--- Page 12 ---
**Extract from the King's Privilege.**

BY grace & privilege of the King, it is permitted to Gilles Gorbin, bookseller in the University of Paris, to print or cause to be printed a book titled *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum*, by Marsilio Ficino. And the said lord forbids all other Booksellers, & Printers, & any other persons whatsoever of this Kingdom, from printing or causing to be printed from the copy, or selling the said book without the will & consent of the said Gorbin, under penalty of confiscation of the said books, which shall be found printed, & of an arbitrary fine. And this until the time & term of ten years, finished & accomplished counting from the day & date that the said book shall be completed printing, as more amply is contained & declared by the letters patent, given for this purpose at Villiers-Cotterêts the seventeenth day of April, The year of grace one thousand five hundred fifty-seven. And of our reign the eleventh.

By the King,

You, Monsieur the Cardinal of Sens, Keeper of the Seals of France, present.

Signed by Vabres.

--- Page 13 ---
**Bookseller to the Reader.**

[Decorative initial V containing floral motifs] That you, candid reader, may understand what benefit can accrue to you from the reading of this volume, take note: whatever was once debated by the ancients concerning divine essence, concerning ideas, concerning divine providence, concerning the soul of the world, concerning intelligences, concerning celestial spheres, concerning paradise, concerning the four elements, concerning purgatory, concerning limbo, concerning hell, concerning matter and form, concerning the kinds of causes, concerning chance and fortune, concerning fate, concerning motion, concerning the infinite, concerning empty space and time, concerning the eternity of the world, concerning the intellectual soul, concerning the souls of brutes and vegetables, concerning genii, concerning demons, concerning resurrection, concerning miracles, concerning dreams, concerning prophets, concerning religion, and similar problems of ancient wise men, is contained in this volume as if in a summary; where, besides the fact that the most recondite Platonic mysteries are explained, many secrets also, drawn from the writings of Moses, Hermes Trismegistus, Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Orpheus, Hippocrates, Aristotle, Hesiod, Posidonius, Xenophon, Lucretius, Virgil, Ptolemy, Plotinus, Porphyry, Numenius, Origen, Iamblichus, Avicenna, Al-Ghazali, Averroes, Solomon, John the Evangelist, Paul the Apostle, Dionysius the Areopagite, Augustine, Thomas, and more recent Theologians, are elucidated and made familiar to all learned persons. For which reason, while we believe that the greatest thanks are due primarily to Marsilio (Ficino), who, like a clever bee ranging through the Elysian fields and flowery meadows, collected these things, having tasted them everywhere, and published them in his own age, we also believe that some thanks are due to us.

we who have taken care to restore to its light and dignity this work, so remarkable, which for a long time now has been contending with moths and cockroaches, and was almost obscured by the very dark shadows of errors; deeming it unworthy that, while so many writings of modern authors are everywhere put to paper, handled, read, and loved—some indeed trivial, some even pernicious and impious—the most weighty, most useful, and most sacred monuments of ancient authors should be scorned and neglected, and held as if unwritten. Therefore, good reader, take this our endeavor in good part, and also show a sign of a grateful mind, for you will reap so much greater fruit from this than from the smatterers of our age, by as much as that golden age, fertile with so many noble and, as it were, heroic intellects, has always been considered, as it was, superior to this our iron age.

Farewell.

TABVLA CAPIT.

[Column 1]

**T**he third book descends from God:
and compares the grades of things with each other to the middle grade: and this (middle grade) to the others.
The descent occurs through five grades, through which the ascent was made: which grades are suitably compared with each other. Chapter 1, letter A, 39.
The soul is the middle grade of things: and it connects all grades, both higher and lower, into one, while it itself both ascends to the higher and descends to the lower. Chapter 2, letter D, 43.

Cap. 4. libri.

**T**he fourth book divides into its species the middle grade of things, that is, the soul.
There are three grades of rational souls. In the first is the world-soul. In the second, the souls of the spheres. In the third, the souls of animals: which are contained in individual spheres. Chapter 1, letter B, 46.
The souls of the spheres move the spheres by a fatal law: and they move in a circle: because

professor of arts & laws: newly edited according to a multiple
alphabetical series.

                                                 A.
    *   *Animabus novem regiones Orpheus distribuit:* Orpheus distributed nine regions to souls.
    *   *& quid unaquaeque sit:* and what each one is.
    *   Translation: Orpheus distributed nine regions to souls, and what each one is.
    *   Reference: lib. 18. lite. K 334

*   **Animus humanus deus quidam, sive stella circumfusa nube, sive daemon, non incola terrae: sed hospes appellari debet:**
    *   Translation: The human mind, a kind of god, or a star surrounded by a cloud, or a daemon, ought to be called not an inhabitant of the earth, but a guest.
    *   Reference: lib. 10. litera D 149

*   **Animus a se quomodo disgrediatur:**

God, just as He is the first in nature,
who acts upon all things and suffers
nothing: so the last, which is corporeal
matter: must suffer from all things:
but to act by itself upon another, not
at all. book 1, letter D 4.
Let no one dare to say that God is
composed of many things.
book 1, letter I 14.
God is the most perspicacious truth:
and the most true perspicacity: or
foresight: light seeing itself:
sight shining by itself: the fount of
intellectual perspicacity and of the
river: and by whose light alone the
perspicacity of the mind beholds
God. book 1, letter C 14.
For God, to be and to understand is
entirely the same. book 2, letter A 29.
God does not exist and act as it
happened, but as it was fitting:
indeed, as it is fitting: otherwise no
order would be found. book 2, letter F 33.
God is most of all His own master:
so that not only does He desire such
things as He Himself exists by His
own nature: but also, in whatever
way He wills, such He entirely
becomes. book 2, letter I 33.
God is a most watchful and perpetual
act from Himself: in Himself, and
entirely about Himself: therefore, as
He acts and watches, so He entirely
exists. book 2, letter L 34.
If God and an angel move something:
and the soul is subjected to them: it
is certainly moved by them: how then
is it moved by itself? book 3, letter H, below 42.
It is proper to God alone to make
something out of nothing: since from
the order of works the order of causes is investi-

God's operation is a certain perpetual
conversion into Himself, by which He
enjoys and rejoices in Himself: and

beholding this, He discerns whatever

nothing, on the contrary, more

THEOLOGY OF PLATO
There is no proportion from the finite to the infinite: Book 8, letter C, page 125
Form is often called 'act' by physicists: Book 1, letter A, page 3
Corporeal forms do not have from themselves a sufficient generation from one another, but demand a higher cause: Book 1, letter I, page 7
Whether forms in God are distinct according to a certain mode of nature, just as in fire, light, heat, dryness, lightness, and through which He acts upon them by a certain necessity of His nature: Book 2, letter E, page 29
Whether God or an angel introduces a new form into the soul, through which it is disturbed: Book 5, letter G, page 63
Each form has its own proper being, nature, and species differing from others: Book 5, letter C, page 64
Form inherent in bodies indeed loses its excellence and entirely becomes corporeal when it has already undergone all the conditions of the body, which are extension according to place, and change according to time—

supreme theologians. (Book 13, Letter D, 211)
Generation is the beginning of nourish-
ment and growth. (Book 4, Letter C, 46)
In every genus, the first principle of the
entire genus exists. (Book 1, Letter C, 4)
In every kind of things, that which is the
highest of that kind, only one exists.
(Book 2, Letter G, 17)
In any genus, whatever is highest ought to
have the pure nature of that genus, un-
mixed with other things, lest it be dimin-
ished by mixture. (Book 2, Letter I, 24)
In any genus that is highest, it has nothing
of a contrary genus, either mixed or
proximate. (Book 12, Letter B, 198)
The Platonists and Proclus distinguish the
kinds of all things, and especially unity
and mind, soul and nature. (Book 14, Letter C, 233)
In any genus that is highest, it has a certain
limit beyond which the genus does not
extend; and many other things to this effect.
(Book 15, Letter B, 237)
Genii, or good daemons, who are named
genii, are constant guides of the intellect
within man himself, who lead to the right
path not by force but by persuading; con-

strangers. (Book 18, Letter B, 341)

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

[Column 1]

Platonists believe that a habit, remaining in the imagination in a certain way, persists; the Peripatetics think otherwise. Bk. 18, letter B, 346.

The soul of Hermotimus of Clazomenae, having left his body, was accustomed to wander, and announced many true things from afar; until, his body having been cremated, his enemies, who were called Cantharidae, took away, as it were, a sheath from his returning soul; which Aristeas of Proconnesus was accustomed to do. Bk. 13, letter D, below 211.

Where the causes of herbs and animals born through putrefaction are said to be. Bk. 4, letter F, 46.

Herus Pamphilus, who rose from the dead, narrated many amazing things about the state of others. Bk. 18, letter F, 345.

The herb Hierobotanum, as the Magi say, contributes to the divinations of physicians: Agate stimulates sight, dulls poison, provides strength and eloquence: the presence of a diamond removes what a magnet attracts: carnelian stops the flow of blood and mitigates anger: onyx ignites anger, terrifies in dreams: finally, coral, as Metrodorus and Zoroaster testify, removes insane terrors, repels lightning and hail. Bk. 4, letter C, 48.

Hippocrates, when he approached Democritus, who was commonly said to be insane,

[Column 2]

to cure him, received through a dream from God that not Democritus was insane, but the common people. Bk. 13, letter E, 217.

No animal would be more unhappy than man, if nature had entirely granted him the same term of life as to other animals. Bk. 1, letter A, 1.

Why the human soul is not subject to heaven, from which it may appear. Bk. 9, letter K, 133.

It is the nature of man that just as the intellect relates to the principle of contemplation, which is that which is everywhere manifestly true, so the will relates to the principle of action, which is goodness itself. Bk. 9, letter C, 133.

Why a larger brain and a warmer heart are given to humans than to other animals. Bk. 10, letter A, 149.

All human speech and every action of life and deliberation is nothing other than a certain argumentation. Bk. 11, letter L, 185.

Man alone among all animals laughs, and alone weeps, from the fact that the movements of the soul have very great power over the body. Bk. 13, letter K, 209.

More ingenious men are often soft in flesh, slender, sickly, and their body is very much affected by the slightest movements...

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

[Left Column]

The opinion of Proclus: that the soul, since it is the principle of generation, generates itself and vivifies itself, so that it has its essence from itself; and many other things about this: book 8, letter E, 123.
The opinion of Proclus: that the creator of the world, while perceiving itself and generating itself, simultaneously generates all things within itself: book 11, letter K, 173.
The opinion or paradox of Proclus: that things composed of elements have neither eternity nor stability, but pure minds possess life; and many other things about this: book 11, letter I, 183.
The opinion of Proclus: that the soul slips away from unity into a discordant multitude, from stability into a change almost devoid of all rest: book 16, letter A, below, 303.
The opinion of Proclus: that even celestial souls move about by understanding; and many other things about this: book 17, letter I, 313.
The opinion of Ptolemy, conceding that particular effects concerning matter do not, however, absolutely follow celestial things (which are universal and remote causes), but rather insofar as intermediate causes contribute, and the mobile disposition of matter is subject to continuous causes; and many other things about this: book 9, letter D, 233.

[Right Column]

The opinion of Solomon: that vanity of vanities and all is vanity: book 11, letter C, above, 184.
The opinion of Serapion, Avicenna, and ancient philosophers: that demons deceive men by the incitement of black bile: book 16, letter H, 306.
The opinion of Sixtus the Pythagorean: that the human soul is made a temple of God, and that the temple of the eternal God will never fall; and many other things concerning this: book 14, letter C, 241.
The opinion of Socrates: concerning forms which lie in formed subjects, since they are imperfect, that there are forms in themselves and perfect, from which the subject forms are formed: book 6, letter I, 82.
The opinion of Speusippus, Xenocrates, Numenius, Plotinus: that the irrational form is called the animation and vivification of bodies, and that it itself is immortal, although Porphyry and Proclus deny it: book 5, letter E and following, 75.
The opinion of Strato and Chrysippus, conceding that life is infused into the world, but that it itself is the supreme God, which the Platonists themselves denied: book 4, letter D, 48.
The opinion of some theologians, saying that God chooses something according to contingency...

PROEM.

MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE'S
proem on Platonic theology concerning the
immortality of souls, to Lorenzo de' Medici.

[Large decorative initial P] Lato, father of philosophers, O magnanimous Lorenzo, when he understood that just as sight relates to the light of the sun, so all minds relate to God, and therefore they can never know anything without the light of God, he rightly judged it just and pious that the human mind, just as it receives all things from God, so it should refer all things to God. Therefore, whether we philosophize about morals, the soul must be purified so that at last, having become more serene, it may perceive the divine light and worship God; or if we investigate the causes of things, causes must be sought so that finally we may find the very cause of causes, and having found it, venerate it. Nor does our Plato only exhort others to this duty of piety, but he himself excels most greatly in it. By which it came to pass that he himself was, without controversy, divine, and his doctrine was called Theology among all nations, since he treats nothing anywhere, whether moral, or dialectical, or mathematical, or physical, without soon reducing it to the contemplation and worship of God with the highest piety. Since indeed he considers the soul to be like a mirror in which the image of the divine countenance easily shines forth, therefore, while he diligently investigates God himself through individual traces, he everywhere turns to the form of the soul, understanding that oracle (know thyself) especially admonishes this: that whoever desires to know God, should first know himself. Wherefore, whoever reads the Platonic works (which I have long since rendered entirely into Latin) most diligently, will con-

THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

We will endeavor to demonstrate in the following discussion that,
besides this sluggish mass of bodies, which limited the consideration of the
B Democriteans, Cyrenaics, and Epicureans, there is some effective quality and power, to which the investigation of the Stoics and Cynics directed itself.
But above quality, which is entirely divided and changed with the dimension of matter, there exists a more excellent form: which, although it changes in some way, nevertheless does not admit division in the body. In that form, ancient
C theologians placed the seat of the rational soul. Heraclitus, Marcus Varro, and Marcus Manilius ascended thus far.
Above the rational soul, there exists an angelic mind, not only indivisible, but also immutable: in which Anaxagoras and Hermotimus seem to have rested. Finally, for the eye of this mind, which desires and grasps the light of truth, the divine sun itself presides:
D towards which our Plato commanded, taught, and strove to direct the purified gaze of the mind. Therefore, when we have ascended thus far, we will compare these five grades of all things, namely the mass of body, quality, soul, angel, God, with each other. Since the very genus of the rational soul, holding the middle place among such grades, appears as the bond of all nature, governs qualities and bodies, and joins itself to the angel and to God: we will show that it is utterly indissoluble, while it connects the grades of nature; most excellent, while it presides over the world's mechanism; most blessed, while it insinuates itself into divine things. And that our soul is thus, and is such, we will affirm by first, common reasons; second, specific arguments; third, signs; fourth, solutions to questions.

### BOOK ONE.

*If the soul were not immortal: no animal*
*would be more unhappy than man. Chapter I.*

[Large decorative initial 'C' within a square floral border] SINCE the human race, because of the restlessness of the soul, the weakness of the body, and the lack of all things, leads a harsher life on earth than beasts: if nature had granted it the very same limit of living as to other animals, no animal would be more unhappy than man. But since it cannot happen that man, who by the worship of God approaches closer to God, the author of blessedness, than all mortals, should be altogether the most unhappy of all: and since he can only become more blessed after the death of the body: it seems necessary that some light remains for our souls departing from this prison. But if human minds do not at all perceive their own light, enclosed in darkness and a blind prison, from which we are very often compelled to distrust our own divinity: let us break, I beg you, O heavenly souls, desirous of our heavenly homeland, let us break as soon as possible the bonds of earthly fetters: so that, lifted on Platonic wings, and with God as our guide, we may fly more freely into the ethereal abode: where we shall immediately happily contemplate the excellence of our nature.
Moreover, so that it may clearly appear by what means especially the minds of men may break mortal confines, perceive their immortality, and attain blessedness: we shall endeavor...

Second, that it be most ready for motion. Third, that it easily penetrates the patient, and that the patient itself is most closely united to the agent. To all these, the mass of the body seems to be an impediment: first, because since it extends into very many parts, the acting power in it is dispersed, and very much distant and distracted from itself. But power, just as it is increased by unity, so it is diminished by dispersion. Therefore, dryness increases the force of both heat and cold, because it unites: but humidity weakens, because it disperses. Next, the greater the body is, the more sluggish it is in itself, and more unfit for motion. Therefore, the more the body is increased, the more it retards motion: and it delays action longer. ...or one single reason, but they operate through their various qualities. Rightly so: because they act by the same reason by which they are. But they exist not by mass in this or that species, but through this form or that: therefore they operate through form: especially since the agent approaches the patient through the qualities of form rather than through the limits of quantity, and through the force of form it passes into alien matter, rather than through the dimension of quantity: [H] and it touches individual points of matter not by dimension, but by quality. Thus, water cools through coldness, fire heats through hotness rather than through mass. For fire burns not because it is most ample, but because it is most fervent. And if all its heat were reduced as it were to a point of itself: because of the greatest union, it will be most powerful for burning. Thus, by the benefit of quality, especially when forced into a narrow compass, action arises. [I] Hence it happens that natural causes produce effects similar to the causes in quality rather than equal in quantity. And if it happens sometimes that equal effects arise, it is necessary that very similar ones appeared first: as if action is carried out through qualities, after which effects necessarily resemble causes in and through them. Therefore, children immediately after birth are almost all similar to their parents in complexion and figure: but equal in magnitude more rarely, and later. But who would not see these things? For if you approach a large body, you do not become large: but if you approach a hot one, you certainly become warm: nor do you perceive quantity by any sense, unless quality has first moved the sense. For who will judge how large a wall is, unless color and light have brought this very magnitude to the eye? For the judgment of quantity is lost more and sooner because of distance, than that of light and color: as if the efficacy of motion lies in quality. [K] Which is clearly confirmed from this, that any thing always moves appetite by reason of good (which is a quality), not by reason of great or many. Otherwise, we would always choose what is greater or more: but now, in those things which we consider bad, we choose the smaller or fewer. [L] Quality, however, therefore cannot be a body: because two bodies cannot be entirely brought together in the same place without mutual offense: but several qualities are equally blended in the same place. Nothing, however, ever originates from itself. For that which provides a beginning to what is generated, must exist prior to what is generated. Nothing, however, precedes itself. Quality, therefore, since it originates from another, and nothing can originate except from something superior, cannot be the principle of nature. But from where does it draw its origin? Is it perhaps from matter?

D By no means: because since matter is a common and unformed subject, and therefore (as far as it is concerned) always and everywhere relates equally to all forms: from where does it come that it is adorned with different forms at different times and in different places, unless from some superior [cause] which affects it differently at different times and in different places? Furthermore, if matter is to give form to itself, we ask whether it possesses that form by its own power before it is to provide it to itself, or not? If it does not have it, it cannot even conceive [it]. But if it has it, it is certainly not prime matter, but something composed of matter and the power of form. And concerning this very power, we will similarly inquire whether it has it from itself, or from another? If it has it from another, it also has the form from another. But if from itself: does it similarly have this through another power likewise proper to itself (and thus we will proceed to infinity), or rather does it possess that power not through another power, but through its essence? If so, the essence of matter will be the same as the power or effective substance of forms, and it will be the fount of forms rather than the subject: indeed, it will be form rather than matter, and the most excellent form of all, a form impervious to all division: nor will it fluctuate (as it does now) with the variety of fleeting forms, but through its eternal essence, it will be endowed with eternal forms.

E From these points, it is concluded that matter does not by its own nature possess any form-generating power: because an unformed subject cannot form itself, since it can do absolutely nothing: inasmuch as action proceeds from form, from which being proceeds. And if matter which is subject to art, although not lacking form, is nevertheless led to the form of the artifact not by itself, but by the form of art: certainly matter which is subject to nature, since it is unformed, is led to natural form not by itself, but by the nature of form.

From where, then, will quality come? Perhaps from another quality, for example, that one fire generates another? Not even that. For quality, because it cannot exist without the nourishment of matter, therefore does not dominate its own matter, much less will it dominate alien matter.

...that it is defiled. Likewise, it cannot be a first form, if it is not true.
For whence does the mind argue this form is not entirely true? unless from there, where it itself discerns something truer: compared to which this one falls short, and is in a way proven to be false. Where then does the mind see the true form itself? Indeed, it either perceives it outside itself, or within itself. If it looks outside itself: certainly somewhere in nature there is a true form superior in quality. If the mind beholds it within itself, a true form is not lacking to the mind: therefore it is not lacking to the world.
Furthermore, truth is indeed stronger than falsehood: [Marginal note: B] since truth can exist without falsehood, but falsehood cannot subsist without truth. For nothing is called false, unless it is at least true that it is false. Nor is anything valid, unless it is true that it is valid: nor is something truly understood to be false, except through truth. Nor is something called false, unless it deceives: nor does it deceive, except through an image of truth. If therefore truth is stronger than falsehood: and a less true form, namely quality, is something in the order of things: much more is a true form found in the order of things: especially since by how much intellect is more excellent and truer than sense, by so much an intelligible form ought to be more excellent and truer than a sensible form. I
Leading through time: it would similarly lead at appointed times.
The human mind daily betakes itself from particular forms to universal and absolute ones. Likewise, it is accustomed to ascend above natural forms bound to certain matters, through mathematical ones (for which uncertain matter suffices) to metaphysical ones (which need neither certain nor uncertain matter). Furthermore, it raises itself from dimensions which need both position and parts, to a point without parts, but in a certain way concerning position; again from points to numbers, which indeed need parts, but by no means position; finally from numbers to unity, which needs neither position nor any parts. And beyond individual, but accidental, unity, it transfers itself to substantial unity, that is, to form, and to individual essence: the foundation and origin of accidents at the same time, as if to a certain fixed pivot, abiding in itself, for accidents which are mutable in themselves and always adhering to another. If the human mind, which is both a certain part of the universe and hindered by bodily chains, has such great power for rational ascent, certainly the universe itself possesses a much greater power for the same; especially since the order of the lowest mind draws its origin from the universal order. But where a greater power for action thrives, there naturally and more and more quickly it is brought forth into act. Furthermore, if any kinds of things are reduced to something in a certain way indivisible in their own kind, by whose simplicity they consist—for example, motion and time to a moment, natural form to the minimum natural degree, geometric dimensions to a point, numbers to unity—why should not also the genus of substance be reduced to an indivisible substance? Just as all figures which partake of inequality are referred to the circular one, the most equal of all, and the circular one to the indivisible center, the beginning of all equality: so accidental and divisible forms should be reduced to a substantial and divisible form, and a form of this kind to a substantial and indivisible one. And just as beyond quality, which is subject not only to decrease but also to remission, there is a substantial and corporeal form which is free from remission, although it may decrease: so above this there must be a substantial form which neither remits nor decreases: so that the ascent which progresses towards the better may be perfected into the op- [timum/highest].

Therefore, the quality of any body cannot by its sole power form another body. Indeed, a natural body, through its very mass, which is subject only to passivity, does nothing; but through quality, it does not act sufficiently. For this (quality), since it does not possess self-sufficiency for existence, does not provide the body with self-sufficiency for action. Indeed, because fire was first generated by something before it itself generated something else, it is more fitting for it to be an effect than an efficient cause. This condition is innate to an effect: that it depends on something else. Wherefore, whenever fire does something, it acts as the instrument of a superior cause. **F** For if this or that fire were the cause of generation, the first, that is, the supreme fire—since from the first cause of any genus the whole genus flows forth—it would everywhere and always produce fire; and thus it would make both itself and any fire that was before it, and that will be after it. Since, therefore, this or that fire is not the primary cause of this kind of generation, we ask of what cause it is the instrument. **G** Is it perhaps the instrument of another fire? By no means. Firstly, because that cause is equal, not superior. Secondly, because that fire from which this one previously flowed is either already extinguished or very remote. Or perhaps it is the instrument of other elements? Not that either. For there is no principle of generating fire in dissimilar and contrary elements, to which this fire, about to generate another, might be subjected as an instrument. Is it therefore the instrument of the heavens? By no means. For this fire cannot become the instrument of that most remote body otherwise than through a medium. But these intermediate bodies are unsuitable. And rather, between the heaven, or the sphere of fire, and the dissimilar elements, for generating this fire on earth, some fire about to generate this fire must be interposed, rather than the other way around. Similarly, we will argue in each species of natural things. Wherefore, besides all forms of this kind, it is necessary that there be in all things and preside over them a certain incorporeal substance penetrating through bodies, whose instruments are corporeal qualities. For in what way would individual qualities, which by their very nature are unstable and disordered, **H** either maintain a stable order in the succession of generation, unless they were governed by the stable order of a higher cause; or always return to the same effects at fixed intervals of time, unless there were one and the same cause which (governed) them at every...

denies that matter, since it is the primary recipient of action, nor dimensions or qualities, since they are the primary affections of the primary recipient, can be the first principles of actions. So Plotinus. But others, although to the same end, distinguish something differently thus. Indeed, they say that matter itself can do nothing; and quantity also, if it is the passive extension of matter itself, proceeding from some cause extending matter, can do nothing, since it is the perpetual affection of the primary recipient. But if it is, as it were, a certain form through which the moving cause of matter extends matter, perhaps it acts somewhat upon its own matter, because it is the medium by which that cause seems to extend matter; but it operates nothing at all upon foreign matter, because it always compels the agent to be distant from the patient, which hinders action. But quality, according to the Peripatetics, operates something upon matter both foreign and its own. But if reason leads us from matter, which acts upon neither matter, to quality, which in some way moves both, through the intermediate quantity, which operates only in some way upon the one, namely its own: shall we not pass from quantity, which in no way moves foreign matter, without any medium, to that thing which entirely moves foreign matter? By no means.
But quality is closest to quantity. Therefore, quality is not entirely sufficient for external action. If, therefore, it is deficient in acting, it is directed by a superior substance, which is entirely powerful. But quality is rightly deficient: because at the very moment it is born, it is scattered through the breadth and depth of matter, and is, as it were, submerged in the river Lethe. The result is that before it itself acts, it is in some way overcome by matter, as if by an infecting agent. Therefore, its power never overcomes matter by itself. For this reason, it will never move by itself, unless it is strengthened by a superior cause. Indeed, it is strengthened and led by a certain life, which even from non-living mud, when frogs and flies are generated, produces life and sensation; from one and the same shapeless matter, it simultaneously creates various and most beautiful flowers through various and most beautiful seeds, which, since they are often not found in dung, must necessarily be in life itself. ...timo. Such will be an incorporeal substance, which primarily has this, that by its nature it cannot be diminished: which must subsist somewhere in nature according to its proper form. Indeed, indivisible and simple things are necessarily prior to divisible and composite things. For each thing must exist before it is extended and swells. These also need those, not the other way around. For from those these take their beginning, and are terminated at those. Therefore, if these subsist according to their proper form in the nature of things, much more must that kind (of indivisible things) also be found somewhere according to its proper form. Indeed, from the fact that nature moves its matter more effectively and better than art moves its own, we infer that the principal form in nature dominates its matter more than the principal form achieved by art dominates its matter. If it dominates more, two things are concluded: first, that it is closer to matter in terms of position than art is; second, that it excels its matter more than art does in terms of substance, and can exist more by itself without it. [Marginal note: D]
Moreover, this reasoning greatly moves me to the same conclusion: that all qualities, because they are forms in another, whenever they generate, generate forms in another: For they cannot beget offspring freer than they themselves are. Therefore, they generate forms in the bosom of matter: but matter itself, which lies least of all in another, is made and preserved only by that form which does not lie in another. For matter is neither from itself, since it is imperfect and does not act from itself; nor from qualities, which it itself precedes; but from a certain form which precedes matter. Such a form is entirely incorporeal. In the virtue and operation of such a form are founded the virtues and operations of qualities, after their works are built upon its work. But of this elsewhere.
Now, however, it is necessary to remember that matter itself, as Hermes Trismegistus and Timaeus think, is formless, yet something: very close to nothing, because it is primarily and infinitely passive. [Marginal note: E]
From which Plotinus believes it follows that the proximate disposition of matter itself, that is, dimension and quality, is something most vain: and whatever little it is, it is entirely a certain passion. For dimensions are nothing other than the extensions of matter itself: but qualities are nothing other than its affections, namely shadowy and fleeting, like certain shadows of tall trees in a torrent. [Marginal note: F]

...quantity: especially since the universe is more perfect if certain substances are freed from the bonds of quantity, than if they were
[Marginal note: A] certain lives devoid of sense. Averroes, following Aristotle's opinion, proves that the corporeal and substantial form of the heavens lacks matter: because, namely, there is no potentiality there for diverse forms, which is the proper nature of matter. There, however, there is dimension: and he considers such a form to be intermediate between natural and divine forms: because natural forms exist simultaneously with matter and quantity; divine forms are completely free from both; but the form of the heavens is intermediate between both, lest one pass from one extreme to the other without a middle. Therefore, he judges it consistent that it exists with quantity, but without matter. From this, we argue in this way. Since a substantial form usually lies in matter rather than in quantity, and has, according to the order of genus and nature, a greater proportion with matter than with quantity: if it can exist somewhere without matter, much more can it exist somewhere separate from quantity.
[Marginal note: B] Moreover, as Proclus holds, there are three kinds of bodies. For some are (to use his words) material and composite at the same time, such as those which are composed of the four elements. Furthermore, there are the spheres of the elements: material indeed,
[Marginal note: C] but in a certain way simple. Finally, there are the celestial bodies, both simple and immaterial at the same time. He also posits three kinds of forms, not unlike Averroes. For he wishes the general definition of forms to be of this kind. Form is that by which something distinctly and actually exists, and acts. In this definition, however, no dimensions are included at all; yet a subject is perhaps signified in a certain way: namely, when it is said, "that by which something," and the rest that follows. From this he concludes that if some forms exist without subject matter, like the celestial ones: much more and many more can
[Marginal note: D] and ought to exist without dimension at the same time. Likewise, Proclus and Syrianus argue to the same point thus. That which is always extended by another is necessarily bound by dimensions; but that which extends, is not at all. Therefore, since matter is always extended by another, it is necessarily subject to dimensions. So great indeed is the power in the genus of forms to this end, that they can be separated from matter, so that even if someone were to say that they are indeed conjoined from themselves, but are separated by the very contemplation of minds: from this he would at least be forced to admit [Marginal note: K] that minds themselves are separated: inasmuch as they themselves separate other things. Which again appears from this, because substance by nature and dignity is prior to quantity and the other accidents. And because what is prior can be separate from what is posterior: there can be a certain substance without division of quantity: and if it can, it certainly is at some time: lest this perfection be lacking to nature, lest this potency be in vain. For in those things which pertain to the principal [Marginal note: L] order of the universe, the matter stands thus, that whatever can be, either already is, as physicists believe, lest change occur in eternal things: or at least will be at some time: lest something always be empty. And if life, which alone by natural origin precedes sense: now already exists by itself somewhere without sense, much more so substance, which surpasses quantity both in dignity and origin, now exists in the order of things separate from quantity.

I That essence, both true and immortal, is judged by the Platonists for this reason: because it neither needs parts into which it could sometimes be dissolved, and through which its dispersed power would be weakened; nor is it bound to a subject, from which, if deserted, it might sometimes vanish; nor is it mixed with a contrary form, by which it could be infected; nor is it confined by place, or subject to time or motion, due to the individual and self-abiding simplicity of its substance.

...is extended, much more can it not only be thought of without dimensions, but also exist. Moreover, every divisible thing is a certain whole constituted of many parts: which parts, unless they had something one and the same common to all, would never make up that whole. For one is not made except from one. Again, unless they were participants of unity, no part would be one, but many to infinity, and any part would be infinitely innumerable. But that one inherent in the parts is not divided individually in each. For it would itself also need another unifier. Therefore, it is the same and whole in each. Such an incorporeal something must necessarily exist.

F
Likewise, since every corporeal thing is a certain whole made of parts, what then is the cause of its union? Does the whole itself unite the parts, or do the parts unite the whole? Or something superior, which is neither a part of anything, nor a whole made of parts, unites the parts to each other and to the whole? The whole rather follows the parts than unites them. And if it is admitted that it unites the parts: will it be incorporeal? For if it itself is also divisible: it needs another unifier in the same way. If the parts unite the whole, that is indeed absurd, that union, which ought to be made from unity, is made from a multitude opposed to unity. It remains, therefore, that besides the individual parts and the whole, there is present something one as the cause of that union, which indeed is incorporeal: lest it too be forced to need a bond, and so we go on to infinity.

Therefore, it is not to be thought that some form divided in a body is the apex of nature and the principle of things: especially since the principle of things must have been, by its own power, eternal, and will be. Indeed, it must have always been: for it could neither have come forth from itself at some time (for it would have been before itself) nor from another: for nothing is before the first. But the rest would never exist unless the first had existed previously. It must also always be: because if the principle is extinguished, all things collapse, and neither it itself any longer, nor anything else can be reborn. Therefore, it must necessarily have infinite power, through which it lives infinitely from itself: it will not have this if it is corporeal. For if it has infinite dimensions: there will be nothing else in things besides itself. If finite, it will also have finite power.

G

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Following the immobile [principle], it is necessary to posit something that is partly immobile, partly also mobile. Therefore, that substance, the proximate generator of qualities, cannot be entirely immobile. What then shall we say? Shall we also assert that this substance is entirely mobile? By no means. For either it would be in the genus of corporeal qualities, in which genus, however, we cannot make a stand. Or the cause which is placed in a higher genus would not exceed its effect with sufficient perfection, if the substance which is the cause of quality should waver no less than quality itself. Wherefore, that substance partly stands, but partly moves. Indeed, it also has three things in itself: essence, power, operation.
[Marginal note: B] Which of these will be stable? Which will be moved? Operation indeed cannot be stable, if the two preceding things are changed. Nor can essence be moved without the subsequent things being moved. Therefore, the first will be stable, namely essence itself; the last will be changed, namely operation. But the middle of both, power, what then? It too will partly stand, and partly also be changed.

**Above the mobile soul is the immobile angel.**
**Chapter 5.**

[Marginal note: C] Up to this point, we have found a certain form above the bodily constitution, which we shall call the rational soul, whose essence always remains the same, which signifies the stability of will and memory. Its operation, however, is changed from this: that it does not think all things at once, but gradually; nor does it nourish, increase, and generate the body in an instant, but over time. Natural power remains, because its natural vigor flourishes
[Marginal note: D] perennially, neither is it intensified nor diminished. Acquired power is changed, because it passes from potentiality to act, from act to habit, and vice versa. Heraclitus, Varro, and Manilius ascended thus far; but one must ascend higher, since this form cannot be the principle of all nature. For a stable operation is more perfect, which most perfectly completes its work in one instant, than that which needs time. Life is more integral which is entirely united with itself at once, not distant from itself, than that which, extended through diverse moments of time, is in a certain way distracted from itself according to intrinsic acts and affections. Therefore, above this form, by whose operation—

Since the elements consist of flowing matter [Marginal note: H] and always mutually affect each other, [Marginal note: I] they would observe no order from themselves, unless they were governed by the most orderly law of celestial motion. But since heaven itself is perpetually immobile and therefore in need, a stable order in its motion does not originate from itself, but from a supreme mover, entirely unmoved and indivisible. For a stable unity does not persist in things so diverse and mobile, except from a most stable and most unified pivot, which ultimately refers to unity itself and stability. Indeed, just as the mobile relates to the mobile, so also the mover to the mover. Therefore, just as the element which is moved changeably relates to the heaven which is moved stably, so the mobile and varied mover of heaven relates to the stable and unified mover; and finally, the stable and unified is reduced to stability itself and unity. Certainly, that action which is called 'to move' follows the mover; that passion which is called 'to be moved' follows this action; nor does the opposite happen. [Marginal note: K] For prior things are not led by posterior things, but conversely. Therefore, it can much more be somewhere that action which is called 'to move' without that passion which is 'to be moved', than such a passion separate from action. However, such a passion in bodies is separate from action. Therefore, somewhere there will be action far from passion: so that just as bodies are indeed moved, but do not move, so angels may move, but are not moved; concerning whom Zoroaster says:

Furthermore, the soul: because it is mobile, passes from one thing to another. Therefore, it has one thing in itself, and another. What it has of these, it also has of multitude. [B] Indeed, we see this clearly in the very spheres of the world. For the more mobile a sphere is, the larger it is; so much so that earth and water, if compared to the higher things, are thought to bear themselves as a point to a circumference. But what is dimension in bodies, that seems to be number in incorporeal things. Therefore it is consistent that intellectual substances, inasmuch as they are the best and exist through themselves, and are the ends of all corporeal things which are created for their sake, are far more numerous than both the motions of the spheres and all bodies, which Dionysius the Areopagite testifies, saying that there are more separate [C] species of intellectual things than of corporeal things. Rightly, the most powerful creator of the universe both could and knew and willed to make his work as similar as possible to himself. But in his dominion, he pre-eminently created that which is most similar [to himself], in that he expanded absolute minds (which are most similar to himself of all things) beyond forms joined to matter, by an immense (so to speak) expanse. Hence that [saying] of the prophet Daniel: "Thousands of thousands ministered to him: and ten times a hundred thousand stood before him." But in distinguishing the orders of angels, Dionysius uses primarily the ternary and novenary numbers, and sometimes also the septenary. Indeed, we also find the duodenary [D] number in Christian mysteries. Iamblichus and Proclus, Platonists, also observed the same after Dionysius. For they divide the supreme and middle angels by the ternary and novenary numbers, the subsequent ones by the septenary, and finally the last ones by the duodenary number of orders. But since among the Platonists the grades of bodies are shadows of rational [E] souls, and the grades of souls are images of angels, therefore some distinguish the orders of angels according to the orders of bodies and souls simultaneously. But of these things elsewhere.

For the mind needs truth, but truth **B** does not need mind. And the dominion of truth extends more widely than that of mind. For intellectual art is found in individual forms, but by no means in unformed matter. Yet matter is truly called matter, and is truly the subject of all natural things. **On the Immortality of the Soul, Book 1, Chapter 14**

Union stands, in unity is power. Let no one dare to say that God is composed of many parts: because if he were rightly composed, he would consist of something that would be like a subject, and something that would be like a form. Therefore, God would not be most perfect in every way, since in him one part would be more imperfect than the whole itself. He would not be the supreme agent: because he would not act by his whole self whatever he acts, but by one part, that is, the form. He would not be most blessed: because he would not enjoy himself everywhere. For he would not embrace his whole self in any member. Moreover, he would see in himself something other than God: because a part is not the same as the whole. He would certainly be more blessed if whatever he sees in himself, were himself: if he were nowhere lacking to himself: but if he met himself whole everywhere. Finally, that part which was posited in God as a subject, because it is conceived as formless in itself, cannot form itself. Furthermore, the other part which played the role of form, because it does not subsist in itself, much less can it exist from itself. Therefore, this composite God would be formed by some superior form: and that (superior form) would rather be God. [Marginal note: I]

This, moreover, is the first discourse by which we prove that God is above the angel. [Marginal note: K]

Furthermore, just as your eye relates to your body, so your mind relates to your soul. For your mind is the eye of your soul. Again: just as the light of the sun relates to the eye of the body, so the light of truth relates to the eye of the soul. Therefore, just as the eye of the body is not light, but a faculty capable of light: so the mind, which is the eye of the soul, is not truth, although it grasps truth. For your mind seeks truth. Yet truth does not seek itself: nor does truth admit falsehood, by which your soul is often deceived. Imagine in your mind, your eye growing so much that it occupies your whole body: and with the varied appearance of members removed, the entire body is one eye. If this eye will see anything more: it will certainly see nothing other than the same light of the sun, which it perceived when it was narrow: but it will receive the same light more abundantly: and it will behold the colors of bodies in that very light from all sides, all at once with a single view: nor will it turn here or there to see: but by resting, it will contemplate all things equally.

Yet there will still be one thing light, and another thing eye. For if sight is instituted to comprehend light, sight is one thing:

Again: those things which have mind, nevertheless do not yet cease; but they still seek the good. For it is characteristic of the mind to make an effort towards understanding. Either after this striving the mind is worse off, or better, or equally. Not equally. For that strives in vain which profits nothing; and nothing strives towards that which it already possesses. Hence some think they have enough in philosophy if they seem to have wisdom, even if they do not have it; but not enough in life, unless they truly possess that which they I judge to be especially good for themselves.

Hence it happens that what it is to understand is not enough for us, unless we understand both well and the good. For often we reject knowledge for a time, if we suspect it will be bad and troublesome for us; but the good itself we can never reject. Often also we prefer pleasure to the contemplation of things; but to the good itself, in so far as it is good, we can never prefer anything. For lower things always receive something from superior causes. Thus, this will not be unity itself, but something composed of a certain unity and power received from above: and it will be a certain multitude, not unity. And also, that which is placed before unity will partake of no unity. For a superior principle receives nothing from an inferior as to its own nature. Therefore, it will be either nothing, or a multitude entirely deprived of all union: of which no part will be a single thing. Nor will the whole multitude be one, nor will any communion exist in the parts either among themselves or to the whole.

Furthermore, above truth there is nothing. For by similar reasoning, this would not be truth itself, but something true composed of a certain truth and a portion of that superior thing. And that which is placed above it, since it is neither truth nor partaker of truth, is entirely false, and nothing. Nor can it be more excellent than truth, unless by the power of truth it is undoubtedly true that it is more excellent.

Similarly, above goodness there is nothing. For this too would not be pure goodness: but something good and a certain goodness contaminated by the admixture of another. That which is placed before goodness will be entirely evil. For it will not be good, since it is beyond the boundaries of goodness. Nor better than goodness: since nothing is better except through a greater portion of goodness. How, however, evil can exceed goodness, I do not see: since excess and dominion belong to goodness. For they are desirable as good things. Therefore, evil through the nature of goodness will overcome goodness, and goodness will provide the power of dominion to evil. Moreover, if there is another principle of things above goodness itself, it will certainly impart some gift from itself to things: as every superior cause is accustomed to do. Furthermore, goodness itself imparts its gift to all, that is, some goodness to each. But we ask concerning that gift which descends from a superior principle, whether it is better, endowed with goodness, or not. Indeed, it cannot be better. For whatever is called better is called better by a greater portion of goodness. Yet it is absurd that the gift of a superior principle is not better than the gift of an inferior cause. Added to this is that since all things desire the good: if there is another principle above the good itself, we ask whether they desire it: or not. If they are said to desire it: it follows that they seek something beyond and more than the good. If they are denied to seek that, it is foolish

...to say they do not want it. Therefore, since in good the highest necessity concurs with the highest liberty, and the dominion of good is extremely necessary for those subject to it, and extremely voluntary: it is established from this that all things derive their origin as from a father, and all things aspire to this as to their homeland.

On the immortality of souls by the same author Ficino,
BOOK SECOND.
*Unity, truth, goodness are the same: and above them there is nothing.*
*Chapter I.*

By three arguments we have now shown that there is something above the angel. First, indeed, we have shown that above it is the most simple unity; secondly, truth; thirdly, goodness. These three are one. For supreme unity is nothing other than supreme simplicity. Because of this simplicity of unity, every thing is pure and true. For the true is one, that which is purely one. Thus the truth of things consists in that simple unity. And because of the same simple and pure unity, all things are good. For anything then behaves well when it is united to itself and to its principle, and remains pure: and is not mixed with inferior things. And if in things, the unity of things, and truth, and goodness consist in the same [principle]: deservedly above them is that very first one, true, and good. That the principle of things is in these, is argued by the fact that traces of these are found in all things, as if all things emanated from them: and all things desire these: inasmuch as they seek their own principle. For individual things are both participants in unity, truth, and goodness, and desirous of them. Above unity there is nothing else: because nothing is more powerful than unity: inasmuch as union provides perfection to all things, and power. But if you wish there to be something above it, two absurdities immediately follow. For if unity is under some superior principle, it is certainly a participant of that superior [principle].

--- Page 114 ---
...it lies subject to, and is circumscribed by the limitations of others: from unity itself, which subsisting in itself is constrained by no limit, flows. Thus, therefore, that common and one nature, for both, comes from elsewhere, and from a higher principle. Moreover, those two proper natures by which they differ, come to them from outside. For besides those, nothing remains in both, except the common and one nature: from which if those two proper natures which are added were to arise absolutely, they would no longer be diverse, as Metaphysicians suppose: but one and the same property would be for both, gushing from the same vein. For it would gush forth through the absolute mode of mere nature: and flow back inwards. If therefore two absolute properties are inherent in them: they necessarily come from outside. Wherefore each receives the property of its essence from elsewhere. And because each obtains its own proper nature from elsewhere,

There are not many gods equal among themselves.

Indeed there are not many gods: because there cannot be multiple E
principles. But let there be (if you please) twin gods: namely two
principles of the entire world, this one, and that one. We ask whether
this is subordinate to that: or that to this: or whether both are equal? If
one is subordinate to the other: that which is superior will clearly be the principle:
the other by no means. If they are equal: we ask whether they differ en-
tirely from each other, or agree entirely: or partly differ,
but partly agree: The first will not be granted. For at least in this they agree,
that both exist, and act, and are equally called principles of things.
And if they agreed in no way: there would be no harmony
in the world's mechanism. If we admit the second, that they agree entirely:
they are no longer two, but (as we desire) one. But if the third is given, that they partly agree in
nature, partly differ: then indeed, because they cannot agree and disagree by the same thing,
a certain common nature is inherent in both, by which they agree:
furthermore, two proper natures in those two beyond the common nature, by which they dif-
fer. Therefore neither of them will be simple: but each
composed of a common nature and a proper nature. Neither
will be primary, because it depends on that which reconciled diverse
parts into one. Neither self-sufficient: since both
the whole needs parts, and one part needs another. Neither most
powerful: since it is not entirely unified. Yet that common nature
by which both have this equality, that they are equally principles: will be a principle rather than those two.

Finally, if there are two gods, and each can equally bring about this whole world: either neither will make the world, and the power in both will be in vain, nor will there be a world anywhere; or one will create the world, and the power of generating in the other will be in vain.
Or each will generate the whole, and thus there will be two worlds, entirely equal to each other and most similar: of which one will suffice, the other will be superfluous.
But if one is able to accomplish the whole, while the other only a part: he who is not able to accomplish the whole, is not a god; and he will in vain generate a part of the world, which the other creates along with the whole world.
If, however, each has the power to create half of the world: neither will be the principle of all things. And because those parts in one whole converge to one end by community of nature, it will be necessary for those two gods to be referred to one superior God: so that the movement towards one, which happens through two, is derived from the communion of the two, deduced from some superior one.
But if anyone asserts that two worlds, entirely diverse and dissimilar from each other, are constructed by twin gods, he will be forced to confess that both those gods and those worlds in no way agree with each other. In what way, therefore, is each of them a single God who lives, understands, and operates? Or is each of these a single world, a work, and corporeal? Therefore, the twin worlds will agree with each other. But one

Moreover, so let the finite unities of species be referred to a unique super-species unity. It is fitting that just as each proper order of things is directed to its own single principle, so the universal order of things should be referred to one universal principle: [Marginal note: I] and just as individual matters to one matter, all members of the world to one body, so all natures of the world to one nature, all lives of the world to one life, all movements to one movement, all movers to one mover of the world. Furthermore, when several things, diverse among themselves according to nature, conspire in a certain single and mutual order, it is necessary that an order of this kind exists in them because of the order which they have towards some one thing: such as is the order of the parts of an army among themselves, which exists because of the order of the whole army towards one leader. For the fact that some things which are diverse among themselves acquire this, that they are united by mutual communion, does not arise from their own natures, through which they are diverse; for from these they are rather disjoined. Nor does it arise from certain diverse orderers. These indeed, through their differing natures, inasmuch as they differ, do not tend towards a single order. And thus that mutual order of many things either happened by chance, or was instituted by one and the first orderer, directing all things to one end. But all parts of the world, although diverse, are reconciled by a mutual order: [Marginal note: A] because they constitute one body: they mutually exchange natures. Lower bodies are moved by higher ones; higher ones by an incorporeal nature. Nor does this order happen by chance: because it is always the same and similar; because it always weaves a similar web, and similarly. Therefore, God, the orderer of the one world, is one. One, I say, by the first reason of the Platonists, because He is unity. He is also one by the second [Marginal note: B] reason of the same (Platonists), because He is truth. For supreme truth is one. For if two supreme truths are said to exist, either one of them has whatever the other has, or not. If the first is granted, it is one, not two. If the second, neither is supreme. For this one lacks the truth that is in that one, and that one lacks the truth that is in this one. Again, God is one by the third reason of the Platonists: because He is supreme goodness. For supreme goodness embraces whatever good can be found anywhere. Therefore, the soul would be no closer or more suitable to goodness itself than the body: therefore neither would it be better, nor would an angel [Marginal note: K] be better than the soul. If there is no first something in things, every thing will emanate from another. Therefore all will be fluid: consequently there will be nowhere unity, equality, similarity, stability, order, and restoration. But now, because these are inherent in things, it is necessary that the flux of things emanating from another be led and restrained by the stability of some cornerstone not emanating from another: just as it terminates the indeterminate flux of liquid bodies, it is necessary not by another similarly flowing liquid body, but by a solid body. Finally, any superior degree operates something upon an inferior [Marginal note: L], and receives something from a superior. If there is no first degree in things, and no last: any middle degree will depend on infinite superior degrees, and in turn will produce infinite inferior degrees: consequently it will receive innumerable perfections from superiors, since it receives some good from each of its causes. And it will exhibit infinite gifts to inferiors. For it will bestow something on each: consequently it will be of immense power, and full of infinite perfections. Thus all things will be equally infinite: no thing will be more excellent than another: no cause will be better than its effect. Or perhaps every thing will be innumerably finite: because it will be innumerably exceeded by antecedents. Again, each will be infinite, because it will surpass innumerable subsequent things. Nor will there ever be any true knowledge: since infinite causes of things cannot be comprehended. Nor will there be anything in the universe to move or stop appetite, if there is no first principle and ultimate end. For by its power every appetite is moved and strengthened. Therefore, whether God recently creates something out of nothing, or continuously brings forth and preserves the prime matter of bodies, and the essence of minds and souls from no older subject, always depending on the first act, that is, the divine (act): beyond doubt he possesses immense power of acting.

What more? The movement and order, so constant through so many ages, of this so immense and so complex machine, teaches that the power in the governor is indefatigable, and therefore infinite.

For finite power, in infinite time, indeed even in a long, though finite, time, becomes weary and falters. Therefore, from the infinite power of God, all intellects receive that they may always and firmly understand, souls that they may be able to range without end: matter that it may have an interminable potential for receiving: movement and time that they may be able to flow without end: and also the generation of things (as it pleases the physicists) that they may be able to be continued by an alternating and interminable succession. For they believe that infinite action and motion derive their origin from infinite power: and whatever things are said to be infinite, either in potential or in any other way, are such and are judged to be such through the supreme and actually existing infinity. Hence the divine nature is called by Orpheus *atelēs teleutē*, that is, "infinite end."

**God is always. Chapter 5.**

[Large initial S] If any thing is more lasting: the more powerful is the virtue by which it remains and is preserved: God, through his infinite virtue, himself remains infinitely, and preserves other things. Likewise, divine truth precedes every beginning of things.

--- Page 121 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. II. 29

The theology of John the Apostle, the most divine of all theologians (whom the Platonist Amelius gladly embraces), calls unity the principle; truth, the reason of the principle; and finally, goodness, the love of the rational principle. And may this very substance, namely unity, true good, or truth one good, or goodness one true, be one good and true God. But because it is unity, therefore it is truth; because unity is true, therefore goodness. In unity it implicates all things, it explicates in truth, it pours forth through goodness. But all things, after they have flowed from there, flow back through goodness, are reformed through truth, and are restored into one through unity.

**God's power is infinite. Chapter 4.**

Just as in supreme dispersion there is infinite weakness, so in supreme unity there is infinite power. An act by its nature does [A] not include a limit. For to be subject to a limit is a passion, which is opposed to an act. An act therefore does not suffer a limit, except insofar as it relies on some subject where there is something of passive potency. But the divine act subsists in itself. Efficacious [B] power itself, insofar as it is power, does not include a certain number of degrees. For what prevents power itself, as it is power, from being thought and existing in one number as well as in another? Therefore, it does not receive a limit of degrees from elsewhere, than either from the passive potency with which it is mixed, or from a terminating cause. But divine power is pure and supreme. Being itself, as it is considered absolutely, is immense, because it can be communicated to infinite things and in innumerable ways, and can be conceived. Therefore, if the being of anything is finite, it must be limited either by its own cause or by a subject. Neither happens to God. But in infinite being itself there is infinite power, just as in finite being there is finite power. In pure nothing itself there is no habit of being, whether true or imaginary. For who can define nothing under the aspect of being? Therefore, in pure being itself there is nothing either of the pri- [C] vation of being, or of the potency not to be, either by true or imaginary reason. Therefore, it can neither be compelled nor conceived not to be, which pertains to its eternity; nor can any degree of power be lacking to it, which can be imagined by the mind. Otherwise, [D] the mind, which is an effect of God, could extend itself beyond God, which is always able to

He succeeds the end of all things: for even before anything's beginning, it was true that that beginning would be; and after every end, it will be true that that end was. Whatever is true at any time is true by virtue of Truth itself. But if Truth itself is said to have begun at some time, long before, through that same Truth, it would have been true that that Truth would begin at some time. And if it is imagined to end, still afterwards, through that same Truth, it will be true that that Truth had ended. Therefore, Truth can neither be thought to begin nor to end. Again: if God [Marginal note: K]
exists entirely above motion and time, He does not undergo temporal change from a prior state to a later state, according to being and non-being. God, therefore, eternal, then offers Himself to us, but enveloped [Marginal note: M]

They would have long since ceased to exist: because since they are by nature in flux, if they were not held back by something else more stable, they would have long since flowed away into nothingness. Therefore, an incorporeal and stable substance presides over the mobile bodies of the world. If this (substance) is equally disposed to being and not being, like bodies, it would again need something else to determine it. Indeed, if it were composed of parts, it would not exist through itself, but through the cooperation of its parts and through him who had brought together the diverse parts among themselves. Indeed, it would be equally subject to the dissolution of its parts as it was subject to their connection: and therefore it would not exist of necessity, since through dissolution it could also sometimes cease to be. Such indeed is God, a simple substance, necessarily subsisting through himself. For which reason Orpheus called God Necessity.

Indeed, if you also wish an angel to be such, so that there are two highest necessities, God and an angel, you will be compelled to declare in what respect an angel differs from God. For not in the necessity of being itself, for in this (respect) they are posited by you to be one. Therefore there will be something else besides necessity itself in the angel, by which it can differ from God. Wherefore an angel will not be the highest necessity, since it is not a pure and sole necessity, but a mixed one. Whatever, moreover, is highest in any genus, ought to have the pure nature of that genus, unmixed with other things, lest it be diminished by mixture. You are also compelled to answer whence the angel has that property added to necessity: whether from its own necessity, or from elsewhere? If the first is granted, God will have the same property, proceeding from a similar necessity of his own. Therefore, by that (property) the angel is not distinguished from God. If the second is conceded, it follows that the angel's own proper nature is born from elsewhere than from the angel, because it acquires the property by which it is distinguished from outside. Therefore, it is more fitting for it not to be than to be. Therefore, it is more fitting for it to be preserved by a cause than by itself. And because what is natural is never lost: it is always such that, if the power of the cause is removed, it does not persevere in being: since it was naturally such from the beginning that it would not come into being apart from the action of a [Marginal note: N] cause. But we properly call God the cause, who alone makes any thing whole: nor is He compelled to need the help of another, or to borrow material from elsewhere: but every thing is compelled to depend entirely on Him always, as a shadow on a body. Indeed, when the cause itself makes the whole effect, and the effect, if compared to the substance of the cause, is something imaginary and vain rather than substantial: then truly the effect, as if vain in itself, continually needs the support of the cause: and the cause which made the whole, preserves the whole. But the world, if compared to God, that is, the finite to the infinite: is more vain and more shadowy than if the finite shadow of a finite body were compared to the body. If God bestows being and action upon an angel, and preserves it: He also bestows the power of acting: He also bestows and preserves the action. Thus whatever an angel naturally operates, it operates by the power of God: just as an instrument acts by the power of the craftsman. Therefore God acts not only the angel, but also the very work of the angel: and much more than the angel brings about the work of the angel, since He Himself is the primary origin of action. If this work which is done by the angel, itself moves something: it acts through the same power of God, through which it was also made by the angel. Therefore, whatever happens anywhere, by whomever it happens, occurs by the power of God: especially since all things that act, in some way provide being to their work. that which is different from being itself would need [something]; certainly, the being of nothing would operate anything by itself. But now the qualities of bodies act upon each other without deliberation. Does the sun illuminate the world, and fire heat, and the soul nourish the body by choice rather than by being? Therefore, even those things which act by choice also do something naturally through their own being, that is, through a virtue naturally inherent in being itself.

Indeed, although the human soul does many things by choice, yet without choice, by its very being, it gives life to the body. Is not choice itself also in a certain way a work of the soul? And a work of this kind is from the very being of the soul without a preceding choice, lest similarly that preceding choice should need another preceding choice, and another again another. Thus any work of the soul would require innumerable choices before it could begin to be done, nor would it ever begin to be done, because it is not permitted to traverse an infinite number of things.

Let us summarize thus: If the action which is performed through natural being itself is inherent in all things, but not that action which is done by choosing, because bodies choose nothing; and also the action itself of choice and deliberation is always preceded by an action which is done through being itself and nature: it is plainly evident that this action which is done by being itself belongs to the universal and first cause, which is God, so that it may be the first and common action of the first and common agent. The action which is done by being is done without care and labor. Thus the sun, by a single act, most easily illuminates in a certain way infinite things, and generates by illuminating; fire most easily heats many things; the soul nourishes the body and digests many things in it simultaneously without solicitude and labor. Thus God, through His being, which is a most simple center of things from which the rest are drawn like lines, with the easiest nod sets in motion whatever depends on it.

But this is the difference between the first agent and the other agents: that the first agent is said to operate through being in such a way that it acts through pure being; but the rest [act] through being, that is, through some natural virtue, or, so to speak, essential virtue. Therefore, the operation which proceeds from deliberation is preceded by the operation which is performed by essential virtue; this [latter] in turn [is preceded by] that which is done by pure being. And by how much that which is done by virtue is easier than that which is done by deliberation, by so much that which is completed by pure being is easier than that which is done by virtue.
