by the virtue of the primary agent, the other agents operate. Do we not arrange the order of causes according to the order of effects? The first effect of all is being (esse): indeed, the remaining effects are nothing other than certain determinations and properties of being itself. For each thing first exists according to nature: then it is this, or that: such, or such. Add to this that the last thing lost is being (esse): for "to be such" is lost before "to be" simply. Therefore, being itself is the proper effect of that agent which is the beginning and end of all things. And if other agents contribute anything to this, they contribute by the virtue of the primary agent. And they themselves, as inferior agents of narrower dominion, do nothing else but everywhere distinguish that universal power and action of God, which tends everywhere to universal being, with God's help: and they induce certain affections of being itself rather than the nature of existing. Indeed, divine virtue distinguishes itself through various media into various effects: just as the light of the Sun, which in itself is equally disposed to any color, if it penetrates through two glass windows, one of which is red and the other green, will produce two splendors on the pavement, namely red and green. That each is a splendor, it will have simply from the light; but that one is red and the other green, it will again have from the light: but insofar as it penetrates through such a glass or such, it forms itself differently.

Let us conclude, first, that the first cause acts more vehemently in any effect than the other causes: because the trace which is imprinted by it, namely being (esse), is imprinted earlier and deleted later than the traces of the other causes, as if it were imprinted more strongly. Secondly, that the other causes establish their traces upon the trace of the first cause: which, just as they necessarily found all their works in the work of the first cause, so they establish their virtues and actions in its virtue and action.

God acts through His being whatever He acts. Chapter 8.

But lest any Epicurean say that God, if He acts much, is troubled by counsel and burdened by work: it is necessary to remember that God, because He can accomplish His work through His being alone, does not need counsel and election. For if divine being itself were not of such magnitude that it could operate by itself, but by some counsel

God understands Himself first, and also individual things. Chapter 9.

**I**ntellect would never become capable of understanding a thing unless there were some kinship between it and the thing itself. Therefore, since there is a kinship between intellect and the thing to be understood: by the same way that something progresses to become intelligible, by that same way it progresses to be intellect. But separation from matter is the only way by which each thing attains that end, namely, to be understood and intelligible, that is, such that it can be properly understood: because then things are properly understood, when they are thought apart from matter and the conditions of matter. Therefore, through the same separation, one can arrive at being intellect. Indeed, if to be separated from matter is the cause that any form becomes one with the intellect: much more and sooner is to be removed from matter the cause that some thing is intellect and intelligent. But because no one is more removed from matter than God, no one understands more exactly. Again, intelligence is desirable as a good. For through it, each thing can enjoy itself and all other things: but to the first good, that is, God, nothing of good is lacking. Add to this that every cause acts through form: and the more ample the cause is, the more amply it acts through form. God is the most ample cause, therefore the most ample form is in God. But nowhere is form more ample than in mind. Therefore God has a mind. Which is also proven from this, because it is not fitting for minds to be instruments of a mover who lacks mind. But all minds are instruments of God. To the same point also contributes that, since in God essence and operation are the same, it follows that His operation is of that kind which does not pass into external matter, but remains in the agent as its perfections rather than those of matter. Such is cognition and appetition. Therefore, in God at least there is cognition: namely, intelligence, or something more eminent than intelligence itself. And since the intelligence of God is the first intelligence: and whatever is first in any genus is pure and sole and in itself: therefore, in Him, to be and to understand are entirely the same: lest if being were one thing and understanding another, we be compelled to place that intelligence in another, that is, in essence. Likewise, if the first intelligence is there, it is certainly most perfect. Such it is clearly, which is most proximate to that object which is to be comprehended by itself.

Do you not know, impious Averroes, that the very good of the universal order is more excellent than the quality of any part? An order of this kind cannot be understood otherwise than if any more precious and viler things are distinguished among themselves: in whose intervals and proportions the whole order consists. Remember, however, that these very things which are commonly called vilest, were each constructed with a most exact art: just as those which are held to be most precious: again, those which, when considered alone, usually seem less beautiful, nevertheless in this whole order, and in the very ordainer of the whole, harmonize most fittingly both with themselves and with others. Orpheus thus sang all this in a hymn to Apollo.

[Marginal note: I]
Nature can certainly make diverse things either through diverse means or from diverse materials; but if the diversity of means and materials is removed, it operates either as one or as something very similar. Nor can it fail to operate when matter is present.
[Marginal note: K] But God alone creates the prime matter of bodies, and very many essences of minds and souls, without any medium or subject. These indeed are widely diverse among themselves, and distinguished among themselves by many degrees of perfection. Rightly, however, God, because He is the first agent, dominates His entire work to such an extent that He Himself can bring about both forms, and the order of forms, and the distinction of degrees. No agent indeed would produce effects both fewer and less varied than God; nay, God would act entirely as one if He operated solely through the mode of mere nature, since divine nature is the simplest of all. Therefore, He is not impelled to act by natural instinct.
      Third argument. If intelligence in us is effective, and more effective in angels, it is necessary that intelligence in God be most effective. His nature and intelligence are the same in God. Also, the same mode of natural operation and intellectual operation usually exists everywhere.
[Marginal note: L] Indeed, both nature and intelligence act through form, and operate something similar in form. Therefore, God is not to be said to operate through bare nature or through an adventitious intelligence, but rather through intellectual nature and natural intelligence. To God, because He is the first, common, and most blessed cause, natural operation is fitting: which is prior to others, more common, and easier. Again: because He is the most precious cause, intellectual operation is fitting: which is prior in dignity in us, although not in time; and therefore is first in the order of things; and as something precious, it is fitting only for more excellent species. Therefore, God's proper operation is both operations. Among the Platonists, however, the unique divine essence, insofar as it is God, is a property. Therefore, both operations are the same in God.
[Marginal note: M]       Fourth argument. Bare nature regards this good or that; intellectual nature [regards] the universal good. Therefore, a cause that acts through bare nature is thus compared to a cause that acts through intellectual nature, as a particular cause to a universal one, and a servant to an architect. Therefore, the architect of the world operates through intellectual nature, insofar as He is intellectual.

[F] Likewise, substance does not depend on accident, although accident depends on substance. That which does not depend on another is sometimes able to exist separately from another. Second argument. The nature of anything is a certain single form and power determined in a certain way to one specific work, doing whatever it does with its whole impetus, and doing it necessarily. [H] Indeed, the hot nature of fire primarily performs one specific work, namely, that of heat; and it always heats with the same tenor; and as much as is in it, it exerts all degrees of heat everywhere. Therefore, that this matter is heated by it to one degree, and that [matter] to two degrees, does not proceed from the ordering of the agent, but from the order of degrees found in the preparations of materials. Therefore, fire does not dominate the whole work. For it is not the author of the order of degrees that are in the work. And if it were to generate two heats outside of subjects, because it would act with its whole self on both, both would be equal; indeed, even now in entirely similar subjects it generates entirely similar and equal [heats].

ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL. BOOK II. 31

Fifth reason. That operation, more than others, is fitting for God, by which God neither deviates from His own state nor from His own simplicity. Such, primarily, is the operation of the mind. For natural operation indeed begins from the agent, but ends in that which is acted upon: just as heating from fire into wood. Intellectual operation, however, retains both terms in the agent. For through this, God, while contemplating Himself, turns all external things, and as Parmenides the Pythagorean says, "He rotates the mobile orb of things while keeping Himself immobile." Moreover, it is necessary for God to be entirely uniform: because He exists above all forms. Indeed, and omniform: because He is the shaper of all things. That He can be uniform and omniform at the same time, only intellectual nature makes possible. For through this, the form of God, by intuiting itself, conceives itself as the proper reason of all forms.

For He sees in Himself whatever is proper to each thing, while discerning to what degree each thing can imitate the divine form, or wherein it falls short: for example, while He understands His own form through the mode of life, but not of cognition: so to speak, He conceives the imitable form and idea of plants. While, however, He conceives the imitable form through the mode of cognition indeed, but not of intelligence, as the proper idea of an animal: and the others in the same way.

And indeed, in all things which come into being not by chance, but either by nature or by design, it is necessary that the end of the making is the form of the work produced. The efficient cause, however, directs the action towards the form not through anything else, but through the form existing in itself. Nor does it direct to certain forms otherwise than either through certain forms, or through certain reasons of forms conceived within itself.

Since, therefore, the marvelous order of the world cannot consist by chance, devoid of order, it is necessary that in the intelligence of the Creator Himself there is a form, according to whose likeness the effect is made. And since, by God's design, the order of the universe is most preeminent: the principal idea with Him is the idea of the order of the universe. The reason for the order and of the whole cannot be held unless the proper reasons of all the parts from which the whole is constituted are held. just as an architect cannot conceive the form of a building unless he has conceived the proper reasons of its parts. Therefore, in God are the proper reasons of all things: nor do the species of things have their distinctness from anywhere else than from where they have their being. Nor does divine simplicity on account of this multitude of them [text cut off]

--- Page 144 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

**Fourth reason.** Where there is no will, which is an inclination of the mind towards the good, there is no pleasure of the mind, which is an expansion of the will into the good, and a rest of the will in the good. If there is no pleasure where the good itself is, pleasure will be nowhere, for wherever it is, it exists by reason of the good. Therefore, in the good itself there is pleasure and will. If an affection of this kind is the beginning of generation in creatures, certainly in the creator himself it is the origin of creation.

**Fifth reason.** If all agents, both according to nature and according to art, always direct their works to an end, that is, to the good, and do so by their goodness; but they receive the order of operating from the first agent, and that is the good itself: it is clear that it (the first agent) orders its own works to the best end. For if particular goods, because they are good, and because they are ordered [Marginal note: A] by the highest good, each order themselves to some good: how much more will the universal good order all things to the good, namely to the universal good? Therefore, God leads all things to Himself as their end. For no end of divine action [Marginal note: B] is outside God, because the end is located in the same order together with that which acts towards the end: and it is a certain good, and it moves the efficient cause. But nothing is located in the same order with God, except God himself. God does not serve an alien good. For the whole good never serves a particular good. Moreover, God is not moved by anything. If God's end is His own goodness: God in His own way desires and loves His goodness. And since God is intellectual and His goodness is intelligible: He loves it with an intellectual love. Love of this kind resides in the will. Therefore, God wills Himself. He wills Himself, I say, as the end [Marginal note: C] of Himself and of all things. From the will of the end, however, proceeds the operation concerning those things which are directed to the end. Therefore, the divine will (as Plato says in Timaeus) is the beginning of all creatures. The same is very often read in Hermes Trismegistus. For they think that the principle of the universe ought to have the most perfect mode of action, that is, that by its will it is entirely the master of its making, who is entirely the master of the things made: a master, I say, disposing by free will. For if it acted by necessity, either of nature or of intelligence, it would act upon all things simultaneously and infinite things simultaneously: it would also compel each thing and snatch it away in a moment.

Second argument. Whatever accompanies existence, that pertains to a being, insofar
as it is a being. What is of this nature must be found in that which is the first being.
But whatever exists has this, that it both desires an absent good and most willingly rests in a present good.
Indeed, nature, sense, intellect desires an absent good:
embraces a present one: All this, nature, devoid of sense, does through a certain
inclination; sense through appetite; intellect through will.
Therefore, since God is (to speak in the Peripatetic manner) the first being:
who will deny that the divine intellect willingly embraces its present good, which is all good, through
will? For just as in its truth it sees all true things, which become true by its
illuminating: so in its goodness it wills all good things, which both are born by its
propagation, and become good by its perfecting. Moreover, any mind
does works by willing rather than by seeing. For by seeing it replicates forms
within: by willing it unfolds them outside: by seeing it regards the true,
to which purity is proper: by willing it attains the good, to which diffusion is proper.

[Marginal note: D]
I consider it sufficiently proven that God creates individual things not by the necessity of nature or intellect, but by the command of his will. How indeed his will is at once necessary and free, I think must now be demonstrated.
First Reason. Let everyone most diligently beware lest he accidentally fall into such rash impiety as to ever suspect that God exists and operates as if by chance it happened. If it never happens by chance to anything to be or to operate, that which is and operates naturally, for example, it does not happen by chance to fire, but it must be hot and heat; but to the supreme being it is natural to be, and to the supreme act it is natural to act; it follows [Marginal note: E] that God, who exists as the supreme being, and more than a being, and the supreme act, in no way exists or acts according to contingency. If where there is more reason, there is less chance; in God, who is supreme reason, or the fount of reason, nothing fortuitous can be conceived. If fortune does not produce reason, since it is contrary to it, indeed it is the privation or defect of reason; in what way then does it produce either God, or any divine action superior to any reason? If God is that very rule, so ordering all things, that from those things which immediately follow, he removes all contingency; how then does it happen to him by some chance to be or to operate thus? Therefore, God does not exist and act as it happens by [Marginal note: F] chance; otherwise no order would ever be found anywhere; but as was fitting, indeed as is fitting. It is fitting, moreover, because it is decorous. Indeed, decorum itself is God himself, by whom and through whom all fitting things are made. Indeed, he exists and acts as is necessary. Necessary, I say, through necessity itself. Necessity itself, moreover, is God, through whom also other necessary things are, whatever are necessary. Therefore, God is as he is. He acts as he acts. And since no necessity presides over necessity, therefore, there is supreme liberty there. Liberty is desirable as a good. But in supreme goodness is whatever can ever be desired as a [Marginal note: G] good. He is free, whoever lives as he wills. Goodness itself lives as it wills, above all others; whose life every will desires, beyond which no will desires anything. God loves, and provides. Chapter 13.

[Marginal note: H]
If God pleases himself, if he loves himself: surely he loves his images and his works. A craftsman loves his works, which he made from external material. A father loves his son much more, whom he generated from intrinsic material: although he first received that material (while eating) from elsewhere. God loves any of his works more ardently: since he did not receive material from elsewhere, but he himself created the very material, who also formed it: with the result that he was both the sole cause and the cause of the entire work. If God loves his works so much, he wills good for them: and what he wills, follows. Therefore he disposes them well: and with his supreme goodness he disposes them as best as possible. For just as fruitfulness and the inclination to act are innate in all agents from the fruitfulness of the first agent: so diligence in guarding works is implanted in each one from the primary diligence of the first agent, the provider for all as if they were sons. In this, the greater the fruitfulness than in others, the more diligent the providence. Again,

[Marginal note: I]
God does all things for his own sake: because if he acted for another end besides himself, God's action would depend on that end: therefore also the will to act would depend on the same: and God himself would depend on the same: since God and God's will are the same. If he makes all things for his own end, and he himself is the supreme good: he disposes all things for good (as Plato wills in the Timaeus): so that each thing, according to its nature, may receive divine goodness. Furthermore, since all things desire good, and the desire for good is good, and therefore it comes from the first good itself, from which all good things are: it follows that, attracted by divine goodness, they desire divine goodness. Who then would deny that God governs things: since he directs them to a good end? The elements and members of the world, contrary to each other in their nature, form, or power, fighting among themselves, how would they come together into one, and remain so long coupled to each other, and mutually exchange natures and motions, and be exchanged, unless they were connected by some more excellent power? Furthermore, if the governance of the world were left to its members, which are contrary to each other: these, balanced by their own weights and separated by their places, would not mix with each other. And if they were mixed: they would do nothing other than hot, cold, dry, humid, rare or dense, and the rest of the same kind; but they would establish no order of forms, figures, revolutions.

of an army is in its leader, so the order of the entire world is in God
alone, the single prince of the world." Therefore, the parts of the world and

that they very often perform their operations as well as they can be done,
just as if they had art within them, and indeed a most perfect art.

human art and reason. And since these bodies are ignorant of their own motions,
and therefore do not know how to prescribe for themselves the end
towards which they tend not by chance but by necessity, yet they have a prescribed
end: (otherwise they would not proceed to this end more than to another) it is clear
that it is prescribed for them by another.

By design, I say, not ambiguous and changeable, but entirely certain and immediate, and by intuition rather than by discourse. Such an intuition we call design by a kind of metaphor, not because there one thing is investigated from others, but because some things are made for the sake of others. Inactive men are accustomed to consult about crafts; but indeed he who perfectly understands an art consults no further, but thus gives it its form, just as nature does with forms. But if there is any most perfect art anywhere, it is certainly there, from where this marvelous work of the world is arranged. Perhaps you will place such an art in nature, devoid of all sense. But I will say that you lack sense, if you are so alien from sense that you do not perceive that if every earthly creature feels, much more ought the whole world and nature, the craftsman of all things, to have sense: a rational sense, I say, if it orders its works more rationally than human reason. However, long custom diminishes admiration. We saw in Florence the workshop of a German craftsman, in which statues of various animals, connected and balanced on a single pivot, were moved simultaneously with diverse motions by the movement of the pivot itself: some ran to the right, others to the left: upwards and downwards: some sitting rose up, others standing bowed down: these crowned those: those wounded others. Also the sounds of trumpets and horns, and the songs of birds were heard: and other things were done there simultaneously, and very many similar things followed by the mere movement of a single pivot. Thus God, through His very being (which in reality is the same as understanding and willing: and which is a certain most simple center of all things, from which, as we have said elsewhere, the rest are drawn forth like lines) with the easiest nod moves whatever depends on Him. Therefore let Lucretius the Epicurean be silent, who wishes the world to be made and moved by chance, and believes that the constant state of most beautiful order proceeds from an unstable and deformed privation of order: just as if someone were to think wisdom to be born from foolishness, and light from darkness. Likewise, just as in the foreknowledge of God, the future events of things are written: so also are the causes of events, and the modes of acting. And just as our works are known to God, so also is our will, which is the cause of our works and the free mode of acting. For just as he foresees that you will do it: so he foresees that you will do it thus, that is, voluntarily and freely. Therefore, if divine prevision, by the positing of some condition, renders our works necessary: it renders necessary, that is, it similarly confirms the mode of acting, which is the freedom of our judgment: because God, the regulator of all natures, preserves for each thing, and does not subtract, the nature which he had given. Thus, while he rules all things, he rules each thing according to its nature: he leads ascending elements to ascent, and descending elements to descent. If he rules the movement of animals: because it is about to advance by its nature, he contributes to its walking. If he guides the heavens: because by nature they are revolving due to their roundness, he contributes to the extent of their circuits. If he stirs souls: because they are freely revolving upwards and downwards: he stirs, and freely: so that he entices, not drags: not compels, but persuades.

Which Zoroaster thus testifies:

For if the adequate object of appetite is the good itself, certainly goodness itself is the reason for the appetite to desire whatever it desires: so that in every thing it desires, not otherwise

--- Page 157 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. II. 38

Nor is the world moved by its own accord without life, nor does it revolve so long and so uniformly without a most powerful life: nor with such order without a most wise mind: nor so optimally and conveniently without the highest good: but a certain single life, queen of the one mundane body, excelling in power, wisdom, and goodness, most providentially and from the beginning and continuously leads the world to the best. This [life] is either the highest God, or the handmaid of the highest God. If it is the highest God: God certainly provides. If it is the handmaid of God: God also provides: because the first principle acts and moves all things for its own sake. Divinely did Orpheus speak of Jove: *panto genethl' archē pantōn, pantōn te teleutē*, that is, begetter of all: and beginning and end. Therefore, if the life of the world provides: certainly, led by God, it provides for God's end. Therefore, all things are finally directed to God's goodness. And yet this goodness, since it has care of its whole work, certainly neglects no parts. For the best state and condition of the whole composite consists of its individual parts. Orpheus expressed all this thus: *pant' esoras, kai pant' epakoueis, panta brabeueis*, that is, you look into all things: you hear into all things: and you distribute all things. But since the whole structure of the world is established for the sake of reflecting divine goodness, and the parts of the world are placed for the sake of this structure itself: not absolute perfection is to be sought in this whole work, but as much as suffices to indicate the more sublime perfection of the author according to its powers. Nor is any perfection of that part to be demanded in any part of the world: but that which harmonizes with the other parts and contributes to the whole. Thus, although sometimes the condition of some mundane particle may seem to be blameworthy in itself: if, however, it is compared to the state of the whole, we will find that the world cannot be well disposed otherwise than in this way. Indeed, the creator of the universe refers not the whole itself to any parts, but rather the parts to the whole. Rightly, therefore, what elsewhere concerning the parts seem either evil or deformed, finally turn out for the ornament and good of the whole. Wherefore, with Orpheus, God is called: *aïdios zōē, ēd' athanatēte pronoia*, eternal life, and immortal providence.

alone: for it does nothing by its own nature. Quality moves an-

indeed stable, but not stable by itself. For it stands through divine
unity. For what else is to stand (as we have said) than
to persevere in the unity of its own nature? It also moves through God.
E  For by the virtue of the first act, all agents do whatever they
do: God moves and acts upon all things by Himself, He indeed being sta-
ble by Himself. Indeed, because all things which are such by another,
are reduced to some first thing which is such by itself:
therefore, whatever things are stable, and moving by another,
we have referred to God, who is stable by Himself, and moving by Himself. And
whatever things are movable by another, for example, bodies and qualities,
we have referred to the soul, which is movable by itself: by itself, I say,
movable: because if you descend from God through the angel, both God and
the angel will seem to you to stand: and the first thing that will seem movable to you
F  will be the soul. Whatever, moreover, is primarily such in any
genus, is such by itself: for example, that which is primarily luminous or
hot, shines and is hot by itself. Thus, since the soul is the first
movable among all things that are movable, it is certainly movable by itself.
A sign of this is that bodies which lack a soul
are agitated only by external impulse: those which have a soul
move spontaneously, and to any part of a place. And since
the soul provides this to bodies, that they are moved in some way by themselves to any
part, it follows that the soul itself is truly and primarily

it is filled thereby at a single point of eternity, and always remains most full of goodness. But since every effect produced outside its cause preserves something of the cause, and also turns out to be inferior to the cause, therefore the angel created closest to God preserves something of God, and loses something. God indeed has unity and stability: the angel cannot retain both. For he would be God himself, not an angel. Nor does he lose both, lest the closest and first work of God turn out most unlike its maker. What then? Will he retain unity alone, or stability? He cannot retain unity alone without stability. For unity itself is utterly immobile. Therefore he will retain stability, but will fall from simple unity: so that the angel is an immobile multitude. Nor do we wrongly assign multitude to the angel: because if it were perfect and most absolute unity, it would be supreme and unlimited power. Indeed, power consists in unity. Unlimited power is God himself. Furthermore, if it is characteristic of a body to receive and to suffer, but characteristic of an incorporeal nature to give and to act: in corporeal nature, power is said to exist, namely, power (as theologians say) receptive and passive; in incorporeal nature, act, that is, efficacy for acting. Therefore quality, because it is in a way incorporeal by itself, has some power of acting, whence it is also called act. But because it is received and divided in matter, and thereby becomes in a way corporeal, hence it is not a pure act, but contaminated by the passion of the body. Therefore quality consists of act and potency. But the soul, although it is separable from matter, and for that reason is called act, and is alien from the passion of the body, nevertheless is not yet a pure act. For it is mobile. If something is moved, through movement it acquires what it previously lacked: as it lacked it, it has that potency which we call receptive and in a way passive potency. As it acts by moving somewhat, it is act; and while it acquires something, it also becomes act. Therefore the soul is composed of potency and act. But is the angel a pure act? By no means. God clearly, because he is entirely separate from matter, in which passive potency exists without any power of acting, is therefore understood to be pure vigor of acting, separate from the nature of receiving and suffering. If God is pure act, the angel cannot be such: because that which is one in itself never becomes plural, unless by the addition of an alien nature.

There must be something between an angel and the qualities of bodies, lest an entirely immobile angel be entirely close to a mobile quality. Let it therefore be partly immobile, partly also mobile. Its substance will remain stable: nor will it be changed into greater or less, or this or that. But its operation will flow: and now it will operate in this way, now in that, and in different ways. The soul's quality, however, is inferior: inasmuch as it is changed through its essence and operation. The body is inferior to quality. For quality is moved and moves: for it moves bodies. The body indeed is moved, but moves nothing. The angel, indeed, that it is a single entity and that it is an act, does not have this from itself, but from God, who is truly one and a most pure act. But that it is manifold through the power of receiving and undergoing, it has from itself: inasmuch as, being produced outside God, it degenerates from the perfection of its producer. Multiplicity therefore is natural to the angel. The soul also, that it is a single substance and that it is a stable act through its essence: it obtains this not from itself, but from God by one and most stable act. But that it is manifold and passive, it possesses from itself: because it is placed under God. Finally, that it is mobile, again from itself: because it is under the angel. Just as therefore unity is natural to God, and multiplicity to the angel: so motion is natural to the soul. An angel does not bind these. Namely, it is entirely raised up to God: it neglects bodies. Rightly, the most perfect and closest creature of God becomes entirely divine, and passes into God.
[Marginal note: I] Quality also does not connect extremes: for it inclines towards the body, leaves the higher things: having left the incorporeal, it becomes corporeal. Up to this point, all are extremes: and the higher and lower things flee each other, lacking a suitable bond. But that essential third thing, being interposed, exists in such a way that it holds the higher things, does not abandon the lower things: and thus in it the higher are bound together with the lower. For it is immobile: and it is mobile. From that side it agrees with the higher things, from this side it agrees with the lower things. If it agrees with both: it desires both. Therefore, by a certain natural instinct it ascends to the higher things: it descends to the lower things. And while it ascends: it does not abandon the lower things: and while it descends, it does not leave the sublime things. For if it abandons either, it will incline to the other extreme: nor will it any longer be the true bond of the world. Indeed, it does the same thing as air in the middle between fire and water: which agrees with fire in heat, with water in moisture. There with fire it is always hot: here with water it is moist. There it is thinned, and becomes clear like fire: here in turn it becomes dull like water. Indeed, it does the same thing as the light of the sun. For it descends from the sun into fire, and fills the fire: nor does it abandon the sun. It always adheres to the sun: it always fills the fire. Indeed, it perfects the air: and by the air it fills, it is not tainted. Similarly, the third essence must both adhere to divine things, and fill mortal things. (as we have already signified) declare [this]. First, because everything that is such by means of another, is reduced to something that is such by itself. Second: because since there are many things that are moved by another: if all things are such, either we will wander to infinity, or we will revolve in the same circle, so that the same thing is the first mover and the last: the same cause and effect: and there is no order in things. Therefore we are compelled to arrive at some mover, which is now not moved by another. But that mover which immediately precedes bodies that are moved by another, is not entirely immobile. For these two are further apart: that which is mobile by another, and that which is entirely stable: their middle is that which is mutable by itself. Third: because if any thing is moved so much better, the closer it is to the mover: and the best motion must be reached: it is necessary that somewhere there is something in which the essence of the mobile and the mover is the same. Fourth: because if something is to be moved, it is necessary either for the mover to turn to the mobile itself, or the reverse: or both in turn. Let there be supposed then in nature only angels, God, and bodies. The former will not approach the latter, because they are immutable: nor the latter the former, because by their very nature they are sluggish. Therefore there will be no motion in things. Therefore it is necessary that there be a certain nature spontaneously mutable, which by itself approaching bodies, may rouse them from their sluggishness: and itself, ever watchful, may first experience its own powers within itself, before exerting them in the body: so that just as from a spiritual substance there is a corporeal substance, so from a spiritual motion a corporeal motion may be produced. Which indeed I believe Plato understood in the Laws, where he says: "If now all things stand still, and a little later something must be moved: what will be moved first?" [H] Namely, that which is active for motion by itself, as being closer to the power of moving: whose motion also other things subject to motion will follow. He calls it in the Phaedrus the source and principle of motion. A source, because it has it from itself: a principle, because it pours it into others. But here a doubt arises. at the same time through any parts of the body. Thus, a point that is
designated somewhere on a line of a circle is neither in all other
lines, nor is it diffused throughout the entire line or circle.
But a point that is the center of a circle is proper to no single line:
it is found in a way in all lines that are drawn from there to the
circumference. And while no point designated on the circumference
equally regards the whole circle: the center, however, which is not
[C in margin] properly fixed on any circumference, equally encompasses the entire circle.
Therefore, that thing which is divisible cannot be whole at the same time
in many places: nor can that thing which, although indivisible, nevertheless
has a certain position in another divisible thing. But that third essence is
neither extended, because it would be a quality: nor situated anywhere in
extension: because it would not move by itself and freely, if it did not
subsist by itself. Therefore, it is like a point living in itself, and entirely
absolved from all quantity and position. For this reason, it equally
encompasses every position of the body: and when it enters the body,
because it is not a proper point of any quantity, it is not confined to any
point of corporeal quantity. Indeed, since it is outside the genus of quantity,
it is not determined to touch any point of quantity: but it is like the center
in all lines, and in the whole circle. From this also follows that this essence
is at once both divisible and indivisible. Divisible, because through the vital
division of the body it diffuses its shadow, while it communicates itself to
diverse parts of the body. Indivisible, because it stands whole and simple
at the same time. Divisible, I say: because its shadow is in the whole divisible
body. Indivisible, because it itself is whole in every part of the body in an
indivisible manner. Indivisible again, because it has a stable and unified
substance. Divisible: because through operation
[D in margin] it is divided into many, while it operates through motion and time.
Indivisible thirdly, because it looks up to higher things, which are very much
united. Divisible, because it inclines towards lower things, which are greatly
divided. Such a nature seems extremely necessary in the order of the world:
so that after God and the angels, who are not divisible either according to

*The soul is the middle degree of things, and connects all degrees, both higher and lower, into one, while it itself both ascends to higher things and descends to lower things.*
Cap. 2.

[Large initial C] But so that we may at last come to that which we desire: let us again gather all things into five degrees: placing God and the angel at the summit of nature: body and quantity at the lowest: but the soul as a medium between those highest and these lowest things: which we rightly call the third and middle essence in the Platonic manner: because it is a medium to all things, and third from every side. If you descend from God, you find this in the third degree of descent. Also, if you ascend above the body, in the third degree of ascent, we judge such an essence to be extremely necessary in nature. For indeed, as the Platonists say, the angel truly *is*, that is, *stands* always; quality *is*, that is, it moves sometimes: therefore quality differs entirely from the angel: both because the latter moves, the former remains; and because the latter *is* sometimes, the former *is* always: therefore there is need of a medium which agrees partly with the angel, partly with quality. What is that? Is it perhaps that which *is*, that is, remains intrinsically sometimes? No. For such a thing is not found. For that which remains intrinsically for some time, that is, either from itself or from its immediate state, remains always. Therefore the medium will be that which *is* always, that is, moves. Insofar as it *is* always, it agrees with the angel; insofar as it moves, it agrees with quality. Hence it follows that there must be a third essence, a medium of these, which always moves and lives, and by its own motion diffuses life into bodies. It is rightly said by the Platonists that above that which *is* in a part of time, there is that which *is* through all time. Above that, again, there is that which *is* through eternity. Finally, above that eternity, there is existence itself. But between those things which are only eternal, and those things which are only temporal, the soul is, as it were, a certain bond of both. To which, in this respect, the principal parts of the mundane body are in some way similar. There are also those who place the Empyrean heaven, as entirely mobile, in eternity: but the other spheres in eternity and time simultaneously:

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**
No subsequent motion descends unless it comes from the first. Therefore, the motion in the third essence is the most perfect of all motions. But it is that which departs as little as possible from its source, which is most closely joined to its foundation, which is supremely one and equal, which is self-sufficient, which imitates the most perfect figure. But such is circular motion, as is clear to everyone, which alone of all motions is eternal. For other motions reach some limit, beyond which it is not permitted to proceed, since there is no infinite space anywhere. But circular motion, as it repeats the same things once, so it does twice and thrice and four times; it repeats in a similar manner; and in it the end is the same as the beginning; therefore when it seems to end, then it begins. Therefore, eternal circular motion is proper to the third essence, so that through motion it is reflected back into itself in a circle. But rightly, if it moves from itself, it also moves into itself, so that some end of motion may occur where there is some beginning. Indeed, the very cause of motion in a certain way produces motion for its own sake. Therefore that essence, beginning from itself, perpetually revolves into itself, unfolding its powers from the highest through the middle to the lowest, and again the lowest through the middle similarly folding back to the highest. If this is so, it perceives itself and what it possesses within. If it perceives, it certainly knows. But it knows by understanding, while it recognizes its essence as spiritual and free from the

...and their connection. But how is it joined to bodies? Does it perhaps, when it enters some body, touch a single point of that body, and is thus said to be united to bodies? By no means. For it would be united to a point, not to the body, nor would it vivify that whole body, but one point would live, the whole body lacking life. Indeed, if, always collected in a single point, it were to persevere thus united to itself: it would be the same as an angel, who is far distant from the body. Or at least it would indeed adhere to divine things in that way, but it would abandon bodies. Therefore, it is not joined to merely one point of the body, but to many: and thus it fills the parts of the body. But does it fill it in the same way that whiteness fills white flesh? And indeed, any quality its proper matter? By no means. For thus it would be the same as a quality: and having abandoned divine
[Marginal note: A]
things, it would entirely incline to the body. Whiteness is in the whole flesh in such a way that it is equally extended and divided into many parts with it: and a part of whiteness, according to the physicists, is in a part of the flesh: and in a larger part of the flesh there is a larger part of whiteness, in a smaller part there is a smaller. Thus whiteness has become corporeal. That essence which we believe to be the third would suffer the same, if it were diffused into the body no differently than that quality: and thus, drawn to the other extreme of nature, it would cease to be the bond of the world. Therefore, when it enters the body, it is wholly present to each individual particle of the body: nor is it divided or drawn apart into any parts for the purpose of being present to the parts of the body distant from each other. For it touches the body through an indivisible power, not through the breadth of quantity. Therefore, remaining whole and simple, it is wholly and indivisibly present to each part: just as the whole voice and its meaning are in a way simultaneously in each part of the house: since it is almost entirely heard and understood simultaneously in each. Nor is it impossible for this essence, since it is something indivisible existing in itself, to be thus wholly present to the ample mass of the body: indeed, from the fact that it is both indivisible and not confined to a place, it can wholly penetrate and comprehend whatever is in
[Marginal note: B]

D But indeed the Platonists will deny that those influxes, since they are certain accidents far separated from their vital substances, can generate vital substance here, because an accident cannot generate substance unless it is subjected as an instrument to substance: to the proximate substance, I say.
E For an instrument, apart from the craftsman, is not moved to the form of art. Thus that influx of celestial life, removed from life itself, will not generate a vital form. Rightly the celestial instinct, because it is common to every element, is determined in each to generate some life in that very element by the common life of the whole element: and to it it is subjected as an instrument. But neither will it itself generate in any way. For since it does nothing beyond its own degree, an accident can in no way generate substance, but merely dispose matter by some accidental preparation. But reason persuades that this formative life must be inherent within the elements, because for generating substance, an agent substance is needed; and for perfect action, the perfect presence of the agent itself is needed. But when a corporeal substance is applied to a corporeal substance for some action, what is substantial in the agent itself remains outside; what penetrates inward is entirely accidental. But there is need of a penetrating substance, so that substance may arise from it, and perfectly. Such a substance is incorporeal and living.
F Furthermore, natural causes, because they act through their own nature, are therefore directed to a certain effect in no other way than by a certain reason of their own nature. Otherwise they would incline no more to this effect than to that. From which it follows that insofar as they are suited to producing the work, to that extent they operate: and vice versa. Therefore, plants and living things which seem to be born in the earth solely by putrefaction ought to arise from their own proper causes no less than those which are born by propagation. But where are these proper causes? Without doubt, the proper causes of terrestrial lives are in terrestrial life. For even if you attribute them to celestial souls, nevertheless, it will be necessary for celestial and common instincts to be contracted to terrestrial and particular souls through the universal soul of the earth, so that you may proceed from the celestial and common to the opposite, that is, the terrestrial and particular, through a competent medium, that is, the terrestrial and common. Nor again does it remain always collected in its own nature like those [things]: nor is it torn into parts like these [things], but it is equally individual and divisible. This is that very essence [Marginal note: E] which Timaeus, Locrian, and Plato in the book 'On the World' said consists of an individual and divisible nature. This is that which inserts itself into mortals, yet does not itself become mortal. For just as it inserts itself whole, not torn apart: so too it withdraws whole, not dispersed. And because, while it rules bodies, it also adheres to divine things: it is the mistress of bodies, not a companion. This is the greatest miracle in nature. For other things under God are each a single something in themselves: this [essence] is all things at once. It possesses within itself images of divine things, upon which it itself depends. It possesses the reasons and exemplars of inferior things: which in a certain way it also produces. And since it is the middle of all things, it possesses the powers of all things. If this is so: it passes into all things. And because it is the true connection of all things: while it migrates into some, it does not abandon others: but it migrates into each individual thing: and always preserves all things: so that it can deservedly be called the center of nature, the middle of the universe, the series of the world, the face of all things, and the knot and bond of the world.

What the nature of this third essence is: we have said enough (as I believe). But that this itself is the proper seat of the rational soul, is most easily seen from this, that the definition of the rational soul is of this kind: Life and intelligence by discursive reasoning, and vivifying the body in time. [Marginal note: F] This is the same condition of that essence. For it lives, it understands, it bestows life upon the body. That it lives, is apparent, because we say those things live on earth which are moved by a certain inner power through every part, upwards, downwards, forwards, backwards, to the right, and to the left. Thus plants and animals are moved. Where therefore there is an intimate and common motion, there is life. Life, I say, is there the very internal power of moving. A power of this kind is there especially, where is the fount and origin of all agitation and the first motion. For the most intimate and common motion is where the first motion is. But the first motion is placed in that third essence. Therefore, life is there: life, I say, of such a kind that by its participation bodies live and are moved. For it is life to bodies by nature most proximate. That third essence, therefore, is life vivifying bodies. It is also intelligent. Therefore, not from itself and matter is one animal made, as the Almarians foolishly
think. For a rational animal is moved from itself,
whence it can be moved and not moved, and sometimes more quickly
moved, sometimes more slowly. But that which is such does not persevere in
perpetual and equal motion, unless by the law of some superior, which in no
way changes. God, therefore, is not the soul of any globe,
lest from Him and the globe one animal be formed, and be compelled
to have a leader above itself. But shall we concede that the life of a sphere is
G an angel, and that natural forms proceed from the ideas of the angelic
mind? By no means. For just as a body, through

Plato in the Timaeus says God joined the mind to the soul, and the soul to the

otherwise than through a transparent soul; just as a luminous

so that what has light by itself and exhibits it to others, may be joined to that which

realm, is far removed from matter.
But since an angel itself is nothing other than mind, and by its very
nature, the mind, in its operation, shuns matter, in what

just as the particular minds of humans reach and move their

powers, so the common minds of the spheres embrace and lead
common bodies through souls.
For thus those spheres will possess an inherent life, and divine

What is human art? A certain nature treating matter externally. What is nature? Art tempering matter internally: as if a carpenter were in the wood. bus. If therefore water and earth have been made fertile and adorned by God: why should not air and fire, besides common souls, also contain many souls of their own, and proper animals? Argue the same about the celestial spheres, where stars, since they are diverse among themselves in quantity, light, virtue, and motion, and each performs its own circuits: they also have diverse souls in kind. Indeed, these stars thus adorn the heavens, as aquatic animals adorn water, and terrestrial animals adorn earth. We clearly perceive those celestial animals because of the great abundance of light; and also terrestrial and aquatic ones: because they are both near to us and show themselves to our eyes by their density. But we do not see aerial and fiery animals: because we do not even perceive the elements of fire and air, since they appear to the eyes of terrestrial beings neither by the benefit of immense light, nor by the density of their mass. If the soul of this lowest globe is not endowed with reason, neither are the souls of the higher globes devoid of reason. In earth and water there is such a distinction of parts, that some terrestrial bodies are less pure, some most pure. The former have irrational souls, the latter rational ones. The same (applies) in water: where there are irrational fish in the muddy parts of the water. There are also aquatic demons whom Orpheus calls Nereids: in certain more sublime exhalations of water: such as are in this cloudy air: whose bodies are sometimes seen by sharper eyes, especially in Persia and Africa, as Zoroaster believes. Porphyry adds that those demons are seen only, in whose bodies fire abounds besides the exhalation of water: and that this happens in the East and South. But in all globes above water, there are no living beings unless they are endowed with reason: because those globes are not divided into dense and subtle parts: and whatever is there is far purer than watery exhalations. Moreover, mixed bodies, which, because of their earthy or watery density, are in themselves sluggish and base, it raises to some admirable actions; indeed, even to both enchanting and strengthening the minds of men: which cannot be accomplished without the power of a soul, and indeed a more powerful one. For by the power [Marginal note: C] of a living and wise nature, which is infused into these very bodies, the herb hierobotanon, as the mages say, contributes to the divinations of physicians. Agate strengthens sight, blunts poison, provides strength and eloquence; a diamond, when present, removes what the magnet attracts. Carnelian stops the flow of blood and calms anger. Onyx kindles anger, terrifies in dreams. Finally, coral (as Metrodorus and Zoroaster testify:) removes insane terrors, repels lightning and hail. Certainly, that nature, by whose power such things happen, is superior to our souls and to tempests; which must be infused into the lowest bodies, [Marginal note: D] so that it may elevate the lowest things with itself, beyond their own natures, to the actions of higher things. Strato and Chrysippus will confess that such a life is infused into the world, but they will assert that it is the supreme God. The Platonists will deny this, because above that life which belongs to something, and is in something, there ought to be that life which is its own and subsists in itself. But the mundane life of any sphere is no less familiar to its sphere than the human soul is to the human body. [Marginal note: E] Therefore, the life of a sphere, whether of a part or of the whole, is neither the first life nor God. For the supreme God is the supreme unity. From the supreme unity, according to the Platonists, some multitude can perhaps immediately proceed; but not such great diversity and discord of qualities corrupting each other. Again, nothing evil and deformed is close to supreme goodness and beauty; but many evil and deformed things occur around matter. Furthermore, if God is being itself, He cannot be the form of matter; for such a form is not being itself, but the principle of being. And because God is being, so to speak, so absolute that He is not in any essence, much less is He in matter. Likewise, since God is the first efficient cause, He acts on all His things primarily; but the form of matter does not act on all things primarily. For the composite acts primarily rather than a part of the composite. Again, the parts of a composite are in a certain potentiality towards the act of the whole itself. But in God there is no potentiality for a further act.

In the fifth, anger dominates concupiscence; in the sixth, conversely. If in the two extreme spheres of the world the number twelve is observed, it is observed in the middle ones as well. Therefore, as we began a little earlier, let us reduce the many souls living in each sphere to the twelve principal ones living in the same spheres in order. Let us again take twelve principles in any one of the twelve spheres—for there are so many spheres of the world among the ancients—let us refer them to the twelve common souls of those spheres. Again, the twelve souls of the spheres to the one soul of the one matter itself. But since the soul is a participant of mind, and above a participant nature there must be a nature full in itself, therefore the genus of souls is elevated to free minds; and minds finally to one mind. And one mind, because it is both mind and one, must be raised to the one simply, which is not this one, or that one, as if one mind, or one soul, but the one itself: which Pythagoras calls universal Apollo. For he wishes Apollo (ἀπόλλωνα) to be called, as if *aplon* (ἄπλων), which signifies simple; and as if *apo pollon* (ἀπὸ πολλῶν), which signifies removed from multitude. He also calls it *to agathon* (τ'ἀγαθὸν), that is, the good itself: because the goodness and perfection of each thing consists in its unity: so that if in things goodness and unity are the same, above things also the first one itself, and the first good, may be the same.

Therefore the first one and good presides immediately over the one mind, and the one mind over many minds. First, perhaps, it presides over twelve leading minds, and over twelve duodenaries under them, and then over many more: and finally over the one soul of the world. The one soul of the world presides over the twelve souls of the twelve spheres. The twelve souls preside over twelve duodenaries of souls. Namely, the soul of each sphere presides over twelve more excellent souls in its own sphere. Finally, the twelve duodenaries preside over innumerable souls. For in each sphere, those twelve principal souls lead the other souls of that sphere.

Moreover, this chorus of Muses sings and dances perpetually, as Orpheus says, with musical measures at the command of Apollo himself,

Add to this that since the heaven revolves with contrary motions simultaneously, if it were led by quality, it would certainly be moved by contrary qualities. However, contrary qualities and natures cannot exist there, where there is no conflict, no destruction. Likewise, since nature is determined, and therefore cannot desire an undetermined and diverse end (such as motion), it moves only for the sake of rest. But circular motion in itself is not directed towards rest; therefore, it is neither driven by nature, nor, if it ever rests, is it stopped by nature. Furthermore, a quality extended in a body is not able to reflect upon itself, since it is bound to the body. In what way, therefore, will a quality give to heaven a revolution upon itself, which does not have in itself the power of reflecting upon itself?

Likewise, since a body does nothing by its own nature, but through [Marginal note: B] quality, and quality does not by its own guidance provide power to the body, but insofar as it is itself moved from elsewhere, if some quality moves the heaven, it is itself meanwhile moved from elsewhere. What is that which moves it: is it God? By no means. The first cause, since it infinitely exceeds all things, is familiar to no body, but is equally common to all, and absolute from all. For if God were the proper agitator of some body, he would no longer be of all. Therefore, in order to be of all, he is not a ruler proper to any. The spheres, however, require very familiar movers (as we have said). And also because they are distinct from each other and are agitated by diverse motions, they demand different and proper movers, inasmuch as there must be a proportion between the mover and the motion.

Nor is their opinion to be approved, who distribute the movers to the spheres in such a way [Marginal note: C] that God is assigned to the first, and the remaining intellects to the rest. For since the distribution is made according to proportion, just as the spheres agree with each other in nature and order, so will God and the intellects agree with each other, nor will God surpass the remaining intellects except insofar as the first sphere surpasses the others, nor will he be immense. He will also be composed of a common nature, by which he will agree with others, and of a proper one, by which he will be distinguished. Furthermore, if God is goodness itself, and this moves any thing as an appetible object of desire, God moves heaven as an end. PLATONIC THEOLOGY

The Platonists likewise freely asserted: Moreover, it is whole everywhere in the entire heaven, so that it may move the whole most effectively. Therefore, that conjoined, indivisible, free, ubiquitous force is a rational soul. By its presence the heaven lives, whose motion is life-giving, since it gives life to all things. Finally, since in animals those instruments live through which souls generate living things, who will doubt that the heaven lives?
[Marginal note: G]
Indeed, it is an instrument of some life for generating living things. Is not spontaneous motion (so to speak), wherever it is, a sign of inner life? Such is most especially present where there is a natural circuit. For what moves more spontaneously than that which naturally returns into itself, and revolves around a natural center, and within a natural surface? Therefore, to no body is life more intrinsic than to the spheres of the world.

Nor should it be doubted that one animal is made from the spheres and divine souls, because since it is characteristic of matter to indeed assume form, and of form to embrace matter and lead it,
[Marginal note: H]
and since all that happens more there where both matter and form are more excellent: who would deny that from those souls which are more excellent than ours, and from the spheres, which are simpler and more enduring than our bodies (and which also contain, draw, and generate our bodies), one and indissoluble animal is formed? Are not those bodies, because of their wonderful simplicity and subtlety, as it were, spiritual? Therefore, in the presence of spirits, they are animated more easily than sulfur is ignited in the presence of fire. For thus the most excellent matter is joined to the most excellent form, that is, to the intellectual, to such an extent that they are never dissolved. If, therefore, mixed bodies, the more they depart from the intemperance of elemental qualities and approach the temperance of celestial bodies, the more capable they become of life and cognition, then undoubtedly celestial bodies are most capable of life and cognition. But the genus of minds is more sublime than heaven, and is more akin to heaven than to earth. Therefore, since many minds are joined to earthly bodies as forms, it is necessary that minds, both more numerous and earlier and more, are joined to celestial bodies as forms than to earthly ones.
[Marginal note: I]

DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. IIII. 51

Now let us return to the Platonic order. We have proved by one reason that the spheres of the world live; let us proceed to another. Since we see the spheres of the world moved, and we conceive of some movers of them, and we know moreover that one sphere cannot be upon another, or other movers upon others, without end, we are compelled to confess that there is some sphere which is moved first. If it is moved first, it is certainly moved by an intrinsic principle. Namely (as we touched upon above), that which is first hot and cold, is hot and cold by intrinsic heat and cold. For we have always said that whatever is such by another, must be reduced to something that is such by itself. And if even the smallest particles of the world somehow have in themselves the powers of their motions and operations—which appears in the parts of the elements and in plants, and in living beings—how much more do the most ample spheres of the world possess in themselves the principles of their revolutions: principles, I say, most intimate, by which the spheres are more closely joined than our bodies are to our souls. Indeed, motion is so much more natural and efficacious, as the mobile thing is more closely joined to the mover. [Marginal note: M] But the motion of the heaven is more alien from violence than others, more natural, more efficacious. But what are those principles? Are they perhaps some qualities? For example, just as the parts of the elements seem to be moved by gravity and levity, and to operate by heat and cold, so are the spheres of the world revolved by qualities of this kind? By no means. For a quality, because it is limited by site and parts, and is assigned to one particular matter, also acts in a limited way, and is fatigued so that it cannot move either always or in the same way; and any quality performs a single operation, and is moved to a single end. What does heat do but heat, cold but coldness? Levity draws only upwards, gravity indeed downwards. Therefore, a quality will never by its nature produce an effect contrary to its principal operation; it will never spontaneously return to the place from which it departed; it will never spontaneously depart from where it naturally moved itself. But the heaven is always moved equally, and produces various and mutually contrary effects; and for this diversity, it disposes the lower matter in contrary ways. It induces various configurations; nor does it have any certain end in its circuit; but whatever point you may mark on the back of the heaven, to that point any part of the heaven will approach innumerably, and again depart most easily, not by any violence. The bodies of brutes and humans live separately from the spheres, because they have their own souls: which is indicated by their figure, equipped with various instruments, being entirely dissimilar to the figures of the spheres; and also indicated by their constitution, which is most alien from the constitution of the spheres.

C As the movable relates to the movable, so the mover relates to the mover. Therefore, as body relates to body, so soul relates to soul. And so, bodies separated from each other by position, nature, figure, quantity, and motion, also have a separate soul; but connected bodies have a connected soul. Yet there is one soul of the world above individual souls. For of one living artisan, there must be one living work. There is not one living thing, except through one life. It does not have one life, unless it has one soul.
Rightly, since (as most argue) one primary and formless matter lies hidden in all spheres by itself, one soul belongs to it.

D What, then, is the reason that, although the members of the world are contrary to each other, they nevertheless conspire into one, and communicate their powers to one another: unless it is because one soul of this immense animal tempers its humors, however diverse, and connects members separated by position and quality through a conspiracy of life and motion? From where does it happen that inferiors follow the commands of superiors, and all members of the world (so to speak) sympathize with each other, unless from one common nature, and indeed one nature from one soul? Nor ought this divine animal to be less united than any other animal: since it is the most powerful of all. Therefore, if among other animals, any body is governed by one certain soul of its own: much more are the members of this mundane animal bound by one soul. And if it relates to its body as our soul relates to ours: it is no less whole in any part of the world than our soul is whole in any part of our body: otherwise, it could not perfectly connect, vivify, and move the universe.

E As nature relates to the body, so the soul relates to nature. Therefore, just as universal nature is everywhere in the entire body: so universal soul is everywhere in entire nature. That the souls of the spheres are rational, the disposition of the mundane movements shows, always proceeding towards that which is better and more beautiful. For just as a motion so swift, free, and enduring, comes from an inner life, so such a marvelous order of moving, and such an artful progression, comes from wisdom—

THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

That celestial spheres have souls, not only Platonists, but
I all Peripatetics confess: which Aristotle teaches in the second book of *De Caelo*; again, in the 7th and 8th of *Physics*, 2nd of *De Anima*, 11th of *Metaphysics*. Theophrastus also, Aristotle's disciple, in the book *De Caelo*. Which Avicenna and Algazel most strongly confirmed. Augustine Aurelius in the *Enchiridion*, and Thomas Aquinas in the second book of *Contra Gentiles*, teach that nothing, as far as Christian doctrine is concerned, matters whether celestial bodies have souls or not.
K But that the spheres of the elements live, although it is plainly established among the Platonists, concerning these, however, the ancient Peripatetics said nothing; but some more recent ones doubt: because elements seem to have been instituted for the sake of composites, and to be so much viler than composites, as they are closer to matter. But to these things the Platonists will respond, that the entire spheres of the elements were indeed instituted for the sake of the whole world, not for the sake of this or that composite; but the particles of the elements, which are both separated from the integrity of the whole element, and mixed in this or that composite body, are mixed for the sake of such a small body. And although the qualities of these particles are very close to prime matter, yet the integral elements, because they are numbered among the principal members of the world, are very close both to the form of the whole world, and to the universal exemplar and purpose of the supreme artificer; and to the divine influxes of the celestial minds and spheres: which flow into mixed particles and small bodies no otherwise than through the integral elements. And in this way the globes of the elements become worthy receptacles of rational souls.
A Moreover, in fire and air, because of their position and transparency, which are suitable for the heavens, there are some parts, as it were, corresponding directly to the stars: which, ennobled by certain direct influxes, are sufficiently prepared to receive minds. But the coarser parts, whether of water and earth, or of fire and air diffused on earth, do not deserve to have souls segregated to them from their proper globes: because they lose the dignity of the globes, and because of the impact of external bodies, they do not preserve their simplicity and purity. But if they are more diligently mixed with each other, until by a long-lasting tempering of qualities they recover a certain equality similar to the equality of the spheres: first indeed wonderful opera-

...operating souls, they judge to be inherent in them. And if anyone asks about the ascent and descent of elements and compounds: the Platonists will answer that this also happens through the soul. Through the soul, I say, of its sphere: which, just as a magnet [attracts] iron, so it recalls the particles of its sphere to itself. Hence also is the movement of a stone descending from on high, the more it approaches the earth, the faster it becomes; and similarly the movement of a flame ascending, the closer it gets to heaven, the more rapid it becomes. Indeed, since the soul of the sphere draws more vehemently from nearby, the soul of the world also draws to the same [place]. And just as if men, seeing the movement of iron itself, but not seeing the magnet, would think the iron moved of its own accord while it is drawn by the magnet: so now those who do not understand the souls of the spheres believe that any particles move of their own accord.

But indeed, since no mind of an artisan moves its own limbs or instruments as correctly as those particles move in the world: it is necessary that those particles are moved and guided not merely by an inert quality, but also by an artful nature.

Furthermore, the natural motion of the elements is that which does not transgress the boundaries of nature and its natural place, that is, a perpetual circuit in its own place and natural sphere, very similar to its own figure. Fire and air circle, like the moon: which the revolution of comets indicates. Water circles by continually flowing back. If the Earth (as Hegesias wished) were moved, it would be moved in a circle: [Marginal note: A] but as most wish, it remains on its surface, its parts somehow circle the center of the world as they mutually press together around it everywhere with eternal effort.

Ascent or descent, however, is not properly a natural motion, but a sudden restitution to the natural place and motion along a straight line: which, because it is terminated by another, and is always directed along a single path, clearly shows us that the parts of the elements are by no means agitated of their own accord. For otherwise they would also rest spontaneously, and would not always follow the same path; and water could sometimes not cool the nearby air, or not flow down into a precipice. For even if the souls of the spheres always maintain the same tenor, it should not be thought that the "animulae," that is, the proper forces of the elemental parts, if they are inherent in them as movers, would maintain such an order: since our own souls [Marginal note: B] do not.

F [Large initial Q] In what way do the celestial souls move their spheres?
Indeed (as it pleases the Platonists), just as your
soul moves your body through appetite, which appetite
there is also excited by thought: but thought by the fatal
law of that soul. Therefore Plato says in the book 'On the Republic':
G "Fate moves heaven, and by innate desire." Which he seems to have received
from Zoroaster, from whom all the wisdom of the ancient
theologians flowed. For he, when he speaks of heaven, says,
ἀϊδίῳ βουλῇ φέρεται, ἀεὶ τρέχῃ ἔργῳ ἀνάγκης,
that is, it is borne by eternal will, it always runs by the work of necessity.
Which we will clearly understand, if we consider the order of things thus.
There is something which is said to be above all: there is something
which is under all. That which is said to be above all, is God: who
cannot properly be all: because He is the simplest unity
above number. Under all are these individual bodies. It is
therefore necessary that between that which is above all, and that which is under all, there
be something in the middle. But that is the all itself and the whole, and the
sum of all things. But there will be a threefold all, or a threefold whole.
Indeed, the first all depends most closely on the very unity of God.
Therefore, it is necessary for it to be united as far as possible, since
it is made most similar to that unity itself. But something can be
united in three ways: by essence, by point, and by moment. By essence,
namely, that it is one substance, not composed of multiple substances.
By point, that it is not dispersed into multiple parts, through which it would be
forced to be drawn into many points of places. By moment, that whatever
it can ever have, it obtains in the blink of an eye: and is not
varied through various moments of time. Therefore, that all
which is immediately from God, is united to Him in all these ways, being more
similar to Him. This is the angel: who, although he can in a certain way
be called mutable insofar as he depends on another, nevertheless, because he is
created especially close to the infinite state of God, and is converted
into it without an intermediary, he becomes entirely stable. The second follows

But let us briefly conclude this whole discussion with this reasoning: that, in the manner of the ancients, we say that those are to be utterly ridiculed who confess that the impure parts of the elements, from which animals are composed, have life and reason, but deny it to the whole and pure elements; as if the part were better than the whole; and they want the world to lack life and sensation, which nevertheless gives life to plants that are not produced from seed, and gives sensation to animals that are not generated through coitus.
