an earthly body is for descent, when our soul leads its body through downward paths. Indeed, the celestial body is equally and easily disposed to any position around the center, just as elemental matter is to any form: nay, much more so. Therefore, just as efficacy belongs to the soul for moving: so proclivity for being moved belongs to the body. For the body, since it comes from act, is in act, and is directed to act: therefore it has the nature that it is always exercised through its forms. But since it has both divisible substance and quality: it is compelled to do or suffer whatever it does or suffers according to a divisible mode, that is, to act and suffer according to motion. Moreover, the motion of celestial bodies and its variety contribute to generation and to the diversity of things to be generated. For heaven adorns with various figures: and transmits celestial powers more vehemently into the elements. It moves the elements: and compels them to be mixed together in many ways: and everywhere equally illuminates and fosters their globe with a certain alternation. Furthermore, the very matter of the world can neither have all figures in heaven at once, nor all forms under heaven at once (since many are contrary to each other) yet everywhere it desires all, as perfections of its nature. Hence it is made prone to perpetual motion: so that what it cannot achieve in a state of rest, it may at least in some way achieve by succession. But why do the spheres rotate especially in a circle? Although I have just now indicated this: let us nevertheless begin more deeply. God is one circle: because He is from Himself, like a circle, and into Himself, inasmuch as He has no beginning or end outside Himself: but beginning in Himself, He ends in Himself. An angel is a twofold circle: both because it returns to whence it flowed, while it understands and loves its author: and because it considers itself. The soul is a threefold circuit: because it looks back to God: because it considers itself: because it descends from the causes of things to effects, and again ascends from effects to causes. If these three movers of heaven revolve: what prevents heaven also from being carried around in a circuit? And since heaven imitates the supernal causes in its figure and substance, why should it not also imitate them in motion and operation? Heaven is subjected to a mobile soul: thence it begins to be moved. As soon as one part of heaven began to be moved, because of its continuity it draws another with it, and pushes another: and they necessarily reflect each other in

everything: which, because it depends on the One in a certain secondary intention, now loses one mode of unity, but retains two: one indeed remains in essence and as a point, but it becomes varied in moments. [Marginal note: H] Such is the soul. The third 'everything' is the matter of the world, which is one substance; but it is not only varied in moments, like the soul, but also diffused through points of places. But why, in this descent, is time found before place? Then because [Marginal note: I] time is the companion of some spiritual action; place is the companion of the body; and therefore time approaches spirit and efficacy more closely than place. Then because one must descend gradually from unity into multitude. It is certainly necessary for the soul itself to be in some way all things, concerning which Zoroaster says:
καὶ ψυχὴ κόσμου πολλὰ πληρώματα κόλπων,
that is, it comprehends many fullnesses of worldly bosoms. For if it is intermediate between the sublime and the lowest, it necessarily contains within itself the gifts and images of those sublime things, but the powers and exemplars of the lowest things. But in that part by which it communicates with [Marginal note: L] the angelic mind, it becomes similar to an angel; in another part, dissimilar. Therefore, the souls of the spheres have all ideas simultaneously in their minds, in habit and in act. In their lowest potencies, moving bodies, they again have all the seeds of things to be generated, in possession and in habit simultaneously, not in act. The middle part of them, namely reason, follows the mind; because their bodies, being most perfect and almost lacking nothing, are ruled by fate only by the lowest part of the soul. Therefore, the middle part of the celestial souls, which by its nature is mobile, because it is at leisure from bodily work, absorbed by the mind, becomes stable.
But in us, because of the indigence of our body, the middle part also moves like the lowest: too difficult and laborious

...that the whole soul may everywhere enjoy all its parts. It flies most swiftly, so that, as far as possible, it may be whole everywhere at once, wherever the whole soul is at once.
[¶] And because it nowhere finds the soul standing still: it itself also nowhere rests. And just as the soul constantly revolves around God as if a center: so the body, drawn by it, always revolves around the soul as if a center.
[☞] But heaven stands on the same axis: because the soul also, due to its participation in the mind, partakes of some rest. All rational souls do this in their bodies. All bodies do this for their souls: whether we speak of the souls of spheres and stars, or of demons and humans. Finally, let us conclude this discussion about the motion of heaven with this statement.
[B] Neither the mobile body of heaven, nor the mover who is moved by the motion of heaven, is the principal beginning and end of this motion: lest in such a motion, labor and transgression should occur. For motion is always made and governed towards the stable and around the stable.

Every rational soul is immortal. First reason:
because it moves by itself: and in a circle.
[A] Chapter I.

[Decorative initial H] We place all souls in the third order of essence: and for this common reason we wish them to be immortal, because they are moved primarily: and because they are moved primarily, they are moved in a circle. Therefore, because they are moved primarily, they are moved always. For there is perpetual motion where there is primary motion. For if the source of motion should dry up, nothing

--- Page 195 ---
That journey is primarily outlined by common thought. From this universal purpose, no specific step is taken, unless a particular thought intervenes, designating the first step. Therefore, the lantern first shows the step: imagination immediately thinks of this very step: appetite chooses this: feet perform this. This being done, the lantern shows the second step: soon Euclides thinks of it: desires it: performs it. Similarly, the third and others. They believe it happens in the same way for the soul of the sphere, where its mind and reason commonly determine to form so many figures in the sky, and forms in matter through the motion of the heavens, because it sees ideas and concepts being formed in the angel by God's own power: so that it itself, to the best of its ability, may produce a worldly work such as God makes angelic, and thus imitate the first artificer: yet it does not begin to move the heavens, or to operate anything, unless the motive power (which is its lowest part), as if a lantern, brings forth one kind of its seeds before others, and as if offers it to the eyes. As soon as the power of some kind of seeds prevails over the other seeds, imagination itself, which is annexed to this lowest power, thinks of it: and desires the same: explains the same in the sky, forms it in the elements: sows it in the sky, gives birth to it in the elements. In the same way, it happens through a series of succession in other seeds. In this series of succession consists the law of fate: in that thought, desire. Thus the heavens are moved by fate and innate desire, in almost the same way as in us spirits and humors are vibrated and formed by vehement thought and affection. Nor should you think that such new effects in the world, such various figures in the sky, are unfolded at every moment, unless through new and various affections of those souls. For from a cause which is entirely stable, the work is also stable. Nor should it be thought that the soul of the heavens is wearied by moving, if our own is not wearied. For movers who are not extended with the movable object are not accustomed to being wearied: namely, if they are close to the infinite goal of all motions. Moreover, as unfit as the lowest and earthly body is for motion, so agile is the sublime body. But if even a light breeze stirs dust, and wind enclosed in the bowels of the earth shakes mountains: will you wonder that sublime souls turn the most subtle bodies with the slightest nod? Especially since they move around their natural axis and in their own orbit: and they themselves are more conducive to such motion by natural instinct.

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

And thus the superior argument demonstrated that the soul is immortal through its motion. The same is also demonstrated through the state of the soul. When we name the soul, we mean the genus of rational souls. For we do not properly call irrational lives souls, but idols and semblances of souls. If that third essence (of which we have said so much), although it is moved by operation, nevertheless remains by substance: it follows that the soul, which is the same as that essence, is not changed by substance. But that which is such: never ceases to be.

Third reason: because it adheres to divine things. Chapter 3.

F For if two things located in the lowest degree of nature, namely matter and quantity, are passive: and two others in the highest are active, God and the angel: how will the soul and quality, which occupy the middle region between passive and active things, behave? Thus, indeed, both become partakers of passion. But quality, because it inheres in suffering things, entirely receives passion through operation and essence: the soul, however, which is further removed, even if it perceives some corporeal passion in its faculty of operating, is nevertheless free from passion in its essence. And just as the passive body, composed of matter and quantity, renders the quality inhering in it subject to corruption, so God and the active angel, by their divinity, make the soul, which is close to them and separated from the body, immortal.

Fourth reason: because it dominates matter. Chapter 4.

G But its immortality appears most especially in this, that the primary matter of things itself, which is moved and formed by the soul, must be perpetual. Art imitates nature. Art performs its works in this order: namely, it impresses various forms upon some subject matter, none of which matter possesses as its own. For clay has no proper form of any vessel, but in turn receives various forms from the potter: and when vessels are broken, the clay remains, from which others can be repaired. Therefore, nature itself, the artisan of things, has some subject [matter] to itself

revolution. The heaven cannot stand still, since its soul knows not how to rest, nor yet does it wish to leave its natural place. Thus it happens that it revolves around the same (point), and in the same (place) the heaven is always moving; since the earth (which is furthest from it) is always immobile. That which moves always, necessarily returns to the same (point). For no space of corporeal things is infinite.

F
Moreover, Plato says in the book *On the Republic*: To divine things alone, of all things, belongs a state entirely free from change. But the world, because it is a body, and now degenerates from the dignity of divine things, therefore cannot be entirely unchangeable. But since it is closest to divine things, it was fitting for it to be moved by circular motion; which, since it revolves in the same (place), around the same (point), according to the same (principles), with a similar and continuous perpetuation, departs as little as possible from local stability. So says he. Add to this that just as among all kinds of motion, only local motion, because it is, as it were, extrinsic, is not compelled to change the substance and natural quality of its subject: so circular motion among local motions, because it alone does not change place, seems able to be called, as it were, "not motion."

H
If someone wished the heaven to stand still, let him fix the heaven of Saturn on its hinge whenever he pleases. Then one semicircle of that sphere (would be over us, and) the other over the heads of the Antipodes. But since all parts of this sphere are most similar to each other without any natural discrepancy, there is no reason why one part should be more here, and another there. Therefore the lower semicircle, because it equally agrees with our place as with the region of the Antipodes, will strive to be here, just as there; and the upper semicircle, because of the same agreement with that place, would contend to be there, just as it was here. From this striving, one part will push the other, while each part, because of equal agreement, will wish to be equally everywhere.

Indeed, the concave surface of the eighth sphere is the natural place of Saturn's sphere. There the convex (surface) of Saturn's sphere touches the concave (surface) of the eighth. Every particle of this sphere, because it equally agrees with every particle of the eighth, strives to touch all particles of that (eighth sphere). If it were to rest, individual (particles) would touch individual (particles), not each (particle) all (particles). But by moving, it almost achieves what it could not achieve by resting: so great is the eagerness of this sphere for that one. lower beings, because they do not have absolute being at all, but some being, and being of this or that kind: therefore they do not have the power to completely remove being, but rather being in this way or that. It would also follow that the sun would generate that new air from nothing, if it had consumed the entire portion of the previous water into nothing.
B Natural agents, however, cannot make something from nothing. For it is easier to make something from any existing thing than from nothing. They cannot, however, generate any kind of thing from any kind of seed: never pears from wheat: figs from millet: an eagle from human seed. Much less will they be able to generate something from nothing. By this reasoning, it is shown that the sun could not have turned that portion of water drawn from the sea into nothing. Therefore, something of the prior nature remains in it. What is that? That water was certainly cold and humid. Coldness has departed: humidity remains: as it pleases the Platonists: which is common to air and water.
C If humidity remains: some matter subject to humidity also remains. For humidity is not a form separated from bodies. Therefore, the matter which previously lay hidden beneath the cold of water: now lies hidden under the heat of air. When, however, air becomes fire, it also loses humidity and receives dryness. Matter of this kind, which, attenuated by rarefaction, ascends into the form of fire, in turn descends by density: swells in air, afterwards condenses into water, finally becomes heavy in earth. You see that one matter in turn assumes all forms, while it both ascends by rarefaction: and descends by density. Which is therefore one, partly because one suffices for one world: partly because, being formless, it has nothing by which it can be distinguished into multiple parts within itself. If the universe is defined into one formable thing, it is consistent
D that it also begins from one former, and that the whole is subject to it. But of this we have spoken elsewhere, and will speak. This matter, however, is never corrupted for this reason, because it is the foundation of all corporeal nature, by the destruction of which the entire machinery of the world would collapse. Nor is it ever dissolved into parts: because it is not constituted of parts by its own nature. For parts are made through quantity: but matter precedes quantity. For it is the subject of quantity and quality. And the subject must always precede that thing which lies in it. Nor will it be destroyed by the accession of any contrary quality. For indeed, no quality is contrary to it: because it equally receives all by na-

will be moved further in nature. Likewise, that which is moved primarily provides to itself internal and external motion. Internal motion is life. Therefore, it supplies life to itself. And because it never abandons itself: since in every nature there is an everlasting love of itself, it never ceases to live. For if that which is moved by another is moved as long as it adheres to the mover: much more so that which is moved by itself, because it is the same as the mover, never abandoned by the mover, never ceases to be moved. Furthermore, if it is imagined to perish at some time: either it will cease to exist before it ceases to be moved: or the opposite: or at the same time. The first is not granted: because motion cannot remain separate from essence. Not the second: because spontaneous motion is a constant companion of that which initiates motion for itself. Not the third: because a destructive change cannot ever break forth from within it, from which vital and life-giving motion arises. But neither will it happen externally. For the source of motion is not moved from elsewhere. This is indeed the property of the third essence: in which, since all rational souls exist by a certain common definition, the same property also belongs to all of them. They are also immortal for this reason, because by the nature of the third essence and the primary motion, they are moved in a circle. [Marginal note: D] For if they are moved in a circle, they never cease. For a circuit does not pour out its strength, but gathers each of its own into itself, and when it is thought to fail, it renews itself: so that for the present they may pass over that reason of Pythagoras which shows that there is no beginning or end in a sphere. And therefore, that which is moved in a sphere neither ever began to be moved, nor ceases. But that rational souls are certain spiritual spheres, and make a spiritual circuit in themselves: since the bodies themselves, which are their shadows, have such a figure and motion. So that visible spheres and circuits are shadows of invisible spheres and circuits: and if the shadows are perpetual, much more will those substances be perpetual, which perform the act of motion without end, through a power lacking end. Nor is there anything contrary to them by which they might be destroyed: just as to their motion, which is a circuit, there is no contrary motion.

Fifth reason, because it is free from matter. Chapter 5.

I [Large decorative initial Q] our causes of natural things are enumerated by physicists:
efficient, final, material, formal. The efficient cause of man
is universal nature, and man: the final cause, human happi-
ness: the material cause, the body: the formal cause is the soul. Whenever something is said to
exist *per se*, it is understood to exist without a cause. Whenever to exist *per aliud*,
to exist by a cause. Only God exists *per se* in such a way that He is by no
cause, wherefore He is entirely *per se*: because He excludes all four
kinds of causes from Himself. A natural body is entirely *per aliud*:
because it includes all four simultaneously. Below God, nothing can exist
that lacks an efficient cause and a final cause. Indeed, God is the one
effector of all things, and the end: therefore nothing besides God will be
found that can be said to exist *per se* in such a way that it does not have an efficient
cause and a final cause. Not all things under God, however, ought to exist
*per aliud* in such a way that they are *entirely* *per aliud*. Namely, these two,
"entirely *per se*", and "entirely *per aliud*", are separated from each other by the

Thus, a universal matter, an indifferent receptacle for any forms whatsoever, is subject to the universal artificer and nature. And now it receives this [form] from natural force, now that [form]: nor does it have any proper [form] by its own nature. For they would not be the lowest, if they had any perfection and a natural faculty of acting for themselves from their own proper form: nor would it be suitable for another form repugnant to its own form. For if coldness were proper and natural to matter, in what way would it receive heat? And if humidity, how dryness? Observe the mutual change of the elements, if you wish to find this hidden matter. For when we perceive where previously there was the species of earth, there afterwards the species of water appears: we cannot say that the form of water, which recently arrived, is received into the form of earth. For these are in a certain way opposed to each other: since earth contains dryness, and water humidity. Therefore the form of earth does not receive the form of water: but with the watery species approaching, it departs into chaos. But the form of water cannot exist without a subject: nor did a new subject arrive in the generation of water. Therefore the same matter which had been subject to the earthly form, now undergoes the form of water. And this is the argumentation which Timaeus the Pythagorean uses. Likewise, when the sun, striking the sea with its rays, thins the water into vapors, and generates air from water [A]: it certainly drew off some small portion of the watery body from the element of water. We ask therefore whether it first reduced that small portion of water to nothing, and afterwards generated air: or preserved something of the water? If it were to reduce the water entirely to nothing, the intention of nature would be towards evil: (which however is always towards good, since it is ruled by the supreme goodness of God). And being itself, which is the peculiar gift of the eternal God, would sometimes be withdrawn from things by subsequent causes after God: which cannot happen: since God always preserves what he once gave, by his own influx: against which the violence of no agent is opposed. The third is: because when it is moved primarily, it is necessarily moved by itself freely in a circuit. If it is moved by itself, it certainly operates by itself. If this is so, it also operates by itself, bound to no bodies. If it is moved freely, it is not bound to matter. If it revolves in a circuit, it returns to itself, abandoning matter. The fourth is: because if it dominates matter by moving it primarily, and in forming it, it is not mixed with matter. Through these things it appears that essence which is the seat of the soul, which Plato also calls the "father of souls" in Timaeus, has no origin from bodies, and also is not constituted from parts of quantity. For such parts are inherent only in bodies and qualities, but not in forms separated from the body. Therefore, the soul will not be dissipated for this reason, that it might be dissolved into some parts. Indeed, it has no spatial separation of parts, because it is not divided in the body, nor will it ever fail because it might be abandoned by some support of its own. For that essence, which by its nature is the mistress of bodies, needs no bodily foundation; nor will it perish by this, that contrary and mutually warring forces of elements sometimes disturb it, for these indeed fight in matter. But the soul is from God above matter, so that the storm of elements and the strife of contending qualities may not touch it. Never again will it be defiled by this, that it sometimes receives some alien and adverse quality to its nature, which inflicts a harmful passion upon it. For the primary subject exposed to passion is matter, through which both quantity immersed in it and quality adhering to quantity are exposed to passion. Therefore, that essence which is separated from matter, that is, potentially separable, has no power in itself by which it might receive anything alien and hostile, from which it might be subjected to passion.

The sixth reason: because it is indivisible. Chapter 6.

Furthermore, since it is indivisible, it does not receive divisible and corporeal qualities. For that which is divisible does not touch the indivisible. For if the indivisible is said to be touched by that which is divisible, we will ask whether this divisible thing touches that indivisible thing by some point of itself, or by some divisible part of itself. Nor does matter need some other seat, which, if perhaps removed, it might fall into the abyss. For it itself is the first support of all things: and if any violence should destroy it: it will either reduce it to nothing, or transform it into something else. The first cannot happen. For whatever acts, from a natural appetite for perfection, is led to act for its own propagation, so that it may generate something else similar to itself, as far as possible: which is clear in elements, plants, and animals: where it appears that natural appetite is directed towards the good, namely towards life, towards being, and similar things, not towards their contraries: [E] because it is implanted in all subsequent things by the highest good (as we have said). For from where they are, thence they are moved, and thither all things are carried. Therefore, every appetite and operation of all things, originating from the good, tends and reflects back to the good. Thus, both it (matter) would be lost, and nothing new would be generated. For that which must be made anew: if it needs matter, it will no longer be able to be made, with that (matter) removed. If it does not need matter, that which is free from matter is free from it, and it transcends it, being created by its author separately from matter. Therefore, while its author acts upon it, since he fabricates it far removed from matter, he inflicts no violence upon it from this, nor does he move matter in any way in its generation, as the work to be completed does not need it. Therefore, that which generates a new thing: whatever it may be, whether it needs matter, or is alien from it, does not reduce matter to nothing. Or perhaps it will transform it into something else, so that one part of matter remains, but another part perishes? By no means. For it (matter) is simple: because it is composed neither of matter and form, since it is the first and formless potentiality: nor does it require a certain aggregation of parts for its existence: since by its natural origin it precedes the dimensions of quantity. Furthermore, if it (matter) is so changed, that after the change is completed, something remains: what will that be? Matter? If it is matter, it does not yet seem to have been transformed into something else, since it remains. If quantity, or quality: that is indeed absurd: because these cannot remain without it (matter). THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

We call one thing essence, another being. Indeed, we say that essence is the reason of a thing, which is comprehended by definition. But being is the act of the essence itself, and a certain presence of it in the nature of things. Take an example concerning a Comet: the essence of a Comet is this reason and definition of it, namely, dry vapor ignited by fire in the highest air, and circling through the air in order. This definition, indeed, is true today, even if no Comet shines forth anywhere today. But the being of such a comet is said to be something such that, namely, that nature of the comet, which is daily designated by definition, now shines somewhere. This being does not occur without a certain place and time. For that essence does not become present otherwise than here or there, at this hour or that. Therefore, the being of natural things requires a certain place and time; essence does not need these. For that reason of a comet is true, even if for the present no comet is hot anywhere. Indeed, if that definition included a certain time and place, for example, today here, or tomorrow there: then at the same hour, and in the same region of the air, in which one comet exists, all comets would exist simultaneously. For in each individual comet resides the common essence and the same reason of a comet. But if this reason were restricted to a certain place and time: all comets would be restricted to the same limits of place and time: just as rational power, when it is included in the definition of man, applies to individual men. Essence and being of natural things therefore differ from each other in this, that being is restricted to a certain place and time.

nature, it is necessary that the work made most immediately by Him, because it is drawn immediately from the nature of the agent, appear as similar as possible to Him. Therefore, that which is made most immediately and with a principal purpose (if I may so speak) by God, ought not to turn out most dissimilar to God. There are therefore between God and body some things which are not said to exist entirely through another. Such appears to be quality: which does not exist through four causes, like body, but depends solely on three causes. Body has matter and form as its causes, and also an efficient cause and a final cause: quality does not have form as a formal cause. For it is itself a certain form. No form, insofar as it is form, is formed: yet quality is brought about by something: and is directed by an agent towards a certain end: and also depends on matter. Just as indeed from the pregnant womb of matter such a fetus is brought forth into light, and with it is extended and divided, for this reason quality surpasses body by one degree, which is said to exist in some way through itself, since it is not formed by another. But why does not also a third essence, which is at least one degree more sublime than quality, surpass quality, just as quality surpasses body by one degree? It certainly does surpass it. But how? Not because essence lacks an efficient cause or a final cause: since this is proper to God alone. Nor this either, that this essence does not have form as its cause. For quality possesses the same. It remains only that it surpasses it in this, that it does not depend on matter: which is by no means proper to quality. Thus it is necessary to proceed gradually from four opposites into four opposites through three and two (stages): so that just as we ascend from the four causes of body to the three causes of quality: so we may ascend from the three causes of quality to the two causes of the third essence. For this reason this essence will have only an efficient and a final cause: but it will not have form and matter. Finally, an angel surpasses this essence by one (degree): because an angel neither depends on matter, nor is inclined towards matter: since it is occupied most immediately by God. [Marginal note: A] Although the third essence does not depend on matter, yet, being made more distant from God, and close to matter, it is in a certain way inclined towards it: on account of which inclination it is called soul. And although it is inclined, it does not however depend on it: which we have demonstrated with many reasons. The first is that which we have assigned. The second is: because if this essence were immersed in matter, it would never emerge into divine things, which are most remote from matter: and thus it would not be a competent knot of the world: because it would not connect the lowest with the highest.

This part of air is called 'the Equal'; that, 'man'. Similarly in nature, matter is not that by which Plato is a man, or a fig is a tree. For indeed the same primary matter of the world is common to men, beasts, and trees. And for many centuries before Plato, and many also after Plato, that same matter exists, but Plato by no means. Therefore, Plato does not have a human species because of matter, but because of such a bodily constitution and a soul, which are called forms. Simi- [C] larly concerning others it must be judged, and in summary it must be concluded that anything whatsoever has its own proper being, nature, and species, differing from others, from its form. Wherefore, whatever ceases to be, loses its very being, from the fact that it is separated from its proper form, just as it had begun to be before when it had obtained its proper form. Therefore, a thing composed of matter and form, for example, fire composed of its mass and natural heat, perishes when it is separated from its form. But the cold of water or earth can insinuate itself into the matter of fire, and from there expel the natural heat, the form of fire; which having been expelled, it ceases [D] to be fire. Thus, that fire composed of matter and a certain such heat loses its being when it loses its heat—its, I say, substantial form with its properties—which we now (because it does not have an obvious name) call "heat" for the sake of discussion. But heat itself, when it loses its being, since it is a form, and being is from form... when, namely, it is expelled from that matter. For in composite things, being is naturally attributed to the whole, not to the parts. Namely, the being of fire itself properly belongs to the composite, not to matter alone, nor to heat. For when heat, in the generation of fire, was drawn out by a natural agent from the seed of matter, it was on this condition, extended through all the matter of fire, that it would depend entirely on it; and that heat would not have its own proper being, but through the common being of the whole fire, heat also would be said to be. But that common being then ceases when those two parts are separated from each other. When the common being ceases, the form also perishes which thrived through the common being. But matter does not perish, because it suddenly receives another form, through which it exists; so that while it loses a certain heat, it loses its fiery being. While [E] it receives a certain coldness or humidity, it begins to be earthy or watery. Conclude, a composite thing, such as fire

It is not touched, I say, by a straight line, nor even by a reflected one. Not by a straight line: because the soul itself does not receive a quality occurring from the opposite direction. Not by a reflected line: because since it is exempt from the body, with qualities raging in the body, it is not carried away by their impulse and fury: and therefore it is corrupted by none.

Or perhaps will it be corrupted by some indivisible [quality], which it might easily receive? By no means. For the reception of indivisible qualities perfects that which receives, it does not corrupt. Which is evident through those indivisible images of things, which are received by water, mirrors, the soul, both through sense and through reason.

Properly, however, this thing does not act upon that by any other reason, [F] except that this may present its form to that. Indeed, all things are led to operate for the propagation of their nature: but no corporeal thing can or strives to generate its corporeal form in the essence of the soul: which is so segregated from matter, [G] that corporeal forms have no ingress into it. But do God or an angel introduce a new form into the soul, by which the soul might be disturbed? By no means: because if they create some form subsisting by itself, they create it separately from the soul: therefore the soul is not disturbed by its creation. But if they infuse some power into the soul, a power of this kind is beneficial: since it comes from the best causes, the preservers of the soul itself: therefore the soul does not perish through it, but is preserved.

...from the thing by which it might be destroyed. Rightly it cannot receive anything at all harmful, since it lacks matter: which is said to be the primary and proper receptacle of such affections. Indeed, if this essence is its own form, nothing will ever intervene between it and its form. For if any medium were ever to fall between it and its form, that [medium] would certainly become closer to the form itself than its own essence. But the essence itself is its very form. Thus something would become closer to it than it is to itself: which is the most absurd of all. Therefore, nothing inserts itself as a medium between it and its form. If this is so, it is not separated from its form by any intervening element. But neither is it spontaneously separated from itself: wherefore it departs in no way from itself and its form. Nor does it depart from the law of its creator. For it was created by that law, that it should subsist in itself. But it always remains so. For from that state it is cast down by no one: Not by itself: for every thing preserves its species and dignity for itself to the best of its ability. Not by superior causes: because those [causes] preserve it by the same law by which they produced it. Not by inferior ones. For the superior is not overcome by the inferior. Therefore the soul, because it is pure form, and therefore departs neither from its own form nor from the law of its creator, undoubtedly remains immortal.

Ninth reason, because being belongs to it intrinsically.
Chapter 9.

What belongs to something intrinsically is never separated from it: Roundness is inherent in a circle by its very nature: and therefore no circle ever exists without roundness. But sometimes roundness is inherent in wood: not because it is wood (for otherwise all wood would be round), but because it receives a circular shape from an artisan, which roundness accompanies: therefore it is then compelled to acquire roundness. Wood sometimes ceases to be round, as soon as it ceases to be circular: then it remains wood, but not round. But a circular shape is so necessarily round, that if it ceases to be round, it also ceases to be circular. Similarly, heat belongs to fire intrinsically, moisture to water, light to the sun. No differently does being belong to form intrinsically. For whatever is something in some species: that certainly

and produces them to be inherent, others it determines to such a being that they exist in a body: whence the being of such an essence or such a form is contracted by the agent to corporeal conditions. When being is contracted to a body, the essence is also constrained by the same limits. The conditions of natural bodies are that they fill a place, and are moved in time. Therefore that form which by [Marginal note: A] itself would have been beyond a certain time and place, now enters its own time and place. Because it enters time, therefore it gradually begins, changes, and ends. Because it enters place: therefore while the body itself in which it lies daily takes on contrary qualities, that [form] too is disturbed by such a storm of qualities: and thus becomes mortal. Such are the forms and qualities of bodies. But that author produces other essences of forms into being in such a way that they do not derive their very being from some other thing or matter, but contain it within themselves. Such are all forms alien to the commerce of matter. For they have their being in themselves, not in matter. Whatever is received from something: it is accustomed to be received according to the capacity of that which receives, and to be drawn to its property. But every essence is immortal in itself. Therefore the being which is received from the essence itself: since it is received by an immortal thing in an immortal manner, it is made immortal. Therefore a form which is separated from the society of matter, from every side, that is, both according to its being and according to its essence, is immortal. Such is the third essence, the source of rational souls.

**G**eneration and corruption are opposed to each other in such a way that they tend towards contradictories: and generation becomes a certain path [Marginal note: B] to being, corruption becomes a path to non-being. But each thing tends to being from the fact that it receives a certain form: and to non-being from the fact that it is forced to lose its form. In the arts, no work is such or such because of matter, but because of form. A bronze horse or man is not called such because of the matter of bronze, since bronze is equally prepared to receive the figures of all living things: but because of a certain form and likeness of a horse or man perfected by the artist.

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

The soul is, it has this, that being belongs to it of itself: of itself, I say, by its own nature. The nature assigned to it is to adhere to itself. Therefore its being follows it inasmuch as it adheres to itself: that is, its existence follows it, not at all sprouting from a subject. And as often as you say, being follows it of itself, so often you say: being follows it adhering to itself. But nothing departs from itself. For what intervenes between itself and itself, that might separate it from itself? If inasmuch as it adheres to itself, so far it is: because it always adheres, it is and always is. Such indeed is the form of the soul. Therefore it is immortal.

But someone can object to this reasoning thus: that just as fire, which is hot of itself, is always hot while it exists: yet it does not always exist, from which it also is not absolutely always hot: so also the essence of the soul, because it is properly and truly a form subsisting in itself, therefore it is of itself: and because it is of itself, therefore it is and always is: namely, while it exists. Yet it does not always exist. Therefore it is not always. This objection is judged ridiculous for two reasons.

First, it contradicts itself when it is constructed thus. That form is of itself: therefore it always is, namely, while it exists: but it is not always. For there are four propositions here: of which that second one which says, "Therefore it always is," contradicts this latter one which infers, "But it is not always."

Secondly, an objection of this kind abounds in superfluities, when it adds: "namely, while it exists." Indeed, this "while it exists" cannot be said to be other than that first [instance] where it is said, "it always is." For thus there would be in the same thing a double "is," and a double "being": nor would there exist one thing, but two. Hence it follows that that "is" which is posited when "namely, while it exists" is added, is the same as that which was already posited when it was said before, "It always is." What are the same: are to be treated by the same reasoning. Therefore if the first "is" is uttered absolutely, so the second "is" ought to be uttered absolutely, without that phrase, "namely, while it exists." Therefore it must be said: "It is, it always is," and not added, "namely, while it exists." Or if you add to that first "is," that afterwards, "namely, while it exists": add also to this second "is," which follows after: "namely, while it exists." Again that "namely, while it exists," and to this third "is": again, "

Those things which are through another are not stable; for left to themselves, they vanish into nothing. Therefore, in themselves they are nothing, whatever they exist as through another. even if it should lose its being, its essence nevertheless remains. This is also evident from the fact that the nobler a thing is, the nobler matter it possesses, and the nobler form. Souls are very much superior to bodies. Therefore, beneath their being, as beneath their form and actuality, there lies a certain matter and potentiality (if any such lies there) which is more excellent than that which lies beneath the form and being of any body whatsoever. But that which holds the place of prime matter and potentiality in souls is their very essence. Therefore, their essence is more eminent than the matter of bodies. The matter of bodies is incorruptible; what wonder then if that (essence) can be incorruptible? From which it follows that if the soul is ever imagined to lose its being, its essence and substance necessarily still remain. If this remains, it certainly exists. If it still exists, its being is not yet lost. Thus, if the soul is said to be corrupted, it necessarily survives even after corruption. Indeed, it even lives. For the being of the soul is nothing other than to live.

But lest anyone say that the very being of the soul is resolved into its essence, and that the essence then ceases to exist because it is without act, even if potentiality perhaps remains somewhere: one must remember that that essence cannot be reduced to matter or the potentiality of matter, because it does not consist of matter as a part of itself, nor does it spring from the potentiality of matter. Again, it cannot be resolved into the potentiality of any efficient cause, unless perhaps into the power of God, who alone created the soul. But the soul does not die because it is resolved into its primal life. It would die, however, if, reduced into God, it ceased to be a soul. But just as a wax figure impressed by a seal, when it is perfectly conformed to the seal, is not destroyed but is restored to its proper form: so the essence of the soul, if ever the Idea by which God had disposed it in a certain species of being is applied to it, is confirmed in its pristine being. For the subsequent act is greatly strengthened by the first. For how can God be the terminus towards which corruption tends, since He is the efficient terminus, from whom and by whom all creation and generation are derived? Or in what way can God, who is pure act, concur in the composition of the soul itself when the soul is born? Thus, just as from the potentiality of matter and an added act of potentiality, a corporeal form comes into being, and finally the act of the form is resolved into that potentiality: so from a certain potentiality of God and a certain added act, the soul comes into being, which finally resolves into the potentiality of God as if into matter.

Furthermore, if being and being hot were exactly the same thing: when you construct the argument, "Fire, because it is hot by its own nature, is always hot," you would immediately add, "To be hot and to be are the same: therefore it is, and always." But now you cannot conclude in that way: because to be and to be hot are not the same: otherwise, whatever things exist, would be hot: and whatever ceases to be hot, would cease to be, which does not happen. **Eleventh reason: because it is not composed of any
potentiality into which it can be resolved.**
Cap. II.

Just as generation occurs through the conjunction of form with matter, so corruption occurs through the separation of form from matter.
Where there is no conjunction of these things, no separation occurs.
But such a composition is not in the soul. But let us pursue this argument more broadly. In the corruption of any thing, the very act of the thing is lost; but after that, something remains which was subject to that act, as it were, some receptive potentiality, lest corruption occur into nothingness, just as generation does not occur from nothing. A thing indeed composed of form and matter is resolved into matter. That form also, which had been drawn out from the spark of matter, is reduced back into the spark of matter. But in the soul, its act is its very being.
But its essence and substance is that very potentiality which underlies the act of being. For in absolute forms, there is almost no other composition than from essence and being, or a similar one.
Essence holds the place of matter and potentiality, but being (holds) the place of form and act. If the soul is corrupted, its being is entirely lost. But what about its essence also? By no means. For no thing is resolved into nothing; because a thing which is so simple that it cannot otherwise be resolved than into nothingness, is also such that it was made by God through creation from nothing. But that which is such is subject only to its author, God. But God's vital and beneficent influx destroys nothing. Therefore, if the soul is destroyed:

...God's vital and beneficent influx destroys nothing. Therefore, if the soul is destroyed: is another foundation permitted? To be and not to be are contradictories. It remains that that potency is founded in God alone, the author of the soul. Therefore, the potency of being, by which the soul is produced into being, is God Himself alone, immortal and stable. But to potency, according to congruence, corresponds act. Therefore, the act corresponding to that divine potency is stable by essence. Such an act is the soul. And just as in God there is the same potency by which God can make the soul, and the soul can be made: so in the soul there is the same act, that is, the same striving, by which the soul subsists in its own nature: and God establishes it in that nature. Whence it happens that God establishes the soul in the nature of the soul with no less desire than the soul subsists in the same. Since it is subject to God alone: if it is to be destroyed by anyone, it must be destroyed by Him. But by Him it cannot be. For how can the efficient and preservative cause of something also be its destroyer? Or in what way is Good itself harmful to anyone? Or is the first life and infinite life the origin of death for anyone? Someone might say, God does not destroy the soul by inflicting some new force, but by taking away the force previously granted to it, that is, by withdrawing His influx by which the soul had lived: just as one who creates his image in a mirror by looking, ceases to produce the image by withdrawing his face. But this cannot happen there: as we showed a little earlier. Again, if God now infuses life into the soul, and afterwards does not infuse it: a change arises there from infusing to not infusing. I ask, does the soul cease to draw life: or does God cease to infuse it? The soul does not cease to draw: for the infusion of life occurs into the essence of the soul: because life is the first act of the essence, when it first received being. The essence of the soul is immobile: because it depends without intermediary on a stable God: because it is perfected by standing and resting. It is disturbed by motion. It attains stable things. It rules over perishable things. It stops mobile things. It gathers scattered things. It reconciles opposites. Nor is there in it that potency to be and not to be at the same time, such as is in bodies: which is the beginning of all change. Therefore, the essence of the soul never ceases to receive the act of life: God does not cease to infuse the same. For God signified that He would cease to infuse His power only to those things in which He implanted from the origin that inclination towards non-being. Furthermore, God, the institutor of nature, never subtracts anything from a thing that is of that thing's

Someone will assert that the essence of the soul is resolved neither into matter
nor into God, but that it immediately receives itself into itself, the [Marginal note: K]

corporeal act, so neither can spiritual [matter exist] separately from a spiritual [act].
Therefore, the essence which is the matter of spiritual things, and is compared to
spiritual being as a kind of act, is never separated from being: from spiritual
being, I say. Unless perhaps someone says that the essence of the soul,
while it sheds one being, puts on another, and that this essence varies in
spiritual being with such changes as matter varies in its forms.
That is indeed absurd to say: first, because the essence of spiritual things
is more stable than the matter of corporeal things; then, because the
essence of the soul, since it is the soul's own proper nature, does not
equally regard one being and another entirely, but only animal being,
namely according to a certain species of soul. Common matter can indeed
exist without this act or that; [Marginal note: L]
but proper matter can by no means exist without its proper act.
Therefore, the essence of the soul which is in such a species of souls
will never receive the act of another species of souls, nor will the
essence again migrate within the same species from this soul to that,
lest it be as mobile as the matter of corporeal things. Indeed, if the
matter of the heavens is always content with the same form, as very
many believe, what wonder is it that the spiritual matter of the mind is always
content with the same act of being? That essence is life; this being is
living. Therefore, it always lives.

Twelfth reason: because it does not have within itself the power to not be.
Chapter 12.

namely, in the form itself, whole and perfect. Indeed, each thing exists
through the integrity of its form. Therefore, the proper subject of its
being there is its form and essence. But where will there be the power to not be,

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

that which is one and common to all, [has] one cause, and [that cause is] common to all. The common cause for all is God himself, one. Therefore, God is truly the cause of being; but of being this or that, in this way or that, there are other causes besides God. Thus, your very existence you have from God alone; your being human, you have also from a human; your being warm, from fire. God will give being to [His] works; other causes, diverse among themselves, [will give] diverse modes of being, and these indeed by the power of God. Indeed, that being which follows after nothingness is called absolute being. For immediately after nothingness follows being simply. After being simply, follows being this or that: or being such or such: for example, being a human or a horse: being white or black. For nothing can become this and that and such, unless there is first that which becomes this, that, and such. Therefore, being such and this and that does not immediately follow after nothingness, but after being itself, simple and absolute. Since, therefore, it is proper to God to bestow being itself, common and absolute, upon all; and indeed that being (i.e., absolute being) follows after nothingness before all modes of being; it will be the office of God alone to produce something from nothing into being: so that the first thing given to all, namely being itself, may be from the first cause; and from subsequent causes, secondary or tertiary gifts. Indeed, that which participates in some nature cannot produce that nature absolutely: because since that which is something such by participation necessarily follows that which is absolute, and indeed is such through that (absolute), whatever it itself is; if this (participating thing) were to generate that (absolute thing), certainly that which is posterior would generate a thing prior to itself, and even the cause of itself, where it would also generate itself. Therefore, Ariston, because he was not absolute man, but this man, constituted in such matter, did not generate humanity itself absolutely, but this man, namely Plato, and in such matter. But since, as far as the nature of being is concerned, whatever is subordinate to God participates in being itself, and does not have being simply, but such or such being, determined in a certain essence and species; it follows that no thing subject to God produces being itself, but bestows a certain mode of being upon a certain matter. From which it happens that for its work it always needs a prior foundation. Furthermore, whatever both art and nature do, they produce from a certain potential into act. just as being is the act of essence. But because created essence is not its own act, therefore neither is its operation its own. Otherwise, such an operation would be subsisting through itself, entirely absolute from every limit of the participant. What is such, we have said, is unique, and exists as infinite. But does operation differ from being, just as it is shown to differ from
L essence? Without a doubt.

For operation is twofold: one flows out from the operator, like heating; the other remains within, like cognition and will. That which flows out, without controversy, differs from being, which does not flow out from the thing itself. That which remains, for this reason also differs, because the being of a creature is enclosed within a certain species of things. Such an operation wanders through many genera; indeed, intelligence itself and will wander through infinite ones. For the object of the former (intelligence) is truth itself; of the latter (will) is goodness itself. But truth and goodness at least extend as widely as that which is called being itself. But operation draws its species from its object; therefore, such an operation is clothed in all species of all things.

But does operation differ from virtue, and virtue
M from essence and being? Certainly. First, because act is always opposed to potency: operation, which is an act, differs from virtue and essence, which are certain potencies; and virtue differs from being, which is an act, and from essence; because potencies are distinguished by their acts, since a proper potency regards its proper act. The act of essence is being; the act of virtue is operation: Therefore, essence and virtue are as distant from each other as being and operation are distant. Why so many of these things? So that you may understand that the operation of any creature adheres to virtue; and virtue and being adhere to essence; and that no creature operates directly through its substance, but through an operative virtue, which is a quality or accident, since it is distinguished from substance on all sides.

Therefore, whenever something operates, it directly generates certain qualities, and gives being of the kind it itself has, that is, always inhering in another. But such things require a preceding foundation. Things that require a foundation are not created from nothing. Therefore, no creature creates anything; and not unjustly. For its operation and virtue, because they adhere to another, and whatever adheres does not remain free and whole, but is received according to the capacity of the recipient, are limited by the boundaries of their subject. But creation requires an infinite operative virtue. Therefore, the soul is created by God alone.

The soul's proper life is, I say, perpetual life: because inasmuch as it is rational, even without discipline and use, through the sole virtue of its nature, it daily brings forth within itself absolute forms, through which one goes most directly to eternal ideas. And because every idea is eternal life: he who, according to his nature, can attain an idea through the mode of an idea, can also attain eternal life through an eternal mode.

The Thirteenth Reason: because it receives being from God without any intermediary.

Chapter 13.

Although Plotinus and Proclus and some other Platonists believe the soul is made by an angel, nevertheless I more willingly follow Dionysius the Areopagite, Origen, and Aurelius Augustine, the most excellent Platonists, who think the soul is begotten by the one God. Which indeed I trust can be demonstrated by this reason. The soul is a form so simple, and so free, that it is neither composed of multiple parts, nor extracted from the bowels of matter. Therefore, when it comes into being, it cannot be generated from any previously existing things. For it is not made from diverse things placed far apart beforehand, then forced into one: since it lacks parts. Nor from a previously unformed, then formed, spark of matter: since it is above matter. Therefore, it is made from nothing. But to make something from nothing is proper to God alone. For from the order of works, the order of causes is investigated, for the effect is adapted to its causes. Therefore, we must reduce proper effects to their proper causes: and that which is found common in all proper effects, we must refer to the common cause of all. Thus, since in all things, besides the proper conditions of individual things, being itself is found common to all: we must adduce individual causes for individual conditions and qualities: but for being itself

--- Page 224 ---

itself, indeed it comes into being in something: but always. But that which comes into being subsequently: neither in itself, nor always by its nature, does it persevere as the same or similar. Therefore, since the rational soul indeed comes into being through the idea of life without an intermediary: by such a power of proximate origin, it is a form always living. But the irrational [soul], since it proceeds thence through the rational [soul]: living sometimes according to itself. For that which is created by the idea alone through action, comes into being by an action entirely stable: and thence has a stable essence. *Fourteenth reason, because it is life in itself.*
Chap. 14.

**T**he soul is essence: it is also life. By previous reasons we have shown it to be immortal, because it is an essence existing in itself: but in the present [discussion] we show its immortality, because it is life living in itself. Furthermore, the soul is life from its very essence: because all that is in it, is life. For if there were anything in it that was not life, that indeed would not be a part of the soul: and the whole animated thing itself would be called something animated rather than a soul. Let us therefore confess that the entire essence of the soul is life. If it is entirely life: it must certainly be called life in itself according to its form. For that which lives through another, not living in itself, is composed of two parts: namely, from its own nature, not living in itself: and from that life received from elsewhere. Thus conclude. If that thing which lives through another is not entirely life: it follows that the thing which is entirely life, lives in itself. Therefore, the soul, which is entirely life, lives in itself: especially since it moves itself. If it is so, it is life in itself. Therefore, the essence of the soul is life. That matter from which art and nature make something, sometimes H is very obedient and apt for the work: sometimes less apt: so that the potentiality of matter sometimes differs less, sometimes more, from the act of fabricating the work. The potentiality of air differs little from the effect of fire: but the potentiality of water differs far from this. Therefore, it is easy to ignite fire from air, difficult from water.
From which it appears that he who acts must be so much more powerful, as much longer as the interval is between that potentiality and the act to which he is to bring his work.
But the distance between nothing and being is infinite: both because in nothing there is no proportion to being: and because no greater distance than this can exist or be conceived.
But that distance lacking proportion and end, only that power can transcend, which has no proportion to other powers: nor has an end. Such a power is God alone. For all other things are surpassed by God's power. Therefore, God alone produces something from nothing into being. Moreover, every thing I apart from God himself is called a creature by theologians: and is necessarily composed of four certain things.

Fifteenth Reason, because life is more excellent than the body.
Chap. 15.

The rational soul is true natural life. True life is by itself the former and ruler of the body: and therefore it is far more excellent than the body. Although the body may be turned into various qualities, or even divided a thousand times into parts, it never ceases to be a body. For the nature of the body, being divisible, always remains when parts are divided into particles without end. Therefore, much more so the rational soul (which is the true life of the body), however much it may change, never ceases to be life. We believe the force of this argumentation to consist especially in this, that the third essence, which is the seat of rational souls, has three endowments, from the fact that it holds the middle ground of all things. First, because in it shine forth the true images of divine things. Second, because it itself forms and contains the entire corporeal machine. Third, because it reconciles divine and corporeal things with each other. All these endowments show the soul to be eternal. Therefore, if not so much that which is in the mass of the body, as that which is in its form, makes a body to be (for a body is so much more, the more comely and beautiful it is; and so much less, the fouler and more deformed it is; which defect happens not by a cutting off of mass, but by the privation of form), it must be thought that that soul, from which as from a principle is given to the body the form by which it is a body, and the connection of parts by which it consists, is never deprived of its own form or union, by which it is and remains a soul; inasmuch as the body is never deprived of all form and union by which it is and remains a body; nor does the soul, however, pass from one species to another, like the body.

For change descends from the soul into the body; and the former is more stable than the latter. Therefore, if this (the body) always remains in the corporeal genus, that (the soul) always remains in the animal species; nor will it be changed from one soul to another within the animal species itself, for there is no underlying matter by which such a change might occur.

If such a change does not occur, and the soul cannot exist unless it lives, assuredly the soul never dies.

But if anyone says that the destruction to be feared by the soul is not that by which something that is becomes nothing, but that by which we call those things dead which lack life, let him consider that no thing lacks itself.

Now the soul is a kind of life. From which it follows that what is animated, lives; but everything inanimate, which can be animated, is understood as dead, that is, deprived of life.

Therefore the soul cannot die. For if it could lack life, it would not be a true soul, but an animated thing, or some semblance of a soul.

But if this is absurd, much less is this kind of destruction to be feared by the soul, which certainly is not to be feared by life. For truly, if the soul dies then, when life deserts it, that very life which deserts it is much better understood as the true soul; so that now whatever is deserted by life is not the soul, but that very life which deserts.

For whatever is called dead, being deserted by life, is understood as deserted by the soul. But this life which deserts those things which die, because it is the soul itself, and does not desert itself, the soul does not die; unless perhaps we ought to believe that true life is some temperament of the body, or something following it, as Aristoxenus and Dicaearchus opined.

In matter, which by its very nature is no less prepared for cold than for heat, opens its bosom to the approaching cold: which coldness, having entered, drives out the color from it; and this color, driven out from there, is extinguished; since it was produced into being by its author with this law, that it should remain as long as it was nurtured by such a bosom of matter. Therefore, forms which are sustained by matter [Marginal note: C], although they do not receive forms contrary to themselves, nevertheless, they are destroyed by their assault and proximity. But those which remain in themselves, and if they sometimes seem to adhere to matter, they sustain it rather than being sustained by it: they cannot admit a force contrary to themselves: but if any force comes to the bosom of matter, it contaminates the qualities and forms bound to matter: but it does not touch that form which transcends matter. Such is the soul: the rational soul, I say: which, since it is the fount of motion and the mover of bodies, cannot be changed from its state by bodies. And since it has an innate life of its own kind, as its proper one, it lives always without the labor of living: especially as long as it lives with itself. But approaching the body, it pours forth from itself an irrational life (to speak Platonically), like a shadow. It is indeed the true soul, and the fount of animal life, and such a life it supplies not only temporarily to the body, but much more to itself always, since it never abandons itself: nor is it compelled to abandon itself by the body, whose quality does not pass into an incorporeal form. Again, nor is it compelled to the same by souls, [Marginal note: H] whose office is to vivify, not to destroy. Such, without doubt, is judged to be the rational soul. But the irrational soul is not a true soul: because it is neither a true essence nor a true life. It is not a true essence, because it does not exist by itself: since [Marginal note: D] it does not operate by itself: inasmuch as it does nothing without the instruments of the body. It is not a true life: because it is deprived of the freedom of motion. For it is not led by itself, but is drawn by force [Marginal note: I] by those things which are offered to the senses. Therefore many Platonists say that the rational soul is both a subsistent soul and life, and vivifies the body from itself. But they think the irrational form is rather the animation and vivification of the body [Marginal note: E], than also being immortal. **PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

D      Such reasons are inseparably inherent in the soul, which always and suddenly uses them at will. In these consists the art of reasoning, which is by no means separated from the rational soul. For if that artificial reason, or rational art, which is a collection of reasons, is separated from it, it will either be nowhere, or in some non-living thing, or in a living thing. It must not be said that perpetual and immutable reasons are nowhere. It is also impossible for true reasons to be in a non-living thing, since life is the foundation of reason. But if artificial reason passes from life to life, it never does so more conveniently than when someone teaches others. But since this does not happen (for no one forgets by teaching others), no transition occurs. Therefore, art is inseparably inherent in the soul. It would also be inherent in the body, if the soul were the harmony of the body; wherefore both reason itself and the soul would be mutable, like the body. But since such reason is immutable, and therefore the essence of the soul is also immutable, in which it inheres as a subject, the soul is not a temperament of the body. And let it suffice to have argued thus from that first member of the previous division, by which it is conceded that reasons are inherent in the soul. Moreover, if anyone admits according to that member, namely, that the soul inheres in them, the same follows. For in what way is the soul a temperament of the body, if it is in the reason of things, separated from the body, as a subject? since the temperament of the body cannot be elsewhere than in the body? If you concede the third member of that division, namely, that both are substances subsisting by themselves, both the soul and the very reason of things, the soul will subsist by itself, nor will it be bound to the temperament of the body. Finally, whatever member of the division you accept, this one reason above all persuades that the soul does not lie in the composition of the body as its origin: because it would not so eagerly, so easily, so assiduously mix itself with immutable reasons while we philosophize, having set aside the mutable body, nor would it be better when it is in them, than when it is in the body. But it is so much better in them than in the body, by how much more excellently it lives in them than in the body itself. But it lives so much more excellently: by how much more perfectly it operates. But it operates more perfectly in them: because it understands more truly, desires more peacefully, enjoys more sweetly, more fully, and more securely. And when the body is often in harmony with itself, the soul itself is in disharmony with itself both in speculation and in morals,

We will then confirm these Platonic mysteries with the opinion of Aurelius Augustine. If the rational soul were to perish when the body perishes: it would necessarily be changed when the body is changed. But it is not changed by the body. For it is itself the principle of motion. Therefore, when it seems to be changed by the body, then it itself changes the body: and guides itself as it commands. If the soul very often moves the body, remaining immobile: much more from the fact that it stops and contains the body, it stops and contains itself. For that which stands firmest in moving another: can always stand firm in stopping and containing itself. Is that which compels it also an animal, or is it not? But if it is not, nothing can be compelled by another. Who indeed would doubt that such a great change could in no way be made to the soul through the body? For it would happen if the body were more powerful than it. Although whatever it is to which it is compelled through the body: it is absolutely not compelled through the body, but through its own desires: concerning which enough has been said. Or because sleep often overcomes us against our will, is it to be feared that the soul might be converted into a body by some such defect? As if, indeed, because our limbs grow weak with sleep, therefore the soul becomes weaker in any part. Nevertheless, it does not perceive sensible things: because whatever it is that causes sleep, it is from the body, and operates in the body. For it lulls and closes the bodily senses in a certain way, yet in such a way that the soul yields to such a bodily change with its will: because such a change is natural, which refreshes the body from labors: yet this does not take away from the soul the power of sensing or of understanding. For it also has images of sensible things at hand with such an expression of likeness, that at that very time they cannot be distinguished from those things of which they are images. And if it understands anything, it is equally true for the sleeping as for the waking person. For example, if one seems to himself to have debated in sleep, and following true reasons in debating has learned something, even when awakened, these same things remain unchangeable, although the other things are found to be false: such as the place where the debate, and the person with whom the debate seemed to have been: and the very words which pertain to sleep by which it seemed to be debated: and other things of this kind which are perceived by the senses themselves and are done by the waking, nevertheless pass away, nor do they in any part attain the eternal presence of true reasons. From which it is concluded that by such a change of the body, which is sleep, not the power of the soul itself, but the life of the body can be diminished. For it is always true in the same way that two and four make six; and that the comparison which is of two to four, is the same as four to eight; and very many other things of this kind.

THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY
On the Immortality of Souls
by the same author, Ficino,

BOOK SIX.

Reduction of opinions concerning the soul
into five chapters.
Chapter I.

[Decorative woodcut initial H] These things I had once discussed in the Regnano countryside at the house of our unique friend John Cavalcante on the Kalends of March under a laurel tree. At these discussions were present three of our principal companions, Christopher Landino, Bernard Nuthius, George Anthony Vespucci: men most renowned for their integrity and learning. But John, having heard these things with the greatest attention, said, "Marsilio Ficino, it could not be said how much I was delighted by the previous discussion. But I desire this furthermore, that after you have discussed the common immortality of rational souls, you would next, if it pleases you, discuss more diligently the immortality of our own soul with specific arguments. Indeed, I agree that there are five grades of things, just as you set forth in the previous discussion: and that the middle of these is held by that third essence, which is freed from matter and is perpetual. Furthermore, celestial souls are not placed in that grade of essence,

--- Page 237 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. V. 78

and conversely, if one assents to a discordant view: whoever has not seen that the soul does not consist in the harmony of the body, that person is discordant with the truth. But let us return to Aurelius: here perhaps arises no small question. Whether [A] just as the soul does not perish, so also it is not changed into a worse essence. For it can seem to someone, and not without reason, that this has been brought about by this reasoning: that the soul cannot come to nothing, but perhaps it can be converted into a body. For if that which was formerly soul has been made a body, it will certainly not be altogether non-existent. But this cannot happen unless either it itself wishes it, or it is compelled by another. And yet the soul will not necessarily be able to be a body, whether it itself desires it or has been compelled. For this follows: that if it becomes (a body), it necessarily wishes or is compelled. But that does not follow: that if it wishes or is compelled, it becomes (a body). But it will never wish (to be a body). For all its appetite towards the body is either that it may possess it, or that it may vivify it, or that it may in some way fashion it, or in any way care for it. But none of these can happen if it itself is not better than the body. But if it will be a body, it will certainly not be better than a body. Therefore it will not wish to be a body; nor is there any surer argument for this than when the soul asks itself this. For thus it easily discovers that it has no appetite except for doing something, or knowing, or feeling, or even merely living: to the extent that its power allows it. But if it is compelled to be a body, by whom then is it compelled? Surely not by just anyone? Certainly by a more powerful one. Therefore it cannot (be compelled) by a body. For in no way is any body more powerful than any soul. But a more powerful soul does not compel into something unless it is subject to its power. Nor in any way is a soul subject to the power of another soul, unless it is subject to its own desires. Therefore that soul compels no more than as much as the desires of the one it compels allow. But it has been said that the soul cannot have a desire to be a body. This also is manifest: that it arrives at no fulfillment of its desire while it loses all desire; and it loses (desire) while it becomes a body. Therefore it cannot be compelled by that (soul) to become (a body), which does not have the power of compelling except through subjected desires. Furthermore, whatever soul has another soul in its power, it is more necessary that it wishes to have it in its power than a body, and either to consult for its good with kindness, or to command it with malice. Therefore it will not wish that it become a body. Finally, this compelling soul is either an animal or lacks a body. But if it lacks a body, it is not in this world; but if it is so, it is supremely good. Nor can it wish for another such a base change. But if it is an animal: either

Chap. 2.

G  Firstly, I believe that common philosophers, who, believing the soul
to be corporeal, followed some opinion out of those four, were
not persuaded by any reason, but compelled to this view by a certain long and most un-

H  Three principal functions of our soul seem to exist.
Indeed, it acts in the body: it acts through the body: it also operates by
itself. In the body it acts through that power which the Peripatetics
call vegetative, but our Platonists call nature,
when it generates the body, and nourishes and increases it. Through the body it acts
according to sense, both external, when it sees, hears,
