DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. V. 79

By those eternal reasons which remain immutably, and are certainly not contained in space, the soul is priorly endowed than the body; and not only prior, but also more so. For it is prior by as much as it is nearer; and for the same reason, it is also more so, by as much as it is better than the body. Nor is this nearness spoken of in terms of place, but in the order of nature. By this order, it is understood that form is bestowed upon the body by the supreme essence through the soul, by which it exists, as much as it exists. Therefore, through the soul the body subsists; and by that very fact it exists, by which it is animated, whether universally, like the world, or particularly, like every individual animal within the world.
Wherefore it would follow that the soul would become a body through the soul; and it could not be otherwise. But because this does not happen (for indeed, the soul remaining in that which is soul, the body subsists through it, giving form, not taking it away), the soul cannot be changed into a body. For if it does not transmit the form which it receives from the supreme good, the body does not come into being through it. And if it does not come into being through it: either it does not come into being at all, or it receives form as closely as the soul does. Nor does the body then come into being; because if it were to receive form so closely, it would be the same as the soul. Is not the soul better by that very fact, by which it receives more closely? But the body would also receive so closely, if it did not receive through the soul: for indeed, with nothing interposed, it would certainly receive so closely. Nor is anything suitable found as a medium between the supreme life, which is immutable wisdom and truth, and that which is ultimately vivified, that is, the body, except the vivifying soul. But if the soul transmits form to the body, so that the body exists as much as it is, it certainly does not do so by *losing* its form; rather, it would lose its form by transforming the soul into a body. Therefore, the soul does not become a body, whether through itself (because the body comes into being through it only if the soul remains), or through other means; because the body comes into being through the soul only by the transmission of form, and the soul would be converted into a body by the *loss* of its form, if it were to be converted. This can also be said concerning the irrational soul or life, that the rational soul is not converted into it either. For it itself, unless it were subjected to the rational [soul] in an inferior order, would likewise receive form, and would be such. Therefore, the more powerful transmit the form received from the supreme beauty to the weaker in natural order. And certainly when they transmit, they do not take away (from themselves); and those things which are weaker exist, as much as they exist, because the form by which they exist is transmitted to them by the more powerful, which indeed

Wash your body, boy, wipe the flesh clean of the clods: you will see yourself as flesh, not mud.
B Dismiss your senses, O wretched ones, those overly impious teachers. Interrogate only your pious mind: yet in such a way that you show it a soul pure, such as you received it, not enslaved to the body, not defiled by the stains of vices. The mind will immediately answer that the soul is not merely incorporeal, but divine. You are something great, O soul, if small things do not satisfy you. And best, if evils displease you. Most beautiful, if you abhor base things. Eternal, if you hold temporal things in slight esteem. Since you are such: if you wish to find yourself, seek yourself, I beg you, where such things are. Great things indeed are there alone, where no place imposes an end with a limit. Best things, where nothing adverse happens. Most beautiful things, where there is nothing discordant. Eternal things, where there is no defect. Seek yourself therefore outside the world.

But that you may seek yourself, and find yourself: fly outside; indeed, look outside. For you are outside, while you yourself embrace the world. But you think you are in the lowest place of the world: because you do not indeed perceive yourself flying above the heavens: but

Or if a bird flying in the air believes itself to be flying on the earth, while it sees its shadow on the earth. Therefore, having abandoned the narrow confines of this shadow, return into yourself. For thus you will return into spaciousness. Know that there is immense spaciousness in spirit, but in the body, infinite (so to speak) narrowness. Which one may perceive from this, that numbers (which approach spiritual nature) since they lack location, and measure and count according to both incorporeal and corporeal form, are nothing other than certain replications of unity itself: and unity is incorporeal: because everything corporeal is manifold. Numbers, I say, which are spiritual, grow without end, yet do not decrease without end: magnitude, on the other hand, does indeed have a limit of increase, although it does not have a limit of decrease. I doubt. I also think it probable that our soul is located there. However, I believe that this cannot be fully affirmed until all the opinions of philosophers about the human soul are reduced to five categories: and four having been refuted, the last one is held. For either the soul is some very subtle corpuscle infused into this coarser body. (B) Whether it be fiery, as Democritus, Leucippus, and Hipparchus think: Or airy, as Anaximenes, Diogenes of Apollonia, and Critias: Or watery, as Hippias: or earthy, as Hesiod and Pronopides: Or consists of fire and air, as Boethus and Epicurus: Or of water and earth, as Xenophantes. Or the soul is something better, that is, not the mass of the corpuscle itself properly: but some quality of it scattered through the parts of the corpuscle, for example, heat, or a warm temperament: which Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Antipater, and Posidonius seem to have intended. Or something purer, like some luminous point of that quality in (C) some more important part of that quality and the corpuscle itself, for example, the heart or the brain, assigned there, residing there, thence governing the remaining members: as is found in Chrysippus, Archelaus, and Heraclides Ponticus. Or something still freer, like some (D) point affixed to no part, but separated from every determined location, and present whole to each part of the body: but such that it is dependent on the very nature of the body. Dependent, I say, in two ways, namely, either because the body's temperament generated it: or because, although the temperament did not generate it, nevertheless its progenitor, whoever he may be, brought it forth from the potential of matter and its depths, that is, brought it to light from some seed or beginning or proportion of matter itself, and entirely committed it to matter as to a natural bosom.
This opinion is followed by Xenophanes of Colophon, Asclepiades, Aristoxenus, and Critolaus, among whom the soul is either a certain agile force of the body for moving, or the harmony of the bodily parts.
Or finally, the human soul is something divine, that is, (E) something individual, standing whole to each part of the body: and produced by an incorporeal author in such a way that it depends solely on the virtue of the agent, not on the inception or capacity or nourishment of matter: as the first [philosophers] teach us.

But it is to call the king of animals the most insane of all. And he alone will be the most insane who will not confess that the object of the mind is as much more excellent than the object of sense, as the mind is more excellent than sense: and therefore that incorporeal natures are truly found in a more excellent kind of substance than corporeal ones; especially because if the objects of the mind move it, just as the objects of sense move sense, then these very objects of the mind must have some substance in themselves, so that they can move the mind. But if it is said that the intellect is not at all agitated by its objects, then it will already be sufficiently proven that at least the intellect itself is an incorporeal nature, since while it creates its own things, it is not moved by another: and it creates incorporeal structures.

But it is necessary to remember that just as a child born blind with difficulty believes in the variety of colors and the existence of light, though nothing is clearer than light to other people: so the soul, recently enveloped by the darkness of the body, can scarcely be led to believe that some incorporeal light exists: though nothing in the order of things is more manifest to angels than it. Plato complains at length about this in the seventh book of the Republic: Aristotle confirms this in the second book of his *Divina*, saying that the human intellect relates to those things which are in themselves most manifest in the order of things, no differently than the eye of an owl relates to the light of the sun.

Therefore, let the petty philosophers sometimes reflect, who, relying on the judgment of the senses, cannot conceive of the soul as incorporeal and divine. Let them realize at some point that from long habituation with the body, they have become so corporeal that they deservedly know nothing but the body, or something born of the body. Let them purify themselves, and they will perceive pure things. Let them sometimes experience within themselves, for they can, provided they wish what they have long desired in the universe; they certainly perceive composites: and they perceive very many forms in composites. Moreover, they desire some forms segregated outside of composites: they themselves are composed of soul and body. They have life imparted to the body by the soul: and they have the life of the soul itself thriving within itself. Therefore, let them despise the former, and look to the latter. Let them lead an intellectual life separated from the body: separated, they will immediately attain separate forms, and will soon prove by the thing itself the Socratic opinion, that beyond the forms which lie in formed subjects, because they are imperfect, there are forms in themselves, and perfect ones, from which unformed subjects

...subjects it gathers through the inner sense, but the very pure and incorporeal power of the soul investigates and finds something incorporeal, which is neither a body nor the image of any body; which action, indeed, we call intelligence. You have, therefore, natural action, sensation, intelligence. The soul uses natural action immediately upon entering the body in the fetus; sensation a little later, namely immediately after the human is born; pure intelligence scarcely at last when the body is already adult: but a large part of humanity almost never, especially those who are still children even in their thirtieth year of age.

If you ask that natural power what the soul is, it will undoubtedly answer that it is body. K
For that power touches nothing else but body. If you ask the external sense, it will similarly answer body. The eyes will ascribe a certain shape and color to the soul, the ears sound, the sense of smell odor, taste flavor, and touch weight, solidity, heat, and similar things. But if you inquire of the inner sense, which feeds on the remnants of external senses, concerning the soul: it too will paint the soul with images of bodies, for it has nothing else to employ.

Our unhappy youth, nourished under these unlearned teachers, compels us throughout our lives to think foolishly about the soul, while we imagine it to be corporeal, taught by these masters who perceive only corporeal things. But this error seems to have arisen, or rather to have been confirmed, especially from this: that if ever, having entirely dismissed these three teachers as sophists, we flee to that mind, the mistress of wisdom, and inquire of her what the soul is: she answers that it is such as she herself sees. This is too much. For now indeed, since we have perceived so many various bodies, we can devise something new which is not either inherent in these, or at least composed or elicited from them: how in that state, ignorant of these bodies, could the soul fashion the nature of a new body? And even if it were possible for it to conceive some member of its own body: it would in no way think that it belonged to its own substance. Therefore that soul will affirm that it exists: yet it will not affirm anything corporeal. But these two things are different from each other, that which is affirmed, and that which is by no means affirmed. Therefore the essence of the soul in that consideration will be something beyond the body. But we think the judgment of that consideration would therefore be true, because it would follow the purely unadulterated nature of the soul: not images received from outside. It would therefore be a very natural judgment, and thus most true. And so if it then awakens, as we are now, and perceives: it will not be (like us) most inept for the inquiry into spiritual things: but it will have a more convenient way, by which it may sometimes prepare itself for the consideration of itself, so that it may declare itself to be something beyond the body. Indeed, by this way the wretched souls are now lacking, who through nature and the senses have touched bodies, both their own and others', before they considered themselves. From which that miserable error has proceeded, that they cannot perceive themselves apart from the stain of the body.
      So far, it is sufficient to have narrated the imagined education by Avicenna. Next, let us briefly touch upon what kind of education our Plato describes in the seventh book of the Republic.
B    "Imagine," he says, "a certain cave beneath the earth: in it, men nurtured from childhood, with their necks and hands bound behind them, and their feet bound to certain pillars, so that they can neither move anywhere: nor look at anything except what appears from the part of the cave facing them. But behind their backs, above, let a lamp be lit: and between the lamp and those who are bound, let many others walk about, and speak to each other, carrying in their hands various images of trees and animals. Those therefore who are thus bound will never truly see either themselves, or any of those other things which we have described, but only the shadows either of themselves, or of others, which, because of the fire lit behind them, are projected only before their eyes onto the opposite wall of the cave. But let us return at last to those things which we had established from the beginning. Arise, I beg you, souls of mortals, now immersed in bodies: you will immediately find your nature beyond the limits of the body. For the body is long, wide, and deep. But since no body is infinite, and therefore has an end to its depth: it is bounded by a surface that is not deep. You now have a surface, long and wide indeed, like a body: but lacking depth, and from this one part rising towards the incorporeal. The finite width of the surface, too, is terminated by a long line, neither deep nor wide. You have a line approaching spirit in two parts. But this very length of the line, because it is finite, is led to a point, deprived not only of depth and width, but also of length. You have a point inclining towards incorporeal nature in three parts. But since this is the end of a line, it therefore has a certain position in the body: it neither fills the whole, nor gives it life. Separate it, if you please, from the line. But that which is the end of a line can at least be separated from the line by thought: and it is in itself in a certain way prior to terminating the line. And what is prior, it is permitted to separate from what is posterior. You have a point in a certain way, that is, freed from the line by thought, now departing from the body in the fourth degree. In this very liberation, it achieves that it equally regards all parts of the body. It is founded through all, and moves: here the irrational soul has its seat. Secondly, what an angel is like, that is, pure intellect, already rejoicing in the infused light of truth. Thirdly: when the soul itself, like an angel, will rejoice in the full light of truth, it will perceive God to be then truth itself shining by itself, and rejoicing: then light itself rejoicing in its own truth: then joy itself shining in its own truth.

But we will begin to know somewhat that the error of the common people is born from corporeal custom, if at least we consider some contrary education to that, such as Avicenna devises in the sixth book of his Natural Philosophy. Let some man be created suddenly by God (says Avicenna), established in perfect age, but so disposed that he apprehends nothing through any of the five senses.

The mind of a man so affected will think something, since he is in adult age, in which the bodily structure does not disturb the understanding, nor is he occupied with the operations of the senses, which impede the operation of the mind. And also let there be something that can be understood. For the very substance of the soul is present to the mind. Therefore, the mind, disturbed by nothing, will think of the substance of the soul present to itself. But what kind will it think? Colored, long, or wide? Not at all. For a blind person does not apprehend such things. Sounding, or well-smelling, and similar things? Not even these. For it has not yet received such things through the senses, so that it could assign such a nature to the soul. Therefore, that soul will be able to attribute nothing corporeal to itself. What then will it assert about itself? Certainly at least that which will be offered to it at first glance. And this is its very essence: wherefore it will affirm that it is itself, yet it will perceive nothing corporeal in itself. Therefore, it will affirm that it is entirely incorporeal. Nor will it even be able to imagine itself to be a body, just as the souls of the common people, now created and educated differently, cannot consider themselves incorporeal.

But if someone were to say that soul affirms nothing about itself of these bodies which we perceive through the five senses, but some other body of a different nature: futile.

**Platonic Theology**

But let us return to the light. Thus you will deny that there is light in the sphere of fire, because it is not perceived by the eyes. But the very splendor of the sun, even if it were not seen, would exist: inasmuch as it exists now, and is not seen by owls: and some splendor of it, mixed with vapors, is seen by us rather than the sun itself: but we infer that it is somewhere from this splendor of it. So also we infer that spiritual light is inherent in celestial souls, from the very light of the stars, which is its image. Do you not know that the act of light is nothing other than to shine: and to glow so much more brightly, the further it is separated from dense bodies? Separate it from all matter: it will glow more wonderfully: and it will live then most of all, if it is ever to live. For where action grows, life also increases: Especially since all these things live through its heat. It will also feel, so to speak, when all these things feel through its rays, yet it itself will be least felt. For both by its subtlety it will escape the keenness of the eyes, and by the abundance of intelligible splendor it will surpass the capacity of earthly sight. You know that in the spheres of the elements, the lowest fire declines so much towards the nature of the highest air, and the highest air, on the contrary, is so elevated towards that fire, that that fire seems to be almost nothing other than thin air, and that air a denser fire: so much so that whoever perceives that air can affirm without lying that he has seen fire. The same comparison holds for the lowest mind, such as the rational soul, to the sublime body, which is heaven. Therefore, the soul is in a way thin heaven, and heaven is a denser soul. And he who looks up at heaven, looks at the soul. Consider some geometric point: which, because it equally regards any part of the space surrounding it, if it ever moves, it moves in a circle through any part: whence what was a point, seems to have become a circumference: where indeed the circumference is a point running around, and unfolded outwards. But the point is a circumference rolled up around a stable pivot. Consider again a certain spark of invisible light: which, because it exists above every place, equally diffuses itself into any part of space: and while it moves in a circle, a fiery orb is formed. An orb, I say, manifest to the eyes: where the spark is compressed flame: flame is diffused spark. A spark of this kind is the soul, the flame is the ethereal body. And how great it is in souls

**L**iving beings and green plants are bodies. Bodies also are wood, and rocks torn from the earth. Those bodies grow; these, however, not at all. What then is the principle of nourishment in them? Not corporeal matter: because other bodies also would be nourished, to which such matter is common. Since therefore that power by which they grow is something else besides corporeal matter, and that is nothing other than the nutritive soul: it follows that such a soul is not a body. For a body does not become such and disposed in a certain way, except through quality itself, and a certain proper affection superadded to the body itself, by which it is not only a body, but also such: by which it also differs from any other body. Just as there is such a great variety of spiritual light in rational beings, so great is the variety of visible light in their proper and celestial bodies. And that light so follows spiritual light, as the pale orb of the moon follows its light in the clouds. But this is the difference among rational souls: that the souls of fixed stars and planets are surrounded only by a luminous body, while the others are surrounded by twin bodies, one luminous and one opaque; or certainly one very luminous, the other less luminous. The same (thing) seems to be a kind of light, which, while it remains a spark, indeed feels, but is not felt; but when it unfolds into a flame, it is indeed felt, but it itself feels nothing more. And just as anyone seeing a flame would lack sense if he denied seeing a spark, so will the soul lack (sense), who, while gazing at the ethereal globes as if they were certain circuits of souls, has not perceived souls to be in them as centers, nor has conceded that souls are entangled globes of lights, and globes are unfolded souls. Which Heraclitus thus signified: αὐγὴ ξηρὴ, ψυχὴ σοφωτάτη, that is, dry light, wisest soul. Hence it follows that nothing is either more pleasing or more wonderful to the mind than light, nor can it dwell elsewhere than in the light of spirits, while it inhabits the earth. Now therefore, here too you have found the soul to be like an invisible, life-giving, feeling, intelligible, intelligent light. And a little earlier, like a point free from the body, agile by itself, warm, life-giving, feeling, capable of higher things, which is called a substantial unity. And this is a first kind of excursion, and a kind of prelude, by which that unhappy disagreement may be removed, which draws the minds of common people very far from the confession of spiritual things.

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

[Marginal note A] A natural body is composed of matter and form. An animal is a natural body. Therefore, matter and form are in it. But it consists of soul and body. Indeed, the body is not a natural form: because a natural form is the form of something, and is in something as a certain subject and formed thing. But the body is the form of nothing: nor is it in any subject, but in a place. It remains that the soul is the form, especially because it is the proper and internal principle of operations and motions: indeed, it is even the principle of being for the animal. All this pertains to form. Therefore, the soul is a form. But if it (the soul) were also a body, there would still be need for some other form for both the soul and the body, by which both together would be called one animal: which other form we would more properly call soul. For through the soul, as through a form, the body which was previously living in a certain potentiality, becomes actually living, and actually an animal. Therefore, the soul alone is form: especially because if it had two parts, namely matter [Marginal note B] and form, three absurdities would follow. First, that it would not form the body according to its whole self: because it would not form it through that part of it which is matter. But a proper form must perfect its proper matter according to its whole essence. Second, that the part of the soul which is called form, would be the perfection of two matters of the same kind: which nature does not allow: just as it does not allow two forms of the same kind to inform the same matter. Third: because the soul would be transmuted into these lower bodies, and vice versa, if it possessed matter common with them. Which is therefore wrong, because if there is a mutual transmutation of bodies and souls, much more will there be a transmutation of any souls into any souls, and likewise of any bodies into any bodies. Therefore, let the soul be form alone. A form, I say, not accidental, but substantial. For since the soul itself is the ruler and mover of the body, so that it does not contain [Marginal note C] it, it stops and twists it, it is more excellent than the body. The body is a substance. But no accident is nobler than a substance. Again, the mover, insofar as it is the principle of motion, does not depend for its being on that which is moved. Therefore, the soul itself, which is truly the mover of the body, does not depend on the body as if it were a follower of the body. Thus it is not an accident of the body. Furthermore

Second argument. The soul is neither an animated body nor an inanimate body. Chapter 5.

**Q** What kind of body do you want the soul to be? An animated one, or an inanimate one? You will not say inanimate, because it bestows animal life on another. For how, if the soul were an inanimate body, would it vivify bodies? Nor can you call it an animated body: because if the soul is said to be an animated body, certainly that body, after it is said to be animated, is said to be animated by some soul. Concerning that soul, I ask again, is it a body or not? If a body, is it animated or inanimate? If inanimate is answered, that is indeed absurd. If animated, I will again ask about that soul by which it is said to be animated. And you are forced to proceed to infinity as long as you assert the soul to be a body, and you are always compelled to answer absurdly. For both responses seem foolish, both that the soul is animated and that it is inanimate: just as concerning wisdom, both that it is wise and that it is unwise. Or concerning light, both that it is illuminated and that it is dark. For just as light is not dark,

Sixth reason. Two bodies are not in the same place.
Chapter 6.

I Two bodies cannot entirely occupy the same place simultaneously.
For if they are to be entirely in the same place, they must
first be divided into parts, and then those parts must be joined
together. If these parts are indivisible, then those bodies are already
resolved into indivisibles. And since they were composed of the same
[indivisibles], and are not dissolved, it follows that the magnitude of the
body grew from certain indivisibles. Which could not happen,
because indivisibles aggregated together never constitute magnitude. If
however those parts are divisible, each will be a body by itself,
and will have its own separate position from the other. Therefore, there will not
be two bodies in one place; rather, in many small places, many

DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VI. 88

and it must be concluded that the soul must always be sought beyond the nature of the body. Nor let anyone introduce some fifth very subtle corpuscle besides the four elements, which, infused into coarser bodies, might be their soul. For the same question will return: whether that corpuscle becomes soul through its own matter, or through some power superadded to the matter. If the former is stated, all bodies will be souls, because matter underlies all. If the latter, we will have already attained what we desire, namely that the soul must be referred to some power in some way incorporeal. Here some brief arguments of this kind are adduced by some.
[Marginal note: D]
If the soul is said to be divisible, it is asked whether its parts live as a whole, or not? If they live, the whole soul is in each of its particles, from which it follows that it does not need quantity, since it is not diminished by division. If they do not live, life will consist of non-living things, which is impossible. Again, every body can become known to one of the five senses; the soul to none. Every body is circumscribed by some figure or boundary; the soul not at all. Every body necessarily performs its operation in an interval of time (for since it is divisible in essence, much more so in action); the soul often operates in a moment of time. A body is in a place by quantity rather than by essence, because by reason of quantity it fills a place; the soul is present to the body by essence. For as it is present to it, it gives it being. Being is given through essence, just as to know is given through wisdom; therefore it is present through essence. A body is in another in such a way that it is contained by that in which it is placed, and is exceeded; the soul in the body is not comprehended, but comprehending. For it itself perfects, contains, and guides the body. Finally, the soul is more excellent than any body and the whole body; wherefore it is more excellent than lines and points which are in bodies as in a subject. The indivisible is more excellent than the divisible. Therefore the soul is more indivisible than either a line or a point.

But if the body were fluid and unstable: the soul would neither bind the body of the living being, nor firmly solidify it: but it itself would also need some other bond (as we said above), by whose stability it would be strengthened, governed, and moved. But that bond we will more readily call the soul, indeed the virtue of the soul. Indeed, the virtue of the soul in the body is almost the same as either the power of rennet in milk, which is thereby curdled: or the force of a Magnet in iron, which is thereby drawn and suspen-
B ded: or the skillful regulation in a clock, which is thereby governed, moved, and sounds with wonderful order. But the soul itself is not a virtue or tempering of humors, but a certain substantial form, simple, indivisible, which by its natural power and skill tempers the spirits, humors, and members.

      Seventh Reason. A body is not simultaneously whole in many things.
                  Chapter 10.

   Neither bodies, nor forms divided through bodies, can be entirely simultaneously in many parts.

--- Page 259 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VI. 89

Therefore, whatever alternately receives opposing things, and itself meanwhile remains the same, is a substance. The soul, remaining the same, receives now this opinion, now that, contrary to each other; now knowledge, now ignorance; and conflicting affections. The soul, therefore, is a substance. A substance, I say, as a certain substantial form. A form, however, is not a body, because every body is designated by some form. A form, indeed, in the respect that it is a form, cannot be formed. Hence it follows that the soul is not a body. I omit for now the reasons by which it is shown that our soul cannot be an accident: because if it adhered to a subject by some necessity, it could not resist it; nor would it ever reflect upon itself; nor would it ascend from the genus of accidents to the genus of substance; or properly define it; or be able to distinguish itself from accidents; or rightly measure by what interval it surpasses accidents.

Fifth reason. A body is by its nature dispersed.
Cap. 8.

**A** body is by its nature entirely dispersed: first, because it admits the distance of parts, so that one part is always in one place, another in another. Secondly, because it is continuously transformed. For if it is subjected to time, just as various moments succeed each other in time, so affections vary in the body with each moment. And this variety, since it occurs in the heavens, much more does it occur by the swift motion of the heavens in the elements. Thirdly, because it is subjected to contrary qualities, to heat and cold, and similar things. Hence it follows that it is against the nature of a body to come together into one, to remain similar, and to be consistent with itself. For the very extension of quantity compels the parts of the body to remain disjoined. Perennial motion compels nature to change: and not to possess its own (qualities) simultaneously, but to lose one thing, to seek another. The contrariety of qualities impels one to flee the other, through which flight the composite body itself is dissipated. Although through these things it appears that a body by its nature can in no way firmly consist in unity, nevertheless, any body is in some way bound in its parts, all conspiring into one bond of the whole body. There is therefore in the body something beyond the nature of the body, which unites, stabilizes, and contains it. It unites, I say, the distance of parts...

but of any body there is a certain and determined nature and
form: just as a place is limited, and time is certain, and power is finite.
Therefore, the operation of each body is determined: and it does not extend
to contrary effects. But the soul seems to have power over any
contraries. For both in diverse animal bodies and in the same body, it produces many conflicting things among themselves.
It stops, moves: contracts: extends, rarefies, condenses: sharpens, blunts: opens, closes: melts, and solidifies. It imparts
contrary odors, tastes, and colors, opposite forces and
shapes to humors and members: it moves light spirits downwards
to the feet: it leads heavy humors upwards to the head:
which happens contrary to the nature of bodies. It agitates the body in
every direction: upwards against the weight of heavy elements:
downwards against the lightness of light elements: sideways and in a circle against every faculty of the body. Since therefore it produces almost all effects contrary to each other, and is so capable of conflicting movements, that it moves contrary to the order of bodies: who will be so mad as to confess that either a body, or its quality, or anything of a quality, is the soul?

Ninth Reason. A body does not move itself.
Chapter 12.

I That which is truly and primarily self-moving, so that it is entirely both the source and the recipient of motion: must be self-moving according to its whole self:
just as it appears in all other things whatsoever are said to be such or such primarily and per se: just as that which is thus clear, is clear according to its whole self. That which is thus good, is wholly good. That which is thus intellect, is wholly intellectual. For the essence which primarily pours forth some quality, and primarily embraces and receives it: because it perfectly performs both, it effects both through its whole self. But it is necessary that an essence self-moving in that manner, or from itself, be found in nature, and that the soul be such: as we have demonstrated in previous books. But a body, even if it is imagined to be primarily and per se self-moving, yet it will not be able to be such according to its whole self: because it would be necessary for any of its parts to be moved by itself, and the parts of parts and particles. If, therefore, two bodies cannot be made equal (or occupy the same space) in the same place: the soul, which everywhere infuses itself into the living body and extends itself through all points of the body, is not a body. That it is everywhere in the body is evident at present from this: that nothing is more intrinsic to essence than being. And therefore the form by which substantial being is attributed both to the whole body and to its parts is intimate to the whole and to the parts. And because [Marginal note: K] just as a thing relates to being, so also it relates to unity: the soul, which gives being by itself, is also united by itself, without an intermediary, to the entire body. That it attributes substantial being is evident from this: that when it is removed, all members change their appearance. Since indeed being flows from essence, and operation from power: the soul, which bestows being and operation upon individual members, also communicates its essence and power to each. For it provides being and operation in the same way it is united. Therefore, if it provides these to individual parts, it is also united to individual parts. Is it not true that if any natural body lacking a soul is a certain unity through one form existing in the whole and in its parts: much more will an animated body be one through the soul present to the whole and to its parts? But if the soul were in only one member, it would be the form of that one alone, and other forms would belong to the rest: from which a truly single natural body would not be made up of all the members, but a certain aggregate, like a house from walls. Nor would there be in any part of the animal such agreement and harmony with any other part as there is now: unless the various members are glued together by one soul: just as all joints are not contracted by the pull of a nerve, unless the same nerve is in all of them. Add to this that in every, however small, portion of the body, there [Marginal note: A] is life, and in most, movement and sensation. These are the intimate powers and operations of the soul. An intimate power and action of any agent does not exist without the substance of the agent. Therefore, the soul is in those parts, if it thrives and acts in them. Which, when it moves in its own way, does not dissipate the body: because no pain arises from the soul's movement through the body. But perpetual pain would occur in the body if its parts were dissipated and disturbed by the soul's movement. And they would undoubtedly be dissipated if the soul were a body: since it itself is perpetually moved through the body by a certain movement of its own. In what way, then, will the soul be a body, which is everywhere throughout the body, and fills and penetrates the whole from all sides without any harm to the body? ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK VI, 91

We think the soul is a certain nature which is either a certain life, or has life as a companion and attendant, after bodies obtain life through the soul. A body is necessarily divided into many parts. For one kind of body is composed of many elements; another is an element, not at all gathered from other elements, but constituted from form and matter. If you say the soul is a body constructed from many elements, we will ask whether each of those elements individually, apart from the others, has life, or none of them, but gathered together they produce life; or one certain thing among them possesses life. If each of them individually has life: there are as many souls there as elements. Nor is there one soul formed from many parts, but many souls inhabiting the same seat. If none of them has life: they will never create life by mutual concurrence. And if life is born from their concurrence: it will not indeed be by their own power, since they themselves lack life, but rather by the power of something ordering that concurrence, that life will be born; especially since it must be admitted, even if life is formed by the concurrence of many, it is not however they may concur, but if they concur in a certain manner and way, life is generated in them. Thus, the innermost orchestrator of that certain concurrence will be the soul itself, exhibiting life in its own way to those flowing together. But if you say one of the many elements has life, that alone will be the soul itself; nor will there be need for other elements besides this one for the soul to be generated. Therefore, the soul should in no way be considered a body constituted from many elements. But neither is it a single element: because every element is composed of matter and form. If that were to live, it would not live through matter: since unformed matter cannot provide life either to something else or to itself. Therefore, such a thing would live through form. Form, therefore, would be the soul. Furthermore, if the soul is a body, whether it is an element, or something similar: and whether simple or composite: certainly, as I shall say, it will be affected in a similar way, namely, hot or cold, dry or wet, light or heavy, rare or dense, fluid or solid, white or black, and similar qualities. If hot, it will only heat. If light, it will seek high places: and whatever kind of body it may be, it will operate according to its own nature: and will never produce an effect opposite to its nature. For the cold does not heat.

bestows into act in an animal, much more and first it bestows it upon itself. For whatever good and vital act is led from a cause into effect, it is first unfolded in the cause. For thus heat itself is hot and boils within itself first, before it heats another material: and animated bodies swell with seeds, and conceive fetuses within themselves first, before they give birth. Therefore, while the soul unfolds a vital progression from potentiality into actuality within itself, it is said to be moved by itself. Indeed, the Platonists
F properly call motion in the soul an action: because it is in its own source, and forms and moves the body. In the body, however, they call motion a passion. And since the corporeal mass of the universe must also be moved by another: they conclude that the motion of the universal body is a passion resulting from the motion of the universal soul, as if from a certain action of theirs. And just as in
G every genus they always reduce imperfect things to perfect ones, so they refer the imperfect motion of the body to the motion of the soul as perfect in the very genus of motion. Therefore, when it is asked by what motion the soul is principally moved, they respond: not by a corporeal one, for it is incorporeal. Not by an imaginable one, for it lacks figure. Not by a cognitive one, for it does not know itself. But by a motion according to its vital essence. For just as the act of
A essence is to be, and the act of intellect itself is to understand: so the act of life is to live. For it does not possess life adventitiously, but from itself: and, to use their words, the soul is life generating and producing itself. But all life is motion. Therefore, if every living thing is moved: then that which lives by itself, is also moved by itself: and that which lives always, is also moved always: not, to be sure, by an intellectual motion, but by a vital one.
Therefore it is always moved: and not always. For mind indeed is according to potentiality: but life is according to actuality. Finally, essence always lives, and perpetually exercises motion from within: because essential life is always mobile: but the powers and acts which occur both concerning life and concerning intellect, can sometimes be interrupted or go astray. DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VI. 92

If there is a particle in a body that does not move itself, that body will not be, according to its whole self, mobile from itself, and thus it will not truly and primarily be such, but by the participation and presence of something else primarily such. Therefore, for it to be perfectly self-moving, it would have to be conceded that each of its particles moves itself. Those (particles) are divided infinitely; whence those particles that move themselves will be innumerable. What moves, acts; what acts, exists in actuality. Therefore there will be infinite parts acting themselves in actuality, and infinite movers in any body in the world. [Marginal note: A] Indeed, those parts will not be parts of another body from the very fact that they will exist in their own actuality, but each will consist wholly by itself; and there will be a certain infinite multitude of corpuscles existing in actuality. But it is impossible for such a multitude to exist in nature. Since therefore the parts of a body cannot be actually infinite, indeed, nor can they truly exist in actuality at all, when they have no proper existence, but are contained under the very existence of the whole composite: it follows that the parts of the body do not move themselves, nor are they compelled to exist in actuality because of this, and to be utterly infinite in actuality. Let us conclude [Marginal note: B] therefore that a body cannot truly and primarily be self-moving, since that (ability) cannot belong to it according to its whole self, when its parts are not able to achieve that, namely to move themselves. Let us proceed to the same point again by another path. When someone asserts that a body moves itself, he is compelled to confess one of these four things especially: either one part of the body is moved by another; or the whole by a part; or a part by the whole; or the whole by the whole, that is, all parts by all parts. If the first is affirmed: since one part is one thing, and the other part is another, the same (thing) will not move itself, but rather one thing will move another. Nor from this will that composite body truly move itself, since it is constituted of some parts that do not move themselves, but it will have two distinct things within itself, of which one moves the other. If you take the second member of that division, namely that a part moves the whole, or the third, namely that the whole moves a part, that composite does not yet truly agitate itself. For we mean one thing by "part" and another by "whole". And that part which moves the whole certainly moves all parts, and therefore, among the other parts, it also changes itself. Similarly, if the whole moves a part,

--- Page 266 ---
[...]mus, old things are corrupted. If therefore growth and decrease require alteration, generation, and corruption, a body which does not move itself through alteration, generation, and corruption, neither does it move itself by growing or decreasing: nor does it condense itself or rarefy itself: because
D without alteration, these things also do not happen. Perhaps someone might say: at least a body changes place by itself through passage or circuit. This too is impossible to say. For if it is powerless for those superior motions which are internal, much more will it be powerless for external ones. Indeed, I call circuit and passage external motions: which tend to more remote limits than internal motions. Therefore, if a body is not able to move itself to its own limits, in what way will it be able to move to alien limits? Wherefore let us now conclude thus. No other motions appear in bodies besides those eight already enumerated. Through none of them are they moved by themselves. Therefore, in no way are bodies agitated by themselves. They are moved, however (as is clear to everyone), by a certain nature agitating from within, even without external impulses.
E No Platonist would deny that this is the soul: which is possible to be moved by itself: because in it certain other motions of a different nature are found besides those eight. As far as the part is concerned by which the body is governed, there is found in the soul a temporal vicissitude of seeds emerging differently at different times in it for generating corporeal things. But as far as the part of the soul is concerned which is engaged in cognition: there is in it a temporal discourse from one cognition and affection to another: a temporal ascent from the ultimate effects of nature to the supernal principles through intermediate causes: and conversely a descent from the supernal principles through intermediate causes to the ultimate effects. These discourses are certain motions, and proper to the nature of the mind: as we have declared elsewhere. For they do not suit God or angels, who simultaneously possess and see all things. They do not belong to bodies, which do nothing by themselves. Nor to corporeal forms, which are not moved towards incorporeal things. But discourses of this kind, leading us to divine things, elevate us above the nature of the body. But neither a body nor anything else is able to be carried above its own nature by itself. Therefore, such revolutions which are alien to bodies, yet are present in the mind: they testify that the soul cannot be a body or a form divided in a body,

Indeed, let us argue thus. If the soul is a body, it will manifestly grow, entirely equaling the magnitude and quantity of this body as it grows, and diminish as it diminishes. In a vast body, the soul will be more magnificent and more divine. And in the same person, when the body grows, the soul will also grow: it will be necessary that it grows by the addition of a body similar to itself. Does such food live in itself before it is taken in by the soul, or not? If it does not live: in what way does it provide and increase life for the soul, since it lacks life, and before it can lend life to the soul, it must borrow life from the soul itself? If it lives, it already has a soul. Therefore, new souls are daily drawn in by us for the nourishment of this soul of ours. Moreover, nourishment always passes into the nature of that which is nourished. Therefore, many souls would daily be lost by nature, so that one soul might be preserved: which the goodness of nature does not permit. Indeed, our former soul will not even be preserved, if its substance constantly escapes, from which it is compelled to always acquire new souls for itself, through which the soul is continually renewed.

But in what way does a new soul agree with the former one? How, if something continuously flows out from our soul, and nourishment flows into the soul, as we see happen in flesh: does the same will always remain in most people, the same custom, the same opinion and knowledge, and a perpetual memory of the same thing? How after a decade do we immediately recognize those things seen which we had seen a decade before, unless the images of those same things, once received by us, are still preserved intact? For if it is to heat itself, it must possess heat which it can impart to itself. It is also necessary that it not possess it, if it is to receive it. For no one receives what he already possesses. Therefore, as it heats, it is already hot; as it is heated, it is not yet hot. Indeed, it is ridiculous to say that something simultaneously has and does not have something, unless perhaps someone says that water has a certain coldness in potential, which it retains even after being heated by fire, and through which, when removed from the fire, it returns again to coldness in actuality. To this the Platonists will respond, either that that water is made cold by external elements, or if its quality in actuality (which inclines somewhat towards an incorporeal nature) springs from that intrinsic potential for producing quality (which potential indeed approaches an incorporeal nature even much more), it follows that a virtue of this kind again springs from a certain substance which is entirely incorporeal. But a substance of this kind will be the principle of motion in the body.

No body, therefore, moves itself by alteration. But neither does it generate itself, because that which generates another gives being to the generated. The generator, therefore, has the being which it imparts to the generated. That which is generated receives being from elsewhere, which it itself does not possess. Nothing, therefore, can impart being to itself. For it would simultaneously have and not have it. And since the generator precedes the generated, he who is the generator and the generated of himself according to a finite nature is simultaneously prior to and posterior to himself, which no one would certainly imagine in a finite nature. But neither does a body corrupt itself: Since every thing generates its offspring from its own nature, and therefore produces what is suitable to itself, not contrary, it follows that the natural instinct of anything, which is a kind of offspring of its essence and its very being, does not rise against its essence and being.

No thing, therefore, is led by its own instinct to non-being, much less its own, nor that of anything else.

Indeed, since the effort of every thing proceeds towards preserving itself, it will not be bent towards the contrary. But neither does a body increase or diminish itself. For this does not happen without alteration, and also a certain generation and corruption. For through the alteration of qualities we grow and diminish. And while we grow, new parts of the body are generated in us; while we diminish-

But a new soul cannot form itself, especially at the very moment it is born, because it itself is also then imperfect. Therefore, in no way can the soul hold in memory the images and knowledge of those things which it once knew, if it gradually flows out and flows in like a body and a quality.

Concerning the immortality of souls, by the same author, Ficino,

BOOK SEVEN.

*The soul is not a body, or a form divided in the body, or some point of such a form; but it is a form whole in every part of the body, as is shown by the power of sensation. First reason. The body does not receive images suitable for sensation.*
Chapter I.

B [Marginal note]
[Large decorative initial N] I know not by what means in the preceding argumentation we fell into the second part of this discussion, in which we are about to prove our proposition through the power of sensation. So therefore let us further pursue this part. If ever the body receives anything, it receives it in a bodily manner: namely, the parts of the thing in its own parts; nor can it contain a thing greater than itself, just as wax receiving a figure from a seal never receives a figure larger than itself. But if the wax had sensation, by which it might judge the magnitude of the figure, it would clearly judge it to be only as large as itself. Nor can it again receive another figure unless it either loses the former, or so confuses both in itself that scarcely mutually

DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VI. 95

especially since the soul, according to them, is stirred by itself, that is, by its own nature and power, and therefore is moved by itself: which the body cannot do. Furthermore, there appear in the soul exemplars of bodily motions: of generation, when it cleaves to divine things. Of corruption, when to mortal things. Of augmentation, when it remembers. Of decrement, when it forgets. Of alteration, when it varies the turns of affections. Of condensation, as it suddenly perceives something, or collects itself. Of rarefaction, as it wanders, or is distracted by many things. Of progression in a straight line, when it first reaches external things. And of circuit, when either in things themselves it resolves the effect into the cause, and deduces the effect from the cause; or reflects upon itself to be considered. Again, it seems to be moved in a straight line, when it inclines towards the body and sense. In an oblique line, when it reflects upon itself or an angel. In a circle, when it reflects upon God, its beginning and end. Upwards to universals. Downwards to particulars. Also to the right and left, namely into opposite differences of genus. Finally, forwards and backwards, when it turns itself to natural causes or effects. Who therefore would deny that the soul is the source of motions, since in it are its own proper motions, and exemplars of bodily motions: in which, contrary to the nature of the body, it somehow generates itself; or (so to speak) as it were corrupts, augments, diminishes, and transfers, and the rest? Rightly therefore, through its presence, living bodies acquire this faculty, that they alter themselves, nourish themselves, augment themselves: while they generate something from themselves within themselves. And again, that they may move from themselves, wherever they have judged it necessary to move. Of these things, those which do not live accomplish nothing: as if spontaneous motion is proper to life.

Tenth reason. The soul does not grow with the augmentation of this body. Chapter 13.

IF the soul is a body, it certainly fills that solid body which you see, so that the whole may live: and it itself is a thin and agile body, which the swiftness of the mind indicates. Therefore, if you divide the animated body into members: just as all fragments of a body are bodies, so those small bodies which remain when the members are cut, are souls, especially since the soul of one (being) is whole in nature, so that it may unite diverse things. Therefore they will live, will be moved and will feel to...

splendors of light striking bodies. But this visible light, although it shines forth in bodies, is nevertheless made and preserved by the invisible light of celestial souls, which overflows outwards from an immense abundance and becomes manifest. Indeed, it is affixed to no bodies; yet it can be joined to the light of our spirit, which depends on our soul, and offer its splendors to it. Moreover, the meanings of words reaching the ear, which are themselves also spiritual, are neither made by the body nor fixed in the body, but are transmitted from soul to soul, and by the power of souls are made and preserved. But let us briefly conclude the preceding discussion with this division. If the soul is something corporeal: either the images of bodies will touch its surface, like a mirror; or their qualities will penetrate into the deep substance of the soul, like flavors and odors into water. If the first happens, perhaps we will perceive present bodies, but we will not be able to think of absent ones. For we will not retain images. But if the second happens, sense will always be gradual and with bodily passion, and similarly memory, and qualities will be confused with each other without judgment of distinction.

*Second reason. The five senses must be led to one center.*
Cap. 2.

[Marginal note: A]
Sight perceives colors, not sounds: hearing only sounds: smell odors. The mind thus compares color, sound, and odor with each other, so that it judges color to be different from sound, and other things similarly. That power by which the mind thus judges, knows both colors and sounds, and other things which it compares with each other. For how would it say that color is different from sound, unless it knew both at the same time? What then is this power? Is it sight? By no means. For it does not recognize sounds. So neither hearing, which is ignorant of colors; nor any one of the five senses at all. For each of them announces only one thing, nor is it able to compare several things with each other. That one power is certainly interior to the soul, to which, as to a center, various things are announced from all sides by the five surrounding instruments of the senses; but that one judges all the objects and operations of those five senses. Nor should you say two

It will also suffer the same thing if the soul is a quality and some combination of humors and members. Nor will the innumerable unity of the animal be preserved, nor the continuity of the motion of nourishment or growth. For it is necessary that that ruler, who orders and stops mobile things, consist in itself. Perhaps someone will object thus: We see the same figure remain for a very long time in our body, although flesh slips away and flows back. Therefore, similarly, what prevents the same images of known things from remaining in the soul, although the substance of the soul is changed from old to new? We respond that the figure does not remain entirely the same, nor entirely similar, but the former often departs as the flesh departs, and in the new flesh, a new one, similar in some way to the former, is restored: and that this is done by a certain most stable artisan working within: who, since he always remains the same and has within himself the principles and seeds for arranging the members of the familiar body, can, with new humors flowing in daily, transmit a complexion similar to the previous ones and provide the new flesh with a figure similar to the old, no differently than a face looking down from above into a river, depicts the flowing and new waves at every moment with new images of itself, so that the same face appears to persist in the various waves. But that innermost and stable artisan of the body is the soul: which if it also flows, certainly the body will not long bear similar effigies and figures, nor will the soul retain similar knowledge: because then it will not hold them by its own power, nor will there be anyone present to it who either stabilizes them in the mind or generates others similar to the previous ones. **Third Argument. The narrower the sense, the more perspicacious it is.**
**Chapter 3.**

C [Marginal note] Indeed, the image of a visible body must be gathered to something impartible. And this is in the pupils themselves. Otherwise, we would not discern immense bodies, and heaven itself, through such a tiny pupil.
D [Marginal note] But if, as far as the eye is concerned, in order to see more acutely, greater quantity is not needed—indeed, the smallest eyes see more sharply than the largest, like the eyes of an eagle compared to an ox—as if magnitude not only does not help sight, but hinders it: if, I say, the outer keenness (acuity) least needs magnitude for perceiving, what shall we say about that inner sight and common sense? Which, the more excellent and acute it is than individual senses, the more sufficient it ought to be: and it will be more sufficient if it needs no bodily quantity. Finally, the very substance of the soul, the foundation of the senses, will be more sufficient than any sense, if
E [Marginal note] it does not need quantity. Who would say that it needs the dimensions of quantity, since the magnitude of the body neither contributes to the soul's faculties nor harms them? If it necessarily contributed, an bee would not be more ingenious than a sheep, a fox more cunning than a pig, an ape more clever than an ass, a lion more daring than an ox. But if it necessarily harmed: an elephant would not be more prudent than a horse, a dog more sagacious than a lamb. But if, for these powers of the soul which are concerned with the quantity of bodies, the quantity of the body has no effect: much less should it be thought to be of value for that power of the soul which transcends the quantity of bodies, namely, reason, which we will discuss in its proper place.

Thus, if the soul is a body, it will receive images of bodies through the eye in a bodily manner: so that the image of Plato in Socrates' eye is no larger than Socrates' eye. Thus Socrates' soul will not think Plato is larger than his eye: or certainly no larger than the brain into which the image would be transferred from the eye. Finally, no larger than the size of Socrates' body. For if Socrates' soul is large, it is not larger than his body. Therefore, if it receives the whole image of Plato into itself: it receives no larger than itself [C]: wherefore it will never consider anything to be larger than Socrates' body. Furthermore, when it receives the images of Xenophon and Alcibiades and Phaedrus, then it either loses the image of Plato, or it then has all of them confused: so that it does not distinguish one of them from another.

Conclude also thus: The soul is either a solid body: or a fluid one. If solid, it is hardly shaped by bodies: and docility and sharpness perish: and one figure of one thing having been received, it either does not grasp others: or if it grasps others one after another, all are mutually obscured. If it is a fluid body, it holds no figures: and has absolutely no memory.

Moreover, is it not clear that the same thing appears small in a tiny mirror, and larger in a larger one? As if you were to look at your face in my pupil, then in a mirror: here you will declare it tiny, there immense. For according to the size and smallness of the mirrors themselves, bodies are judged larger or smaller. But in the soul of man, images of almost all bodies shine, through which the soul judges bodies as they are in size: and there is no body so huge, so immense, that it cannot either behold or conceive it, and always another body greater than the conceived body [D]. From which it appears that there is no prescribed limit of magnitude for the soul, both concerning those things which it is about to comprehend, and concerning what pertains to the soul's own substance. For if it had any specific magnitude in itself, it would be especially as great as the magnitude of its own body. Hence, in such a tiny animal mirror, things so varied, so clear, so immense could not shine: since, according to the different quantity of mirrors, larger or smaller things usually appear. We ought not, however, think that spiritual images of colors are either made by bodies, or received in mirrors and the brain. For they themselves are nothing other than [N]

**Fifth Argument. The Soul Feels Wholly Everywhere.**
**Chapter 5.**

**D**o you not know that a part of any body cannot be equal to the whole itself, and therefore that a form, which is such that it extends through diverse parts of the body, cannot exist whole in any part of the body? Otherwise, a part would be [Marginal note: A] equal to the whole. I admit these things. What then? Namely, the soul is present as a whole to every part of the body: because it feels as a whole the suffering of any bodily particle. For if the foot, injured by some accident, aches: immediately the eye is turned there: the hand is moved there at once, the mouth cries out, and the other members almost similarly. This certainly would never happen, unless that which is present from the soul itself in all parts of the body, also felt in the foot. But that which has happened somewhere, an absent (thing) could not feel. Nor indeed is it to be believed by any messenger that this happens without the one who announces it feeling it: because what does not feel, does not announce. Nor can suffering, which occurs through the continuation of a mass, always happen so as to reveal the other parts of the soul which are elsewhere: because pain does not always occur everywhere. But the soul feels as a whole that which happens in a particle of the foot: [Marginal note: B] and it feels only there, where it happens. Therefore, it is present as a whole to each part simultaneously, which as a whole feels simultaneously in each (part). But to forms scattered throughout the body, for example, whiteness, the same thing happens in this respect as to the body: namely, that the suffering of one part does not necessarily change all the other parts. For what prevents one part of the body and of its whiteness from being infected and defiled while the rest are not polluted? But nothing happens in any single particle of an animal without it immediately pertaining to the whole soul. Our Augustine thus confirms this Platonic mystery. The soul extends through the entire body which it animates, not by local diffusion, but by a certain vital intensity. For it is present as a whole simultaneously through all particles, neither smaller in smaller parts, nor larger in larger parts: but somewhere more intensely, somewhere more remissly: and it is whole in all, and whole in each. For otherwise, whatever it feels in the body, even if not in the whole, yet the whole

Therefore, answer: whenever the soul is about to compare color to sound, does it apprehend both, namely color and sound, through both powers: or one through one (power) and the other through the other? If each power apprehends both: what need is there for twin powers, since one suffices for the work of comparison, and one does as much as both? In necessary matters, nature does not fail; in superfluous matters, it does not abound. But if it knows only one thing through one power: [marginal note: B] it will compare neither of them to each other through either power. Nevertheless, it compares through some power. If you say it is a line from 'a' to 'b', such a line 'a b', I will ask you in this manner. Whenever the soul is about to compare color to sound through such a line, it is certain that each of these touches that line. Therefore, does color only reach the head of the line which is 'a', and not reach 'b'? And does sound only touch 'b', the end of the line, and not pass to 'a'? Or rather, do both color and sound simultaneously come to both, that is, to both 'a' and 'b'? If you grant the first, namely, that one (stimulus) only comes to one end of the line, and the other (stimulus) to the other: certainly those two ends will be two distinct powers from each other: each of which will recognize what is its own, and will be ignorant of the other. Therefore, the mind will compare those things through neither power. But if you grant that both of those (stimuli) concur at both ends, so that the power at each end perceives both: one of them suffices, the other is superfluous: since both powers do no more than either one (alone): indeed, both powers will be indivisible. Thus we are compelled to confess that that one power of the soul through which it judges many things is not partible. Therefore, that power, the mistress of the senses, is neither a body nor a quality diffused through the body. If such is the power of the soul, what prevents the soul from being such? Eighth Reason. Complexion acts through the power of qualities.
Chapter 8.

I
**T**he action of complexion, and of its form, is always carried out through the qualities from which it itself is composed: and therefore the complexion never performs anything so sublime that the powers of the qualities do not extend to it. It is the work of heat to penetrate and dissolve: but the nutritive power of the soul, through heat as an instrument, not only dissolves foods (which is proper to heat itself) but also cooks and digests them, and brings them to the form of living flesh and human shape: which action indeed exceeds the power of heat. The growth of an animal also cannot come from heat as a principal cause. For it does not occur except through nourishment: and when it is brought to a certain limit of magnitude and a certain shape: but heat, if matter is given, spreads itself without a certain limit or shape: and since the limit and shape must be prescribed to the work by the principal agent: it is clear that heat cannot be the principal maker of growth: indeed, no other accidental form can do it, if heat, which is the most excellent of all, cannot. Nevertheless, growth occurs from the soul. From this it is concluded that the soul is not an accidental form: which must very often be proven by us. It is also concluded that it is not constituted from accidental forms: because it could not rationally order qualities, which wander without a certain limit, degree, proportion, or shape, to these very things. Finally, it is concluded that the soul is not some substance, a form of an element or a mixture. For the motion of such a form is directed to a single limit, as we have said: but growth extends equally to any part.

**Sixth argument. The soul does not necessarily suffer by sensing.**
Cap. 6.

A The soul itself (as true philosophy teaches), since it is most pure, is joined to this crude and earthly body, far distant from it, in no other way than through a certain very thin and very bright little body, which we call spirit, generated by the heat of the heart from the thinnest part of the blood, thence diffused throughout the entire body. The soul, easily insinuating itself into this, its closest kin, first indeed pours itself through this entire spirit, then by this means through the entire body: it first imparts life and motion to this [spirit], and makes it vital: and through this [spirit] it rules and moves the body: and whatever flows from the body into this spirit, the soul, present to it, immediately perceives, which perception we call sensation: then it notices and judges this perception: which noticing we wish to be phantasy (imagination). Why these things? When a physician cuts the outermost skin of the body, the flesh is broken, the spirit is dissolved and contracted. Touch, which is the universal sense of the soul throughout all members, feels all these things: it judges these things: and the phantasy grieves. How can flesh be cut, without the spirit infused into it being partly dissolved with the dissolved flesh, and partly also contracting, fleeing into itself? By what means also could the dissolution and contraction of the spirit lie hidden from its soul? And if it does not lie hidden: why should the soul not bear with annoyance the destruction of its work? Indeed, the spirit and the body are the work of the soul. But all things love their own work. In the flesh D indeed there is suffering: torment in the spirit: sensation in touch: compassion and fellow-feeling (so to speak) in the phantasy. To sum up briefly. Let there be a certain pernicious and substance-corrupting dissolution or contraction both in the flesh and in the spirit: let us call this a harmful injury. Does such an injury also pass into the soul? By no means. For this [injury] destroys substance. Therefore it destroys the virtue of the substance itself: then it destroys the operation of that virtue. Therefore, in any [injury] of flesh and spirit, or

Tenth Argument. The harmony of the temperament does nothing in the body. Chapter 10.

C  Nor should Aristoxenus or other musicians be allowed to imagine that the soul is a certain harmony born from the temperament itself. For thus the soul would similarly be not a substance, but an accident. Does not harmony draw all its power from the strings? Nor does it exist at all by itself, nor can it accomplish anything at all in the strings. For it does not itself move the strings, but harmony is born when they are moved from elsewhere. Therefore, if the soul is a harmony of humors composed in a certain way, it will depend entirely on them; nor will it itself move them, even if the soul arises when they are agitated by another. Nor will it rule them, but they will rule and sustain it.
D  Therefore, there will be no movements in the body beyond the condition of the humors, no operations beyond their control, as they are now, as we have explained in previous sections. No artificial shape, no disposition. The mind will never resist bodily affections, nor will it reflect upon itself, nor will it, being separated from corporeal things, unite with incorporeal things; nor will it operate anything by itself, if it has not existed in any way by itself. But concerning this we have spoken elsewhere and will speak again.

Eleventh Argument. In every composite body there is harmony. Chapter 11.

E  In every body composed of many parts, there is some harmony of its parts, through which they unite by mutual agreement. Cap. 7.

AND if by the preceding arguments we have proved not only that the soul is not a body, [H]
but also not a form scattered through bodies: nevertheless, we think this second part must be shown by specific arguments. And so that we may speak more conveniently about this matter: we will call such a form (as we have said elsewhere) sometimes a quality, sometimes an affection of the body, in the manner of the Platonists. If the soul were a corporeal quality: it would either be a simple quality: or a complexion: or a form bound to these. It cannot be simple. For any simple quality, or form following it (as we have declared elsewhere) makes only one thing: it does not extend to opposites: the soul [does] many things, and contrary things. Nor will it be a complexion, or a form following a complexion: because in this, one quality always dominates above the others, whose operation thrives in the body before others. The soul is bound to no quality, to no specific motion.

**Thirteenth argument. The harmony of humors takes nothing without matter. Chapter 13.**

[A]
**W**hatever effects something: it must be more excellent than that which is made by it. The freer something is from matter, the more sublime it is. Therefore, the cause must always be freer from matter than the effect. No effect, therefore, can be freer from matter than its cause. The power of nourishing is very free from matter: which has been shown elsewhere to operate in many ways both above and beyond the order of the elements. The power of sensing is even more free from matter: because in its very act of sensing, it receives the forms of things without the matter of the things themselves. For sight does not receive the color of the wall along with the wall itself: but it apprehends the spiritual image of the color. Much more does intelligence do the same: as will appear in what follows. Since, therefore, these powers of the soul are very free from matter, they cannot proceed from a cause which is matter, or immersed in matter. Humors are entirely corporeal: therefore, in no way can humors, by some mixture or consonance of theirs, procreate powers of this kind: much less the soul itself, the fount of such powers. Indeed, if the soul has its substance in the qualities of humors: whatever it receives, it will receive through the affections of the humors. But through these, only corporeal forms are received. This complexion, therefore, both from what I said, is not a substance; and from the fact that it has something contrary to itself, for example, the excess of some extraneous quality dissociating its own composition. Furthermore, it admits of more and less. For the natural force and operation of the complexion is intensified and remitted. But substance neither has something properly contrary to itself, since the very contrariety of things consists in another genus than substance, that is, in the genus of quality; nor in its own nature is it intensified in more, or remitted in less, so that now more, now less, this or that substance is what is once a substance; that is, this stone is more or less a stone than that one. But that the soul is substance is also clear from this, because through it an animal obtains a certain and substantial nature and name of its species and genus. Through this soul, this indeed is a dog; through that, that is a horse; through another, that is a human. That quality indeed which is an accident comes to its subject after that (subject) is already perfect in its species. But the soul itself fabricates its own body for itself; it preserves what is made; and when it fails, it restores it; it connects warring elements into one. With the soul departing, the body collapses; nor is the prior complexion or species retained. Such indeed must necessarily be the nutritive soul. Nor are there in the same body two souls, of which one fabricates instruments for the other. Indeed, that which nourishes is the same as that which senses. For perturbations of the senses hinder or augment the work of nourishing. For sadness weakens it through imagination; joy strengthens it; as if there is one soul in man, whose both are functions. Which is therefore substance, because it is the artificer of the body, not a handmaid. Therefore it is not complexion.
