*Twelfth argument. Harmony is understood either as the composition*
*itself of the members, or as some principle of composition.*
*Chapter 12.*

[Marginal note: F]
When someone asserts that the soul is consonance: I think he can mean two things: either the composition itself of the humors and members, or some principle of that composition. The soul assuredly is not composition: because it would be necessary for any part of the soul to be a composition of some parts of the body. How this plainly happens, we cannot explain. Indeed, the composition [Marginal note: G] of the body is manifest to physicists: but the soul is unknown. And how it is composed of its own powers, namely intellect, sense, appetite, and the rest, is difficult to know. Again, it is most difficult how individual powers are composed. Furthermore, composition [Marginal note: H] is nothing other than the union of many things: but many things are not united except by one. By one, I say, which is inherent in the many: so that they are glued together by an inner coagulant. Therefore, that one power inherent in the members, from which the union of the members proceeds: that is the soul itself, rather than the union resulting from it. Nor is it the principle of composition itself. For since different principles and proportions of composition are inherent in different members of the body: each member would possess its own soul: indeed, the bone would have one soul, the nerve another, the flesh another: and similarly for the rest. Since these members are composed with different proportions among themselves. But we would by no means be able to assign one life to a single living being, unless we attribute to it a single form, a single mover and ruler, that is, a single soul. We also observe that the principle of consonance is more suited to the qualities of the body than to the soul. Health [Marginal note: I] is the consonance of humors. Strength, the consonance of bones and nerves. Beauty, in a certain way, of the members: and of color—

Indeed, to it, as to something prior, various properties supervene for constituting persons. Fourteenth Argument. That which is more in harmony, is more harmony.
Chapter 14.

Harmony thus consists in the concord of many, so that with strings that accord more, there is more harmony; but with less harmonious ones, less. The soul of the most wicked man is least in harmony with itself, for sense disagrees with reason; and appetites also fight among themselves. The soul of an upright man is in harmony everywhere. If the soul is harmony, the soul of an upright man, which accords more, is more harmony; therefore, the soul is more [harmony]. The soul is a kind of life; therefore, it is also more life. THEOLOGY OF PLATO

Nearly all agree, however, that the universal nature is known by it (the intellect/mind) before the particular. Indeed, it primarily acts according to the nature of the intelligible form. But this, since it is conceived through a certain abstraction, is absolute: hence it primarily refers to the universal nature. And it acquires this power from the virtue of the intellect, in which and from which it is, as if the intellect itself were absolute. But from the image that is in the imagination, only the particular is represented. Indeed, both Platonists and Peripatetics largely believe that this particular is perceived by the intellect only by a certain secondary and reflective act, inasmuch as the intellect, after having suddenly and directly intuited the universal through a species, then by a certain discourse through act and species into the image (by which the species had been conceived), reflecting itself, now perceives the particular. [Marginal note: E] Therefore, the movement towards incorporeal and absolute things is most natural to the mind: since it first suddenly and directly applies itself to them: where it appears that the power of understanding is entirely incorporeal. If, therefore, through the operations of nourishing, and likewise through the operations of sensing (of which the first occur in the body, the second through the body and concerning bodies), we have shown that the soul is not divided in the body: how much more ought it to be thought that the same is evident also through the operations of understanding, and moreover that the soul neither derives its origin from matter nor is mortal? Indeed, it performs the work of understanding by itself: in which it entirely leaves matter behind, and ascends to incorporeal and perpetual reasons. Come then, let us see by what way we can find what we seek, through the operations and effects of intelligence.

The intellect then receives the divine Idea itself, whether existing within itself, or in the divine light. For reason dictates that natural species, because they are eternal, cannot come from a moving cause: otherwise, if made by motion, they would sometimes cease to exist. Yet they are made, because they are parts of a universe which is composed from elsewhere: and all are from one cause. Hence the human intellect concludes that above the moving world, in the immobile mind, mover of the world, there are exemplary species of natural species, not in a corporeal or animal nature (for they would be mobile), but in an intellectual, indeed intelligible, nature. Third argument. The virtue of the soul: because it is indivisible, it cannot be a quality of the body.
Chapter 3.
*

D What is indivisible cannot be a quality of the body. For if it is assumed to be a quality of the body, we will ask thus: does it touch some divisible part of the body, or some indivisible point of the body? If the first is granted: certainly a quality of this kind will be divisible, since it touches in a divisible manner. And thus it will not be the indivisible quality of the divisible itself, but the divisible (quality) of something divisible. If the second is granted: certainly that quality is the quality of that point alone which it touches, not of the body. Therefore, what is indivisible will never be a quality of the body. But the virtue of the human soul is an indivisible quality. Therefore the soul is not E a body.

E body. Indeed, this kind of demonstration will be considered sufficient if we show those two things more clearly: namely, both that virtue is a quality of the soul, and that this virtue itself is indivisible. The first is most evident to everyone: since through the presence of virtue, the soul becomes such and such, and is called wise, prudent, just, brave, and temperate. And virtue can be absent from the soul while the soul remains. But this is the F condition of qualities.

F condition of qualities. exults, not temporarily, as for the body's uses: but it rejoices
perpetually: it is enlightened: it grows: it becomes magnificent:
so much so that because of its own greatness, those things which
usually seem very great to a hungry little soul appear very small to it. By this
nourishment also it becomes unconquered, temperate, just, a governor
and lord of men, higher than heaven, equal to angels, similar to God. Who
then would further doubt that truth is the natural food of the human mind?
All minds desire the same food, and each mind always desires the
same. This stable agreement in desiring signifies that minds
wonderfully agree among themselves, and that each mind remains
stable in its own nature: inasmuch as their appetite is not varied or
changed as the appetite of the senses: which, due to the diversity of bodies, is diverse
and is changed by the alteration of the body: as if the senses follow the
change of bodies, but the mind follows the stability of divine things.
For it hates bodily foods: and feeds on the same food
as heavenly and eternal minds. This food is truth.
But truth is not corporeal: otherwise it would not be inherent in incorporeal things. E
But now it is inherent in God, and in angels, and in numbers:

Or how will it be mortal, if it is nourished by immortal truth, since neither a corruptible stomach desires or receives incorruptible food, nor does incorruptible food pass into a corruptible body? Indeed, truth is immortal, and it is the continuous food of the soul; as it certainly is, whether truth itself is converted into the soul, or converts the soul into itself, it makes the soul immortal. But since, while it feeds on this familiar food, it is suffused with such pleasure, which has neither annoyance mixed in, nor turns into weariness or pain, it is clear that the mind is never wearied, nor disturbed by the encounter of anything contrary, nor can it in B be corrupted into anything contrary. Again, because nothing is naturally more desirable to the mind than truth, but truth is obtained through a certain separation from mortal things, nothing is more natural and familiar to the mind, insofar as it is mind, than to be separated from mortal things. But from that which is most natural, not a remission of life follows, but an intensification. Therefore, the mind will live especially then, when it has departed from here.

But we can confirm this argumentation of ours with a certain argumentation of Olympiodorus the Platonist, which, drawn partly from Pythagorean, partly from Platonic mysteries, accepted from C Phaedo and Gorgias, he thus wove together. The mind, by its natural avidity for truth, continuously separates itself from the body, and forms from matter, and thus desires and strives to live separated, although daily the body and senses twist it in the opposite direction. But it naturally desires that life separated from the perishable body, as naturally, that is, truly good, especially since life is entirely dedicated to truth and goodness. If such a life is good, therefore it is also possible. For what is impossible is also useless. But good should not be called useless. Likewise, if impotence belongs to evil, power belongs to good. Therefore, every good is possible by its nature. From this it follows that the natural appetite for good is an appetite for a possible possession. And if even that which appears good is possible, certainly the truly good itself is most powerful, and true goods are possible for those who truly and well seek them.

Fourth argument. The intelligible species and conception cannot be received by the body.
Chapter 4.

[Marginal note: B]
All Greek Platonists believe this. We can confirm the same by the opinion of the Arab Platonists. The intellect does not understand a thing, for example, a human, unless it acquires a certain universal form signifying humans, which they call an intelligible form and species. Having acquired this, it thus judges what the nature of man is: man is a rational animal. This judgment is called both a concept and a conception of the mind, and also the reason and definition of the thing to be known, which we also usually call knowledge.

If the intellect were extended through the breadth of the body, both the intelligible form and the conception would adhere to the breadth of the body. In this very breadth, two things are considered: namely, a point, and the extension of the breadth. Therefore, the seat of that form and conception will be either merely some point of the body, or the extension. But if neither ought to be conceded, as we shall demonstrate, it follows that the intellect is not extended in the body at all.

Let us first show that a point cannot be such a seat. First, it must be noted that a point does not exist by itself, but is so affixed to the measure of the body that it is always its boundary. If it apprehends a thing according to its nature, it certainly never receives anything but some boundary of some magnitude which is received in that measure of the body, of which the point is the boundary: so that just as the bodily measure receives the magnitude of the incoming thing, so the boundary of such a measure receives the boundary of the magnitude. Therefore, whatever is said to be received by a point of the body is not free from magnitude. Thus, if the receptacle of the intelligible form is a point, it will not be possible for that species not to be divisible, and to have its boundary in a point of the body, while the remaining parts are in the breadth of the body. We shall prove, however, that it is indivisible in what follows. Furthermore, if it is said that a point thus apprehends that form, so that it alone is its seat

Furthermore, knowledge which is the understanding of the largest bodies would be greater and clearer than knowledge which is of smaller ones. But we know many things whose magnitude we are not able to equal; and the whole mind perceives a great thing equally and in the same way as a small one. But in summary, what else is speculative virtue, if not clarity of the intellect? What else is moral virtue, if not a stable ardor of appetite kindled by the clarity of the intellect? That clarity H

Suddenly the light of truth (as Plato says) shines forth in the mind: not suddenly struck out from things, but by a certain long discussion, like a spark from a stone often struck. Similarly, by long custom, youth is disposed to morals. C Again we ask the Epicureans, who divide species in the intellect as if a form in a body, and locate one part of it in one part of the mind: for example, genus in the right part of the mind, but difference in the left: why should the right part rather correspond to genus, and the left to difference? Is not any part of the mind equally mind? Lest the mind be made of mindless parts. Therefore, any particle of the mind equally regards both genus and difference: therefore any part grasps both. But if any part receives both, and both are in each: it follows that they are not separated from each other.

But, as the Epicureans wish: chance causes one of those two to fall into the right, the other into the left. But let them answer us: whether they then remain thus distinct: or are mixed with each other? If they grant the first: it follows that knowledge does not arise therefrom. For no definition is made from genus and difference separated from each other. In neither of them placed separately is perfect knowledge of the thing itself held. They must be mixed into one, so that one knowledge of one thing can be held by one mind through one definition at one time. Indeed, both must be in the whole mind, so that it may be truly understood. For what is in a part of the mind is not yet fully understood. For the action belongs to the whole thing, not to a part. Therefore, they must admit that those things are mixed. But from where are they mixed? By chance, or by mind? By chance, they say. This is too impious to say. For such a mixture would be most rare: and when it did occur, then at last they would concede that those things thus united are incorporeal: which is what we ourselves want. Finally, they will concede that those things are mixed by the mind. From this concession we will immediately infer two things. First, that the mind is incorporeal, if it leads accepted forms to an incorporeal state, which opinion is contrary to the Epicureans. Second, that that mixture made by the mind will not be true unless such a union exists in the things themselves. For what is fabricated by the mind contrary to the nature of things is a figment rather than knowledge. Is it perhaps cut into dissimilar parts, like the body of an animal into bones, flesh, and nerves? By no means. For through this form, [Marginal note: B] the mind knows what the substance of a thing is: as we have said. The substance of a thing is best understood by definition. A definition consists of genus and differentia: as the definition of man consists of animal and rational. Animal is the genus, by which man commonly agrees with other animals. Rational is the differentia, by which he differs from animals lacking reason. Therefore, if there is any diversity of parts in that form, this will be primarily through genus and differentia. Let these two be: if you wish, parts of the intelligible form. Let them be extended through corporeal breadth.

Hear what follows from this. Because the parts of a body can be divided infinitely, therefore, along with them, both genus and differentia will be cut without end: and in one definition there will be innumerable genera, and innumerable differentiae: nor will there truly be a definition: because it will not be comprehended by the intellect if it is infinite, nor will it be bounded by its own limits: and (what is more absurd) we will either infinitely replicate the same genera and the same differentiae, or by resolving the genus we will ascend into genus infinitely: similarly by dividing the differentia we will descend into differentia. Such ascent and descent is impossible: because true reason finally arrives at the primary genera of things and the ultimate differentiae, beyond which it is not permitted to proceed. Indeed, substance is the supreme genus in man: which is not resolved into another genus. But a certain power of reasoning is the ultimate differentia: which it is not permitted to narrow into another differentia. This increases that error above all else, that if genus and differentia are in a thing, there will be infinitely many such in effect. For it would only know those things which are themselves grasped by breadth. But these are only those things which are themselves extended by breadth. This appears plausible, but it is not true. Firstly, through a point, it will only reach those simple things which are applied to a body as a point; but it will not reach separated forms or numbers. Secondly, through its breadth, it would traverse the entire magnitude of the body to be known, so that it might understand the whole. But no breadth can traverse an entire space of magnitude, unless with every part of itself it traverses in length every part of that space. Therefore, the mind will apply each of its parts to each part of the body to be known, by moving through them in order, and by applying them, it will know. But it will apply parts that are in a way infinite. For the mind will have so many parts, if it is a corporeal breadth. And so, in a short time, it will understand, as it were, innumerable portions of that body:

Whatever things are understood: either they are simple by their nature, or at least they are understood when they become simple through resolution. Therefore, if the mind is said to be corporeal, it will not grasp those things by its breadth; but rather by something indivisible. If it grasps by this alone: it understands by this alone. Therefore, this indivisible part of it alone will truly be the mind. What need is there for the remaining parts for it to be intellect, when there is no need for others for understanding, since that one indivisible thing suffices? Indeed you cut the body, because you tear it into members, which are bodies: you do not cut man: because you do not cut into men. But that which is such a certain thing in itself, and is not divided into multiple such things: that certainly, insofar as it is such, is individual and simple.
The denary also, insofar as it is a denary, is not divided. For there is only one species, and one form: which we cannot divide into multiple denaries. Where the mind inserts itself as a medium between any things participating in equality and equality itself. And if it is most closely commensurate with the highest equality, it is not disturbed by the injustice of unequal qualities.

*Seventh reason. The intellect, by receiving the forms of things, does not lose its own; bodies, on the contrary. Chapter 7.*

**A**
Bodies are accustomed, when they receive the forms of other bodies, to lose their own. For how will water take on fiery heat, unless it sheds its own coldness? But if, when foreign qualities are received, its own also remains, it becomes more imperfect: as when sweetness remains in wine, even if water infused into it becomes sweet: the flavor is thereby weaker. But the mind receives the forms of all things, while it recognizes all of them, and turns over those known within itself: and by receiving them, it neither loses nor weakens its own form: since the habit of any form is always designated by its operation: and the operation of the intellect is intelligence: it follows that the form of the intellect is (so to speak) natural intellectuality itself: which is then judged most perfect, when its operation is most perfect intelligence. And this is more perfect, the more forms of things it attains. For it becomes more sublime, swifter, and more lu-
**B**
cid. Wherefore the intellect, by receiving the forms of all bodies, not only does not lose or diminish its own, but (which is contrary to the nature of a body) it greatly perfects—

--- Page 315 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VIII. 117

It reduces those concepts of our mind, which always shine within us concerning the principles of sciences, to concepts either more known or prior. Where resolution ceases: division ceases. Where division ends: perfect simplicity is possessed. Therefore it must be concluded that the primary concepts of the mind are simple: and that those things which are known from them are partly such that, although they seem to be divided, they are nevertheless known by a reason by which they are least divided, and therefore their notion is indivisible. Partly they are such that they are entirely simple: and therefore their perception is simple, if only the intellect is equal to the things understood. If concepts, notions, perceptions are simple, the intelligible forms from which these arise are also simple. If this is so, the mind also is simple: which is the subject of simple things. And since the simpler something is, the more indissoluble it is: and the mind attains the highest degree of simplicity, as we have said, in knowing: it also attains the highest degree of indissoluble nature in living. For intelligence is the reflection of life into itself. Therefore, if through intelligence, which follows life, it attains the highest simplicity: which precedes an indissoluble nature: much more through life, which is prior to intelligence, it attains an indissoluble degree, posterior to simplicity itself.

Fifth reason. If the mind is a body, it understands by touching, and by traversing. Chapter 5.

IF the mind is a body, or a form diffused through the magnitude of a body, it has two things in itself, as we have judged elsewhere: namely, a point and breadth: and it is subject to the same conditions as a body. Therefore it will not comprehend things to be understood otherwise than by touching them, and by expanding itself through them, and by traversing them like a body. Therefore it will be said to touch either by a point alone: so that it may understand, or by breadth alone, or by both. If it uses a point alone, and needs touch for knowing: it will not know the magnitudes of things: for through a point it touches points, not magnitudes. But even if it were to touch, it would never, however, know them entirely, either as a whole or as wholes. For points in it are infinite. Infinite also in magnitude. The accumulation of all those is the intellect: of these

nor will it ever be corrupted. For corruption arises from the treacheries of matter.

Ninth reason. Minds embrace each other, bodies by no means.
Chapter 9.

F **T**wo corporeal things cannot contain each other in mutual embraces. For that which contains another by quantity is greater than that which is contained. But one body cannot be at once larger and narrower than another single body. Thus the sphere of Saturn encompasses and contains the sphere of Jupiter: not vice versa. But one mind contains another, and is equally contained by the same. Indeed, my mind considers yours: yours, mine. Therefore, our minds, by considering each other, in turn grasp each other: by grasping, they understand: by understanding, they embrace. And (what is greater) one mind embraces all, when it considers the nature of all minds. Wherefore if any mind beholds any other mind: which it can indeed do, if it pays attention: any mind is comprehended by any other mind. But any body cannot be enclosed by any body. If any species of things is immortal, it follows that a singular substance which equates itself to its own species, is immortal. But any mind, if it happens, looks into any other: and in each it discerns the species of all: where by a reflexive act, which is cognition, it equates itself to its own species. Therefore, also by a direct act, which is life, it first equated itself to the same. If this is so: it follows that either any mind has always been, or will be, just like the species of minds itself: or at least it will always be like it.

Tenth reason. The mind operates through all bodies, and above bodies.
Chapter 10.

G **S**ince form is the principle of operation, each thing acts according to its own kind: from which all things generate offspring similar to themselves, if they can, in species: but beyond its own kind, nothing acts. But neither do these lower things operate beyond their species (for a dog never generates a sheep) and much less do they operate something above their own species. For in what way will a dog procreate a human? Whence it happens: that a body acting-

--- Page 317 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VIII. 118

a line without breadth, a surface without depth, numbers without position, beauty without a mixture of ugliness. For thus it distinguishes these things separately by considering them: nor does it consider them otherwise than it receives them. But a corporeal form does not entirely receive these things separately in this way. If that clearly shows the soul to be simple and indivisible, which comprehends simple and indivisible things: much more clearly does this declare it, that whatever things would be simple or indivisible in themselves: and yet because they are joined with others, they become composite and divisible: the soul separates them from their opposites, and renders them entirely simple and indivisible. But it could not restore to them a simple and indivisible nature, unless it itself were simple and indivisible. Finally, if it restores purity to infected things, it itself is outside and above infection.

*Sixth reason. The intellect receives whatever it grasps according to its whole self:*
*which it would not do, if it were corporeal.*
Cap. 6.

[Large initial N]o body contains anything within itself, except by that equalization of quantity, by which it comprehends the whole thing with its whole self, but a part with a part, and a larger part of itself a larger part of the contained thing, a smaller part a smaller. [Marginal note: C]
The intellect does not grasp things themselves in this manner. For it grasps whatever it receives with its whole self. Indeed, it grasps in the same way that it understands. But it understands whatever it understands with its whole self. For if someone were to say that the intellect has two corporeal parts, of which one indeed grasps and understands a thing, the other not at all: we would refute him, asserting that the intellect is truly that part which grasps and understands the thing. (since the intellect is named from understanding) but that part which does not understand, is not the intellect. Therefore, that nature which is truly the intellect, grasps and knows any intelligible thing with its whole self. When therefore it understands the body of a human, it understands also the members of that body: with its whole self it knows the whole human body: with its whole self it knows any of its members. For he who compares any member to any other, and refers any members to the whole, it is necessary that the same [entity] knows individual members as well as the whole body. Nor

--- Page 318 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...nor would it comprehend incorporeal things. Therefore it is not a body: since, beyond any bodies, it apprehends even incorporeal things. But neither is it some form mixed with a body: for a mixed form, just as it becomes divisible through the division of the body, so it becomes qualified through the quality of the body. And therefore the mind would contract a certain quality for itself from the body, by which, determined to a certain species of corporeal things, it would know only a certain species of corporeal things: just as sight is contracted to colors through the eye. And it would not grasp very similar forms, as we said: nor even very dissimilar ones. And this is Aristotle's opinion, approved by the Platonists. But the Platonists add that if the mind were mixed, it would neither grasp incorporeal things: because what is mixed does not comprehend pure things: nor would it aspire to attain something separate from the body, otherwise it would aspire to be separated from the body and dissolved. Nor would it know otherwise than it is moved: as a material power usually does. But now it does not know as it is moved, but as it itself produces species for itself: thus it abstracts, reasons, and reflects upon itself almost without end. Nor should any Epicurean here object to our ears, denying that the intellect grasps incorporeal things. Indeed, it always desires those things, and grasps them alone with the greatest pleasure, as if they were most similar to itself. Nor does it only desire and grasp those things: but it also creates them. For what else do we strive for now in these discussions, but to fashion some thing with the hands (so to speak) of our mind, most alien from the body? Which we have already fashioned and are fashioning, and we handle it with those very hands of the mind: and before we fashioned it, we foresaw that it was to be fashioned. Indeed, when we first decided to demonstrate that the soul is incorporeal: we already saw some degree of incorporeal nature somewhere, to which we wished to lead the soul. What do we do daily in disputing? As often as we assert that something exists: which indeed exists, but truly has no length, breadth, depth, or any quality, or figure, then certainly we create a certain spirit in our mind above the body, and the passions of the body. There indeed is our mind, where it gives birth: it gives birth, I say, to offspring very similar to itself, in no way superior in its substance. **A** Therefore our mind transcends bodies and the conditions of bodies. Wherefore it is neither confined by place, nor circumscribed by the limits of time.

Indeed. It penetrates their substances: and observes all things in individual ones, while in simple things, through composition, it sees mixed things, and in mixed things, through resolution, it perceives simple things. Therefore the mind seems to be in all things in such a way that in individual things it is all things itself. Again, it is outside and above all corporeal things. Otherwise it could not separate these from incorporeal things, and discern those from these. If it is in all corporeal things: it commands all things, and even outside all things, it commands over all by nature. Therefore it is not cast down from its state by the violence of any body.

Eighth reason. Form is universal in the mind. Such a form cannot exist in the body. Chapter 8.

**C**orpus, and form extended through the body, are so (so to speak) material, and bound to a particular place and time [Marginal note: C], that they have no universal power. For the more something approaches corporeal matter, the more confined it is: the further it departs, the more expansive it becomes. Therefore if the intellect were a body: or a form diffused through it: all forms received by it, even if they were universal in themselves, would at least become entirely particular and material in it. For forms in a subject that is bound by the passions of matter retain no power to represent anything universal. Thus, whatever the intellect might think: it would conceive through a material form, bound by singular conditions. [Marginal note: D] Since the true operation of anything follows the form of the operating thing, the intellect operating through such a form, that is, conceiving, would operate only singularly. And what the operation is like, such is always the work. Therefore the intellect, thinking singularly, would think only singular things: and would not know anything common and universal. Indeed, it would revolve one man, for example, Socrates or Plato, within itself: but by no means the human nature equally common to them. Nor would it establish a universal rule in morals and arts for many things: nor would it ever establish a law regarding the actions of many men. If the mind, even without choice and daily use, gives birth to universal forms within itself, it must be that it is their natural source and natural receptacle. Forms of this kind are by no means bound to any particular matter: therefore the mind is not bound to matter: nor—

Thirteenth Argument: The Mind is not changed by receiving forms. Chapter 13.

A body cannot extend its power beyond its own kind, and much less be-

First, that it would neither receive nor conceive the forms of many bodies. [H]
Indeed, it would not grasp the forms of bodies similar to itself, because it would already possess them.
For how can fire receive the form of another fire? But it would by no
means conceive or produce the forms of dissimilar bodies. For every nature produces something similar to itself. But for it to
understand, it is necessary that it first receive the form of the thing to be understood,
then from that, conceive the definition or reason of the thing. Only then is understanding perfected. Therefore, the intellect would know few bodies, if it were a body; since it receives the form of no similar

and conceives equally. But if it could somehow happen that it receives or conceives some corporeal form,

If it receives a form from elsewhere, it will draw it into its own nature.
If it conceives from itself, it will bring forth according to its own nature.
Therefore, through any form received or even conceived by it,

Therefore, it can be everywhere, and always. For this reason, nothing prevents it from being perpetual.

**Eleventh reason. The mind profits by stillness, the body by motion.**
**Chapter 10.**

[B]
A body never receives a new form, except through motion. For through alteration (as physicists say) form is introduced into matter. But the mind neither receives forms through motion, nor is it moved by receiving them. The more it maintains quiet from all motion of disturbances and affairs, the more it profits by contemplating. Here also appears its eternity: because by its very nature it desires only the contemplation of truth, and therefore stillness: without which contemplation is not perfected. But the body profits by motion: because it is born through motion. Therefore, that which profits by standing (stillness) depends on stillness: and therefore has a stable and perpetual substance.

**Twelfth reason. What are contraries in matter, are not contraries in the mind.**
**Chapter 12.**

[C]
The forms of contrary elements, while they are in matter, are contrary to each other: because they repel each other, and destroy each other. In the mind they are not contraries: because there they not only do not repel each other, but also help each other. Indeed, our mind simultaneously holds the forms of contrary elements, when it considers the elements simultaneously. It also simultaneously comprehends good and evil: useful and useless: beautiful and ugly: light and darkness: voice and silence: sweet and bitter: and the rest: and from the knowledge of one contrary, it judges the other more truly. Therefore, it is not corporeal: nor properly corruptible. For that which is corrupted: for the most part [D] is corrupted by its contrary. But what can be contrary to the mind, which has such power over contraries, that it removes contrariety from them, and reconciles hostile things with its own peace? Nor again is that corruptible, which is separated from its preservers. For if it reconciles alien and contrary things with alien and contrary things: much more does it apply itself to its own causes and preservers.

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**
*Thirteenth Argument: The Mind is not changed by receiving forms.*
*Cap. 13.*

[Large initial C] The form of any body, when truly received by another body, renders that which receives it entirely such as is that body from which the form is imparted: just as when the flame of fire is received by wood, it makes the wood hot and fiery. But that flame, shining back in a distant mirror, does not render the mirror hot or fiery, because it is not truly received by it, since, due to the distance, it is not prepared for the true flame of fire. Indeed, in no way is that little flame, that is, that image of the flame, since it is spiritual, fixed in the body of the mirror, but in the spiritual light of the sun, which surrounds the surface of the mirror. But images of this kind of things are made not by those bodies whose images they are (for a body does not procreate anything incorporeal), but by the spiritual light diffused around bodies. The light itself also is not born from the globe of the sun, but from the soul of the sun, whose light, though invisible within itself, when diffused further, is invisible; yet in which the soul itself is conspicuous. For as it pleases the Orphics and Heraclitus, light is nothing other than visible soul, whence through this all things revive; but soul is invisible light. But lest we digress further, the forms or images of bodies are not in mirrors. But the mind receives the forms of all bodies when it judges concerning bodies. Does it truly receive? Truly indeed. For as it receives, so it judges. It judges truly. Therefore, it truly receives. It receives from itself (as the Platonists believe) when, excited by the images of bodies, it brings forth into light the forms which lie hidden in the mind's recesses. Furthermore, where the form is more perfect, there it is also truer. And how much more perfect the form of bodies is in the mind than in the bodies themselves, we have declared elsewhere, and will declare. And hence it is clear that human nature in Plato or Socrates is proper to Plato alone and to Socrates alone. But that human nature which is conceived by the mind, when it considers the conditions of humans under one definition of man, has force for individual humans, since it embraces all. Furthermore, if the truth of each thing consists in pure integrity, or in integral purity, and the form in matter does not retain its integral force because of pas-

--- Page 325 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. VIII. 122

...the admixture of passions, and is surrounded by extraneous accidents: a truer thing is found in the mind, where the naturally inherent idea of the thing itself gives birth to the notion of the thing, indeed including all necessary elements, but entirely excluding superfluous ones.

The mind, therefore, so truly grasps the forms of bodies that it possesses them even more truly than the matter of bodies. Therefore, if it itself were something corporeal, it would become entirely such as bodies are. It would then become water when it understands water; fire when it understands fire. And because it simultaneously understands heat and cold, it would become contraries at the same time. But now it receives the forms of all things, and is not cast down from its own state; rather, it is perfected by receiving. From this it appears that the intellect is not corporeal. It also appears not to be mortal. For it receives whatever it receives in the way that it is. Its being is purely intellectual. Therefore, it receives nothing otherwise than by understanding. Through this kind of reception it not only does not diminish, but also profits. Therefore, it receives nothing from elsewhere that might change and destroy it; and what is greater, it gains so much in receiving all forms, that it even seems to gain in evils. If it becomes so much more perfect the more it knows, certainly it is more perfect if it discerns the privations, defects, and evils of things, than if it ignores them. Therefore, what are evil and harmful in themselves [Marginal note: G] become good and wholesome in the mind: So far is that nature from being destroyed by evil and harmful things, which so converts evils into goods, that all things are good to it.

Fourteenth reason. The operation of the body tends towards a composite thing, that of the mind towards simple things. Cap. 14.

The operation of each thing always follows the very being of the thing, so that the operation belongs to that whose being it is; and the mode of operating is the same as that of being; [Marginal note: H] and the work to which the operation is directed becomes similar to the operator. In things composed of matter and corporeal form, being is not proper to matter or to form, but to the whole composite made from the conjunction of both. Therefore, the operation is properly that of the composite itself; wherefore it operates in a composite manner, and produces a composite work. We observe this in elements, plants, animals, which indeed generate composite works just as they themselves are. If the intelle-
Q ij

--- Page 326 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...if the intellect were some body composed of matter and form: since its operation is intelligence, this very intelligence would always terminate in some composite thing: whence it would never understand anything other than composite things. But now our mind so far excels natural composition, that it resolves composite bodies into matter and form: and thinks of each separately. But each of these is simple in itself. And in this its excellence is especially seen, that it comprehends as true those things which in matter are in a certain way false, such as figures, and the principles of figures. What are impure in matter: it discerns as pure. For the qualities which are mixed with each other in matter, and tainted by contraries: it judges them according to their proper reasons. What are many in themselves, it beholds as one, as if infinite humans under one species. What are mobile in themselves, it contemplates as stable, when it gathers together the parts of time which flow in themselves, and connects the past and future to the present. What are distant in themselves, it very often beholds as united: when it sees the whole world in a point. Neither intervals of time, nor spaces of places restrain the mind's intuition. What (so to speak) are dead as if living. Indeed, stones which lack life, the mind possesses as living within itself: when it compares them to the first life from which they were made. What are corruptible as if perpetual: when the mind, by its intuition, exempts individual bodies which are subject to place and time, from places and times. From all these things it is gathered that the intellect is neither something corporeal, since it operates far differently than bodies: nor is it impure, tainted, dispersed, mutable, corruptible: since indeed, by a certain power of its own, it frees even those things which are such from such passions.

**Fifteenth reason. The action of the mind terminates in action: the action of the body in body. Chapter 15.**

[Marginal note: A] [N]o body's action properly terminates in the action itself, but passes into external matter. For if it were to terminate in action, that action would remain in the operator, where it would operate on itself: for example, fire would heat itself. Which cannot be done by a body: because if a body does not act from itself, also...

--- Page 327 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL. BOOK VIII. 123

it does not act upon itself. Again, if whatever a body does, it does by moving: certainly, since they cannot move themselves, it cannot act upon itself. But we see the operation of the mind, namely intelligence itself, terminate in itself: nor does it do anything externally by itself: unless perhaps it sometimes moves the will, which, by moving the arms, produces some external work, such as what had been thought. But we say that sense in a way flows outside itself: Because it is moved from elsewhere: it perceives external things: it operates for the sake of an external end: nor is it conscious of itself. The mind, on the contrary, moves itself freely, and inspects its own things, it operates for its own sake. Therefore, essence, according to Plato, is called 'status' [Marginal note: B] (standing/state): because if it is without life, it is inert: life, 'motion': because it now proceeds into action: mind, 'reflection': because without this, life would flow out into external work. But the mind stops the vital motion of essence in itself: it reflects it into the essence by a certain self-awareness. It also draws all other things to itself: insofar as it considers things rather as they are in the mind itself, than as they exist externally. It is also called infinite reflection: because the human mind terminates in its own operation not only once, but also innumerable times: when it perceives itself to understand something: and recognizes that it perceives: and when it wills itself to will something: and wills that it wills itself to will: and so on in the same way: where either one operation terminates infinitely in another, or the same is replicated in itself innumerable times. From this it is clear that the intellect is not only incorporeal but also immortal. Indeed, through its own operation, it always forms and perfects itself, always by understanding and willing. This is nothing other than continually making, or preserving, or renewing itself: which indeed the Apostle Paul called by the name of daily renewal. Whence it happens that it never departs or is absent from its perfecter or preserver, since it can never be absent from itself: and therefore it is always formed and perfected. Furthermore, if the end of natural generation is a certain immortality: much more is the end of intellectual generation immortality. But [Marginal note: C] because nature generates offspring outside itself: its immortality is fulfilled in the succession of those being born. But because the mind generates in itself both itself and other things: insofar as it conceives the reasons of both itself and all other things, when it either understands itself or other things: it follows that the power of this immortality resides in the mind itself, the generat-
Q iij

--- Page 328 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...the generating mother is preserved. Here also lies a certain argumentation of this kind. It is more excellent to fare well than simply to be.
**D** Whoever, therefore, provides well-being for himself, can much more provide being for himself. The intellect seems to give itself well-being when it forms and perfects itself both by speculation and by morals. Therefore, it can also provide being for itself according to its form in such a way that it never ceases to be.
**E** I omit what Proclus says, that the soul, since it is the principle of generation, so generates and vivifies itself, that it has its essence from itself. And in summary, concerning every indivisible substance existing in its own essence, he affirms that it both produces and contains itself. But concerning every divisible substance, even concerning heaven itself, he says it is necessarily produced and contained from elsewhere. But he himself may see to this.
Moreover, another such argumentation lies hidden. When the intellect first comprehends and loves its own operation, and then its own power and substance: then undoubtedly it acts upon itself. Therefore, also through itself. For nothing is interposed as a medium between the intellect and itself. Add to this that just as the body, because it does not act from itself, therefore does not operate upon itself: so the intellect, because it operates upon itself: is therefore considered to operate from itself. If it acts from itself upon itself, therefore also through itself. For if both terms of action are in it: then also the medium. What then prevents the intellect, separated from the body, from operating and living? especially since its operation, which is completed from itself upon itself through itself, necessarily occurs: and resides in itself? But this will be explained more clearly thus. If the mind's operation properly ends in the mind itself, the mind itself is in a certain way the end of its own operation.
**F** But the end of anything is the same as its beginning: since all things desire their origin, and propose it to themselves as the end of their own motion. Therefore, the substance of the mind is the principle of its own operation: therefore it operates through itself: which our Plato calls "moving itself." As it operates, so it lives. For life is an interior operation. Therefore it lives through itself. As it lives: so also it is. For life is the first act of existence. Therefore it exists similarly through itself. What prevents it from being always: since it is the cause of itself? A cause, I say, not efficient, but formal: by whose virtue being is attributed and preserved. Quality and life, whose every operation flows out into other things: necessarily, according to its nature, fails in four parts,

end,

--- Page 329 ---
**On the Immortality of the Soul. Book VIII. 124**

First, because by flowing out it wavers, it needs an external support.
Secondly, by flowing away it is weakened. Thirdly, while it flows into others, it is defiled by external things. Fourthly, because of its need, weakness, and defilement, it is sometimes forced to flow away from its own nature. If this is so: it follows that rational life, which flows back into itself, sustains itself, is not weakened, is not defiled, does not flow away. Rightly, just as life which is entirely forced to flow out of itself, while it departs from life, tends and is consumed into death: so life which overflows into itself, grows and is perfected into life. Finally, if a more abundant motion is an indication of a more abundant life: rational life, which exercises, fulfills, and terminates every kind of motion: also fulfills every kind of living: and therefore neither the privation of life is mixed with it, nor any condition subject to death. However, that it exercises all species of motions in the body, fulfills the exemplars of all motions in itself, terminates all motion in itself, and its own principle through the reflections of the mind itself, we have declared elsewhere. [Marginal note: A]

**\*Sixteenth Reason. Corporeal form does not have infinite power: the mind does. Chapter 16.\***

[Marginal note: G]
It is agreed among physicists that corporeal form, especially elemental form, is so limited that it can in no way have any infinite and indefatigable power: But the mind wanders without limit, and is never wearied. In principle, in itself, it is as if without limit: For it understands itself. Therefore, its understanding, proceeding from the very substance of the mind, revolves back into the same. Revolution is infinite motion. For it does not aim at any external end to be acquired, by which it might rest: but it embraces its own substance, eager for itself. But its eagerness for itself is never extinguished. Therefore, the substance which, by desire for itself, once began to encounter itself everywhere, and by circling itself, to contemplate itself everywhere: with the same desire perpetually instigating it: will perpetually embrace itself similarly at will. Therefore, the motion of the intellect: since it is circular, revolving into itself, insofar as it is intellectual, is certainly eternal. It also lacks an end, as we have said: for the reason that intelligence is infinitely replicated.

--- Page 330 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

For he who understands either himself or anything else whatsoever, can, just as he understands the thing itself, so too understand his own understanding, and likewise another and another without end: while he both recognizes the thing, and perceives that he recognizes it. Again, that he thus perceives, does not escape him: and similarly without end. Such a course of understanding is accompanied by that rational appetite which they call will. This [will] indeed wills itself, or anything else whatsoever: and wills to will itself: and again wills what it wills: and similarly thereafter.

Furthermore, it divides bodies into very many parts, and the parts into particles. It increases numbers upon numbers without end. It discovers innumerable modes of figures, and their mutual proportions, and also comparisons of numbers: it extends a line beyond the sky, beyond any limit on all sides. It produces time into the past without beginning, into the future without end. And not only does it think of another time more ancient and longer beyond all time, but also always thinks of another place more ample beyond all place. It also fashions innumerable degrees in individual qualities. [Marginal note: A]

Moreover, the mind is not content with one certain kind of things, as the senses are. Not with colors alone, like sight: not with voices alone, like hearing: but it runs through all things: through all things, I say, not only those which are, but those which were, or will be. And not only that, but also through those things which neither are, nor ever were, nor will be. For it devises many things which perhaps could be, but will never happen: and many things which perhaps could never be, it itself imagines. Although those things which the mind paints by itself within itself seem no less to exist in the nature of things, than those it paints through language in the air, or through the hand on a wall. It also always fabricates new forms of things by its own power and in a certain order, and again renews others.

Does it not also, after it has gradually ascended through the spheres of the world, gradually consider angels in such a way that it always sees one higher than another: nor does it ever find one so sublime that it cannot find another greater by at least one degree, and again another by another degree? And it does this for as long as it declares each angel to be finite, from which, for any finite spirit, it finds another higher. And thus it would progress without end: unless it itself imposed a limit upon itself, and concluded that there is some infinite spirit, which surpasses every angel, both that which can exist and that which can be thought of, by innumerable...

--- Page 331 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK VIII. 125

...and concludes that there is some infinite spirit, which surpasses every angel, both that which exists and that which can be conceived, by innumerable degrees. What progresses infinitely? What in a certain way terminates infinite progress? What reaches that infinite limit of progressing? The Mind certainly does these things. Therefore, the mind's power is in a certain way infinite. Which also appears in this, that it not only discovers infinite act, which is God: but also infinite potential, which is matter subject to God: and suitable for receiving innumerable forms from it. Hence also we find an infinite vicissitude of generation: which can be poured out from infinite act into infinite potential through infinite time. It appears again from this, that it grasps the universal reasons of things. But under every universal, whether species or genus, innumerable things are contained. It gathers innumerable men under the human species in perpetual succession, and likewise infinite individuals under other [species] into one species, many species into one genus, many genera into one essence, one essence into divine unity, truth, and goodness. Conversely, from this one, it gradually descends into an infinite multitude. A truly wondrous power: which renders the infinite one.

But who would deny that it runs? when we comprehend creation, which comes into being from non-being, and destruction, which happens conversely, by the most certain reasons, and we describe the nature of both extremes: and we grasp by intellect the power of common being itself, which communicates to things born by its progression through in-
D numerable modes of being. Finally, to speak summarily: that the mind possesses a somehow infinite power will be able to serve as testimony to us, because hunger of the body, and thirst, and sleep, are quickly satisfied by a small thing, the ardor of the mind is never extinguished, whether it regards human things or divine things. If it desires human things: what accumulation of riches, what extent of empire terminates this? If divine, it is filled by no knowledge of created and finite things. Rightly it never rests, unless it grasps infinite God: who fills its infinite capacity flowing from Himself. If this (capacity) were finite, it would either be filled by some finite thing, or at least its thirst for both (human and divine) would be relieved. But now, through the acquisition of any finite things whatsoever, it is not only not extinguished, but burns more ardently: because the more it approaches infinite God by grasping more things, through a certain preparation, the more it burns with its own fire, having become closer: and thus it runs more rapidly, now very close to the infinite end of its own motion. Which the element of fire also does, when it returns to its own sphere. The stone also does the same more evidently, when it descends from on high: for the closer it gets to the earth, the more vehemently it is carried down to the earth. Who would say that the mind is an elemental body, or anything corporeal, if it possesses infinite power? Power, I say, both of persevering and grasping, and of embracing and traversing: whether it has this (power) by itself, or (to speak more truly) by a certain divine amplification: inasmuch as, namely, the absolute infinity of God implants and continuously preserves intellectual and vital infinity in minds and souls immediately dependent on it: and recalls them from an infinite beginning to an infinite end. For if it is accustomed everywhere for some similar communicated quality to flow from an absolute
E quality: what wonder is it for such an infinity, or such an infinity, to flow somewhere from absolute infinity? But especially into minds and souls, through which the Platonists believe that in the world also an infinite succession of time and generation proceeds. Who then will be so mad as to wish the mind to have a-

PLATONIC THEOLOGY
On the immortality of souls, by the same
author, Ficino,

BOOK NINE.

*It is proven by rational virtue that the soul is not only an individual form, but also does not depend on the body, so that immortality may be more clearly demonstrated. First reason: because the mind reflects upon itself.*

Chapter I.

[Large decorative initial H] Up to this point, we have proven by rational virtue that the soul is an individual and immortal form. Next, it must be proven that it does not depend on the body: from which immortality is properly concluded. Divisible things do not reflect upon themselves at all. But if someone should say that some divisible thing revolves upon itself: we will immediately ask thus. Whether one part of this thing is turned into another, or a part into the whole, or the whole into a part, or rather the whole into the whole itself? If the first is granted: not the same thing is turned into itself: since the parts are diverse among themselves. If the second or third is conceded: the same follows. For a part is one thing, and the whole is another. Only the fourth mode seems to remain, that the whole is turned into the whole. This happens no otherwise than if all parts are turned into all parts. Granted. Finally, this kind of conversion having been made, we will ask: whether any part in the thing remains outside another, or differing from another, or none. If it remains, one part will be in this position or manner, another in that: and thus they will not yet have been converted into each other.
A

--- Page 334 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

But if none, certainly no part in that thing will be distant or differ from a part. What is such, is entirely indivisible, so that it is constituted neither from parts of quantity, nor from matter and form. Therefore, either something does not reflect upon itself: or if it reflects, it is indivisible. We have said elsewhere that the soul revolves into itself in four ways, namely through the intellect into its own nature, when it seeks, finds, and considers itself: Through the will into the same nature, when it desires and loves itself. Through the intellect into the very act of understanding, when it both understands a thing, and understands itself to understand. Through the will into the act of willing, when it both wills something, and wills itself to will. And these four [B] wheels Plato attributes to the chariot of the soul: and I believe this to be that fourfold fount of perpetual nature, which Pythagoras says was bestowed upon the souls of men by Jove. If no divisible thing returns into itself, assuredly this rational quadriga of ours, which runs back into itself through four wheels: and that innermost fount itself, which flows back into itself through four streams, is simple, and utterly indivisible. But a conversion of this kind is not from body to body, but from soul to soul: which has been proven to be indivisible both from many other things above, and here from the fact that it returns into itself. Therefore, such a conversion is free from the body: since it neither originates from it, nor returns into it. Much more is the substance of the soul free from the body, if the conversion, which is its motion, is free from the body. Therefore, the rational soul in no way depends on the body in its being: just as neither in moving and operating. Likewise, if it reflects upon itself through operation, it also reflects through its essence. Thus the essence of the soul is converted into itself. Moreover, where the conversion of anything occurs, from there is also its origin: and vice versa. Therefore, the soul which turns into itself, is from itself. From itself, I say, in three principal ways. First, according to form: because it is not formed by another form: otherwise it would not return to itself, but to that other form. Secondly, according to its foundation: because it is not sustained by another. For this form, which leans upon itself when it strives towards itself, does not lean upon another. Thirdly, according to simplicity: because it is not composed of parts. For in what way is that form unfolded through the surface of parts, which is entirely folded back into its own center? What is thus from itself, is always: because what ceases to be, does so either because from a formative cause

Third argument. The mind resists the body. Chapter 3.

G   No thing can spontaneously resist its own origin; other-
wise, it would spontaneously be carried to its own destruction, which neces-
sarily follows from the loss of its origin. Moreover, whatever
effect something produces, it does so by the power and aid of its origin. If,
therefore, it were to fight against its cause, in that struggle, that cause
would be at odds with itself. The soul resists and opposes our
body, indeed, all bodies. Therefore, it does not derive its origin from any
H   body. Its two principal functions are: to contemplate, and to deliberate.
In both, it resists bodies. First, let us see how it resists in contemplation. In many
ways daily, external bodies, variously disposed, move the instruments of our
body assigned to the senses in such a way that they deceive for a time: which
fallacy reason corrects and amends: as we have explained more
fully elsewhere, where reason judges differently than either the
external body indicates, or the proper body reports:

often judges in a contrary manner: in which matter it condemns the affection of its own body as well as that of others. Let us set aside for now the speculations about other things; let us take up the highest contemplation of the Highest, so that we may know how much in it the mind refutes corporeal nature. Imagination follows the external senses; the senses follow the disposition of its own body and of other bodies. Therefore, we attribute the judgment of the senses and imagination to the disposition of bodies, and we say that it occurs according to corporeal affection. When our mind, desiring to find out what God is, inquires of such teachers: imagination, a teacher and a too-rash craftsman, devises some statue from five materials which the external senses have offered to it as the most beautiful of all others, received from the world, yet in such a way that it renders those materials somehow more excellent than it received them from the world through the senses.

Therefore, imagination offers us a light so clear that no other can appear brighter. So vast that none is greater, and almost diffused through immense emptiness: which is adorned with innumerable colors, and revolves in a circle: because of which revolution it resounds with the sweetest melodies, both filling and soothing the ears. May it [Marginal note: A] smell of the most pleasant odors. May it also abound in all flavors, which can be imagined as the sweetest of all. Soft to the touch in a wonderful way: delicate, smooth, and temperate. Imagination proclaims this to be God. The body of the world gives us nothing more beautiful. No corporeal sense either touches anything better, or announces anything more excellent. Imagination, friend of the senses, fashions nothing more sublime. But reason, meanwhile, looking down from the highest watchtower of the mind at the games of imagination, thus proclaims: Beware, little soul, beware the deceptions of that empty sophistry. Do you seek God? Receive a light so much clearer than the light of the sun, as the light of the sun is brighter than darkness: to which, if the light of the sun were compared, even if it were a thousand times and a thousand times brighter, it would seem a shadow. And also receive it so much more subtle, that it escapes the keenness of sight. Nor should you diffuse it through emptiness, lest it consist of parts: and thus require the support of parts, and a place. Gather the whole (if you can) into a point: so that from this infinite unity it may be infinitely powerful. Let it then (if you please) be present everywhere: not scattered in place, but whole, standing by any place. Nor

--- Page 338 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

be tinged with a manifold variety of colors. For pure light is more splendid than colored light. Nor let it revolve or sound. For I do not wish it to be moved, or struck, or broken. And I consider stability to be more perfect than motion. Remove also odors, tastes, and tangible softness: lest it be composed of a coarser nature. Here shines that which no place contains. Here sounds that which time does not snatch away. Here smells that which no breath scatters. Here tastes that which voracity does not diminish. Here clings that which satiety does not tear apart. Do you desire again to behold the face of God? Behold the entire universe full of the sun's light. Behold the light in the matter of the world, full of all forms of all things, and changeable. Please subtract matter from the light, leave the rest. Suddenly you have the soul: namely, incorporeal light, all-formed, mutable. Remove again change from this animal light: you have now obtained an angelic intellect, namely, incorporeal light, all-formed, invariable. Remove from this that diversity by which any form is diverse from the light, and is infused into the light from elsewhere: so that the essence of light and of any form may be the same, and the light itself may form itself: and through its forms may form all things. This light shines infinitely: because it shines by its own nature: nor is it tinged or contracted by the mixture of another. It is through all things: because it is in nothing. It is in nothing, so that it may shine abundantly through all things. It lives from itself: and grants life to all: inasmuch as its shadow, such as this light of the sun is, alone is life-giving in bodies. It perceives everything: and bestows sense, if its shadow excites all senses in all things. Finally, it loves each individual thing, if individual things are most truly its own. Therefore, what is the light of the sun? The shadow of God. Therefore, what is God? God is the Sun of the sun. The light of the sun is God in the body of the world. God is the sun above angelic intellects. This is yours, O soul, this is your God. Phantasia had shown you its shadow. Such is the shadow of God, that it is the most beautiful of sensible things. Of what kind do you think the light of God is? If the shadow of God shines so much, how much does the light of God shine? You love the light of the sun everywhere above all others: indeed, alone. Love God alone: O soul, shine alone. Love infinitely the infinite light of the benevolent God. You will shine now: and you will be delighted infinitely. Seek therefore, I beg, his face: and you will rejoice forever. But do not be moved, I beg, to touch it: because it is stability itself. Do not be distracted by various things so that you may grasp:

--- Page 339 ---
...that you may grasp it: because it is unity itself. Cease motion: gather the multitude: you will immediately attain God, you who have long ago thoroughly attained Him. In this investigation, O immortal God, how much the mind resists all bodies: how much it destroys their images and deceptions? how much it condemns imagination, and the senses, companions of bodies? Indeed, just as it is a substance by itself, drawing no origin from any [marginal note: C] body, so it sometimes performs its own work by itself without any aid of bodies, nay rather (which is more wonderful) against any contrivances of bodies. Certainly, this would never separate itself by its operation from all bodily stain, unless it were much more alien in essence from every bodily origin. And because it cannot resist the universal nature of bodies by any bodily force (for a part does not rise above the whole), it follows that it acts by its own proper force in the present without the aid of bodily things: and therefore much more in the future it can accomplish this. How the mind resists the body by contemplating, we have already said enough. Let us say next how much in deliberating.

Often when the stomach is hungry, or the lung is thirsty, or the brain is heavy with sleep, or the genital members are swelling with semen, the bodily sense, a companion, invites to food, drink, sleep, and coitus. It incites, I say, or rather, it announces the body's incitements to the soul. But reason, for the sake of contemplation or virtue, judges that one must abstain from these: and as it pleases, we often abstain. When insult or injury is inflicted, blood around the heart is kindled for vengeance. Then the moving force of the soul, companion and guest of the body, moves feet and hands for avenging: but reason sometimes, for the sake of peace and leisure, commands to stop and restrains. When dangers are often presented, the heart trembles: but reason commands to meet the battle for the sake of defending the homeland: whence even with an unwilling heart, one goes against enemies. But the ends for which reason thus deliberates are incorporeal: namely truth and virtue. When our Plato, a heavenly man, for the sake of taming the body, chose the unhealthy place of the Academy in [marginal note: D] Attica to be inhabited, did not his soul oppose the nature of the body? When Xenocrates, beloved disciple of Plato, and Origen, their follower, castrated themselves so that they might completely extinguish the fires of lust: did not the unconquered soul declare war on the members of the body? Before these, the Magi of the Persians, the Egyptians

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

priests, Pythagorean philosophers, to enervate Venus (sexual desire), abstained from wine and meat. I pass over those ancient priests consecrated to the Great Mother or to Saturn. The former castrated themselves, the latter tortured themselves. I pass over the early Christians, than whom the world never saw anything stronger, anything more wonderful. Therefore, let no one object to us that there were few in the past, or that there are very few today, who resist the body's affections: nay, rather, we all resist daily, some for the sake of health, others for honor, others for peace, others for justice, the contemplation of God, or blessedness.

[Left margin:] A

And even if we never broke the body's impulses, the struggle itself, which is continuous within us, would still be enough to show that the soul resists the body. If there were no other nature in us than the corporeal, immediately when a bodily affection drew us to something, we would rush forward like brute beasts, nor would we have any hesitation or deliberate whether that to which the body entices us should be done. For nothing fights with itself. Yet there is almost always a struggle in us, brought upon us by the whole body. Therefore, there is something in us besides the body itself, separated from its root. Separated, I say, both from the nature of all humors and elements, so that it can resist all the inclinations of these and transcend them by thought and affection; and also from all celestial nature, infused into these humors by heaven itself and brought to their property. So that it can sometimes also oppose celestial inclinations, which astrologers themselves concede to us, and always conceive and cultivate a certain substance far superior to heaven. I pass over the fact that whatever is effected by the corporeal and mobile power of heaven is both corporeal and entirely mobile, and cannot surpass corporeal and mobile nature. Therefore, the soul can live separately both from elemental nature and from celestial nature infused into the elements. But if any of the Platonists should say that it (the soul) is always in a celestial vehicle, we will respond that the soul does not depend on the vehicle, but the vehicle depends on the soul, and that the eternal soul, among the Platonists, always vivifies the eternal vehicle. But let us return to our established order. Nor should it disturb us that the soul often obeys the body, because it does not obey by force, but by love, with which it is affected towards the body, living through itself, as if it were a son and its own work. *Fourth argument. The soul operates freely. Chapter 4.*

But most of all, we will know that the soul does not arise in any way
from the human body, if we consider how free it is. [Marginal note: C]

...judgment, if we comprehend it by its own reason. For that which is bound to a body whose nature is determined, cannot have a free and unconstrained operation. Indeed, no action arises from some common consideration unless some particular judgment intervenes; because movements and actions occur concerning particulars. Just as when someone commonly considers physical exercise to be useful: although he considers it so, he is not yet exercising unless he first consults what the modes of exercise are, and which are more conducive. But when he has chosen one particular exercise out of many, then he undertakes the work. If walking: he walks; if riding: he rides. The intellect by its nature is occupied with the conception of universal principles. Therefore, for any action to arise from its apprehension, its universal conception must be led down to certain particulars. A universal notion, by its power, contains many, indeed infinite, singular things; for example, the common genus of exercising contains innumerable modes of exercise. Therefore, that universal notion can be derived to diverse singular things equally. A judgment about what is to be done follows this kind of derivation. Therefore, a diverse judgment can follow. And so the intellect's judgment about things to be done is not by its nature determined to one single thing. Therefore, it is free. Indeed, some things lack freedom of judgment [Marginal note: D] because they have no judgment at all, like plants. Others, although they have it, have it from nature determined to one single thing, like brute animals. For by natural estimation, a sheep judges a wolf to be harmful to itself, and flees; nor can it not flee, nature impelling it. By natural instinct, swallows are carried to building nests; bees to beehives; spiders to webs. Therefore, all animals of the same species always construct their things in the same way; nor do they ever learn; nor do they ever vary; because the natural species by which they are led is inherent from the beginning and remains the same. Humans, however, both learn and always vary their works; yet they have one nature from the beginning. Therefore, they are not drawn to action by nature, but they themselves conduct themselves otherwise at different times by their own counsel. For whence do we think it happens that trees and beasts never err in their certain movements, arts, and choices, but man very often does? Not indeed from the fact that intellect is inherent in them through...

--- Page 343 ---

more perfect, for they have no intellect at all: but because they are drawn by the never-erring divine intellect, while man is led by his own, which can err. [E] If he also at any time takes rest from his own actions, then he too is led by God and does not err: which is declared by prophecies and miracles. And if he were always led, like other things, he would err less than those, by as much as the instrument is more perfect. Conversely, if other things led themselves like man, they would err more, by as much as they have received a less perfect species. Therefore, since man does not have a judgment about things to be done determined by nature to one thing, he is necessarily free. That he judges freely, we infer from this: that he leads himself to judge. That he leads himself: from this, that he reflects upon his own judgment. That he reflects: from this, that he knows himself to judge, and defines judgment. Indeed, he obtains this freedom by the power of his intellect itself. [F] For the intellect apprehends not only this or that good, but the common good itself. And since the intellect moves the will through the form apprehended by itself; and in all things, the mover and the moved correspond to each other in proportion: the rational will is not determined by nature except to the common good itself. But under this common good, individual goods are contained. Therefore, whatever is offered to the will as good, the will can incline towards it, with no natural inclination preventing the contrary. It often prescribes for itself a way of life harmful to the body: it hates the body, weakens it, kills it: which beasts never do, whose every impulse and action serves the use of the body.
