The second sign is that the irrational soul never judges, desires, or pursues anything other than what pertains to the use of the body. For in every action of it, the end is the body's advantage. But the ultimate end in things is almost the same as the beginning. The beginning of fire is the concave of the moon; the concave of the moon is the end of fiery motion, because every cause acts and moves towards its own end. Therefore, in a brute, the principle of actions is the nature of the body or the soul. Not a pure soul, but a corporeal one; and as it serves the whole nature and the artificer of natural life, since the end of acting is to be preserved in corporeal nature and life.

The third (sign) is that a beast never regrets having acted in this way or that, nor does it retract or amend anything; which signifies that there is a single principle of acting there, since there is no resistance. Corporeal life certainly moves as its proper end. Therefore, nothing else proper is present there besides corporeal life to move it.

The fourth (sign) is that (as we said above) in the works of brutes of the same species there is no diversity. One spider does not weave a web differently than another. All swallows also make a nest similarly, and each one in the same way each year; just as all fire heats similarly, all stone descends similarly, all plants sprout similarly according to their species. For the nature of each thing is a certain single form affixed to itself, and a certain force implanted from the beginning; through which one and always similar (form/force), one work is always done and is similar. Therefore, the soul of beasts, following the instinct of nature, preserves the familiar tenor of its species. The same also happens to us H whenever reason is sluggish, and we live at the beck and call of the senses and imagination. But with reason awakened and attentive, we deliberate long in matters to be done; and we condemn the impulse of imagination; and we act differently than what the nature of either external bodies or our own members demands. And if ever we indulge them, we regret it, and we try to amend it, and we often tame and subdue the nature of the body. For we have in our mind a certain common exemplar of good things, to which, comparing individual things, whether we reject them, or approve them more or less, we ourselves are indeed not drawn by the things themselves or by the body, but rather drawing the things themselves to the exemplar, and the body to the mind. Therefore, even while the affection of things and of the body remains similar, we often choose dissimilarly, that is, differently at different times. And while it becomes dissimilar, we often choose similarly; indeed, almost at the same moment, because of various conjectures proposed by reason, even while bodily things remain similar, various and in a way contrary choices are made. For it happens through deliberation that we subject not the soul to things, but things to our soul,
[Marginal note: I] indeed, as Plotinus often says, and Proclus confirms. We have an indication of this in sciences and morals. In sciences, in this way: When we are content with the mere contemplation of truth, communicating nothing at all with the body, nor desiring to do anything outside ourselves, who does not see that that contemplation of ours is in no way dependent on the body? In morals, again, in this way: When we direct all the pursuits of life to our soul, to be adorned with morals, who does not understand then that the end of our duties is the soul, and therefore that the soul is their principle? The principles of these actions are not humors, because humors do not invite to anything against their body, and above bodies. Not heaven, which moves through humors. For the body of heaven, far removed, neither moves our four humors before it moves the four elements, nor will it move the soul unless the humors are agitated. But the soul opposes the agitation of the humors: while it despises their impulses with the intention of speculation, restrains them with the pursuit of morals, and breaks them with the industry of the arts. No one was more inclined by nature to love than Socrates, or to lust and drunkenness than Alciphon the Megarian; yet no one became more continent through study than they. Did not Xenocrates, Demosthenes, and Cleanthes repel the impediments of nature through diligence? If we resist humors, we also resist elements and heaven; indeed, even if we are not subjected to heaven, much less are we subjected to other bodies.

But that the human soul is not subject to heaven is evident from this: first, knowledge foresees future events; then, either prudence avoids them, or magnanimity disregards them, as if they pertain not at all to the human being himself, who is the soul itself, but to the prison of the soul. Furthermore, it uses prosperous fortune happily because of temperance, and adverse fortune best because of tolerance, so that both equally advance it towards virtue and salvation. But how then does it follow events that precede it, or necessarily undertake what it avoids by diligence? Or does it dread nature, which it often despises? Or is it overcome by good things, which it directs towards its own happiness? Or would it be overcome by evils, which it converts into good? Or is it compelled by some necessity, who, while willingly consenting with the divine will out of piety, makes even those things that are necessary and seem terrible, voluntary and light? We demonstrate the same again in this way, through intellect and will. First, thus through the intellect. A celestial body has a corporeal, singular, local, and temporal form. The form by which every mind understands is incorporeal, universal, and absolute. Therefore, this is not born from heaven. For a form that is enclosed somewhere does not generate an absolute form. And therefore heaven does not generate any form in the intellect. Does it perhaps generate intelligence in it? By no means. For intelligence follows form. Therefore, what cannot give form will not give intelligence. Indeed, no body at all understands anything through its own form. For such a form is entirely singular. Much less will it generate intelligence in another. Since therefore the intellect has neither its own action nor the principle of action from heaven, it is not subject to a celestial body; especially because our soul, according to that power by which it is joined to those things which are said to be above heaven, not only is not subject to heaven, but even presides over it. But insofar as it understands truth, it is joined to the angels who preside over heaven. For it understands to the extent that it obtains intellectual light from there. Thus, therefore, it is established that the intellect is not subject to heaven. Thus again it will be established that the will is not subject. Indeed, those things which happen by nature are led to their end by determined means, from which they almost always proceed in the same way. For nature is determined to one thing, but human choices tend to an end in diverse ways...

in morals as in arts. Moreover, those things which are of the same species in natural actions, which follow the species itself, differ minimally among themselves. For just as every swallow (as we said) similarly builds a nest, so every intellect similarly understands those first principles of arts and morals, which are known to each by nature. And every will similarly desires the good itself: because the will naturally desires the good. For this is the nature of man, **C** that just as the intellect relates to the principle of speculation, which is that which is everywhere manifestly true, so the will relates to the principle of action, which is the good itself: and we necessarily assent to both. Choice, however, is a certain action following the human species: just like the discourse of reason. For these two are proper to man. Therefore, just as if men were to reason by instinct of nature, the opinion of all men would be the same in individual matters: so if they were to choose guided by nature, the choice of all would be one. But now, some choose different things in different ways: just as they also judge variously in reasoning. Wherefore the heavens do not move our will by instinct of nature: they do, however, move the body. Sense follows or announces the motion of the body. Hence the will is often enticed. However, this enticement is not a necessary cause of choice: because the will sometimes assents to it, and sometimes not at all. Nor, however, is the human body or sense moved only by celestial bodies. For **D** Ptolemy himself concedes that particular effects concerning matter by no means absolutely follow celestial bodies, which are universal and remote causes: but rather insofar as intermediate causes contribute; and the mobile disposition of matter, subject to contrary causes, receives them differently at different times and places. Indeed, we prove this daily by experience itself: especially in those things which, though born at the same time, follow rather the nature of the species and the individual, and also of place and nourishment, and custom: so that they behave in diverse ways, rather than the same moment of birth causing them to behave entirely similarly. Rightly, therefore, Ptolemy instructs astrologers to deliver a common and possible judgment, rather than a distinct and necessary one. He adds that the wise man can resist threatening stars, or favor promising ones. **E** Therefore, one must not believe the assertors of fate, who say that individual things proceed from determined causes—

--- Page 349 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. IX. 134

—namely, that with a cause posited, the effect necessarily follows. Firstly, indeed, from a remote cause, however necessary, an effect does not necessarily arise, unless an intermediate cause is also necessary: just as in arguments from a necessary major premise and a contingent minor premise, a necessary conclusion does not usually follow. But between celestial causes and terrestrial effects, the intermediate causes are elemental forces, whether simple or mixed, whether active or passive: which indeed are contingent and mutable, and can very often impede each other. Secondly, it is not necessary that, with this or that determined and even sufficient cause of an effect posited, the effect immediately follows: since it can be impeded by the concurrence of another cause. For often a sufficient cause here is for bile, but there a certain sufficient cause is for phlegm: and they can impede each other.

Lastly, we cannot designate the determined causes of all things. For that you are white, you have a proper cause: likewise another proper cause that you are a grammarian. But that whiteness and being a grammarian concur, you do not have a proper cause. For if the concurrence of the two things I mentioned proceeded from some common and determined cause: they would certainly have some order among themselves. Therefore, concerning any effect, we will say that it does not necessarily proceed from its cause among us: since it could be impeded by some other cause accidentally concurring.

And although someone might reduce a concurring cause to a higher cause: nevertheless, no one can reduce the very concurrence that impedes to a certain cause: so that from that he might prove that an impediment of this kind proceeds from some celestial principle. Therefore, if things pertaining to the body do not necessarily follow the stars: much less are the minds and their actions subject to the stars.

Nor should anyone dare to say that the minds of men are moved by higher minds through the heavens as if through some instrument and medium. For minds agree more with minds than with bodies: therefore, the heavens are not interposed between those minds and ours: but rather our minds hold the middle ground between those minds and the heavens. And therefore the heavens are (moved) by divine powers through minds—

--- Page 350 ---

...human minds ought to be moved, rather than our minds being moved from there through the heavens. Perhaps someone might say: that our minds are moved by those minds without any intermediary. Let them move us then, if you will; indeed, let them lead us. For thus will human minds be divine, if they are moved directly by divine beings. For they will be closest to them by nature. Otherwise, they would be moved as if through a medium, by another nature closer to them. They will certainly be closer to them than the celestial sphere, since they are moved from there without the heavens.

But if they think the heavens will be perpetual, why not also the human soul to be eternal, since it is closer to divine beings? Therefore, the infusion which passes into lower minds from higher and angelic ones should rather be called illumination than motion. For the former transmit in their own way, and the latter also receive in their own way; but both are intellects. Therefore, it is an intellectual light both that which is given and that which is received. A gift of this kind does not prevent our soul from turning to that light in its own way, from using it according to its nature, and from reasoning and choosing freely through it; especially since our soul sometimes turns to the worse part in its counsels, but the instinct of divine minds would always draw towards the best.

G Wherefore the human soul draws the inspiration of divine powers into its own nature. For from there descends the stable (inspiration), which renders the mobile (soul) itself mobile, since the soul itself is mobile, and then acts in a mobile way. Therefore, nothing prevents the soul's action from being free, since it is not subjected to any specific mover.

Plotinus, Proclus, and Avicenna argue that celestial motions are not the causes of inferior things, but rather instruments obedient to divine movers as to craftsmen; whose various thoughts are indicated to us by celestial bodies, figures, and motions, as if by their eyes and nods, and portend future events.

A They add that divine notions are explained by celestial dispositions as if by letters; and just as birds, by their flight and chirping, are believed by augurs and soothsayers to show not what they themselves do, but what they signify, so too the heavens, by their figures and motions, which happen from elsewhere, daily signify to us. This indeed astrologers show, when, in judging someone's nativity, they bring forth many things which pertain to fathers, grandfathers, brothers, wives, friends, and enemies; whose fortune does not depend on another's nativity, but is only signified. Indeed, the supernal motors not only conceive of those things of which they themselves are the causes, but also of those things of which our minds will be the future causes, and they ponder within themselves, and often demonstrate these by celestial signs. As often as some good is proposed to us, so often can the soul thus reason: Because the greatest good is liberty: I wish to experience it in myself at some time. Therefore I prefer now, by retaining the act of choosing, to be my own master, rather than by willing to serve this or that. Nevertheless, it chooses liberty as a good, which it often otherwise postpones for other goods. Therefore we choose no good necessarily, although we necessarily desire good itself. Finally, either motion is nowhere free, or it is free where it is primary. Primary in the soul. But the primary must be free, if indeed whatever is such primarily, is such by itself. Indeed, it ends in the dominion of the mind itself, as when I say I do this for that: that for the other. That, because I will. To will, because it pleases. But to please me, and moreover to will what pleases. I add furthermore that if by chance I were unwilling: I would will to be unwilling. Fifth Reason. The Mind operates without the body.
Chapter 5.

[C]
The mode of operating follows the mode of existing. Therefore, if
the soul exists in any way through the body, it never acts without the body
or with the help of the body. But now the opposite happens.
Therefore, it is not through the body. Let us first hear
Plato's mind concerning the mode of knowing by which the human
soul operates. Since the soul is much more excellent
than the body, and that which continually forms something is more
excellent than what is formed: therefore no bodies, whether they are outside us
or inside, paint their forms or images in the soul: but with certain
qualities or powers or images of their own, they strike that
warm and vital vapor, which is in a certain way the knot of the body
and the soul, and is called spirit by the natural philosophers.
For if those bodies agree with this spirit in matter,
but do not agree with the soul: it is more reasonable for the spirit
to be formed by them than the soul: which is so far from
being formed by the body, that it is rather in truth both the form of the
body, and its shaper. Indeed, it is the shaper of its own body by
nature, but a part of others. The rational soul, therefore, which
is the fount of bodily motions, itself indeed moves
bodies: but is not moved by bodies. But it would be moved
by them, if it were formed by them. But the spirit, which is the
chariot of the soul, is struck by all bodies. A pulsation of this kind
does not escape the soul. Thus, we are said to feel such a passion
or agitation of the spirit, which is not hidden from the soul. But immediately from this
sudden act of sensing, the inner power of the mind is excited
to another work very similar to this. For when it has reached colors
through the spirit of the eye, sounds through the spirit of the ears,
and other things through other [spirits]: it (the soul) by a certain
power of its own, by which it presides over bodies and possesses
their seeds, no less in the power of knowing than in that of nourishing:
soon it either conceives anew in itself the utterly spiritual
images of colors and sounds and other things, or it brings forth those
conceived long ago, and gathers them into one. This, we have called
imagination in earlier [discussions]. We have placed afterwards phantasy a little-

--- Page 353 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL. BOOK IX. 136

Then, the faculty superior to this [phantasy], wandering almost similarly
through images of bodies. Finally, the Intellect, superior by a long
interval, as we have declared. When the soul perceives something,
among the Platonists it is said to operate through the body: not because
the soul itself and the body perceive simultaneously. For just as the soul D
is the source of living (as Plato says), so too is it the source of perceiving.
Moreover, objects are often present to the eyes or ears: yet if the mind
more attentively considers something within itself, these are not perceived
until the mind returns to such things: as if not these members, but the
inner nature of our mind itself has the power of perceiving. However,
this power of perceiving does not perceive unless the corporeal spirit is
agitated by bodies. Therefore, when it is said to act through
imagination or phantasy, it is said to operate through the body's aid:
because it revolves through individual images, which individually refer
to bodies, and were conceived through the impulse of the corporeal
spirit caused by bodies. And also because there is such a close
connection between these internal images and the spirit, that the
vibration of the spirit itself always follows the internal revolution of
images, and conversely, the revolution of images is for the most part
committed to the vibration of this spirit: when it speculates and
chooses something through intelligence, it is said to operate both
without the body and without the body's aid: because even without that
impulse of the spirit, and without images collected from it, it sees and
chooses something utterly alien from them. E
I omit for now that the Peripatetics place all powers of sensing in the
soul indeed according to their origin, but in the composite according to
their form: but they locate the power of understanding in the soul alone:
and in this way they believe the former (sensing powers) act through the
body, but the latter (understanding) even without the body.
Nevertheless, it naturally turns itself to images of corporeal sense as
long as the mind naturally inhabits the body.

But that this last operation sometimes occurs without corporeal aid,
and those former ones always through the body's aid: the signs I shall
present will show us this. First, the very power of the soul that uses the
body, whatever it may be, does not perceive its own instrument. For who
tastes his own tongue with taste? Who through imagination or phantasy
has known the nature of spirits and images, which scarcely after

--- Page 354 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...is recognized after long mental discussions? But it would be clear to everyone, and very easily, if it were known through imagination and phantasy.

**Second sign.** Such a power, which, as we said, uses the body, neither knows itself nor its own action. If sight properly perceived itself seeing from what it sees: always while we see something, we would notice that we see: which is certainly not the case. For often we see a person present with open eyes: but because then the interior power of the soul is intent on something else, we by no means notice that we see: as if an act of this kind is perceived not by sight, but by a certain interior power when it is unhindered. Moreover, the act of seeing, and similar acts, are in a way incorporeal, but those senses only know corporeal things. If these powers are ignorant of their actions, they are also ignorant of themselves. For what else is a certain power, if not a principle of operating in a certain and proper way? Therefore, he who does not know the operation, does not know the mode of operating: nor does he know his own principle of operating in this way. Therefore, the five sen- [Marginal note: A] ses are ignorant of themselves. But neither do imagination and phantasy know themselves. For since all always use these two powers of the soul, all would most easily know what nature these powers have. But now scarcely do those know these things who have sought them through long mental examination.

**Third sign,** when something vehement is presented to these powers, which more violently agitates us: it so occupies them: that weaker things are not well perceived, neither at that very same time, nor afterwards for a time. Our eye, sometimes overwhelmed by opposing sunbeams, discerns other colors neither then nor afterwards for some space of time. The same happens to the ears from a loud noise and violent thunder. The same also to the other senses. The same to imagination and phantasy, whenever they are occupied by certain horrifying images. Which shows that the action of powers of this kind concurs with the vibration of the spirit, and vice versa: just as the sensation and movement of a spider, remaining in the middle of its web, with threads stretched everywhere, and flies flying towards it, follows the tremor of the web everywhere, and conversely the tremor of the web follows the spider's movement. Indeed, this demonstrates that these powers are close to matter: since they are often, as it were, overcome by the object, and the remnants of corporeal passions remaining in the spirit confuse them for a time.

Fourth sign: by a more powerful object, not only is the act of discerning confused, but injury and discomfort occur in us, as if the corporeal spirit were injured, and from these powers, by a certain mutual use, some offense arises.

Fifth: they do not apprehend the quality of sensation and the image familiar to them. The eye does not see its own whiteness or the image through which it perceives. Touch does not judge its own heat. And even if some foreign heat becomes familiar to it, it does not feel it: which usually happens in those who suffer from hectic fever: whose touch by no means perceives the fever. Imagination and phantasy also completely ignore their own power, habit, and conceived images. For reason scarcely discovers such things.

Sixth: after the seventh or eighth septenary of age, [Marginal note: B] when the bodily constitution gradually begins to decline towards an earthly quality, with the spirits dissolved or too much thickened and warmed, sight grows dull, hearing is blunted, smell is obstructed, taste stiffens, touch dries up: the usual speed of imagination and phantasy is slowed down.

Seventh: the longer the senses labor, the more debilitated they feel worse and more confusedly. For if you have fixedly looked at something for an hour, you will become dim-sighted: because with the spirits dissolved or obscured, the qualities and images of sensible things which you perceive do not become clear in them.

Eighth. They attain a certain kind of things, not all kinds: each of the five senses (as is clear) its own kinds [Marginal note: C] of qualities: imagination and phantasy their own conditions of these qualities. These and other similar things usually happen to the powers of the soul using the body: but the contrary happens to the intellect. Therefore the intellect does not use the body. But note that the contrary things happen to the mind. Those powers are ignorant of themselves: but the mind knows itself. For it finds that it exists: and in what kind of things it is: and what power it has. Those powers have certain instruments, and they are ignorant of them. The intellect has no instrument: and if it had one, it would know it, since it knows both itself and other things. And that instrument would be placed between itself and other things. But if anyone should say that the mind has an instrument, we will inquire whether it is corporeal: or whether it behaves otherwise. If he answers that it is corporeal: it will thus be refuted by Peripatetic argumentation. Every [Marginal note: S]

--- Page 356 ---
THEOLOGIAE PLATONICAE
corporeal instrument is contained in some species of bodies by some form proper to it. If the intellect uses such an instrument, it will not form a sincere judgment about corporeal things. For whatever is perceived through such an instrument, being infected by its quality, will not appear entirely as it truly was, but as the instrument was; just as through reddened eyes the air appears red, but through jaundiced eyes, yellow. For this reason, the pupil lacks all color, so that it can purely receive all colors. Thus, the instrument of the mind ought to lack all corporeal quality, so that through it it might sincerely discern all things. Yet it would not lack all, if it were a body; therefore, it would have some. But what it would have, it would not perceive. Therefore, the mind would not recognize qualities similar to its own through it; just as the sense of touch, whose instrument has a certain warmth, does not feel warmth that is entirely similar. But neither would it purely discern qualities dissimilar to it, because these would first be infected by its quality before the mind would perceive them. Finally, through an instrument that was a body, that was of a certain kind of bodies, that was something singular circumscribed by place and time, the mind would not recognize anything more excellent than bodies; nor indeed all bodies, but a certain kind of corporeal things; just as each of the five senses, through individual instruments, perceives individual kinds of corporeal things.

Lastly, it would not comprehend anything universal through a singular instrument. Yet we experience that we know universals through the mind, when things that seem diverse, we find to agree together in some nature; when we reduce individual things to one species; when, comparing a singular and proper thing with a common one, we judge the universal to differ from the particular. But we cannot compare these two with each other otherwise than by a single faculty that comprehends both.

As often as by right reason we so separate a certain kind of most true things from every kind of bodies, that we discern nothing corporeal in it: so often we reject whatever can be called corporeal. Yet we cannot reject all corporeal things through a corporeal instrument, because at least the instrument itself cannot be repelled by the instrument itself. And when we behold the abstract

--- Page 357 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. IX. 138
species, and through it we unite ourselves to abstract forms and reasons, and them to us: then a corporeal instrument interposed between them would be an impediment rather than an aid. For it is both most diverse from them, and inferior to a degree: and it brings much more distance than union. Since these things are so, the mind cannot use any corporeal instrument. But what about another? Absolutely none. For if anyone were to attach any other instrument to it, we would ask whether it can understand anything without it: or nothing. If it can, it would not need an instrument. But someone will say it cannot. We, on the contrary, will assert that it can. For now everyone will admit that the intellect knows itself: in which cognition it uses no instrument. For if it were to use some instrument to grasp itself: that certainly would fall as a medium between the mind and the mind's own essence, which would be comprehended by the mind through that instrument: where something external would be closer to the mind than the mind's essence. And when the power of the mind reflects upon a power, or an act upon an act: no instrument is interposed there. For a medium is usually assumed because of its convenience with the extremes. But no instrument is more convenient with power and act than power and act themselves. Everyone will also con [marginal note: E] fess that if the intellect has an instrument, it does not ignore it. For primarily for this reason we seem not to ignore it, because we are accustomed to its existence: and we add that it is such as to serve the intellect. Furthermore, if the intellect knows itself, and also external objects: it is necessary that it also sometimes knows the instrument through which it passes from itself to objects in understanding. Moreover, when through already known objects it turns itself to its act, and through the act to its power and substance: is it not compelled in this very regression to also encounter its instrument, if it has one, since that instrument would be a medium between the act of the mind and its power? Where it is compelled to recognize its instrument. But does the mind recognize its instrument through some instrument, or not? If through some: I ask about another and yet another, again ad infinitum. If through none: therefore it does not [marginal note: F] need an instrument for knowing, since it knows the instrument itself without an instrument. There, indeed, what is called an instrument is rather a certain object than a medium. And if from this it passes to another in knowing: not from a medium to an object,

but the object runs from the prior object to the posterior. But perhaps
someone might say: the instrument is known by the mind not

But I will ask: whether through the very essence of the instrument,
or through its image. Not the first: because the mind would always

Hence, by the very fact that we truly conceive of simple things and true simplicity,
the Platonists conclude that what thus conceives in us
is constituted neither by intellect and instrument, nor
composed of soul and body: but that the mind exists as simple
and alone. Therefore, the mind operates by itself: and in this way
Plato also calls it 'moving itself'. Therefore, it lives by itself:
and it lives always.
      Let us proceed to the third sign. Those powers are confused by a vehement
object, so that they do not discern weaker ones. The mind, on the
contrary, when it sees magnificent and arduous things: then, in them and after them,
it discerns smaller and lighter things more clearly and easily: inasmuch as it
is great, and is nourished and grows by great things. Let us proceed to the fourth,
and the rest. Other powers are offended by a powerful object: the mind
is offended by the consideration of no thing, however immense: as if
it were not subject to a certain commensuration of humors.
Indeed, it discovers the greatest things more slowly: because, being entangled with external things,
it does not investigate. When unencumbered, it finds things more quickly: and when found, it then shines
wonderfully, as if entirely ready for them, and is filled with incomparable
pleasure, as if most proximate to them. Who
here would not see that the power of the mind is in a way infinite, which
is overcome by no finite object? Moreover, other powers are ignorant of qualities
and images familiar to themselves: but what familiar thing does the mind
not know? Which also defines familiarity itself:
and sees itself by understanding its own act: and the
species through which it understands, and its habit and virtue.
Therefore, the mind dwells with itself. Is it therefore its own dwelling place? What kind of thing—

--- Page 359 ---
...any thing is preserved in its natural place. Therefore the mind is preserved by itself and remains thenceforth always unharmed. It is added that the more robust, as far as natural operations are concerned, always, and often the sensual, are better off than others; but as for intelligence, neither always nor often: as if intelligence were not a companion of the body. Add that the natures of the senses fail in operation through old age. But the eye of the mind then sees more clearly, the mists of youthful vices having been dispelled. For divinely Plato says, "The virtue of the soul does not flourish unless the virtue of the body [Marginal note: B] fades." The keenness of the mind is not sharpened unless the keenness of the body is dulled. Then the wisdom of divine things thrives: the prudence of human things is consumed: equity and constancy prevail. And what is greater, not even the very power of properly sensing, which is in the soul, is lost by old age or disease: although its act is interrupted when the eye is injured, because objects are not represented sincerely enough. For even with a broken pen, the act of writing ceases: but the art of writing remains intact in the soul. That the art has suffered no detriment from this is clear from the fact that in the meantime it writes within itself: and with the pen restored, it writes at its own discretion. The same would happen if the tongue of a mute person were cured: and if the foot of a lame person [were cured]. The same if the eye of a blind or bleary-eyed person were cured: as if the damage were in the body, not in the soul. For often, with the eye cleansed, we see immediately. Which either would not happen, or would happen late even with the body already healed, if the very power of seeing had failed: which would require a certain time for its restoration, after the body [Marginal note: C] had completed its own. Aristotle wisely says: "If you provide an old man with the eye of a youth, he will see completely like a youth." If the senses, which are ascribed to certain parts of the body, lose no power either when those parts themselves are injured or through old age: the mind, which is ascribed to no parts, will neither fail when the whole body is injured, nor ever.

Here occurs to us that argument which Socrates presents in Plato's tenth book of the Republic: that the rational soul does not die through any bodily disease. "For in what way," he says, "will that perish by a bodily [Marginal note: D] disease which does not fail by its own disease?" Indeed, our body does not perish by an alien disease, but by its own. If it perishes by a defect of food and the putrefaction of air: it does not perish by these before it falls from these into its own disease: by which proper disease it is dissolved. And if it would not perish by its own disease: never also by an alien one. For if it is not harmed by fever, by unhealthy food...

--- Page 360 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...or by air, it will not be harmed. But the soul does not perish by its own defect, that is, by iniquity. For an iniquitous soul is no less a soul and vital than one that is just. Therefore, it does not perish by bodily illness.

Furthermore, bodily illness does not inflict upon the soul a defect proper to the soul itself: because when the body is sick, the soul does not become more iniquitous, but is often improved, and profits from the study of morals. Therefore, bodily illness not only does not destroy, but also does not corrupt the soul.

And if sometimes, when the body is sick, [Marginal note: E] the mind seems to be harmed: it is not so, however. The mind perhaps rests there, or acts within itself: or busies itself with human affairs: it is not harmed.

Socrates, when he either played with his children or cared for them when they were ill, did not lose the habit of higher philosophy: although he might not philosophize at all then, or not philosophize excellently, while the consideration of baser things distracted the act of knowledge.

Our soul often plays with the body in its pleasures. In its illnesses, it rules and cares for it. In both states, that sublime consideration of reason is interrupted or relaxed: because it either rests for a time: or anxiously busies itself too much with baser things: but when things are calm, it rises again.

Thus it is arranged by nature, that for diverse works simultaneously, as far as human powers are concerned, we are not sufficiently capable. Guests intent on feasts do not hear the lyre's melodies well. While the soul digests much food in the stomach, it relaxes the duty of human contemplation: therefore, we seem dull then. While it contemplates more attentively, food is digested with difficulty.

Hence, philosophers are often weak in body, but not weak in soul: but they excel in intelligence as much as they are deficient in body. Therefore, what wonder if, when the body is feverish, the soul, most intent on sustaining and curing the sick person, ceases from contemplating, and, most occupied in forming the body of a child, and also in sustaining the body of an old person, uses its intellect less?

And when black vapors of the brain have occupied the spirit, and by vibrating it, have moved horrible images in the imagination, from which, by the novelty of the dreadful spectacle, almost the entire power of the soul is directed to the imagination: will you wonder if in the meantime it has interrupted the work of contemplating, which it finally restores when the vapors are resolved?

Often also, when vapors are boiling, reason itself, ever watchful, refutes the illusions of images: which happens in those who suffer from dizziness of the brain: whose heaven does not deny...

--- Page 361 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. IX. 140

or the earth to fall, although sense asserts it. Furthermore, those who are agitated by rabies because of a dog bite, or are instigated by the fury of a demon, sometimes even at the very onset of their fury, perceive the impending madness. [Marginal note: F] And those who are terrified by horrible dreams cry out against the phantasm, often saying that they are dreaming. Therefore, the mind does not always need inferior powers; it often idles when those are active, but is active when they are idle. It condemns their chatter and orders them to be silent. But if anyone should say that the mind needs them to be excited, and therefore without them operates absolutely nothing, I respond thus: because while the soul inhabits the body, it is always occupied with its sustenance, and is distracted by many things far removed from divine matters; therefore it is not turned to the contemplation of divine things, unless, by comprehending some more express likenesses of them through its subservient powers, which it uses very much, it is excited to them. But after it is sufficiently turned, and through frequent turning is aptly prepared for the infusion of divine things, it no longer needs the obedience of those (powers) for that contemplation; indeed, it puts them to sleep as much as possible, lest it be hindered by them. And it would always willingly persevere in that state, if the necessity of caring for the body did not press upon it. Which signifies that the mind can continue contemplation by itself; and when it is no longer drawn back from this on account of the care of the body, it will freely contemplate by itself without the ministry of other powers, for which it will have been sufficient beforehand to be minimally hindered by them. But as long as it is enclosed in the body, because of that ministry of the senses by which it is prepared for conversion, it happens that with the body injured and the spirit clouded, because neither are objects clearly represented nor is there clear perception in the senses and phantasy, the mind is not easily excited from there to true contemplation. It also happens that some appear more ingenious than others because of the diversity of spirits. Although I judge that the difference among people in learning arts should be attributed not so much to a difference in talent as to a difference in will. For anyone attains even the greatest things, if they are striven for diligently. Furthermore, it happens that some are called mad because they either do not use their mind, or abuse it. Indeed, since all the intention of the soul in these cases is too much occupied with the more vehement illusions of phantasy. But with the bile, whether black or yellow, which provides the cause of the illusion, [Marginal note: A] emptied, they suddenly recover their senses, as those who have not lost their mind. I omit that Origen and Plotinus dispute that human souls

PLATONIC THEOLOGY

human souls are in a way minds fallen from their purity: when, namely, having fallen from the mind's intention concerning ideas to the intention of the vivifying power of bodies, they descended into bodies. And the more intently and deeply some have turned to matter than others, the less (as they say) intellectual light they retain. Hence a great diversity in intellects and morals arises among souls. To which also contribute the ethereal bodies of souls, adapted to different figures and stars of the sky. Finally, the variety of natures brings about a variety of intellects. But if someone does not grant that souls existed in time before bodies, yet wishes to imitate the Platonists in some respect, he might perhaps say that souls, at least at the very moment they are created and joined to the body, are almost affected and disposed, as Origen and Plotinus argue: indeed, some angelic minds having fallen to lower things, others not at all; and of those that fell, some more, others less. But the minds of humans, as the lowest of all, by natural instinct, as soon as they are created, tend towards the natural part and bodies: and some immerse themselves more deeply than others into the river Lethe, that is, matter. And in this way, Pamphilus seems to have corrected Origen, as far as he could. But of these things, another time. Now therefore, let us return to the proposed topic.

If someone, having injured a part of the head, seems to lose memory, the Peripatetics will respond that the images of things retained in the spirit of the brain are confused: but the species (forms/ideas) that are in the mind are not properly harmed, but rather (so to speak) are idle. For the mind, as long as it inhabits the body, must contemplate corporeal species not without corporeal images.

The Platonists will add that insofar as the soul's intention is more vehemently occupied with the healing of the injured limb, to that extent knowledge or memory is diminished and interrupted.

Avicenna and Alganteles will say that the mind, turned towards lower things, is diverted from a certain divine mind: from which they believe every act of intelligence continuously depends.

But since Lucretius especially distrusted immortality for this reason, that the powers of the soul seem to fail at the approach of death: it must be noted that the life of the body consists in the temperament of humor and heat: and therefore the body dies when either heat dissolves humor, or humor extinguishes heat.

--- Page 363 ---
**ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK IX. 141**

But since humor is the nourishment of heat, heat the vehicle of spirit: and spirit is the uniter of the soul to the body: it happens that when humor is gradually dissolved in the members of the body, the soul also gradually abandons the members. And because it is then less occupied in governing the body than it usually is, it gathers itself into its own mind: it discerns secrets: and foretells future things. Far be from us the Lucretian suspicion, namely, that the soul will die with the body: for it is strengthened when the body is weakened. And since union is opposed to dissolution, the mind must then be considered to be very far from dissolution, when it most gathers itself into itself, and, having laid aside its animal nature, rises into the mind. And this clearly happens in death which occurs due to resolution.

But in death which occurs due to the extinction of the vital soul, the vital force is intent on curing humors and swellings, the senses on judging pains, the imagination on seeing images which are stirred up by the vapors of the humors. Therefore reason temporarily suspends its office, just as it sometimes does in sleep: which it resumes after the clamor of death: just as it is accustomed to awaken after dreams. But that it by no means loses its powers and faculties in that very time, that is an argument for us, that many who are recalled to life from imminent death by the diligence of doctors, indeed recover the body's strength either never or late: but the mind's (strength) immediately, once the humor is purged: as if the body's powers had been extinguished, but the light of the mind had rather lain hidden, as fire under ashes, than vanished. Who would say that the departure from life of the body and the soul would be the same, when the return is not the same? For the body returns scarcely and late: the mind returns easily and suddenly. Nor did it lose anything of itself at that time, since it suddenly brings forth again into light both its natural and acquired faculties, no less than it was accustomed to before: inasmuch as it had then gathered its furnishings, not dispersed them: and had been prepared like a serpent to shed its old skin: not otherwise about to emerge from those confines into the light, living and whole: than when it was once sent forth into the light from the maternal womb. But the wise man thinks, when he leaves the body, that he is not deprived of a part of himself, but is freed from a most troublesome burden. And enough now about the sixth sign. Re- [F] ceive that seventh sign. The senses are fatigued by prolonged work, but the mind never is. The longer you look, the more dully you will perceive. The longer you investigate with the intellect, the more in-

--- Page 364 ---
...you will understand more clearly that every work of the body and sense is worn out by use, but that of the mind is strengthened. However, the head is accustomed to be weighed down by prolonged thought, and the eye to grow dim: because the exercise of the mind is often accompanied by movements of the imagination, and these by a vibration of the spirit, and this (vibration) by an injury to the brain or eye. But the very keenness of the mind becomes lighter and sharper. Which (keenness) would certainly remain directed upwards without any interruption, unless, pitying this body entrusted to it, it were to interrupt its own proper work for the sake of recreating it. This is clearly seen in those who, while contemplating something more attentively, bear with difficulty the fatigue of the body, in whom the mind, as it were, unwillingly ceases from its work, but the body and senses cease most willingly: as if not the mind were fatigued by working, but they (the body and senses). That which is tireless is also immortal.

G The eighth sign is that other powers are assigned to some genus of things, but the mind to none. For what is there among those things which are said to exist, to which the keenness of the mind cannot be directed? Which comprehends by description the nature and power of what is called being, essence, and existence. And under these (concepts), all things that exist are contained. It also finds the difference between being and non-being: and thus knows both: and in a way divides being into its parts and particles: while it arranges every genus and species of things under being. And, what is greater, it ascends above being itself, and descends below being: when it posits the One itself, and the Good itself, above being: and places matter or the privations of things below being. The mind is bound to no genus of things, if it encompasses all. It has nothing outside itself by which it might be destroyed, since it somehow encloses all things within itself. Let us conclude the discussion in this manner. If the human soul were in some way through the body, it would never act without the instrument or aid of the body. But it acts without the use of the body by understanding and willing: as we have explained through eight signs. Therefore, it is not through the body. Therefore, it is either through itself, or through divine causes. If through itself, it never abandons itself: If through divine causes: therefore, through eternal causes it is eternal.

Sixth Reason. The soul agrees partly with divine beings,
but partly with brute animals.
Chapter 6.

--- Page 365 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. IX. 142

IF the soul of man were to spring from matter (which they call the ethereal stream), it would never be joined in operation with divine things which do not spring from that stream. A
But that it *does* agree with them in operation, indeed even in essence and life, we shall thus show. Because we see all things then B
most especially operate something, when they are adult and perfect in their species, we are compelled to assert that God, because He is the most perfect of all, is not idle, but does something, since operation is a sign of perfection. Indeed, neither would we do anything, unless He acted: by whose moving, we are moved: just as by whose making, we are: and by whose breathing, we live and breathe. But what is the operation of God? Not one that begins from elsewhere, or tends somewhere else, lest God be compelled to depend on something else. C
Therefore, the operation of God is a certain perpetual conversion into Himself, by which He enjoys and delights in Himself. Therefore, He contemplates Himself: contemplating Himself, He sees His power. Beholding this, He discerns whatever He can. Therefore, He contemplates both Himself and His entire work simultaneously in a single act. By contemplating, He conceives all things within Himself. By conceiving, He brings forth outside Himself whatever He wills. A nearly similar operation exists in His holy ministers and celestial spirits. For they too contemplate themselves and their own works. They also contemplate God and divine works. Contemplation is certainly the only suitable activity for them: because it is the most perfect of all operations. Which also appears in us. This [contemplation] does not need external matter, like fabrication. Nor corporeal instruments, like the senses. Nor is it moved from elsewhere, or tends elsewhere, like other operations. Nor does it shape alien matter: but it cultivates and adorns the mind, when it is not terminated by something else, but defines itself within itself. Nor is it quickly fatigued, like others: but remains indefatigable. Nor is it troublesome or unworthy, as those are: but easy, full, and suffused with incomparable joy.
If therefore any of those operations which are inherent in us is to be attributed to the supernal divinities, contemplation is certainly to be attributed, being the most felicitous of all operations. D
From these things it is clear that the soul of man agrees with divine things in contemplation. We also do not doubt that it agrees with beasts in nutrition, sensation, and bodily affection. But certain operations, directed to objects suitable for them, require certain suitable virtues and substances: and what proportion is ob-

--- Page 366 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...of one object to another, the same is of one operation to another. The same comparison also holds for virtue and essence to virtue and essence. Therefore, just as in us that which pertains to the use of the body is an operation common with beasts towards an object common with them: so a nature common with them appears. This is the operation of nourishing and sensing, and the power and constitution of the body: which in us are almost as perishable as in beasts. It is also necessary that there be found in us a power **E** and substance common with those celestial beings, from which arises that operation which we have in common with them towards an object common to us and them. Wherefore, just as in us the nature of nourishing and sensing and the bodily constitution are in a way perishable, which are concerned with perishable things and are common with perishable animals: so the power of contemplation will be immortal, which is concerned with immortal things and is common with immortal beings: because the same operation cannot proceed except from the same nature and power. Who, moreover, would doubt that our contemplation is very similar to that of the supernal beings? since through it the soul, like those celestial beings, considers itself and its own works: and also investigates supernal causes and their effects: likewise ascends from lower effects through intermediate causes up to the supreme cause: and conversely returns in a circle from the supreme cause down to the lowest events. Where it seems to embrace the entire series of divine work by no other virtue than divine, and to survey it as if some god. Not only does it truly have intelligence in common with the divine powers, but also will: since it yearns for their blessedness. **F** Furthermore, it has a similar action, inasmuch as it acts freely: and commands its own body almost as they do. From all these things it is gathered that our soul agrees in essence with the celestial beings. If it has a common and proximate essence with them, and they have no origin from matter: it follows that our soul also has no such origin. Moreover, if those divine powers are eternal, because they always move the spheres of the world in the same order, and are never wearied: it follows that the essence of the mind is eternal: since a finite and mobile life is in no way proximate to an infinite and immobile life. But it agrees with them even more in the immortality of life than in the intelligence of truth and the desire for blessedness: inasmuch as life

life itself is prior to intelligence or will. And if will
is the striving of intelligence, and intelligence indeed the highest peak
of a maturing life: the soul is directed to a right will
in no other way than through true intelligence; and to this (intelligence) also in no

(It has) true intelligence: both because insofar as it is intelligence, it is not

we will show elsewhere. Therefore, it must necessarily have a true and mature
life. Such a life is one that is not subject to death. To this argumentation
of ours, that of Origen is greatly favorable, where he says:
All natures which are partakers of the same principle are [Marginal note: G]
similar among themselves: just as eyes, because all are partakers of light,
since by their nature they are similarly turned towards light: all are
similar: but nevertheless, according to a diverse participation of light, one is sharper than another.
All rational substances are partakers of God, since all
are turned towards God: therefore they are similar both
among themselves and to Him. And so, just as the highest are immortal, like
angels: so also the lower, like souls. But all are immortal,
because they are very similar to the immortal God. This similarity
is shown by that very turning towards God: towards whom indeed, like
stars towards the sun, the higher angels are turned: but the
soul towards the same: like the moon: which, although it is changed by a
certain vicissitude of divine light, and therefore receives it in a certain mutable
way: nevertheless perceives it by an inextinguishable reason. For indeed,
it comprehends by certain reasons both that it is itself inextinguishable, and by what reason it becomes inextinguishable.

Chapter 7.

Dicaearchus, or some Epicurean, will struggle against these (arguments), [Marginal note: H]
as if it were similar to a monster, namely, that something is partly

But we will affirm that the order of nature cannot be preserved without this.
There are some bodies entirely removed from all corruption, like the heavens:
of which neither the sphere itself, nor any particle is corrupted.
And there are bodies entirely opposed to these, namely, entirely
perishable, for example, wood, stones, metals, and other things from the four (elements).

composed of elements. Indeed, some particles of wood sometimes decay: then also the whole wood itself ceases to be wood: although whatever is thus composed, for that reason at least consists of the incorruptible and the corruptible, because it has in itself a perpetual primary matter, but a mortal form. Therefore, the conjunction of mortal with immortal is neither impossible nor rare. But let us return to the established order. There are also middle bodies: namely, the four spheres of the elements: partly incorruptible, partly corruptible. Indeed, the entire sphere of an element preserves its species, its position, its tenor: but some of its particles are sometimes lost from here, and restored from there. But since bodies have been constituted either by spirits or by the grace of spirits, the order of bodies must proceed from the order of spirits, or at least imitate the order of spirits.
K. There are therefore some spirits entirely immortal, like angels: whose entire substance itself is not changed, nor any power, nor even operation. There are others entirely mortal, as common opinion holds: namely, the souls of brutes: whose power and operation are changed, and the whole substance is also changed. Moreover, there must be spirits intermediate between both: so that there may be one continuous context of all nature. These will remain through their entire substance: they will be changed through some particles. Such will be our souls especially, whose substances that common contemplation, will, and action with celestial beings compel to be perpetual. But that common operation with mortal brutes, entirely enslaved to the service of the mortal body, indicates to us that some powers or operations will sometimes cease. Indeed, since natural affections are founded in proper natures, and diverse affections in diverse natures: but we see that our souls have an affection for eternal things, and also an affection for temporal things: we rightly say that they are composed of two natures, namely eternal and temporal: just as if we were to see some body by its nature moving almost equally upwards and downwards, we would say that it is almost equally composed of gravity and lightness.
A. We have seen three bodies and also three spirits: let us now take three species of animals. Animals eternal on both sides, both in soul and in body, like the spheres of the world, the stars—

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

The work [matter] is the most remote of all divine works from God, but the intellectual kind [the lowest intellect] is closer. And that [matter] comes into being apart from mind; much more can mind come into being apart from matter. If the ultimate intellect holds such an order in the genus of intellectual things as matter holds in the genus of natural things, and matter cannot be made from any natural thing, it follows that the ultimate intellect cannot be made from any species of intellect that is in that genus. But if an intellect of this kind does not depend on any genus of intellect of the same kind or a much more excellent one, much less should it be thought to depend on the genus of natural things, and much less still on matter. From this it follows that the ultimate mind is not drawn out from matter. It also follows that it is incorruptible. For since the order of minds is more excellent than the corporeal order, and the order of corporeal things finally descends into eternal matter—since that matter is never corrupted—who would be so mad as to concede that the order of minds, which is more stable and more divine than bodies, would finally end in a corruptible mind? Therefore, the ultimate intellect must be perpetual, which is related to intelligible forms just as prime matter is related to sensible forms.

Matter **A** is neither corrupted by any sensible form through corporeal corruption (for it is formed by these) nor by any intelligible species (for it is perfected by these). Therefore, the ultimate mind is neither destroyed by any intelligible species through spiritual corruption (for it is perfected by these) nor does it perish through any sensible form by corporeal corruption. For mind presides, it is not subject to corporeal species. Nor does corporeal corruption pass into the mind, just as spiritual corruption does not pass into matter. Indeed, if spiritual violence does not pass into the mind, much less will corporeal violence pass into it because of the grossness of bodies. Indeed, if the corruption of corporeal things does not affect the matter subject to them, much less will it defile the mind, which is higher than them. Let the ultimate intellect **B** be perpetual. But what is this? This, I say, is the human intellect. Who doubts that intellect is in us, since we cannot dispute about intellects except by the power of intellect? And just as the eye does not perceive the light of the sun except through a certain internal light of its own, so our soul neither investigates nor intuits divine intellects except through its own—

--- Page 373 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 146

...its own intellect. But what kind of intellect is this of ours? I do not care about this any further. For whatever kind it may be, it will be eternal. For intellects, the higher ones are undoubtedly perpetual [Marginal note: C], if the lowest one is perpetual. But I indeed believe our mind to be the last, as it also pleased many of the ancients: because it does not act its own (things) simultaneously, but turns forms in itself in turn like Proteus, and understands by succeeding (sequentially): just as the moon, which is the last of the stars, in turn changes its light, while the others do not change. Let our mind therefore be the last. Let it also be eternal. Because it is eternal, it always yearns for eternal things: and as often as it is not disturbed by the body, it immediately attains them: and rejoices in them as its own and familiar. Moreover, that movement of anything is natural, which occurs immediately after an impediment is removed. But it occurs towards the most similar end: but because it is the last, it loves the nature of bodies, to which it approaches as if to a relative, it vivifies and governs them.

*Objection of Epicurus and response concerning the series of things. Chapter 2.*

Here again Epicurus rashly exclaims that it is a monstrosity for divine things to cling to mortals: inasmuch as he does not see [Marginal note: D] that mortal things cannot subsist without the companionship of divine and stable things. I think it must have escaped him that the series of things is so arranged in its parts, that although there are many and various orders of things in nature, the lowest parts of each superior order [Marginal note: E] are somehow joined to the highest parts of the immediately subsequent inferior order. The kinship of aether with the nature of the elements teaches us this. Indeed, the moon, the lowest part of the aether, closest to the elements, seems to have something not insignificant of the elemental, both by that frequent change of its shape: and by the very variety of its bright and dark body. Again, fire, the highest element, imitates the nearest heaven: because it moves and shines like heaven. The natural disposition of the four elements among themselves also shows the same, where the lowest part of fire is more humid, and as it were, grows warm like air. The highest region of air is thinned and as it were, glows like fire. There, fire is airy: air is fiery: and thus they are joined into one structure. The lowest region of air and the highest of water do the same, where clouded air liquefies like water, and water likewise thinned by vapors...

[Marginal note: E] Therefore, the association of an eternal mind with a human body, however perishable, is not so absurd, as the Epicurean and Lucretius believe: especially since our mind is the lowest of minds, just as the moon is the lowest of the stars: and as the moon relates to the sun, so our mind relates to God. The moon revolves around the sun in such a way that it shines at different times: it is figured differently and variously, yet is never entirely deprived of the faculty of receiving light. Moreover, it has something bright in itself, and it has something dark. Finally, it has something opaque, which prevents it from shining entirely. The human mind similarly always shines with the ray of the divine sun, but at different times differently: and it changes its form: it never shines entirely. Nor does what shines in it, shine equally. Besides its divine and rational virtue, there is a certain opaque part beneath it: and empty of reason: which, just as that lunar opacity (relates) to the elements, so it itself, inclining towards matter and the body, is left devoid of light.
Therefore, it seems consistent with the natural order of things that the lowest mind, although it may be eternal, can be joined with a certain body, however perishable. I omit that Xenocrates and Speusippus, Iamblichus and Plutarch believe that an eternal power proceeds from eternity itself, not only as far as the lowest minds which reflect back into it, but also as far as the souls of beasts. ...it may deserve to receive an eternal mind as a guest? Without a doubt, we ought not to be disturbed by the fact that nature has equipped the bodies of beasts with various defenses and supplied aids for sustenance, while giving us nothing of the sort. For it did not wish to deform the delicate equilibrium of our body; nor could it supply innumerable defenses or instruments for the infinite actions of man, which follow infinite thought; but, as Aristotle says, while it gave mind and hand, it granted all arts and all instruments. But beasts it easily equipped with finite defenses, by which they might execute determined actions of imagination, directed by nature towards a certain specific thing. Indeed, we believe our bodies are suitable abodes for the mind, both because of their upright figure, looking not at the ground but upwards, and recognizing heaven as its homeland more closely; and also because of the altogether wonderful beauty of its various limbs. Then because fire and air, the purest elements, are most potent in us, which is also indicated by the body's agility, tall stature, and upright gaze. But most of all because of the most temperate constitution, which is indicated by the delicate, smooth, firm, and shining softness of the flesh, which is not achieved except by the most exact tempering of the elements. [Marginal note: I] The eagle surpasses man in sight, many birds in hearing, the dog in smell; but no animal in taste or touch. This is clearly seen from the fact that men indulge more immoderately in feasts, drinks, and venereal pleasures than beasts, although they are sometimes restrained by reason. For it is fitting that they embrace those pleasures which they perceive, and more acutely, more eagerly than beasts. Those three higher senses are then most acute when the brain is dry. God did not grant this dryness to man, whose brain never rests, lest perhaps if it were [Marginal note: K] naturally dry, also drying out from continuous activity, it should dry out sooner than is proper. Taste is nothing else than a kind of touch of the tongue. Since touch is a universal sense, both of every animal and of the entire body, where it is most acute, it declares the best constitution to be present in the body; for this reason especially, because it occurs in the nerves, which, when they are drier, feel poorly; where touch is acute, it signifies the presence of softness, which tempers the dryness of the nerves. Furthermore, the instruments of the senses ought never actually to possess those qualities which they perceive—

--- Page 379 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 149

which the sense is to perceive. For the pupil lacks colors, hearing lacks sounds, smell lacks odors, the tongue lacks flavors. But since touch is concerned with the four qualities and those of the elements, it is necessary that it either lack them entirely (which cannot happen in a composite body) or be far removed from their excess, so that no quality seems to dominate in its instrument, but rather a certain harmony, as it were, with the qualities banished. It was necessary, however, that a large amount of earth and water, in terms of mass, be present in us, so that the abundance of water and earth might temper the much more vehement force of fire and air. Also given to us is a larger brain and a warmer heart than to other living beings. The former, so that it may provide for contemplation through various instruments; the latter, so that many and clear spirits may be present in the brain. The head is also suspended, lest the impurities of heavy humors descend to the brain and contaminate the purity of the spirits. Also, the intense coldness and humidity of the brain, and the heat and dryness of the heart, temper both each other and all the members. Therefore, in man, the most temperate constitution of all seems to exist. If this were earthy, like that of almost all beasts, we would be covered with horns, teeth, claws, harder beaks, rough and hairy skin, and scales. But now, on the contrary, the human body is so constituted that it is neither rough from an excess of heat and dryness, nor rigid or sluggish from excessive cold, nor fluid and slippery from superfluous humor, but equally delicate and solid. This is also understood from the foods we constantly consume: airy, sweet, ground, thinned, liquefied, and most temperately prepared; while beasts consume the opposite. Moreover, what kind of constitution one has, such foods one desires; and what kind of foods one uses, such one becomes. Let us conclude, therefore, that man is born for contemplation, as Anaxagoras says, since both the brain and the rest of the body are so constituted in him as to continuously serve the office of contemplation; which requires both the softness of the brain and a temperate bodily constitution: the former, lest it be too much dried out by speculation; the latter, lest it be diverted from contemplation by the tumult of humors. But since the moderation of our body is so great and sublime that it imitates the temperateness of the heavens, it is no wonder if a celestial soul temporarily inhabits this dwelling, so similar to heaven. Yet it is not infused into the flesh first, but is led by suitable means, so that

The Persian Magi teach. First indeed, in its very descent, it is enveloped in a celestial and airy body; then by a spirit generated from the heart, which in us is most temperate and most lucid, like heaven. By these intermediaries it is enclosed in a grosser body. And to all these it becomes equally close, although it may have transfused itself from one to another, just as the heat of fire adheres most closely to air and water, even though it is drawn to water through the air. And deservedly, the immortal soul is joined to mortal bodies through that immortal ethereal body. Indeed, it always inhabits that perpetual one, and these mortal ones for a short time; so that the soul may deservedly be called a kind of god, or a star surrounded by a cloud, or a daemon:
[Marginal note: D] not an inhabitant of the earth, but a guest. Guest, know thyself. Know that you are a citizen of a celestial homeland. A citizen born for contemplating heavenly things. Remember, if your end is contemplation, your life is augmented and perfected by contemplating. When indeed from this very thing the life of the body is in some way diminished, it follows that in the very detriment and destruction of bodily life, your life does not decrease, but increases.

*Second argument. Just as in natural things there is a resolution to the first*
*immortal matter, so there is to the ultimate immortal form.*
Chapter 3.

[Large initial O] rder of natural bodies is so instituted that it descends to the first
[Marginal note: E] matter and ascends to the ultimate form. And the more any matter approaches the first matter, the more potent the matter becomes: that is, truer and purer matter. The more any form approaches the ultimate form, the more perfect the form becomes. For the first matter is the matter of matters. The ultimate form is the form of forms. Take this example that we wish. We divide the body of an animal into members as if into its matter; each member into four humors, which are a kind of matter of the member. Similarly, each humor into four elements. And an element into simple matter, to which it is finally necessary to arrive, lest we descend into infinity, lest we be compelled, conversely, to ascend without end. For nowhere will there be a mixed act, if nowhere there has been a mixed potentiality. Nowhere again will a pure act be found, if nowhere a pure potentiality can be found. And

--- Page 381 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 150

Since action has its beginning from pure act, and passion from pure potentiality, actions and passions will be nowhere. Therefore, there must be simple matter. This simple matter, which is subject to the form of an element, is indeed called primary matter, because the artificer of nature itself, in fabricating bodies, first takes this matter bare; soon it clothes it with the qualities and forms of the elements; then it produces the elements into the species of humors; then it arranges the humors into the forms of members; to the members it adds the capacity for nutrition; to this, the form of sensing [F]; to this, finally, the form of understanding.

The intellectual nature, however, is twofold. One is so alien from bodies that it provides no life to them; therefore, this is not called a form of matter or body, and that order of bodies does not terminate in this nature of mind as its proper form. This rank, among Plato's followers, is held by the sublime angels. But there is another nature of mind, which, joined to the body by a kind of covenant, conspires with it [G]; into which, as if into the ultimate form of matter, the progression of bodies ascends.

Of this progression, there are two termini: matter is the lowest, that mind is the highest. If they are very far apart from each other, they have opposite conditions. Therefore, just as primary matter is mere matter, by its nature entirely devoid of form, subject to all forms and matters; so that ultimate form, namely mind, is mere form, namely entirely devoid of matter, presiding over all forms and their matters.

Likewise, just as primary matter is furthest from primary being, and is closest to nothing, whence it is placed by Plato between being and nothing [H]; so the ultimate form is furthest from nothing, and is closest to primary being. From this, three things follow. First, that the ultimate form in no part springs from matter. Second, that it is made by God alone. Third, that it will be able to remain immortal [I].

The first of these is concluded from the first comparison which we introduced. The second from the second. The third follows from the first and second. From the first, thus: If it is entirely devoid of corporeal matter, which is the beginning of destructive change, it is far from destruction. And if it is the head of mutable things, it neither succumbs to mutable things, nor undergoes any change except a vital one. From the second, however, thus. If the term closest to nothing does not tend towards nothing, what wonder that the term furthest from...

--- Page 382 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

farthest from nothingness, and closest to first being, is never thrust out of being, nor thrust into nothingness? Again, the nature of form is more perfect than that of matter: since matter is perfected and adorned by form. Therefore, just as descending from matter to matter we gradually arrive at the eternal prime matter of bodies: so also ascending from form to form, we are gradually carried up to the eternal ultimate form of bodies: lest the ascent be more imperfect than the descent: and the supreme term be more imperfect than the lowest. It is fitting for that intellectual form, towards which the whole endeavor of universal nature tends as its end, to be so absolute and complete that it is far from death: but it is not necessary for intermediate forms to be immortal. For nature seems to hold them in little regard: since it chooses them not so much for their own sake as for the ultimate one. In this, they seem wisely to exist as certain preparations of matter for receiving the ultimate form, rather than as principal forms themselves. Through those, as it were, paths, the very motion and impulse of nature passes: in that (ultimate form) nature stops its motion. Rightly, therefore, those (intermediate forms) will pass from being into non-being: that (ultimate form) will rest in being: so that the end of nature may remain without end. But we say that the whole endeavor of universal nature is directed primarily to this, that an intellectual animal may exist from the intellect being present in the body: but that the intellect itself, in itself, can only confer divine action. And since it depends solely on eternity itself, it will be eternal. But what shall we say about the intellectual animal? The Magi do not doubt that it too would have remained in its temperance, as Plato writes in Charmides, if only the soul had remained in its, that is, divine, temperance. For from it (the soul) proceeds all the body's consonance and dissonance. The Mosaic and Christian law teaches precisely the same thing. But that the universal order, which it once lost due to the disordered motion of the soul, must finally be restored to order by order itself prevailing again: not only Moses, but Zoroaster, Mercurius, and Plato agree. But of these things elsewhere. Now let us conclude what was proposed. Therefore, let the two terms of the corporeal order be perpetual, both the lowest and the supreme.
