If it were entirely free and operated nothing through the body, it would not be a form of the body. If it were entirely overwhelmed and acted nothing without the body, it would not be the ultimate form. For there would be something further than this, whatever might be found to be such: that it would be partly joined to the body, partly not joined. And indeed, it is necessary for there to be some such [form]: [Marginal note: C] so that between that angelic substance entirely separated from the body and acting nothing through it, and another form entirely joined to the body and acting everything through the body, such as the soul of beasts, there might be a certain middle form: partly joined to the body, partly also separate: so that it might accomplish something through the body, something through itself. And every rational soul is such: because it both governs the body and speculates. The human soul is also undoubtedly such: which performs the operations of nourishing and sensing through the instruments of the body, but perfects the act of understanding and choosing through itself. Thus an angel is separated from matter both by substance and by operation: and entirely in eternity, because entirely in a state. The souls of brutes are joined by both, and entirely in time: because they are changed by both. Rational souls, because they must be partly joined and partly also separated: nor could they be separated in any way if they were joined by substance: necessarily they are separated by substance, or are separable: because, namely, they have no origin from matter or from an agent—

Objection of Epicurus: & response concerning forms most similar to God. Cap. 4.

Epicurus says we are dreaming when we assert that forms in any way exceed the matter by which they are sustained. He thinks they are absorbed by matter to such an extent that it is impossible for any form, however excellent, to operate anything beyond matter. G [marginal note] But we believe that all the works of nature (as Plato writes in Philebus, and Aristotle confirms) are perfected by a certain divine intelligence, which, indeed, revolving the heavens as its instruments, and, as Plato says, "summoning the celestial chariot," thereby forms this lower matter of the elements.

And just as in art the form of a work has a threefold degree (for it is first in the mind of the artisan, second in the instruments moved by him, third in the matter thereby for- H [marginal note] med), so the forms of things which God generates or creates here through the motions of the heavens, either transmitting or preparing, are first in God himself: then in the heavens as if in channels or seats: finally in this lower matter.

But this matter, since it is thus moved by divine intelligence, must receive and bear forth some most exact form of divine intelligence. Which we also observe happening in nature and the arts. Indeed, the vital nature of the soul, through natural heat as a kind of instrument, moves the matter of the food taken by us, and renders it vital. This life imparted to food imitates not the form of that heat, but of the soul. For heat by itself does not generate life. A painter also, through his instrument, the brush, marks some form on the wall: not one similar to the brush, but rather to his own mind, which had first conceived it within itself, and afterwards brings it forth. Therefore, both according to na-

...ture as well as according to art, the form of the work reflects the form of the agent.
I of the agent. But indeed, in this, we find a threefold degree. One form we see closer to matter than to the agent: another closer to the agent than to matter: and some intermediate one. Take first some example in nature. For the soul, through that instrument of hers, namely natural heat, bestows a threefold form upon digested food. For to the coarser parts of the food it imparts the form of bones: for it generates and nourishes bones from them. But to the finest parts, for the most part, it applies the form of its own spirit: because from these it recreates the spirit. Finally, to the middle parts it provides the form of flesh and nerves. All these things that natural heat performs, not by its own power, but by that of the soul. For it itself only burns by its own nature, and dissolves: but for works of this kind it is tempered by the power of the soul. The form of bones is most remote from the soul, and closest to matter. These five senses, I say, which nevertheless do not yet depart very far from the body, since they never act unless external bodies are present. Receive moreover an example in the arts. Indeed, the instruments which artisans use have only their own certain nature and figure: yet they do not have the very beauty of the artist's intelligence. But through these, the artist's mind performs certain three things, some very close to itself, others most remote, others intermediate. Indeed, all works of the artist that pertain to sight or hearing almost entirely declare the artist's genius. Those which pertain to the three remaining senses, very little. For in preparing odors and flavors, or in tempering beds and baths, the artist's intention appears little or scarcely. However, in paintings and buildings, the artist's counsel and prudence shine forth. Moreover, a certain disposition and, as it were, figure of the mind itself is observed. For thus the mind expresses and shapes itself in these works, as the face of a man looking into a mirror shapes itself in the mirror. But most of all, in speeches, songs, and sounds, the artistic mind brings itself forth into light.

These forms of the elements surpass those preparations of theirs in that they are the ends of those preparations: and in that they distinguish proper species: and they remain in a way firmer. For the coldness of water seems to change more quickly than the species of water: and similarly in other things. Nevertheless, they are entirely immersed in matter: because they are not resolved into other species or principal forms, but are soon introduced by qualities into matter, close to the shapeless bosom of matter. Hence, because of the passive nature of matter, they are scarcely partakers of a single action. What else does fire do but burn? This indeed signifies, above all else, that the nature of this mind is excluded from the bonds of matter, since it has obtained an operation free from commerce with matter. For matter indeed impedes the power of knowing. This appears from the fact that the forms of elements, mixtures, and plants, which are close to matter, know nothing. And in animals, those parts serve multiple senses to which coarser matter ascends less: such as the head: and there the sense is sharper, where the instrument is purer, and the spirit most abundant.

Hence sight, because it is purer than the others, senses more quickly and acutely, and impresses the marks of things more deeply upon us. And therefore, through those things pertaining to sight, we recognize anything more clearly after a long time, than through the indications of other senses.

Moreover, even in dreams, sights present themselves to us more often than sounds. Nor does matter only impede the power of knowing, but also the thing to be known. Therefore, when the sheer mass of things presses upon a sense: we either sense nothing at all or with difficulty.

The forms of things also present themselves to us first: and through them, we, as it were, implicitly understand matter. Furthermore, we necessarily infer privations through habits, and matter through a certain relation to form.

However, we do not think of all forms through a relation to matter: which signifies that matter depends on the genus of forms: and that there are some forms free from matter.

Again, we know things most clearly and most firmly when we consider the very reasons of things without the conditions of matter.

If matter is an impediment both to the power and to the object of knowledge: it follows that the soul...

And if through lower cognitions we conclude that the soul is not from matter, through supreme cognition, namely through intelligence, we can conclude that the soul is not from matter: so that just as what knows without matter, is without it: so what comprehends without the conditions of matter, may exist far from its passions. For if the soul of man were such a form, that it were referred to matter as its origin: it would not know any forms except through some relation to matter. But now, as mistress of matter, it subjects it to forms, while it refers matter itself to forms: and, like God, it refers subsequent forms to the first form, and God himself. But he who in this very act rises most above matter, because he raises it above itself: also becomes closest to God, because he reduces all forms into God. From which it is clearly established what we have long sought, namely that the rational soul emerges as most similar to God among all bodily forms, to such an extent that no other can become more similar after no other can be made further in matter: since this one shines forth at the very extreme threshold of the body.

But it was necessary to express some form in nature most similar to God: if indeed the divine artisan is to overcome matter, as Plato taught in Timaeus. He wishes such a mind to be that which is in the body, derived from the mind which is outside bodies, as if a certain face of that mind shining in the mirror of a more sublime matter.

Consider to what extent fire elevates matter to its own likeness, and by what degrees. The sphere of fire possesses a threefold quality: heat, light, and lightness tending upwards. That sphere moves the lowest bodies: and infuses heat only into the coarsest and most inept bodies: as usually happens in stones. To purer ones, heat and light: which it easily does in wood. Finally, to the thinnest, beyond heat and light, also that lightness drawing upwards. Lucretius's Objection: & the response that the mind can operate without a body.
Chapter 6.

Two impious men, Lucretius and Epicurus, will disturb our discussion, as they usually do, not with any reason, but with clamor. We indeed assert two main things here: that God creates the soul similar to Himself, and that in matter. Against the first, Lucretius will object: If the soul is so divine, first it is against its nature to be joined with a body to form the species of an animal: then, even if it is joined, why does the mind never speculate anything when the imagination is not thinking? Against the second, Epicurus will object thus: If God creates the soul in matter, then also from matter: and therefore mortal. We have responded to the first objection, and we will respond more extensively elsewhere. **Epicurus's Objection: & the response that God does not make the mind except from Himself, & through Himself. Chapter 7.**

"In what way," says Epicurus, "does God produce this soul in matter, unless also from matter?" But we ask him, in what way does the sun produce light in the air, yet not from the air? A face in a mirror (produces) an image, not from the mirror? The mind of the speaker (produces) the meaning of a voice in the air, yet not from the air? Therefore, just as the sun indeed generates heat in the air from the air, yet light not from the air itself, although in it; and the mind of the speaker generates sound from the air, but the meaning of the sound not from the air itself, but in it: so God draws out other forms from the depths of matter; but intellect, which is the ultimate form, He spreads over the face of matter: He does not draw it from its bosom. Epicurus ought to have considered that matter itself has no proper formative power of itself (for nothing formless forms itself), yet it has a formative power and preparation, which we call the inception of forms, and the ancient theologians called ancient chaos: to which God, as Timaeus teaches, applies a formative power: not as proper to matter, but as some instrument of God Himself

--- Page 397 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 158

one will observe in four degrees, both of forms and of the subject. Rational souls are kindled by the sole and pure ray of God upon the pure face of indivisible matter. Irrational souls are brought forth into light through a celestial and also an animal influx, applied to that divine ray, from the bosom of matter not yet extended. Familiar forms of elements and mixtures are drawn out through familiar qualities of elements from the already extended bosom of matter: extended, I say, through non-terminated dimensions. Foreign forms of the same are brought forth through moreover foreign qualities of elements from the womb of matter already extended through certain terminated dimensions. But we therefore believe these forms, besides rational souls, to be bound to matter, because they have absolutely no operation without some contribution from the body's nature or instrument; and they always propose to themselves the use of the body as an end, inasmuch as they depend on the body, while through a celestial or elemental formative instrument they are accommodated to the formable virtue of matter. A sign of which thing is that none of them is turned towards God, as if God C is not their proximate cause, but rather an alien one. But we conjecture especially that the rational soul is made by God without any instruments from this, that it is proximately turned towards God, which we will declare in the following. Therefore, instruments concur not to the production of the human soul, but to preparing the matter which the soul of man is about to inhabit. But God himself produces it when the matter is prepared. Which Plato D teaches in the book On Nature, where he wishes the rational soul to be attributed to the sole artificer of the world, but irrational ones also by his ministers favoring this work. Aristotle also, having followed his master E in this, says in the second book On Animals: "When man is generated, the intellect is infused from outside, and to be solely divine, whose operation is not completed by anything corporeal." As if it is not brought forth from the innermost bosom of matter, as he thinks other forms are brought forth. Therefore, God himself infuses this without an instrument. You have an example in the light of the sun, and in the soul. The light of the sun, through heat as a medium, having dispersed the clouds, clears the air; it illuminates the clear air by itself. The soul, by natural heat, by cooking food, prepares it for the form of life.

--- Page 398 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

To cooked and prepared food, it (the soul) gives the form of life not through heat, but by itself. The soul again, through the tongue as an F instrument, breaks the air: the broken air sounds: by sounding, it signifies. That sound is as it were a certain animal constituted of broken air as a body, and of the signification itself as a soul: which signification indeed, like a soul, lies hidden in words, and is as it were a certain unheard life of the heard voice. From where then is such signification given to sound? From the very soul of the speaking person. But does the soul give signification to the voice through the tongue? G By no means. For the tongue is a body, and gives only a corporeal and sensible function: nor does it give any signification by itself whenever someone speaks by chance, with the mind not attending to the matter. Signification, however, is an incorporeal and insensible thing. Otherwise, whoever heard a voice would immediately know what is signified by the voice. Therefore, signification, which is something insensible, becomes as it were a certain soul in the voice, that is, in broken air as a body. It happens, I say, from the thought alone of the soul itself: not through the service of the tongue. And therefore, while you pronounce "Plato", that broken air is divided into many parts. Plato, namely. Which pass through three moments of time. Signification, however, is not divided into parts: because in the indivisible mind of the speaker, it is conceived in a moment before it is pronounced: and it often signifies very great things, whose mass it cannot itself equal in magnitude. It also signifies motion and time often without motion or time. And when it is pronounced by sound, with a part of the sound itself pronounced, very much is not yet comprehended by the listener: nor is it perceived gradually, but when all syllables are pronounced, what is signified by all of them is understood immediately. Which signification indeed often remains perpetual in the listener's intellect while the syllables perish: just as it had been in the speaker's mind before he spoke. H Signification therefore, produced by the speaking soul without a medium, is incorporeal. And the soul of the voice is simple, and in a certain way immortal: but sound, fashioned through the tongue as a medium, is dissipated into parts, and perishes. If the sun and the soul accomplish something in matter without instruments, much more will God be able to impart some form to matter with no instrument intervening. And that will especially be the rational soul: which thinks and chooses something without an instrument. Which it would never be able

--- Page 399 ---
if it were made by the operation of an instrument. If it is made by God through no medium, it is made by Him only through God Himself. God is eternity itself. Therefore, it is made through eternity itself. What is made through eternity is eternal. And what is closest to the highest state is so stable that it is most remote from mortal change. For this is the ultimate change. Rightly, just as in other kinds of things, besides that which is such by itself, there are also others which are such by another: so in the order of eternity, beyond God, who is eternal by Himself: many things become eternal through Him. Indeed, Timaeus teaches that those things which are begotten by God without a medium are such. [Marginal note: I] Therefore, the soul of man will be both immortal: and inserted into this body as an aerial signification when God speaks. If anyone observes this signification, he will understand the mind of the speaking God.

Panaetius' Objection: and the Response that the Soul is from God without a Medium.
Chapter 8.

Perhaps Panaetius will grant us that something can be created by God in [Marginal note: K] matter without matter and instrument: but he will not concede that our soul is made in this way, unless we show this again by some more manifest sign. For we believe that the soul of the newborn is generated from the soul of the parents, just as the body is generated from the body: because children are often born similar to their parents both in body and in character. But Panaetius' conjecture seems to have little weight, because they are often born dissimilar in body, and most often in mind. And those who follow paternal customs, imbibe them by habit rather than by generation. And if some do not acquire them by use, they nevertheless imitate them: they do not imitate for this reason, because the soul is born from the soul: but because the soul from a tender age is drawn to its own body: in which, due to the parents' constitution, certain similar incitements occur: but as age progresses, they change their customs by their own will both for the worse and for the better. Therefore, Panaetius' conjecture must be rejected. But since he would demand a sign from us: by which it might be shown more clearly that the soul comes from God: such will be our sign. Whenever some thing occurs to the rational soul, it investigates not only what that thing is, and of what kind: but also what its origin is. Nor does it ever cease unless it has found its cause. Nor yet

--- Page 400 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...halts its progress at any cause, but always investigates the cause of the cause: so that it does not rest before it has attained the supreme cause. Every single thing rests in its own proper end. [Marginal note: L] The proper end of a thing is its own proper cause. For there it is perfected: and all things desire natural perfection as their end. But if they seem to seek a common end, they do not, however, adopt it unless it is suitable and accommodated to them, and becomes their own. It becomes such when it is received in a proximate, sufficient, and higher-ordered cause. Air does not seek Venus or Jupiter, although it also draws its origin from there: but fire seeks its natural concavity: where its proper principle is, and its domestic place. Other things likewise do not seek just any cause of themselves. For no things would cease before they are transformed into God: who is the first principle of all things. Or if they were never transformed into God, they would move in vain and rashly. Therefore, they do not seek just any cause, but a proximate one. For it is sufficient for each to preserve its own species incorrupt and whole. But this is preserved by its proper cause, which is sufficient and higher-ordered: The highest cause, however, would change the species of a thing more remote from itself into a more sublime nature, where that thing would cease to be what it was, and would perish: but things do not desire that, but to remain unharmed in their own state. In which, insofar as they remain, they also attain a likeness to the first cause. To what end are these things? So that you may understand that any thing, only when it has reached its proximate cause, immediately rests, and does not seek further. And therefore, the mind, which rests in no thing unless in the first, has no proper cause except the first. A sign of this is that the human mind turns to God without a medium. For if things turn back to their [Marginal note: A] cause, as they proceed. Those things which proceeded through a medium, turn back through a medium. Those things which proceeded without a medium, also turn back without a medium. The soul is reflected back to God without a medium: when it beholds God neither in any creature, nor in an image of sense and fantasy, but absolute and naked above all created things. It beholds such a God, indeed, when it argues that God is so infinite that He surpasses by an infinite interval all things that can fall into thought, where nothing created is interposed between God and the soul. But in what way would the soul's gaze be fixed on God without a medium, unless also the power of beholding

appetite

--- Page 401 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 160

...unless also the power of seeing had proceeded from Him without a medium? But if the soul seems to need certain media for this, from the fact that it ascends to God through the disposition of the world and the orders of angels: know that the soul does not use these media to behold God in them or through them as if the sun in water or through glass, but as if by certain steps, so that it, which once fell below itself, may return through these steps to its own citadel: where, having returned, it sees God without a medium.

Furthermore, through the disposition of the world: it is invited, having abandoned the cultivation of the body, to return to its own reason: through the investigation or inspiration of angels it is admonished, having abandoned the customary discourse of reason, to receive itself into the light once divinely infused into it: where, having reflected, through the very light of God it now beholds God: like one who through a sunbeam no longer beholds the colors of bodies, but the sun itself: concerning which Zoroaster says:
χρή σε σπεύδειν πρὸς τὸ φάος, καὶ πρὸς πατρὸς αὐγὰς [B]
ἔνθεν ἐπέμφθη σοι ψυχὴ πολὺν ἐσσαμένη νοῦν,
that is: You must ascend to the light itself and the father's rays, whence the soul was infused into you, surrounded by much light of the mind.

But that the mind sometimes reaches this state, we infer from this: that it so separates itself from all thought of created things, that it asserts a divine summit to exist through infinite space, transcending every concept of any created thing, however sublime. While it thus describes God, it comprehends God according to its powers. It therefore has some power capable of God without a medium. And this is attributed to God alone. For He who alone forms, He alone disposes. He who fills, He amplifies: just as sight receives that innermost and inborn ray from its origin, by which it most closely sees the light of the sun, daily from that same light of the sun itself. And so that power capable of God needs no medium beyond God to receive God: just as the visual ray needs no medium to receive the solar ray: because both ray from ray, and power capable of God from God, without any medium interposed.

Hitherto we have proven our proposition chiefly through the intellect. Again, we prove the same chiefly through the will. [C] Every appetite is fulfilled by the possession of its cause. For the thirst of appetite is quenched by perfecting the very thing that ignited—

--- Page 402 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...and bringing it into being. The will can be filled by the possession of the sole infinite good. For it desires good only as far as the intellect presents good to it. The intellect finds the common nature of good itself separated from all the limitations of participating things, which for this very reason remains infinite in itself. It also spreads infinitely, since goodness can be communicated to innumerable things in infinite ways. If the will desires good only as far as the intellect offers it, but the latter offers infinite good and infinite goods, it follows that the will desires as many. Therefore, it is filled by the possession of the sole infinite good. Furthermore, just as the object of the intellect is God Himself under the aspect of truth, so the object of the will is being itself under the aspect of good. But since every faculty can be content only with that in which the complete nature of its object is found, it follows that the intellect and the will can be satisfied only by God, in whom alone is the complete nature of truth and goodness. And because the former (intellect) always moves from one truth to another, and the latter (will) is carried from one good to another, it is sufficiently clear that rest can be obtained for them only from that which embraces all such things. For a settled state, indeed, stops motion; and an infinite settled state (stops) a motion that is in a way interminable.

Finally, the legitimate intellect is that which understands things as they are; the legitimate will is that which desires things as they are desirable. But things are as they are ordered by God, and they are desirable as they are ordered towards God. Therefore, neither the intellect nor the will can rest in things themselves; but the former resolves into God, the latter refers to God. To the former (intellect), God alone is proposed to be contemplated by natural instinct; to the latter (will), God alone is to be loved. If infinite goodness alone is able to fill the capacity of the will, then surely infinite goodness alone creates the nature of the will, especially since the will itself sometimes directs itself to infinite goodness without any intermediary. Which it does most evidently then, when the intellect no longer proposes this good or that good to the will, but either shows the accumulation of all goods together, or the very source of goodness from which the harvests of such a heap have sprung forth. Finally, no effect extends beyond its cause. The human mind transcends any finite thing, because whatever finite truth or good you offer, the intellect can understand more, and the will can desire further. Therefore, no finite thing is the cause of the mind.

Which

--- Page 403 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 161

Which seems to be confirmed most strongly from this, because a particular cause and mover cannot produce a power and inclination tending towards the universal. And because in the intellect there is a power towards universal truth, and in the will an inclination towards universal good: it is plainly evident that the intellect and will are not made or moved by any created thing. For whatever is created is only particular truth and good. Can the soul not reject any particular good, although it cannot reject universal good? What does this signify, except that it is subject to the action and dominion of universal good alone? Let us conclude therefore, through the acts and conversions of the intellect and will, that the human soul has proceeded from God into light out of nothing, with no intermediary, and that infinite power of God, by which it was thus produced, is in a certain way so infused into the soul itself, that it becomes as it were proper and natural to it, through which it, whenever it wishes, turns itself to God. The Platonists think that no less infinite power is needed for someone to turn himself to the infinite God, and to recognize and love infinite being under a certain aspect of infinity, [marginal note: G] than for something to be made out of nothing. By His infinite power God created the soul out of nothing: by the infinite power of God the soul reaches that same infinite power of God, which begot it out of nothing. Which infinite power indeed: whether it is infused into the soul once, or rather is continually infused and preserved by God: demonstrates that it is a participant in infinite power, and (so to speak) capable in such a way, that through this very power it attains the infinity of God. We know that the infinity of God is whole, at once, and complete: the infinity of time, by which it continually vanishes, and is continually renewed: has partly flowed away: and will partly flow away: [marginal note: H] nor does it ever have anything in the present except a moment. A moment is immeasurably surpassed by complete infinity. From which it follows that the infinity of God immeasurably surpasses the infinity of time by an infinite distance. The soul attains that. Therefore it far surpasses this. Wherefore it exceeds all limits of time: and lives perpetually. Which is most strongly confirmed from this, that if God does not make it through angelic and celestial powers, much less through material seeds. And therefore it does not undergo a destructive change. If therefore you desire to worship your parent: worship only Good itself. Do you seek a parent? The nature of the body is not your parent, O soul.
X

--- Page 404 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY
For the better you are, the more you obey your parent. But you are so much more excellent, the more you oppose the body. It is entirely good for you to be with the father: it is in a way bad for you to be with the body. No mere mind begot you, O soul. The operation of the mind is changeable. If therefore you had been made by it, you would entirely have a mutable substance: and therefore you would halt your progress in the very mutability of the mind, nor would you demand a truly stable nature, nor would you think anything beyond the mind. No complex intellect created you. For you would not attain the highest simplicity, and the attainment of intellect itself would suffice for you. But now you ascend to life itself, to essence itself, to absolute being itself, by understanding and loving, above any intellect: nor is intelligence enough for you, unless you understand both well and the good. But the Good itself is certainly enough for you. For you do not seek anything for any other reason, except because it is good. Therefore the Good itself is your creator, O soul: not a good body: not a good mind: not a good intellect: but the Good: the Good itself, I say: which consists in itself, infinite beyond the limits of any subject: and grants you infinite life, either from eternity to eternity, or at least from some beginning into eternity.

Third Argument. As is the object, such is the power. Chapter 9.

**Q** These four things, essence, power, operation, object, have this order: that from essence flows power; from this, operation; operation seeks an object; and such an essence operates through such a power, that is, its proper power, in a certain way concerning an object suitable to itself. It is not to be thought that from essence flows any power other than one proper to it, nor that from power is produced any operation other than a natural one: nor that operation is concerned with any object unless it is similar, convenient, and suitable. For why does that natural power of the essence, in operating, seek one object rather than another, unless because such a thing is more proper, more apt, and more convenient to it? For unless it were more suitable with a certain one than with others, it would either seek none, or it would seek all equally. Thus the innermost ray of the visual power through the ray of the sun...

--- Page 405 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. X. 162

sees colored rays. The innermost air of the ears draws in through the external air what is broken, that is, sounds: The sense of smell, generated in the misty air vapor, perceives through such vapor (diffused from an apple into the thick air) the fragrant vapor within the apple. [C] The sense of taste, submerged in the moisture of saliva, perceives through the liquefaction of food in the mouth flavors that are either naturally liquid or already liquefied there. The sense of touch, accommodated to earthly nerves, easily perceives earthly and solid things, and very much corporeal qualities. You see that objects always agree with natural operations and virtues. You are compelled to confess the same regarding the mind: that the mind is free from matter, whose object is free from matter. Such, however, is the universal reason and idea of every thing. Such an object, the primary one, the Platonists and Peripatetics call it, because it presents itself at the first and direct glance. They consider the adequate object to be the entire breadth of being itself, because the intellect traverses universal being by abstracting, dividing, composing, and defining. [D] Being, however, is common to all incorporeal as well as corporeal things, and is infinite. And lest anyone be so deceived as to say that the intellect perhaps agrees with the universal reason in some other thing rather than in separation itself, we must consider that it agrees most of all in that which it necessarily does itself in order to understand. But what does it do most of all? Certainly, it separates both itself and the universal reason/idea from the passions of matter. [E] Nor does anything more impede either the intellect from understanding or the universal reason/idea from being understood than the conjunction of passive matter. Therefore, if not only such a power seeks such an object, but also such an object, by its approach, makes the power much more of that nature (just as sight, naturally luminous, both seeks light and becomes more luminous when light approaches), it follows that the mind is not only removed from matter and ample on that account (because it naturally and constantly directs itself to remote and ample things), but also that it becomes much more remote and ample from that very fact, because those things which are remote and ample strike, seize, and occupy it. But it can be separated from matter only so much, namely, that it may escape the passions of matter. For it naturally desires the reason and idea, both of every thing and of being, absolute from these (passions of matter). But it can attain this through the very same nature by which it is moved towards it. And finally, the ideal reason itself, which is entirely in eternity, since it is in God, can entirely raise the mind, elevating itself towards it with all its might, above the limits of place and time.

*First Argument. The mind is united with a perpetual object, and receives species*

Chapter 1.

[Marginal note: F]

[Large decorative initial R]eason itself, thoroughly absolute, is that very thing which is understood by us actually, primarily, correctly, and properly. That which is understood in act becomes more one with the intellect through an intellectual species, than that which is seen in act through a visible species, with sight: and so much the more, as a closer bond arises from purer things. This bond is further increased by the fact that the visible, indeed, is outside sight; but the intelligible reason itself, which is present to all matter of the world capable of being formed by it, and to every place (since it does not regard a proper location), undoubtedly resides in the innermost parts of minds, which are by nature most proximate to it: whence they are always affected both by it and towards it. If, from the understanding intellect and that intellectual species (or reason signified by the species), a unity is formed; and if that species and reason, as such, is separated from place and time and the other passions of matter, the intellect in this very act will be removed from these same things. An act of this kind is proper to the intellect itself. A proper act accompanies a proper essence: and vice versa. Therefore, the intellect, not only through its proper act, but also through its proper essence, will be separated from all contagion of matter. And just as that common reason, as far as it is in itself, encompasses all place and time (although as it regards matter, it inclines towards place and time), so the mind, accommodated to it by nature, although as it regards the body, it confines itself to parts of place and time, nevertheless, as far as it is in itself, it in a certain way encompasses both in their entirety, especially because a species cannot be absolute according to its power of signifying, if the mind

Objection of the Epicureans and response concerning the union of the mind with absolute species from sempiternal reasons.
Chapter 2.

[Marginal note: E] [Large initial N] Let no Epicurean here bother us, objecting that the light of the sun is indeed received by the eye, the eye perishes, but the light of the sun remains unharmed. Similarly, that universal species (that is, universally significant), and sempiternal reason, are grasped by the intellect; the intellect sometimes perishes; but the species or reason remains. We respond that the light of the sun is by no means received by the eye, because not even for a moment is it held by it; and when the sun sets, sight loses the light in a moment. For if it had received any light, it would certainly retain some of it, even for a short while, just as water retains heat for some time after the fire is removed. Therefore, we can affirm that light is present to the eyes, but by no means that it is inherent in them and received. But the mind is said to receive that universal species and reason of man and other things precisely because it retains it in memory even when the man is absent. Add to this that this very
[Marginal note: G] light, which is light and visible, is not derived from the eyes. For it is such by its very nature; and the eyes obtain from it that they may become clear and see. But that universal species of man, this very fact that it is universal, it does not have from the individual persons of men themselves, in whom whatever exists is particular. Yet it is universal in the mind. Therefore, in order to be universal,
[Marginal note: F] it has it from the mind. But in what way, especially as Aristotle pleases. Our mind has two powers: one active, the other

--- Page 409 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 164

...indeed receptive. The agent is that which produces universal species; the receptive is that which receives them, conceived by the agent. When therefore the imagination contemplates in itself such an image of this man, like Socrates, immediately the light of that agent power strikes that image, no differently than a sunbeam strikes water. And just as this sunbeam, reflected from the water onto the opposite wall, there creates a splendid and trembling circle: so the very light of the agent power, striking the particular image of a man conceived by the imagination, and reflected from that image into the receptive power of the intellect, thereupon gives birth to a certain species in this very (power), which no longer refers to this Socrates placed in this location and time, but to the nature of man equally common to all individuals, freed from the specific limits of place and time, where both the species itself is universal, and the nature referred to by it is universal. In this, the marvelous power of the intellect appears.
Indeed, he who creates a species freed from matter, place, and time, and therefore in a way receives into himself something eternal and created [Marginal note: G]: through which he also apprehends a similar nature, why should he not also be freed from these same (limits) and be perpetual? Finally, those things which the intellect grasps as thus separated: if they are such by their nature, such also is the intellect; for when it grasps separated things, it is then there where they are themselves; therefore, it too is separated. But if by nature they are enslaved to those passions, but the intellect by its own power frees them: much more and primarily is it itself free, so that it may free other things. Tell me, why can the form of any thing not become one with the intellect before matter is entirely separated, unless it is because the intellect itself is much more and primarily separated from matter? But in what way one is made from that species and the intellect, that comparison which we introduced concerning the ray and water teaches us. But if it falls upon a mirror, it will be more closely united. Finally, if the same (light) returns to the sunlight from which that ray had been sent forth which had created the splendid circle: it will completely coalesce into one. **PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...of that active power by which the mind gave birth to it? What, moreover, is our mind, if not a certain spark of the superior mind? Therefore, that species is infused into our mind in the same way that a spark of things [is infused into] a spark of the superior mind; and as that splendid circle [is infused into] the light of the sun by whose ray it had been created. Therefore, from the mind and the species, one is formed in such a way that from two sparks joined together, one flame [is formed]; or from the rays of two candles, one light; or from that splendid circle and the light of the sun, one radiance. Moreover, that which is thus united eternally through the species becomes, without controversy, eternal: especially for this reason, that the intellect, perhaps by understanding, is not only united with the eternal thing understood, but it is also the eternal thing itself which is understood. For it is in a certain way the same ray which strikes the water from above, which shines in the water, which is reflected in the air; where, poured back into itself, if it should acquire the power of seeing, it will immediately see that radiance of its own which flowed back from the water. It will do the same if it has rebounded from gold or silver. For it will always see its own radiance, although affected in various ways according to the variety of objects from which it has been reflected. If a more suitable example concerning those two powers of the intellect and [Marginal note: A] this union is desired: let us consider the eye of the *muscipula* (by the name 'muscipula' one understands a cat, which the common people call 'cat'), in which, almost as in our mind, there are two powers. There is in it a glassy transparency; and there is also a spark. The former power is receptive, the latter active. The spark shines forth at night: it draws the image of this or that color from bodies opposite to it: it imprints it upon the transparent power, which through it perceives the object body. Indeed, perhaps it does not so much perceive the opposite body, as its own ray which was unfolded and folded back; and when it was folded back, it rebounded into the eye, already painted with the image of the body. Therefore, although it seems to discern now this color, now that, it always nevertheless discerns itself in a certain way, but in a varied manner, shining back from various colors. What prevents that active power, which is a ray of our mind, shining forth differently in various images of fantasy, from being reflected back into itself, and seeing itself affected in a diverse manner according to the diversity of the images? Where that species or reason which we understand as absolute and perpetual, is perhaps nothing else than a ray of the intellect reflected into itself: which

--- Page 411 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 165

then it easily perceives itself, when it directs itself into images: just as a face does not see itself, unless it looks into a mirror: from which it is also reflected variously according to the variety of the mirrors themselves: just as the mind's ray is reflected back into the mind, varied according to the diversity of the images. But more fully on these matters in what follows.

Epicurus's Objection and the Response that Species are Innate to the Mind.
Chapter 3.

[Large initial N] Epicurus will perhaps deny that those species which the intellect daily conceives are perpetual: because they begin to exist [Marginal note: B] when they are brought forth: and cease when they are committed to oblivion. But we, according to the opinion of our Plato, think we have enough in this, that if those species are born, they are brought forth by the perpetual reasons of the soul; and they refer to eternal ideas beyond the soul. First Reason. Indeed, to sense and to understand, because they are vital operations, proceed from an intrinsic and vital principle: from an active principle, I say. For there are certain o- [Marginal note: C] perations common to living things and those lacking life: such as generation, alteration, change of place. Those things which lack life suffer operations of this kind rather than act. For they do not in any way generate themselves, or alter themselves, or change place. But living things perform these operations in themselves: because by nourishing and growing themselves, they alter and generate something within themselves: and by judging and desiring, they change place. If nature ought to instruct living things better for their proper actions than for common ones, and that which is active is better instructed than that which is passive, and it (nature) has handed over an active principle to them for common operations: much more for their proper actions, namely sense and intelligence, it (nature) has so disposed them, that they would act through these more than they would suffer. Therefore neither the mind, nor [Marginal note: D] even the sense (as it pleases many Platonists), in order to perceive anything, is formed by external bodies: but just as the vivifying part through innate seeds alters, generates, nourishes, and grows: so the inner sense and the mind judge all things through innate formulas, indeed, and excited by external things. Nor is this judgment anything other than the transition of a formula from a certain potentiality into act. For no operation ought

--- Page 412 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**
...for no operation ought to transcend the limits of the agent.

Therefore, a vital and internally permanent operation is not from an extrinsic principle lacking life, [Marginal note: E] but from an intrinsic and vital one. A sign, moreover, that the interior sense is very effective is taken from this: that it composes, divides, reasons, and by its affection turns the body into contrary qualities. A sign that the mind is most effective is taken from Boethius against the Stoics, from this: that beyond those things which the sense does, it itself devises universal rules beyond the nature of objects; it descends by composing; it ascends by resolving; and referring itself to itself, it refutes falsehoods with truths. Finally, since other powers of the soul judge the same thing differently (for imagination or phantasy judges differently, and reason judges differently), it is consistent that the judgment itself should follow the form and nature of the one judging, not of the thing judged. And because judgment exists as an act of the one judging, it is probable that each judge performs his work not from an alien, but from his own power.

Second Reason. But let us return to the mind. Just as images of particulars are not impressed upon the phantasy by bodies, as we have also proven elsewhere, so too universal species are not figured in the mind by images; but the mind produces them by its own power, just as phantasy invents images by itself. For in what way will an image (which is also called a phantasm) create something freer and more ample than itself? The image itself is indeed singular and restricted by the conditions of matter; but a species, because it is universal, is therefore freer and more ample. If this species, which is also called universal, is not formed by images, much less is it formed by external things, which cannot form the mind through any other medium than through images. Again, for one and a spiritual species, there must be one spiritual cause, or at least one united and ordered in a spiritual manner. But the individual things that are external are many and corporeal. Yet none of them, taken by itself, since it is properly only of a corporeal nature, will create an incorporeal species, and one signifying a common nature. But neither will all singulars joined together achieve this. For they are scattered; nor do they have such an order that, when such things are joined to others, they arrange a single series of causes. Therefore, just as by the conjunction of stones one simple thing is not formed, but a heap, so by a multitude of singulars perhaps something will be formed—

--- Page 413 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 166

...a certain confusion of images rather than one and simple species. Furthermore, in every singular thing, three things are found: the nature of the species, accidents which are not necessary to the species, and [Marginal note: F] the thing itself composed of both. For example, in Socrates there is humanity, which is called the nature of the species; there is whiteness, such and such a figure, which perhaps happen to the species and are called adventitious. From both, the person of Socrates is composed. Is that common species, which is the equal likeness of all humans, imprinted in the mind by these persons? Certainly, it will not be imprinted from the accidents of persons (for it would relate the accidents of man, not the substance), nor even from the nature itself which is subject to accidents. For that (nature) is not the whole person of any man, but a part of him. Therefore, such a nature is not predicated of any man. Who would say: 'Socrates is humanity'? But we say 'Socrates is a man'. Therefore, 'man' is predicated of Socrates: of Socrates, I say, as a whole: not of humanity alone, or of accidents. Similarly of Plato as a whole: and of all others. Here it appears that man himself, whom our mind commonly predicates, conceived in itself concerning each whole person, is much broader than this or that nature of each person. What it comprehends, truly, is other and broader: it is not made from that which is also comprehended and is narrower, especially since that nature becomes singular in individual men. But what has become singular does not create the universal.

But is that species conveyed to us by all and complete persons? By no means. Indeed, that species [Marginal note: G] equally regards innumerable persons. But we have nowhere observed innumerable (persons), nor have we received from some persons that which comprehends infinitely many others besides. Nor can anyone safely enough prescribe a common rule from some singulars; for whoever would attempt that would be deceived, just as if someone, when he considered only the animals of the earth and saw them breathe, would conclude that every animal breathes. Since, therefore, the species is generated neither by singular persons nor by their images, it remains that it is made by the intellect. The intellect does not generate it from a phantasm, or in a phantasm. For a phantasm, because it is singular both in being and in signifying, if it were to become the matter or place of the species, it would render it similarly singular.

--- Page 414 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

But it is doubtful whether it generates it through a phantasm as a medium cause between the intellect and the species to be generated. We believe this cannot happen for the reason that a medium cause, and one closest to the effect, agrees more with the effect than a more remote cause; as in the generation of man, because the sun generates man through man as a medium, the generating man agrees more with the generated man than the sun itself. If, therefore, a phantasm were the proximate cause of the species, the species would be born more similar to the phantasm than to the intellect; from this, two absurdities would follow. One, that such a species, immediately born, would adopt the phantasm itself and phantasy, as being closer to itself, as its natural seat rather than the intellect. The other: that even if the intellect were to receive it through such a species, it would understand something singular, both more and sooner than the universal; for it would primarily announce the singular, because it would be more akin to the singular phantasm. Nor should those be listened to who interpose a phantasm as some instrument between the intellect and the species. Does not the active power of the mind agree more with the receptive power than a phantasm? In what way then will the agent form the receptive power through an extraneous phantasm, since it is necessary for the instrument of formation to be interposed between the former and that which is to be formed, but an extraneous phantasm cannot be interposed between those two mutually akin powers? Therefore, when the intellect creates that form, it does not procreate it neither from an image, nor in an image, nor through an image. But perhaps it inserts some ray, or power, into the image of phantasy, through which the image itself, as a former of the mind, generates a form of this kind, which we call an intelligible species. But we do not think this can happen either. For that power, received in the image, will be bound by the same conditions of matter as the image. Therefore, it will not generate an intelligible form which is free from those conditions. And if someone should say that form is grasped by the intellect in an absolute manner, even though the phantasm did not create it as absolute: from that very fact we will conclude (which we primarily desire) that the intellect is not subject to phantasy as the formable is to the former, since it has forms in a more excellent way than phantasy itself can bestow. From which it follows that if an intellectual form is born, it is born from the intellect alone, and without a medium. For if the mind

--- Page 415 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 167
(On the Immortality of the Soul, Book XI, 167)

...generates that form, and by generating it, receives it into itself without a medium: certainly it produces it by itself: and produces it with no other intervening. From all these things it is concluded that the intellect forms [Marginal note: A] itself. And since if it were entirely formless, it could not form itself: it is necessary that before those forms or notions which it produces in itself almost every moment throughout its life, other forms, natural to the soul, lie hidden in the innermost parts of the soul, as many in number as there are species of created things in the world: by which it can produce the intelligible forms of those species.

Third Reason. For certain things need certain seeds. Nature does not make anything out of anything: it does not make something out of nothing. Therefore the essence of the soul, which is one and regards almost all things equally, cannot produce many and various forms in species, and some at some times, others at other times, unless through several inherent formulas differing in species: by which it may create or bring forth some rather than others at different times.

Fourth Reason. For these it often brings forth into light suddenly, even without any preceding deliberation or will, by a certain natural instinct alone. But effects which occur by natural order bear a form such as their causes possess. For hot things are made hot by a hot fire: because a cause which naturally produces something from its own being makes an effect such as itself, albeit in an inferior manner. The mind, therefore, which naturally generates universal species of all things through its own being, seems to have acquired universal species of all things in its own essence from the beginning: so that like may be generated by like. For if the efficient cause of those species is one, namely the intellect, and the subject is one, namely the same intellect: no reason can be assigned why many and different species should be made, unless because the intellect brings them forth as diverse through diverse reasons natural to itself. For the diversity of images is not sufficient to effect this variety: which contribute nothing else to this production than some occasion for operating: while through their presence the mind is excited to bring forth species. But this is nothing other than making those idle reasons more ready.

Fifth Reason. Therefore, if the divine mind, full of all ideas through its own essence, so full, without a medium, ani-

--- Page 416 ---
THEOLOGY OF PLATO
...mind, without an intermediary, creates the soul: it is necessary for the soul to flow forth from it full of ideas. Indeed, since God is in no way hindered in creating the soul, He makes it as perfect as it can be made in that kind. It certainly comes forth more perfect if it descends into such a difficult province full of notions, than if empty. Moreover, it is capable of notions from the beginning in that part where it agrees with angels. For just as in its temporal part it has the capacity to continuously search and reason, so in its eternal part it has the capacity to possess from the beginning: especially since it is closer to God than prime matter. And therefore, if matter receives all species from it, and grasps them as soon as it is ready, it is necessary for the soul also to receive all of them. But the soul is ready to receive all things as soon as it receives being from God. Since its essence is simple, stable above time: and therefore it cannot be increased, or become more ready through time. Which Zoroaster thus sang:
σύμβολα πατρικὸς νόος ἐνέσπειρεν ταῖς ψυχαῖς
that is, the paternal mind inserted conjectural signs into souls.
And Orpheus thus:
πάντα γὰρ πρώτῳ πρώτῃ φύσις ἐγκατέθηκεν:
that is, for primal nature placed all things in Proteus. Orphic theology calls Proteus the third essence, the seat of rational souls. Archytas of Tarentum also, in his book on wisdom, says that man was born the wisest of all living beings: because God infused into him the ideas of all things: through which he is able to create notions of things with his mind no differently than he forms the names of things with his mouth through his tongue. So he said.

Sixth Reason. Indeed (to speak Platonically), in matter lie the inchoations for receiving all forms. Also, in the nature through which matter is moved towards forms, the seeds of forms lie hidden. Hence, in the natural constitution of a tree, a seed is enclosed for propagating a similar tree. In the seed, the entire tree to be generated is contained. The same happens in the natural constitution and seed of an animal. Therefore, in that part of the soul which nourishes the body, and which nature uses as an instrument for moving and forming matter, there are present, and indeed much more excellently, the reasons of all forms: so that from the reason of the head which is in the soul, that seed of the head which is in nature may arise: and from this seed may sprout the form

--- Page 417 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 168

this of the head which is observed in matter. And the same may happen in the chest, arms, and other limbs. If this lowest part of the soul is fertile, and itself forms bodies, and is not formed by bodies, and contains the principles of generating forms: will the mind, which is the highest part of the soul, be sterile? Or will it only be formed by bodies? Or will it lack principles for producing species? By no means: but rather, just as the lowest part, which is closest to individual bodies, through principles inherent in it from the origin, generates individual and corporeal things: so the mind, which is closest to corporeal and utterly perfect minds, has principles inserted from there, through which it may produce those species free from the affections of bodies.

Seventh reason. For thus the soul will hold a middle place between divine and corporeal things, if it appears to partake of both: and will have within itself the principles of both kinds of forms, both intelligible and sensible.

Eighth reason. Nor is it fitting for it to be inferior to bodies. Therefore, if bodies, before adventitious qualities, possess natural qualities: much more does the mind have its own proper forms within itself before it receives foreign ones. [E] A twofold commonality of matter is fitting: natural, and adventitious. The natural is that nature in which individual things under the same species mutually agree: just as humanity, in which individual humans agree: which commonality (as most think) is perpetual, and superior to each individual. The adventitious is that universal notion which the mind thinks about the natural commonality, with all individuals set aside. Which is not only adventitious as far as matter is concerned, but also as far as the mind is concerned. If, before this adventitious commonality, matter possesses another, natural one, the mind also, being better than matter, similarly possesses another before this one. For it is necessary that some common form in the mind be more excellent than in matter. But the natural is more perfect than the contingent. Therefore, it is necessary that common forms be inherent in the mind before those which it fashions from the encounter with corporeal things. But often, while we contemplate innate forms, we think, due to ignorance, that we are looking at adventitious or external ones: no differently than those who, affected by sleep or some disease of the brain or eyes, imagine they see certain things flying hither and thither outside their eyes: which nevertheless both move and are seen intrinsically.

Ninth reason. Why do brute animals, having inspected individual things, a common

--- Page 418 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

do not conceive a notion: but man, by his rational nature, by which he differs from brutes, does this? Is it not because his very nature possesses the seal of such forms? For if he creates forms through nature and his own proper species, he certainly creates them through a formative nature. And who would say that such a nature lacks characteristics?

   **Tenth Argument.** Moreover, when in the sciences we construct perfect demonstrations from certain more excellent and broader principles, we are accustomed to demonstrate certain properties concerning species. But among those notions that are newly formed by the mind, that which is broader is more remote from the substance, and therefore the notion of species approaches the substance more closely than the notion of genus. Whence it happens that what is less common among them is judged more excellent. Therefore, there are other notions in the mind besides these, which are at once broader and more excellent: from which true demonstration is constructed. Since indeed demonstration proceeds not only from universals, but from universal causes: and the notions which are innate to the mind are not effects of a demonstrated cause: and furthermore, forms in bodies cannot be universal: it follows
[A small triangle symbol pointing to the right] that beyond the forms, both those which are in bodies and those which are in our minds, other forms must be sought in the divine mind, the creator of all: which are the universal causes of all: whose formulas the human mind possesses: so that through these, as likenesses of causes, it may, by demonstrating, refer conclusions to those [divine forms] as the causes of effects. But more on ideas elsewhere.

   **Eleventh Argument.** And this very demonstration always infers things somewhat unknown to us from more known propositions: these again from others: until it arrives at certain principles known to the mind by themselves: lest either the progress become futile to infinity: or a rash circle be woven back from the same things to the same things. But those things which are known to the mind by themselves, shine forth to the mind's gaze through the nature of the mind. Moreover, concerning individual species of things, proper demonstrations are made from their own principles, and in various faculties, various ones. Therefore, according to various species and various faculties, diverse principles of doctrine known from the natural light of the mind are present to the mind. And in these very principles all subsequent things are contained. Hence it follows that the mind by nature abounds in all doctrines.
                                                                           **Twelfth**

--- Page 419 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 169

Twelfth reason. Just as both trees and animals, and their parts, sprout from their own seeds: so sciences arise from innermost principles, lest the mind be more barren than nature, which brings forth its offspring from implanted seeds: not chance pours forth by impulses.

Thirteenth reason. When we seek truth among ourselves by asking and answering: how could the argument which is concluded reach its culmination, unless something were first conceded? But what could rightly be conceded, which was unknown? Thus this argument (as Aurelius Augustine says), unless it found something known in us, by leaning on which it might lead to the unknown, we would discern nothing at all through it. Therefore there is in us a certain understanding before reasoning, from which reasoning may take its beginning.

Fourteenth reason. Is not our reasoning mobile: and while it seeks truth, it descends from one thing to another: and when it examines something found, it ascends from one thing to another? But all motion begins from rest: or from something stable, and tends towards the stable. But motion of this kind is a complex of notions. But every thing has its own beginning and its own end. Therefore reasoning, because it is a progression of notions, is reduced to notions: because it is mobile, into some stable notions: by whose impulse it may seek what it desires: by indications it may find what it sought: by light it may examine what it found: by firmness it may rest in what has been found. Therefore it began from there by seeking, and returns to the same by examining. Therefore there are in the mind certain stable and perpetual notions, which are both the beginnings and the ends of reasoning.

Fifteenth reason. Not only of reasoning, but also of understanding in any way whatsoever. For just as sense, which [Marginal note: A] always knows through adventitious forms, which are called accidental, also always apprehends accidents, as the Platonists think: so conversely the mind, which defines the essences of things, understands through essential forms. And because sense, which trusts in fallacious and suddenly vanishing images of things, is often deceived, and does not discern the image from the true thing, but for this, the judgment of reason is needed: therefore the mind must rely on essential (so to speak) reasons, lest it also be deceived, and need the judgment of some higher power.

--- Page 420 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Sixteenth reason. Moreover, if we know angels, and we are not able to know them through species drawn from the senses—which, since they depend on bodies, do not represent angelic forms that do not incline towards bodies—it follows that we know them through innate species. For by what means do we judge angels to be natures not inclining towards bodies, unless through species in no way dependent on bodies?

Seventeenth reason. Finally, intellectual cognition is intermediate between divine and sensitive cognition; therefore, it also has intermediate conditions. God knows through His immobile essence; the senses know through mobile qualities, that is, foreign species. C. Therefore, the mind will know through immobile qualities: which are called innate species. Finally, the order of the universe requires that just as pure minds look into themselves, and the senses only into other things, D. so the soul, participating in both mind and sense, not only looks at forms outside itself, but also within itself.

But where, in the manner of Aristotle, we are accustomed to say that the mind procreates new species, we can also, more appropriately in the Platonic manner, say that innate species are drawn forth from the inner recesses of the mind. It is the nature of kindred powers that they accompany each other in operation, just as in existence: and that they mutually arouse each other to action. Kindred powers are smell and taste: whence the soul is often invited to taste through smell. Kindred, the power of desiring and the nature of being angry. Easily therefore are we provoked to anger from lust. The kinship of the eyes also causes both to turn simultaneously to the same thing. The kinship of sense and imagination causes that when the sense operates towards something, the imagination also operates towards the same thing. Because of a similar kinship, when imagination brings forth its species into act, the mind also brings forth its own into light. The species of the mind are not properly generated then, but those which were more narrowly confined, open wider and flourish: those which were lukewarm, become fervent: those which shone by themselves only at the apex of the mind, gleam brightly from afar: and in the reason that follows the mind, E. having become clearer, they now shine forth. Therefore, what Aristotle would call creation in species, Plato will name coruscation: through which the awakened eye of reason is irradiated by the species of the mind. That first coruscation in the mind is intelligence itself; the subsequent irradiation is the very discourse of reason. Through intelligence, the essences of things are defined. Through reason, compo-

--- Page 421 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 170

compositions
of defined essences are formed: and arguments are constructed. But the mind cannot fabricate true definitions of essences through accidental images of things, but it constructs them through reasons infused from the origin of all things.
   Eighteenth reason. Infused, I say, from the reasons of things which God possesses. These, indeed, in God are God's very essence, understood by God himself under various reasons. Therefore, the forms of all things are in God: and there they are nothing other than God's very essence: and all are simultaneously in habit and in act. All forms are also in an angel. They are not, indeed, the very essence of the angel: but certain essential reasons, that is, those which always accompany the essence. Where they flourish simultaneously in habit and in act: because according to all of them, the angel understands all things simultaneously in act. Furthermore, all are in the human intellect. In which they are also called essential reasons, all simultaneously in habit, just as in an angel: but not simultaneously in act: because it does not use all of them simultaneously. Therefore, it is called the lowest intellect, and in a certain way similar to matter: yet because it is more excellent than matter, it therefore has forms in an effective habit: which is not granted to matter: which habit is called the active power of the mind: because it brings itself to act. Also a receptive power: because it receives the perfection of act. Finally, all forms are in matter. Where they are also called essential reasons, because they are certain sparks or dispositions or relations to forms, perpetually accompanying the essence of matter. These are indeed powers of forms: powers, I say, capable of forms, not effective: and in a certain way forms themselves, but imperfect. Hence all are also in matter perpetually: according to potentiality indeed: but not according to effective habit or act.
   Nineteenth reason. Who would deny that the soul, from a tender   A
age, desires what is true, good, honorable, and useful? But no intellect desires unknown things. Therefore, some notions of these things are present in the soul even before it desires them: through which, as forms and reasons of these things, it judges them to be desirable. The same is proven by inquiry and discovery. If Socrates seeks Alcibiades in a crowd of people, and is someday to find him: it is necessary that some image of Alcibiades be present in Socrates' mind: so that he knows which of the people he is seeking above others: and in-
                                             Y ij

--- Page 422 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...and when Alcibiades is found in a gathering of many, he may be able to distinguish him from others. Thus, the soul would neither investigate those four things, nor would it ever find them, unless it possessed some notion of them—that is, of truth, goodness, honesty, utility—through which it would seek them in order to find them; so that whenever it finds what it had investigated, it may recognize it and distinguish it from their opposites. And we prove this not only from appetite, investigation, and discovery, but also from judgment. For whoever judges someone to be a friend or an enemy to himself, does not ignore what friendship or malevolence is. In what way, then, would we daily judge many things true or false, good or bad, as we are accustomed to, and judge correctly, unless truth and goodness were known to us in some way from the beginning? How again would the works of architecture, music, painting, and other arts, as well as the discoveries of philosophers, be often rightly approved and disapproved by many, even those not versed in these arts, unless some form and principle of those things were granted to them by nature? Comparison also shows us the same thing. For whoever, comparing honey to wine, declares one sweeter than the other, recognizes what a sweet taste is; and he who, comparing Speusippus and Xenocrates to Plato, judges Xenocrates to be more similar to Plato than Speusippus, undoubtedly knows Plato's form. In the same way, when from many good things we rightly consider one better than another, and one appears better or worse than another by a greater or lesser participation in goodness itself, it is necessary not to be ignorant of goodness. Furthermore, when from many and diverse opinions of philosophers or even of others, we often judge very well which is more similar to the truth and more probable, it is necessary that we do not lack some intuition of truth, so that we know what things are more similar to it. Therefore, some in adolescence, some even without a teacher, and most, from the very few rudiments of doctrine demonstrated by teachers, are said to have become most learned. Which could never have happened unless nature, as we said, greatly assisted. Socrates abundantly demonstrated this to the youths Phaedo, Meno, and Theaetetus, and taught that boys can answer correctly in individual arts if someone prudently questions them, since they are endowed by nature with the principles of all arts and disciplines.

--- Page 423 ---
**ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XI. 171**
**Confirmation of the foregoing: and moreover concerning ideas. Chapter 4.**

But we can argue again thus from those three books of Plato, Phaedo [B], Meno, Theaetetus, and moreover from Parmenides, Timaeus & Symposium. If by 'head' one is properly and especially denominated greater, and the other lesser, that indeed is absurd. Firstly, because by the same thing it will be both greater and lesser. Then something will be placed by one species into another species: for example, by the species of head into the species of greater or lesser. It is better however to call something 'headed' by head than 'greater' or 'lesser'. Finally, it is absurd to call something greater by something small. Therefore, if a formal cause is to be asserted, it will be called greater by greatness, lesser by lessness. Similarly, we will not properly call the number ten greater than nine by unity, since we properly call one by unity; but rather greater by plurality, and we will say another is lesser by paucity. Likewise, we will assert that the dual number is made not by the division of one into two, because it will also sometimes be contended to be made by the conjunction of this thing and that. And altogether, it must not be said that the same thing is properly effected by opposite causes. Therefore, we will rather assert that the dual number is made by the participation of duality itself according to form. But let us set aside these as lighter matters; let us proceed to more serious ones.

If color or figure is beauty itself, in what way will some color or figure be deformed? Likewise, by what reason would many subjects participate in one beauty as common, unless one common nature of beauty were both inherent in each and presided over them, so that what is inherent depends on what presides? Therefore, goodness itself is one thing, and things which become good by participation in goodness are another. Beauty is one thing, and beautiful things are another; and similarly concerning the other species, which Plato calls ideas [C]. For beautiful bodies are many, but beauty itself is one. For everything first and highest in any kind of things is only one. Again, these beautiful things [D] have two natures: both a corporeal matter, which participates in beauty, and a quality of beauty. But beauty itself is nothing other than beauty, because whatever is primarily such in any genus is nothing other than such. Likewise, these bodies are partly beautiful, partly also ugly- Y iij
