Many Platonists, furthermore, argue from the objects of the mind in this manner. Since our intellect naturally grasps forms, and understands principles either separate or by separating them, it follows that the common principles of things themselves, separated from matter, are its natural objects. But since objects of this kind move, form, and perfect the intellect, they are therefore constituted in a more excellent and truer degree of the universe, and are very far from fictions, lest the mind, both judge of truth and corrector of the senses, be further from truth than the senses. For this reason, those principles are deservedly considered to be of a more sublime, truer, and more efficacious nature than the intellects which are formed from them. But are they in turn to be called intellectual? Not properly, indeed. For rational souls are intellectual by participation, but angels are intellectual by form. Finally, those principles and ideas are intellectual according to cause, but intelligible according to form. For the intellectual relates to the intelligible almost as the desiring and the movable and the formable relate to the desirable mover and former. But where are they? Indeed, Platonists generally place less common ideas in more common ideas, and finally all kinds of ideas in the first being itself, the most common and most perfect of beings, which they call the highest intelligible: intelligible indeed according to form, but intellectual according to cause. To this, they next subject very many minds, intellectual according to form, but intelligible according to participation. To these, however, they subject rational souls, intellectual by a certain participation, but not intelligible at all. Therefore, they consider being itself, and the intelligible itself, to be the same, because being is natural and adequate to the intellect itself, in which respect it is the object of the intellect. Furthermore, they place the intelligible itself under the first principle of things. For that (the intelligible) is such that it can somehow be comprehended, but this (the first principle) not at all. They properly call the first principle unity itself and goodness. And because unity refers to eminence and light separated far from all things, the intelligible, however, refers to a certain light already proportioned to intellects...

Furthermore, because minds desire both to understand and the intelligible, not simply, but also well and the good, yet they desire the good simply: for this reason also they prefer the good, that is, the supreme God, to being itself, which is also intelligible. Not to mention that the intelligible relates to the intellect, but the good relates to the will. Therefore, not only is this different from that, but also more excellent, since that which ravishes the will is more excellent than that which is comprehended by the intellect. Wherefore, they think being itself is perceived by the intellect according to its powers, but the good rather draws the soul to itself through the will, and, having been drawn, transfuses it into itself as well; and if it is touched in any way by the soul already occupied in its own manner, it is properly touched through the unity (E), the head of the mind, which God, who is the prince of the unity of the universe, inserted in us from the beginning. But to return to our subject: (they hold) that in the good itself, ideas exist by way of cause, distinct from each other only by certain relative reasons; but in the intelligible itself, properly by form, and moreover differing from each other by absolute forms; in the subsequent minds, whether separated from the body or conjoined, already distinct by a certain participation and gradually more and more distinct; but in nature, certain lowest seeds of forms infused from ideas; finally, in matter, shadows. Plato indeed names the good itself (F) in his letters as God the Father, but the intelligible itself as God the Son. Plotinus also (calls it) God from God, and light from light, and reason, and the Word of God. Again, Plato in the Epinomis, through such a divine reason or word (which he calls the intelligible world), affirms that the sensible world was adorned. Similarly, in the seventh book of the Republic, he says the idea of the good, that is, the good itself, in whose form all ideas are one form, is the cause of beautiful ideas, namely, those which are many in subsequent (levels).

Plotinus and Proclus confirm the ideas with the preceding arguments: and place them differently in the first God (as they say), and differently in the second. [marginal note: G]
But some others proceed to the same point thus. Indeed, in the lowest matter, the shadow of ideas emerges; but above matter, the face of all ideas shines, of which the source is God, the author of things, as Plato's Timaeus most clearly teaches, and the tenth book of the Republic, and Parmenides. For if mind and nature are full of forms, and through them act in a way that appears in natural and artificial things, deservedly also God, who is the shaper of nature and mind, ought not to be formless. Therefore, he acts through forms, which we call ideas. These Plotinus and Proclus call not only exemplary, but also essential forms. [marginal note: H]
For they think the maker of the world uses no consultation in making the world. For such an operation would be imperfect: and he who consults about perfecting a work would first have conceived an imperfect work in himself in some way, then inquire about its completion. Which is alien to a perfect mind. Likewise, if the universe were arranged only by a mutable discourse of providence, there would be nothing stable anywhere, nor would the world's motion be perpetual and stable. Therefore God makes and arranges the universe through his very being: especially since such an action is the first and most common and easiest of all actions: and therefore, from some first, most common, most easy cause, it exists wherever it is, and it especially suits it. But every cause that makes by its very being, makes such an effect in the next degree as it itself is in the first. Since therefore the world is a complex of all species, it follows that the maker of the world is a complex of all species in a way more excellent than can be conceived, and has the exemplary forms of all things, and, to speak in their manner, essential to himself. Which they again confirm thus. If art imitates nature, and produces works through the reasons of works, then nature also possesses the reasons of its own works. Again, since nature itself lacks reason, and is moved and perfected by God, it receives reasons from the very ideas of the divine mind. And by how much the reasons of nature are more internal to nature itself than the reasons of art are to art, by so much at least ought the divine reasons to be more internal to God than the reasons of nature are to nature itself.

They add that sensible forms are not entirely and truly what they are named. Indeed, equality and likeness everywhere partake of inequality and unlikeness. But true beauty cannot exist in a subject that is in itself deformed and formless. Nor can true good exist where there is defect and a tendency towards evil. Moreover, they deny that there is a true line or surface in celestial things, or a true point of the center and poles. Since their essence is indivisible, they cannot exist in a divisible thing. But our mind has and generates true forms, through which it refutes other false ones, observing how much they differ from the true ones. Therefore, much [Marginal note: I] more does the soul of the universe possess and [Marginal note: H] generate the true principles of forms. For where virtue and intelligence are more excellent, there is the conception and birth of more expressive forms. Finally, the [Marginal note: K] creator of the world generates even more certain and more perfect forms in himself; and (to use the words of Proclus) while observing himself, he generates himself, and simultaneously generates all things in himself. Added to this, since the members of the universe conspire among themselves in a perpetual order, they are reconciled and governed not by chance, but by reason. That reason which orders all things cannot be ignorant of itself. Otherwise, the highest reason would be irrational if it had no reason of itself. For that reason is more rational which embraces itself by knowing itself, than that which abandons itself by being ignorant of itself. Therefore, it understands itself as the ordering reason of all things, by which it is brought about that it always understands by what reasons and ways individual things are disposed. Therefore, in the highest reason of all, are the reasons of all. Is it then because God was about to make all things that he knew all things? Certainly not. Otherwise, he would refer his essential operation and his very conversion to himself to external things, and would depend on something else. Therefore, just as the sun, by shining in itself, illuminates all things, so God, by understanding and willing himself, both knows and effects all things. Who would not see that if by seeing himself, he sees and makes all things, it follows that in his substance there are substantial forms which are the exemplars and causes of all things? For always in the very order of nature it is so, that from an interior action an exterior one proceeds, and the work itself is very similar to the action; just as from shining comes illuminating, from illumination comes the illuminated, [Marginal note: A] similar to illumination and light. Likewise, plants and animals are generated from seeds. But there must be in the seed the ra-

...principles which are, in a way, of the living being rationally procreated from it. They are not, however, in the corporeal seed except potentially. For the seed is uniform, and almost formless: but what is generated from it is multiform and beautiful. Likewise, if a seed is divided, many wholes are born from it: as if the wholes that are generated lie hidden in the parts. From this it is clear that the seminal power hidden in the seed itself is in a way incorporeal, in which is the principle of this motion and generation. But it is necessary that multiple principles of a manifold living being reside in the seminal power, which we call nature. For the same thing, insofar as it is the same, could not immediately generate such great diversity. Moreover, it is necessary that they exist actually. For that which is such potentially, as imperfect, cannot be produced into something actually such, except through something which is actually such, and more perfect. Therefore, individual principles of the individual parts of the living being, differing in kind, inhere: by which [B] each part may be procreated in its own time, place, and order: and, if possible, very often recreated if cut off. But are the seminal powers in the seeds of living beings the highest causes? By no means. For the species itself does not come from any of them, but rather something particular under the species: and each of them derives its origin from another under the same species. Therefore, one must have recourse to universal nature: in which are the universal principles of all their species. To the nature, I say, of the earth, the creatrix of earthly things: especially since corporeal seeds are often lacking for plants and animals spontaneously growing everywhere: from which it follows that for their production incorporeal seeds are necessary. [C] And so that we may proceed in a convenient order, let us refer each species of earthly things to the universal nature of the earth, and similarly in the other elements: then the natures of the four elements immediately to the nature of the moon, in which are the principles of all elemental things: and the nature of the moon to the nature of the superior sphere: and similarly thereafter. Finally, all natures to the very nature of the universe: in which necessarily are the principles of all natural things as well as of all natures: principles, I say, both exemplary and effective: so that it may direct and produce all natures according to certain rules towards certain ends. But nature cannot be the highest reason and cause of things: first, because it is irrational in itself (which is evident in our nature), for it knows neither itself nor other things: then, because it is a cause mixed with its effect: just as if a craftsman with wood in-

But nature, even if it is irrational by itself, must nevertheless have the reasons (or principles) of corporeal things, by which it can intrinsically and rationally order, move, and form individual things in suitable ways towards a fitting end; and since it is irrational by itself, it ought to be guided by that which is rational by itself, and formed by reasons. Indeed, it is irrational to commit the order of the universe to a nature that is irrational by itself. Therefore, in the superior cause, it is necessary that the reasons of things exist so rationally that the cause itself, perceiving itself and its own (reasons), has a certain understanding of itself and of its own reasons. It would certainly be absurd, since we have understandings both of ourselves and of our works and of the universe, for the cause of the universe to have understandings neither of itself nor of its own (creations). Wherefore, if the creator of the world knows all things, he certainly did not look to other things in order to perceive them; since his knowledge undoubtedly precedes other things produced by that very knowledge. For who does not know that external work follows intrinsic action? Therefore, God, looking into himself, knows all things. Whereby it happens that in Him are the species of all things, through which He knows and makes all things. And (to speak summarily), just as in this material world all matters are finally reduced to one ultimate matter, so much more in the formal world are all forms necessarily reduced to one ultimate form. From these things, the madness of certain dogs barking that Plato placed ideas outside the divine intelligence is condemned.

A single heaven full of stars figures a torrent at night with images of its stars: which images are neither stars, though they seem to be to infants, nor do they remain, but are continually renewed by the flowing water: although they are commonly thought to remain. **B** Similarly, God, a single overflowing fullness of ideas, always shapes fluctuating matter with simulacra of ideas: which simulacra, indeed, are neither true species according to the Platonists, although some physicists consider them to be true: nor do they ever rest, as Heraclitus says, as matter flows away: even if the ignorant believe them to rest. And this is the way by which temporal things, as Parmenides the Pythagorean wishes, become participants of eternal ideas. But since that which measures is more excellent than that which is measured: the human mind, insofar as it measures all temporal things through relations to ideas, which are contained under those very ideas, is more excellent than those things. And therefore it is closest to the ideas, because it measures whatever follows them, inasmuch as it falls in the middle between the source of ideas and the streams flowing from there. But although it measures in relation to ideas, it does not, however, measure through the ideas themselves as if through certain proper and proximate means. For universal ideas are not the proper instrument of this or that human mind; nor do universal ideas fall in any way in the middle between a singular mind and other singular things. But since the mind cannot measure the singular images of universal ideas otherwise than through formulas of ideas proper to the mind, and, as it were, inclining towards singular things, it is necessary for formulas of ideas to inhere in the mind, through which it may compare images to ideas, and approve what agrees with the formulas, and disapprove what does not agree.

F But from where do these formulas come to the mind? Is it from images? Or from a fiction of the mind? Or perhaps from ideas? Not from images: for through these formulas the mind measures images, whence the formulas precede the images, and are so much more excellent as they are closer to the ideas. And if they were made from images, they would not truly measure them, but rather would be measured by them. For measure is a correspondence.

*Confirmation of the foregoing by signs. Chapter 5.*

Now, we find many signs of this matter. First, that rustic men, who never thought anything about ideas, and adolescents who heard nothing about them, when beautiful bodies first meet their senses: provided they use reason, they refer them to ideas: in two ways (as we said). In one way, when they affirm this to be beautiful: which they do only because the figure of such a body corresponds to the seal of beauty innate within. In another way, when they affirm this to be more beautiful than that, and that more beautiful than the other: inasmuch as one approaches the seal more closely than another. Such a seal they acquired neither previously through doctrine nor through invention: because they neither thought anything about it, nor heard about it: nor even then do they collect it from individual beautiful bodies. Indeed, through that which is least fallacious, they refute the fallacy and defect of individuals. Nor from some common nature which is in individuals. For what lies in fallacious things, itself also turns out to be fallacious, and from itself creates a fallacious notion. Moreover, when they think about it more diligently: they find it either to be or to refer to something one above many, subsisting in itself. For above that nature which is in a certain way one in many, there must be such a nature which is one before many: so that it may be equally common to many. Such a seal, because it is in no way enclosed by the multitude of singular things, is in no way collected from that multitude: nor is it conceived by the contrivance of thought. For through it we find that above the mobile and manifold beauty of each soul, there is one beauty abiding in itself. Therefore, the seal raises its power higher above souls: but the contrivances of the mind fabricate nothing more eminent than souls. If therefore, when we first use reason, we refer very many things to this

The second sign is, that both relations happen suddenly, often even with no preceding intention of the will, or discursive reasoning. Which signifies that the rule for relations of this kind is not to be acquired by the soul from above or externally, but has long been possessed internally: by which it can make use at will, as often as it directs itself to it.

The third sign is, that all experience in themselves whenever they wish to find the definition and cause of something, they attempt nothing else than that, with all obstacles of sense and imagination removed, they penetrate the innermost parts of the deep mind: to whom then first most clearly shines what they seek, when first they have penetrated into the inner sanctuaries of the secret mind: as if in-

The fourth sign is taken from approval. The bodily complexion which abounds in blood demands certain tastes, as well as other uses of things: that which abounds in bile, others; that which abounds in phlegm, others. When to each complexion that which is its own is offered, such a nature does not accept the offered thing otherwise than fire itself accepts sulphurous fuel. Hence the sanguine person commends sweet things, the choleric person sharp or pungent things, the melancholic person sour things, the phlegmatic person soft and insipid things. What we say about the sanguine person, is similarly to be transferred to others. The sanguine person does not know for what reason he approves sweet things: because he does not commend by counsel, but by nature.

...by the instinct of complexion. Indeed, through natural instinct it also desires kinds of qualities: red and green by sight; A joyful by hearing; sweet by taste; temperate by touch and smell. If it desires and approves these five qualities through complexion, it is necessary that in the very constitution of the complexion there are five inherent seeds of these five approvals. For just as among those five qualities there is one reason and another, so by such a complexion they are approved under one reason and another. Therefore, in every person there are five natural seeds for approving five qualities congruent with the five senses. And because in other people there are different complexions of humors, therefore the desires for bodily things among people are diverse.

But since there is one human species in all, and since the species of mind is one, therefore the approbation of those things which pertain to the mind is common. Every mind praises a B round shape in things immediately considered, and does not know why it praises it. In buildings likewise, it praises such things as the squareness of houses, or the equality of walls, or the disposition of stones, the opposition of angles, the shape and arrangement of windows. Moreover, in the same way, it praises a certain proportion of human limbs, or the harmony of numbers and voices. It commends moral gestures and habits as decorous. It commends the light of wisdom and the intuition of truth. If any mind immediately accepts all these things always and everywhere, and does not know for what reason it accepts them, and cannot but accept them, it accepts them by instinct, necessarily and entirely naturally. But because there is a diverse reason among those things which are desired here, it is necessary that by the mind, from diverse reasons of its nature, they are desired as if by seeds, and approved as if by formulas and rules: so that by the same rules their contraries are rejected. Indeed, their contraries, as soon as they are presented to us, offend by their nature, even if we do not know the reason. Therefore, the reasons for those things and similar ones are innate to the mind.

Hence, he who teaches is a minister rather than a master. Wherefore Socrates, in Plato's book on knowledge, the Theaetetus, says that he is the son of a midwife and very similar to a midwife, inasmuch as in educating people he does not introduce knowledge, but draws it out, just as midwives draw out already conceived fetuses. Therefore, when some teacher endeavors to demonstrate something to the listener from many arguments, he who listens is not gradually formed, like clay by a potter, or some stone by a sculptor; but after many indications, he suddenly perceives the truth, even in the absence of the master, when he has been sufficiently provoked: just as a field cultivated by a farmer, after his long labors, itself produces fruits in its own time, with the farmer doing nothing. Who taught eyes to see? Who taught ears to hear? A doctor does not provide sight to the eyes, but either dispels the mists poured over them or directs them towards an object; so a teacher does not pour knowledge into the mind, but purifies its keenness or directs it. No one provides hunting sagacity to dogs, no one provides the virtue of running to horses, no one provides warlike strength to elephants; yet often men compel those very virtues, latent and dormant in their limbs, to awaken through use. The teacher does the same in the mind, as Plato teaches in his own book, the Republic. For the mind possesses its own virtue (which is the intuition of truth) no less firmly and naturally than the senses and animals possess theirs. Socrates, the leader of teaching, provokes it by questioning; it itself, when rightly questioned, answers truly. It cannot answer truly unless it has known. But since things themselves are connected to each other, and similarly the reasons of things are joined to each other, from which one easily passes from one to many, it often happens that from one certain trace shown by the teacher, the keen mind of the student hunts out many things in a long sequence with its own nose. Add to this that the mind has no weaker faculty for seeing truth than feet have the power of progressing. Socrates leads an infant by an outstretched hand so that he may walk; he questions a youth so that he may learn. He does not provide the virtue of walking to the infant, but both provokes him and leads him more safely to the goal. He does not bestow understanding upon the youth, but makes him more ready for the accomplishment of his own work. But if Socrates himself is ever said to have acquired his knowledge, he acquired it as new, either by discovery or by learning. If he himself discovered things by himself, he would never have used the discovered things, unless for using

But where an idea shines in an absolute and clear manner, it not only shines clearly, but almost entirely. For all the properties of the idea which we narrated at the beginning of this discussion, according to Plato's mind, consist primarily in this, that it is universal and detached. But that not shadows of ideas, but clear images are inherent in us, is especially clear from this: that we distinguish their shadows from their images by right reason, or that their inherent forms clearly represent them to us and turn us towards them; and the shadows of ideas in bodies do not refer them to us until they are purified and reformed by the forms of our mind. Finally, if they shine in our minds through distinct images, and in a complete and detached manner, they also shine in a thoroughly immortal manner. But if the natural subject of an immortal thing is immortal (for when the subject is dissolved, whatever adhered to the subject is dispersed), without doubt the mind of man is immortal, which naturally and firmly receives the forms of immortal ideas in an immortal manner.

**A**urelius Augustinus, a man of divine genius (than whom no Latin expressed Platonic majesty more exactly, both in wisdom and eloquence), having built upon the foundations laid by Plato, constructs arguments of this kind. (F)
One thing is the true, another is truth: just as one thing is chaste, another is chastity: and truth is more excellent than the true: since every true thing is true by truth. But when something that is called true perishes, truth nevertheless does not perish: just as if a chaste person perishes, chastity nevertheless does not perish. If this world will always remain, it is true that it will always remain: but if it will not remain, it is true that it will not always remain. What, when it has perished, if it is destined to perish: will it not then be true that the world has perished? For as long as it is not true that the world has perished, it has not perished. Therefore, it is contradictory that the world should have perished, and it not be true that the world has perished. But something cannot be true where truth is not. Therefore, truth will exist, even if the world perishes. What if truth itself perishes? Will it not be true that truth has perished? But I do not think it can be true if truth does not exist. Therefore, truth will in no way perish. Thus Augustine. But where, then, is truth? Not in bodies: for it would change when bodies change: since truth is nevertheless eternal, from this follows that Platonic paradox, that bodies do not truly exist, because, of course, truth does not remain in them. (G) Therefore, what we call gold, if it is not truly gold, is false gold. If this is the case, it is not even gold. And so concerning the other kinds of corporeal things. Furthermore, a bodily state does not remain entirely the same through two points in time, as we have shown elsewhere: and now we show in this manner. Just as stable and simple eternity is the measure of stable and simple things, so flowing and varied time is the measure of mobile and multiple things.
Points in time never remain the same, but always creep upon each other, with one succeeding another. The mobile body of the world has time as its own proper measure. If this is so, then the disposition and change of the heavens certainly fit the flow of time. Therefore, the disposition of the heavens cannot be entirely the same in two moments of time. For if it were to remain the same through two moments, in that very brief interval, time would indeed have flowed from one moment to another, but the heaven would have rested in one.

--- Page 446 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Flow, however, is by no means compatible with rest. What is not compatible, does not measure. For how does motion measure rest, or
A a flowing thing through two [moments] measure a thing standing in one [moment]? Therefore, in that brief interval, time would not have measured the heavens. But in reality, time always measures the heavens, no differently than eternity [measures] those things which are above the heavens. Therefore, just as those [things] remain in eternity continuously without any change, so the heavens under time continuously pass without any rest. If the configuration of the heavens in no way remains permanent: much less do the tiny bodies which are under the heavens, and are carried away by the heavens' swift current. For it is necessary that these [bodies] continuously vary through influx and efflux, condensation and rarefaction, intensification or remission of qualities, consonance and dissonance of temperament, and other motions.
This indeed Plutarch and Proclus have abundantly demonstrated: and before them Heraclitus says. Just as we cannot enter the same water of a torrent twice, or similarly touch the same particle of a running wheel twice: so we are unable to attain an entirely similar disposition and temperament of a body persisting through two points. If the affection of no body persists entirely the same and similar through two moments: in the same moment such a quality begins, and ends. What begins in nature does not yet possess a complete act of existing or operating: what ends, no longer retains such an act. Therefore, at that point in which that quality is said to be,
B it can also be said not to be: since it has not yet entirely departed from non-being, and is already slipping into non-being. And because the swiftness of time surpasses the swiftness of the tongue: while you pronounce that quality to be, it flees as you pronounce it, before you have uttered this very word "is" with your mouth. And as Timaeus says, it deceives the one pronouncing: nor is anything ever truly pronounced or perceived about this. Nor can it be said to be more than not to be: since it both is and is not equally, while it is uttered. But since those things which are continuously changed, insofar as they are changed, to that extent they become: but those things which become, while they are becoming, are not truly: therefore, whatever things are thus changed and become, are not so much said to be, as to seem to be.
But what shall we say about time? which is always falsely said to be: since its being (so to speak) is non-being. Indeed, of any present moment it is truly said, this is not time: but

But concerning the past or future, they are only affirmed to be time. Indeed, we think that a certain continuous succession is signified by time. But the past and the future do not exist. Therefore, we somehow place the being of time in non-being. But the moment, which is the limit of time, while we pronounce it to be, turns into non-being: and compels those pronouncing it to lie. And what we demonstrate concerning time, must also be judged concerning temporal things: namely, that they have their being (so to speak) in non-being.

To these things agrees that Pythagorean saying: "He who is called a man, is more non-man than man: because if you consider his innumerable parts, you will be able to judge innumerable times: this part is not a man, and that similarly." Only once will you say of the whole: "this is a man." Whence also Timaeus, distinguishing two parts of an element, considers them to be matter and form: because of matter, it is not called fire or water: but because of form, therefore, according to a part. Therefore, this alone is called fire according to a part, and that water. And in truth, this is not fire: but fiery. That is not water: but watery.

Add that that is truly such, which is purely such: for example, pure wine, which is purely wine. But the nature of each species, when it is in matter, first indeed has an admixture of potentiality towards non-being: as we proved in the fifth book. Then it suffers many additions, and often contrary ones. Indeed, in air there is often something fiery: always some position beyond the nature of air. In this or that man there is often some complexion contrary to his nature: always some habit, or affection, figure or position beyond the necessity of the human species. And the remaining species of natural things are similarly constituted.

But since above all things which are such partially and impurely, there must be those things which are wholly and purely such in themselves: Timaeus thinks that above the defiled and imperfect forms of matter there are other pure, integral, separate forms. And he trusts most in the strength of that reasoning, which argues thus. Forms which are in another, namely in matter, are also from another: Not however from the unformed nature of matter: and form must be from form, and ultimately from a form subsisting by itself: and one formable matter is ultimately reduced to one former. For even if someone were to introduce many formers, never would many, insofar as they are diverse, have a mutual order among themselves: and to one work

and will lead to an end; but only insofar as they are led by one form-giver of all. Therefore, it is necessary that forms are given to matter by a certain mind full of forms, where the forms are the very essence of the mind, and therefore are true species. But because that mind is the first being, and matter is truly closest to nothing; and the former is pure act, the latter pure potentiality: it follows that matter is almost innumerably inferior to mind. Moreover, whatever is received from something passes into the nature of the receiver. Therefore, forms immersed in matter are so much inferior to the species of the mind that they are certain shadows of those rather than images; and retain their denomination, and indeed a false one, rather than their nature. Just as artifacts are imitations of natural things, so natural things are imitations of divine things. But artifacts approach closer to the truth of natural things, because they agree with them in matter, than natural things do to the truth of divine things. If therefore a painted horse is so deficient from a natural horse that it is not a true horse, much more does a natural horse so much from a divine horse—that is, from the Idea and the true reason of a horse—that it ought to be called a shadow of the horse itself rather than representing its form. And if the true reason and nature of man and horse is the Idea itself of man or horse, and matter, being very far distant from it, does not preserve this, then that saying of Socrates in the Phaedo and in the Republic is concluded, namely, that true men and true horses are not found in matter; which so deceives the little souls of the ignorant with the shadows of the Ideas that, like dreamers, while they see the imitations of true things, they think they are looking at the things themselves.
[Marginal note: I] To these things agrees that paradox of our Proclus: "Composites from elements have neither eternity nor stability." Pure minds possess both, and comprehend all things simultaneously; the middle ones of these are those which have their eternity in a certain motion. Souls indeed closest to minds admit motion only in operation; but subsequent souls in a certain way moreover in power. Finally, the entire machine of the corporeal world, as if inferior to the souls in essence, operation, and power, has also acquired an essence so mutable that it is entirely temporal on all sides. And just as a thing entirely eternal always remains whole in one, so the entirely temporal machine of this world always flows out entirely from the divine world in every moment of infinite time,

Indeed, what indivisible eternity itself measures, must necessarily be indivisible. Therefore, that which has a divisible essence, constituted both from parts and from multiple natures, such as the world machine, does not agree with indivisible eternity, but rather with divisible time: by which it is measured, by which it perpetually glides along. Moreover, it acquires a divisible power and action through motion: wherefore the mass of the world begins to be entirely at once from non-being in single moments, and ceases, and is born again: just as in motion and time (to which it is entirely subject) moments flow out entirely one by one at the same time and flow back in. This is moreover confirmed by the fact that infinite power is needed for the perpetual motion of the heavens. Since the finite body of the world can neither have this from itself, nor receive it entirely at once from another, it must draw it gradually in single moments from its maker and mover. To draw, I say, a momentary and suddenly vanishing power.
Indeed, a temporal essence receives entirely temporally: and a finite nature cannot be capable of eternity, whose power is infinitely and entirely at once. Certainly, the nature of the world cannot receive infinity at once. And eternal infinity, since it consists of an indivisible whole at once, cannot be received gradually by anyone.
Here Proclus distinguishes these points: Immovable essences are indeed from God in a certain way once, but are preserved by themselves through their own power. A For since they are entirely from there without motion at once, they can therefore in a certain way persevere as stable by themselves afterwards: and by their own power can now proceed from certain of their own potencies into their own acts. Wherefore he calls such essences self-subsistent: and affirms that they in a certain way produce themselves: but the corporeal machine, flowing forth after the motion of the soul and time, and together with corporeal motion and time, has nothing stable, and no power to preserve itself. Therefore, not substantial or true, but entirely shadowy and false, which he calls by the custom of the Manichaeans, perpetually dissolving, and perpetually

...altogether needing the restoring influx from above, like shadows of a body in very swiftly flowing water. Hence that [saying] of Timaeus: B We say that the intelligible world always is, but never becomes; but the sensible [world] certainly always becomes: it never is. Here Proclus adds that that world always exists as numerically the same; but this one is never properly one and numerically the same, but rather one, and numerically the same, is continuously recreated. And insofar as it is body, it always becomes and begins; but insofar as it depends on the divine mind, it has always been made, and suddenly attains its end. But let this paradox now have an end.

Since therefore the whole sensible machine is a certain vanity, and daily a cause of vanity to the senses, therefore C Solomon exclaimed: Vanity of vanities: and all is vanity. Therefore there is no truth in sensible things. But is it in the soul? Perhaps it is in the soul: but not (as Protagoras and Epicurus believed) in that part of the soul which is sense: because it looks outside itself, and is compelled to perceive with a certain passion, and is deceived by the frequent trifles of sensible things. Therefore Xenophanes, Parmenides, Zeno, Melissus, Stilpo said that nothing true is comprehended by the senses. Almost the same view pleased Anaxagoras, Empedocles, and Plato.

For even if someone were to say that there are some sensible things always remaining in the same way, and bring us the question of the sun and the stars, in which it cannot easily be proven that they deceive us by swift change, D certainly no one is there who is not compelled to admit that there is nothing sensible which does not have a false likeness, so that it cannot be distinguished. For to omit other things: as Augustine says, all things which we perceive through the body, even when they are not present to the senses, we nevertheless experience their images as if they were entirely present, either in sleep or in madness. When we experience this entirely, we are unable to discern whether we perceive them with the senses themselves, or whether they are images of sensible things. If therefore there are false images of sensible things, which cannot be distinguished by the senses themselves, nothing can be perceived unless it is distinguished from the false: the judgment of truth is not established in the senses. And it may perhaps happen that the senses perceive some things truly, as pleased Aristotle; E yet it never discerns whether it perceives truly or on the contrary: and since the truth of natural things consists in this, that they agree with the reasons of the divine mind, just as the truth of artificial things, as

--- Page 451 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XI. 185

so that they may agree with the ideas of the artificial mind: the sense does not recognize this kind of congruence, and therefore does not have the test of truth.

Again, since the truth of the knowing faculty arises then, when the faculty agrees with the things to be known: but it is perfected when the sense is made equal to the ideas of things: he who perceives neither that congruence nor that equality, lacks the judgment of truth.

Add that the sense does not comprehend the intimate and pure substance of a thing: or in what order any thing is arranged in nature, which whole pertains to the very truth of the thing: but is attracted by a sudden impulse of qualities to pursue or flee: in which it indulges its own bodily comfort rather than the truth of things to be comprehended.

Therefore, the judgment of truth is not established in the sense. But it is established in reason.

For the privations of things are known through their positive states: darkness through light: and silence through sounds.

The privation of truth is falsehood. Our reason refutes sensible things and the senses of falsehood: which it cannot do except by the examination of present truth.

Again, reason describes truth itself thus: Truth is the pure integrity of each nature, and integral purity.

But truth is not defined except under the natural and proper reason of truth. In the very reason of truth, there is truth. Therefore, truth is in the mind defining truth: just as in the mind refuting falsehood.

Moreover, it is in the mind describing any thing. Indeed, the definition of a species embraces the very essence of the thing, both whole and separated from extraneous contingencies.

If therefore in the species themselves there is the truth of things, but species is comprehended by definition, and definition by the mind: who does not see that truth is in the mind of man?

Which if it is immortal, sufficiently declares that the mind to which it adheres inseparably, is incorruptible.

For a quality which adheres inseparably to some subject: is destroyed when the subject is removed.

But that truth adheres to us inseparably, this can be a testimony, because either constantly, or at least at our discretion, suddenly, and by the mind's sole collection into itself, we both condemn many falsehoods, and define some common natures, whether of natural things, or moral, or artificial.

Moreover, the same is concluded from what we showed in the preceding (pages), that the clear reasons of ideas adhere stably to the mind.

But in the very truths of all things.

are comprehended. Above all, however, this is supremely declared by the rational faculty itself, which is no less natural to man than flight is to birds, or barking to dogs. Through this, Socrates is a man; through this, man is distinguished from other species of animals. At present, we call the rational faculty the very virtue of reasoning: which discerns consequences, that is, it gradually observes what follows from each thing, and proceeds in order from antecedents to consequences. This is a certain natural dialectic, that is, the art of discourse, inherent in humans from their origin. Through this, children and the most unlearned people defend their positions with whatever conjectures and assertions they can. And every human discourse, and the whole action and deliberation of life, is nothing other than a certain argumentation. And no one is so insane that they do not infer one thing from another by arguing, and thus almost argue from images to images: just as a sound mind proceeds from things to things themselves. The rational faculty, therefore, is never separated from man. But if truth is not separated from this [faculty]: truth will never be separated from the soul. In this virtue of discourse, two necessities are inherent: one according to its subject, the other according to its use. The first necessity, indeed, is because the faculty of discourse itself is so inherent in the entire human species that it cannot be separated. The second necessity, however, which is observed in its use, is twofold: absolute and relative. Absolute necessity indeed appears in three things: namely, in the principles of discipline, definitions, and properties. Principles are of this kind: Whatever exists, either exists through itself, or through another. Opposites repel each other by their nature. Every whole is greater than its part. To each must be given what is his own. These and many similar things necessarily hold true in such a way that they are necessarily known: because they can never be otherwise, nor can they be unknown to anyone, however unlearned. There is also necessity in definitions: as when a circle is thus defined: A circle is a figure from whose center all lines drawn straight to the circumference are equal. For although such a combination of words in the mouth, or such a figure drawn in dust, may be contingent: yet that truth is necessary and eternal: because it is the very nature of a circle. Similar necessity exists in properties, that is, that a circle is the most capacious of all figures. And to omit other things, is it not in numbers from a necessary

If reason grasps necessary truth in some things, and in others it makes it, and it always grasps and makes: who will deny that there is perpetual truth in it? Indeed, who will deny that it is necessary, since it accepts what is necessary by itself exactly as it is, and does not change it; but what is not such by itself, it makes necessary by its own power? And it is much more necessary than all things which are made necessary by it through positions, conditions, and arguments. Therefore, it is absolutely necessary, almost like those principles of disciplines, definitions, and perpetual properties. Therefore, human reason either necessarily always was and will be like those [principles]: or at least it will necessarily always be. For what prevents reason from being perpetual, whose perennial action is nothing other than to provide relative eternity to any temporal and contingent things, from an absolute eternity firmly remaining within; and to arrange one necessary and perpetual series from necessary and contingent things? If it will always be: it will also always live. For reason does not exist unless living, and in a living being.

**Objection of the Sceptics and response, that something certain is known.**
**Chapter 7.**

[Marginal note: C]
Nor should the Sceptics be listened to if they deny that truth exists in our minds, because they seem to doubt about individual things. For the mind does not doubt about everything: as appeared in all the necessary truths which we have recounted and similar ones. I know that this appears white to me. I know that this smells pleasant to me. I know that this touches the taste sweetly. Who does not know that the highest good exists, than which nothing is more excellent? And that it exists either in man, or outside man: and if in man: either in the soul, or in the body, or in both. Who does not know for certain whether God exists, or does not exist? And if he exists, whether he must be one, or many: and if many: either finite in number, or infinite? Whether God must be corporeal, or incorporeal. And if he is not corporeal: he must necessarily be incorporeal. Likewise, effects declare many rules of astro- [Marginal note: D] logy and medicine to be certain: not to mention arithmetic and geometric rules, than which nothing is more certain.

--- Page 455 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XI. 187

And what is greater: if ever the mind doubts about something, then it is also certain about many things. For it does not doubt that it then doubts itself. And if it is certain that it is doubting, it holds this certainty from a certain truth. Indeed, he who understands himself to be doubting, understands truth; and concerning this thing which he understands, he is certain; therefore, he is certain about truth. And everyone who doubts whether truth exists, has truth within himself, from which he cannot doubt. Nor is any truth true except by truth. Therefore, it is not right for him to doubt about truth, who was able to doubt about anything whatsoever, as Augustine says: especially since he not only understands himself to be doubting, but also perceives that he understands this, and recognizes what he perceives, and so on to infinity. Moreover, it distinguishes a doubting mind from an undoubted one. Nor is it hidden from him how much better it would be not to doubt, and how ardently he desires truth. It compares certainty with doubt, by which it comes to be certain about both. Furthermore, it is certain that it investigates, feels, lives, exists. Indeed, he doubts nothing who does not exist, live, feel, and investigate. It is also certain that it is not the primary truth, since the primary truth itself does not doubt about itself. It knows that it is not entangled with doubt and error. It knows that in judging, it must either be mistaken or not mistaken. It knows that, whether it is mistaken or not mistaken, while it judges, it undoubtedly lives. Finally, it does not ignore that there is something else in nature outside its mind which causes it to doubt. Such certain truths are perceived even in doubt itself. [Marginal note: E] By this, we are warned not to fear Aristo, Pyrrho, and Herillus, who, while they opine that nothing true is known by us, themselves undoubtedly know that this opinion of theirs must be either true or false. They know that if it is true, something true is understood by man. They know that if it is false, the opinion opposite to it is true, namely that something true is known by man.

*Objection of the Peripatetics, and response, that truth familiarly dwells in the mind. Chapter 8.*

But are the Peripatetics to be feared, who deny that truth familiarly dwells in the mind, on the grounds that so few seem to be skilled in it, and whoever has known it has been unlearned for such a long time from infancy? Certainly not to be
A a iij

PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Augustine, where he expounds the mind of Plato, thus testifies concerning those to be feared. Either there is something in the mind which is not in present thought: or the art of music is not in the mind of a musician when he thinks only of geometry. But this is false: therefore that is true. Yet the mind does not perceive itself to have anything, unless it has come into thought. Therefore, something can be in the mind, which the mind itself does not perceive to be in itself. But as long as this happens, it makes no difference. For if the mind has been occupied with other things for a longer time: although it can easily reflect its attention on previously thought things, it is called oblivion or unskillfulness. But when either we ourselves reasoning with ourselves, or well questioned by another, perceive truths about certain liberal arts: we find those things which we have discovered nowhere else than in our own mind. For for this very reason, the mind must withdraw into itself, leaving external things, to find these. Nor is it the same to discover as to make or generate. Otherwise, the mind would generate eternal things by temporal discovery: for it often discovers eternal things. For what is so eternal as the concept of a circle: or if anything else in arts of this kind is understood to have always been and always to be? From this it is manifest that the human soul is immortal, and that all true reasons are in its secrets: although it seems either not to have them or to have lost them through ignorance or oblivion.

Imagine yourself to have forgotten something, and others wanting to, as it were, recall it to your memory. So they say: is it this, or that? bringing forth diverse things as if similar. But you neither see that which you wish to recall: and yet you see that it is not what is being said. When this happens to you, does it seem to be complete oblivion? Not at all. For the very discernment by which that which you have falsely suggested is not admitted, is a certain part of recollection. Such people, therefore, do not yet see the truth: yet they cannot be deceived or misled: and they know well what they are seeking. But if someone tells you that you laughed a few days after you were born, you do not dare to say it is false: and if the author is one to whom faith must be given: you will not recall, but you will believe. For that entire time is hidden from you by the strongest oblivion. This therefore differs greatly from that oblivion: but that is a middle kind. For there is another (kind of oblivion) closer and nearer to recollection and revived truth. To which it is similar when we see something, and we certainly recognize that we have seen it some-

--- Page 457 ---
...when, and we affirm we know it, but we strive to repeat and recall where, or when, or how, or from whom it came into our knowledge. Just as if it happened to us concerning a person: we also ask where we knew him. When he has recalled this, suddenly the whole matter is, as it were, infused with light into the memory: and we labor no further to remember.

Such are those who are well educated in the liberal arts. Indeed, they undoubtedly unearth those [truths] buried in oblivion within themselves by speaking, and in a way, dig them out: yet they are not content nor do they restrain themselves until they behold the entire face of truth, of which a certain splendor already glows faintly in those arts, most widely and most clearly. But in these [arts], certain false colors and forms, as if into a mirror, pour out thoughts, and often deceive and mislead those inquiring: thinking that what they know, or what they seek, is the whole [truth]. Those very images are to be avoided with great caution: which are found to be deceptive when they vary as the mirror of thought is changed: while that face of truth remains one and immutable. For although thought may depict for itself squares of different and varying magnitudes, and, as it were, present them before the eyes: nevertheless, the inner mind, which wishes to see the truth, rather turns itself to that [idea] according to which it judges all those [shapes] to be squares.

What if someone tells us to judge according to the same [standard] that one is accustomed to seeing with the eyes? Why then does it say, if it is truly learned, that a true sphere is touched by a true plane at a point? What has the eye ever seen, or can it see, anything of this kind, when by the very imagination of thought nothing of this kind can be conceived? Do we not prove this when we describe even the smallest circle in the mind by imagining it, and draw lines from it to the center? For when we have drawn two [lines], between which one could scarcely prick, as it were, with a needle, we can no longer draw others in the middle by imaginary thought itself, so that they arrive at the center without any mixing: while reason cries out that innumerable [lines] can be drawn: so that a circle can even be inscribed in every interval between them. Since that imagination cannot fulfill this, and the eyes themselves fail even more (since it is infused into the mind through them), it is manifest: both that it differs greatly from the truth: and that the latter, while this is seen, is not seen. The same happens when reason divides a line into infinity: which neither sense perceives, nor imagination grasps.

On the immortality of souls by the same author Ficino,

BOOK TWELVE.

Many reasons and signs that the human mind is formed by the divine mind in understanding. Chapter I.

B Plato, father of philosophers, discussing the acquisition of wisdom in his letter to the Syracusans, says that five things are especially necessary for the knowledge of any subject: name, description, image, formula, and idea. Let us take the example of a circle, as he himself does: so that we may judge the same concerning all other things. Our mind is often prompted to the knowledge of a circle by hearing, when it hears both this name "circle" and a description of a circle like this: "A circle is a curved figure, which is equally distant from the center on all sides." It is also prompted by sight: when it sees a circle made of wood by a lathe, or drawn on a wall: which is not a true circle, because it is not perfect: but an image and likeness of the true one. Prompted by these three, the mind, eager for truth, brings into action the innate formula of the circle within itself: Through which, as if by a character, it directs its gaze to the very idea of the circle existing in the divine mind: which direction is indeed the knowledge of the circle. Plato shows in that letter, however, that the mind enclosed in the body cannot rise to the idea without those four steps: because it is necessary for it, having long since fallen below itself, first to return to itself through those three: then through the formula it has within itself, to ascend above itself to the idea. For just as the forms of things from the divine mind into ma-

THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY
Friends, let us return to Platonic matters.
   Now, that we cannot truly know things unless we are formed by ideas, Plato seems to have persuaded himself of this by these reasons. First. The name of a circle is mutable. For it can be called otherwise if the use of language is varied. If this is so, the description is also mutable, which is composed of names. The image is also mutable. For a wooden circle can be destroyed, and one that is painted, abolished. The formula is also mutable from this, because it migrates from potentiality or habit into act, and from act back into habit. But that which is comprehended by the knowledge of a circle is entirely immutable, because it is both universal and cannot be otherwise. Therefore, an immutable idea is necessary to comprehend the immutable concept of a circle.
   Second. A circle, which is either made by a compass or painted, is not pure, because it has something of a straight figure mixed in. Similarly, the phantasy which follows its appearance does not attain the pure concept of a circle, which is entirely separated from its opposite figure. Reason also, if it listens to phantasy, is deceived. Therefore, it is necessary that it recurs to a pure idea, by which it may discern the pure.
   Third. True knowledge of a circle consists in knowing what a circle is. But those four (i.e., name, description, image, formula) signify quality rather than substance, because they themselves are qualities.
   Fourth. The true and perfect mode of knowing follows the mode of being. And so, just as both the circle and the other species of things are conceived and brought forth by the divine mind through ideas of ideas, so they seem to be known by subsequent minds through the same (ideas), so that all sciences imitate the primary science according to their abilities. The truth of a created thing consists in this, that it [A] corresponds everywhere to its idea. But knowledge consists especially in this, that the mind agrees with the truth. But it cannot fit the truth of the thing itself unless it also fits the idea, in whose congruence truth is situated, so that thus through the idea, which is the cause of the thing, it may know the thing, since true knowledge is through the cause. Therefore, the theology of John the Evangelist, which calls the idea the divine reason, calls that very reason truth, because through it things both truly subsist and are truly known.
   Fifth. The intellect understands and judges any created things in their absolute concepts. And just as for the most part...

--- Page 461 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XII. 190

...the same sensible things by their nature are present to all sentient beings, nor are those (sensible things) changed from there when these (sentient beings) are changed: so the same intelligible reasons everywhere and always show themselves to all rational beings; and they remain stable in themselves, while the minds of reasoning beings approach them more or less. Reasons of this kind are superior to all created things, not only because through them, as rules, all created things are approved or disapproved, but also because they are prior both on account of their amplitude and on account of their simplicity. Therefore, they are in B [marginal note] God himself, through which He himself both discerns and disposes individual things. When, therefore, the intellect apprehends reasons of this kind, then it apprehends in a certain way both God in whom they are, and the things of which they are the exemplars; yet first, according to a certain natural origin, it apprehends in a certain way God in whom they are, rather than the things in which they are not inherent, although they are present (to them). Nor should it seem incredible to anyone that any corporeal things are known through incorporeal exemplars, rather than the other way around. For through spiritual images of sensible things, whether they are in the senses or in mirrors, we perceive sensible bodies, not the other way around. But that we are thus deceived in this matter, so that while we contemplate the spiritual exemplars of things, we often think we are only contemplating the corporeal natures of things: what wonder is it, since even infants, when they see incorporeal images of bodies in mirrors, and dreamers, when they contemplate spiritual images, believe they are seeing bodies? But more plainly about this in what follows. Add to these reasons two signs, one through the intellect, the other through the will. Through the intellect in this manner: In the knowledge of a natural species, such as beauty, first indeed we devise some description of beauty common to individual beautiful things. We immediately add some properties of beauty deduced from the description. Perhaps we will concede that these notions can be devised through a formula of beauty innate to the mind. But when we dwell longer on this very consideration, we find that nature of beauty which we have defined, because it is pure, to be infinite; and because it is infinite, to be God. But no one of sound mind would concede that through a finite formula, existing below God by a very long, indeed incomparable, interval, an infinite nature, and God himself, can be apprehended.

the whole revolves. Pythagoras began his philosophical studies with the morning singing of sacred hymns.       *First Question concerning the ascent to God: how the mind*
            *is elevated to the divine idea.*
                  Chap. 2.

[Large initial T] Here three questions arise. First, in what manner
the mind is elevated to the divine idea. Second, for what      D
reason we by no means perceive ourselves seeing God in that
state.
Third, in what manner God continually infuses this very understanding into us:
which Plato affirmed in earlier passages. To the
first, we respond thus for the present. When the imagination,
excited by the figure of some human being absorbed by sight, is formed
into a human image: then the formula of the human species, which
lay hidden in the mind's secrets, being stimulated, shines forth: and it
actually forms the keenness of the mind or reason, which it had formed habitually. Such a
formation: is either a certain ambiguous understanding, or the birth
of understanding. After it is thus sufficiently formed, the idea of man
is formed, that is, that reason by which God generates
man. Thus indeed the mind, through the formula of the human idea, conforms to the
human, just as wax which has been shaped by a ring, when
carefully applied to the ring, corresponds to its exemplar. That very
conformity is the true and distinct understanding of man.
Therefore, Plato says in the Symposium that the soul, a lover of
divine beauty, when it attains divine reasons, then
no longer gives birth to images of things, but to true things within      E
itself: and nourishes those things which have been born: becomes intimate with God: and, above all others,
immortal.

--- Page 466 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

But no one seems to have revealed this secret more clearly than John the Evangelist: who, when the mind of man touches something true, does not say (as others usually do) that it sees some true thing, but that it makes truth: because, in fact, it thereby achieves that God, who is truth itself, is, as it were, made its form. For then the mind, clothed with the idea, becomes the very truth of that thing which was created through such an idea. This is what all contemplators do, whom John says receive from the fullness of divine reason: because, in fact, whoever truly contemplates some form of things, has already received into himself some from the number of ideas: the fullness of which is divine reason itself. But accomplished theologians call the mind ignited gold: because just as gold is clothed with the form of fire, by which it is heated, refined, and shines: so that mind, clothed with the ideas of the divine mind, through them both shines with the light of truth and burns with the fuel of goodness. Paul the apostle also affirms that the mind contemplating divine things is both daily renewed, and transformed into the same image as God, and becomes one spirit with Him. Trismegistus likewise says that from a pure mind and divinity, one spirit somehow coalesces. And all Platonists prove that in contemplating reasons, divine reason is touched by a certain substantial rather than imaginary touch of the mind: and that the mind's own unity is joined to God, the unity of all things, in a certain inestimable way. Which Plato often confirms in the *Phaedrus* and in the *Epinomis* and elsewhere: especially when in the *Phaedrus* he says that the contemplator of divine things is separated from others: completely purified: cleaves to God: is filled with God; and in the *Epinomis*, that the soul perfected by contemplation completely becomes one with the divine unity. He holds the same in the books *On the Republic*.

*Second Question: For what reason do we in no way perceive that we see God in that state.*
*Chapter 3.*

**T**o the second question, we can respond thus. Just as the eye, formed by the species of color, sees color, but does not perceive the species by which it sees: so perhaps the intellect, somehow formed by an idea, immediately understands through this the natural species itself, which was made through such an idea:

--- Page 467 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XII. 193

idea: the idea itself, however, it does not yet clearly perceive; indeed it does not recognize it, although it may be looking at it. Perhaps this is what happens at the beginning of contemplation and assimilation: but when it proceeds in contemplating, and becomes more congruent, it also perceives the idea itself more clearly, and recognizes it: but it does not yet discern where it perceives it. For just as children, while they look at their own reflections in the sunlight that surrounds the surface of the water, think they see them not in the external light, but at the bottom of the water: so the mind, still unrefined, while it sees the reasons of things in the sublime God, thinks it sees them in itself [Marginal note: H] or in other things: especially since the reason of a natural thing in God, for example, the reason of air, does not refer to God entirely as God, and as the unbound and free principle of the universe, but as the exemplar of air: with the result that the mind, when it is surrounded by the very reason of divine air, understands God not as God, but as air: for it sees God as airy, that is, circumscribed to the nature of air. But angels, who are formed simultaneously by all ideas, perceive the source of universal nature through the very collection of all ideas. For thus they insinuate themselves almost entirely into the divine substance, not from some part of it, as we do. Therefore, where they see those things, they perceive them. The same will happen to us when we are thoroughly reformed into God. But now, almost all of us are deceived in this, no differently than common people who, when they see by moonlight late at night, say they see in the light of the moon: when in fact that is the light of the sun, by which they also see at night. Thus ungrateful humans affirm that they perceive truths in their own and natural light, which they perceive in the common and divine light. And if the very globe of the sun either did not rise and set, or was in no way perceived by us in its own form: then no one would know whence this light is sent into the air by which we see all things: just as now no one knows whence light is sent down into the mind by which we discern all things: because God, from whom that descends, is hidden. But it descends in such a way that it is the beginning, middle, and end of our understanding. The beginning: because just as the vision of the eye itself comes from external light as a universal cause, and also from a certain inner spark ignited from it as a particular cause: so in us the act of understanding depends on the ample mind of God, and on our own. The middle, however, because in it we discern eternal reasons which are only in eternity. The end, de-

But it places the Good itself above mind and above essence. Above mind, that is, that which is the invisible eye capable of truth, eager for goodness. For God is not said to be capable of truth, nor desirous of goodness, but is truth and goodness itself. But in a more excellent sense, it can be called mind: both because divine truth is not ignorant of itself, and because from a certain exuberance of divine goodness, many minds flow forth from it. God is also placed above that essence which is the subject of being itself. [Marginal note: D] Furthermore, it is placed above that being which is the act of essence. For such an act, because it is mixed with passive potentiality, is impure and infinite. Nevertheless, it is called "being" by the Peripatetics, insofar as it is a pure and absolute act, through which [Marginal note: E] all essences receive the act of existing. But Plotinus and Proclus place the One and the Good itself above Being for these reasons. The influx of the One and the Good itself propagates more widely than the influx of Being. Indeed, matter and formless potentiality are more to be called participants of the One and the Good than of Being. Since being comes through form, but matter is formless; yet matter is called one, and eager for good. And they seem to have received this argumentation [Marginal note: F] from Dionysius the Areopagite. Furthermore, just as multitude is not the same as nothing, so Being itself is not the same as the One. Nor, however, are Being on one side and the One on the other equally disposed, lest two principles of things be foolishly posited. Nor again is Being above the One; for if the One were to participate in Being, it would no longer be one, but two, that is, one and being simultaneously. It follows, therefore, that the One is above Being. Finally, the more simply unity signifies something than being, in which essence and existence are enclosed, the more it corresponds to the first principle of things. Nor do they permit existence to be separated anywhere from essence, lest a proper act be separated from its proper potentiality. Nor do they want it to seem strange to anyone that they name the principle of things [Marginal note: G] "unity." For thus they distinguish: Either it must be named unity, or multitude, or a composite of both. But not a composite, lest it be forced to depend on that which reconciled diverse things into one. Not a multitude devoid of unity, because both it itself would lack all virtue, and the universe would lack all union. Again, in the principle of all things, all potentiality must exist. Therefore, if it itself...

multitude itself comes to be: insofar as anything might fall into multitude, to that extent they would become more powerful. Again, the Good is above it: because all things always desire the good: but beauty only those who know it, and after they have known it, Likewise, we desire beauty for the sake of the good, hoping, namely, that it will be beneficial. Finally, we truly wish to have the good: yet it often happens to us, if we openly appear to have beauty. Exceedingly blessed are those whom the universal beauty, the splendor of the Good itself, transforms into the Good itself through love: especially because while it transforms into the good, it equally reforms into the one: and therefore unites to the good itself as one. Indeed, the One itself and the Good, as the same, are equally diffused through all things, and above these things, and are equally desired by all, even without knowledge, by natural desire. Nor can they differ from each other as two things equally disposed: lest there be two principles of things. Nor can the One be above the Good: lest anything better or more desirable than the Good be said to exist.
