...and evil are equally shunned as if they were the same. Blessed is he who is entirely united with the good. But he is not united properly by intellectual virtue. For since this [intellectual virtue] is manifold, and is placed below the intelligible, it neither suits unity nor can it attain that which is intelligible, that is, the universal being that transcends it. Add to this that since the one and the good are desired by a certain instinct preceding intelligence, it follows that they are attained by a certain touch above intelligence: a unifying touch (so to speak): namely, through our unity, which surpasses intelligence, and which joins the soul itself to the very unity and goodness of all things, not by an imaginary bond of intelligence, but by a true union of its very substance. Hence, there does not follow some slight, external, and particular joy, as if of one seeing or hearing the good, but a vehement, intrinsic, universal pleasure is produced, as if of a taste and touch superior to intellect, already thoroughly tasting and touching that very sweetness which is superior to the intelligible. Indeed, natural thirst desires liquid before we recognize by sense that we are thirsty; and after we have recognized it, we desire it again. The appetite that follows sense is imaginary and more remote from our substance; the preceding one, however, is most intimate to our substance. Therefore, when we obtain liquid by taste, we embrace it not properly by the virtue of the subsequent appetite, but by that of the antecedent appetite, and we perfectly transfer it into our substance. Similarly, it is not so much the appetite that follows the action of the mind, as that which precedes it as the principle of motion, that enjoys the end of motion while it effects a substantial union; and therefore, it alone thoroughly fulfills the vow.

*Third Question. In what way God continually infuses intelligence into us.*
Chapter 4.

But from here let us now descend to the third question. I believe this to be the meaning of our Plato, when he writes that both knowledge is infused into the intellect and truth into intelligibles by the Good itself: namely, because that benevolent and life-giving act of all things, which is God, always embraces His works and inserts Himself into all things. But especially shining in the secrets of the mind, He continually purifies, sharpens, illuminates, and kindles its keenness; then He vivifies the innate formulas in the mind: so that whenever we are free from cares...

--- Page 472 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

whenever we are free from cares and apply our mind to the investigation of truth, those formulas, made more vivid by God vivifying, may burst forth more readily into the open; and the mind's keenness, ignited by God irradiating, may inspect more clearly and ardently. Where, for the very act of understanding, God acts as the first and common agent; the formula as the proper and secondary agent; the image as an incitement; the mind holds the place of matter. But let us consider this matter by example, so that we may see more clearly by what reason the act of understanding descends into us from God. If God, according to the idea of creating a mind, which is vibrant within Him, tempers our mind by procreating it, and configures it most closely to Himself; and as motion and sound pass from one lyre to another similarly tuned: what wonder is it that when the divine mind sounds forth in understanding, the mind of man resonates? A certain craftsman makes a thousand mirrors, and having made and arranged them in order, he presents himself to them. In a thousand mirrors, a thousand images of the craftsman result. Sometimes the craftsman moves himself in such a way that he turns his eye to survey his other limbs, and turns his limbs as much as possible towards the eye. The images in the mirrors imitate these movements. At the movement of the living eye, all the imaginary eyes move; at the movement of the living limbs, the imaginary limbs. Similarly, God procreates souls; then presents Himself to them as if to mirrors; through which presentation, images of God are made in each. These images are indeed the very minds of souls, so that the minds are then many, because there are many souls in which they are, and yet all are one, because God whom they reflect is one. Moreover, each mind, through its power of understanding, reflects the power of God conceiving ideas; but through formulas, it reflects the ideas themselves. From this, that prophetic saying which we touched upon above is also opened/explained: "The light of Your countenance is signed upon us, O Lord: and in Your light we shall see light." Namely, God, through His fertile power by which He conceives ideas by discerning, grants and preserves to the mind the power by which it may attain ideas by understanding. Again, God, through the ideas themselves already conceived and distinguished by reason, imprints and preserves in the mind the formulas of ideas. At the motion of God, that is, at the act of God, a continuous motion occurs in minds. In what way? The power that is in God, conceiving ideas, in a certain way bends itself towards the ideas themselves; the ideas mutually reflect back to that power. Meanwhile, by a certain harmonious tempering, it happens that the power in

--- Page 473 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XII. 196

...the power of understanding in the human mind, if it is unhindered and directed towards God, turns itself to formulas, and the formulas are turned back to the power of understanding. And thus the acts of the mind perpetually imitate the acts of God with wonderful harmony.

But since a face in a mirror, when it seems to look at the face from which it originates, is in reality more looked at than it looks: therefore the Apostle Paul says: "When you have known God, rather, you have been known by God." [B]

Thus therefore the higher face of our soul is named by the Platonists an imitation of the divine face: to such an extent that Plotinus, Theodorus Afinis, and Iamblichus believed that mind of man, which is not human but divine, lives and operates continuously in the intelligible world through a continuous intuition of ideas.

But two main reasons moved Plotinus, Theodorus, and Iamblichus to this conclusion.

First, the soul's supreme mind, because it is an intellectual essence in itself, therefore understands by its essence: just as fire is hot by its essence, and water is cold, although the power of the soul, inferior to the mind, does not understand by its essence. Therefore, just as fire is always hot, so the mind always understands.

But the objects of understanding are the eternal forms themselves of things. But the intellect, in understanding, does not cling to deceptive images of objects, but so that it may truly understand, it is united with the objects themselves. Therefore the mind is always united with eternal forms: by which it happens that it diligently cultivates the temple of eternity. [C]

To this points that saying of Iamblichus: "The being of our intellect is nothing other than to understand divine powers." For he thinks that just as it is the same act by which the sun illuminates the moon, and the moon is illuminated thereby, and looks back at the sun with a likeness of light: so it is the same act by which the divine mind creates and illuminates our mind, and ours is created and illuminated thereby, and by a certain natural intuition turns itself back there.

Similarly, an image in a mirror looks back at the face by the same act by which it is looked at by the face. And just as it comes into being by being looked at, so it is preserved by looking back. The same is the likeness of the soul to God.

The second reason is this. The rational soul is made by the divine mind, and is joined to the body: and holds the middle ground between mind and body. If it clung only to the mind, it would not bestow life upon the body. If it clung only to the body, it would certainly understand nothing. Therefore it clings to both mind and body simultaneously: just as a line that touches both the center and the circumference: just as the light of the sun is simultaneously joined to the sun, and diffused through the air. But just as the soul

Nor without reason do we place intelligence in the soul as essential and perpetual: because it is in the soul inasmuch as it agrees with the perpetual causes of its essence. And just as there is an innate, perpetual, and essential appetite for the good in the soul: so too is there a natural and essential intuition of truth itself, or rather a certain touch, to use the words of Iamblichus. A touch, I say, prior to and more excellent than all cognition and discursive reasoning. The divine Iamblichus confirmed this kind of opinion with the following additional reason, that just as we attain temporal and contingent things through temporal and contingent cognition, so it is necessary to attain necessary and eternal things through an essential and perpetual notion: which precedes our inquiry no differently than a state precedes motion. Hence it ought to be no less immortal than that, especially because the purer and simpler the mind is from bodies and souls, and for this reason the more it is one, so much the tighter a bond arises from those two minds coming together than usually arises either from any corporeal things mixed together, or from souls concurring with each other, or from a soul uniting with a body. This strengthens the bond, because God is unity itself, and goodness itself. And since through the power of unity, the bond of all things is united, and through the power of goodness, attraction and drawing near occurs everywhere, nowhere does a truer union arise than where the mind conspires with divinity. Likewise, if God, into the mind closest to Him and perpetually emanating, both glides in with infinite subtlety of purity and thoroughly fills it with the amplitude of virtue, and He Himself, like a nerve, intrinsically connects the parts of the mind, as if joints, to each other, and He Himself, like an innermost knot, binds it to the whole, and to its whole essence with being, and therefore is more interior to the mind than the mind is to itself, what wonder is it

power of divine amplitude, through its force, in its light, to its end,
the mind is continually formed by eternal ideas. And because all

PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...such that it is continually formed by eternal forms. If prime matter is incorruptible, into which certain eternal forms penetrate, although it itself does not penetrate into them: will not the mind also be immortal, which is not only penetrated by them, but also penetrates by knowing, and reflects into them by recognizing? [Marginal A] Furthermore, where there is a prime mind, there is prime life: because mind is the reflection of life into its own being. Where there is prime life, there is also prime being: because life is the first and innermost motion of being itself. Indeed, God, insofar as He exists through Himself, and truly that which exists perpetually remains: is called by many the prime being. Insofar as He does not languish in idleness, but works assiduously with Himself: He is called life. Insofar as His act is such that it does not flow outwards: but flows back into itself, He is called mind. [Marginal B] For by that reflection He perceives Himself. Since indeed that which is supreme in any genus has nothing of a contrary genus either mixed in or near it: it follows that neither the prime mind suffers anything insane either in itself or near itself: nor prime life anything mortal: nor prime being anything destined to fall into nothingness: nor prime unity anything dissoluble: nor prime goodness anything subject to disease. Therefore, the mind which is joined to the prime mind, just as in that conjunction it reserves nothing for madness: so it admits nothing mortal or perishable, or dissoluble, or subject to disease: because through the prime mind it is also coupled to prime life, and to prime being, and similarly to unity and goodness. What wonder if intellectual life, because of its encounter with prime life, remains immortal: since celestial bodies (as the Platonists wish) are indeed dissoluble by themselves, because they are both mobile and composed either of several natures or parts: [Marginal C] yet they endure undissolved from this, that they are coupled to an immortal soul with no other body interposed. But those which are dissolved by another medium: such as bodies composed of several elements, which receive an immortal soul (as the Magi transmit) through a celestial body.

First Confirmation of the preceding argument by sight.
Chapter 5.

[Large initial D] That the souls of men transmigrate from bodies into bodies, and the arts of a preceding life are recalled in subsequent ones—

--- Page 479 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XII. 199

that souls of men transmigrate from bodies into bodies, and recall the arts of a preceding life in subsequent ones, Plato did not treat in his own sense, but recounted it from the opinion of certain Egyptians, whose opinion Aurelius Augustine rejected. But that the soul of man descends from its very own creator, marked by the forms of things, and by these forms does not sufficiently comprehend the substances of things, but through them, as if preparations, being reformed by ideas, it may be able to comprehend: this, I say, Plato himself often seems to have affirmed from his own mind, and Augustine to have greatly approved. Therefore, treading in Augustine's footsteps, let us again strive for the confirmation of the preceding statement. Let us proceed by a threefold path: by sight, by hearing, and by reason. First by sight, in this manner.
E The soul by which bodies live is superior to all bodies, because it gives life to bodies. That [soul] which has sensation is indeed more excellent than this. But indeed in the human mind there is something more excellent: I do not mean that by which it senses sensible things, but that by which it judges concerning sensible things. Now indeed it is easy to see that the judging thing is more excellent than that about which it is judged and which does not judge.
F But not only does rational life judge concerning sensible things, but also concerning the senses themselves, for example, why an oar must appear broken in water when it is straight, and why it is necessary for it to be perceived thus by the eyes. For the sight of the eyes itself can report this, but it can by no means judge. Therefore, rational life is superior to sensual life. And so if reason judges according to itself, then no nature is more excellent. But because it is clear that it is mutable, when it is found now unskilled, now skilled: but it judges so much better, the more skilled it is; and so much more skilled, the more it partakes of some art or discipline or wisdom: the nature of that very art must be sought.
G Nor do I now wish art to be understood as that which is noted by experience, but that which is investigated by reasoning. But certainly it must be asked why it offends us if, with two windows placed not one above the other, but next to each other, one of them is larger and the other smaller, when they could have been equal; but if they are one above the other, and both are unequal by half, that inequality does not offend so much; and why we do not care much how much one of them is larger or smaller, because there are two. But in three, sense itself seems to demand that they not be unequal; or that the middle one be so between the largest and smallest, that it precedes the smaller by as much as it is preceded by the larger. For thus, first, as if nature itself

it is considered what it proves. Where it is especially to be noted, how that which, when viewed alone, displeased less, is rejected in comparison with something better. Thus it is found that common art is nothing other than the memory of things experienced and approved, joined with a certain use of the body and operation: if you lack this, you can indeed judge works, which is much more excellent: although you cannot perform artificial things. But since in all arts congruence pleases, by which alone preserved all things are beautiful, and congruence itself seeks equality and unity either by the similarity of equal parts or by the gradation of unequal ones: who is there who would find supreme equality or similarity in bodies, and dare to say, when he has diligently considered, that any body is truly and simply one: since all things change either from species to species, or from place to place: and consist of parts occupying their own places, by which they are divided into diverse spaces?

Furthermore, true equality and similarity themselves, and true and primary unity itself, are perceived not by any sense but understood by the mind. For whence would any equality whatsoever be sought in bodies, or whence would it be convinced to differ very greatly from the perfect, unless that which is perfect were seen by the mind? And since all things that are sensibly beautiful, whether produced by nature or elaborated by arts, are beautiful in places and times, like a body, and the movements of a body: that equality and unity known only to the mind, according to which corporeal beauty is judged by the senses as intermediaries, is neither swollen by place nor unstable by time: For it cannot rightly be said that a round temple is judged according to it, and not a round vessel, or a round coin, according to it. Similarly, in times and in the movements of bodies, it is ridiculously said that equal years are judged according to it, and not equal months according to it. But whether something is moved congruently through these spaces, or through hours, or through shorter moments: it is judged by the same one and immutable equality. But if smaller and larger spaces of figures and motions are judged by the same law of equality or similarity or congruence, that law itself is greater than all these, but in power: otherwise, in space or place or time, it is neither greater nor smaller. But if it were greater, it would not judge according to the whole—

--- Page 481 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XII. 200

...we would judge smaller things; but if it were smaller, we would not judge greater things according to it. But now, since by the entire law of squareness both a square forum and a square stone are judged: again, if by the entire law of equality the movements of the feet of a running ant and of a walking elephant are judged to agree with each other: who would doubt that it is neither greater nor smaller in intervals of places and times, since in power it surpasses all things.

Now this law of all arts, since it is entirely immutable, but the human mind, to which it has been granted to see such a law, can suffer the mutability of error: it is quite clear that the law, which is called truth, is above our mind. Nor is it now to be doubted that the immutable nature which is above the rational soul is God: and that there is the first life and the first essence, where there is the first wisdom. For this is that immutable truth, which is rightly called the law [K] of all arts, and the art of the omnipotent artisan.

Therefore, since the soul perceives that it does not judge the form and motion of bodies according to itself: at the same time it must acknowledge that its own nature surpasses the nature about which it judges: but that the nature according to which it judges, and about which it can in no way judge, surpasses itself.

For I can say why the members of any body ought to correspond symmetrically on both sides: because I delight in supreme equality, which I contemplate not with my eyes but with my mind. Therefore, I judge those things which I perceive with my eyes to be better, by as much as they are, by their nature, closer to those things which I understand with my mind. But why those things are so, no one can say: nor would anyone soberly say that they ought to be so, as if they could be otherwise. But why they please us, and why we most vehemently love them when we are wiser: no one, if he rightly understands them, will dare to say.

For just as we and all rational souls rightly judge about inferior things according to truth: so concerning us, when we adhere to it, truth itself alone judges: but concerning truth itself, not even the Father judges.

For it is not less than He Himself. And therefore, what the Father judges, He judges through it. For all things that seek unity have this rule, or form, or example: because it alone has fulfilled His likeness, from whom it received being.

The mind judges all things: because it is above all things, when with

is with God. But it is with Him when it understands most purely and loves with all charity what it understands. Thus also, as far as the law itself can, it becomes that through which it judges all things: and concerning which no one can judge. Just as in these temporal laws, although men judge concerning them when they institute them: yet when they have been instituted and confirmed, it will not be permissible for a judge to judge concerning them, but through them.
**A** [marginal note] However, the maker of temporal laws, if he is a good and wise man, consults that eternal law itself, concerning which no soul is given to judge: so that through its immutable rules, he may discern what is to be commanded and forbidden for the time being. Therefore, it is right for pure souls to recognize the eternal law: it is not right to judge it. Indeed, according to it we can judge concerning mind and body: "this action is less, or less vehement than it should be; this is less pure than it should be." But concerning the law itself, no one judges in any way. For when someone has said that eternal things are superior to temporal ones, or that seven and three are ten: no one says it *should* have been so, but merely "it is so," recognizing it: not correcting as an examiner, but delighting as one who discovers. But for many, human delight is the end: nor do they wish to strive for higher things: so that they may judge *why* these sensible things please. So if I ask an artisan, having constructed one arch, why he builds another equal one opposite it on the other side: he will answer, I believe: "So that equal parts of the building may correspond to equal parts." Furthermore, if I continue to ask why he chooses that very thing: he will say, "this is fitting; this is beautiful; this delights those who see it." He will dare nothing further. For he leans back on his eyes: and does not understand whence it depends. But I will not cease to admonish the man who is inwardly sighted and sees indivisibly *why* these things please, so that he may dare to be a judge of human delight itself. For thus he is superior to it, and is not held by it: while he judges not *according to* it, but *it itself*. And first I will ask, whether things are beautiful because they delight, or whether they delight because they are beautiful. Here it will be answered to me without doubt: they delight because they are beautiful. I will therefore ask next, why they are beautiful: And if he hesitates, I will suggest: "Is it because their parts are similar to each other, and by some joining they are reduced to a single harmony?" When he has found this to be so, I will ask: "Whether they supremely fulfill this very unity which they are convinced to desire, or far below..."

When the soul is agitated by many illusions of phantasms disturbing it hither and thither, and yet recognizes that these are false: where is the truth that is perceived by the mind? That light is true, by which you recognize that all these things are not true: through this you see that one thing, by which you judge that whatever else you see is one; yet whatever mutable thing you see is not that which that one thing is. Furthermore, ask in bodily pleasure what delights you: you will find nothing else than congruence. For if resistance or discrepancy produce pain, congruence produces pleasure. let us grant that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true: where, I ask, do we see this? Certainly neither I in you, nor you in me; but we both see it in that immutable truth itself which is above our minds. There, indeed, we behold with the sight of the mind the very form according to which these temporal things were made; and from there we have the conceived truth and knowledge of things as a word within us. From the light which illuminates every man coming into this world: which cannot be seen by these eyes, nor by those by which phantasms are thought: but by those by which it is said to the phantasms themselves: "You are not what I seek: nor are you that. From which I order you. And what appears ugly to me among you, I disapprove: what is beautiful, I approve: since that from which I disapprove and approve is more beautiful, therefore I approve this itself more: and I prefer it not only to you, but to all those bodies from which I drew you." Where these things are
[Marginal note: D] seen, there is light without space of places and times: and without any phantasm of such spaces. Can these things be corrupted in any part, even if every reasoner should perish? For reasoning does not make such things, but finds them: therefore before they are found, they remain in themselves: and when they are found, they renew us. Thus the inner man is reborn, and the outer man is corrupted from day to day. Between our mind, by which we understand the Father and the truth, that is, the inner light through which we understand Him, no creature is interposed. Therefore let us also venerate truth itself, in no part dissimilar, in Him and with Him: which is the form of all things that were made by the One: and strive towards the One. Whence it appears that all things were made through this form: which alone fulfills what all things desire.

*Second confirmation by hearing according to Augustine.*
*Cap. 6.*

Hitherto, through those things which are perceived by sight,
with Augustine as our guide, we have arrived at the point
of finding our mind to be formed by the divine mind.
Next, with the same guide, let us proceed to the same
conclusion through those things which are heard. In harmonious sounds there is
a certain rhythm; hence also in the act of sensing, a definite rhythm is
established, because a rhythmic sound is sensed rhythmically. There is also a rhythm
in the very nature of sensation. For otherwise it would not be either soothed
by the harmony of sounds, or offended by their absurdity.
Therefore, whatever that very thing is by which we either assent or recoil,
not by reason, but by nature, when something sounds, I call it the rhythm
of sensation itself. For this power of approving and disapproving
does not then come into being in my ears when I hear a sound. For the ears
are open no differently to good sounds than to bad ones. Consider rather
that these two things are by no means to be confused. For if any
verse is pronounced sometimes more briefly, sometimes more lengthily,
it is necessary that it does not occupy the same space of time, even though the same
metrical structure is preserved. Therefore, that it may soothe the ears
by its very nature, that power causes it by which we accept harmonious things,
and reject absurd ones. But that it is perceived in a shorter time when it is uttered more quickly
than more slowly, nothing matters except how long the ears are touched by the sound.
Therefore, this state of the ears, when they are touched by sound,
is in no way such as if they were not touched. But just as hearing differs
from not hearing, so does hearing this voice differ from hearing another. This
state, therefore, neither extends beyond nor is confined below
the measure of the sound which produces it. One [measure] is therefore in an iamb,
another in a tribrach; longer in a longer iamb,
shorter in a shorter one; none in silence. If this happens in a rhythmic
voice, it is necessary that it itself also becomes rhythmic, nor can it
exist when the sound that produces it is absent. For it is similar to a footprint
impressed in water, which is neither formed before you impress a body,
nor remains when you withdraw it. But that natural
and judicial power which is present in the ears does not cease
[Marginal note: A]
to exist in silence; nor does sound insert it into us, but rather, sound,
whether to be approved or disapproved, is received by it. Who would deny
that there is a power of rhythms in the soul, when the soul performs these rhythms
which we find in the pulse of the veins and in reciprocal breathing?
When sometimes more briefly or more lengthily, while I serve
the law of times, by which feet correspond from simple to double,

Therefore, those judicial (numbers) are also held by certain limits of temporal spaces, which they cannot exceed in judging; and whatever exceeds these spaces, they do not attain so as to judge. Yet these temper individual actions. For that which restrains and checks us in any attention of doing something with the limbs of the body from unequal movements – whether walking with unequal steps, or striking with unequal intervals of blows, or eating with unequal movements of the jaws, and finally scratching with unequal movements of the nails – and tacitly commands a certain equality, that very thing is a certain judicial something, which causes humans to have a sense and appreciation of beauty and decorum more than beasts, who rush to any of their impulses for the sake of appeasing bodily passion, and are not attracted by the grace and desire for beauty. Hence horses do not choose a more beautiful mare to love, but are drawn to any (mare) with equal frenzy. But that judicial (something) suggests God as the creator of animals, whom it certainly befits to believe as the author of all suitability and harmony. For that number which consists of temporal intervals, unless we are aided by memory in it, to be judged by us, no...

...in that way it can. For any short syllable, since it both begins and ends, its beginning is at one time, and its end sounds at another. When that verse is sung, "Deus creator omnium" (God creator of all): we hear the numbers of that verse through the numbers of sensing; and we are delighted by the judicial numbers; and we form an opinion about this delight, which is, as it were, the judgment of these judicial numbers, by I know not what others: whereas through others we could form a broader, but certainly truer, judgment about these things. For it is one thing to be delighted by sense, another to form an opinion by reason. For it is one thing to assent or dissent to rhythmic movements: which happens in the delight of harmony, and the offense of absurdity of such movements; and it is another thing to judge whether these things delight rightly or wrongly: which happens by reasoning. This art of rhythm or meter, which those who make verses use, we think has certain numbers, according to which they construct verses. Whatever these numbers are, they do not pass away with the verses, but remain. It must therefore be agreed that fleeting numbers are fashioned from certain permanent numbers: and we think this art is nothing other than a certain affection of the artist's soul. Those numbers will not pass from the one who teaches to the one who learns: but the learner will move himself inwardly in his own mind towards something from which these numbers are impressed upon his mind, and create that affection which is called art: and he will understand and answer that the things he is asked are true. But since these numbers about which we are thus inquiring are unchangeable, they are therefore eternal: nor is there any inequality in them. Third confirmation through the mind according to Augustine.
Chapter 7.

First, we have sufficiently investigated our purpose through the indications of sight, then through the admonitions of hearing. Now let us investigate through the indications of reason. Each person expresses his mind differently by speaking, attending to what is happening within himself; but defines the human mind differently by special or general knowledge. And so, when he speaks to me about his own (mind), whether he understands this or that, or does not understand, and whether he wills or wills not this or that, I believe him. But when he speaks truly about humanity, either specially or generally, I recognize and approve. From this it is clear that each one sees one thing in himself, which he believes another speaking to him, yet does not see (himself); but another thing in truth itself, which another also can behold; of these, one is changed by time, the other subsists in unchangeable eternity. For we do not gather a general or special knowledge of the human mind by seeing many minds with bodily eyes through similitude; but we behold inviolable truth, from which we may perfectly (as much as we can) define not what kind of mind each person has, but what kind it ought to be according to eternal reasons.

Moreover, when the impious think of eternity, and rightly reprehend many things and rightly praise many things in the morals of men, by what rules, pray tell, do they judge these things, unless by those in which they see how each person ought to live, even if they themselves do not live in the same way? Where do they see them? For not in their own nature, since these things are undoubtedly seen by the mind; and it is established that their minds are mutable, but whoever sees these rules in them, sees them as immutable; and he could see this not in the habit of his own mind, since those rules are of justice, but it is established that their minds are unjust. Where then are these rules written? Where what is just, even the unjust person recognizes; where he perceives that what he himself does not have ought to be had. Where then are they written, unless in the book of that light which is called truth, from which every just law is described; and into the heart of the person who practices justice, it is transferred not by migrating but as if by imprinting, just as an image

--- Page 491 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XII. 205

just as an image passes from a ring onto wax, and does not leave the ring. But he who does not act, and yet sees what ought to be done, he is the one who is turned away from that light, by which, however, he is touched. But he who does not even see how one ought to live, indeed sins more excusably: because he is not a transgressor of an unknown law. But even he is sometimes touched by the splendor of the everywhere present truth, when admonished, he confesses. [B] Finally, this preceding Aurelian discourse is concluded by four points: namely, that the mind does not rise to the highest things unless it is drawn by the instinct of that which is highest; that it would not use eternal reasons for judging according to its will, unless it could equate itself with eternity; that it would not apprehend immutable things by immutable reason, unless it touched the very rule of immutability; that many minds would not grasp the same truth, unless either there were one human intellect in many, which cannot happen, or at least many human intellects immersed themselves in the same fount of truth: as if then some would best know the order of an artifice, when they have penetrated that one reason by which the artisan constructed the work. But this opinion of Augustine is especially confirmed in two ways: first, by the common power of argumentation; then, by the common notions of truth, goodness, and being. Every intellect apprehends a necessary consequence in things both contingent and non-existent. For this consequence is necessary: If Plato runs, Plato moves: although Plato, and his running, and his movement, are contingent. Furthermore, this is necessary: Plato, while he was discoursing long ago, was speaking: although neither Plato, nor his disputation, nor his speech are present. Therefore, the immutable necessity of such consequences is not founded in those temporal things which either do not exist in any way, or are contingent: nor in the mere thoughts of the soul: otherwise it would not be true necessity, but a figment: indeed, nor would it be immutable, since our thought is mutable. It is founded therefore in the eternal and necessary series of things, which the divine mind, the ordainer of all things, contains within itself: where it attributes a mutual relation to things. Wherefore every light of true reasoning is kindled by the first truth, and is reflected back into the same, [C] since all necessity of consequence is founded in the supreme necessity of the whole of nature. These common (things) teach this...

notions also of truth and goodness, and of intelligence itself, which we have proven in previous (discussions) to be inherent in the minds of all, and from the fact that they constantly compare true and good things. But if truth itself and goodness is God, it follows that God shines forth into the minds of men as often as we judge true and good things through God as a standard. The same is also taught by the notion of itself implanted in all. For all men judge that one thing indeed to be in no way, but this one to be, but in an imperfect way: this (other) to be in a way of perfection. But such a gradation in being neither occurs nor is known except through access to the highest being (which is God) and a withdrawal from it. But access to it, and withdrawal A from it, cannot be seen except by one who sees it. But more skilled men see it in yet another way: namely, when they resolve all subordinate kinds of things to the most general, and those (most general) all the way to that which is called simple and absolute being. Such a being is either a false figment, or it is God. But being itself cannot be false, if only something truly exists in things. If that comparison of the grades of things and this resolution does not happen except through the very power of the highest and absolute being, it certainly happens through God: by whom the intellect, being formed, both compares and resolves.

To these things is added, that being itself shines so clearly B that it cannot be thought not to be. For just as that which is called nothing occurs to us as entirely devoid of being, so being occurs (to us) as utterly devoid of non-being. Therefore, in being, neither any power whatsoever appears towards non-being, nor any defect of being.

From the first part, it is eternal; from the second, it is most full with the whole perfection of being, that is, God. For this reason, being occurs to us most evidently: and to those rightly observing, it occurs as God. Which is moreover confirmed by two reasons. First, because being is so manifest that in each thing that C is known, it (being) is always known as well. He who affirms Plato to run, affirms him to be running. He who calls him a man or white, says he is in the species of man, and of white. Finally, in each of the modes of being by which individual things subsist, being itself is so understood, just as in all species of animals, animal is understood. Second reason: because through being itself other things are known, but it (being) itself through itself. Indeed, in knowledge which happens through intuition, that which is called

*How much the soul dominates the body is shown by many*
*signs: and first by the affections of the imagination.*
Chap. I.

[Large decorative initial H] C Hitherto we have demonstrated the divinity of the soul by arguments; next, indeed, we shall confirm the same almost similarly by signs.
Four affections follow imagination: appetite, pleasure, fear, and pain. All these, when they are most vehement, suddenly affect their own body entirely, and sometimes even another's. How great are the passions that either the desire for revenge arouses in the heart, or the lust for pleasure in the liver, nay, even in the pulse? From whose change the physician Erasistratus recognized that Antiochus was smitten by love for Stratonice. Again, how perniciously does the desire to harm, by a frequent gaze, fascinate boys and any other more delicate individuals? How manifestly does the craving of a pregnant woman infect the tender fetus with the mark of the thing thought of?
D What various gestures and figures do parents impress upon their sons, and how dissimilar to themselves, due to the vehement imagination of diverse things by which they are affected by some chance during conception? Whence it happens that men are very much more dissimilar among themselves in figure, gestures, and manners than any brutes are among themselves in any species. How often is malicious will commonly said to have harmed men, and beasts, and plants by its curses and sorceries?
E Add that some gluttons, thinking more eagerly of certain dishes, taint their saliva with a certain similar flavor. Boys also and pregnant women, on account of an excessive craving for forbidden food or drink, melt, flow away, and perish. These and similar things are effected in many ways by appetite. Vehement joy also effects no less. This can suddenly destroy the body, and often relieve it from illness.

Moreover, concerning our motions, this must be diligently observed: that some, starting from the body, do not penetrate to the soul, while others do; and some, starting from the soul, do not overflow into the body, while others do. The first kind are such, when a very temperate air, surrounding the body, as it were, moves the body in some way, and yet provides us with no sensation of heat, nor of cold. The second kind are, when it moves in such a way that we feel something. The third kind are, when the mind calmly contemplates something, or the imagination moderately observes something slight. For from such thoughts the body is not agitated. Finally, the fourth kind, whenever either the mind or the imagination applies itself more vehemently to something, and considers it either very harmful, or very useful and pleasant. For then the body suffers something.

Indeed, when some motions, through an affection of the soul, overflow into the body, they seem to descend into the body not by the force of the body, but by the command of the soul. For the body has no power of acting: and it suddenly receives motions brought upon it by the soul, with no delay intervening. For the face suddenly grows pale when the soul fears: and it turns pale solely through the agitation of the soul. But when the body is excessively heated, and the soul bears it with difficulty: such a disturbance does not happen to the soul before it has both felt the body's suffering and judged it harmful. To feel and to judge is an act of the soul. Therefore, the soul is disturbed properly by its own act, not by the violence of the body: and therefore it moves itself: it is not moved by the body. This is clearly seen from this, because from a more vehement thought and affection of the soul, the body is always agitated: nor can the body resist it: but from the suffering and torment of the body, the soul is not necessarily cast down from its state. Diogenes the Cynic, naked, trod on ice and snow in winter, and burning sands in summer: and meanwhile he laughed and joked: Polemon the Academic, while feeling the most rabid bites of dogs, did not even turn pale. Anaxarchus the Abderite philosopher was ordered by Nicocreon, tyrant of Cyprus, to be thrown into a hollow stone and beaten with iron hammers: but the philosopher, disregarding the body's punishment, said: "Strike, strike Anaxarchus's vessel: you terrify Anaxarchus himself not at all." He heard Xenocrates disputing about chastity. The same Diogenes, when he heard Antisthenes disputing about liberty. Nature is accustomed to abolish whatever has grown strong over a long time, no otherwise than over a long time. Therefore, to weaken in a moment a habit strengthened by long custom is not of corporeal nature, but of a higher and divine nature.

**De poetis.**

Furthermore, consider poets, whom Democritus and Plato affirm to be seized by a certain divine frenzy. This is shown above all others by two dialogues of Plato, Phaedrus and Ion. For this very thing, he offers three proofs. First, because individual men scarcely attain individual arts without divine aid over a long time: but true poets, such as he wishes Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, Pindar to have been, have inserted into their works certain signs and arguments of all arts. Second, because, raging, they sing many things, and those indeed wonderful things, which, a little later, when the frenzy has subsided, they themselves do not sufficiently understand, as if they themselves had not uttered them, but God had cried out through them as if through trumpets. Third, because not the most prudent of all, and those most learned from an early age, became the best poets, but rather some madmen, such as Homer and Lucretius are known to have been, or ruder ones, such as Hesiod testifies himself to have been, and such as Plato writes Ion and Tynnichus of Chalcis to have been, who, beyond art, suddenly emerged as wonderful in poetic matters. He adds that certain most foolish men are therefore seized by the Muses, because divine providence wishes to declare to the human race that excellent poems are not human inventions, but heavenly gifts. Of which he offers that sign in Phaedrus, that no one, however diligent and learned in all arts, ever excelled in poetry, unless to these things was added that more fervent stirring of the soul, which we feel when God is within us, we grow warm with Him stirring us. That impulse has the seeds of a sacred mind. Let us come to the priests.

**De sacerdotibus.**

His writings and the deeds of his disciple show that the divine Paul, the theologian, ascended the three heavens of the celestial hierarchies in divine abstraction of mind. The Galileans also
Dd iij

--- Page 504 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Some once, suddenly inspired by God, emerged as the greatest theologians from fishermen. All antiquity testifies that many priests, long before these times, accustomed to rave by the impulse of demons and utter certain marvelous things. Aulus Gellius writes that Cornelius, a most chaste priest, was moved in mind at Patavium at the time when Caesar and Pompey were encamped in Thessaly, to such an extent that he saw both the time and the order and the outcome of the battle. Pliny also relates that the soul of Hermotimus of Clazomenae was accustomed to wander, having left the body, and to announce many true things from afar; until, when he was cremated, his enemies, who were called Cantaridae, took away from the returning soul, as it were, its sheath. Maximus Pyrius the Platonist and Herodotus write that the soul of Aristeas of Proconnesus was accustomed to do the same. Aurelius Augustine relates that a certain priest from Calama was accustomed to withdraw himself from his body at his own
E arbitrament, especially when soothed by plaintive harmony. "He lay," he says, "most like a dead man, without breath; and though he was burned and cut, he felt nothing." But having awakened, he said that he had felt nothing during that abstraction except the melody itself and the voices of those speaking. Which signifies that that soul was accustomed to do nothing in the body then, when there was no movement or sense of touch, or breath; yet to do something within itself when it pondered the harmony heard before and perceived voices. And that Cornelius, and Hermotimus, and Aristeas, whom I narrated above, when they had withdrawn themselves from the body, would have seen nothing more distant than before, unless the soul, when it is freed from that little body, lives more freely and wanders more widely; nor would the soul of the Calamensian have withdrawn itself from the body of its own accord and, being separated, done something, if it had been entirely an attendant of its body. These things seem to be confirmed by these words of Plato in the Phaedrus. "He who rightly uses
F divine meditations," he says, "and is always imbued with perfect mysteries, truly alone becomes perfect. But separated from human studies, and always adhering to the divine will, he is commonly taken as if out of his mind, but he himself, full of God, is hidden from the common people."

**Concerning soothsayers, and prophets.**

augurs, haruspices, auspices, astrologers, mages.
Indeed, the works of these indicate most skilled minds. But those prophecies indicate divine minds above all others, as Plato wishes in the Phaedrus, which happen without art and counsel: such as those which Plato relates concerning the prophetess Diotima and Socrates and Epimenides: those which Varro [relates] concerning the Sibyls together with Plato: those which historians narrate concerning the Pythian oracles: and almost all philosophers confirm, especially the Platonists: those which all experience concerning dreams: those which the Hebrews transmit concerning divine prophets. The minds of all these then most extensively surveyed many places, and embraced three times in one, when they separated themselves from the body.

Therefore, when the human soul will be entirely separated from the body: it will comprehend every place, and every time (as is among the Egyptians). Indeed, such a soul is already almost [Marginal note: H] by its very nature everywhere and always: which, so that it may survey many and most remote places, and so that it may recall all past time, and anticipate the future, is not compelled to go outside itself: but having left the body, returning into itself, it entirely achieves this, either because its nature is everywhere and always, as the Egyptians believe: or because when it withdraws into its own nature, it is immediately joined to the divine power comprehending all limits of both places and times. Moreover, by what path prophecy falls into the soul, if you please, I will trace back more deeply.

Three orders of things seem to pertain to the human soul: providence: fate: nature. Providence is the series of minds: fate the series of souls: nature the series of bodies. In the beginning, under God, we place those minds [Marginal note: I] entirely freed from the body according to Plato: whom Dionysius calls angels, that is, the purest intellects. We add a lower degree of minds, namely those which are already united to bodies, and seem to be, as it were, certain angels: holding in a certain way the lowest degree of angels: among which are all rational souls, whether of the world, or of the mundane spheres, stars, daemons, and humans. In the third place are the globes of the heavens, of the elements, of moistures. Therefore, God is the head of the angels: who, sending down his ray endowed with the reasons of all things to be created, through all angels, gradually forms all things: so that in each he describes the universal figure of the world. the brute powers of sensing which are in the idol, namely confused phantasy, which follows natural instinct; and imagination, the gatherer of the five senses. Nature is the handmaid of the Idol. The Platonists compare our Mind to a certain sun of ours, Reason to the light of this sun, the Idol to the ray of this light, and Nature to the reflection of the ray, that is, to splendor, or, to speak more accurately, to shadow. And to return to the rational power, they often say that it relates to the Mind as we see speech relates to the soul; and that it is engaged in perpetual and free motion. Finally, that rational faculty which is properly the nature of the true soul, is not determined to any one thing. For it wanders up and down with free motion. For the primary mo- H
tion is that which is located in the proper nature of the soul: since it itself is the third essence, whose power is mobile by itself. But the primary motion is not this motion or that, it is not carried only here or there: but it is a common motion: and like a fount of motion, it flows freely, and pours forth with equal impulses in every direction. Wherefore, although through the mind, the idol, and nature, we are in a certain way bound to the common order of things—through the mind to providence, through the idol to fate, through singular nature to universal nature—nevertheless, through reason, we are entirely our own masters: and as if unbound, we follow now these parts, now those. Sometimes reason adheres to the mind, when it rises into providence. Sometimes it obeys the idol and nature, where fate arises with a certain love of its own: while trusting in the senses, it is distracted here and there by the encounter with sensible things. Sometimes, having omitted other things, it withdraws into itself: where it either investigates other things by reasoning, or it examines itself.
To such an extent is this middle and proper power of the soul both free and restless. And when something encounters our extremes, for example, the mind, the idol, or nature: it is indeed possible for the soul to perceive it immediately in some way: yet it does not first notice that it perceives it, until it passes into the middle power.
For since it is the middle power, through which we are human beings, indeed, and what we ourselves are: what pertains to it, most evidently pertains to human beings. Often colors or voices move the eyes or ears: immediately sight and hearing fulfill their function: the one sees, the other hears: yet the mind and vi-

--- Page 510 ---
dere se and hear, unless our middle power applies itself to these things. This is evident in those who do not perceive people they meet, while they are thinking more intently about something else. Thus superior minds always move our mind annexed to them; yet we do not perceive such an impulse for this reason, because the middle power, wandering through lower things, turns itself away from superior things. For the same reason, the images of superior souls always strike our image; yet we do not recognize this influx, when that middle part contemplates something else more firmly. Similarly, the natures of larger bodies continually provoke the nature of our body; and we A very often do not perceive this instinct for the same reason. We have an example of this in the body. For often, provoked by nothing, we become somewhat angry with ourselves; disturbed by no evils, terrified by no messages or portents, we grow sluggish, mourn, and tremble; soothed by no good things, we ourselves rejoice with ourselves and sing. Whence these? Such new effects certainly have a new cause. This is, indeed, a varied affection of the body according to various times: whether yellow bile boils over in the gall or liver, or black bile ferments in the spleen, or the heart abounds with clear blood. Such affections and natures of the body, because they are closest to the vivifying power which is contained in the idol and which contains them, incite it with various impulses, while they offer an opportunity for it to operate both differently and more strenuously in vivifying the body's complexion, than it usually does. Such an operation, rendered more agitated, gradually tickles the power of sensing (which is contained in the same idol), especially touch, or secretly pricks the imagination of the same idol; just as the stomach is pricked by a natural need. That hidden pricking and tickling does not pass to the middle part of the soul when it is intent on something else; but it passes when it is free. Then, through the thinking reason, we suddenly become somewhat angry in a certain way, or we mourn, or we rejoice. The intellectual reason perceives these things; whence it sometimes assents, and B sometimes it also flees and puts these things to flight with counsels and remedies. In summary, we are often struck by these affections in a long order, descending to us from universal natures through our own (nature); and we are utterly ignorant of whence they are brought upon us. when our middle part is so occupied with its own activities that the influx of mind does not pass through to it. But when it is vacant, what prevents some angelic thought from creeping into our rational faculties, even if we do not see whence it may steal in? This is indicated by those who, without a teacher, from the mere intention or even tranquility of an unoccupied reason, have often produced many most excellent things, even when they were not seeking them, as if the light of the sun of its own accord suddenly pours itself into a clear sky. And although the disposition of the world, which is inscribed entirely at once in the minds and reasons of the superior souls, offers itself entirely at once to our mind through a certain perennial continuation, nevertheless, the temporal vicissitude of worldly seeds, just as it gradually succeeds itself in the idols and natures of those souls, so by a similar certain continuation of succession, it descends through the idols of all souls and the natures of all bodies, even to the idol of our soul and the nature of our body. [C] For example, the reason for tomorrow's rain today reigns in the idols of celestial souls and the natures of the heavens. The same emanates through the idols of elemental souls and the natures of the elements, until it strikes the idol of our soul, and simultaneously the nature of our humors. The striking of our idol comes from the idols; the striking of our nature comes from those natures and our idol. When that influx of minds finds our reason strongly idle, or vacant in mind, it shows it something of those things which pertain to the universal knowledge of eternal things or the governance of the world, so that it may foresee either the law of God and the orders of angels, or the restitutions of ages and changes of kingdoms. When the instinct of idols and natures finds reason and imagination entirely vacant, it portends to itself something of those things which pertain to the vicissitudes of times and the disturbances of the elements, so that it may foresee future rain, earthquakes, and similar things. [D] By what way is this done? That power of the superior idols, about to induce rains, prefigures the wheels of the heavens for rains; these moisten the air; the moist air moves our phlegm, that is, the watery humor; phlegm moves the spirit, especially from that part where it is also watery. Since the spirit, being a vapor of blood, and in blood there are four humors, in the spirit there are four virtues of humors and elements. Therefore, that watery virtue of the spirit is...

In the same way, the power of the superior [beings], about to produce heats and fevers, by suitable means moves cholera, that is, bile in us, and the choleric spirit: the latter [moves] the vivifying virtue; the former [moves] fiery images hidden in phantasy and reason, so that we imagine fires, and red and yellow colors.

Seven kinds of vacancy.

[Marginal note: E] But when we are so vacant that we perceive such influxes, there are seven kinds of being vacant. We are vacant by sleep, syncope, melancholic humor, a temperate constitution, solitude, admiration, and chastity. Since the soul performs its operations of moving and sensing in this coarser body through the spirit closest to it, therefore when either due to the exhaustion of the spirits in the exterior members they are dissolved, or due to vapors and humors, those cerebral passages are blocked, through which such spirits, suitable for sensation and motion, are accustomed to be transmitted to the members: then the mind in a certain way collects itself: neither is it occupied in sensing corporeal qualities, nor in governing and moving the members of its body, nor in handling external affairs: which easily happens in sleep. But the more the exterior act is relaxed, the more the interior act is intensified. Interior acts are the visions of phantasy and the discourses of reason. But phantasy is so greatly intensified (by whose nod we largely live our life) that it revolves its images within itself with the keenest gaze.
[Marginal note: F] Those images, more keenly revolved, shine back up to that common sense, which in the Platonic manner we call imagination: thence into the lower senses, and the spirit. But the image shining in those senses and in the spirit is accustomed to be asserted as a true thing. But those images shine forth more than others, to which the imagination is more affected: whether past thought or disturbance, or present turmoil of dominant humors causes it. And these dreams are vain, and offer nothing of prophecy: for they arise either from the remnants of waking thoughts, or from a disturbance of the body. By such dreams are those men usually deluded, who, dedicated to a life of pleasure, are vehemently affected by those things which move the senses: and most keenly fix their imagination on these things, either as good things to be acquired, or as bad things to be rejected: with the result that their remnants disturb the imagination in sleep. Furthermore, because burdened by too much food or drink, they never have their imagination free in sleep. For because of the immoderate superabundance of humors and vapors, those images are often moved in the imagination, G
which present earthly spectacles. In these (men) also, because of the heat of wine, with the expelling power of the generative seed incited, images of the beloved person, which the imagination preserves, are moved: H
whence an embrace is imagined. From these reasons Plato in the ninth book of the Republic concludes that reason is often so occupied in sleep that it does not freely perceive higher influences. But it will perceive truth, he says, whenever it is not disturbed. C
There are also many who despise a life of pleasure, yet are zealous for civil affairs, or desirous of power and glory. In these sleeping men, the imagination is sometimes even lulled to sleep: but reason then handles private and public affairs: and is greatly occupied by them. There are some who despise both pleasures and human glory, but are dedicated to the investigation of divine and natural things. In these, in sleep, not only the imagination sometimes ceases, but also the anxious deliberation of active reason.
But that accustomed investigation of speculative reason rises again, so that we seem either to measure the heavens, or to divide the elements, or to enumerate the species of animals. To none of those whom we have enumerated does prophecy commonly belong: although these last philosophers truly reason even while sleeping: indeed, and sometimes they discover things which, though long sought, they had not found while awake: because reason is more tranquil. [Large initial T] The third mode of detachment occurs from the contraction of melancholic humor, drawing the soul away from external affairs: so that the soul is as free in a waking person as it sometimes used to be in a sleeping person. Certainly, just as a very convenient instrument ought to lack its own motion, lest perhaps when the craftsman decides to move it to the right while working, it meanwhile carries itself by its own motion to the left: so that soul which divine providence has decided to use for prophecy as if it were an instrument, it is necessary for it to be quiet, as melancholics often are.
But even these, when seized by divine power, become so much more agitated than others, as dense bodies, if ignited, burn more fiercely than rare bodies. For this reason, Socrates, whom Aristotle judged to be melancholic, foresaw many things by the inspiration of his familiar daemon: of which matter Plato, Xenophon, Antipater the Great, Apuleius are witnesses.
Indeed, when Timarchus had departed from that banquet where Socrates was reclining, Socrates' daemon forbidding it: he then committed those acts for which he was killed. Charmides competed in Nemea, Socrates forbidding it: and he regretted having competed.
To Crito, who was farming against Socratic advice, a branch struck his eye.
The same Socrates also, while fleeing with some others the attack of enemies: when they came to a crossroads: he did not want to flee by the same way as the others, because he was deterred by his daemon. Then indeed those who had fled by another way fell into the enemy cavalry. Aristides and Thucydides and many others, as long as they were near Socrates, even with Socrates himself silent, made very great progress in the studies of philosophy by means of that daemon.

[Marginal note: E] **A**nd there is a fourth mode of detachment stemming from a temperate temperament, since such a temperament introduces no tumult of any dominant humor which might stir the imagination to any image. For men of this kind are moderate in their affections and actions: therefore they live with such a tranquil mind that even while awake they are subject to heavenly influences: which is said to have happened to Pherecydes of Syros, Pythagoras, and Plotinus. I admire Plotinus above the others: who (as his disciple Porphyry narrates) foresaw the ways of men, their errors, and events: and when Porphyry himself was thinking of killing himself, he [Marginal note: F] divinely perceived it and prevented it. For this reason, as Pliny the Younger writes, when Curtius Rufus was governing Africa and was walking in a portico at the close of day, a woman's figure, larger and more beautiful than human, appeared to him. This (figure) predicted that he would come to Rome and hold honors: and also that he would return to the same province with supreme command: and die there. And all these things happened.

[Marginal note: G] **A** fifth mode of detachment seems to occur from solitude, where the mind, distracted by no human concerns, by a slight impulse of either deities or heavens, daily contemplates the same things that the heavenly deities contemplate doing: [Marginal note: H] which Zoroaster, prince of the Magi, is said to have achieved by twenty years of solitude, where he wrote and performed many things concerning the entire art of divination. His writings to Musaeus declare that Orpheus accomplished similar things in the deserts of Thrace.

[Marginal note: I] **L**et the sixth mode of detachment be from admiration. When the Sibyls and Pythian priestesses withdrew into the cave of Jupiter or Apollo, they believed the deity itself was present there, they contemplated the majesty of the deity with such stupefaction of admiration and veneration that their senses, imagination, and reason immediately abandoned their functions. Then the mind, exposed only to the deity, whether that was a god or a demon, perceived heavenly promptings: especially those pertaining to the matters about which they had recently deliberated. Aurelius Augustine affirms that he was often present at his divinations.

The seventh and most excellent of all is that alienation of the soul which occurs through the chastity of a mind devoted to God: just as Orpheus teaches Musaeus in the hymn of all gods. Such a mind, indeed, is not temporarily, like others, but almost always a peaceful temple of God: whose door (as John the theologian says) God knocks at first: which, immediately opened, He enters: which He diligently inhabits: in which He feeds man [Marginal note: L] with ambrosia. Through this (as Aurelius Augustine relates), a certain rustic in his time would withdraw from the body, and knew himself to be awake, while nevertheless seeing certain wondrous things with non-corporeal eyes. Through this, John the theologian, most divine of all, in Patmos [Marginal note: M] saw the entire order of the ages. Through this, Ezekiel inspected a field filled with the bones of the dead, and the bones later rising again: through this, Isaiah saw God sitting, surrounded by seraphim. But all these, just like those dreaming, whatever they perceived with the mind, they immediately covered with the veils of fantasy: so that the visions of the mind, obscured by the shadows of fantasy, needed an interpreter. Let us now conclude, through the seven kinds of prophecy, that there is such an excellence of the human soul against matter, that even with the body subdued, asleep, and half-alive, it sees much more clearly and operates much more excellently than when the body is operating: as if for accomplishing any magnificent things it does not need the aid of the body. Where it is evident how great is the soul's harmony with celestial beings: how great its kinship with God: which, as often as it returns to itself, becomes a partaker of celestial secrets and divine providence.

...dence, which is proper to God, who is the universal cause. Therefore, man,

E is a kind of god. He is undoubtedly the god of animals: who uses all, commands all, instructs many.
It is also established that he is the god of the elements, who inhabits

But arts of this kind, although they shape the matter of the world and command animals, and thus imitate God, the artisan of nature, are nevertheless inferior to those arts which, imitating divine rule, undertake the care of human governance. Individual beasts barely suffice for their own care or the brief care of their offspring: but one man abounds in such perfection that he first commands himself, which no beasts do; then he governs his family; administers the republic; rules nations; and commands the whole world. And as if born to rule, he is entirely impatient of servitude. Add to this that for the sake of the public good he undergoes death, which beasts do not do: inasmuch as he despises these individual mortal goods, trusting in the stability of the common and eternal good. Moreover, arts of this kind will perhaps seem to some to pertain to the present life: although such great care is not necessary for the present life, but rather looks to imitating the providence of divinity.
F Let us therefore consider those arts which are not only not necessary for bodily sustenance, but are very harmful, such as all liberal sciences: whose studies enervate the body and impede the conveniences of life: The subtle computation of numbers, the curious description of figures, the most obscure movements of lines, the superstitious consonance of music, the prolonged observation of stars, the investigation of natural causes, the investigation of long-lasting things, the eloquence of orators, and the frenzies of poets. In all these things, the human mind despises the service of the body: inasmuch as it can sometimes, and even now begins to, live without the aid of the
G body. He administered justice through an interpreter. Cyrus and Lucius Scipio knew the names of all their citizens. Fabius Maximus and Lucullus held in memory all the histories of all nations. Seneca says that he repeated two thousand names recited in the same order; and that he recited two hundred verses pronounced by his students in reverse order. Augustine writes that there was a certain man in his time who had read many things, and had never forgotten anything of what he had read. That there was another man in Rome who committed an entire comedy to memory while it was being recited. The capacity for so many and such great things, such stability in what has been received, cannot be contained in a narrow corner of the brain, and cannot be preserved by its fluid and perishable matter, but requires the most ample and most stable receptacle of the divine mind.

There is also that prediction of future things, in which the Chaldean and Egyptian mathematicians excelled. Certainly, that substance does not fail in the future, whose prophetic power so anticipates the entire future, just as a remembering faculty recalls the entire past. Now, this eternal substance gathers the fleeting intervals of time into an eternal moment. Finally, the use of speaking and writing, proper to man, indicates to us that a certain divine mind is inherent in us, which beasts lack. Without speech, we could live just like beasts and mute men. Therefore, speech has been granted to us for some more excellent work: namely, as an interpreter of the mind, a herald of infinite inventions, and an infinite messenger. Nor should Epicurus dream that beasts possess reason like us, but rather that they lack the use of speech and hands, through which they might outwardly signify the reason hidden within: because nature does not fail in necessary things, nor does it abound in superfluous ones. It did not give feet or arms to trees. For their earthly body, fixed to the soil, is nourished everywhere by earthly food. For the bodies of brute animals, as being less earthly, not all earthly food is everywhere sufficient: therefore, they are equipped with feet to seek more convenient food. Their imagination has a few and confused concepts, and only those necessary for the use of the body, which can be sufficiently expressed by mooing, barking, neighing, chirping, growling, roaring, or gestures. But the human mind, the inventor of infinite and distinct things, is supported by the use of innumerable speech, as if by a certain worthy [instrument] of its
