as an interpreter: also equipped with hands as most suitable instruments for fabricating the innumerable inventions of the mind; which instruments nature would indeed have given to beasts as well, if there were in them the same inner artisan to use such instruments. Therefore, the mind conceives as many things within itself by understanding as God makes in the world by understanding. It expresses as many by speaking, and in the air. [C] It writes as many with a pen on paper. It shapes as many by fabricating in the matter of the world. Wherefore, it is clear that he is mad who would deny that the soul, which in arts and governments is an emulator of God, is divine.

*Fourth sign from the effect of miracles. Chapter 4.*

But not only in forming and shaping matter through the reason of art, as we have said, does the human mind claim for itself a divine right, [D] but also in transforming the species of things by command; which work indeed is called a miracle, not because it is contrary to the nature of our soul when it becomes an instrument of God, but because, since it is something great and happens rarely, it produces admiration. Hence we admire: that the souls of men dedicated to God command the elements: summon winds: compel clouds into rains: dispel mists: cure the diseases of human bodies, and other things which poets sing, and historians narrate, to have been openly done in certain ages among various nations; nor do our most excellent philosophers, especially the Platonists, deny them; ancient theologians testify, Mercury first and Orpheus; and later theologians also proved by word and deed. Perhaps you will wonder if I seek out the reasons for miracles. But listen. In the first book it was argued that the third essence is below the angel and above all the matter of the world: to be formed by the divine power, and to form matter: indeed to receive spiritual forms from the divine power, but to give corporeal forms to matter. In the third book it was also established that the third essence is nothing other than rational souls, both our own and those superior to ours. Hence it follows among the Platonists and followers of Avicenna that every rational soul, through its essence and power, is above all the matter of the world: and can move and form the whole, namely, when it becomes an instrument of God for these things.

--- Page 526 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Nevertheless, such is the order of things. All rational souls
E (as we have said) have an intellectual head, a rational middle,
and a vivifying lowest part. This middle power is the soul's proper
characteristic. The intellectual power, however, is a certain ray of the superior
intellect sent down into the soul, and reflecting itself back into the superior intellect.
And the vivifying power is an act of the soul overflowing into the body,
and thence redounding into the soul: just as the light
of the sun in a cloud, according to its own nature, is splendor: as it
regards the sun, it is a ray; as it fills the cloud, it is paleness. The intellect
apprehends the intelligible: and remains in itself around the intelligible itself.
Reason runs: but within itself. The vivifying power runs below itself
to another, while it fills the body. But since through this
lowest part of itself, or shadow, souls depart furthest from their dignity,
approaching bodies: it has come to pass that the powers
of this kind, governing bodies, having somehow relaxed or
interrupted that amplitude of domination which the soul
possesses over the universality of bodies, are distributed individually
to individual bodies: to which, while they are bound, they attend to the proper
care of their own bodies, and almost neglect others'.
F What binds them to bodies? As Plato would have it, love, that is, the overflowing
affection of life, more inclined to vivify what is nearest to itself.
But to diverse species of rational souls are proximate
diverse species of bodies. Hence it is willed that some rational
souls have conspired with other bodies, some with
spheres, some with stars, others with others. Finally, others with
human bodies. And from certain dispositions of inner
seeds established by providence, some human souls are more
suited to governing other human bodies. And to speak summarily:
that vivifying power of each rational soul, since it pertains
to the third essence, has equal power over any bodies whatsoever:
but through a certain loving instinct, some accommodate themselves
to moving certain bodies, others to others: divine temperament
contributing to this, namely: and when one instinct ceases, that vivifying
power becomes free, so that, affected by a new instinct, it may
govern and move another body in some way. If this lowest part
surpasses all natures of bodies: much more so do the middle and highest parts.
The supreme part, that is, the mind, so far transcends that it never
savors anything corporeal, being eager only for divine things, stable by nature, intelligent

--- Page 527 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XIII. 223

sudden intelligence. The middle part, that is, the faculty of reasoning, is itself more pre-eminent than the lowest: and sometimes (as we have said elsewhere) it ascends to the mind, when, having received principles of demonstration from the mind, it investigates the universal reasons of natural things by arguing. But now it declines to the vivifying power, when it trusts imagination, listens to the senses, and flatters the body. G
It ascends to the mind out of love for grasping higher things, it descends to the lowest power out of love for governing lower things. Rightly, since it is the middle of both, it loves both: and as being more eminent than the lowest, while the lowest governs only one body, it itself moves and governs many. For while the governing faculty of your body alone nourishes your body, and through sense and desire serves the nourishment of your body: your reason takes care of your body, and of others: and fabricates works of art in external matter. This [reason] also, although it is equally capable of handling any matter, nevertheless at different times it undertakes to handle different ones, wherever love carries it. When the love by which it carves stone ceases, it suddenly abandons the statue. When love draws it to earthenware vessels, it undertakes pottery. When we speak of handling bodies, we temporarily set aside that mind which utterly despises bodies; we speak more of reason and the governing power. These two, indeed, although they have equal power over any bodies of the world due to the common nature of the third essence, nevertheless act most powerfully upon that which they are more affected by: that divine tempering of seeds not preventing it.
The affections of those souls who are above us are more stable than ours: and they always retrace the same order, H always progressing with a customary tenor: because in them both the highest power and the middle power incline upwards, devoted to eternal contemplation. Only the lowest power varies its works: but it performs changes, and indeed very orderly ones: so that even in change itself there appears to be stability, while the same tenor is observed, and the same things are similarly retraced. But however it happens: the forms of things inherent in those three powers of souls are the causes A of the forms which are expressed in mundane bodies. And, so to speak, the destiny-shaping imaginations which gradually arise from the idols of those souls: as if the most vehement affections of pregnant women, whatever they imagine for themselves in the sphere

...as if the most vehement affections of pregnant women express whatever they imagine for themselves in their spheres and subsequent things as offspring. Our soul also, being affected towards this body, shapes this body from the very directing power of the body, according to the order of its own seeds. What provides to this body a certain complexion of four humors, what the colors and features of the face, if not the soul? The soul also drives the heavy body upwards against its nature; and it overcomes the four contraries in turn: nor does anyone wonder at this miracle. Indeed, how much the same power through imagination can do in shaping the body with more vehement affections, we have said in previous discussions. Indeed, according to the diversity of affections, it produces diverse qualities in the members: with anger, heat, redness, and a bitter taste, and a flux of the bowels; with fear, cold and paleness; with sadness, the humor of sweat and a bluish paleness; with anxiety, dryness and blackness. Indeed, the affections of the soul themselves are the authors of these qualities: because they often move to such qualities contrary to our prior complexion. And, as Hippocrates and Galen teach, a long-standing affection changes the prior complexion of the body and draws it into its own nature. Imagination does this. What reason, however, accomplishes in arts and governance, we have declared elsewhere. Therefore, what is done by the directing power of the body in its own body through the vivifying power, and the affections serving it, we have explained here. Moreover, something is done by it in other bodies which approach it: sometimes through natural heat it digests foods, and warms those touching it. The maternal soul also acts upon an alien body when it nourishes fetuses in the womb: which indeed it accomplishes through continuous bonds by which the fetus is bound to the maternal body. Nor does it only form a nearby body, but sometimes also a distant one. Indeed, when seed is cast by a man into the womb, and long afterwards the man being absent, the formative power left in the seed thrives there, and performs the role of the paternal soul in the seed, and shapes a human body: just as when someone throws a stone far away: the expulsive power imparted to the stone by the thrower, as long as it reigns in the stone, so long does it propel the stone, namely by that stroke of air, and to that mark, where and to which that thrower had directed it. But let us return now to those souls, through whom God performs miracles as if through instruments. What does a temperate bodily constitution contribute to their excellence? So that their reason may be more unhindered, disturbed by no tumult of excessive humors. What about a moderate and pure diet? So that the soul may not be weighed down by the burden of its own body. What about that honorable and pious upbringing? So that it may both wish good things for humans: and, being in some way similar to God, may be helped by God, indeed, may be guided by God as an instrument. Finally, since reason is superior to phantasy, when it, wholly dedicated to God, is directed to this one work of bestowing benefit, that former natural affection of the soul by which it is joined to its own body is greatly relaxed, and, freed from it, it acts upon another. For it can easily be guided by God as an instrument for these things, since its nature is above all bodies: although some affection may have formerly drawn it to the governance of one [body]: no differently than if a most wise and powerful king, whose providence and dominion all parts of a most vast kingdom are equally subject to, should neglect the others for a time, enticed by the charm of some part: but when the love for that part eventually cools, he applies himself to governing others. Our Plato seems to have touched upon all these mysteries, indeed that tyranny of phantasy, and again this dominion of pious reason in the Timaeus, where he discussed the power of the soul over the body: but in the Phaedrus, he hints at something more wonderful, when he says that every soul has care of the universal body: and that our soul, when it is free, wanders through the whole heaven, and governs the world together with the celestial souls, circulating at times in different forms. But when it is such, he revealed in the Epinomis, where he affirmed that the necessity of the mind and of the soul joined to the mind surpasses all necessity, and that every such decree is fatal. Indeed, the influx of the most high God, flowing through angelic minds even to the soul of man, daily incites the soul immersed in the body, so that, having cast off its fleshy shell, it lays aside its animal powers and operations, and instead of a soul, becomes an angel: just as a ray of the sun thins vapors, draws them upwards, and converts them into a fiery nature. If the soul by its nature exceeds the world's mechanism, and through lower powers works wonders even in alien bodies: what do we think it will do when it has risen to its own head, and become angelic? Which must be possible sometimes, since it often becomes brutish by the blandishments of the senses: and the inspiration of God ought not to be more vain than the blandishments of the senses. Then therefore it will no longer enchant one tender person, or heal a sick man, but will command the spheres of the elements. ...be called intelligible. But that light of God, when it is infused into an angel, immediately becomes intellectual light and can be understood. When it is infused into the soul, it becomes rational, and can not only be understood but also thought about. Then it migrates into the image of the soul, where it becomes sensitive, yet not corporeal. Then into the ethereal vehicle of the image, where it becomes corporeal, yet not manifestly sensible. Finally, into the elemental body, whether simple and airy or composite, which is the vessel of the ethereal vehicle, in which it becomes manifestly visible. And I believe this to be that golden chain which Homer saw hanging from heaven and let down even to the earth, by grasping which, men can raise themselves to the heavens. Indeed, celestial souls so divinely abound with light that a huge abundance of light overflows from them into their bodies, which we see in the stars. If ever the soul of a man so fixes its gaze on God, and is filled with divine light and carried away, he then likewise shines and pours out most abundant rays into his vehicle, and through the vehicle and airy body, into this body manifest to the eyes. Which then, that most full abundance of rays shines forth, becomes rarefied, is lifted up, with the ethereal vehicle and airy body contributing to this, as if [G] tow lifted by flame. By such a fiery chariot, the Magi and Platonists would say that Elijah and Paul were snatched up into heaven, and finally, after the judgment of the world, the body which our people call glorified, would similarly be snatched up. Six Questions concerning Miracles: & Solutions. Chapter 5.

**M**When the mind of man sheds bodily cares, why does it affect the passions of the elements? Because the divine soul, son of the highest and common good, does not despise the public good: therefore, like some god, it will providentially move the elements for the benefit of animals and men. Can it be lifted so far above its own body as to reach the spheres of the world? It can indeed, if it is everywhere: as some think. But does not light, enclosed in a thick lantern, when the lantern is opened for a short moment, shine forth from afar, and illuminate even the most distant things, yet without departing from the lantern? When the lantern is closed again, it is gathered into a corner without detriment to itself, even though it previously filled a very ample space and was diffused without dissipation? Wonderful power of light. It rests in the narrowest place, it fills the amplest. This it does indeed, because light is in a certain way incorporeal. The soul does the same: because it is divine light. Is this divine

**THEOLOGY OF PLATO**

Does the soul, in performing these miracles, withdraw from the body through all its parts? There is no need for it to entirely abandon the task of reconciling opposites. The soul indeed in the body, through its idol, as if the hair of a long-haired woman in vapor, first reconciles contrary elements into one: then if anything is dissolved, it restores it by nourishing; it also augments, governs the body, and moves it; and so on. We see most clearly that the work of moving and governing the body is sometimes relaxed and interrupted. When the soul is seized by a stronger imagination, the task of augmenting and nourishing is diminished because of the most intense investigation of reason. Therefore, philosophers do not digest food; **E** and the soul in an adult body speculates more acutely than in an adolescent one, being less occupied with augmenting bodies; and a sober body hinders speculation less, while the soul is solely intent on speculation. Wherefore, when through the mind such an abstraction of the soul occurs that both imagination and natural reason are interrupted, which themselves usually weaken the nourishment and governance of the limbs: what prevents the body from falling, and nothing in the body being nourished? Perhaps only the office of reconciliation will remain, by which the soul does not yet allow humors to dissolve and dissipate. But then such a reconciliation will not happen as usually happens through the idol: which entirely abandons the earthly body, when the soul tastes nothing earthly. For then the idol thus leaves the nature of earth, just as the reason **F** of earthly bodies leaves images. I am of the opinion therefore that the body of a man entirely abstracted, in that very brief time in which the soul is angelic, through the previously accustomed virtue of the idol, is neither moved, nor sustained, nor even contained. But if it is moved, or sustained, or contained: I believe this happens through that center of the soul which a little while ago we called the unity of the soul bestowed by God, through which it is reconciled to God, the center of all, and to pure unity; through which it reconciles not only the elements of this body, but also of the world; through which alone God can be reached, as Zoroaster thus revealed.

it is granted, what he says, that the soul raptured by God is neither clearly in the body nor outside the body: namely because it is not *in* the body through the idol, but *present* to it through the center.
   How long does the soul perform these wonders? As long as it remains thus abstracted. But it remains for a short time, a certain natural affection of an inferior power drawing it back to the care of the body: just as a stone thrown upwards is said to remain in the air for a little while, between its ascent and descent. But does the human soul confuse the order of the world by performing miracles? By no means.
   For, to speak Platonically, in the universal law of things and a certain perpetual series of causes tending to the same end, such miracles are prescribed. To this very thing contributes the providence of minds continually conspiring under God, down to our own mind. To the same end, the divine fate of animated idols flowing from the first soul to the idol of our soul. To the same end, a certain divine disposition of all natures concurring from the affection of the first nature down to the constitution of our nature. The same things are often foretold to us by celestial signs: through which, as if through the eyes and nods of the divine powers, thoughts are signified. "The heavens declare the glory of God: and the firmament announces the work of His hands." Therefore, it is not when that angelic soul desires to accomplish some wondrous work, for example, to summon winds, that the superior causes immediately favor this wish and desire new things because the soul has desired new things: but on the contrary, because the celestial powers have decreed that very thing, this soul desires it. How so? The foreknowledge of future winds stands in the supernal divine powers. A disposition of this kind (as we have said elsewhere) immediately flows down through those three series even to our souls: especially through providence in the mind: in a certain way also through fate in the idol: and through nature in the constitution of our body. But the disturbed minds of men do not grasp these impulses: a peaceful soul, however, receives the supernal impulses from all sides: whence it secretly begins to think the same things that the superiors think, and to will and not to will the same things, since it is inclined by a natural, that is, divine and intimate instinct. To this soul, all thoughts and affections succeed according to its wish: and whatever it asks from the superiors, it receives.
Indeed, it asks for what they were already about to give: and because they were about to give, they provoked it to ask: just as a mother
                                       Ff  iiij

PLATONIC THEOLOGY

who offers an apple with her hand before the eyes of her son, so that, invited by this, the son may ask for the apple. The son sees: asks: receives: receives, I say: not only because he asks, but he also asks because he is about to receive. Nor does the mother wish to give after the son wishes to receive, but the other way around. We indeed for the most part do not proceed with natural or divine desires, but with those which chance daily ignites. For as different things occur to our senses, we are affected differently. And thus occupied with contingent things, rarely do we achieve what we desire: because rarely and by some chance do we concur with the will of the supernal powers. But the angelic mind both consents with them, because it lives tranquilly: and commands the world, because of its own accord it is freed from this small body, which is a particle of the world, returning into its most ample nature. Indeed, God perhaps foresaw such a mind: such a mind, I say, not only by supernal aid, but also by its own will: which indeed then acts especially freely, when, having dismissed actions, it turns itself to contemplate and love itself and its origin. [Marginal note: I] God also chose such a mind to perform miracles. Whose prayers are not in vain even concerning public changes in the world. Avicenna in his Metaphysics, and Proclus and Iamblichus discuss in the Timaeus. For they prove that the vows of a most holy man, especially if the vows of the people also concur with him, wonderfully join minds to God in such a way that in a certain way one operation of God and the mind occurs: but of God indeed as an artisan, and of the mind as a divine instrument. But concerning those miracles which God performs by himself without an instrument, which are far greater: we do not treat them at present.
Are miracles of this kind natural to the mind? They are natural in a certain way, as the Platonists believe: and again, not natural. Natural indeed inasmuch as it recurs to the mind, and becomes the attendant and instrument of the highest God. Not natural, inasmuch as it serves only the use of one body: captivated by the love of which for a time, it neither unfolds the amplitude of its virtue nor becomes a participant in the divine. He who as often as he both unfolds and becomes a participant: shows that he will not be dissolved by any blow of bodies: inasmuch as in a certain way he surpasses all things: and twists all things according to his will. **That the soul strives to become God, we have shown by twelve**

**Chapter I.**

[I] N the beginning of the discussion, we laid two foundations
of signs pertaining to the immortality of the A
soul. In one, it is discussed how much
the soul dominates bodies: which we have covered through
four signs. In the other, it is argued
that the soul strives to become God. Concerning this, we will discuss through
twelve signs according to the twelve attributes of God.
In this will appear the wonderful greatness of the soul: for which it will not have been enough
to emulate God in those wonderful ways we have mentioned, unless it also
becomes God. Hence Zoroaster thus exclaimed:
ὦ τολμηροτάτης φύσεως ἄνθρωπε τέχνασμα.
that is, O man, artifact of a most daring nature. It is agreed B
among all theologians, that God is the first, the very true and
good. To be all things. To be the author of the universe. Above all
things. In all things. Always. To provide for all. To justly administer.
To persevere strongly in His own state while administering.
To treat temperately and gently. To live most opulently, and
most pleasantly. To behold Himself so blessed, to admire, and
to worship.
All theology among all peoples attributes these twelve divine attributes.
Whatever men do everywhere, they refer to the possession of these:
nor do they seek or strive for anything else than to acquire such attributes most fully for themselves.
The sole fullest possessor of these is God. Therefore, the entire endeavor of our
soul is that it may become God. Such an endeavor is as natural
to humans as the striving of birds for

--- Page 540 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

to fly. For it is inherent in all humans, always and everywhere,
and therefore it does not follow a contingent quality of any particular human, but the very nature of the species. But a natural movement directed towards some end is not determined to this end rather than to another for any other reason, except because of a certain affection of its nature: through which it is more congruent with such an end than with another such: and because of this congruence, it loves: and because of the same, it can attain what it loves: just as air, which by its lightness is congruent with the hollow of fire, strives and moves towards it by the same means. By the same means, it can again reach it: and in it, after it has reached it, find rest. Therefore, human striving directed towards God can sometimes be fulfilled. For who implanted this in our souls, if not that very God whom we seek? Since He alone is the author of species: He implants in species their proper appetite.
[Marginal note: A] For from the first principle of things, as from the first and desirable good, every natural appetite is drawn. The same is the first mover. The same is also the ultimate end. Indeed, an order in ends follows the order of agents: because just as the supreme agent moves the subsequent agents, so the ends of the other agents must be referred to the end of the supreme agent.
[Marginal note: C] For whatever the first agent itself does, it does for its own end. But the first agent leads and drives all actions of all subsequent causes, by moving all towards its own action: and therefore to its own ends. Hence it follows that the ends of all inferior agents are ordered by that very first agent to its proper end. God is the first agent. The end of the divine will is its own goodness. Therefore, all subsequent things are necessarily ordered towards God as their end: especially because nothing tends towards something as an end, except insofar as it is good. From which it follows that
[Marginal note: D] good is the end, in the respect that it is good. Therefore, that which is the supreme good: is most of all the end. Add to this that the first good is the cause for all things to be good: therefore it is the cause for them to be desired. But if it is that for the sake of which all things are to be desired: it follows that it is both most of all and by all to be desired. Therefore, it is the end of all things: yet in such a way that for minds, it is the end according to its form: but for other things, according to a shadow. Therefore, for humans too, it exists as the end according to its form: when nothing else satisfies them. Thus, therefore, humans desire the form of God, so that such an appetite is granted by God. Nor is it less—

--- Page 541 ---
**ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XIV. 230**

...nor is it strange, if human appetite is kindled by God, by which we desire God, more than a bodily appetite is enticed by any object presented to the senses. Indeed, and so much the more, as the highest good is more powerful to draw than the least goods. Truly, as I discussed in the book on love, the splendor of the highest good itself shines in each thing: and where it shines more fittingly, there it especially entices the beholder: it stirs the one considering it: it seizes and occupies the one approaching it: and compels him to venerate such splendor above others as if it were a divine power: and to strive for nothing else than that, having laid aside his former nature, he himself might become that splendor. This is evident from the fact that he is not content with the sight or touch of the beloved person: and often exclaims: "This person has I know not what that burns me: and I do not understand what I desire." Where it is clear that the soul is burned by divine radiance, which shines in a beautiful person as if in a mirror: and is secretly seized by it, as if by a hook, and drawn upwards so that it may become God.

But God would be (so to speak) an unjust tyrant, if he commanded us to undertake things which we could never accomplish. But he commands us to seek him: while with his little fires he inflames human desire for himself. He would also be an unskilled and overly rash archer, if he directed our desires like arrows towards himself as a target: and had not added little feathers to the arrows, by which they might sometimes hit the target. [Marginal note: E] Finally, he would be unfortunate, if his effort by which he draws us to himself, should never achieve its end. For this reason, our soul can sometimes become God, since it naturally strives for this, with God urging it on. But it does not become God, except insofar as it puts on the form of God: just as nothing becomes fire, unless it receives the form of fire. Therefore, just as the matter of air, which was previously under the humidity and heat of air, through the power of fire sheds its moisture, retains its heat: and having received dryness, puts on the form of fire: so the essence of the human soul, which now has mind and lower powers: with God stripping it, in a way sheds its lower powers: and with the mind, indeed with the head of the mind's unity preserved, it puts on divine substance, as if a new form, through which it almost becomes God: through which it then performs all operations as a kind of god rather than as a soul. That this can sometimes be fulfilled is necessary: lest it be attempted in vain by the human species seeking, indeed, lest it be rashly attempted by God drawing. The soul, surrounded by the dark dwelling of this body, relinquishes all lower powers either never or scarcely and for a moment. [Marginal note: F] Therefore that wonderful work in

is not fulfilled in this body: and is scarcely ever tasted by anyone. But natural desires must be fulfilled in many ways: and not by a momentary quality, but by a stable habit such as they desire. But if the mind is elevated higher to contemplate spiritual things, it departs further from corporeal things: and the supreme limit, which intelligence can reach, is the very substance of God: it follows that then at last the mind can take on the divine substance, when it has been entirely alien from mortal senses. Therefore, the soul, freed from the bonds of this body and departing pure, becomes God in a certain way. But God and God's eternity are the same. Therefore, by a similar reasoning, it becomes eternity: and much more does it become eternal. Indeed, John the theologian calls this state "becoming like God," but Paul calls it "being transformed into the image of God."

<center>Fifth sign of immortality from the fact that the soul desires the first truth and the first good.</center>
<center>Chapter 2.</center>

Thus at last a higher reasoning will make us more certain about immortality, if, by individually examining those twelve attributes of God, we show that the soul naturally strives in some way to equal God in seeking these.
Our mind therefore conceives a common principle of truth and goodness: through which it seeks common truth: and desires common good. In common truth all truths, in common good all good things are contained. Hence it happens that it naturally seeks all truths: it naturally desires all good things. This is evident from the fact that, having known one truth about something, we do not rest, but seek another, and again another: as long as we think some truth remains to be known. The same is observed in acquiring good things. But all truth, and all good, is God himself: who is the first truth, and the first good. Therefore, we desire God himself. But what do we especially strive for in him? To become like him. For all things, according to the capacity of their nature, tend towards him as their end: and they desire in their own way to become like him: bodies lacking life, according to being only: living things, according to life: sentient things, according to sense: according to intellect

--- Page 543 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XIIII. 231

rational beings. But we cannot become like God through the intellect, unless by understanding God: since the intellect becomes similar to any other things when, by understanding them, it transforms itself into their images. Therefore, our end is to see God through the intellect; to enjoy God, once seen, through the will: because He is our highest good: the highest object of our highest power, or the most perfect act concerning Him. Our highest powers are the mind, the head of the mind, and the will. The highest object of these is the common truth: and the common and complete good: and that is God. Nor let any of the Arabs object to us that it is sufficient for us to enjoy some angel. For a natural desire is in us always to find the cause of every effect, nor does inquiry cease until the first cause is reached. Since, therefore, we desire to see the cause of every known effect, and our intellect recognizes that it is the universal itself: it follows that we naturally desire to know its cause: which indeed is God Himself. Nor are we said to have attained the ultimate end unless all natural desire rests. Wherefore, the ultimate human end consists in the sole knowledge or possession of God: which alone terminates natural appetite. This is clearly apparent from the fact that the attainment of one's proper end delights everyone exceedingly. But the soul rejoices in the possession of no thing so vehemently, so purely, so firmly, as in even the slightest taste of divine contemplation: for which, if it is truly experienced, all possession and the whole world and life itself are scorned. For whoever lives piously with God sometimes, exclaims: that then alone in life he has lived removed from evils, and has tasted something good: as if then only he had received himself into his own harbor. To this points that saying of Plato in the book on knowledge: "Evils cannot be entirely avoided." For it is necessary that there always be something contrary to good. But among the heavenly beings, it is impossible for evils to exist: but they necessarily revolve around mortal nature and the lower region. Wherefore, one must flee from here to there as quickly as possible. But to flee from here to there is nothing other than to render oneself similar to God, as far as possible. And justice and holiness with prudence make one similar. So he says. Rightly does he thus command. For where all good things

[marginal note: C]

[marginal note: D]

--- Page 544 ---
...Where indeed all good things flourish, there alone is found the medicine for all evils. Nor should we believe Panaetius when he says that we indeed desire divine things, but will never attain the highest, because the full possession of divine things and a quiet life does not pertain to the souls of men, but to angels. The very nature of things teaches us the opposite. Indeed, elements which by their natural desire seek their places are carried so much more swiftly, the more they approach their places and boundaries. Therefore Aristotle in the book 'On the Heavens' shows that natural rectilinear motion cannot wander to infinity; otherwise, in its progress, it would not be sometimes slower, sometimes indeed faster. Therefore, that which is such that it tends more vehemently towards something later than before, does not stray into infinity, but directs itself to something certain. This, moreover, we experience in the very desire of knowing. For the more one understands, the more ardently he burns for what remains. Therefore, the natural desire of knowing is directed to some determined end. What is this end? The Cause of all causes: which, once discovered, terminates all natural inquiry into causes. Nature gave to dense bodies an appetite and inclination by which they would desire lower places; it also applied to them gravity and cold, as a means by which they might descend to the desired place. It gave to more subtle (bodies) an appetite for a higher place, and added lightness and warmth, and through these means they might attain the desired end. It gave to brute animals an appetite for food and coitus, and added members prepared for eating and coitus. The guide of nature gave to the soul a universal desire for all truth and goodness: which indeed is more natural than the appetite for food and coitus, in that it is more continuous. Indeed, the body rarely demands to eat, and more rarely to copulate; but we desire truth and goodness at every moment. For we are always desirous of new things, imaginations, and reasons. We always open our eyes to whatever occurs, and we are excessively delighted by the longest and widest prospect; indeed, we are content with the immense alone. We always prick up our ears for whatever is to be heard: which infants and adults do, both knowledgeable and ignorant alike, and all artisans in any art, with nature as their guide. Add that the lust for coitus can be tamed, the voracity of eating diminished; but the desire for truth and goodness by no means (can be diminished): indeed, those (desires) decrease with age, this (desire) increases. Add moreover, that those bodily...

Such things are desired for the sake of something else; but these for their own sake. Therefore, the more natural the desire for truth and goodness is than the desire for food and coitus, the more has it been provided by the leader of nature that it should completely attain its end. Indeed, for this very reason it is more natural, because it is more ready to acquire its end. Certainly, if the property of each species is necessary and wisely disposed by the author, it follows that the striving of the rational species, which is directed towards the possession of the whole good as its end, should be able to attain what it strives for. For indeed, if the attainment of the ultimate end is impossible, then the entire species and the action of the species is contingent, fortuitous, and vain. The eye sometimes rests at the sight of a graceful form; the ear rests with melody; and each sense is sometimes satisfied and filled by its objects. Nature has endowed the senses with such great happiness. But will reason, the queen of these, which, although inferior to angels, is nevertheless superior to brutes, be so unhappy, so neglected by the artisan of nature, that it should always wander, never rest? Certainly never in this life. Nor should any of the Arabs be listened to here, feigning that the human intellect can attain in all humans collectively what it cannot attain in individuals in this life. First, indeed, there is not one intellect in all men, utterly repugnant among themselves (which we will show elsewhere); then, neither in all men simultaneously does the soul ever attain the desired habit. And while in individual men it is blind to divine things, it is almost similarly blind to the same things in all. Finally, it is not permitted to feign that we ourselves can comprehend the very substances of divine forms from natural substances at will. For these substances incline towards matter, but those by no means. But the human intellect, insofar as it inhabits this body, to that extent, in knowing, it somehow inclines towards corporeal things. Furthermore, natural effects cannot equal and demonstrate the powers and substances of divine causes. Add to this, that divine forms differ much more from natural ones than natural ones differ from natural ones. Therefore, if colors are not known through sounds, which is evident in the blind, much less are divine things ever comprehended through natural things, as Plato writes to Dionysius of Syracuse. I omit that the divine substance and power, being infinite, cannot be perceived by us at will before we are absolutely formed by it itself. Which

--- Page 546 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Which indeed cannot be perfected in the soul joined to this body thus affected. But to return to the argument of this chapter's purpose: the capacity and desire of reason requires not merely some truths, or some goods, but all and complete ones. Which here it therefore never seems to attain, as Plato says in the Epinomis, because the intellect is always ambiguous: the will is always anxious. These things therefore the soul, stripped of the body, will achieve. If it obtains the universal good, it will in no way lack immortality: which is as great a good as death is an evil, which deprives of all goods. But the mind which will see all truths will rejoice in no goods if it suspects itself to be mortal. So that therefore the attainment of the end may be secure and tranquil, it is necessary for the mind to be certain of the eternal possession of the end. Which indeed Aurelius Augustine thus confirms in the thirteenth book of On the Trinity. All wish to be blessed, and therefore do not wish to perish and be consumed, because they are blessed. Nor can they be blessed unless living. They do not wish therefore to perish because they live. Therefore, whoever are truly blessed, or wish to be, wish to be immortal. But he does not live blessedly to whom what he wants is not present. In no way therefore can life be truly blessed, unless it is eternal. So he said. But lest the Panaetians further doubt that a truly blessed life is fitting for man, thus we will conclude. Since it is proper to intellectual nature to taste every good by knowledge, certainly it is proper to the same (nature) also to feed on every good, that is, the complete good, by affection. Therefore blessedness is proper to intellectual nature. But what kind of intellect each person has, such a blessedness he can attain. If a true and formal intellect, then also a true and formal happiness. But if a shadowy intellect, then also a shadowy happiness. Although the human soul is a certain image of a more divine intellect, nevertheless it has in itself the true form of mind, which is proven by three signs. The first is, that it understands many truths according to their true reason. The second, that it understands the true reason of truth itself. The third, that if our soul had only the shadow of intellect, it would never understand or define the form and substance of intellect, but would only confusedly perceive accidents. Since therefore the soul possesses the power of understanding not merely shadowy, like some more sagacious beasts, but truly also expressed and

and formal: therefore it can sometimes attain a truly blessed life. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that I posit one intellect as shadowy, another as formal. Indeed [C] the Platonists, as Proclus argues, thus distinguish all kinds of things: and primarily unity and mind: soul and nature. But let us set these aside for now: and let us see by what reasoning Origen confirms the above in his books 'On First Principles'. When Origen considered that God, the artificer of things, in each particular consults not only necessity and utility, both proper and common, but also (and indeed no less) strives everywhere for the beauty of things and the admiration of onlookers, he concluded that just as a human artisan constructs works as beautiful as possible, so that viewers may be drawn to consider and admire the ingenuity with which he constructed them: so too God, the most skillful artificer, constructed the work of the world. From this he wishes it to follow that the inquiry into the reasons by which all things subsist is implanted in the minds of all by the very reason of God the artificer, and is moved daily from there: so that our mind desires them no less by nature than the eye desires colors, and taste desires foods. He adds that we have received such a desire from God on the condition that it could someday be fulfilled: lest it be implanted by God in vain. Moreover, whoever indulges this love and zeal of will: even if he attains little truth in life, is nevertheless prepared by this affection to comprehend the fullness of truth in the future. And since such preparation is made by God: the formation will someday be by God. Indeed, active causes dispose matter for no other reason than that they may someday form it when it is disposed [D]. We briefly confirm this opinion of Origen thus: namely, insofar as we consider what the universal forms are in effect, and whether they benefit or harm us: to that extent we seem to be led by created nature, and to obey the life of the body: and to wish to transform external forms into our own form, as use demands. But when we investigate by what reasons individual things are thus created and ordered, which indeed we naturally inquire into: then by the very reason of the artificer of things we are drawn to it itself: and we strive for eternal life: and we try to reform the soul into the all-forming form of the artificer. Hence the Apostle Paul says that the inner man is daily re-Gg

The sixth sign, because the soul strives to become all things.
Chapter 3.

E [marginal note]
It has been shown that our soul, in all its actions, strives to acquire, to the best of its ability, that first gift of God, that is, the possession of all truth and all good. But does it seek that second [gift]? Does it not strive to become all things, just as God is all things? It strives in a wonderful way. Indeed, it lives the life of a plant, insofar as it indulges the body by nourishing it. The life of a brute, insofar as it flatters the senses. The life of a human, as it consults with reason about human affairs. The life of heroes, as much as it investigates natural things. The life of daemons, as it speculates on mathematics. The life of angels, as it inquires into divine mysteries. The life of God, insofar as it works all things by the grace of God.

DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XIIII. 234

Who would deny that one thing is made from corporeal matter and the form attributed to it, when from that composite one act and one motion arise? But much more (as the Platonists and Averroes hold) ought one thing to be made from the potentiality of the intellect and the form of the thing to be understood: both because a more stable composition often arises from these (for they often remain together longer than corporeal matter and its form), and also because the intellect itself is a kind of form. A form, I say, yearning for matter, as matter for a further form. Therefore it agrees more with the form to be received than corporeal matter agrees with its own proper form.
G
H
For all forms descend into the matters of the world from the supernal mind; wherefore they agree much more with our mind than with matter. Finally, the more excellent the mind is than matter, the more effectively it takes to itself and unites the form which it desires. Nor is it to be believed that the soul unites to itself what it grasps less than the body does. For the body turns even the most diverse foods into its own substance, with the soul digesting. So also the soul, what it receives, nay, conceives, it turns into itself, and much more so. Indeed, the dimensions of bodies impede mutual union in bodies; but spiritual things are much more apt for union. Therefore the reasons of intelligible things pass more into the substance of the intellect, as Plotinus holds, than foods into the substance of the body. Through these things it is clear that from our mind and the form of the thing to be understood, one thing is made.
I
But that which thus takes on the form of something, so that from it and itself it renders one thing, almost becomes that very thing whose form it took on. Who does not know that the matter of air, when it receives the form of fire, becomes fire, or fiery? Therefore the intellect almost becomes that thing which it understands. It becomes, I say, that thing in act. For both in potentiality and in a certain habit it was the same thing even before it understood, as Plotinus thinks. Then indeed the intellect understands a circle, when it itself actually, as it were, becomes the reason of the circle. Nay, this very becoming in act is understanding itself. But the intellect was the very same reason of the circle even before, both according to potentiality, which pertains to the substantial idea of the circle itself, and according to habit, as regards the formula of the idea familiar to us. But the truth of individual things consists in their own firm reason. And thus any mind becomes true when it understands the things themselves by converting itself into their perpetual reasons. But of this elsewhere.

But it suffices for us at present that since the intellect seeks to understand all things, and by understanding is thoroughly clothed in their forms, it follows that it seeks to become all things; whence it strives to become God, in whom are all things, while it strives to become all things. Enough about the intellect. Our will also desires the same thing:
[Marginal note: C] because it always yearns to enjoy all good things. But by enjoying things, it unites itself to the things it enjoys. But there is a difference between the intellect and the will. For both indeed become all things, the intellect all true things, the will all good things: but the intellect unites itself to things by transferring them into itself, the will, on the contrary, by transferring itself into things. In what way? Indeed, our intellect understands things more in its own way than according to the nature of the things themselves. For it understands the forms of bodies, which are particular, immersed in matter, divided, confused, imperfect, and mobile, in a certain universal, absolute, simple, distinct, pure, and stable way: but God and angels, who are stable and simple, it comprehends mostly by mobile and manifold discourse. Thus our intellect perceives both those things that are below it, and
[Marginal note: D] those that exist above it, in a certain way of its own. For this reason, it is said to transfer all things into its own nature. From this, that saying of Plato also seems to be confirmed, that the mind understands through innate forms, since it understands according to its own nature's mode. The will, however, first of all, does not remain in itself like the intellect, but moves the soul and body to act, so that they may approach desired things: then it does not desire things in the peculiar way they exist in the soul, but rather in the way they exist in themselves. For the intellect, when it is to know gold, that universal and incorporeal species of gold suffices: but for the will, it does not suffice. For as far as human life is concerned, it wants that particular and corporeal gold, such as it is in itself. Let us conclude, that our soul flies to God through the intellect and will, as if by those twin Platonic wings, because through them it flies to all things. Through the first, it applies all things to itself; through the second, it applies itself to all things. Therefore, the soul desires, strives, begins to become God, and progresses daily. But every motion directed towards some end, which begins first, then proceeds, is gradually intensified and progresses: indeed, it is perfected at some point. For it is intensified by the same faculty by which it began. Afterwards, it progresses by the same (faculty) by which it was intensified. Ea-

finally perfected by that by which it progresses. Therefore, our soul will someday be able to become in a certain way all things, and to emerge as a kind of god.

The seventh sign, and the eighth, because the soul attempts to do all things: and likewise to overcome all things.
Chapter 4.

**S**Other attributes of God follow: the third, that he is the author of all things: the fourth, that he is above all things. Our soul also pursues these. We have said elsewhere how, through various arts, it emulates all the works of God: and thus, like God, it accomplishes all things. We have also said that man always strives to dominate both himself and all others, both men and beasts. To be impatient of all servitude. Who, even if compelled to serve, hates his master: inasmuch as he serves against nature. Moreover, he strives earnestly to overcome in any matter: and is ashamed to be overcome even in the smallest matters and the most trivial games, as if that were against the natural dignity of man: and altogether the feeling of shame and modesty proper to the human race, signifies something narrow yet widespread in us, I know not what: which it would be wrong to violate: or which is most worthy of veneration. On this elsewhere. But as far as the desire for victory is concerned, one can clearly perceive the immense magnificence of our soul from this, that the empire of this world would not be enough for it if, having subdued this one, it should learn that another world remained which it had not yet subjugated. Hence Alexander, when he heard Anaxarchus the Democritean disputing that there were innumerable worlds: Alas for me, he exclaimed, who have not yet even gained possession of one. Thus man desires neither a superior, nor an equal: nor does he suffer anything to remain excluded from his rule. This state belongs to God alone. Therefore, he seeks a divine state. Which we can clearly infer from this, that many, both philosophers and princes, have sought divine honors for themselves. Nor was it enough for them to be considered good men, unless they were also considered divine. Indeed, they wished to be worshipped as gods: which, while innumerable men have attempted, then among philosophers Empedocles especially, among princes Alexander the Macedonian is said to have desired. Finally, all aspire to the same thing: and if succes-

Dionysius. From which he wishes it to be inferred that a sense of human affairs remains for the souls of men: which he also confirmed in the laws according to the order of divine providence.

Another way in which our soul desires to exist always, indeed, and to live (since for the soul, to exist is the same as to live) appears as follows. The human soul, and indeed every one, conceives of some eternal life: which, as soon as it is conceived, it desires: and always wishes to exist.

Altogether, the appetite for existence is natural: because it is inherent in all things as soon as they are born, and is continuous. [Marginal note: A] Nor does it come by design: because it is inherent in things as soon as they are born. Nor does it happen by chance, because it is in all things, and because it is continuous.

Indeed, the elements, through the power of their natural qualities, resist things attempting corruption: lest existence be taken away from them. Again, they seek out places convenient to themselves most eagerly, and repel things obstructing their movement, so that they may preserve their existence. This appetite for existence is therefore called natural, because it follows the natural qualities of things.

Plants also, by the instinct of their vital constitution, seek out more wholesome moisture, extending their roots very far towards it: by which they preserve their existence. Likewise, they avoid shadows by withdrawing their small branches: and with certain hooked tendrils, they entwine supports: lest they lose their existence. Which appetite we call natural: because it follows the natural constitution of life.

Brutes, through natural desire, acquire those things which preserve their existence: they repel destructive things through natural anger.

Therefore, in them likewise, the appetite for existence is natural: because it does not follow design or chance: but follows natural and inherent powers.

But since the natures of these have no power by which they might properly exhibit eternal existence to their own subject and body, therefore none of these desire to exist always in their own proper substance: for they would strive in vain: yet they desire, according to nature, to be eternal in their species: for which their natural powers sufficiently serve. Hence they generate things similar to themselves in species: through which propagation, such a species of things remains perpetual in the world.

This appetite, indeed, not only in elements [Marginal note: B] and plants, but also in brutes, lacks cognition. Namely, the power of generating, which serves this purpose, has absolutely no cognition.

But if there are any bodies whose principles are sufficient for existence in their own substance, those desire to exist eternally according to nature: eternally

[Marginal letter: C] But it desires to be always. Is this desire for eternal being as natural as the desire for being? It is, clearly. Nor let any Epicurean object to us that, although the soul naturally desires being itself (because it would desire it even if it did not know it),
[Marginal letter: D] yet it desires eternal being contrary to nature, perhaps because it first knew that eternity, and afterwards desired it. For that knowledge does not prevent the avidity for eternity from being natural. For our senses also recognize foods, which nevertheless they desire according to nature. A wolf desires a lamb, a dog a hare, after they have seen them; yet they desire them naturally, because from their natural constitution they are immediately so compelled to desire that they cannot but desire.
[Marginal letter: E] And just as it is natural for the eyes to perceive such objects presented to them, so it is natural for the power of concupiscence to immediately seek such things once seen. By the same reasoning, it is natural for the intellect to know clear objects, and for the will to desire what has been judged good. Whatever is clearly presented, the intellect naturally recognizes. Whatever is presented under the aspect of good, the will naturally desires. Therefore, it is natural for the intellect to know eternal being;
[Marginal letter: F] and, once known as good, for the will to naturally seek it. And just as irrational appetite follows sense, so the will, which is rational avidity, follows the intellect. Therefore, if the appetite for food is natural because it is sudden, not born of deliberation, so the will for immortality is natural because it is a sudden act following the pure nature of the intellect and the will. For when eternal being is first presented to the mind, it is judged desirable without discursive reasoning, and it is desired without any preceding deliberation. If it were desired either by chance or by deliberation, then not everyone, nor always the same people, nor equally always would desire it; but this would vary according to the variety of chances and deliberators. But now, all necessarily and suddenly adopt it, nature impelling them; just as we necessarily will good itself: but this (specific good) not necessarily, nor by nature. Thus to be such or such,

here or there, we do not naturally desire: but absolute being itself, to which no privation of being is mixed, we desire by nature's drawing. And just as we always dread the eternal privation of life by nature's impulsion: so we cherish eternal life by nature's drawing. But the artificer of nature has tempered cognition with being, appetite with cognition, and the attainment of the end with appetite. Therefore, just as a brute recognizes only temporal being according to the capacity of its nature, and naturally desires temporal being: so our soul, by the magnificence of its nature, recognizes eternal being and naturally desires it. For being itself is naturally desirable: and indeed naturally desirable in the same way it is naturally knowable. Therefore, just as by the nature of a brute, being is recognized only as temporal and present: so by it (the brute's nature) it is similarly desired naturally. But by human nature, just as being itself is recognized as perpetual, so as perpetual it is naturally desired by it: so that what is known only according to its own intellectual nature, may be naturally desired according to the same. Indeed, according to the same, we shall obtain what we desire. For it is reasonable that we attain in obtaining through the same faculty through which we attain in knowing and willing: so that to the same may be the natural end of motion, to which motion is natural. Therefore, he who attains eternal life through cognition and will, I do not see why he should not attain it through life itself: by the virtue of which life, surpassing temporal things, both intelligence and will, which depend on it, extend themselves beyond temporal things to eternal things. Moreover, since natural desire is not in vain, it follows that the human soul should attain perpetual being, naturally desired. Perpetual being, I say, not only in species, but in its own substance. For it desires that. Rightly, corporeal things, because they are born by propagation, desire perpetual being according to propagation: but the mind (desires) perpetual being of its own substance: because each mind subsists in itself, and is from God: it does not lie in any subject of generation, nor is it produced by succession. But who naturally desires impossible things? For who (desires) either to fly, or with dry feet to cross rivers? Indeed, sometimes some vain boy, by some chance, moved by sense, such wonders for himself—

--- Page 556 ---
the ability to desire such things: but neither do children themselves often think or desire such things, nor do men ever. But we all desire eternal life, and always, even when we do not realize we desire it. Therefore, the attainment of this is not impossible. But I think this should be particularly noted, that
[Marginal note: K] life is more natural than knowledge: because life is prior and more interior, and more continuous and substantial, than knowledge. Therefore, the appetite for true life is more natural than for true knowledge. True knowledge is that which is so devoid of its opposite, that is, ignorance, that it neither has it actually mixed in through deception, nor can it ever fall into it through oblivion. True life also is that which is neither actually mixed with a death-bringing quality: nor subject to death by any inclination. Since, therefore, the desire for true, that is, eternal life, is much more natural than for true knowledge: it follows that the attainment of eternal life is far more natural and possible than that of true knowledge. Indeed, since life much more than intelligence and will is in harmony with eternal life: if by understanding and willing, certainly much more by living do we attain eternal life. If indeed it communicates itself to the later acts of the soul, namely to intelligence and will: then assuredly it has first communicated itself to life itself, which is the prior act. Otherwise, the author of nature would not so vehemently draw us daily to the eagerness for this thing, just as he does not draw us to any other impossibilities. For divinely, Zoroaster [says],

οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ πατρικῆς ἀρχῆς ἀτελές τι τροχάζει,
[Marginal note: A] that is, Nothing proceeds or revolves imperfect from the paternal principle.

*Sign. 11. 12. 13. 14. that we desire to attain the four virtues of God. Chapter 6.*

[Marginal note: B] THERE are four other gifts of God pertaining to four virtues. For we have called Him provident, just, strong, and temperate. Who would deny that God oversees all things individually. Governs by due and natural orders. Remains unmoving in His own state while doing these things,

--- Page 557 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK 14. 238

nor to be wearied? To be tranquil, and to handle each thing gently and moderately? Look at the human soul, an imitator of divine prudence. How curiously it recalls past events, not only private or its own, but all public and worldly ones. How intensely it inquires into present things, even those of others and foreign? How eagerly it yearns for future things. How diligently it anticipates future ages? What more serious insult can a man hear than if he is called ignorant and improvident? Hence it happens that no one willingly wishes to confess ignorance of any thing or art: inasmuch as, nature showing the way, he judges that ignorance of nothing pertains to man, but that he naturally possesses skill in almost all things, just as God does.

**I**ustice, too, our mind pursues divine. By how many laws does it subject its own body, govern the family, temper the state. It also moderates kingdoms. [Marginal note: C] With how many punishments does it rage against sinners? With how many rewards does it affect the good? How gravely does it feel indignation towards the most wicked? How ardently are even the most upright men loved by the wicked. Finally, with what order, and almost heavenly, is human society arranged, and in every governance is it directed towards one elder and wiser person, just as the whole world is directed towards one God? Indeed, even robbers justly divide the spoils among themselves, and unjust men, if they inflict any injury, think they inflict it justly, either avenging received injuries, or removing from their midst men who would be harmful, or stealing those things which they themselves need while others abound: and they wish to appear to commit each act most justly. In all these things it appears that the human race wishes to claim for itself no less justice than God himself possesses.

**D**o we also strive to attain the fortitude of God. [Marginal note: D] Indeed, the fortitude of God is an unmoving state. The most prudent men acquire this state for themselves, as far as their strength allows, from the fact that they resolve to live content with the goods of the soul: and to make nothing of the advantages or disadvantages of the body and fortune: as if to themselves, who are souls themselves, nothing pertains. Those who neglect these movable things persevere with an unmoving spirit. The less prudent, however, desire the same state of life, but they approach it by another path: thinking that things will more easily succeed for them

E  **M**oreover, who would not desire divine temperance? The prudent strive to moderate the movements of the soul in such a way that they do not disagree in any part; the imprudent arrange both their body and their affairs in such a way that they do not disturb the soul. Both seek the complete harmony of their soul; and indeed, for the prudent, the matter sometimes succeeds; for the imprudent, never. Finally, just as with all other things, so too the highest principles of these four virtues are in God: so much so that God is supreme prudence, supreme justice, and the other supreme virtues. Men who are zealous for these virtues seek their highest principle, desiring that nothing pertaining to their perfection should be lacking to them. All humans desire this, although some proceed by different paths. Therefore, all seek God. But those seek God by the most direct path who first, through civil virtues, cut off secondary affections of the soul;
F  then, through purgative virtues, they eradicate them; in the third place, through the virtues of a soul already purified, they moreover moderate the primary affections; with these tempered, finally they are formed by the exemplary virtues which are in God. Indeed, we can undoubtedly sometimes be formed by exemplary virtues. For preparation or affection regards form and habit, and a certain affection regards a certain habit. Therefore, a cause that gradually prepares some subject more and more, prepares it for this reason, so that it may induce a substantial and principal form; and that subject, according to the common order of nature, just as it is a participant in that preparation, so too can it be made capable of the principal form. God, who is the exemplary virtue itself, affects the human soul from the beginning with certain seeds and incitements of
G  virtues, through which, by human virtues, that is, civil and purgative virtues, purified souls are suitably prepared for the exemplary and divine virtues. That three such human virtues are preparations for divine ones, we infer from this: that they are instilled in us and excited by the divine; that their images are so clear that the divine virtues are recognized through them; that they gradually approach them more and more; that they thus affect us...

The sixteenth sign, that we worship ourselves and God. Chapter 8.

It remains for us to speak about that twelfth divine gift, by which He loves and worships Himself; which men claim for themselves in two [Marginal note: H] ways. First, because all, not only as they do all other things, love and protect themselves, but also greatly worship themselves, and venerate themselves as if they were certain deities. The prudent do this insofar as they subject external and bodily things to the soul as to a ruler. They depend entirely on the mind as if on God. They also consider it a sin to defile the august majesty of their mind, like a divine statue, with base thoughts and earthly impurities. This natural notion indeed instilled shame and reverence in the human race, so that we revere not only the sight of other men as if divine, but also the conscience of our own mind (as Pythagoras taught) as the face of God; which constantly stimulates us with repentance for misdeeds, even if we do not fear punishment. But the memory of good deeds delights us. As if the heavenly soul always recoils from earthly stains of vices. The imprudent do the same in a certain way, but they are surpassed by the more prudent in accomplishing this work. Again, the most foolish men do the same, but differently, inasmuch as they are too pleased with themselves; they persist most stubbornly in their own opinion; they hold their opinion tenaciously as if it were a divine decree. [Marginal note: A] Finally, all men, the most excellent souls, and those who have deserved best of the human race in this life, as divine-

Hence the soul is made a temple of God, as Xystus the Pythagorean
believes. He believes that the temple of the eternal God will never
fall. The human mind daily considers God.
The heart burns for God. The breast sighs for God. The tongue sings of Him.
The head and hands and knees adore Him. The works
of men represent Him. If God does not hear these things: perhaps He seems
ignorant. If He does not grant them: perhaps He will appear ungrateful.
Cruel in a way, if He compels us to cry out daily, whom
He does not hear. Nor should anyone dare to say that God despises
human things as insignificant. Indeed, a suitable dwelling,
as an end, moves the craftsman as an efficient cause, so that he may
devise a certain form of house: for which form, in turn, he may seek
certain material. Where the end moves the agent: the agent [moves] the
form: the form [moves] the material. The same happens in civil
and military counsels. From which it follows that the end is the cause of causes:
D and therefore precedes all causes. Moreover, all natural things are
instituted for the sake of some certain end, since individual things seem
to lead to individual, most particular uses. For example, the tendril of a vine
(which they call a capreolus) is born for this purpose, that it may bind the vine
to the nearest shrub. This act of binding is the cause that—

But whether an act of this kind in that nature presided according

a divine mind presides over all bodies, which embraces the forms
of all corporeal things in an intellectual manner, and
like an archer directs each thing to its own ends: and finally,
all things to one end.

This divine farmer cultivates the vine shoots, tendrils, and roots.
For how else do the vine shoots turn towards the sun, avoiding shade?
Or how else do the tendrils, like hands, especially stretch towards that
part where support is nearest? Or how else do the roots,
fleeing dryness, spread most towards moisture? A choice that does not err,
is the work of artistic counsel, indeed, of the most true intellect.
Yet a true mind is not inherent in vines. Therefore, it is present.
Moreover, it is present even to the most humble little animals,

Does He despise humans alone? who [Marginal note: E]

Far from it: indeed, if God neglects no parts of the world, not even the smallest,

which is such a precious part of the world, that it is the middle ground between

So close to God, that insinuating itself into the secrets of the divine mind,

of the worldly order is more excellent than that order itself. Since
indeed, an order of this kind is made by intelligence, and is governed by it.
If through knowledge our soul is more excellent than the world:
through life it will also be more excellent.

By whose virtue, being separable from the body, it possesses the ability to be separated from the body through its operation, and to transcend the world itself by the virtue of a super-mundane life (if I may so speak). How much intelligence surpasses the order of the world is apparent from this: that such an order is dispersed in time, while intelligence possesses the whole simultaneously and stably. Order, in turn, follows its cause but does not attain it; intelligence attains the cause of order when it finds God, its artificer, where it grasps so much about God that it subsequently regards the world as a mere shadow.

Indeed, one does not scorn such a great thing unless one conceives of greater things. If the human soul is so much greater, why should it be neglected by God, the provider even of the smallest things? If the soul perceives God, why should not God also perceive the soul, especially since God has given this very power and act of perception to the soul, and preserves it, and guides it? Hence David asks: "He who planted the ear, does He not hear? And He who formed the eye, does He not see?" Moreover, if the soul ascends to God, why should not God in some way descend to the soul? If the mind demands what is just from God, while it asks for its paternal inheritance, why should not God hear it? What does this most dutiful child ask from its most indulgent parent?

Eternity. It will certainly obtain it. For the eternal God can bestow it; the life of the mind can grasp eternity, which its knowledge and will grasp. For it does not will unless it knows, nor does it know unless it lives. Furthermore, eternity ought to be given to the mind, which both transcends time and, for the sake of the eternal God, despises temporal things. This is something not only the more religious, but even the impious in some way do. For those whom the love of God does not attract, at least fear terrifies. Those whom fear does not terrify, at least suspicion troubles. Therefore, many men, indeed all, or certainly very many, cast aside the comforts of temporal life, out of love for God, or suspicion, or fear. God, therefore, ought to bestow eternal things in exchange for temporal ones.

But no other animal refrains from present goods because of the desire for future ones. From which it follows that man is the most foolish of all animals, and the most miserable, if he enjoys neither the present life nor the future. And this miserable foolishness of his, and foolish misery, will arise from this: because he has trusted himself to God, who is most wise and most happy. But just as nothing can become most cold by the proximity of fire, so man cannot,

--- Page 567 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XIV. 243

...because he alone clings to God, most wise and most blessed, [he cannot] become most foolish and most miserable from this; but rather, for this very reason he is most blessed, because he joins himself to the most blessed one. He joins himself to Him by despising temporal things and desiring eternal things. If he becomes blessed by despising temporal things, he is not made such otherwise than by the acquisition of eternal things. Furthermore, if God is the first and highest life, the animal that clings more closely to Him lives longer. But we do not live longer in the body. If God is supreme wisdom, man is so much wiser than other animals, as much as he clings more closely to God. But in this drawing near, he judges himself immortal. But because such a judgment is true, as it comes from the soul when it is wiser than other animals and men, it is true that the soul is eternal. If the first truth cannot deceive, then the hope of immortality, which is inserted into us by the first immortality to such an extent that we always retain such a hope even when all things among which we live are unwilling and protest, will not be deceived. If the first goodness is not malevolent, the avidity for the first good infused into us by it does not deprive us of temporal goods except to bestow eternal ones. If every opinion is truer the better it is, and better the better it makes those who hold it, then the opinion of immortality is the truest of all, because above all others it makes men most good, most excellent, and therefore most happy. Who is ignorant that that is most true in the nature of man which most leads to human perfection? If the intellect by nature loves God as truth itself and goodness itself; and God both loves the intellect, especially the pious one, as most akin to Himself, and loves it back as loving: it follows that there is a certain natural friendship between them. The end of friendship is communion of life. Therefore, God's life can be communicated to the intellect: namely, in that way in which it is loved by it. [A] Indeed, the end of friendship is such as the friendship itself is, and vice versa. But a perpetual one is loved and desired. Which seems to be confirmed from this, because since it is characteristic of the good to attract all things to itself and to communicate itself to all, it is necessary that the infinite good, which is God, should draw and communicate infinitely. Therefore, He communicates Himself to each according to their wish, because the same God who drew also communicates. But the intellect by nature desires the perpetual life of God no less than a certain understanding of Him. Finally, if God
