That religion is of all things most proper and true to the human race. Cap. 9.

B That man is superior to beasts, his works are the most evident testimony: which Aristotle shows in the 12th book of animals. Let us therefore inquire by what special gift he is most excellent. He certainly seems to excel in the genius for arts and governance: especially because (as we have declared elsewhere) men vary their crafts: inasmuch as they themselves are artisans, not instruments of another artisan. But beasts do not vary, because they are instruments of an artful nature rather than possessing art themselves. But although we excel other animals in the genius for art and governance: this ingenuity is nevertheless common to us with beasts. But the human species, since it is distinct from beasts, ought to have some distinct and proper perfection, of which no beasts are in any way partakers.

Will it be speech here? But beasts imitate speech by nod, cry, and song. Is it reason? Reason certainly: yet not every operation of reason. For active reason indeed has certain vestiges in beasts through indications of arts and governance. Speculative reason concerning natural things also seems to have something imaginary in beasts. For they themselves cure their diseases by the choice of certain foods and remedies: and as if provident of future storms, they present signs of future events: C and they change places: so that they may avoid the coming dangers of the seasons: although they are led to this rather by nature than by leading themselves. What then remains: which belongs entirely to man alone? The contemplation of divine things. For beasts show no indication of religion: so that the elevation of the mind to God, the king of heaven, is proper to us, just as the elevation of the body to heaven is proper. And divine worship is almost as natural to men as neighing to horses, D or barking to dogs. But if any curious person should affirm that some beasts moreover venerate celestial things: (which I by no means believe

--- Page 569 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XIIII. 244

do) the Platonists will respond that beasts of this kind, or anything else, do this when they seem to honor celestial things. Or if perchance they do honor them, yet they do not know what they are doing. Or if they know: that they too are participants in intelligence and immortality. But in truth, to return to our purpose, the most perfect animal excels most in perfection by that property, and differs from inferior animals, by which it is joined to the most perfect, that is, divine beings. Again, if man is the most perfect of mortal animals in what respect he is man: he is the most perfect of all by that special gift which among these he himself possesses as his own, not common to animals. That is religion. Therefore, through religion he is most perfect. If religion were vain: through it again he would be the most imperfect of all: because through it, as we explained a little earlier, he would be most insane and most miserable. But he cannot through the same part of himself suffer such contradictions, that through it he is at once supremely perfect and supremely imperfect. Therefore, religion is true. Or do we ignore that prophecy which is made by an entire species of animals, to be true? Many reptiles creep out from the bosom of the earth at sunrise: a mist of air spreads forth. A very large flock of crows flies in the evening from a certain region of the air: winds are foretold. Also by the common prophecy of men, religion is true.
  For all everywhere always worship God for the sake of a future life. Therefore it is true that there will be another life, if only the most perfect species of animals has that very true judgment, which is most natural to it of all things. But that the assertion of religion is such appears not only from the fact that it belongs to man alone, but also from the fact that all human opinions, affections, customs, except religion, change. When I speak of religion, I understand that very instinct, common and natural to all peoples, by which everywhere and always a certain providence, queen of the world, is conceived and worshipped. To which piety certainly we are led especially by three causes. First, by a certain natural (so to speak) sagacity, infused into us by Providence itself: then by philosophical reasons proving the architect's providence from the very order of the edifice: lastly by prophetic words and miracles. ...vicenna adduces in metaphysics, to confirm. Man (as

Moreover, that he is sociable, speech indicates, as a certain

Therefore, association is natural to man. But if they come together without

unless the legislator is and is considered divine. Finally, for him to be
and be considered such, it is necessary that he be sent to men by divine
providence with certain manifest miracles. Whom indeed, as a
prophet, a divine leader of the human race, Plato and Avicenna
call. To this tends that Platonic saying in the book *On the Kingdom*:
Just as beasts cannot be led successfully by a beast without man,

Again in *Protagoras* he says that men could not live together

will, and a bearer of law both divine and human.
That God, moreover, sends prophets in certain ages for such an
office, we can show thus, together with Avicenna.
If God provides most accurately for the human body not only in things
absolutely necessary, but also in conveniences, as in the eyebrows
and eyelids, and the concavity of the feet:
much more does He provide for the soul, and for the entire human race in
principal matters, and especially in those necessary for our good:
especially since lesser goods exist for the sake of greater ones.
Therefore, if lesser goods are immediately present to us from the beginning,
without doubt greater goods are also present: which can be present, and are
the causes why lesser ones are not lacking. Therefore, God concerning divine law,

...and God so provides for its founder, the prophet, that concerning his goodness, if individual members of the body cannot justly complain, much less can the soul itself, the master of these, or the entire human race ever complain for any reason. [Marginal note: A] Moreover, Avicenna proves that the soul, imbued with prophetic law and virtue, is sent solely by divine providence; but the body, suitable for receiving the prophet's soul, is disposed by God, yet not directly, but through the moving souls of the heavens, as if through ministers, and also through the heavens themselves, as if through instruments of God. Thus, divine law, being incorporeal, although it cannot be effected by celestial bodies, can somehow be signified by certain signs received from heaven. This is also confirmed by many of Plotinus's disputations, in which he demonstrates that what pertains to our mind can never be done by a celestial body, but can nevertheless be signified. Indeed, the moving minds of the heavens foresee these things of ours, [Marginal note: B] and often seem to indicate their thoughts with their celestial eyes and nods, as it were.

Three objections of the Lucretians: & solutions. First. Cap. 10.

**N**one should believe the Lucretians who say that religion [Marginal note: C] does not arise from natural judgment, but from corruption of temperament, laws of counsel, or the impulse of heaven. Indeed, I do not think it arises from corruption of temperament, because the temperament in humans is not worse than in beasts, especially regarding the judgment of truth and the choice of good. But humans alone are diligently occupied with religions. But neither among humans who have a depraved temperament are these properly the ones who worship God. For not all have a corrupted temperament. Yet all somehow worship God, and have always worshipped Him; nor has human nature always been depraved. Nor do only unlearned people worship, but also the ingenious and wise, as demonstrated by the Magi of the Persians, the Egyptian priests, the Hebrew prophets, Orphics, [Marginal note: D] Pythagoreans, Platonic philosophers, and the ancient theologians of the Christians. All these, without controversy, excelled in wonderful wisdom and incorporeal sanctity. Porphyry concerning

Porphyry, discussing devotion, says that the most excellent men among all nations dedicated themselves to the study of wisdom with vows: such as the Brahmins among the Indians, the Magi among the Persians, and similar ones among the Greeks and Chaldeans. So he said.

Nor should it be thought that they feigned it, who confirmed the sanctity of their speech both by perpetual works and by the danger of their life.

There were also many other very learned philosophers, barbarians, Greeks, and Latins, who, even if they did not excel in such great chastity of life as those whom I mentioned before, nevertheless led their lives with honest morals and and did not hesitate to favor religions.

Indeed, it is possible that some of these may have feigned it in some part; yet I do not believe all feigned it, nor that those who feigned it were entirely devoid of religion.

For it is difficult to entirely shed one's nature. Indeed, Diagoras, Dicaearchus, Epicurus, and Lucretius are said to have been impious above others, who were even compelled by nature sometimes to assent somewhat to religions, as their books testify.

But just as these men brought forth some things against religions with impunity, so too would many other philosophers have openly vomited forth the poison of impiety, if very many had been impious.

But it is one thing not to admit this or that religious practice, which many do; it is another thing to utterly abolish all religion, which very few have attempted, and those indeed rather suspecting than entirely asserting.

Furthermore, if any ingenious and learned men are found to be ambiguous in religion, it is not to be wondered at.

For Plato writes that two ages are very religious: childhood and old age.

For children suck in religion with milk, and they remain in what they have imbibed until reason is awakened in adolescence, which by its nature seeks the causes and reasons of individual things.

If in this age they either undertake those studies or fall into those discussions in which the causes of things are diligently sought out, they begin, as it were, to want to assert nothing unless they themselves have thoroughly understood the reason for it.

Then for the first time they largely cast religion behind their backs, unless perhaps they commit themselves to laws and the counsel of elders, because the most hidden reasons of divine things are perceived only after a long time, with the most exquisite diligence, and a purified mind.

Those adolescents do not yet attain reasons of this kind; and because they assert almost nothing for which they do not see a reason, if by their own judgment—

Indeed, I call a healthy and natural human complexion sanguine, and [Marginal note: D] most temperate. The sanguine is airy, consisting in vital heat and moisture. The temperate is like the sky: nor does it disturb the judgment of truth. Such are most human complexions, adapted to a sound mind and prudence: which indeed do not bring religion to us (for this is divinely infused into the mind, since the grace of divine things commands other things to be neglected) but they do not impede it at all, nor do they cast vain suspicions into the mind. But that which is in many and in perfections, is considered natural. That which is in very few and sick people, is monstrous. But indeed, the natural is truthful; [Marginal note: E] and the monstrous is usually deceptive. Moreover, judgment favoring religion is found in many and more serious men; but in very few and most frivolous men, the contrary: by whose example others are also sometimes infected. And in those very few, this is not a judgment of reason, but a disease of the mind, and a fearful suspicion arising from a depraved bodily complexion. This is evident from the fact that often such men indeed have reasons favoring the soul's eternity, yet they are suspicious: just as those whose reason either judges wine should not be drunk, yet their lungs thirst nonetheless; or judges there is nothing on the road that can harm, yet their senses shudder in the dark. And not only an unfavorable complexion contracted either from parents or from the stars, but a quality induced by habit, as we indicated from the beginning, leads the human race away from religion. For men who are too curious in any discipline, [Marginal note: F] due to excessive brain agitation, are in a way driven mad by a dried-up brain: which he writes in the Theaetetus.

Plato, against those who said that nothing ever stood still in things, stated that they, affected by dizziness due to constant motion, believed everything was turning: when it was they themselves who were turning. Therefore, it is not surprising if men curious in the arts sometimes clearly rave both in religion and in other matters: whose madness is revealed both by their very frivolous morals and by opinions in many things that are excessively ridiculous, and by the contradictions of these very opinions. Therefore, religion is not born from a corruption of temperament, but rather
G impiety. And Plato asserts in his letters to the Syracusans that impiety arises not only from a depraved temperament, but also from depraved morals, saying that one must always believe the ancient and sacred oracles which assert that the soul of man is immortal, and has judges, and suffers the greatest punishments when it has been separated from the body. Wherefore it must be considered a lesser evil to suffer the gravest injuries than to inflict them. Which indeed a greedy man and one devoid of mind either does not hear, or is accustomed to deride: and given over to pleasures, as if blind, he does not perceive how great an evil necessarily always follows him living impiously: and how miserable a departure awaits him after death. All these things are there. Similar things also in the Gorgias and in the tenth book of the Republic and in the Laws: where he adds
H that this opinion about the soul has been proven by necessary and adamantine reasons. Which was so thoroughly persuaded to Cleombrotus that he deprived himself of this life out of love for another. Demosthenes also says that it is better to die honorably than to live shamefully,
I after he had heard Plato and Xenocrates discoursing on the immortality of souls. Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that the greatest cause of impiety is usually attributed by the Platonists to the class of inferior demons, who, by a certain silent persuasion, either because of false ambition or because of envy, drive us with all their might into irreligion.

K [Large initial C] Onfutavimus the first objection of the Lucretians, by which it was said that the worship of God arises from the depravity of human nature. Where it became clear that the Lucretians themselves are rather depraved: who judge human nature to be most wicked from this very fact,

...because it is joined to the best God. But what if they bring forward in the second place, that the veneration of divine things arises from human counsels and civil institutions? By no means. For it cannot be said how quickly human inventions change, even true ones: let alone false and simulated ones. All human institutions are changed into contrary institutions in a short time. Also, at the same time, laws are diverse among peoples: and what are considered shameful by some, are considered honorable by others. But what is older than religion, or what is more extensive? Nor did the founders of laws invent this to restrain peoples. For before cities and homes, religion flourished in the world: and scattered and wild men worshipped God, and these very lawgivers themselves feared the divine powers. Which indeed [L] Plato confirms in Protagoras: saying that men, even before they gathered together, or spoke, or practiced any arts, from the very beginning, out of natural kinship, adored God: and made altars and sacred rites. Therefore, such a hard yoke of religion, contrary to so many good things in life, men would have rejected it somewhere at some point, if it were fictitious and did not consist of the stability of truth. But perhaps Protagoras will say that religion is not natural, but appears to be so, because we imbibe it from our tenderest years. We will thus respond to Protagoras, that we learned to speak and drink from infancy: nevertheless, speech and drink are natural. Everywhere and always men speak and drink: because it is natural. But at different times and places they speak and drink in a different order: because the order of operation consists more of custom than nature. Similarly, among all peoples in all ages, God is adored, because it is natural: although not with the same sa- [M] cred rites and methods. Speech, because it is natural, attains its end, that is, to declare one's will to another. Drinking also attains its end, that is, to restore the body's moisture. Why religion should not attain its own end: I do not see. Its end is to enjoy God: its desire is to enjoy Him perpetually.

Third objection: and solution.

[Large initial A] re men led to religion by the stars: which the impious object in the third [A] place. By no means. For the stars influence the humors of bodies. Religion is inimical to bodies.

--- Page 578 ---

Nor can the sky instill a deeper longing than for the celestial spheres, which even the religious person scorns. Moreover, religion condemns fate and asserts liberty. In what way, then, will that very thing (religion), which opposes fate, have its origin from the fates? Furthermore, a certain conjunction of planets provides fertility, while an opposite one brings scarcity. This one brings plague, that one health; similarly, war and peace. We see how quickly the gifts of the heavens are changed into their opposites. Therefore, if a certain position of the stars compels one to worship God, soon an opposite position will erase divine honors from the memory of men. Yet nowhere and never has there been an intermission of religion, although elsewhere and at other times God is honored differently. This very variety of human minds has secure counsels, which are by no means subject to the stars. For the human mind, by its nature, as if divine, is led to perceive, worship, and fear God, just as by its nature it is led to love good and avoid evil. **B** Nevertheless, through the free choice of its own deliberation, it varies the rites of worshipping God, just as it proceeds along various paths towards good, according to its will. From the preceding discussion it is gathered that this common religion of all peoples to one God is very natural to the human species, and a virtue proper to man, and therefore most excellent. Indeed, there are two most excellent acts of men: **C** namely, those which are in the most excellent part of the soul and are concerned with the most excellent object. Such are in our mind the knowledge of God, and love (of God). In this life, human love for God surpasses human knowledge, because no one truly knows God. But truly love God, however known, those who scorn all things for His sake. Again, just as it is worse to hate God than to ignore Him, so it is better to love than to know. Add to this that by scrutinizing God, in the longest time we profit very little; by loving, in the shortest time, very much. For this reason, love connects the mind with divinity more quickly, more closely, and more firmly than knowledge, because the power of knowledge consists more in distinction, while that of love consists more in union. Moreover, it is more pleasing to God Himself to be loved than to be contemplated. For we attribute nothing to God by contemplating Him; but by loving, we attribute to Him whatever we are and whatever we possess. Therefore, God repays Himself to those who love rather than to those who scrutinize. Next, by knowledge

He who has already offended divine justice for so long – to whom future ages are present – as long as he is, if he were to live, destined to sin: an infinite punishment is already owed to this infinitely sinning person. Furthermore, if the reward of true virtue is eternal (for it looks to God, from whom it depends as its beginning, as its end), it follows that the punishment for vice, which falls short of the eternal reward of virtue as much as it falls short of the principle of life, should be eternal. No such thing exists in this very brief span of life. Therefore, it will be in the future. In this way, the adversities that befall the good in this life, and the prosperities that befall the wicked, seem to be compensated: lest piety be a detriment to the good, and, as is read in the Phaedo, impiety be a profit to the wicked. Indeed, good ought to be beneficial; evil, harmful. Yet in this life, piety is detrimental, as it compels one not only to despise present goods, but also, for the sake of God and honesty, to undertake labors and death. **F** Conversely, impiety is exceedingly profitable. Therefore, lest justice lack its place, judgment must be rendered elsewhere. Nor should it be thought that this part of justice, which concerns human affairs, does not pertain to God, to whom belongs the administration of the entire world. In this, if He makes individual things by understanding and loving, as Plato desires, it follows that by making, He understands and loves each one, and in caring for the whole, He does not neglect the parts **G** (without which being cared for, the whole is not cared for). These things Plato states in the Laws. Indeed, a not insignificant part of the world is the human species, itself an administrator of justice. If, therefore, divine justice, as Orphic hymns sing, distributes each element to its own place, if it dispenses small gifts to each and every thing, even the smallest, according to its nature: why should it not also dispense to humans places, rewards, and punishments according to their merits? God frequently leaves either the good unrewarded or the wicked unpunished, so that by these indications He may show us that another life remains, in which justice, which cannot be deceived, may be fulfilled according to merits. Sometimes, however, He punishes crimes, especially the most grievous, even in this life, so that by this we may recognize His providence. So great also is the observance of order, that the soul which seems to depart from order by sinning: even while it departs, it proceeds within the order of free movement itself: and immediately returns to the order of justice by suffering, while on account of the habit of transgressing, it suffers such things as are fitting for that habit. These things I had to say concerning immortality, as far as the testimonies of signs are concerned: but it is necessary next to most diligently resolve the doubts which compel one to distrust immortality.

ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL. BOOK XV. 251

Five questions concerning the soul follow. First, whether there is one intellect for all humans.
That there is not. Chapter I.

[Large decorative initial M] Any things which are usually brought forward against the
soul, we have already refuted in previous discussions. Five remaining (as I
believe) doubts are to be clarified. The first is,
concerning which the Peripatetic Averroes doubted: Lest perhaps there be one
mind for all humans, and eternal, while many souls are
mortal: so that the eternity of the mind itself profits nothing to perishing human souls. The second, concerning
which some doubt, why souls, if they are divine, are joined to such lowly earthly
bodies. The third, for what reason they are so greatly disturbed in these [bodies].
The fourth, why they depart unwillingly. The fifth, what the state of the soul is before it comes to the body,
and what it is after its departure. Averroes, a Spaniard by birth, an Arab by
language, devoted to Aristotle's doctrine, ignorant of the Greek language,
is said to have read Aristotle's books translated into a barbaric language from Greek,
rather perverted than converted: so that it is no
wonder if the mind of a very concise writer escaped him in certain recondite
matters: which the Platonist Plethon testifies happened to him,
and all the most skilled of the Greeks. And what is most
important, Aristotle's Greek words cry out against Averroes. Plethon himself
says that Aristotle, without controversy, judged human souls to be many, and eternal. He
adds that he does not wish to pervert Aristotle's words, even if Aristotle perverted the
words of Plato and other philosophers. Thus he [said].
However, Alexander of Aphrodisias seems to have perverted Aristotle's meaning
concerning the soul, where he says that Aristotle judged the soul to be mortal.
Themistius more fairly explained Aristotle, saying that by him the active
intellect is considered unique, but the receptive [intellect] multiple,
and both perpetual. What Alexander himself truly thinks, he declares in his natural
questions, where he says: "Medicine, although it is a science, yet in
its operation it appears as an art: just as the soul, although it is
immortal, yet immersed in a mortal body, seems to be
mortal." And again he says, "The creator of the world did not wish..."
li iij

--- Page 584 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...to connect our heavenly human souls to earthly bodies without some suitable medium. But a medium of this kind he names "spirit" and "vehicle" in the manner of the Platonists. But Proclus affirms that not only the Platonists, but also Aristotle, posited an immortal soul. And Themistius asserts that he posited it for the same reason [Marginal note: H] as Plato had also posited. And after he proved in the third book of *On the Soul* that both intellects, namely the agent and the receptive, are perpetual: he added that only this one, namely that which is mixed from both, is such; but the passive reason, that is, imagination, is by no means such: for which reason he concluded that we do not remember human affairs after death: because the recollection of these things usually happens through turning to phantasms and on account of affection for corporeal things. Therefore, he says, that we do not remember, Themistius wants this to have been added for the reason that it might indicate that souls live after death, and that there are many souls: but that it is nothing to wonder at if they do not remember corporeal things; because if he had thought souls perish, there would have been no reason to assign why they remember so little. But let us return to Averroes.

***Narration of Averroes' opinion.***

[Marginal note: I] **A**verroes, when he often read in Aristotle that the intellect undoubtedly has nothing of corporeal and mortal nature mixed with it, understood it thus, so that from it he concluded three things. First, that the intellect is not a body, that is, it is not composed of matter and form. Second, that it is not some quality divisible with the body, or in any way dependent on the body. Third, that it is not such a form as to be able to perfect, vivify, and govern the body, and thus to adhere to the body, so that from matter and the substance of the intellect one composite is made, whose being is one. We grant the first and second to Averroes; the third, if we follow the ancient Peripatetics, we concede in no way. He denies that the substance of the intellect can be the perfecting form of the body and the vivifying act. [Marginal note: K] His first argumentation is of this kind: If the intellect were such an act of the body, from it and the body one composite would be born, and the being of the composite would be one. But one cannot be made from its conjunction with the body without it itself becoming a participant of the body.

The mind does not admit this participation, which reason shows to be separate from bodies.

Second argument. If the mind were the form of the body, it would receive everything in the same way as corporeal matter receives. For that which is the form of a body receives nothing without its matter. But whatever matter receives, it receives in a divisible manner: whence the forms of things divided in it become temporal and particular. The intellect would also grasp such things: therefore, it would never comprehend any universal nature through its forms.

Third argument. Matter does not recognize the forms it possesses. Thus, if the mind, joined to matter through its companionship, were to receive in the same way as matter, it would recognize absolutely nothing.

Fourth argument. It is impossible for there to be infinite power in a body in any way. But the power of the mind is in a certain way infinite. From this he wants to conclude that the mind has no commerce with matter.

But since there are many species of mind in nature, he wants one certain species of it to be the human mind: namely, that which contemplates the order of things in us: inasmuch as in all humans the mode of understanding is the same according to species, and the soul is the same in species: through which life is one according to species in all humans, and the figure is the same. But since the human mind is one in species, it must also be one in number, that is, unique and singular: not divided among individuals. For a form that is one in species in itself is not cut into many, except by the addition of matter. But how will the human mind, existing as one in itself, be divided into many, since it is not a participant of any matter?

Furthermore, if there were one intellect in me and another in you, it would be necessary for that species which is the likeness of the thing to be understood to be one in number in me, and another in you, but the same in species. For since the species of things to be understood are in the mind as if in a subject, it is necessary for there to be other and distinct species in other minds. Distinct, I say, in number, just as minds are distinct in number. But species or forms which are many in number, (though) one in species, are particular forms, which cannot contribute to understanding: because that which is truly to be understood must be universal.

Furthermore, when one teaches another, the teacher seems to transfuse his knowledge into the disciple. Therefore, either he transmits to the disciple exactly the same knowledge that he himself had, or another in number, but the same in species. If he transmits the same in species, but another in number, he will generate knowledge in the same way

Ii iiij

--- Page 586 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

by which nature is accustomed to generate its work. Namely, that which acts through nature generates its form in another, very much agreeing in species, but differing in number. This, however, pertains to those things which agree with each other in matter. But the mind, both of the teacher and of the learner, is above matter: and knowledge itself is not an effective quality like heat and similar things. It remains therefore that he must communicate to the disciple exactly the same knowledge in number that he himself possesses by teaching: which can never happen unless there is a single intellect in both: lest the same quality of knowledge pass from one subject to another: nor that the teacher, by teaching, be forced to lose knowledge. Add, that in our minds, if they were diverse in number and congruent in species, the notions of known things would agree in species, but differ in number. But those things which, besides their diversity, agree in some species: they certainly agree in some common notion. Both my intellect and yours will see such a common notion: to which it will collect those diverse notions. Thus, both of us will conceive a notion of this kind, I one, you another: differing also in number: but congruent in species. Therefore, we will again similarly reduce it to another common one. And [Marginal note: A] so on to infinity. But it is absurd to introduce an infinite regress in ordered things. In the species of things, however, order is necessary. By these reasons Averroes concludes that the human mind, because it is without matter, is and has always been, and will be, unique: and that this is the lowest of all minds. And just as he attributes individual minds to each of the superior orbs, so to this inferior orb he attributes one mind: which should be called not properly the mind of this man, or of that man, but the mind of the human species: so that for the unique species there is a unique intellect, in this inferior orb (as some interpret him) whole everywhere. For he believes that this man whom we see consists of this body, and a sensitive soul, as he himself calls it: but by no means an intellective one. But this sensitive soul is the most perfect of all such souls, differing in species from those in brutes. There are as many souls as there are human bodies, arising and perishing with the bodies. He calls the supreme power of this soul the cogitative faculty, which the Greeks call phantasy. [Marginal note: B] He adds that the souls of beasts have some estimative power, by which, through natural instinct, what is good for them or

the receptive power another substance. And that the former is by its nature lucid and formative, the latter utterly obscure and formable, that from the eternal coupling of these, one soul is constituted as a being, just as from matter and form, one composite being is made in nature. They call the former the agent [Marginal note: F] intellect; the latter the formable and receptive intellect. They believe the agent intellect, because it is an act existing per se, always understands itself per se: so that looking upon its own essence it sees itself, and per se also the supernal minds. That such intellection is its very essence. But since its essence is always conjoined to the receptive intellect, they think it follows that through this same intellectual essence, the receptive intellect always understands the agent intellect: whose intellection is as much its own as its essence. Moreover, it also understands the superior minds. They believe this intellection to be in the universal intellect or soul a single, stable, and eternal act. And that there is also in its formable part another intelligence, indeed sempiternal but varied: temporal and manifold: which it borrows from us. And because it adheres more closely to the agent intellect than to fantasy: and on account of its conjunction with temporal fantasy it obtains temporal cognition: they think that what we said a little earlier is clear: namely, that on account of its conjunction with that eternal intellect, it possesses eternal intelligence, so much clearer than the other, as it is more familiar to the agent intellect than to fantasy. But in us, they believe it individually pursues doubtful and mutable knowledge: so that while Pythagoras was alive, through the images of things shining in Pythagoras's thought, it gathered that Pythagorean knowledge: but with Pythagoras's death, and those images ceasing, the intellect lost the species and knowledge received therefrom. For those species are made and preserved by the images. Moreover, even while Pythagoras was alive, the intellect among Pythagoras omitted its act as often as Pythagoras's thought omitted its own. It received together, it forgot together: it received together. It acted similarly in Plato, and in individuals daily in the same manner. To be imbued everywhere and always in various ways through the various souls of men, and in a certain way to be nourished: to receive as many species as there are images in us, like a mirror [receives] images from bodies: to produce as many acts of understanding: and also diverse habits of discipline—

--- Page 589 ---
...of disciplines, according to the diversity of human studies. And because daily an innumerable multitude of men strives for the knowledge of all things, daily from this (intellect) they learn all things. And through those species drawn from our images, the capable intellect (can know) not only inferior things, but finally, both in all men and in the wisest men, to know itself. From this, the agent intellect, and from that, the superior minds. They believe that in this consists a wonderful connection of things. For there are forms entirely separate from matter, namely the angels themselves: among whom there are not many angels in one angelic species: but as many angels as there are, so many species of angels there are. Moreover, there are forms entirely corporeal, very many in the same species: for example, the souls of animals, and forms inferior to them. (Marginal note: A) Between these is placed this composite of man and mind: of many human souls, with one mind, as if a certain huge monster composed of many legs and one head, where both the absolute form unites with corporeal ones, and the corporeal ones with it in turn. And as is fitting: that which is absolute, remains unique in itself. That which is corporeal becomes manifold: while one mind suffices for innumerable souls. And that composite indeed, of the mind and each one of us, they call the intellectual man: but each one of us apart from the mind, the cogitative man. And they affirm that the first man (the intellectual man) indeed understands something: because a part of him, that is, the mind, understands, just as we are accustomed to call a man snub-nosed because his nose is snub-nosed: but the second man (the cogitative man) understands absolutely nothing.

Refutation of Averroes. That the mind is the form of the body, is clear first from the order of nature. Chapter 2.

Great was once the controversy among the Peripatetics concerning the mind of man: and the dispute is still before the judge. (Marginal note: B) Dicaearchus affirmed it to be a form both of the body and corporeal. Of the body, because it vivifies the human body. Corporeal, because it is drawn from the bosom of the body. Averroes, on the contrary, (affirmed it to be) neither a corporeal form nor even a form of the body. Avicenna, prince of the Arab theologians, and Alganteles, following a middle path, asserted the mind to be indeed a form of the body, but not corporeal: (Marginal note: C) so that between forms which are of the body and corporeal, and forms which are neither corporeal nor of the body, as if greatly differing, there are certain middle forms, partly agreeing with the former, partly with the latter in some way. Rightly between forms entirely divine, which are so separated from matter that they cannot be joined: and forms entirely natural, which are so joined

--- Page 590 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY
are, that they cannot be separated, intermediate forms are interposed, partly indeed
natural, and partly also divine: they are so separated that they can be joined:
they are so joined that they can be separated. Which indeed is shown by their powers
and actions, which are distinguished by such a certain difference of both conjunction and sepa-
ration among themselves. Finally, not without reason, between
sense, which is both in the form of the body and needs an instrument,
and angelic intellect, which is free on both sides: there is
human intellect, which is indeed a form of the body, but needs no bodily
instrument. This opinion is indeed more probable by the common
judgment of men, and most consonant with the books of Plato, Aristo-
tle, Theophrastus, and Thimistius. We have already sufficiently

and Aristotle. Indeed, from the foundations which we have laid elsewhere,
we will show it to be probable that among the forms which are only bound to the body for vivifying it,
D there is an intermediate form which both vivifies the body and understands: so that the
image of the divine countenance may not everywhere succumb to matter, but may
triumph somewhere. Now, forms in bodies are nothing other than
images of divine ideas: just as figures which are impressed
in wax are images of a golden seal. If in all waxes
a confused impression is made, you would call him who impressed it
so inept, inert. Thus the divine mind, which in moving matter is
eager for its own likeness, will perhaps seem inert if it is never
made master of its desire. But this will never happen, unless forms
of this kind appear in bodies, which almost rule their
bodies as God rules the world, and thus are reflected in themselves and in God
through intelligence, just as God turns himself into God.
Indeed, the divine mind, by agitating matter through the motion of the heavens,
E is said to generate something, nay, all things, or to produce them:
although it does not produce every form or permutation,
or draw it out from matter itself. But since
the very first term from which this universal generation or production
takes its beginning is the divine mind itself, and also the ultimate

must exist. But the ultimate term of generation
is in that which is begotten: and that is its form. Therefore,
it is necessary that there be some divine mind which is the form of matter. For

--- Page 591 ---
If generation made by fire ends in the form of fire, and that made by man in the figure of man: why should not generation or production, which is arranged by the divine mind, end in mind? Generation does not end except in a form, which is the proper and intimate perfection of what is generated. If art, through instruments, finally imparts to matter a form most similar to that which the mind of the artisan contains; if the nature of the human body in generation first moves the seed to the form of milk, then of blood, thirdly of flesh, finally of man; if fire first moves wood to warmth, then to heat, thirdly to ignition: what prevents the divine mind from moving the matter of the world to the forms of elements first, of mixed things secondly, of plants thirdly, of brute animals fourthly, and fifthly to its own form, that is, mind, which would be the form of the generated body, so that in the noblest offspring the parent's countenance shines forth? However, it moves matter to lower forms through change to be drawn out from matter itself; but to mind rather to be induced by a divine act. For if it were drawn out, it could not be mind. This pertains to the divine order, that since forms superior to the rational soul are neither drawn out nor induced, but lower forms are both induced and drawn out, the soul itself should be induced, not drawn out. And if the form of a mixed body is of such great value that it has the power and action of the elements; again, the form of plants is so powerful that it does whatever lower forms do; and likewise the form of brute animals: who would deny that the mind has the power and action of lower forms, so that its very essence, while it understands, is also perceived through the body, and nourishes the body? Indeed, since a superior nature both includes and surpasses the entire power of an inferior nature, and is capable of performing the same work that is done by the inferior, provided the same instruments are supplied to it: it is necessary that that mind which thrives within us can accomplish the work of nourishing and sensing no less than a thinking soul. For if the spirit of our constitution is a sufficient instrument for the mind for the service of intelligence, as the Averroists believe: much more will it minister to the substance of the mind for sensation and nourishment. And because nature does not abound in superfluities, there is in us only one principal soul and form, just as in other bodies, since superior forms contain inferior ones. ...the rational soul not only enters the depths of the body by nourishing, but also transcends the sublime parts of the body by understanding. Rightly so, because what is more excellent ought to depend less on what is inferior than vice versa. Just as, therefore, the lowest souls are, as it were, contained by bodies, and the middle ones are in a certain way contained and contain, so the sublime ones entirely contain bodies. They do not entirely contain a body unless they both penetrate it internally and encompass it externally. And just as by encompassing the surface of the body, the soul receives intellectual life from above, so by penetrating the inner parts of the body, it bestows animal life upon the lowest part. While it encompasses, insofar as it is from God, it obtains an active intellect; insofar as it resides in itself, it possesses a receptive intellect. While it penetrates: insofar as it insinuates itself into spirits, it feels and moves; insofar as it immerses itself in humors, it nourishes and sustains.

G But let us return to the universal order of things. We can say that God is a form which neither inheres, nor forms, nor is formed; but the irrational soul, on the contrary, is formed, forms, inheres. But an angel is indeed formed by God, yet neither inheres in matter nor forms matter. Rightly, therefore, between the angel and the irrational soul, we will place the rational soul, endowed with such a nature that it does not inhere in matter, yet it is formed and it forms.

H That Platonic distinction in Avicenna's metaphysics seems very commendable, namely, that in the intelligible world one must proceed from the highest intelligible to many intellects, as from a former to powers thence formable: and first from that absolute to absolutes, which in no way deviate thence; then to intellects which incline a little towards sensibles, that is, to be governed only externally; so that to them also such a function seems to happen, as it were, externally. Thirdly, to intellects which, as far as is possible in intellectual nature, now naturally incline towards sensibles, that is, to be governed internally by life and motion. For not otherwise is the sensible world perfectly connected with the intelligible, and the lower things are most beautifully and excellently arranged according to the exemplar of the higher. But let us return again to divine matters. Indeed, no one denies that God exists;
but the very being of God is not determined by a certain kind of being,
through which it might become such or such a being, lest God be composed
of the common nature of being and some added difference, that is, a property
of being. Therefore, being itself is absolute, circumscribed by no limits,
which exists as utterly infinite, the immense root, containing
and procreating all those things which have such or such a being. For from a simple
source, all composition flows. Therefore, angels have being;
but each of them has such or such a being, that is, with this or that
property in different species of angels. Therefore,
the being of an angel is not infinite, like divine being. For it does not
contain the entire fullness of all being, nor does all being exist [in it];
but it is enclosed in a certain species of things,
through which it is determined to a unique mode of being. For it is fitting
that divine being, which precedes ideas (that is, species),
and through species distributes being to things flowing from itself, should impart
this very being in species, and therefore diverse modes of being to diverse species.
Thus, angelic being is limited within the angelic species.
But the angelic species, which we also call essence, which is the foundation
of such being, is in a certain way infinite: not indeed like God,
but because it remains with itself, and preserves the entire integrity of its species;
nor does it receive anything into itself beyond the species and the properties of the species,
since it approaches no inferior nature by whose contagion it might be infected.
But if this angelic essence did not differ from its being,
then its being would also be called infinite, since it would subsist
in itself and through itself; but to be infinite on all sides,
and to exist through itself, is proper to God alone. Likewise, if its being
did not differ from its essence, since being is act: certainly, the angel would be
pure act. But since participation occurs only through potency,

which can only be fitting for God alone. Thus God is altogether infinite:
because He alone exists as being, and as whole and complete
being. An angel is finite according to being; infinite according to essence;

G  God the Father, as it pleases Timaeus of Locri, broods over Mother Matter, about to generate forms as offspring. There is in the Father an effective fecundity of all forms: there is in the Mother a receptive fecundity of forms, especially of corporeal ones. There is in the Father an effective act of forms: there is in the Mother a receptive potentiality of forms. Offspring similar to the Mother are born, namely many forms, which emerge from the depths of matter, and finally are immersed into the same, just as the shape of a golden vessel from gold, and into gold. Again, it is necessary that certain offspring very similar to the Father be born, if only the Father prevails somewhat more than the Mother in this union. Forms of this kind will be those leaping forth from the Father's act onto the face of matter, and from there leaping back into the Father's act: just as splendor from the sun into gold and back into the sun. Those forms, indeed, more similar to the Mother, first lie hidden in a certain way within the bowels of matter, just as the shape of a vessel in gold. They also lie hidden in the virtues of mundane souls and bodies, which are the instruments of the divine artisan. God brings them forth from the bosom of matter through the movements of the world, and according to the capacity of matter, produces them into being. But whose is this kind of being, properly speaking? Of that composite body which is made from this generation. Why? Because the instrument through which they are generated by God is composite. If therefore the proximate cause is composite, and the effect usually comes forth most similar to the proximate cause: it follows that what is properly begotten is that which is composite. But to that which is begotten, being properly belongs. Therefore, that being is proper to the composite. For it does not come from the form or matter, but from the composite. In addition, such forms adhere to matter in a certain way according to potentiality first, before they attain being. And in the bosom of matter they are produced into being at the very moment when the being of the composite is completed. But since by adhering to matter itself according to their virtue, they become,

--- Page 599 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XV. 259

and begin to be: therefore, by adhering according to the act to the same matter, they retain being: and they exist as long as they adhere. Therefore, they do not exist by their own being, after they both come into being and exist, and remain by adhering: but by the being of that composite of which they themselves are parts, or which is the terminus of generation. And deservedly, since they do not have their own being, nor do they possess any power or operation of their own, such are the forms which seem more similar to the mother than to the father. But those which are more similar to the father, such as rational souls, are brought forth from the pure act of God: therefore, they are immediately brought to the act of being. For this reason, they have being, as it were, in themselves first, afterwards they are joined to matter. They have being before they adhere to a body: and before the body, by the very order of nature, they retain being: and after the body, they have their own being in themselves. They have some distinct power in themselves, not common to the body. They impart their being to the body in some part: they produce some operations in the body, and through the body.

How the mind approaches the body. Chapter 3.

B But in what way do they impart their being to the body? A Do they mix with it? Not at all. For that which is mixed perishes and is confounded. Do they touch the body? By no means. For touch is proper to two bodies. Are they enclosed in it? B Neither that. For nothing is enclosed in a place except a body. What then do these forms do to the body when they communicate their being to it? They penetrate it everywhere with their essence: they dedicate the power of their essence to it. But since being is derived from essence, and operation flows from power: by joining the essence, they impart being: by dedicating the power, they communicate operations: so that from the coming together of soul and body, one animal being emerges, one operation. This being is indeed the soul's own by essence: it becomes the body's by participation. The soul does not immerse its own being into the body, but elevates the body to itself. Nor does the body grasp the whole amplitude of that essence, but it reaches something according to its own nature: nor does it sustain it, but is sustained. But in what way a non-extended form fills the mass of a C body, anyone will clearly understand who considers that even an extended form mostly relates to the body in such a way that

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Let any part of it relate equally to any part of matter, and vice versa. Therefore, we can conceive of any part of this form being in individual portions of matter, and forming them in such a way that the whole is present at any point. But let us take away extension from this form, and meanwhile leave it the function of forming the body. For we can. For to form is both different and more excellent than to be extended. Therefore, if matter is indeed extended, but does not form, some form of matter can form and not be extended. Thus we shall see an individual and whole form simultaneously forming the whole of matter, and equally any part of it. And if that Pythagorean saying is true, [Marginal note: D] namely that a point by its motion makes a line, and a line makes a surface, and finally a surface by similar motion makes a solid, we will easily be able to conceive that the same point by its motion diffuses itself, whole and individual, through length and breadth and depth. Hence it happens that wherever you divide or touch, you find a point. If this is indeed an accident, it will necessarily be sustained by mass. But if it is a substance, like the soul subsisting in itself, it will indeed be present to the mass, and separated from the mass, it will perpetually remain in itself.

**How the mind is present to the body. Chapter 4.**

[Marginal note: E] This soul, so excellent, is it joined to unformed matter without an intermediary? A more perfect form always contains less perfect forms within itself, just as a quadrangle comprehends a triangle. If a rational soul has the most excellent power of understanding of all, it also has the power of sensing, nourishing, and governing. Therefore, within the power of the rational soul is enclosed the sensitive and nutritive soul, and also the form of lifeless mixtures. The rational soul approaches matter, endowed with all these forms; and through its form or power, which acts as a substitute for lifeless mixed bodies, it adheres as closely as possible to unformed matter, and in it establishes the complex composition of the four elements, while it binds the parts of matter into one and tempers the elements. Through its rational form, it commands the rest. And so, through its lowest power, it is the form of matter; through its second, it is the form of a mixed body; through its third, of a plant; through its fourth, it is the form of an animal; indeed, the form of forms. From this it follows that the rational soul forms bodies more than other forms, because it forms through more virtues and forms more purely, because it touches unformed matter closely with its 'foot,' but with its 'head' it looks afar.

Just as fire, from four degrees of its proper heat, infuses the first into cold wood, the second into wood already warm, the third into wood already hot through the two (previous degrees), and adds the fourth in addition to those three degrees, through which it shines from above. So the essence of the rational soul, filled with certain four degrees—mixed, vital, sensual, intellective—applies the first to matter; applies the second to the first; adds the third to the second; adds the fourth to the third, where it seems to form matter both according to its whole essence and according to all its degrees; although according to its whole essence it forms in the same way, but according to all the degrees, in one way and another.

The first, indeed, is the form of matter; the second is the form of a mixed body; the third is the vital form; the fourth is the form of forms of all corporeal things. Through the three degrees, the particular soul emerges; through the fourth, it remains absolute and capable of absolute forms. What wonder if, in this most excellent degree of it, some power and operation appears very similar to divine ones, to which this degree becomes closest because it is most removed from matter; since in some forms of mixed bodies, because of some temperament suitable to celestial bodies, some power and action results which is indeed alien from the elements from which the subject of that form is composed, but consonant with celestial bodies, to which it becomes similar by temperament?

Nor should it seem strange that the soul, although it is the form of the body, nevertheless has some power not common to the body; because angels are drawn from matter neither according to their essence nor according to their preparation for essence; but irrational souls are drawn through both. Therefore, since rational souls are in the middle, their condition ought to be in the middle.

How the mind is in the body.
Chapter 5.

BUT in what way is the rational soul joined to the
body? Not as a solid body to a solid one. For these
solid bodies, which are joined by touch alone, are not entirely
together: nor do they act together: as the soul and body are entirely
together, and operate together. Therefore, it seems most
absurd of all to compare the soul, the most efficacious origin
of vital motion, to dense and crude bodies: which, the more
they are said to possess corporeal properties, the less
they seem to possess natural action and vital motion.
Indeed, if they are divided, they remain scattered: nor do they, like
purer things usually do, quickly return to their unity. On the
contrary, those things which have the least corporeal density, while
they seem to be struck by more solid things, most easily avoid the blow: while
they seem to be penetrated, they penetrate most effectively: while they seem to be divided, they return to their
unity so quickly that they seem not to have departed from it at all.
Therefore, as we were saying, the soul is not joined as a solid
body to a solid one. Again, not as water to wine. For these
soft bodies, by mutual mixture, lose their former power,
and cease to be what they were. Since the soul is incorporeal, and
does not have matter in common with this body: it cannot
be mixed and confounded with the quality of this body.

--- Page 604 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Or perhaps like the heat of fire to water? Rather, in this way. For heat
is not a body: therefore it is more similar to the soul. But even
that does not satisfy us. For a part of the heat is in a part of the water, not
the whole in the whole. Perhaps like a voice to the air. For perhaps a single
and same voice is whole in any part of a hall, since it is heard
whole in any part. It moves the ears: it announces something to the intellect.
Just as the soul is whole in any particle of the body.
It rules the body and at the same time understands. But the voice has I know not what
fragility, and is subject to passion. It is born from the breaking of air:
and is pushed back by a light breeze. But in the meantime, I have something more
similar: namely, the image of color coming to the eyes in the air.
This is spiritual. It travels in an instant. It reaches far.
It appears whole everywhere. It does not suffer the impact of wind. It
colors the air. It forms vision. That is indeed very similar:
but it differs in this, that it neither rules nor governs the air, as
the soul does the body. But behold, a governor governs some ship,
and is in the ship. Does the soul also relate to the body in this way?
No: because the governor does not fill the ship: is not present to the whole:
does not move it solely by himself, but by means of the rudder. But now I
find the soul in this rudder: because when the sailor rules the ship
through it, the art of governing is not only in the sailor, but also
passes into the rudder. It becomes whole in the whole rudder: and rules
it. This itself is the soul of the rudder. But this (soul of the rudder)
attributes nothing of its own nature to the substance of the rudder: but
only agitates it, itself indeed being agitated externally: whereas the soul
truly attributes something to the body, and moves by its own nature.
Please, philosopher, lift your eyes to the sky: you seek the celestial soul
on earth or sea. Look up at the light of the sun. This is one and
indivisible, so to speak: whole in any part of the air. It illuminates
and heats the air: but it itself takes nothing from the air: nor does it
suffer force anywhere: nor is it stained by any dirt. The air fluctuates
with the winds, the light remains: as Plotinus wishes. It is from the sun:
in a moment it passes into the air. It is not separated from the sun again:
it is also reflected back into the sun. Without it, the air is dead,
being cold and dark, deprived of any form. Light has two qualities:
brightness and heat. It indeed exercises brightness in the air, but does not
attribute it to the air: it attributes heat. Hence, when the sun sets, it
is not extinguished, as Plotinus thinks: but the whole light suddenly
recedes together with the sun: the remnants of heat remain until late night re-

...are left: as if the air had become a participant of heat, not of splendor. But let it be granted, if you please: let it not bestow splendor. Indeed, what else is the being of that light than to shine? Without it, the air does not shine: without the air, it (the light) shines. If indeed Plotinus's opinion is true, that light in no way depends on anything transparent, but continually depends on the sun alone: and that it (light) always accompanies the sun, as it were, being a certain perpetual act of the sun itself. But let us proceed to the rest. Light approaches the air: there the light shines, just as before in itself. The air shines, which did not shine by itself before; that light shines, and it is through this light that the air shines. Is the shining of the light different from the shining of the air? By no means: otherwise, the air would remain luminous when the light departs. Therefore, there is one shining, by which both shine: but to the light it belongs by essence: to the air it belongs by participation. [F] Therefore, to be one in a certain way is common to both: nor is light *in* the air, although it is commonly said so: but the air is *in* the light, if indeed that which is narrower and subject to passion is contained by that which is ampler and impassible. Similarly, the soul of man is sent forth by God into matter: it passes into it suddenly, and does not depart from God, but acts as both simultaneously: It governs the body: and also touches the very truth of all things (which is God himself) in a certain wonderful way (as Plotinus argues) through the intellect. Again, just as light is reflected back into the sun, so the soul itself is reflected back into God through the will: inasmuch as it always desires the goodness of all things, which is God himself. It fills the body without offense, as light fills the air: and similarly, the whole (soul) is present to the whole (body): when the body suffers, it (the soul) does not suffer: but it perceives and judges the passions. It does not flow away when the body decays: but remains firm. It has two principal powers: the judicial: and the vital. It does not hand over judgment to the body, but performs it itself. It lends or bestows life upon the body, inasmuch as it communicates to it a certain imaginary power of its own life. Whence the soul alone judges, not the body. However, both the body and the soul live. Therefore, when the soul departs, sensation immediately ceases: but traces of life seem to remain for a time: namely, heat and motion. For the soul to be, is to live: since the essence of the soul is life: through which the body formally lives. Also, for a living being to be, is nothing other than to live. Nevertheless, the living of the soul itself, united to the body, is not different from the living of the composite itself: [G] indeed, just as through one and the same life, that is, the essence of the soul, both live; but the soul by its own (life), the body by an alien (life):

...so that most people judge that it lives through one alone: both, however, are and are called living things: the soul through its own [life], the body through another's. And as we touched upon above, the soul is not in the body, although it appears so to those who indeed see the body, but not seeing the soul, suppose the soul to lie hidden in the body as in a vessel. But those who observe the soul penetrating the body inwardly, extending beyond it outwardly, embracing and sustaining it, and moving this tiny dust on all sides, would undoubtedly confess that the body is in the soul. Who would doubt that it is larger than the body: since in one part of itself it is somehow equal to it, namely in its vital power, but in another part it exceeds it, namely in its judicial faculty? Therefore the body, as something narrower and perishable, is in the soul, which is entirely larger and stable, just as that which is contained is in that which contains it.

B Although therefore the whole soul is present to the body, yet the body is not present to the whole soul, but only to its lowest part, that is, the vital [part]. Which seems to be confirmed from this: because since the soul is much greater than the body in power, and from power comes motion and amplification, it is necessary for the soul not only to be present to the whole body, but also, according to its presence (as Iamblichus holds), to exceed the body. And because it is indivisible: wherever it is, it is there whole. But the body, just as it is not equal to the whole power of the soul, so it is not equal to the whole of its presence. Plato understood this in the Timaeus when he said that the creator of the world placed the body in the soul. Again in the tenth book of the Republic where he says that the body of the world revolved between the knees of necessity, that is, to be ruled and moved by the lowest part of the celestial soul. In the Phaedrus he also affirmed that souls raise their head above the heavens. But although the soul thus exceeds the body, it should not seem impossible to anyone that it draws matter to itself to such an extent as to make a single composite.

But any lowest forms do this: what prevents even sublime forms from doing it, provided they naturally desire it? But if angelic forms do not do this at all, it arises from the fact that they have no inclination whatsoever to complete any species of animal by their conjunction. Therefore, his difference is taken from universal reason, and this is in the mind. The mind, therefore, is that form by which each of us is placed in the human species. But if it were separated in being from man, from it and this man, one species would not be formed; and man would more properly be called "fleshly" because of his inner flesh, [Marginal note: F] than "rational" because of his external reason. Nor let Averroes say that man is something aggregated from a cogitative animal and a mind, and that the whole (man) is called rational because of one of its parts: just as a body is called snub-nosed because the nose is snub-nosed. For first, the nose is continuous with the body; but the mind is by no means continuous with cogitation. Secondly, the mind is a certain species of this kind, separate from the cogitative animal; and this animal is a species by itself, separate from the mind. But the appellation of a difference does not pass from one species to a separate species. And just as, according to Averroes, the mind is not called cogitative and sensual because of the cogitative soul to which it is near: so neither will the cogitative soul be called rational or intellectual because of the mind. Nor again will the appellation of a difference pass into some third thing that is made from them. For one difference requires one species: and vice versa. But those (the cogitative animal and the mind) do not constitute one species: because they do not come together into one essence nor into one being. But it is altogether ridiculous for man to receive the difference by which he is man, from a single and separate mind. For thus, individual persons will be one man, (but) many animals: and the nature of the species will remain universal, the nature of the genus having already become particular. Nor is it less ridiculous to place the human species in such a heap: because just as it will not be simply one, so it will not be (if I may so speak) simply a being: nor any substantial species of things, but a contingent heap, especially because from two things which exist actually by themselves according to a perfect species, there is not made one true thing per se, but a false one: and that indeed by another binding it. For that which can exist entirely by itself does not cast itself into the bosom of another: nor does it naturally admit within itself another which is sufficient unto itself. Indeed, when each thing by its own acts mutually...

**Second Reason, because man understands. Chapter 7.**

[Marginal note: A] [Marginal note: ri] Aristotle holds that man is an animal composed of body and mind. --- Page 610 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Everyone also experiences in himself that he understands something: and he does this only through the intellect. How could we also investigate the nature of the intellect in the present situation unless we ourselves understood? And since we use the intellect more by our own will than imagination, which is often compelled from elsewhere, the intellect is more familiar and natural to us than imagination.

If the Averroists are asked what that is which properly understands, when Aristotle and Averroes say that man properly understands, they will answer that it is neither the mind—for among them the mind is not man—nor the cogitative animal, because it does not have the faculty of understanding; but a certain collection of mind and such an animal: and the action of the mind, which is intelligence, is attributed to this whole because the action of a part is often ascribed to the whole.

That is indeed foolish. Firstly, because such a collection is not in any one species, or one genus: nor does it have that union by which it might concur in a single operation such as intelligence. Secondly, because the action of a part is then ascribed to the whole when that part is either continuous with another into one essence, just as we say that man sees, because the eye sees. Or into one being, as when we say that fire heats through the heating which proceeds from heat and form: which is such a part of fire that by forming the other part of the fire (the matter) it leads it to one being. Or into one effect of agitation: as when we say that the soul vibrates the sword together with the arm: because such a motion passes from the soul into the sword through the arm.

But the mind among them is neither continuous with the animal into one essence, nor into one being, as is evident: nor even into one effect of agitation: because intelligence never leaves the mind so that it can be communicated to another besides the mind: nor is it completed by any instrument. From which they are forced to admit, against their leader Aristotle, that the mind is properly said to understand, but man cannot be said to understand, except very improperly and absurdly.

Nor should they bring up that usual example of the heavens, that the heavens are sometimes said to move themselves, because one part of them moves another: and thus man understands: because a part of him understands. The example does not agree. For motion from the mind of the heavens passes into the heavens: but intelligence neither passes from the human mind into the animal, nor vice versa: But they assert

But since a syllogism ought not to be made from equivocal terms, it follows that that word 'act' should signify the same thing everywhere, that is, the natural act of a body: which he himself immediately reveals, when he adds the division of substance into matter, its form, and that which is composed of these. And he says that every soul is that form which is the other part of the composite. Again: where there is the power of understanding, there are also the powers of sensing and nourishing. And just as a triangle is in a quadrangle: so is the vegetative soul in the sensitive soul. And this (the sensitive soul) in the intellective soul. And although he says the power of understanding is separated, that is, distinguished, and is separable from others as the perpetual from the perishable: nevertheless, he says furthermore that the intellect is distinguished from others: either by subject, as the ancients thought, who seemed to attribute reason to the head, anger to the chest, and lust to the liver: or rather to be distinguished by a certain mode, just as in the same surface the concave from the convex.

Furthermore, he praises those above others who thought that the soul of man is indeed incorporeal: but nevertheless something of the body, that is, such an act in such a subject. Hence in the third book On the Soul he says: Since the intellect is not separated from the body, it will have to be investigated elsewhere whether it can understand forms separated from the body. Most clearly, however, he reveals this in the second book of his natural philosophy: where he holds that the soul of man is a natural form, and separated from matter, and conjoined. He says it is conjoined indeed, because it is the completion of human generation: but I think he says it is separated on account of intelligence. These things, however, can be rightly understood neither concerning the cogitative soul, nor concerning a single mind. Also in the twelfth book On Divine Matters, where he denies that forms precede their matters, but rather follow after matter: he grants that form alone which is the intellective soul: clearly declaring that our soul is the form of the body: to begin with the body: and yet not to cease. Nor can those words be understood concerning the Averroistic mind: which would be numbered among moving causes rather than formal ones: and precedes the human body: nor is it joined to our body from its very generation: which is against that order which Aristotle uses in the second book On Animals, where from the very origin he applies the intellect to us, although descending from outside. Third reason, because man moves himself freely.
Chapter 8.

All Platonists and Peripatetics agree that man moves himself, and that human actions are so arranged that man himself, who acts, is the master of his own operations. And to act rationally by reasoning in a certain way before executing. First to take a universal rule, then to subjoin a particular opinion, thirdly to infer a conclusion, in this manner: Every good is to be chosen, that food is good. Therefore, that food is to be chosen. The first part of this kind of argumentation belongs solely to the mind: the second can also belong to imagination, and similarly the third. And just as in the mind alone there is a universal rule for judging good: so in it alone is the universal will for desiring good: In imagination there can only be a particular opinion, and a particular appetite. When they affirm that man moves himself freely, they do not take only the mind, in which to move is rather towards works than to be moved: Nor only the animal, in which to be moved and to be compelled to work is rather than to lead freely: but they take both together.

However, let us now set aside nourishment and sense: let us indeed take up phantasy and mind. I certainly experience this in myself, that when phantasy is too intent, human intelligence or reason is weakened, and vice versa: so much so that the mind or reason is largely vacant when phantasy commands too much, even if it is a sound and sober phantasy: and conversely: just as sense, even if it is sound, when it is too intently occupied with external things, distracts phantasy: and conversely: Again, when in dreamers, drunkards, angry people, lovers, madmen, and frenzied people, phantasy rolls its images within itself with the whole attention of the soul: is not all judgment of the human mind or reason put to sleep? But when in contemplatives, reason fixes its ardent gaze on divine things to be considered: does not phantasy fall silent most of all: and if anything interrupts, is it not immediately commanded by reason to be silent, nor is it permitted to be carried away too much by affections, or to wander more widely through customary digressions? Who then will deny that mind and phantasy are powers of the same soul, since they mutually debilitate each other by their intention?
Moreover, let us grant to the Averroists that there is as great a vicissitude of motion between mind and phantasy as there is between common sense and particular sense: and just as the image of a thing shining in the eye thence reflects into common sense, and similarly the act of seeing from the eye redounds into common sense: so from phantasy both images and acts continuously shine back into the mind. Although it seems to me that there is even a greater vicissitude between mind and phantasy than between interior sense and exterior sense: because from the mind into phantasy both images and acts are reverberated: but how this happens from the interior and common sense into the eye, I do not clearly see: nor do they themselves declare it. But if they assert that this sometimes happens in dreamers: so be it. I shall find again another thing in which the vicissitude of mind and phantasy surpasses the vicissitude of interior and exterior sense. Indeed, between mind and phantasy there is a mutual interchange not only of species and acts, but also of affections and habits: which never occurs between these (the interior and exterior senses). are of the soul: why should not mind and imagination also be in the same soul? By what means does the finite power of imagination often accompany the in some way infinite power of the mind in action, so that as far as the mind speculates, so far does the imagination itself think: unless the same substance makes both equal?
