Fifth reason: because the separated mind does not need imagination.
Chapter 10.

B **M**ind's nature, according to Averroes, does not have a common being with the body: it does not communicate its proper being to it. It does not have its origin from it, neither according to its essence, nor according to its preparation for existence. It does not form any species with it: nor is it numbered according to the number of bodies. Therefore, just as it has a mode of being entirely separate from this animal, so it will have a mode of cognition completely segregated from the body. Therefore, there is no reason that compels it to draw species from the images of imagination: and to need a temporal and mobile discourse for the knowledge of things, especially eternal ones. Indeed, it will be very similar to the supernal minds: and much closer to them.

--- Page 621 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XV. 270

closer than to the qualities of bodies. Therefore, it will understand those [minds] and their manner more than these [qualities]. Which is against Averroes' leader, Aristotle, who writes that this mind understands nothing without images. But images are of bodies, not of minds. But since the first and most familiar objects of human intellect are the common reasons and natures of natural things, indeed conjoined with bodies, but separable from bodies: it is permitted for us, from a certain proportion of power to object, to argue that the intellect of man is such that it is both conjoined [with the body] and can be separated from the body: and because it is conjoined, therefore it almost always turns itself to images. Indeed, because it is conjoined, therefore it turns itself to conjoined things. And because it is conjoined in a separable manner, therefore it turns itself in a separable manner, that is, by abstracting and separating. But minds which are not only separable, but also separated, contemplate both in a separable manner and as separated things equally. Therefore, to speak summarily, nothing seems to me to demonstrate the middle nature of the human mind more than its natural inclination to both. For whether through the intellect it begins from bodies, it soon transfers itself thence to incorporeal things: or if it sometimes begins from incorporeal things, it conversely slides to the images of bodies. Or whether through the will it desires eternal things, in the meantime it is deflected thence by the affection for temporal things: or if, on the contrary, it desires temporal things, it is conversely often restrained thence by reverence for eternal things. But let us now return to the Averroistic question. The Averroists will respond that this intellect indeed understands the higher minds without the images of fantasy: [C] but by no means the natures of bodies. To this we will infer: that in those minds there are incorporeal species of bodies, through which they judge concerning bodies. Therefore, if this intellect understands them, it receives the knowledge of bodies from them. There is therefore no need for it to receive it from bodies. Then they will assert that this intellect is the lowest, subsisting in itself, and adhering to us. Insofar as it subsists in itself, it is compared to higher minds as a transparent and vitreous body to light: and it perceives them. Insofar as it adheres to us, it draws species from images: and understands corporeal things. To this we will first indeed say that it is superfluous that an intellect which always inspects bodies in the causes of bodies, should also always see the same things in images: and that one who has in eternity, should daily borrow from time.

D Then not because it adheres to us does it receive species from images, but because it takes them from here, it adheres. For as Averroes thinks, the intellect is joined to us only because it is formed by species received from us. Therefore, the intellect must be considered first as if prepared by a certain power to take such species, before it adheres to us. Therefore, it is not by this, that it adheres to us, that it is prepared for such species; unless perhaps one thinks that it adheres to us as far as the proximity of nature is concerned, that is, that the nature of that intellect is in some degree close to our soul. If this is so, nothing more will follow than that such a mind moves and forms our soul. For a more worthy degree, when it approaches an inferior, does not receive from it, but gives. The sphere of the moon moves the sphere of fire; it is not moved by it. Why then does this mind borrow knowledge from the soul rather than lend it? Indeed, if it is superior, and so much more excellent as Averroes thinks, it ought indeed to know by itself alone, and the soul through it; especially since this mind is joined to the body in the same way as the celestial mind is to the heaven, as Averroes holds. Therefore, just as that receives nothing from the heaven, so this receives nothing from the body. Nor let the Averroists object to us that just as the celestial body is full of its forms, so its mind is full of its own; but our mind always receives new forms, just as our body continuously varies its forms. This objection accomplishes nothing. For that action of the artisan takes its mode from the instruments, which is carried out through instruments, such as cutting, and similar things. But that which remains only in the mind of the artisan, such as the deliberation of arranging the work, does not receive its mode from the instruments. Therefore, it is not fitting to give a mode to the intellect from the body itself, through which the intellect is not completed. We will then ask Averroes whether the mind, while it understands in us, becomes more perfect, or more imperfect: or neither. If neither, this perpetual activity will be in vain, accomplishing nothing by its operation. Indeed, it will not even operate; for there is no motion towards an indifferent end.

*Sixth reason, because both intellects are a power in the soul.*
Chapter II.

But as for the fact that they affirm the agent intellect and the potential intellect to be two essences, from which one being of the intellectual soul is constituted: that indeed is superfluous and [Marginal note: C] absurd. Superfluous, because one essence, equipped with two powers, would suffice: so that through one it produces species, through the other it receives them: just as fantasy draws certain intentions from images, and itself receives those drawn. And the eyes of animals which see at night possess twin powers in the same essence: through one they elicit images of colors, through the other they receive them. Light itself also both makes and receives certain colors in clouds or water. But in what way is a twofold power, productive and receptive, founded in the same essence? Namely, from different principles or relations. Indeed, light, insofar as it is from the sun, makes colors: insofar as it is, as it were, in itself outside the sun, it receives them. So also the soul, insofar as it is from God in purest act, obtains the power to produce species. But insofar as it is in itself below God, it becomes, as it were, passive, and is formed by receiving species.

--- Page 626 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Hence it follows that that Averroistic fiction is superfluous and absurd: because from two essences which actually both exist, one substantial being is not constituted. [Marginal note: D] For two acts of existing are two beings, not one. That the agent intellect among them is actually a certain substance, after it performs some action, is not doubtful: nor do we fight against it. But what they add, that the receptive intellect is also another substance, and such that it is pure potentiality, just like prime matter: we do not accept. For if the receptive mind is pure potentiality, it will not be distinguished from prime matter. And wherever there is matter, there will be intelligence: so that even stones themselves understand. It is certainly true that prime matter is pure potentiality. But pure potentiality cannot exist in nature except as one, just as pure act cannot exist except as one: and vice versa. For if whatever things are said to be in potentiality are such by one common reason, and whatever things are in act similarly, it is necessary to arrive at a single source of potentialities and a single source of acts. Again, if that first and common distinction or composition in things is that which is made through potentiality and act, and from one, many are not made except through a certain order of some things to others: and from many, similarly, one is not made except through such an order in which one thing is referred to another as potentiality to act: it follows that multitude in things takes its origin from the very mixture of potentiality and act. Hence it follows that neither pure act nor pure potentiality can be multiple, since neither potentiality except through the mixture of act, nor act except through the mixture of potentiality, undergoes number. From which it is concluded that the mind cannot be pure potentiality. And if it is said that the mind is also simple potentiality no less than matter is, and nevertheless differs from it: we will inquire in what way it differs from matter. Clearly not insofar as it is potentiality: both because in this very thing they agree; and because through potentiality confusion and chaos reign: distinction is made through act. Therefore something beyond potentiality will be added to the mind, by which it differs from the potentiality of matter, and that indeed will be some act. And if this act is infused into the bosom of the mind, it will cause the mind not to be pure potentiality, since it has an act mixed in. But if it rests extrinsically, it will not first cause the mind to differ from the potentiality of matter, than
[Catchword: tum]

But if it (the act) lies externally, it will not make the mind differ from the potentiality of matter before then that potentiality is, inasmuch as by acting through its own proper act upon the mind, it might bestow some intimate act upon the mind, through which it might differ from pure potentiality insofar as it is potentiality. For such a discrepancy does not arise except through some act, insofar as it is an act, and thus again the mind will not be pure potentiality. The Averroists will imagine that the mind differs from matter for this reason: because the mind regards another act, namely the absolute and universal, while matter regards another, namely the concrete and particular. As if indeed these very regards were not some acts. Indeed, if the regard of the mind is nothing other than the mind's potentiality itself, it will not introduce a difference. But if it were something else, it will be an act. Furthermore, if mind and matter exist before they regard forms to be received, and as they are in themselves, so they regard, certainly from the fact that they are diverse among themselves, they regard diverse acts, not the other way around. Nor should it be thought that the mind regards a more perfect act than matter regards, unless from the fact that the mind is more perfect. If this is so, it departs further from nothing and approaches closer to the highest act, from which is all perfection. Therefore, it is not mere potentiality. it will indeed be subject to accidental act, but by no means to substantial act.

That substance will bestow in a stable manner; this substance will receive in a stable manner, since both are eternal. Therefore, the very same substance that has receptive power will also have efficient power; nor will there be need for the conjunction of twin substances for those two functions of the mind. [Marginal note: E]

From this also is refuted the error of Alexander, who, in order to remove all divinity from the human race by a violent exposition of Aristotle, asserted that receptive minds are indeed in us and distinct in number, but the agent mind is outside humans and unique, in which alone resides the whole divinity of the mind, which is the universal cause of intelligible species. But since in all natural things there are certain virtues that are the producers of their own motions, it is wrong for the substance of the human mind, most preeminent of all natural things, to be deprived of efficient virtue. And because operation proceeds from virtue, the universal mind does not first bestow the act of understanding upon our mind before it bestows the efficient virtue of intelligence. Furthermore, if a universal cause is utterly opposed to a particular effect, namely, both as cause to effect and as universal to particular, it is necessary to interpose a particular cause as a medium between these two. Indeed, the universal power of the sun does not produce this human, who is a particular effect, except through another human as a particular and proper cause. By the same reasoning, that universal agent mind will not produce this or that effect of species and intelligence in the receptive mind without some particular agent mind residing within us.

For just as we use the receptive mind at our discretion for understanding, as if it were a familiar form, so too, as we please, we fabricate species through the efficient mind as if through an art proper and inherent to us. Wisely did Aristotle never call the agent and receptive minds [Marginal note: F] two essences, nor did he place them above the soul.

(G) **F**ROM all things that have been brought against Averroes, we conclude two
things. One, that the soul in man is the same, which forms corporeal things,
and is formed by incorporeal things.
For by this means alone are the rays of divine things transmitted even to the lowest,
if the same thing that is illuminated by them, illuminates these.
Indeed, and by this means the lowest are reflected to the highest, if the same thing
rules the lowest, and is ruled by the highest. And we conclude a second thing,
(H) that human minds are numbered according to the number of men:
so that they are distinguished from each other either by species, as the
Magi believe; or certainly by number, as later theologians assert.
For as many bodies of men as there are, so many are there vital com-
plexions, so many life-giving souls, so many minds of souls.
For almost as complexions are distributed according to the distribution of bodies,
and lives according to these complexions: so minds, which are powers of
souls, are distributed according to the number of life-giving souls.
Not, however, does the distinction arise from the distinction of the body as from the
cause of an incorporeal substance and power, but it proceeds from the incorporeal
former itself. But those arguments of Averroes by which he denied from the
beginning of the question that the intellect is the form of the body, are of no avail against us.
For they bring about this, that it is not a corporeal form lacking its own proper being,
and dependent on the body by essence. But we want it to be not
such a form, but one subsisting in its own being, and mistress of matter.
Moreover, in order to refute some additional sophistries by which the Averroists
strenuously strive to ensnare the Platonists, it is necessary to remember that it is not
contrary to the nature of the human soul to be joined to a body, but it is natural
for this eternal soul to be always with an eternal and celestial body, and to be
with a temporal and terrestrial body for a time: just as it is natural for each
planet to be always in its sphere, but for a time under such and such a sign.
But after it has departed from the body, it is natural for it to be reconciled again: so that it—

just as it had not extended itself by rarefying itself from east to west by temporal flux.
For in a moment it had made itself present: in a moment it makes itself absent.
If the soul is entirely everywhere throughout the body, and it alone understands: it understands everywhere. In
no member, however, does it understand: because it itself is not in the members,
but rather the members are in the soul. Nevertheless, it commonly seems to
understand in the brain, because intelligence is very much accompanied by imagination,
and this (imagination) by the agitation of those spirits which
are in the brain: just as the affection of imagination is accompanied by the agitation
of the spirits of those who are in the heart or liver: indeed, the
spirits of the heart follow the affection of anger, the spirits of the
liver follow the affection of lust. If someone asks what man feels or what he understands,

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

For they will say that sensing is primarily an act of the composite, because the power of sensing in the composite itself comes from the matter and form of the mixture, and of the soul; then also an act of the soul, because sensation occurs by its virtue. And that understanding is an action of the whole composite. For although intelligence is in the soul alone, and therefore can remain in a separated soul, nevertheless, while the soul is so the form of the composite that it concurs into one common being, that whole, whose being it is, is said to operate through the form just as it is. [F] To this tends that Aristotelian saying: "The intellect is the act of no organ." And rightly so. For it is not in the body like sensation, but in the soul. Nor, as Averroes thought, is it to be considered as separated from man, but rather as separated from an organ. Nor again is it to be explained in the manner of Alexander, that indeed individual senses have each been allotted individual instruments, but that the intellect itself has the whole body as its instrument. For we see that the noblest powers use not just any instrument, but only the noblest; whence touch uses almost any, while phantasy uses a unique and distinct one. Therefore, the entire body will not satisfy the mind. Nor is it to be said that from the cooperation of all instruments, one harmony is produced, which the intellect uses as an instrument. For if the matter stands thus, the intellect will need all instruments, and will be most organic and mixed of all powers; nor will that Aristotelian saying stand any longer: "Sensation indeed is not without the body; but the intellect is separate and unmixed, using absolutely no organ." For if it used organs, it would become such and such, and would no longer be able to know all things. Nevertheless, it is not so separated that the substance of the soul in which it resides does not vivify the body. Otherwise, they would not say that man understands. For it is separated because it is not in the composite like sensation, but in the very substance of the soul, which is separable from the composite. Nor does it use an instrument in understanding: which indeed he confirmed in the book concerning animals and sleep and waking by saying, "whose are the actions, theirs also are the powers of acting." But since sensing indeed happens through an instrument, but understanding not at all, therefore the power of sensing can be of the composite, and the power of understanding proper to the soul.

**Solution to the Averroistic arguments concerning the single intellect. Chapter 13.**

--- Page 635 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XV. 277

[Large initial S]We have already refuted the arguments of Averroes and the Averroists, who thought it could be demonstrated that the substance of the mind cannot be the vital form of the body. Let us now refute those arguments by which Averroes tries to show that the mind is unique.
"From matter," he says, "comes the number of forms under the same species. But the mind lacks matter." Although this is the opinion of some Peripatetics, nevertheless many Pythagoreans and Platonists believe that the one nature of a species is diffused into many individuals not because of external matter, but because of certain inherent modes of the form itself, into which the form, when brought to actuality, becomes this or that individual. For the angelic species is present in every angel, brought to an angelic individual without the mixture of matter. But so that we may follow for now partly the Peripatetics, partly some Platonists: perhaps we will concede that the number of forms arises either from matter, or because of matter, indeed because of the composite of matter and form. For corporeal forms, just as they somehow derive their essence from matter, so too do they derive their number placed under the same species. But forms that are not corporeal indeed, but of the body, such as rational souls: because they do not have their origin from matter, nor do they have number from it. But because divine providence instituted them not only for the contemplation of divinity, but also for the governance of bodies: just as it willed there to be a certain number of various bodies, that is, composite human beings, for the adornment of its work: so it orders a certain number of souls. But to speak with Plotinus, what distinguishes the soul of Plato from the soul of Socrates? That divine concept, which first tempered the vivifying power of Plato's soul to the garment of a certain celestial body: and through this adapted it to generating and governing a certain particular complexion of an elemental body. So too for certain aspects of Socrates' soul. Thus, therefore, it distinguished the vivifying powers of souls because of matter, indeed because of the composite of matter, for the sake of worldly adornment: but it distinguished the intellectual powers of these same souls for the distinction of souls. But for what reason? Because of different contemplations of divinity. Under various ideas we can enjoy the divine mind, investigate it through various traces, va

--- Page 636 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...to proceed by various paths to this end. Indeed, infinite goodness willed to communicate itself not only to corporeal, but also to spiritual eyes, in infinite (so to speak) ways: and to show innumerable faces of itself to almost innumerable eyes. Therefore, it tempered the intellectual eyes and affections of various souls in diverse ways: so that we might proceed by diverse paths to diverse possessions of manifold divine goods. Proclus, following Plato's mind in the Timaeus, saying [Marginal note: D] that God adapted the souls of men, some to some leaders and stars, proves that the differences of souls do not arise from bodies or inclinations towards bodies: but from that essential adaptation made by God to different leaders and stars: whence also the difference of inclinations and actions arises, both for seeing eternal things and for governing temporal things. Therefore, just as Scotus and his followers argue, every nature except the first, which alone is pure act, has a certain power mixed within it, in a way formless in itself and formable from elsewhere: which relates to multiple and singular modes of existing no differently than matter relates equally to multiple forms: and therefore, just as the human species and the equine species, so also any intellectual species, both of angels and of souls, can be derived into multiple individuals. Moreover, the number of minds in the same species contributes to the complete fulfillment of the order of the universe. Indeed, that is a full order, in which superiors are ordered to inferiors, and these in turn to those, and equals are likewise ordered among themselves. And we clearly perceive such an order in corporeal things. But if incorporeal things have a fuller order, we are compelled to conceive a similar order in them too, that is, a threefold one. However, there can be no order among equals unless multiple entities are comprehended under the same species. Again, the number of very many minds in the same species conduces to their more perfect happiness. For they, contemplating themselves in a way in one another, rejoice with equal and mutual (as is naturally accustomed to happen) recognition and familiarity. Finally, the universe is far more beautiful if everywhere below species, as above species, there is multitude. Above, indeed, by general and special (categories): below, however, adorned by a certain numerous variety. Nor do they think that the number of individuals conduces only to this: that the species them-

**ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK 15, 278**

it may be preserved: because even in bodies there are far more individuals everywhere than is necessary for preserving the species. Moreover, we see nature in individual species do many things not at all for preservation, but also for the sake of ornament: [Marginal note: E] which we clearly see in colors and shapes and lines and a certain most ordered disposition. Finally, the principal end for the sake of which God wills all things to exist, is not properly that they exist, but rather that they exist well, and are in a good state. And if for this sake they exist principally, of whatever kind they are: certainly for the same sake they exist, however many there are. Therefore, God did not will there to be more minds in the same species merely so that the species itself might exist and be preserved: but rather that it might be well, and be in the best state. Such a state, moreover, consists in a certain varied ornament everywhere, and in activity blessed in various ways everywhere. If anyone, however, should prove that the multitude of human souls contributes to the preservation of the species, we will concede it thus: namely, that such a number is necessary not properly for the species of the soul itself, but for preserving the species of composite man. For God wills there to be more men perhaps for this reason, because the human species is not preserved in one. But more men cannot be made, unless there are also more souls. The number of souls seems to serve not so much the number of bodies, as it serves the number of composites, the whole species, and indeed the order of the universe. Nor should anyone think that souls differ among themselves for this reason, because their differences relate to bodies. For they are different in themselves first, before they relate in a different manner. So much for them.

Let us now return to our purpose. What Averroes adds, however, is this: if my intellect and yours differ in number, the species of things to be known will similarly differ, and will be particular. Yet what is to be understood must be universal. It is solved thus. It is not so much singularity that opposes understanding, as the aggregation of corporeal accidents. Indeed, individual intellects and their individual conceptions can be most conveniently understood. Furthermore, just as the image of a color in the eye is not that which is properly seen, but that through which the color itself is seen: so the species and likeness of things in the mind is not that which is properly understood, but that through which the universal reasons of things are understood. Nor is that species in the mind so singular as to impede the understanding of universal reasons.

[Catchword: ita]

--- Page 638 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

For if indeed a statue, which is singular and corporeal, in a certain way refers to us the common form of men: how much more does that species refer to the common nature, since it is in the mind, which is free from all passions of bodies, and therefore is itself free from them: whence it also refers to us a thing neither confined to a certain place nor time?

But it is necessary to remember that this order in species is posited by most, namely that in angels they are universal, both as regards referring and in a certain way as regards existing: in brutes they are particular in both ways. In the souls of men they are indeed singular in existing, because they are in entirely singular essences: but universal in referring, because they are in essences free from the limit of matter. But let them see to these things themselves. Moreover, he brought forward I know not what concerning the knowledge which a master imparts to a disciple: which, from those things which we have otherwise discussed concerning innate species, is easily resolved. But indeed that argumentation of Averroes is easily retorted against himself.

For if the knowledge of the teacher does not pass into the learner, nor generates another knowledge in him: one of two things follows: namely, that the very same intellect which is in both, either possesses the same habit in both: or from the habit which it possesses in one, generates another habit in the other in itself. Neither can happen according to Averroes. Not the first: because since that mind of his daily knows all arts in all men, and all teach these to others, in a certain perpetual succession of teachers and learners: it follows that the habits of all sciences are always entirely the same in the mind: which Averroes openly rejects. Not the second: because knowledge would be an effective quality, which he denies, and innumerable qualities similar to each other in species would be simultaneously in the same subject: which he would also by no means admit. For how much beyond the purpose of nature that fortuitous accumulation of superfluous qualities is, especially in an eternal and divine substance, whoever does not see this: he will be beyond the purpose of nature.

Finally, Averroes reasoned. If in two singular minds there are two singular species, it will be possible to reduce them to a universal one: and each mind will reduce to its own certain one: and in each mind again each species will become particular. Therefore it will be possible again to collect both to another without end. That is indeed vain. First because

--- Page 639 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XV. 279

the mind's gaze is clearly aroused by a species, yet it does not terminate in the species, so as to necessarily inspect it as an object; but through it, it inspects the universal reason of the thing: which, indeed, as one and the same, and as one, two minds behold through two species, just as the eyes of two men see the same thing through two images of it. Therefore, minds do not intend to reduce their species to other species, but through them to see the reasons of things. But if it ever intends this, they will not, however, proceed to infinity, because these species have a universal power and signification. Therefore, it is not permissible to always resolve them as singulars into others that are in reality more common; but let them proceed without end, if it pleases. For what prevents the mind, which in a certain way has infinite power, from wandering without end, provided that it never actually completes this infinite course? [Marginal note: B] A similar argumentation can be made concerning notions and concepts; the answer is also very similar.

**Signs that there is not only one mind. Chapter 14.**

After we have responded to Averroes' arguments, it remains for us to bring forward what are those signs or arguments especially [Marginal note: C] which dissuade (from the idea) that there is one intellect in all humans. First sign. If the mind is so divine that it has no commerce with matter: that it is one, lacking beginning and end, whole everywhere under the moon: it is not probable that it is so ignorant of itself that in almost all men, except for Averroes alone, it has always thought and thinks itself to be numerically multiple. I certainly not only understand, but I also understand that I understand, and similarly that I feel. Therefore, I am one and the same who understands and who feels. One, I say, by being one. Otherwise, it would not be affirmed for so long by me and by everyone that the understanding and feeling (being) are absolutely the same, but the understanding (being) would be clearly distinguished from the feeling (being). For in what way is it probable that a separate, eternal, divine mind, knowing all things in eternity, should so ignore itself that it always and everywhere thinks itself not only to understand, but also to feel and move and nourish: since, as Averroes opines, it does not effect such things.

--- Page 640 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Second Sign. The Mind is the place of truth: Truth is the food of the mind: from which it happens that they willingly embrace each other in turn. But since the human mind is never or scarcely made capable of Averroes' opinion, we can infer that that opinion is not true. Moreover, Averroes himself did not fall into an opinion of this kind by the free judgment of his own mind, but because he did not know how otherwise to interpret Aristotle's books, which had been corrupted into the Arabic language. Nor does he put forward a definitive opinion, but he tests the powers of his [Marginal note: D] intellect. He only affirms this: that the mind is immortal. But he does not affirm that it is one, but he opines and doubts: And he says that he is trying and hypothesizing, and leaving to posterity an opportunity for dispute. And if any assent to his doubt, they do not do this so much from their true conviction, as from a certain zeal for ambition, so that they may seem able to defend paradoxes. Scotus rightly says that this paradox is so far from being able ever to become probable to anyone, that not even Averroes himself could persuade himself of it. But Averroes would have spoken much more probably, indeed more truly, if, either with Themistius, he had introduced a single illuminating intellect, but many partly illuminated, partly illuminating: or if, with Plotinus, he had posited God as the sun: to this he had subjected a single intellect, whole everywhere, as light to the sun: to this, moreover, very many intellects, as rays to the light: finally, to these, also very many souls, as eyes to the rays. Or at least if, with Avicenna, he had posited many minds to one mind, as things capable of being formed relate to a former. For anyone can easily grasp these things, and soon confirm them with some example. But Averroes' invention is entirely alien from all mental capacity. But that human minds cannot grasp some invention, either it arises from this, that it is above them, and divine: or from this, that it is against them, and false. Averroes' invention, because it is about the mind, is not above the mind. Therefore it is false.

Third Sign. As often as we conceive of the unity of the mind, so often we are accustomed to hate it: and to desire a plurality of minds, if only we wish to survive. Nor should it be thought that we hate the mind's unity through imagination. For if there is any hatred in us against the mind, the same mind can hate its own unity, which it can also know. But it is not probable that a divine and most blessed thing should always scorn, reject, and hate its own nature.

THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY
If the power of seeing, through some agent sense joined to itself, always saw individual things, it would be said in vain that the eye needs a power by which it is moved and formed by external things. Just as from the words of Averroes, a superfluity arises in these three cognitions, so too it arises in three formations. If the capable intellect is formed by the Agent (Intellect) once through its essence, as he himself thinks: it is superfluous for it to be formed again always by the same thing through the images of all men, and also superfluous for it to be formed daily by the same thing through the images of wise and happy men. All these superfluities follow from the sayings of Averroes, which we have reviewed from the beginning. Which clearly shows us that his opinion should be rejected as superfluous. Let him therefore boast that he has discovered a divine mind, which, though wise in itself, always raves in us. And since innumerable men daily consider the same thing and are often mistaken, that mind considers the same thing a thousand times over at every moment, and is often deceived. If the mind itself never perceives this superfluity and fallacy cast upon it by phantasms, it is always ignorant of itself. The contrary of which we experience in ourselves, when we refute our own fallacies. If it does perceive, but does not turn its intention away from these digressions into itself, though it could: it is always weak, always incontinent. But the eternal mind can eternally turn its keenness away from the trifles of temporal phantasms. Indeed, the temporal soul often for a time withdraws itself from the trifles of the senses: nor can affection for individual things that are below men detain that mind in those errors and confusions, which is not even so affected towards human nature as to conspire with it to fabricate a species. In what way, therefore, will it concur with this animal for intimate operations, unless it first comes together for existence? For the form of fire communicates indeed the very heating of external matter, which is an external operation, even if it has by no means communicated its own being: but to be hot by itself, which is an intimate operation, it communicates only after existence.

Nor is the mind to be compared to the exterior senses, which lose forms when objects are absent. For they do not have true forms, but images: nor do they themselves, by their own power, contribute to the making of images. But the mind possesses true reasons, through which it comprehends the true substances of things: and it itself fashions them for itself: And therefore, it can preserve them by the same power by which it fashioned them. But if the species of the mind depended on images no differently than shadows depend on bodies, they would have nothing more excellent in themselves than the images. And if they had anything more sublime, it would be the gift of the active faculty, by which they will be preserved even when images are removed. But that they do not depend on images like shadows can be a proof to us, because they are so deeply implanted that they impress a habit that is utterly indelible. Nor should it be said that species therefore have a small essence, because they refer to universals: and therefore always need the foundation of images, as a preserver.

Firstly, indeed, because they contain and refer to more and better things, and things more pertinent to the essence of things, than simulacra: and therefore possess a nobler and ampler essence. If anyone diminishes the concept of genus because of its confusion and dispersion, and the concept of particulars because of their shadowy nature, we will readily concede.
C But Plato bids us honor species. For in them consists the perfection of the world and the truth of knowledge. To these, individual things are referred as parts to the whole, and also as to an end. Then, even if because of their universal condition they need a preserver, the active intellect will preserve them, especially, from which they acquire a nature of this kind. Nor do we think this species needs simulacra because it signifies nature existing in particulars: because if it signifies nature as absolute, it refers rather to a thing separate from particulars than in particulars: namely, the eternal reason of things which according to essence is in the divine mind, but according to intermediate participations in minds following God, and according to a certain ultimate similitude in bodies: reminded by the images of which, the intellect, absolutely participating in divinity, immediately either conceives the species, or recognizes the idea in itself and above. Thus, by the very condition of the species, it is clear that it is not, as it were, a completely unstable shadow of an image, but a certain excellent and stable nature.

D We can also infer the same from the nature of the mind. Indeed, wax and dust preserve the figures of things for a time, even when the things themselves depart. The brain also, as Averroes opines, preserves the simulacra of bodies when the bodies are absent. But the mind itself, which is stable because of its eternity, and above motion: will it not receive species stably and above motion, according to its nature? Will it not eternally preserve what it has received into its eternal bosom? Is not the intellect a power superior to sense, and therefore more unified? And therefore, it alone can do all that multiple powers of the senses accomplish.

But that the mind is mindful, this signifies that when we first learn something, we apply ourselves to those things with great difficulty and scarcely: but after long use of thought, we most readily meditate on what we once received, according to our will, as if they had already become ours, and were stored deep in the mind. After our mind has once formed within itself certain definitions of figures, or numbers, or virtues, or angels, succeeding each other in order, it can scarcely recall the first without taking up the second and the third: and just as at the beginning when it discovered them, it scarcely wove them together: so when it again encounters the discovered ones, it scarcely unravels what it had previously woven together: and much more easily and quickly it recurs from one species to another, than the inner sense usually does when it too returns to prior images by gradually reminiscing. This clearly declares that memory is present in the mind much more than in the sense. But if someone should say that the mind has not preserved formed species and definitions so much as the habit of reforming them: we will respond that the same power of the mind which both contracts and preserves habit, having already almost turned into [Marginal note: A] its nature, contracts the species into its innermost parts, and preserves it. Indeed, habit is founded on species: species are contained in habit. Therefore, if habit comes from the mind, species, and act: it acquires its stability from one of these. Not from the mind alone: otherwise the mind could also bestow stability upon the act. Not from the act: because it has no stability. Therefore, from species. Therefore, the species remains stable. Nor is it necessary, as often as we contemplate the same thing, to receive new forms from the agent each time, with the previous ones suddenly vanishing. Which signifies (as we have often already sought) that the mind, even while present in the body, sometimes operates without the body's help: and therefore, when it has departed from it, it will operate much more by itself. If the Averroists here should bring forward that those who have such and such a bodily constitution are usually stronger in intelligence and memory, because intellectual notions continuously depend on the senses: we will be able to respond Peripatetically, that a certain bodily affection serves the sense *per se*, but the mind *per accidens*: because the mind, while joined to the body, in a way fabricates its own species through the images of the senses: and as often as it has turned itself to its own species which it has made and preserved, so often it almost reverts to images. It reverts, I say, both because of a certain kinship between them, and because of the habit conceived from the condition of the soul united to the body. And although in every constitution we daily see sharpness and memory, from which we are compelled to confess that these proceed from a higher principle: let it be, however (if you please), that a dry nature is more retentive: provided that dryness is the *per se* cause of memory in the sense, but in the mind *per accidens*: not only because the memory of the sense itself serves the mind in a way, as we have said: but also because the dryness of the spirits, by contracting itself inwardly, does not prevent the soul from collecting itself. From this it happens that due to vehement and assiduous thought, the intellect is sharpened and memory is strengthened. Humidity, however, is the opposite. To these things, however, the Platonists would say that as many stars as there are, so many are the armies of souls: and that they have such a nature and denomination from them. Hence, therefore, souls are called Saturnian, and Jovian, and Martian, and Solar: and others similarly: and that they have various gifts concerning sharpness, memory, will, morals, arts, fortunes, from them: all of them, however, insofar as they are from there, are good: although here, from the multiple concurrence of causes, they often degenerate. Furthermore, that they receive spiritual gifts from the souls and divinities of their stars, both those leading and those following them, but corporeal and sensual gifts from the bodies of the stars. Finally, that a great excellence of sharpness and memory very much arises from vehemence of will and assiduous attention. But it is not permitted to digress further here. Why all this? So that we may reject that Averroistic opinion, which asserts that the absolute species of the divine mind depend like shadows from corporeal images of temporal fantasy: [Marginal note: D] But let us give credence to Plato, who says that what has once truly been understood can never be entirely committed to oblivion, but that the species of the thing comprehended is turned into an eternal habit in the eternal mind. For it has nothing contrary by whose approach it might be destroyed, nor is it ever abandoned by its subject. Wherefore, if the Averroistic mind is affirmed to draw all species at every moment through the fantasies of all humans, from which it understands all things, and if this mind lacks a beginning, and there has always been a generation of humans: certainly, thousands of thousands of years before us, it had all species and habits not once but innumerable times; indeed, it never received the first species from anyone, if there was never a first understanding human. Hence it formed species through no one's images, but its species are itself, or from its very essence. Which Aristotle would not have granted: but [he would have said that the intellect] received species, and all of them long ago. But it preserves whatever it receives immovably, if only it receives it intellectually according to intellectual reason. If it once acquired each thing infinitely, and is full of all things and overflows: what does it seek further? What does this superfluous reception of forms without end mean? Therefore the mind now understands nothing in us, since it receives nothing from us. Perhaps Averroes will reply that if the mind once possessed the species of something, for example, gold, it does not receive another species of gold recently from my fantasy thinking about gold, but that the very species of gold, which as far as I am concerned, was in a way sleeping in the mind, is awakened by the image of gold; and thus the mind recently looks upon my fantasy, and understands gold in me, just as it understood it before in another. If this is so: the active intellect no longer creates any species; the receptive [intellect] accepts none, since all species are possessed long ago. Which

indeed contradicts Averroes and his followers who hold that new species are daily created and received. It contradicts the Peripatetic sect asserting that the intellect is like a tablet on which nothing is written: which indeed Averroes, while defending his opinion, will never be able to explain except foolishly and ridiculously. But it does not disagree with us, who, led by Plato, believe [Marginal note: A] that the intellect is not compelled to generate a new species of man as often as phantasy presents us with various images of various men, but rather that a species conceived beforehand awakens: just as Socrates' phantasy does not form a new image of Alcibiades in itself as often as he sees Alcibiades encountered on the same day, but rather brings into act what is hidden within. And the eyes would do the same, if they retained images.

Thirdly, because as often as two people understand the same thing, so often do absurdities entirely follow. Chapter 17.

My phantasy now thinks of gold, and yours also of gold: [Marginal note: B] the Averroistic mind, excited by our images, gives birth in itself to the species of gold: and understands gold: we inquire whether now in both of us it grasps one species and one understanding of gold, or twin species and twin understandings: or rather one species and twin understandings: or vice versa. Some followers of Averroes follow the first part of this division: who are refuted by reasoning of this kind: because if the diversity of our images makes no diversity in the mind, they babble too rashly as often as they assert that that mind in me and in you, indeed I and you, understand gold. For the mind itself alone will understand, and in itself, while we think: just as Xenocrates himself discerns in himself a common truth, one and consistent with both, while he hears Speusippus and Polemon disagreeing in words through ignorance in their disputation. Furthermore, if the mind, by the same act of understanding, now understands gold in me and in you: as soon as it ceases to consider it in you, it likewise ceases to consider it in me: the contrary of which we experience. But they will deny that this follows: and just as in us the same soul vivifies the arm and the hand, and if amputated—

--- Page 650 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...with the hand amputated, it ceases to vivify this, not that: thus they will say that the mind, ceasing in your image, considers only in mine what it previously considered in yours as well. The example does not fit: because the act of vivifying passes into the body, the act of understanding does not descend into images. Therefore, in two limbs, diverse acts of vivifying are received: the act of understanding remains one in one mind. But this example fits better: just as the soul, through one life, lived in both limbs, afterwards through the same life it lives in one: so the mind, through the same intelligence, considered in both, through which afterwards it speculates only in the other. But neither does this example quite fit: because we can rightly say to live here and there: but to understand here or there, by no means. Indeed, intelligence is perfected by the segregation of place. But what if the eye, with the same gaze, sees simultaneously the right and left part of a small surface, and meanwhile, with the left withdrawn, the very same gaze that perceived both remains whole, but is only terminated in the other, which previously was terminated in both: so does the same act of understanding regard one image, which had regarded two? This also disagrees. First, because the eye does not properly cease to see while vision remains whole: but rather that part of the surface which is broken ceases to be seen. But let it cease to see: what then? Is not the gaze directed to local parts of the surface? So that it can rightly be said to see here as well as there. And therefore perhaps it will sometimes cease to see here, not there. But intelligence does not extend itself to local images: but to reason excluded from places. Therefore it is not rightly said to perish here, not there: but either nowhere, or to cease entirely everywhere. What then does that rash answer mean, that intelligence sometimes regards two images, sometimes one? Not that it contemplates the images themselves, for it looks higher. Not that it moves them: because the mind does not properly understand from this, but it affects the images in such a way that they themselves understand, or move something else to understanding. Or perhaps that the mind is moved by the images? If so: why did they not say that the mind is regarded by the images rather than regarding them? But they might say, What does it mean for it to be regarded by them? Does the species of the mind depend on the images as shadows on bodies? Indeed, this itself is the magnificent Aver-

A similar comparison also applies to the acts of the senses regarding imagination. Nor do I think there will be lacking among those who dare to assert that from twin simulacra of gold, twin species are attributed to the mind, yet only one act of understanding concerning the gold itself results from them. This we will therefore reject: because if the diversity of simulacra has such great power as to produce diversity in species, although simulacrum and species exist in different substances: how much more will the difference of species produce a difference of understandings, especially since they are in the same essence of the mind? Do not even among these thinkers one movement lead to contrary ends, when through one understanding contrary judgments are made, and contrary affections? What also will they answer us when we ask, whether either species taken separately from the other can produce understanding, or not? If it cannot, the mind will not be able to perceive anything unless the images of that thing are twinned in the mind: of which one will always be superfluous. THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Therefore, there will be two aspects in the two forms: not indeed differing in species, inasmuch as they are referred to one nature of gold in species. Differing therefore in number. But by what do they differ? Not by themselves, otherwise they would differ in species. Not by the subject, for they are located in one mind. Nor should it be said that they are therefore doubled because they are placed in twin forms. For it is granted that the forms themselves are doubled rather by aspects, not by something adventitious, because otherwise we would again add aspects to aspects, and dispute about the latter as about the former. Again we inquire, whether those respects are founded in the forms or in the simulacra. If in the simulacra, the forms would be looked at by the simulacra rather than looking at them. If in the forms, they do not pertain to the essence of the forms themselves, because they would introduce a specific difference to the forms; they are added to the essences of the forms extrinsically by the simulacra, the fabricators of the forms themselves. From which it follows that forms of this kind are particular because of the very corporeal singularity of the simulacra. How much this impedes the purity of intelligence, no one of sound mind is ignorant. Indeed, since simulacra are compared to forms as extrinsic agents, they will never cause one form to be distinguished from another, unless individual simulacra apply certain conditions to individual forms emanating from them, by which the forms will differ among themselves no otherwise than the simulacra do from each other. Therefore, the forms will not be absolute as long as they are constrained by the limitations of the simulacra. Moreover, it is entirely incredible for two absolute forms to be found in the same subject, differing only in number. For by the very fact that they differ neither in reason nor in essence, nor in subject, they will be forced to differ from each other by foreign qualities, whence they will not be absolute. However, for them to be in two subjects is not impossible. For at the same time they will be distinguished from each other, because they will form distinct subjects; and they will remain absolute, because they will not be formed by the subjects, when the subjects are simple and free from imperfections.

Fourth, because either the knowledge of many men would be the same, or there would be superfluous qualities in the same.
Chapter 18.

--- Page 655 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XV. 287

All qualities, absolute both from their end and from an external preserver, which are one in species, if they come together in the same subject, also become one in number. For what agrees in species also agrees in form. But if they moreover agree in matter because of the subject, they are entirely one. Therefore, in one drop of wine there is sweetness and redness at the same time: which two qualities are diverse in species: yet there are not two sweetnesses there, or two rednesses. Although images and splendors of qualities can be in the same [subject] differing only in number, just as the images of two eggs in the eye and imagination, and also the two lights of two candles in the same air, because they depend constantly on external things, and therefore follow the number of those things whose images or lights they are, rather than the subject's: those qualities, however, which are both true and follow the nature of the subject rather than the object, become one in number through the subject, if they have been one in species. The absolute form of the mind, however, is therefore its true and stable quality, because it is not an image or shadow or splendor of foreign accidents, but the offspring of intellectual substance, an exemplar of substances, a rule of truth depending on the intellect, not on external things. Therefore, there are not in the mind certain absolute forms differing among themselves only in number. Here it is permissible to scorn that Averroistic objection. "A simulacrum," they say, "is the principle of an intelligible form: therefore, as many simulacra as occur at the same time, so many forms are made, because each of the simulacra can sufficiently produce a form apart from another." We, however, say that a simulacrum is neither the principle of a form, if the form is universal, nor a preparation of a capable mind for receiving the form (lest it be in the mind before the form, or certainly more similar to the mind), but is a certain occasion for the incitement of the active power. Which it will also never accomplish, if it itself is in another substance in another form. But if they are in the same soul, as they certainly are, how it provides an occasion, we have declared elsewhere. When therefore the simulacrum of gold presents itself: if the mind had never before received the form of gold, it itself produces it, having found an occasion for producing. But if it has produced it previously, and possesses it, it does not produce another, but brings into act that which it possesses. But only one

PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...produces and brings forth, even if a thousand images of the same species occur. Do you not notice when you see a thousand men with your eyes in the theatre, and afterwards recall a thousand images of these thousand simultaneously in your imagination, meanwhile the mind thus considers: Man is a beautiful animal, delighting in society, skillful, religious? Here the mind does not pronounce thus about any of those thousand, but about the one common nature of all: about the common substance of a rational animal: about the common definition of society itself, of skill, and of religion. This one judgment about the one nature of all men or virtues the mind cannot make more conveniently than through one species and likeness. Where it appears that it has drawn only one species of man from a thousand images of men: and always does the same in all images of the same species, however diverse: from all images of horses collected together, one equine species: but not one species from images of a horse and a man, but two. Whoever understands anything experiences this in himself. Therefore, when a hundred men see a horse, a hundred collect images of the horse in their imaginations. But the mind, if it is one for all, provoked by a hundred images, conceives one species of horse, which one intellection follows. Therefore, there will be one act of understanding among a hundred men. How then, if one ceases to understand, does another not also cease? Certainly, innumerable men succeeding one another can understand through that same intellection remaining in itself. From this it will follow that the very speculation of temporal things is eternal. Which Averroes will not concede. The mind does not consider a horse as this particular horse: but simply according to the universal concept of the equine species. A concept of this kind is one, even if there are a thousand images of a thousand horses in one or more human souls. Therefore, there will be one consideration of the horse in many men. From such consideration, the habit of knowledge is contracted in the mind. In the mind, I say, not in the imagination: if indeed the act of understanding is a disposition towards a habit: and where there is a disposition, there a form is made, that is, a habit: a universal habit from universal acts and forms. THEOLOGIAE PLATONICAE

If therefore the mind is one: either the knowledge of two will be entirely the same, two will think together, together they will cease to think: or innumerable qualities of the same kind will be in the same subject: and daily the intellect will receive very many qualities of the same kind as those it has, as if honey at every moment received one sweetness after another, very similar to its own. And in this Averroes' opinion will greatly contradict itself, who in the books on the soul three times repeated (according to Aristotle's opinion) that every subject ought to be bare of the kind of quality which it is about to receive. Therefore, since we experience in ourselves that the mind not only understands, but also perceives that it understands, and very easily transfers itself in a moment from one understanding to another, often similar, often even opposite, and connects many things into one: and even to grasp many notions of one who disputes with it, through the expression of a single one: and what is greater, often to perceive what another has in their imagination, which is more remote from the mind: without doubt it is wonderful that the Averroistic mind, unique, eternal, indivisible, uniform, equally present to all, never perceives in me that which it understands in you. It never connects what it observes in one person with what it observes in another: it never infers by itself in one person what it thinks in another. Nor is it permitted to resort to the diversity of images: which are both outside and below the mind: and many things are certainly understood at a time when an image is neither intervening nor properly accompanying by itself.

Fifth, because contradictories would be in the same (subject).
Cap. 19.

Contradictories oppose each other much more than contraries, inasmuch as there is a greater repugnance between being and not being, than between being such and such. Therefore, if contraries cannot meet in the same subject, much less can contradictories. Hence it happens that each of us experiences in himself that his mind never affirms and denies something entirely at the same time: to wholly will and not will: even if there are many images of the thing itself in his imagination. -roists, that the image of whiteness and blackness are simultaneously in the eye and imagination, and again their species simultaneously in the mind, in which also there are cognitions of contraries simultaneously: because forms of this kind which are contrary outside the soul, for this reason are not contrary in the soul, because they lose their nature. For they are transferred into a certain quality of the soul, and that indeed in a certain imaginary way. But to assent and not to assent, to will and not to will, retain a contradictory force: because they are rather essential than imaginary: and they signify being and not being concerning the same act or affection of the soul. Therefore, although the species of whiteness and blackness in sight are not contrary: nevertheless the vision of some object as white, and the vision simultaneously of the same as black, are so opposed to each other that they cannot coincide: although the visions themselves continuously depend on different species and objects: thus in the mind the affirmation of the divine trinity and simultaneously its negation cannot agree, even if they are said to depend on different images and species. Indeed, the diversity of agents does not prevent contrary effects from opposing each other and expelling each other. What then causes the Averroist intellect to assert in Plato that the One itself is above essence, and the Good itself above mind: but to reject it in Aristotle? Certainly, no variety of images causes this. For such contemplation is rightly performed only by setting aside images. Or what causes that intellect to affirm in Plato that the heaven is fire, but simultaneously deny it in Aristotle? Would the diversity of two images perhaps cause this, if the mind judged in images or through images or about images: but now, having taken occasion from them, it immediately withdraws into itself: and through a common species judges in itself about the common nature of heaven and fire: but to the imagination itself it leaves the intuition of images, and even a very slight one: which is weakened all the more, the more the mind's speculation is strengthened: and vice versa. Which is a most evident argument for what we were discussing above: namely, that a species is neither made by an image nor preserved. Do diverse species conceived in the mind through the occasion of diverse images produce those diverse opinions? By no means. For the mind receives one species from two of the same

...of the heavens' *simulacra*. But for the sake of argument, let it accept two. Although these two may be ways through which conflicting opinions seem able to proceed into the mind, nevertheless there are not two distinct parts or powers or proper forms in the mind in which discordant opinions can be received: but they are gathered to one and indivisible center of intelligence. There, a single and most simple judge delivers the sentence. But one cannot so clearly contradict itself at the same time. The duality of *species* can do nothing further than variously instigate the mind, if only they themselves are various. But the intellect delivers its judgment, neglecting the weaker *species* through the other: and through the dominance of one prevailing *species*, it produces only one judgment: just as the imagination, although agitated by various conjectures through various senses, nevertheless brings forth one judgment and affection. Indeed, anyone experiences the mind doing the same thing in various conjectures within itself. But if that one mind should waver through two *species* in two men, and be carried hither and thither, because it is nevertheless conscious of itself within itself: it does not ignore what it wavers about there: and with the conjectures weighed, it inclines to the other side in a short moment. And if it is absurd to say that heat and cold are simultaneously received in the same subject, even if these two are brought about by different causes, namely fire and water: will it not also be ridiculous for contrary opinions to enter the mind, even if they are introduced by different causes? For what is received, is received according to the disposition of the subject. But the same subject cannot be disposed in simultaneously contrary ways to simply receive contrary forms. Furthermore, the argumentation will be stronger if we argue concerning contrary habits. For since confirmed habits no longer depend on *simulacra*, and are now even (which is greater) independent of their own actions: the Averroists cannot say that contrary habits can concur because of certain contrary agents, that is, *simulacra*. Therefore, one mind is one subject, although it may receive two species: and by reason of itself (not of the species) is whatever arrives received. How, therefore, an entrance for contradictories may be open, cannot even be imagined: unless perhaps they add that the mind relates to species as matter itself relates to quantity. Therefore, just as matter, extended by quantity, receives contrary qualities: so the mind, clothed in species, receives repugnant opinions. [Marginal note on the right: A] For it is the nature of a contradictory that they cannot dwell together simultaneously. But they cannot be simultaneous, even if someone should try to reconcile them through some medium. Add that if repugnant things are to be received by certain preparations: the preparations themselves demand repugnant things. If preparations contribute to certain habits, and are in some proportion congruent with them: they only impede diverse habits: and are dissonant from their preparations. And if preparations for repugnant things are again received by the same subject through other discordant affections: we shall err to infinity. But if no affection intervenes, that is indeed absurd: and repugnant habits will be able to be received equally like affections without a medium. Wherefore, if our mind is to be disposed to the repugnant acts and habits of contradictories: there will first be need of species mutually opposing each other, and also of dissonant discursions, which, excited by discordant species, assume conflicting principles of reasoning, and through dissonant means arrive at contradictory conclusions. All this repugnance which distracts towards contradictories, cannot be received by the mind without a medium, just as contradictories cannot. If a medium is sought: it will be sought without end.

--- Page 662 ---
PLATO'S THEOLOGY
Just as we have disputed concerning contradictory assents, so it is permissible to discourse concerning contradictory affections: as, for example, when that mind in Plato both desires some universal object, and at the same time, in Aristotle, does not desire it: an affection of this kind does not pertain to phantasms, which do not grasp anything universal by desiring any more than by thinking. We also see contrary affections in the mind, when people simultaneously desire two universal objects that are mutually dissenting; and when, regarding incorporeal things, some rejoice, while others simultaneously grieve. Finally, the same mind will be both upright and wicked simultaneously: wise and ignorant: certain and ambiguous: happy and miserable. What will they say to this? That from repugnant acts and affections, repugnant habits will coalesce in the same mind, namely both contrary and contradictory ones. But this is the most absurd of all, because a habit is not something imaginary, but takes the place of a natural form: and a natural form and inclination is destroyed by the advent of an opposite form and inclination.

Perhaps longer than was fitting, we have disputed about the mind with those who deprive themselves of mind when they separate it from the human species: which is so familiar to the human species that neither can we adopt the mind without mind, nor can they reject the mind without mind. We believe, however, that in the preceding, we have refuted not only Averroes, but also those Moors who are of the opinion that there is one soul for all. For if there is distinction in minds, there is much greater diversity in souls: both because human minds are more united to each other, inasmuch as they are more excellent than souls are to each other; and because if one soul were sufficient for governing our bodies, much more would one mind be sufficient for comprehending truth. Therefore, it should not be believed that some adulterated Platonists assert that all living things live through one world soul: because we would not be led by free movement and variety of counsel, but would be carried by sudden impulse like arrows. And if we all breathed by one world soul, we would also only speculate by one mind above the world. However, the very diversity and distinction of worldly bodies signifies a distinction of natures: the distinction of natures follows the distinction of souls: the distinction of souls accompanies the distinction of minds: and minds inherent in souls...

--- Page 663 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVI. 291

tain their number. One may also laugh at a certain barbarian
Dinant and the Manichaeans, who wished our souls to be certain
portions of God, or God Himself. [marginal note: B] For that this cannot
be is sufficiently declared from those five grades of things
set forth in the first book. Nor can God either be torn into many
souls, since the highest unity cannot be divided: or become the matter
of many souls: lest He be viler than souls, nor the highest
act play the role of a subject. Or He Himself, existing in His own form,
be changed so frequently in us: since He is the stable center of mobile things
from true to false, good to evil, joy to sorrow:
and vice versa. Finally, if God were the soul of all,
there would be one mind in all: which has been refuted in earlier parts.
But since Themistius asserts [marginal note: C] that there was one
opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus concerning the mind: if we wish
to conclude this Peripatetic discussion with a happy end,
let us thus gather into one the very Platonic and Peripatetic truth,
scattered among many interpreters. Let us accept
from Averroes that the potential intellect is immortal. Let us accept
from Alexander that potential intellects are certain powers naturally
inherent in our souls, equal in number to the souls.
Let us conclude that human souls are immortal.
And this is the conclusion of the Platonists, Christians,
and Arab theologians, most consonant with the ancient Peripatetics.

On the immortality of souls
by the same Ficino

*The second question follows: why are souls enclosed in earthly*
*bodies.*
Chapter I.
