**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

[Marginal note: D]
[Large decorative initial P] After we have answered the first question,
and shown that the divinity of the mind
is fitting for our souls: let us answer the second [question]:
and let us show why souls, if they are divine,
are enclosed in such lowly earthly bodies.

First reason, that they may know individual things.

[Marginal note: E]
[Large initial E] The essence of God, if indeed it is to be called an essence, is not one
particular kind of thing: otherwise, it would only act upon things of its own kind;
just as water makes things that are wet, not dry;
fire, on the contrary, generates dry things, not wet. But since God
produces all kinds of things through His essence, and what
He produces remains above all that is made: God is in no kind of thing,
but above all kinds. Therefore, when He contemplates His
essence, the origin and exemplar of all things: He contemplates all
kinds of things: and also all species, and individual things.
For the essence of God is the beginning, middle, and end,
not only of specific principles, but also of individual things
pervading under any species. Indeed, the divine essence,
since it has nothing in itself similar to matter, which tends to obscure
cognition: it is light and supreme perspicacity. Therefore, God
properly, through His essence, as through an efficacious light
and a discerner of individuals, perceives individual things: and since
the essence of God is utterly absolute, not only from all matter
and the property of matter, but also from every specific condition
and relation to this created thing or that, and is
infinite: therefore, it relates (so to speak) indifferently to all things.
Therefore, either it knows nothing besides itself, or it knows all things. To know nothing, however,
is impious to say, since it is the supreme reason of both knowers and things known
and of knowledge itself. Nor should Averroes object to us,
that God would be debased if He considered lower things. Indeed, because
He knows Himself to be the principle of all things that are below Him:
therefore He knows what it means to be inferior. Therefore, He comprehends by what reason they are deficient.
But indeed, while He recognizes the very reason of the defect itself:
He Himself does not suffer the defect. For if God, in considering the very
foundation of imperfection, which is most alien from Him,
does not Himself become more imperfect: certainly much less
does He become imperfect in thinking about other, even most imperfect, things.

--- Page 665 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVI. 292

...he becomes imperfect. What more? The knowledge of oneself and of others is desirable as a good. For it is a certain possession of oneself and of one's minds. However, one mode of knowing can be less desirable than another. Indeed, the mode by which the external sense knows is imperfect. Less imperfect, however, is that by which the internal sense (knows); less also that by which reason (knows); and least of all, finally, that by which the angelic mind (knows). Therefore, that mode of knowledge by which God discerns particulars, since it is infinitely more perfect than the angelic mode by infinite degrees, certainly comprehends no imperfection, nay, rather, it entirely comprehends all perfection. Such, indeed, is the mode of divine knowledge, which is infinite through perfection itself. Finally, just as for us finite beings it is better to know certain finite things than to be ignorant, so it is more fitting for the infinite God to see infinite things, rather than either none or finite things. Indeed, He distinctly knows particulars everywhere, since He who perfectly holds the cause of causes, possesses all and individual causes most perfectly. And distinct perception, as being much more perfect than confused (perception), is much more to be desired. But lest we digre- [Marginal note: F] ss further, let us proceed to the rest.

The angel also beholds all and individual works of God. Indeed, if the object of our mind is being itself and the common truth, and therefore the human mind directs itself (though gradually) to all existing and true things, it is fitting that the mind of an angel, which is superior to ours, should grasp all things: and, as the Platonists wish, all things simultaneously. But where does the angel look to see all things? Does it direct its gaze to bodies? By no means. Because the angel's mind is stable, and discerns all things simultaneously, therefore it cannot learn those things from bodies, which, often changed in their course, show now one thing, now another, and different things. And if [Marginal note: G] the mode of acting follows the mode of being, an angel, who in being is entirely free from body, will also be free in understanding. Nor will he be formed by bodies, he who is superior to bodies and has no commerce with them. Or perhaps will he turn his gaze to the angelic essence? He will indeed turn it: but in the angel he will only perceive an angel. For he will see only as much in the angelic nature as it extends itself. It is only in the angelic genus. Therefore he will see an angel in it: he will not clearly discern the other genera of things. Indeed, if matter impedes knowledge, and created essence has something not unlike matter, formless and obscure: it follows that no created mind, insofar as it is in
O o iiij

--- Page 666 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...sees a bare, as it were, darkness, can attain clarity of vision: just as if the moon were looking at itself, not yet illuminated by the light of the sun. Therefore, just as the eye does not discern colors except through the very forms of colors, so too the mind does not clearly see the kinds of things except through their forms; since form is the principle of action. The essence of an angel alone is the form of an angel; and that, indeed, is in a certain way dark. But the essence of God, or rather, truth and goodness, is the form of all things, and the purest light, the ra-
[Marginal note: H] dix, reason, and exemplar. Therefore, through this alone, as through the sun, all things can be seen. Will the angel then discern all things through the very essence of God? Not indeed through the absolute essence of God without a medium. For in what way can infinite essence, as a form, be congruent with a finite mind with no intervening preparation? It is necessary, however, for the mind itself to have some form within itself, through which it acts in understanding. Therefore, the angel receives the forms and exemplars of things from the essence of God; and just as the eye, through the sun's light, which is effective for all colors, receives the forms of those same colors and sees colors, so too the mind of the angel, through God's light, which is effective for all things, receives the species of those same things and understands. Rightly does God first and more fully form the spiritual matter closest to Him, that is, angelic minds, than the matter of the world most remote from Him. But there are many grades of minds, and many more than of bodies, as Dionysius the A-
[Marginal note: A] reopagite relates. For the best artisan wished to establish more grades in His excellent works than in His baser works. Thus the city of God will be more glorious, if there are more grades of nobles and freemen in it than of mercenaries and slaves. Such, indeed, is the comparison of minds to bodies. How many principal orders there are in the angelic grades, we have sufficiently discussed from the mind of Dionysius, both in the book on religion and in Paul's rapture.
[Marginal note: B] In what way the Platonists divide them into nine orders, we have indicated elsewhere: namely, because angels are certain intellects contemplating the supreme intelligible itself, in which they contemplate essence, life, and intelligence. But there, in essence, both life and intelligence exist according to the mode of essence. Again, in life, the other two similarly exist according to the mode of life. Likewise, in intelligence, the other two, that is, life and essence, exist according to a certain mode of intelligence.

--- Page 667 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVI. 293

There, therefore, the supreme and one intelligible is divided
into three, and then through these three it is multiplied into nine. In the same C
order also, intellects considering it are distributed into nine
orders. And in this way the Platonists divide angels dedicated solely to contem-
plation. But those who also govern the world, some divide by
twelve and seven, primarily according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac and the seven
planets. Then to these they add certain other armies of angels,
attending to certain duties according to the number of stars in each sphere of the world;
and as many throngs of demons and heroes obeying the angels;
and finally, as many orders of particular souls adapting
themselves to the supernal deities. But let us now dismiss the demonic
and heroic armies: it is enough to have understood that the Platonists
placed innumerable minds above us; in naming which, Iamblichus
takes not only the names of angels, but also of archangels and principalities
from our (tradition), and he thinks that the divine light descends
through all of them, as if through glass, down to us. Wherefore,
through almost innumerable grades of intermediary spirits, that
divine ray, the shaper of minds, descends even to the lowest
minds, such as human souls. But four things seem to be considered D
here. First, indeed, that divine ray; then the species of things in it,
which we call both the reasons for things to be created, and ideas;
third, minds; fourth, the powers of minds. The ray, inasmuch as it consists
in the simplest unity of God, is entirely one and most simple, and E
offers one idea to the divine eye, namely, the one essence of God,
but that (essence) indeed communicable to things to be created through many
modes of being. Which modes, according to Plato, are those very ideas of things
which are to be produced through such modes. Therefore, the one essence
of God is one idea, representing all ideas; and through this
one, God surveys all things. That ray, while it emanates
from God, the further it proceeds from divine unity, the more it becomes
manifold; and which had first offered one idea to the eye of God,
now offers many, and then more, and finally very many to angelic
eyes; just as a line drawn from a center, which was
indivisible in it, the further it departs, the more it extends
into more parts. Indeed, just as the sun's ray in the sun itself
presents a single form of light, many in fire, more in air

--- Page 668 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

and in water, very many in earth: just as that divine ray behaves, so too do the minds into which it is infused. For the closer a mind is to divine unity, the more united and simple it is. The more remote, the opposite. However, each mind receives the incoming ray according to its nature: therefore, the supreme minds receive it more simply, the others more multiply. Hence, few ideas are painted by the ray in a sublime mind, in the next (mind) more, and very many thereafter. But since the simpler and more united something is, the more powerful it is: therefore, in higher minds, the power of understanding thrives more acutely, (and is) duller in the subsequent ones. From which it follows that through those very fewer ideas, superior minds see no fewer things than the others through more ideas: Just as a most skilled physician foresees future cases in a sick person by a single sign, an unskilled (physician) needs more signs to judge, and a most unskilled (physician) needs very many. And a shrewd minister understands with a single nod.

Indeed, Platonists consider that higher minds, just as they contain the immaterial ideas of material things, and the ingenerable ideas of generable things, so too do they possess only universal ideas of particular things.

Let us imagine the human soul now first emanating from God, and not yet clothed in a body, so that, free from the occupation of the body, it may direct its entire intention to its own mind, where, according to its nature, it receives only the influx of that ray perpetually assisting and inspiring it. What will the soul naturally grasp through such a ray? As many ideas as there are species of created things: one idea for each species. What will it understand through the idea of man? Only the nature common to all men; it will not see individual men under it. It will do the same for the idea of a horse, and for the rest. Therefore, the cognition of this soul will remain confused, since the distinct progression of species lies hidden from it.

into particulars: and its natural appetite will be empty, and its desire always restless, for it wishes to lack no truth, no good. But why can't the human soul clearly discern, in the ultimate ideas, both species and the particulars subject to species, just as angels see genera, species, and
A particulars in their ideas? Because, as we have discussed elsewhere, in every order of things, nature is so arranged that action at the summit of that order is free from passion, passion at the lowest is devoid of action, and in the middle, there is a middle composition. It has also been established that our souls are the lowest minds. Therefore, as far as intelligence is concerned, God will act alone; the angel will act and receive; the soul will receive only through the nature of its mind, it will not act. For God indeed pours out ideas elsewhere; He does not draw them from elsewhere. The first angel receives two (so to speak) ideas, that is, those two broadest genera of things, in receiving which it somehow undergoes a passion. Having received these, because of the inherent efficacy of those genera, it penetrates their depths, and clearly discerns all subsequent species within them; and forms for itself proper concepts of any species whatsoever, which it also derives into particulars. And this is no longer passion, but action. The same second angel acts, and others; and always the subsequent angel receives more ideas from above by being passive, and will form fewer concepts of species for itself by acting. Therefore, passion gradually increases, while action decreases, until the lowest mind is reached, which does nothing, but is nourished by received ideas, and devises nothing new. Whose intelligence is nothing other than the reception of ideas, by no means hidden from itself. And since ideas are universal by nature, no
B mind can, without its own action, deduce them to distinct concepts of individual things. Therefore the human soul, which, in that part where it is mind, is the last among minds, and understands only by being passive, does not distribute universals into particulars. Nevertheless, in that part where it is divine, through its center, as if a character of God, it has some action by which it produces or educes species, but it by no means divides. Furthermore, in that part where it is soul, because it is not the last of souls, it is capable of animal and corporeal operation. Hence, coupled with earthly bodies, the most excellent of all earthly things, it indeed rules them: and through its vital power brings vital affections to them from within: but through sense it judges alien affections inflicted upon them from without. Since the human body consists of four elements, and is located in the middle of the world: it suffers the impulses of all elements and all surrounding things through the five instruments of the senses. The soul discerns such impulses, inflicted from all sides by individual things, one by one through the senses: and by its animal power, it forms their images within itself through phantasy, and preserves them in memory. Whence it happens that in a short time, phantasy is full of almost all individual things in their individual forms. Hence reason, being aroused, first indeed gives birth to universal species: and through them, by simple intuition, conceives common notions. Soon however, **C** from this intuition, directly from the act of understanding, it reflects itself into an intelligible species, and through this into an image: and through the image it perceives the individual, at first indeed vague and indeterminate, for example, some honey: then determined, namely this honey or that. But after such shorter acts, it is accustomed to range more widely in this manner: What is this sweet and yellow body that phantasy **D** now offers to me? Why is it sweet? Is this sweeter, or wine? Here reason seeks three things: which, as it seems to the Platonists, had lain hidden from phantasy. First, the substance of that thing: when it asks what this is. Second, the cause of that quality, when it inquires why it is sweet. Third, its relation to others: when it asks whether it is sweeter than wine. After these things, it answers itself three things. First: This is honey. Second: This is sweet because its humor is rich and moderately cooked. Third: It is sweeter than wine, because its sweetness delights the tongue more and longer. These discourses of human reason, since they follow the impulse of phantasy, are particular, and wander through individual things. Indeed, it also tackles other questions. What is honey? What is sweetness? Now it does not ask about this honey any more than about any other: similarly about any sweetness. And having neglected that particular image of honey which phantasy brought, it investigates the common reason of universal honey and sweetness. This is a universal question. The answer also becomes universal, thus,

--- Page 672 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

Honey is the juice of bees, hot in the second degree: cleansing in its property: sweetest in taste: fatty to the touch. Furthermore, sweetness is a taste arising from the moderate concoction of aerial humor. Reason sought these common definitions of honey and sweetness for a long time, and finally found them. If it sought for a long time, it did not possess them itself. For it received from elsewhere that to which it arrived by discursive reasoning. From where then did it receive them? Not from phantasia. For if it (phantasia) had possessed them, it would have offered them plainly at once, just as it offered simulacra: especially since that light of common definition, by how much it is more illustrious and divine than simulacra, by so much more clearly ought it to have shone forth to the eyes of reason adapted to it. Therefore, reason receives them from the mind: and since it (reason) is very close to the mind, it acquires that very power through which, sometimes neglecting singular questions, it applies itself to universal questions. And because it seeks definitions universally, it brings back common ones from the mind.

It was asked what profit might come from the body. Very much, without a doubt. Indeed, if the soul remains outside the body as soon as it is born, it will indeed know universals: but it will not discern particulars, either by its own power or by a divine ray comprehended through itself, because its mind will not descend beyond the ultimate ideas, and reason will rest in the intuition of the mind. In this body, however, because of the senses, reason becomes accustomed to run through particulars: to apply particulars to universals: to derive universals into particulars. It runs through particulars in this manner: This is sweet, and yellow: therefore it is honey. It applies particulars to universals, thus: this is sweet. Every sweet thing is a humor moderately cooked. Therefore this is a humor so cooked. But it applies universals to particulars thus: Every sweet and yellow thing is honey. Therefore, because this is such, it is honey. Reason, thus accustomed, when the soul has been separated, will easily distribute the common ideas of the mind into singular notions: because just as reason here, by a certain temporal discursive process of its own, provokes that divine and efficacious center of the soul and head of the mind to gradually bring forth into light the formulas lying hidden in the mind, and translates them even into reason: so there (in the separated state), by a sudden and continuous affection generated by long custom, it will inflame the formulas, so that, sparked by certain sparks of singular things, they may sometimes flash forth from the mind into reason. *Second Reason, that singular forms may be reconciled with universal forms. Chapter 2.*

[Large decorative initial M]
Truly wonderful is this human reason, proper to the rational soul, through which we are human beings. It receives particulars from imagination, universals from the mind, and gathers both into one: and just as in man mortal things are coupled with immortal ones, so in this kind of reason temporal images are joined to eternal species. If this were not brought about somewhere in the world, the series of forms would remain interrupted. But it cannot happen, unless the rational soul is joined to an earthly body.

Third Principle, that both the divine ray and its forms may be reflected back to God. Chapter 3.

[Large initial F] In this, it does yet another, more marvelous thing: because that divine ray, most full of ideas, after it descends all the way to the soul, passes through the vital force of the soul, and through nature into the matter of the world: in which it forms certain extreme and shadowy resemblances of ideas: just as light forms images of colors in a mirror: indeed, just as shadows of bodies are outlined on the earth by light.

Such resemblances or shadows, however, depart very far from divinity itself. For from pure they become impure, while they are defiled by contraries: from united, they become scattered: from common, they become individual: from stable, they become utterly unstable. If all things seek their origin, from where the sun's ray striking the earth is then reflected back to the sun: what wonder is it that these shadowy resemblances of ideas also, by a certain hidden instinct, seek their pristine purity, and that the ray itself, their creator, after it has descended, strives ardently in turn to ascend? Will such a great effort be in vain? By no means. Who will help? Not the souls of beasts, which gape only at individual images. Not those minds superior to ours: which, since they do not have bodies subject to all the storms of all bodies, do not receive any particular passions or forms of any bodies. Only the soul of man remains: which, because of its earthly body, being in a way struck by the individual commotions of individual bodies, indeed takes in through sense these resemblances of ideas infected by the matter of the world, but gathers them through imagination, purifies and refines them through reason: then binds them with the universal ideas of the mind. Thus that celestial ray which had flowed down to the lowest things, flows back to the highest, while the resemblances of ideas which had been scattered in matter are gathered in imagination, and the impure are purified in reason, and the individual finally become universal in the mind. Thus the soul of man restores the world, now weakened: because by its office, the spiritual world, which had once become corporeal, is continually purified, and daily becomes spiritual. a pyramid: and in that very opening they are so much deflected, that they are led across by it: and when they fall onto the pavement below, they form a shining circle, so much larger, the further the pavement is from the opening: where they seem about to equal the width of the solar globe, if they have fallen from the opening by the same distance as they flowed from the sun. Also, the influx of ideas sent down from higher minds into bodies, become most narrow from being most ample, and while they become entirely particular from universals, finally, reflected from bodies into the human mind, they regain their pristine amplitude. From this they clearly show that the human mind is almost as remote from bodies as are the higher minds. And therefore, since it is equally separated from mortals as divine minds are; it exists as equally immortal: especially since it restores to eternity forms that have fallen from eternity into time and parts of time.

Fourth reason, that the soul may become more blessed. Chapter 4.

Furthermore, the descent of the soul into the body contributes to the soul's [Marginal note: G] own blessedness. For if someone is duller in intellect, and always strong in body: he will not know how much good bodily health is to be valued. He must sometimes fall ill, so that by that comparison at least he may recognize the value of health: and having recovered health again, he may enjoy it more sweetly. The human soul, duller than all minds, needs comparison for the fullest judgment of the greatest things. Therefore, agitated by worldly storms, how quiet and sweet is the harbor in God: and here it will prophesy more rightly, and there it will discern more acutely: it will adhere more intently, and enjoy more sweetly. Indeed, Plotinus seems to approve of this reason not moderately: but especially Porphyry: who says that the soul, having often experienced these evils, at last adheres entirely to its parent, never to these [evils] again.

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

never again to return. Perhaps God himself ordained that divine joys should be obtained by nature for the higher grades of minds, but acquired by labors for the lower order: so that there might be those who become blessed by birth, and those who make themselves blessed by living: lest either sublime spirits be esteemed more than they are, since they obtain blessedness from elsewhere, or inferior spirits be despised, since they themselves are the authors of their own blessedness.
[Marginal note: I] What if angels, inasmuch as they are more remote from time, as soon as they are originated, through a certain sudden conversion to God, instantly obtain blessedness? But we acquire a similar happiness by a longer circuit. And what is lacking in nature is repaid by our industry. And while the endurance of honest and pious labor is compensated by the weakness of our origin, in a certain way, equaling angelic excellence, we also equal the rewards. Thus, four grades are found in good. God has his good only from himself; corporeal things only from another; an angel and a soul not only from another, because from God, but also from themselves, because they provide good to themselves: but an angel by an eternal act, a soul by a temporal act. Nor should we wonder that the soul can not only stray to extreme evil, like the wretched, but also progress to the highest good, like angels. For the first and free movement has its limit nowhere but in the infinite.

**Fifth reason, that the lower powers of the soul may proceed to action.**
**Chapter 5.**

[Marginal note: K] Moreover, this dwelling is conducive not only to reason and mind, as we have explained, but also to those three lower powers of the soul, imagination, sense, and the faculty of nourishment: which must be in the soul no less than mind and reason, if indeed it holds a middle place between angels and beasts. Indeed, that power is empty and restless which never comes forth into action. Of these three powers, there is no action without a body, or certainly it does not begin without a body; without a terrestrial body, I say, they do not perform their operations, neither individually nor entirely.
[Marginal note: A] Add that Plotinus says that the soul clearly perceives its powers and nature through actions; and unless all are brought forth, it will not perfectly know itself and its own.

--- Page 677 ---
ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL. BOOK XVI. 298

But since their acts and effects are entirely changeable and temporal, it is fitting that they operate for a certain time: that which acts temporally, operating on temporal things for a time: for this reason, such a body is given for a time. But since the operation of the mind and its handmaiden reason can be continuous towards perpetual objects, they rightly operate perpetually, even when the three other powers are sometimes inactive.

But for what reason is the soul's dwelling here so brief? Plotinus answers, that having laid down its burden, it may depart more quickly to better things. A brief life suffices for fulfilling these duties, for the sake of which it came here. But in what way is it fitting for the eternal soul, that now it descends to the earth, now it ascends, and as if playing, now it is in the body, now it is outside?

(The souls) of men manifest themselves always and continuously, though at different times to different people. The souls of the succeeding spirits (manifest) always, but not continuously. Always: because they do this in all ages. Not continuously: because they intermit. Our souls (manifest) neither always, nor continuously. But if it is not against nature for something to descend from sublime bodies at individual moments to lower regions and again ascend, like the rays of stars and flames, then it is also not against nature for something from the sublime [Marginal note: E] spirits to descend here daily, as it were, and ascend.

Likewise, it seems consistent to the Platonists that just as angelic lives are always separated from bodies, but brute (lives/souls) are never separated, so there are two intermediate types: first, the happier souls, which are always partly separated, partly conjoined, without any impediment to action; then also the less happy (souls), which are sometimes segregated, but sometimes conjoined – [Marginal note: F] conjoined, I say, to an elemental body, which in some way impedes intellectual action. For according to the Platonists, they always have an ethereal body; but according to Christians, they will eventually always have such a body. I [Marginal note: G] omit that the Platonists believe not only our souls, but also the souls of many daemons, sometimes change their own bodies.

Indeed, they believe that divine goodness both pours itself into others and converts others to itself. Hence (they believe) souls have the ability to rule bodies; hence (they have the ability) to apply themselves to incorporeal things; and those which can perfectly do both at once do not change bodies; but those which are otherwise, rightly change (them).

Hence [Marginal note: H] arises that common disagreement. What is this? The dead do not return; they are not seen; they do nothing. The Platonists, however, think they do return in other forms. But in truth, what need is there for a veteran and retired soldier to return to battle? If the return to battle were according to nature, then all would certainly return. If it is against nature, do not seek anyone's return. A superfluous return is certainly against nature, if it was according to the laws of providence for those who had fulfilled their duty to depart from here.

The sphere of fire often ignites a flame in the air; the flame a little later returns into the sphere. Do not seek a more frequent descent of that flame. If he had sailed, he would have perished in a shipwreck. Simonides returned; the others suffered shipwreck. All these things teach that the souls of the dead have some effect on us.

Sixth Reason, that the world may be adorned, God may be worshipped. Chapter 6.

But so that we may conclude the preceding discussion with a fitting end, the divine craftsman wished to make the work of the world as similar as possible to himself. And it is such, if it is everywhere most full of reason. Indeed, just as in Him there is reason, both uniform and omniform at the same time, so in His handiwork He wished there to be one rational soul, and many: namely, one for a single sphere, and many for many. And because each sphere imitates its whole, therefore He also placed many (souls) in each sphere, so that just as sphere contains sphere, so soul might contain souls. But He decreed that there should be at least as many souls in the highest (heaven) as there are stars, which, since they imitate their own sphere, each also revolves around its own center, and have been endowed with their own movers for their own motions. For it is probable that they also have their own lives beyond the life of the sphere, if only they are more excellent bodies than those of terrestrial animals, which have obtained their own lives. I omit that each of the celestial souls—

and of air and water flow everywhere. Wherefore, no one should find it strange both that celestial souls are sent down to earthly things, and conversely, that foreign inhabitants of the earth are sometimes sent back to heavenly things. Finally, whatever the nature of the earth, man is its master. He is indeed a god on earth. Nor should the human soul be considered less divine because it is surrounded by a fragile body, but for that very reason, most divine: because even in the earthly dregs – if indeed the earth be vile – despite both the nature of the place and the burden of the body, it performs such divine works that while it governs lower things, it does not depart from higher things. All Platonists, with whom Dionysius the Areopagite agrees, consider it to be the natural office of divine minds that they remain in their own nature, that they proceed by providing and acting, that they themselves are converted by recognizing themselves and their origin, and that they convert what follows. Therefore, the soul, being divine, fulfills these three things to the best of its ability: and it is not so much attracted to this governance of lower things by a loving affection due to kinship, as by a certain innate zeal for providence because of the excellence of its nature. For all the most excellent things, overflowing with inner perfection, propagate themselves most widely. And as Plotinus says, the Good itself begets intellect with its outpouring splendor. The intellect also, while it unfolds, brings forth the rational soul. The soul itself, propagating itself, produces life and corporeal form. Hence Dionysius the Areopagite. Indeed, the divine unity, being united with all things, in turn unites all things, while it gathers into one those things that are equal among themselves, due to similarity of quality, by a certain mutual consent; but it turns lower things towards higher things due to their need, with a desire to partake; and it bends higher things towards lower things due to their abundance, with a zeal for providing, so that they may imitate divine providence. But the Platonists assert that rational souls imitate divine providence in four ways. Indeed, in the first degree, they place the soul of the world: in which there is universal providence concerning the world, under God, through which it bestows all things upon all. But in the second, the souls of the twelve spheres, in which there is universal particular providence: through which, namely, they distribute certain things to all worldly beings. In the third, the souls both of stars and of any deities reigning in any sphere of the world. Among whom they believe there to be particular universal providence: by which, namely, to certain ones...

...to the members of the world, which are appropriate to them, they distribute individually. Finally, in the fourth [degree], particular souls: those, namely, which recur from the intelligible to the sensible, and vice versa. They believe that their particular providence is such that they impart only some things to some [beings]: moreover, they fulfill [this] through many courses of life: which the higher [souls] accomplish in fewer periods, and the first [soul] completes in a single circuit. Indeed, Plotinus and Proclus argue that just as one circuit of the world embraces many, Saturnian, Jovian, Martian, Solar, and others in succession: so one inner circuit of the mundane soul, through its species, contains many particular souls: since a higher soul traverses a longer orbit around intelligible things, and a lower [soul] a shorter one. Indeed, I wanted to be more extensive in recounting these things, because the Platonists believe that through these, especially, both what is in this chapter and what is touched upon in the preceding chapter, are explained and confirmed. But let them see to such matters themselves. For me, it is sufficient to have narrated [them].

**Third question: for what reason are souls, if they are divine, affected by disturbances? Chapter 7.**

It was asked, thirdly, for what reason souls, if they are divine, are subject to disturbances. But no one would ever wonder at this, if we would sometimes consider that no mind has been given a body more burdensome than the human one. Indeed, the minds of the spheres, stars, and higher demons preside over simple bodies, which are so constant in a certain unity of similar parts that nothing of themselves flows out: and therefore, nothing new needs to flow in. Again, by natural agility, they are so inclined to motion that they live and are moved by the slightest nod of those minds. On the contrary, the human body is composed of four warring elements, and is slowed down by the weight of water and earth. Therefore, by the dissension of its parts, it is dissolved almost every moment, and by its weight, it falls, becoming less fit for life, and slower to move. Also, because of the internal dissension in which humors expel each other, something always flows out of the body: and again, it is necessary for something to flow in.

--- Page 686 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Therefore, to reconcile, move, and restore a body of this kind, our soul needs the most intense attention. To this points that Platonic saying: "Sublime bodies approach sublime souls; inferior souls approach bodies." Because, obviously, the former yield to the latter most easily, while the latter yield to the former with the greatest difficulty. And if any of those higher minds were enclosed for a decade within the confines of our body, perhaps it would be burdened and troubled by care not much less than our soul; and we would distrust its divinity, just as we now distrust our own.

But someone will say that the soul of the world has a body composed of four elements opposing each other, yet it is not wearied by such care as our soul is by our body. This is indeed true. But the very elements that are members of the mundane body are not parts of other elements, but whole and complete elements, not outside their natural places, but each disposed in its own regions. They are not confused with each other everywhere, but are distinct in their proper seats. They are not subject to external bodies. For no body exists outside the world. On the contrary, the fire of our body is not whole fire, but some part of a larger one. So too the other three. Therefore, the elements of this body are imperfect. They are also outside their own proper places; therefore, the fire and air that are in us always flee from here to the sublime, while water and earth fall to the lowest. But it is most difficult to perfect the imperfect, to reconcile warring elements, to detain bodies outside their natural place. Moreover, those four are mixed in us in every particle of the body, which causes the struggle to rage more vehemently everywhere; in the world, however, they are somehow discerned in certain places, and rest more peacefully. Many things, also, and uncreated things outside us, which threaten us from all sides, afflict the body; by these burdens and labors neither the soul of the world is oppressed, nor even the souls of the elements, to whose bodies whatever approaches or departs has scarcely the momentum of a single atom. Restoration is also tempered everywhere; nor does natural harmony ever jar: harmony, I say, of the spheres conducive to salvation. But not even they, however divine, can so restrain the impetus of the spheres that parts of the elements and composite bodies do not devour and destroy each other, and floods of fire and water often per-

--- Page 687 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVI. 305

often disturb. Yet such conflicting qualities could not in any way be produced and guided by heaven, unless their virtues were in it. Nor would they be in heaven, unless they were in the movers and the creator of the heavens. But in God they are one form, distinguished only by reason; in angels, however, they are further distinguished by forms; in souls, by motion, and also by time; in heaven, also by place and at the same time by virtue; finally, under heaven, by effect and by conflict. [I] Why these things? So that we may understand that the souls of the elemental spheres do not have such great power as to so moderate and reconcile qualities which do not conflict with each other in heaven, that under heaven they do not fight each other and destroy themselves. There are those who say that celestial substance, by its excellence, reconciles them; but matter which is under the elements, being formless, unstable, ineffectual, can neither contain them simultaneously, nor reconcile them. Be that as it may: it appears that the souls of the elements, if they have souls, cannot entirely pacify them simultaneously; which not even the soul of the world can do; so it is not surprising that our souls labor so much in tempering the humors, and are discordant in a region of discord. But entirely, a governance both easier and more fortunate has been assigned to higher souls. But if our soul presided over the reins of the mundane body as they do, it would perhaps dispose with the same ease as they. But some divine minds also had to be sent into the particles of the earth, lest the king of the world be celebrated less in the parts of the earth than in the heavens and the whole elements. This lot fell to our souls. Hippocrates writes that changes which are both sudden and greatly to the opposite bring about very great and lasting diseases. [A] Plato, however, in the seventh book of the Republic, believes that the soul, slipping into the body, suddenly rushes from the highest light into extreme darkness; so it is not surprising that it is blind and disturbed for a very long time. Its disturbance increases (as Proclus argues in the Timaeus) because it slides down from unity into a discordant multitude, from a state into a change almost devoid of all rest; whence it is always distracted, and as if affected by dizziness, it stumbles and wavers. Nor does that vital shadow of its own, naturally delivered to the body, easily permit it to emerge from so many waves and such great storms, for which shadow, as if its offspring, it (the soul) is affected by vehement love; and while that (shadow/body) suffers daily, it (the soul) also suffers in its own way. Perhaps indeed as long as

--- Page 688 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

the soul by no means perceives itself, thinking itself to be nothing other than a shadow openly appearing in the river of the body, just as Plato teaches in the seventh book of the Republic. Nor does it disturb itself otherwise, when this shadow is disturbed, than if uneducated boys, when they see their shadows confused in the water, were to lament grievously.

The Platonists indeed posit such an order among souls: namely, some never descend into generation, that is, into a generable body, such as divine or proximate souls; others indeed descend into generation, and from a better life into a less good one: yet in such a way that they are by no means corrupted by it, nor undergo any evil; such as they count among daemons and heroes; others descend at the same time, and are in some way corrupted, but can be purified again and transfer themselves back to better things.

They add that in the highest souls, no fault is found either according to essence or according to action; but in the lowest shadows of souls, according to both. In our souls, however, action can indeed be corrupted, but essence by no means.

Most people think that the difficulty of human life is furthermore increased by this, because the movement and state of the soul, insofar as it is intellectual and rational, ought to be circular. Similar also is the movement and figure of the ethereal vehicle. But in the composite body, the soul, by vegetating, sensing, and progressing, in some way undergoes a rectilinear motion, having abandoned its circular motion. The vehicle also is compelled to change its movement and figure. And although it is not destroyed according to its substance, because, as some think, it lacks matter: nevertheless, it is disturbed according to its figure and movement. Which it will finally recover, when first the mind, raised into its head, that is, its intellect, will be completely restored to its proper state. Which it seems to have entirely lost for so long as, through intemperance, it fixes its head, that is, its mind, to the ground: but lifts its feet, that is, the lower powers of the soul, on high: by which state indeed nothing more deformed or more laborious can be conceived.

But why was no aerial body given to us, in which we might cultivate the earth and more freely contemplate celestial things?

Because its own spirits are present to the air: in this way, they would have been lacking to the earth.

And if simple bodies are not devoid of reason, then some composite and earthly bodies must in turn possess reason: so that this corporeal world may be entirely rational, just like that spiritual world.

--- Page 689 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVI. 304

...according to whose model this is made, is entirely reason. But that best father wished his priests, who sing to him in the higher spheres, to remain there always the same: because, due to the blessedness of the place, they lead a life without labor there. But on earth, he did not wish his priests to endure long stays: because perpetual or long labor is not owed to those who diligently praise God. Therefore, he sends them down here daily, and calls them back: so that through succession on earth, what always happens through the same life in the heavens may always happen. I omit that many also in [Marginal note: E] the air think the souls of demons and heroes change their bodies, though more slowly, yet sometimes for the better. But let it be, someone will say, that our soul has a more burdensome body than other minds, and therefore is sometimes troubled, and is more hindered from contemplation than others: but why does it have a more fragile body than beasts? Not because it has a more fragile body is it therefore to be thought less divine: rather, because it is more divine, to have a more fragile bo- [Marginal note: F] dy. We have argued elsewhere that our body is the most temperate of all earthly things, and most similar to heaven: so that it may offer a more peaceful service to the functions of the celestial soul. But this temperance is necessarily followed by weakness. A constitution in which heat excessively prevails is scarcely harmed by heat and cold. For immense heat overcomes lesser heats, so that by comparison with it they scarcely appear: and it breaks the assault of cold. And if in some constitution cold prevails: not every coldness applied from outside is perceived, and heat is easily tolerated. Similarly, where humidity or dryness prevails. But where these four qualities are moderate and are mixed in harmonious temperance: whatever new quality arrives forces one of those four qualities to exceed; and with that exceeding, the harmony of the former constitution perishes, and the natural state is dissolved. Therefore, because the most temperate constitution of all earthly things was necessary for man, but this (constitution) is harmed by any slight offense: it followed that the nature of the human body would be weak. However, to this weakness comes aid from the diligent industry of our arts: by which it happens that our temperance may persevere longer against the storms of the world. For thus the divine artisan balanced all things: so that in beasts, with the weakness of the soul, he endowed strength of body; but in us, with the weakness of the body, he compensated with strengths of the soul; and thus signified that of beasts

--- Page 690 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY
that the souls [of beasts] are destined for the death of the body, but ours [human souls] are dedicated to the perpetual life of the mind; yet these must always labor outside their homeland.
G For the temperate constitution, which is most natural to the human species, as we have said, is compelled to become discordant from all sides due to innumerable causes, both from the beginning in many individuals and daily in each. And therefore, continuous and most intense attention of the soul is necessary, even if we scarcely notice it, to restore the very temperateness of nature. This most difficult and perpetual labor of the vegetative power not only greatly relaxes and interrupts the mind's intention, from which we, as it were, do not use our mind, but also secretly affects us with many disturbances and agitates us as if dreaming. Indeed, while it operates, subject to tempering these or those qualities, it meanwhile, using its appropriate seminal reasons for these, arouses in the higher sense images and affections especially pertaining to those qualities. Therefore, in secretly dealing with bile, a propensity to anger thus arises. In stirring the blood, vain joy. In phlegm, weariness and laziness. In black bile, fear and sadness. But often, images and affections of this kind grow so strong that, with reason being entirely absent concerning such things, madness follows. Moreover, in many cases, while it strives to thin out coarser spirits, it reveals the dullest. While in others, it strives to gather looser spirits, it shows them to be unfit for the assiduity of contemplation and memory. If ever we say that the mind collects the dryness of the spirits, we wish it to be understood thus: not that it acts upon the mind, but that the mind does not labor in gathering the spirits, from which it is compelled to be diverted from contemplation. Finally, just as the external sense is offended when it deals with troublesome things, so too the interior sense, perceiving many intrinsic offenses of the spirits brought about by various humors and causes, arouses troublesome images and affections.

H Enough now concerning the causes of burdensome governance. But concerning the vices of the soul, although we have said something, something more must be said. I omit that Plato proves in the Laws, and Plotinus confirms, that since the soul precedes the body and dominates it: it does not A so much have a corporeal affection from the body, as it immerses itself into the body through such an affection of its own. Indeed, this B opinion agrees with Zoroaster and in a certain way with Moses, who say that the evils of the body proceed from the faults of the soul. From the very beginning, three such powers undertake this kind of work with such great intention for the fabrication of the nascent body, that there is almost no attention of the soul to reason until, with the body matured and the senses purified, the intensity of this work subsides. But when reason first awakens: with the greatest difficulty it weakens the dominion of imagination, confirmed by long use in the soul: since it is indeed arduous to resist either nature or habit. Here, however, one must fight both against a habit confirmed beyond nature, and against a natural affection. This it nevertheless achieves at last through more diligent discipline. But in the meantime, reason itself, because of its natural kinship and providence, loves those three lower powers as if they were sisters or daughters. Therefore, it often obeys them. They naturally take care of the body. Therefore, reason also, through them, declines towards the body out of love. From long declination, it contracts for itself a habit of inclining more readily. A habit of this kind we call a vice, indeed even a certain (if I may say so) destruction: because just as it usually happens in many species of animals, after the lower power has enveloped itself in natural threads in fabricating the body, often the higher power gradually weaves the commenced work with a stronger web: and finally, enclosing itself secretly beneath the hardest texture, it destroys itself: not to rise again into the light until the concrete texture is broken. D For in every age we seek all truth through the intellect: we love all good through the will: we worship God, who is truly all good, through our actions. These three duties of virtue signify that the soul, even in such a tempest of this sea, always looks up to heavenly things: by contemplating which it is daily seized by a more vehement love for them. By love of this kind, as it grows fervent, the love of the body, by which the soul had been corrupted, gradually cools down: and the stains of vice are abolished. Therefore the soul is never forced from elsewhere: but by love it plunges itself into the body: by love it emerges from the body. To this tends that divine saying:

E 'He who loves his soul in this world, loses it. He who hates it here: receives it in eternal life.'

But what kind of [soul] it becomes and appears to be in this sea, Socrates expresses thus in the tenth book of the Republic. For it is not fitting that the divine mind should be so deceived and attacked by the senses, otherwise than when demons are striving for the same end. But the Platonists think that the violence of such envious and ambitious demons can be overcome through philosophy and sacrifices, which the Orphic hymns demonstrate to us. But Christ, the true physician of souls, commands this to be done by fasting and prayer. If it were permitted to expound the oracle of God himself philosophically, I would interpret fasting as abstinence from those things which either increase a certain humor, or move an image and affection. And I would explain prayer as such a vehement turning towards God, that the mind neither perceives the goads of demons, nor do the demons despair of being able to overcome a mind dedicated to God. But let us now conclude the discussion. Let no one therefore say that the soul of man is less divine on this account, because it is troubled in caring for the body, because it is corrupted. For a much harder province is assigned to our mind than to other minds. Nor is the soul corrupted by the body, but by loving the body too much, it corrupts itself: it purifies itself. Nor should it be thought that divinity is lacking to us on this account, because we live much more anxiously than beasts. Indeed, it is precisely from this that we are most divine, because, deprived for a time of our heavenly dwelling and homeland—namely, as long as we are God's vicars on earth—we are continuously troubled, even if we hardly notice it, by the desire for our heavenly homeland: nor can any earthly delights console the human mind, desirous of better things, in this exile.

**Fourth question: Why do souls unwillingly depart from bodies.**
**Chapter 8.**

[Marginal note: A]
The fourth question proposed to us was, why, if souls are heavenly, do they depart from earthly things so unwillingly? First, indeed, not all depart unwillingly. And those who keenly gaze at the splendor of the mind with eyes of reason not yet purified by philosophy: are struck back by its rays, grow dull, and waver. For since nothing is more present to the eyes of reason than the very substance of the mind, it is not likely that it is unknown to us because of its minimal light, but because of its maximal light. He, therefore, who will behold both the pure mind and with purified eyes of reason: he will not only not distrust, but will revere it as a divine power. But although some distrust, very many nevertheless trust. And those very ones who seem to distrust, at the same time hope that they will be perpetual. Nor can such a hope ever be entirely uprooted from our mind, inasmuch as it is naturally implanted in us. Those kinds of ideas are usually fallacious which have their origin either by some chance or by use from the senses: which the opinion of eternity certainly does not have, since the senses perceive nothing but what is perishable: and sometimes compels us to suspect, lest perhaps those who have departed from life are nothing more after they are seen nowhere. Therefore, the hope of immortality follows the natural instinct of reason, since the mind hopes for it not only without the senses contributing, but even against their will. I certainly am accustomed to admire nothing more than that each of us hopes for this, inasmuch as we are always engaged among perishable things, and yet we do not cease to hope.

I also deem that worthy of consideration, namely, that it would not be surprising if men, even if they had more evident reasons concerning immortality than concerning all other things, would still distrust these very reasons more in this matter than in others. For what we love greatly, we greatly fear for it. But we love nothing more than eternal life, for this reason especially, because it is most natural to us. Indeed, from the very fear of death, we can conjecture that some sense remains for us after death. For if the soul therefore fears death because it hates perpetual darkness, and hatred proceeds from a diversity of nature, then the soul is perpetual light. Or at least it discerns eternal darkness no otherwise than through some eternal light; it cannot behold this without immense light. If the light of the soul, which is its mind, relates to light itself as the life of the soul relates to life itself, and the light of the soul is reflected upon immense light, then necessarily the life of the soul embraces infinite life. Furthermore, because life agrees more with life than light with life: if the light of the soul in its own way, that is, by understanding, reaches immense life, much more does the life of the soul in its own way, that is, by living, attain infinite life.

Moreover, he who dreads darkness consults with himself whether he will always live without a body, or cease to be. This very consultation signifies that the soul, having left the body, then withdraws into itself. For the body does not reflect into itself, nor is it raised to a life separated from the body. In that very consultation, it judges how much more excellent is eternal life, free from a mortal body, than either present life or the privation of life; and it desires a free and eternal one. But it could not judge and desire thus, unless it first experienced such a life within itself. If a free life is far different from a servile one, and yet the soul, enclosed in the body, experiences and exercises it, how much more can it fulfill it when freed from the body? Moreover, in the same deliberation, the mind debates whether it can do something by itself, with the body laid aside, or not. And if it can, it does not doubt that it will live apart from the body, where even now, although it leads life with the body, it nevertheless acts somewhat without it, when it judges what that very thing is and of what kind it is, which is said to operate without the body.

DE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS. BOOK XVII. 309
Fifth question: what is the state of the soul before it approaches the body, and what is it also after its departure. Chapter 1.

[Decorative initial S] But now let us undertake the fifth discussion, through which that question may be resolved, [Marginal note: B] which inquired what the state of the soul is before it approaches the body, and what it is also when it has departed. In these matters which pertain to theology, six supreme theologians once agreed: of whom the first is said to have been Zoroaster, head of the Magi; the second, Hermes Trismegistus, prince of the Egyptian priests. Orpheus succeeded Hermes. Aglaophemus was initiated into the sacred rites of Orpheus. Pythagoras succeeded Aglaophemus in theology; Plato succeeded Pythagoras, who comprehended, augmented, and illuminated all their wisdom in his writings. But since all of them covered the sacred divine mysteries with poetic veils, lest they become common to the profane, it happened that their successors interpreted theology differently. Hence [Marginal note: C] the multitude of Platonic interpreters divided themselves into six Academies: of which three were Attic, the rest foreign. Of the Attic ones, the Old flourished under Xenocrates, the Middle under Arcesilaus, the New under Carneades; of the foreign ones, the Egyptian under Ammonius, the Roman under Plotinus, the Lycian under Proclus. But although there were six schools of Platonists, those three Attic ones along with the Egyptian understood whatever was written by Plato concerning the circuit of souls differently than the words sounded; but the two subsequent ones observed the very face of the words more carefully. Now, in what manner these two Platonic schools explain the mysteries, let us diligently review.

Plato's exposition on the soul according to the two last Academies.

Such a power they call the most common matter, that is, a force equally receptive of all forms: which by its nature neither inclines towards being itself, otherwise it would not need a divine shaper; nor towards non-being, otherwise it would not obey the shaper; but equally towards being and non-being: likewise it holds itself equally as a kind of medium towards such and such forms, and is determined by the shaper. --- Page 702 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**
For the present, I will set aside the mixture of other things; and in what manner the Pythagoreans **A** and Platonists mix the soul from these kinds, I will soon explain, if first I warn, lest by chance we think that, even if most of these say the soul has always existed, they nevertheless believe it to be entirely from itself. For since the soul does not unfold its entire operation, through which it always operates, all at once, but gradually, it is clear that it does not possess this infinite power of always operating entirely at once. For if it possessed it entirely at once, it would also produce it entirely at once and as a single entity. For every operation of a power (as they say) is one of one. Therefore, it always receives the power of always acting. Therefore, it does not act similarly, but differently at different times; so that it can be said in summary, whatever acts temporally, whether body or soul, indeed continuously receives the power of operating gradually, but never possesses the whole entirely at once. Wherefore **B** the soul is judged by the Platonists not only to always exist, but also to be always generated, namely, insofar as it gradually draws its power and internally unfolds forms differently at different times, and continuously varies its affections and actions. Therefore, insofar as it is itself the vital cause of its own motion, it in a certain way supplies to itself an essential and unending life, and is thus considered to exist; but insofar as it unfolds this over infinite time, and gradually receives such power from higher sources, it is indeed judged to be perpetually generated by another. Added to these points is that the supreme principle of things is present to all things, so much so that individual things everywhere participate in the principle according to their nature; otherwise they would suddenly vanish. But the soul is not present to all things. For not all things live. Likewise, the first principle itself must be absolutely one. For if it were a multitude, it would undoubtedly have the cause of its unity above itself, since to unite is not the function of a multitude, but rather of unity; but to say that the first principle is a scattered multitude **C** is an abomination. Yet every soul is a multitude. Again, the first principle is conceived as being above all essence, since every essence admits of multitude within itself, at least such as we have enumerated in the preceding parts. But the soul is a certain essence, namely, vital and life-giving. Finally, the first principle can neither be contaminated anywhere, nor ever, nor in any way; yet very many souls are sometimes, and somewhere, and in a certain way, infected. Wherefore the soul necessarily [derives] from a higher [source].

--- Page 703 ---

its essence is somehow composed by its own principle. Moreover, in things composed by God above the soul, the functions which look to the end surpass the opposite kinds by a very long interval; but in things following the soul, the opposite happens. But indeed, in the composition of the soul, kinds are more equally fitted to kinds. For since the soul is the truest medium of all things composed by God, it is fitting that it be composed in a certain most equal and middle way (as far as possible). Therefore in it, to omit other things, the divisible is harmonically tempered with the indivisible, the other with the same, motion with rest, as if a sharp note with a grave one. Indeed, in those things which are above the soul, three things are especially considered: essence, life, intelligence. [D] In these also which are below the soul, three in turn: quality, nature, sense: so that sense is a likeness of intelligence, nature of life, and quality finally is the ultimate image of essence. In the superior things indeed, according to essence and life and intelligence, the indivisible surpasses the divisible; the same also exceeds the other, and rest (exceeds) motion; but in the inferior things, the exact opposite happens. But in the soul, as being the medium of all things, a mode, as it were, middle through all things, is observed. Hence, whether you compare it to the extremes of the world, it is judged to be a medium between minds, as being very indivisible, and qualities, as being entirely, that is, divisible in time and place. Or to its own extremes, namely to its mind on the one hand, and on the other hand to the life immersed in the body, likewise it is equally considered to be a medium between the individual and the divisible. Or finally, if you compare it to its very own medium, namely reason: even this very reason, when it rises to the intellect and universals, is called indivisible; but when it declines to the senses and particulars, it is named divisible; and there it attains identity (so to speak) and rest; but here in turn it undergoes alterity and motion. And while it somehow ranges in considering eternal things, it intermingles divisible motion in a divided state. But on the contrary, while it somehow rests in itself in attaining temporal things, it in turn tempers divisible motion with a certain divisible state. Moreover, just as the soul of the world, in moving the heaven which is called ἀπλανὲς, that is, inerratic, shows alterity in the same; but in moderating the planets which are somehow erratic, through itself

--- Page 704 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...it seems to preserve the order of motion in the other in turn. But up to this point, the same surpasses the other. Finally, in governing inferior things, the same now allows itself to be surpassed by the other. Similarly, the human soul seems to relate to three quasi-vehicles, namely the ethereal,
E the aerial, and the composite body. Now therefore, what Timaeus means when he uses musical proportions in composing the soul can be sufficiently understood. For he means nothing else than that the soul is composed both from the very kinds of things and from its own powers in such a way that it most aptly corresponds,
F first to its own ideas, then to itself, and thirdly to other things. The Pythagoreans are accustomed to use mathematical figures as well as numbers in depicting the soul: because just as mathematics, so too do souls hold a middle position between natural and divine forms. They therefore construct a triangle: at whose apex a unity is placed: from which three numbers flow out on each side, here even, there similarly odd: specifically in this way, that on one side first, two, then four, finally eight: on the other side first three, then nine, lastly twenty-seven. By these, they believe all parts, powers, and functions of the soul are designated. For those things that are above the soul are considered unified rather than numerous. But those things that are below the soul are indeed numerous, but in themselves most dissonant. But the soul is first called numerous because, since it is closest to corporeal multiplicity, it is now understood to be manifold both in its motions and in its powers. Then, since it is the nearest principle of ordered motion and generation, it is concluded by probable reason that its numerosity is most consonant: from whose consonance, the continuous consonance of the body, both celestial and elemental, depends no differently than that harmony which is in the mind of the musician, and that which is subsequently felt and accustomed to flow in voices and sounds.
G Therefore, Philolaus, having named God unity in the Pythagorean manner, soon after called extended matter duality, because just as duality itself is the first division among numbers: so the dimension of matter is primarily the cause for forms to become separated and repugnant to each other. Therefore, they believe that the soul, depending on divine unity, infuses itself into matter as if into duality, no differently than a triangle from its highest angle similarly ends in two angles. Kinds and circuits of souls according to the two last academies. Cap. 3.

There are four kinds of souls. There are divine souls, that is, the souls of the spheres of the world and of the stars: which are therefore called divine, because they are both closest to God and exercise the common providence of the world in the perpetual region. There are profane souls, that is, the souls proper to beasts, devoid of all divinity. But let us dismiss these for the present. Between these extremes, there are two middle [kinds], namely souls always following God: such as the souls of demons and of sublime heroes: which, although they are not properly called divine, nevertheless never depart from God. In this first kind of souls, principles are so arranged that there, indeed, essence, but here (so to speak) identity, in a way, surpasses the other principles. Below these are souls which sometimes follow God, and sometimes abandon Him. In these, the principle which is called "the other itself" seems in a way to surpass the others. Such are the souls of inferior demons and heroes; but more clearly, the souls of humans: which, since they are the lowest of all minds, do not have that power by which they can perfectly fulfill two very different things at the same time, that is, to contemplate divine things through human reason, and to govern earthly bodies. Yet it is necessary for them to do both, since they are born for both. Therefore, they do in turn what they cannot do at the same time. Moreover, they use this alternation in three principal ways. First, they transfer themselves from the intelligible world to the sensible, and vice versa. Furthermore, in the intelligible itself, they perform various kinds of contemplation in turn.
Rr

THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

G Again, in the sensible region, they change diverse species of living.
These vicissitudes, indeed, Plato describes often elsewhere, and especially in the Phaedrus, and there more clearly, where he says that some souls are companions of other gods in heaven, and in contemplating ideas, they perform a mental discourse similar to their god, according to their powers: yet, above heaven concerning divine things, then in heaven concerning celestial things, then under heaven concerning natural things, to be considered gradually. And insofar as they can imitate the gods, to that extent they remain among the superior beings. Likewise, when they repeat multiple circuits from causes to effects, and vice versa: he says that the soul which has beheld the Idea, which is the head of the circuit, does not fall in that circuit which is properly continued through the Idea itself: but then it slips when the bad horse, that is, the power of desiring, incited by the power of generation, already growing strong at its own time, diverts it from contemplating to generating. Then he enumerates nine lives: not because there are only so many, but because they descend through the seven planets, and fire and air: Finally, he describes many transmigrations through lower realms, and a return to higher realms: where many things are undoubtedly more poetic than philosophical.
Therefore, let us now turn to a more philosophical order.
H Indeed, many Platonists think that there is something which has infinite life from itself: something which has it from another: something which has it from neither. Again, that which has it from another, either tends rather to the highest, or to the lowest, or possesses the middle entirely. Namely, that God possesses infinite life, abiding from Himself entirely: and the angel also abiding, but received from God: then divine souls superior to ours, indeed have infinite life from elsewhere, but a flowing one: yet flowing in a certain order, discoursing from species to species, free from all defect and oblivion. Finally, that our souls similarly have infinite life, but not only flowing but also inordinately, and from a better state to a worse: and conversely, mutable both by remembering and by forgetting.
I But souls below ours are in no way partakers of infinite life. Here the followers of Proclus confirm their point, namely that celestial souls also discourse by understanding: because between the gods who behold intelligible things both always and abidingly, and particular souls which behold them both sometimes and by flowing: celestial and sublime souls appropriately hold the middle ground.

Indeed, the soul of man will always be, because it yearns for eternal things. [Marginal note: L]
And it always was, as they say, because it would sometimes have an end, unless it

the four alternating phases of the moon), so our souls,

Which Zoroaster calls palingenesia, that is, regeneration; [Marginal note: A]

PLATONIC THEOLOGY
...all the seeds of things, and that he tempered them in turn with musical measures (as we said above); from which tempering he created rational souls distributed in three grades, so that in each soul there are all the seeds, so that since it is mixed from all kinds of them, it could easily recognize all things through a certain kinship, to move all things and to vivify, and more easily experience an all-form life. What else do we understand by God's bowl than a third essence, midway between divine and corporeal things, sparkling with divine sparks, pregnant with the seeds of corporeal things? From this source three principal kinds of souls flowed forth: divine; always following God; sometimes following God. To the first, the Pythagoreans assign wisdom; to the second, right opinion; to the third, wavering opinion. From this is gathered what we have often said already, that our soul is in a certain way all things, and therefore contains the progressions of all living things within its depths. It does not, however, unfold all of them individually. For it operates more in the first soul than in the second; and these (the second) also more than in the third. Wherefore, although it pertains to all, the soul of man seems to be instituted for many progressions of life. Nor by some violence inflicted from without, nor by a deliberation of counsel is it transferred from life to life, but by a certain natural instinct, such as in this life, teeth, hair, seed, and the rest emerge each in its own time. For just as in the very nature of the universe, so in the natures of individual souls, all things are ordered by a certain eternal law, and they proceed into action in such a way that it is consistent both with themselves and with universal nature. Certainly, a certain harmony arises from all the members of the mundane animal, through which individual parts resonate with each other and with the universe everywhere. Therefore, just as the soul of the world itself produces certain things at certain times, so too individual souls, with implanted seeds, are naturally inclined and disposed at a certain time towards certain kinds of living. And while gradually the affection and action of a past life is relaxed, in turn, that of the succeeding life is intensified, with the nature of the universe everywhere bestowing (it) upon individuals. But it is necessary to remember that, as the tenth book of the Republic teaches, souls descend by fate—that is, because they desire generation—and that they desire it at a certain time arises from a natural instinct connected to the order of the universe; but by free will they choose such a life or such. Lachesis, that is, the lot-giver: because she inserts individual lots into individuals. Clotho, that is, the spinner: because she unwinds for each person their lots, spun from the beginning, in certain orders and times. Atropos, that is, the unchangeable: because in unwinding the lots, she proceeds with unchangeable reason. Plato asserts that the soul, inclining downwards, goes to all these goddesses in this order, namely, that after Lachesis' lots falling upon it, it has naturally desired an elemental life, and with multiple examples of lives proposed, it has chosen by free will a certain life and its guiding daemon, then Lachesis confirms the choice. Then from the same daemon it is led to Clotho and Atropos and Necessity. Who would not see here that the soul, because of the sole affection for this body, soon falls into all the power of the Fates, finally to the Lethaean river of oblivion, namely into this body, from which it immediately forgets divine things? Therefore it signifies that the soul which has drunk first from that river, that is, which has acquired a body for itself with a more vehement affection, forgets more of the higher things, and remembers more slowly; and conversely, the opposite.
