*That Plato is more rightly explained in the manner of the four preceding academies, especially the first and fourth.*
Cap. 4.

[Marginal note: A]
But the four academies older than these differed from them in this: agreeing among themselves that Plato's writings were entirely poetic, but differing among themselves in that Carneades opined that Plato had both thought and treated all things in the manner of the Sceptics, as ambiguous, and had made no choice in any matters. Arcesilaus, however, (believed) that Plato had indeed held nothing certain, but something probable and plausible. Xenocrates and Ammonius together affirmed that he (Plato) had held some things not only as probable and plausible, but also as true and certain: and that these were a few things concerning the providence of God and the immortality of souls. We, therefore, following the footsteps of Xenocrates and Ammonius, do not deny that Plato affirmed certain things about the soul: but many things concerning its circuit, which are treated by him, we understand as poetic, differently than the words seem to signify: especially since he himself did not invent such circuits, but narrated those of others. [Marginal note: B] First, indeed, invented by Egyptian priests under the guise of purifying souls, then sung by Orpheus, Empedocles, Heraclitus in poetic verses only. I omit that Pythagoras always inserted the transmigrations of souls into his customary conversations and symbols. Wherefore we will thus respond to the latest academies. But they rely on two principal foundations: their own reason, and Platonic authority. As for the kinds of things, and the music of the soul Rr iiij

--- Page 714 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...they explain by composition, and again, what they assume in their argumentation, that there are four species of souls: we admit. Again, that our soul can scarcely accomplish both at once, namely, to see divine things and to govern bodies, especially the more inept ones: this too we grant. But we do not think it necessary on this account for it to perform innumerable turns up and down: since it sufficiently performs both duties, if, while it lives on earth, it sometimes cares for corporeal things, sometimes cultivates itself and God; and when it has departed from here, it may more easily govern its vehicle, and more intently apply itself to divine things. Moreover, we concede that the soul is pregnant with the seeds of all lives: and therefore can accomplish the progressions of all of them, yet in such a way that those seeds exist in this very soul according to the mode of the human soul and species: and from them may sprout affections and habits [Marginal note: A] suitable to other species: but never let there be a true transmigration from species to species. For whether the soul is compared to the body as a proper form is compared to its proper matter: or as a proper art to its proper instrument: any soul will not be able to enter any body. For who would dare to say that the form of the moon shapes the matter of a stone: or that the art of music enters the instruments of a potter? Rightly did the divine Iamblichus reject the transmigration of the soul from man into [Marginal note: C] beasts. Porphyry also rejected infinite transmigration: and conceded that it only wandered in the human species for certain ages: and finally asserted that the purified soul of man always adheres to the heavenly father, never to return to the misery of this life: because it could never be blessed, if either it were ignorant that it would return here, when it was at some time to return here: or if it foresaw and feared future evils. Which indeed is confirmed by this, that an unstable good cannot fulfill the natural appetite, which properly recognizes and desires the eternal and infinite. Again, a soul enjoying infinite power, truth, and goodness, neither violence tears it away from there, nor deceit removes it, nor any will diverts it. Not the will of God, whose property it is to convert. Not the will of the soul: which, since it never chooses anything except for the sake of good, has nothing to choose outside of that, in which it entirely recognizes the whole nature of good. Nor does any change of life fall upon a soul living beyond time in eternity. Finally—

DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVII. 317

Finally, to say that the soul, enjoying itself, is sometimes separated from it,
is just as if someone were to say that either the earth, enjoying itself very near the center, or
fire, enjoying itself very near the moon, or iron, adhering to an immense mass of Magnet,
is diverted from there. Moved by these and similar reasons (as I believe),
Porphyrius blushed to rashly tear away the soul, once fixed in its own center, from there.
It also shamed Proclus, Syrianus, and Hermias to cast the celestial soul into the bodies of beasts.
And so that they might repay immense vices with due punishments, they thought that
sacrilegious souls were observed among the souls of beasts: yet not to rule the bodies of brutes:
because if the soul should escape as a brute, it will not be purified thereby, but will be utterly defiled.
For purification does not occur unless there reigns a certain protest of conscience.
Moreover, they assert that if the soul has not always existed, it will not always exist in the future:
how it is condemned, we have said elsewhere, and will say. Therefore, their reasons do not persuade us
to give credence to infinite errors and wanderings of souls, and absurd confusions of species.
But lest they defend their position with Platonic authority, we must remember that
Plato learned Pythagorean wisdom, which had emanated from Zoroaster, from Archytas, Eurytus,
and Philolaus; and when he had traveled the world and examined all other opinions of philosophers,
he finally chose the Pythagorean sect as more probable than the others, which he then illustrated
in his writings. Therefore, he introduces Pythagoreans disputing in his principal dialogues:
Timaeus of Locri, Parmenides of Elea, and Zeno: from whom Socrates in Plato learns what he himself
relates to others in Plato's other dialogues. But three signs, more evident than others, seem to allow us
to judge that he by no means affirmed those Pythagorean doctrines.
First, because he introduces the same people disputing who had once said such things.
Second, because he portrays Socrates as ambiguous in relating what he had heard:
Socrates, who proclaimed that he knew nothing else than this very thing, that he knew nothing.
Third, because what he had written about such matters, he did not confirm in old age.
Indeed, in the books *On the Laws*, which he wrote in his old age, in which only Plato's own person speaks,
he asserted nothing of the kind. And in a letter to King Dionysius, when he was very old,
he said that he had never composed anything about divine matters.

to have been: nor is there any work of Plato about these things, nor ever
will be: as if he had not revealed his own mind, but narrated another's.
Also, in the letter to the Syracusans, which he wrote later as an old
man, he repeated the same things: where he added that no one existed then
or would exist in the future who understood Plato's mind on matters of this
G kind. Rightly so: because he did not write. Does Plato then affirm nothing about
divine matters? Some things, beyond doubt: namely, that God cares for
human affairs, and renders rewards or punishments to the immortal soul for its deeds.
But he affirms nothing else. For these few things he asserts not
only in other dialogues where other persons speak: but also in the *Laws* and letters, where
he himself speaks. He does not assert that the world always existed, but rather
generates it in the *Timaeus*: he generates it, I say, from the beginning of ordered
time, almost by the same reasoning as first Moses, then
Mercurius, as Severus, Atticus, Plutarch, and
H many other Platonists explained. Hence Numenius the Pythagorean ex-
claimed that Plato was nothing other than Moses speaking with an Attic
voice: although Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus,
and Proclus wish for a perpetual generation of the world to be understood
there from Plato. But if perchance it must be explained thus, it will be the
opinion of Timaeus the Pythagorean rather than Plato's. Indeed,
Plato himself says in the *Epinomis* that the stars will either be immortal,
or so long-lived that their own life suffices for them: and they do not
need a longer one. This is consistent with him in the *Timaeus*, namely that the stars
would be dissolvable by themselves, because they were composed from the
beginning: unless they are preserved by the will of the composer. Again, in the sixth book
of the *Laws*, he says that the human race either always existed, or
originated many ages ago. Where he seems to have preferred to choose a beginning
rather than eternity. Aristotle also, when he discusses the nature
of questions, says that the question of the world's eternity is neutral:
as if to say it is not so much a demonstrable opinion as one
probable in some way for both sides. But Plato perhaps means in the *Laws*
that souls exist before bodies in such a way that this is attributed to the
A dignity of nature rather than to time. Although some Christians
also believe that souls precede bodies by some brief interval of time.
He does not confirm in the *Laws* that human souls pass into beasts.
But in the ninth book, he says that according to the fables of the priests,
they (souls) go into other men. And in the seventh [book] concerning-

--- Page 717 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVII. 318

He clarifies how it should be explained if ever they are said to insert themselves into other bodies. Where he teaches that he who is ignorant of necessary doctrines will never be among other men a god, or a daemon, or a hero. As if both these things and those which he sometimes relates about animal bodies are said by comparison to other men; although in the Phaedrus he does not say that the soul of a man passes into the body of a beast, but into an animal life; and in the Timaeus into an animal nature, not into the body of an animal. In the last book of the Republic, the soul of Thersites (goes) not into the body of an ape, but into an ape. In which is understood a change of habit and life rather than of species or body. Moreover, in the Phaedo, after he related in the manner of poets the passage of souls into beasts on account of the punishments of sins, he added that it is not for a prudent man to confirm such things; but that only can be prudently asserted, that they pay some penalties for their misdeeds. He adds that souls purified by legitimate philosophy will live eternally with God without bodies; which indeed he confirms in the Epinomis, saying that a pious soul separated from the body spends the rest of its time in the contemplation of all the most beautiful things. In the Gorgias also, and the Theaetetus, and the tenth book of the Republic, he describes perpetual punishments of the impious on account of many sins which cannot be expiated, and he asserts that such punishments were instituted more for the sake of justice and example than for cure, where he found those inexplicable wanderings of souls. Through these things it is clear that Plato, in the manner of Christians, signified eternal good or evil. But what Christians call purgatory, Plato understood there, where, about to purify the soul, he often revolves it through lower things: namely, not so much through bodies, as through the lives and interactions of beasts. Finally, he restores the purified (soul) to heaven. In the ninth book of the Republic, he depicts the soul of man in this manner. There is a certain mass of many animal heads, as if gathered into a wild globe. From this multiple mass of animal heads, as it were, a trunk sprouts from roots: which trunk on one side is a lion, on the other a dragon. Upon this trunk a man is placed, holding a club in his hand, with which he beats the raging beasts. Finally, the skin of a human body surrounds all those things, through which it appears to be one animal, which is a multiple animal. He wants the mass of many beasts to be the insatiable part of desire. The trunk composed of a lion and a dragon, (he wants to be) the force of anger: which is called a lion when it supports reason, (and) a dragon when it resists.

--- Page 718 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY
Man is reason. After this, Plato commands that we nourish that inner man rather than those beasts: lest, with man failing due to hunger, only beasts remain in us.
Through these things, we are admonished to understand the transmigration of souls not into various species, but into habits. Thus, there will be a tree according to Plato, which, dedicated to nourishment, will be sluggish day and night. A kite, which will live by plunder through concupiscence. A lion, which will fight nobly. A dragon, which will rage cruelly against the human race. A man, who will live by civil reason. A hero, who will investigate natural things. A Demon, who will investigate mathematics. An Angel, who will investigate divine things. For the soul becomes such as the habit it assumes. Such, I say, in the body: such also outside the body. Socrates confirms the same in the Phaedrus, saying: "Therefore I consider whether I myself am a beast more manifold than Typhon, or a more divine animal." And afterwards in the same book, he places a charioteer in the soul, and twin horses: good and evil: namely, the power of reason and of anger and of concupiscence. Where it appears that in the very D powers of the soul there are both man and beasts. In the same way, Parmenides the Pythagorean had depicted the soul in his book "On Nature". Timaeus, also a most noble Pythagorean, says that migration into beasts is falsely introduced to terrify impious men. But Pythagoras himself signified the whole matter thus:
ἢν δ' ἀπολείψας σῶμα, ἐς αἰθέρ' ἐλεύθερον ἔλθῃς.
ἔσσεαι ἀθάνατος θεὸς, ἄμβροτος, οὐκέτι θνητός.
That is, if, having laid aside the body, you ascend into the free ether, you will be an immortal god. Immortal, no longer mortal. As if to say: Thus you will become an immortal god, so that you will be entirely E far from death, never again to return to mortal things. Orpheus also, in the very hymn of Terrestrial Mercury, says concerning Mercury:
κωκυτοῦ ναίων ἀνυπόστροφον οἶκον ἀνάγκης.
that is, dwelling in Cocytus, the irreversible path of necessity. In these words, he places eternal punishments in the underworld: and entirely removes that manifold return from life to life. But not even F all Egyptian priests truly believe that the transits of souls occur from species to species: rather, they wish it to be understood concerning a bestial or heroic habit of the soul, when they assert that a man becomes a beast or a hero: since among

among these, man alone is spirit. This was revealed by Mercury, the chief priest of the Egyptians, who, when he had described a certain such migration in a poetic rite, added a divine law G that did not permit the migration of our souls into the bodies of beasts. He also assigned eternal punishments to impious souls in the lowest elements of this world; and he clearly asserts that the souls of the impious are subjected to eternal torment by an immortal decree. He also gives thanks to God, because He consecrated good men to eternity. Likewise, he says that the mind is so united with God that it is never again entangled in errors. σὸν γὰρ ἀγγεῖον θῆρες χθονὸς οἰκήσουσιν.
that is, your vessel, beasts of the earth inhabit. But if beasts are within us, then also within, not externally, do we pass from man into beast, and from beast into beast. Nor are there lacking those who explain transmigration into beasts thus: that souls which have led a life similar to brutes, I are found among various throngs of beasts. Olympiodorus judges this to be very consistent with Plato, because Plato held that the purest souls dwell among the gods, while impure souls often revolve among tombs: by whose shades we are sometimes terrified: since they have drawn something corporeal around themselves as well as into themselves. By this he means that they can sometimes be seen. K Similar to this is what Pliny the Younger writes, that there was an infamous house in Athens, in which both a noise was heard and the apparition of a dreadful old man was seen. And that Athenodorus the Tarsian philosopher, having rented the house, saw that apparition, and guided by it, discovered bones inserted with chains beneath the ground in the courtyard of the house. He buried them as was the custom. The house was then freed from that noise. He adds that he believes these things affirmed by many. Therefore, it is not surprising if impure souls, among these things, likewise also dwell among brutes. From all these things, we conclude that Plato affirmed only those things concerning divine matters which he approved in his letters and laws L (in these, however, infinite cycles of souls are not approved); and that those things which he merely recounted in other works as ancient discoveries, he held to be probable rather than certain. And if anyone should contend that Plato also affirmed these things, perhaps our discussion

PLATONIC THEOLOGY
On the immortality of souls
by the same author, Ficino,
BOOK EIGHTEENTH.

*That Plato does not forbid giving credence to the common theology of the Hebrews, Christians, and Arabs, that the world was created.*
Chapter I.

[Marginal note: A]
[Large decorative initial P]lato, therefore, seems to not forbid giving credence to the common theology of the Hebrews, Christians, and Arabs, [which states] that the world began at some point: that angels were created from the beginning: [and] that immortal human souls are created daily. To these things we are compelled by divine authority. To these things we are led by reasons of this kind. The mass of the world cannot exist by itself, in such a way that it does not depend on something else, nor can it establish itself in its own being: otherwise it would in a way make itself. But to make something does not pertain to a body: for whatever it seems to do, it performs through a certain incorporeal power lying in the subject: indeed, it pertains to the essence itself, which is entirely incorporeal and remains in itself, and to the origin of that power. Furthermore, a corporeal mass cannot contain itself. Since it cannot contain unless by doing something, especially since it cannot contain without union. But to unite seems to pertain not to a divisible nature, which itself also needs union, but ultimately to a power that is entirely indivisible. Again, the same mass cannot operate or be moved by itself: because if it cannot give being to itself, much less will it be able to perform an action. And conversely if

it could act by itself, it could also act through itself. But
that it cannot operate by itself is also clear from this, that it
cannot move itself, as we proved in the sixth book. We have shown
moreover elsewhere that infinite power is necessary for the perpetual and most ordered motion of the world, which a finite and determined
nature of a body cannot have from itself. And therefore the world,
as if wandering and dissoluble by itself, borrows an indissoluble
order from elsewhere. But from where does it borrow? Certainly,
if the world can neither subsist by itself, nor contain itself, nor
act or be moved by itself, it necessarily depends on a cause existing by itself
and containing itself: a cause, I say, utterly indivisible,
lest it (the cause) similarly either be through another, namely through parts, or a gatherer of parts;
or be contained by another, namely by a unity connecting parts
to each other; or be insufficient, since it would lack parts;
or have non-being mixed in, since a composite of parts
is none of the parts. Therefore, since the world is composed of dissimilar things,
it is necessary to investigate the cause of such a composition.
For a body does not compose itself, which is neither the principle
of action nor of union. Nor must it be said
that the parts of the world flowed together into such a
composition by some motion of their own, for bodies are not moved by themselves.
Nor as if compelled to it from elsewhere, and compelling each other.
For what is it that impels? And what impels first? Again,
it is wrong to entrust such a wonderful order to impulses lacking order.
In what way is such great order and adornment produced from ordered and unordered things,
since the acting cause is always accustomed to be more excellent than the effect? [Marginal note on right:] B
Moreover, if you say that the parts of the world are the material causes of this composition,
we will inquire about the efficient cause. But if (you say they are) efficient causes, again
we will inquire in what way a rational work is produced from things lacking reason.
Therefore, if the world is composed neither from itself
nor by chance, it certainly has a definite cause of its composition.
Nor should anyone assert that it has only a final
cause. For it has it (a final cause), since it is rightly directed towards the good as its end.
But since it is not moved towards it in vain,
it certainly obtains something good from it. But it receives
according to its essence, inasmuch as it desires and is moved
according to its essence. Therefore, it receives being from the same (source) from which
it receives essential goodness.

--- Page 722 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY
Therefore, that cause is as much efficient as it is final. It is also an exemplar. For if the world is carried by a certain reason towards the good, certainly God continuously directs it by a certain reason, as an exemplar, towards that good. But since to lead to an end and to seek the good is the office of will, doubtless God moves the world by will, which He similarly composed by will.

The same is moreover thus confirmed. What is called fortuitous and contingent is accustomed to be posterior to that which is ordered, or consists of determined causes. Therefore, the order of the world cannot have happened by any prior chance. And if someone brings forward many causes of worldly effects, unless he reconciles all under one, he will not be able to state why the world, although it consists of diverse things, is both one and united; and by what reason one whole is better than many parts, unless he finds one cause that is both common and superior to many causes, by whose virtue all converge into one. Wherefore, there is one cause of the universe and of its very union, to which all things are coordinated.

If this (cause) were devoid of reason, men who use reason and know themselves would be superior to the first cause, and human work would be rendered more perfect than divine work. Therefore, God rationally knew His infinite goodness to be propagable through all things; whence His goodness pleased Him to be propagated through individual things, since it is characteristic of the good that it pleases, C and of the highest good, that it pleases supremely. By this affection of rational will, all things were both rationally and optimally created, and are continuously disposed. That the world is disposed by divine reason and will is signified in the Chaldean oracles which Proclus recites, with these words: "The Intellect of the Father, emanating with perfect counsel, understands all-form ideas, which indeed all proceeded from one source." "For from the Father was the will and the end." "But they were distributed by a certain intellectual fire, and then divided into certain other intellectual ones." "For the King placed an indeficient intellectual figure over the multiform world, of which the second world is a trace, hastening together with the form; and the apparent world is endowed with all-form ideas." "One source, from which innumerable other divided ones erupt, producing around the bodies of the world." "Which, rightly assimilated by a certain circuit, are carried everywhere, turned around; but elsewhere other intelligences from the paternal source as from fire..."

--- Page 723 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVIII. 321

...as if from a vigilant spark of fire around the primordial ideas. For the first idea flowed forth from the Father, and a voluntary source. Thus far the oracle, in which mention is made of the father, son, spirit, ideas, angels, and the voluntary disposition of the world. But let us now return to our established topic. Whatever elements and plants do, they operate by a certain necessary affection of their nature. That is only one. Therefore, each operates a single thing. Furthermore, brute animals operate through appetite, which, as it is provoked in various ways through sense, undertakes various things. And just as elements and plants act by innate necessity, so brute animals operate by an imposed necessity. The rational soul acts through will, which indeed is moved to action not by the forms of things, as appetite is, but by the notions and counsels of the intellect. This free operation is deservedly fitting for the perfection of an animal. Such an operation of God ought to be preeminent among others. Therefore Plato in the Timaeus speaks of the will of God as benef-

**THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

were led to confess that the world had a beginning of time. The Egyptians say that the first day of the world dawned in such a way that Aries was in the middle of the **E** sky, Cancer was rising, the Moon in Cancer, the Sun in Leo, Mercury in Virgo, Venus in Libra, Mars in Scorpio, Jupiter in Sagittarius, Saturn in Capricorn; and they say that each of the planets is the lord of those signs in which they are believed to have been when the world was born. The Chaldeans think that the sun was in Aries when the world was born. Both (groups) believe the world was born at some point; and they call Aries the head of the signs, either because the sun was in it, or because it traversed the middle of the sky. Therefore, astronomers judge the fortune of the entire year especially from the sun's entry into Aries, as if almost everything **F** depends on it. I omit that the Egyptians assigned only Leo to the Sun, only Cancer to the Moon; but to the remaining planets, besides those signs to which they then adhered, they added the remaining five in such a way that the second order began from the end of the previous order. Thus, Aquarius, which succeeds Capricorn, is assigned to Saturn, who was the last; then Pisces to Jupiter, who was next to Saturn; Aries to Mars; Taurus to Venus; and Gemini to Mercury. But having omitted these things, let us return to our purpose. Proclus demonstrates that the world, because it has an extended and composite essence, and is therefore inherently divisible and dissipable, is connected solely by a certain individual virtue infused from **G** divine unity. Again, because it is always moved in an orderly fashion by a natural appetite towards the good, therefore the nature of such appetite and motion has received its origin from the divine mind and goodness. And this virtue, by which it is connected and moved, must be infinite, through which it can be connected and moved without end. Which, since it is finite, it cannot have from itself, but always receives from divine infinity: not all at once (for it cannot contain it), but rather, according to its temporal nature, as if it drinks drop by drop at each moment. He shows that this (virtue) flows away suddenly no differently than moments, and likewise, with the moments, a momentary (virtue) is drawn in; and always in this way, as we have narrated elsewhere, the corporeal world flows and comes into being, but in reality never *is*, like the shadow of a prominent tree in a torrent: which, even when it appears to be a tree, is not a tree; and even when it appears the same for a long time, to persist, yet it is continuously renewed by the continuously renewing waves. For to whom then...

--- Page 727 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVIII. 323

...to whom then, therefore, should it seem strange that the world from the beginning proceeded from non-being once into being, since among some it is so shadowy and unstable that in single moments it passes from being into non-being and vice versa? But let Proclus himself consider these matters. Plato, in the book on the generation of the world, shows that the world was created by the grace of divine goodness. But a work of this kind was not established for this purpose, that it might make God, who is goodness itself, better: but that it might reflect divine goodness.
[Marginal note: H]
Just as parents do not generate children for any other reason than that their image may be seen in their children. But especially the world reflects the goodness of God the creator, if it shows not only how munificent it is, but also how excellent. How munificent it is, it shows inasmuch as it is always preserved unharmed by God, which, if left to itself, would dissolve, as Plato says in the Timaeus. How excellent, it testifies inasmuch as it began to exist at some point: through which beginning it is clearly perceived that the world is not from itself but from God. Because God exceeds the world by an infinite interval: who was infinite (if I may say so) before the world: because he produced the world from nothing by infinite power: because he acts by freedom of will: not by necessity of nature. Such an origin of the world's generation Trismegistus Mercurius taught more plainly. Nor should it seem strange that he knew such things, if this same man Mercurius was also Moses, which the historian Artapanus shows with many conjectures.
[Marginal note: A]

That angels and souls have not always existed. Chapter 2.

We have established order in bodies: let us establish order in spirits. There is that supreme spirit, which has always been and will be. This is God.
[Marginal note: B]
And there are the lowest spirits of beasts: which neither have always existed, nor will exist. There must be two certain middle spirits between such disparate extremes: who have a part of that first spirit, and a part of the lowest spirits. In what way, therefore, shall we compose these middle ones? Shall we say that they have always existed, but will cease at some point? By no means. For that which has always existed: it has lived infinitely through infinite power. Infinite power is never diminished. Therefore, if they have always existed: they will always exist. And parts in duration belong to God: not to middle spirits. Therefore, that they may be middle in perseverance: o-

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

it is necessary that they began at some point, but never cease. And even if
they were made from nothing, they will not, however, turn into nothing. For
that very thing which we call nothing, in their creation, is neither the
matter nor the efficient cause from which they are made, but perhaps the
limit from which they are made. Nor is it truly a limit: but it is said to be.
Therefore, they are not compelled to follow the nature of nothing itself, by
which they might return to nothing: which nature indeed they had
rejected before, when they first came into being. Rather, they preserve
that nature of their cause, from which they received their essence: so that
by the same infinite power they are preserved in being far from nothing,
by which they emerged from nothing into being, with nothing set aside.
**C** It is not absurd to think that what is immediately begotten by an infinite
beginning and an infinite end, that is, by God, will have no end:
since many things also which proceed from a finite beginning and a
certain finite end, are rightly considered to proceed without end.
For thus, from unity, number; thus, from a point, a mathematical line;
thus, from the present moment, future time is thought to progress
without end, with nothing preventing it.
**D** But that something created will exist forever, especially the soul, not
only religion but also Avicenna and Alganteles prove as philosophers.
Therefore, angels indeed hold one intermediate position between God
and beasts: human souls have obtained the other intermediate position
immediately after angels: these agree with angels in that they will always
exist: they differ in that they did not exist at least through all time like
angels: who, having arisen from the beginning of things in natural order
before the course of the heavens, of which time is a companion,
although they did not exist through all eternity, yet existed through all
time. Our souls, born after the origin of time, yield to angels, yet they
are not temporal. For God, through that very point of His eternity, which
is always the same and transcends the universe, and encompasses the
circuit of time by which He created angels, also creates human souls.
Therefore, human souls are made above the passions of time, although
they are made after the origin of time. But the souls of beasts are
generated both after the origin of time and under the passions of time:
because they are not made by God directly through God's eternity, but
through the revolutions of the heavens and the virtues of souls: which
results in them not living forever. For they are also subject to the change
of time, which were made under time through the motion of the heaven. And

      Souls are created daily.      Cap. 3.

BUT why are new souls created daily by God? Or could not God, having constructed the world, create all souls at once, G
just as He created all angels at the beginning of the world? It was not fitting. For if they had lived for a long time freed from the bonds of bodies, they would have sincerely judged how much more precious a freed life is than an embodied one, nor would they ever have wanted to enter bodies, namely, insofar as they are intellectual. Neither God nor an angel wishes to compel the free will of the soul. For the mind is moved by nothing other than persuasion. Indeed, neither would the soul have known each individual body which it could choose, since it would lack sensory knowledge of particulars beforehand. And so, this middle part of the divine temple would lack divine priests and sacred hymns. It is necessary, however, that in each of the circles of this temple, proper choirs of priests singing to God be led. Moreover, it is consistent with reason that just as the souls of the spheres, or angels, were not created after some delays of time before their own spheres, so neither were our souls (created) before their own bodies. Likewise, the soul is the form and act of the body. H
But although act in the universe, according to the order of nature, is prior to potentiality, yet in the same subject, according to time, it is posterior, because motion is effected from potentiality into act. Therefore, the seed, which is potentially alive, was prior to the soul, which is the vital act. Furthermore, it is natural for every form to be united with its proper matter. Otherwise, that which is composed of matter and form would be some collection contrary to nature. I
But that which is fitting for each thing according to nature is attributed to it first, rather than that which is contrary to nature.
                                Sf iiij

--- Page 730 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

For what is fitting according to nature is inherent in each thing by itself; what comes contrary to nature arises from something contingent. Therefore, for the soul, insofar as it is a soul, it is more fitting that it be joined to a body than separated. How then did it live before the body? Add to this that if any higher mind (as some think) is both one in species and immortal, while any corporeal form is both multiple in the same species and mortal, and the human soul, which succeeds those minds and precedes these forms, will thus participate in both, so that it is either a single soul in one species of humans and mortal, or immortal and multiple. The first cannot happen. For if a single soul were to represent the entire species of souls, it would encompass with its powers innumerable souls that can exist under that species. Thus it would be of immense power, and immortal, especially since the species of things are eternal, and what comprehends an entire species is eternal. Furthermore, because it would have no communion with these corporeal things, it would be very far from destruction. Indeed, if it were such, it would preserve the pure simplicity of its species. That species is separated from a perishable body. Therefore, it would remain in its own purity, alien from mortal bodies, and would not provide life to them. From these points, it is clear that the human soul cannot be single in all humans; again, it cannot be single and mortal at the same time. Therefore, it will be immortal and multiple. By its immortality, it will imitate minds; by its multiplicity, it will imitate thoroughly corporeal forms.

Perhaps this will be consistent with the order of things, that the ideal species of things themselves hold the first rank, and those things that receive species hold the second. And among those that receive, first are those that receive their entire species, according to the creature's capacity, and always. Second, those that do not receive the whole, but nevertheless always. Third, those that receive neither the whole nor always: just as at the highest we place the exemplar of lights, that is the sun; in the second, the stars, each of which receives its entire light from there and always; in the third, the moon, which always receives, but not the whole; and if it seems to suffer an eclipse, nevertheless it suddenly receives it back: similarly air and water. In the fourth, those composites from the elements which are in some way transparent and bright, indeed desire such things, but neither always nor entirely: to omit the opposites, which in no way admit light into themselves.

admit. But how does this one species of soul receive multiplicity? Perhaps not from the fact that it imitates minds. Therefore, from the fact that it imitates corporeal forms. What kind are these? They begin with the body, and end with the body. If our soul is entirely such that it begins and ends at the same time, it does not imitate them: but is of the same kind. And if it has neither of these, it does not imitate, does not agree, does not adhere to them: it does not vivify. Therefore, it will have one or the other: either it will begin only with the body, or it will only end with the body. The mind cannot end with the body, for it is directed towards immortal truth and goodness as its end. For it does all things for the sake of this. But just as concerning the beginning of things we form a conjecture from the efficient cause, so concerning the perseverance of things we are accustomed to draw a conjecture from the end. If therefore the mind is properly directed towards an eternal end by a certain natural kinship, it is capable of eternal perseverance. For a proper end corresponds to a proper agent: the perseverance of a thing directed to an end holds the middle ground between both. The mind therefore, since it has an eternal proper end, also has an eternal proper agent: and therefore, from both sides, perpetual life and perseverance. If it does not end with the body, it at least begins with the body: the soul of man certainly becomes multiple in many bodies. Which indeed is signified by the contrary opinions and affections of men. But such a soul is not made from its own species, through which it is one; but (as some think) in a certain way from bodies; indeed, from God, the reconciler of souls and bodies. Not because it is divided in the body. Not because it is from matter like a body. Not because it is born from the body. From where then, unless because by divine will it becomes the companion of the body? When God at the same time provides a beginning for both, he does not however provide the same principle. Therefore, neither the same nature, nor a similar end: but the same beginning, as we said. From which also he transmits the same number. Hence the affection of the soul towards the nature of the body is increased, because it accompanies the beginning of the body. And in its creation, the change which seems one, is threefold. Indeed, the change of the soul from nothing to being, made by God alone, is creation: but the change of a non-living body to life itself to be received from the soul, is indeed the formation of the body, but is called the generation of an animal. It is fitting for God's immense power to always show itself powerful to the eyes of minds, so that they may see God, in the lowest degree of minds because of the lowest place in the world, continuously creating something out of nothing; so that by this continuous effect they may more clearly recognize God's altogether infinite power, carrying out an infinite act of creation infinitely, if it pleases Him. Let them venerate it illuminating in [marginal note: E] the heavens. Let them admire it (as I might say) creating on earth. Indeed, creation is a more excellent operation than illumination. Therefore, the former is more fitting for God than the latter; the latter is continuous from God. Therefore, the former becomes continuous by God's will. The ministers of God move the heavens. By this motion, subsequent things are generated, while any species of things on earth does something; and in acting becomes a minister of heaven. Does God himself alone do nothing while all other things are working? Far be it that the first act should do nothing, while others are acting. But you will say that He acts sufficiently, while He does not abandon the other agents, but supplies them with the power of operating. That is not enough. For from this, the proper works of other causes follow, and images of those (causes) are made in the world, not of God: why should God not also continuously make His own works and His own images, always creating many things without an intermediary? Therefore, since creation is God's own operation, but external generation is the proper operation of others, God will not cease to create something as long as others do not cease to generate something. God is truly the center of the world, as we discussed in the book on love, because He is one, simple, stable, and in all things; [marginal note: F] and all other things whatsoever are altogether multiple, composite, mobile, and revolve perpetually around Him by their natural appetite for Him. Thus God is the center of all things, because He is in all things in such a way that He is more interior to each thing than it is to itself. He is also the circumference of the world, because existing outside all things, He so surpasses the universe, that He excels the highest peak of dignity of each thing by His immense dignity. Likewise, the more He is the least of all in quantity (if it is permissible to say so), the more He is the greatest of all in power. As He is indeed the center, He is in all things; but as the circumference, He is outside all things. In all things, I say, not enclosed, because He is also the circumference. Outside all things also not excluded, because He is also the center. What then is God? As I might say, a spiritual circle, whose center is everywhere, its circumference nowhere. But if that divine center has some imaginary or clear seat of operation in some part of the world, most of all

Which is a familiar seat to God, not so much because it is a species of soul, as because it is the middle of the divine city, a public treasury, and a harmonious moderation of the urban parts. Someone might be able to suppose that Aristotle thought something of this kind in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*: where, having proved that the intellectual soul is separable from the body, because corporeal operation does not communicate with its operation, he added a little later that some body, separable from the body of generation, is suitable for this soul. From this also appears what we were seeking against Averroes in the preceding discussions, namely that the intellectual soul is a form vivifying the body: especially because when Aristotle had proved in the same place that among the three souls, namely the vegetative, sensitive, and intellectual, only this one (the intellectual) is both from outside and separable from the body, because only its operation can be performed by itself without an instrument, he added that all these three souls are equally in the seed according to potentiality. But truly, if anyone considers these things diligently, he will find that no potentiality can be common to these (souls), by which the body might be in potentiality in an equal manner to the three souls, unless it is a certain faculty by which it receives life and motion from the intellectual soul similarly as from the others. But now let us return to the body closest to the soul. [C] The Magi call this the vehicle of the soul: namely, an ethereal corpuscle received from the ether, an immortal garment of the soul: indeed naturally round in shape because of the ethereal region, but transforming itself into a human likeness when it enters a human body, and restoring itself to its former (shape) when it departs. Which the Magi consider necessary for this reason, because angels are such that they are both separable in potentiality and actually separated from bodies: irrational souls are neither separable in potentiality nor in actuality. From which it follows that rational souls, as being in the middle, ought to be such that they are always separable in potentiality, because if bodies are withdrawn from them, they will not perish: but are always conjoined in actuality: who acquire a familiar body from the ether, which they keep immortal through their own immortality: which Plato calls a chariot of both gods and souls in *Phaedrus*, and a vehicle in *Timaeus*: which [D] the souls of the spheres and celestial beings use, being of the purest (ether), the souls of daemons use a less pure (ether), and ours also less pure because of the earth...

**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**

...of the mixing of the earthly body. For this reason, Zoroaster thus commands:
μὴ πνεῦμα μολύνῃς, μὴ δὲ βαθύνῃς τὸ ἐπίπεδον.
that is, do not defile the spirit, nor increase into the deep what is flat. He calls the spirit and the flat/level the vehicle itself: not because it is not a body and deep, but because on account of its most subtle and splendid purity, it is as if not a body. Therefore, he commands that you do not, on account of too much affection for the elemental body, force it (the vehicle) to remain even after this life, sordid and heavy, **[Marginal note: E]** by the addition of elemental darkness, which ancient theologians called the shadow of the soul. Nor, however, do they wish the rational part of the soul to cling to the nearest vehicle, but the rational soul itself, insofar as it is rational and a companion of the celestial souls, to perform a life-giving act upon the vehicle which we have often already called the idol of the soul: which kind of soul Plato calls mortal in the book 'On the Generation of the World': not because it dies at some point, but because, if the vehicle were removed, it would collapse, as some think. For just as the moon's splendor in a cloud emits paleness from itself, so the soul in the celestial body emits an idol like a comet its tail. Which would vanish, if that body were to vanish, just as paleness is extinguished when the clouds are dispersed. Because, however, the vehicle will never be removed, Zoroaster says:
**[Marginal note: F]** ἔστι καὶ εἰδώλῳ μερὶς ἐς τόπον ἀμφιφάοντα.
that is, there is also a place for the idol in the all-shining region. Because, namely, together with the vehicle and the rational soul, it will return to heaven. Plotinus, however, thinks it (the idol) is simply mortal, **[Marginal note: G]** even if the vehicle is removed from it. And similarly he says that the light of the sun in the air, indeed present to the air, would not be extinguished even if the air were removed from the midst: for it depends on the sun alone as its perpetual act, nor is it a passive affection of the air, or a quality proper to the air. Indeed, it is present and absent in a moment: nor does anything of it remain in the air when the sun is removed. Nor is it only present to the air, but similarly to everything transparent, even if the transparent things are of contrary natures among themselves: as if it does not depend on a specific nature of the subject. Nor does it in any way depend on the transparent, in the way that it is transparent: but it is only present to it, because it is not hindered from being present to it, just as being present to the opaque seems to be hindered. For the sun always emits this act: it does not send it away: it does not send it in. By chance, however, it happens that there is something beneath that can receive it: indeed, that seems to receive it. This act, in turn, perpetually accompanies the sun.

*When the soul is infused into the body: and whither it is led while it lives in the body. Chapter 6.*

[Marginal note: D]
**W**hen is the soul infused into the body? After, in the womb of the woman, the seed itself, which had previously flowed from the whole body of the man, and had drawn with it a formative power from the soul of the man, through this very power, for about forty-five days, it has been so affected, that for the first six days it became milk, for the next nine blood, for another twelve flesh, and for the remaining eighteen it was formed: then the soul is created and infused.

Those who think that souls lived before their entry say that they naturally chose a demon as a guide for life at the very beginning of their descent, before they entered the body. Others, however, say that after they began to exercise choice, by choosing their habits, they meanwhile secretly choose a demon as a guide for life. Often, the same demon is also chosen by many. For many souls can use one genius, that is, one demon as a guide of their nature. Those who believe in choosing beforehand, wish to receive from that particular crowd of demons which is accommodated to the same star to which the soul was assigned by the world's creator himself. For there are as many legions of demons and heroes as there are stars in number. And from such a crowd, to obtain that one above others, who most agrees with that chosen life and the configuration of the heavens, which is composed at that very moment of the descent of choice: and that from these causes, the greatest difference arises in the natures and fortunes of men, while those who say that souls acquire different genii after birth due to the adversity of their habits, also concede that such guides are changed when habits are changed: and they seem to attribute more to counsel than to fate or fortune.

But however it may be, we always need the perpetual guardianship of divine powers. Which indeed Plato, while he says it in the Symposium, Protagoras, Politicus, Critias [Marginal note: E] thus proves in the Laws, namely because we are engaged among false goods and innumerable evils: whence perpetual deception and disturbance arise. And therefore, like sheep, we always need the wonderful guardianship of divine shepherds. He adds that, since our own vice indeed destroys us, but our own virtue, being as it were small, cannot save us: therefore, we can only be saved by the virtue of the superior guardians (whose virtue our own virtue is a certain small image): especially since, as Her[mes] says elsewhere

Through what part of the body the soul enters, through what part it exits, and by what guide it proceeds. Chapter 7.

[Large initial G] As to what part of the body the soul enters, and what part it exits?
The soul, which is the middle of things, by the command of God (who is the center of the world), is first infused into the central point of the heart (which is the center of the body). Thence it spreads itself through all the members of its body, when it joins its chariot to natural heat, and through heat to the spirit of the body. Through this [spirit], it immerses the spirit in the humors: it inserts [itself] into the members through the humors. Finally, when those mediums are dissolved by illness, it immediately gathers itself (so to speak) with that chariot of its own, and flows back into the heart: whence it had first flowed out. When the heat of the heart is extinguished, which was the proper receptacle of that vehicle, it finally leaves the heart, that vehicle accompanying it: just as when an eye is closed, the light of the sun that had flowed into it flows out whole, its own heat accompanying it. And as Plotinus proves, it is not extinguished, but [Large initial H]perpetually follows its sun. I omit for the present that their own genii and demons lead all departing souls to the common judge: but, the judgment having been given, a violent and evil demon drags away the former [souls] and the evil ones; but God tranquilly leads the good ones. These things are in the Phaedo.

This is most fully realized in souls separated from this changeability.

But why do the souls of the elements, and their chariots, not strive towards a heavenly dwelling? Because, so that I may answer according to the opinion of the Platonists rather than my own, a duty has been assigned to them by God, that they should always be there. [Marginal note: L] Souls yield to the divine will. Chariots also yield to the desire of the souls. Those souls do not lose a more excellent duty by this office. The chariots maintain an unimpeded circular motion around their souls. And just as it is natural for the heavens to turn there around their souls, so here for these vehicles around theirs. But our soul, having duly performed the task enjoined upon it here for a time, chooses for itself that region of the ether above others, to which it had been assigned by birth. It flees to that star and deity, as Plato says, to which it made itself similar by living. But let them consider these things.

Therefore, just as on earth, by considering, it proceeded from individuals to common natural species, and from species to divine reasons as natural causes; so in heaven, in turn, it perfectly converts itself from divine reasons, that is, ideas, to natural species, and from these, in a certain way, to individuals.

And what it diligently inspected here individually, it perceives the same things there effortlessly. Again, what divine things it foresaw obscurely, it perceives the same things there so clearly. And what it saw here individually through instruments in external light, there it sees according to species, by itself, in intrinsic light.

Indeed, as much as it was formerly turned to sense, so much is it then turned to the mind, in whose eye divine light shines. Which, although it can be said to be intrinsic to minds, nevertheless depends much more on God himself, and is always preserved by Him, than a ray infused into the eye depends on the sun; and it is full of forms, just as the light of the sun is full of colors. And it shows the forms themselves, and all things through forms, to minds to the extent that they are purely and ardently turned towards it. But to those entirely converted, it reveals at least as many things as the species of things it makes in the world. For it is not fitting to form the mind less than the matter of the world. Nor to attribute less to the mind than it naturally desires; but it desires to comprehend the order of the universe, by which it is also comprehended...

is: which it has long sought with admiration. In which it itself obtains the office of a certain providence. But it foresees individual and lowest things only in light, whether those things were past, or present, or future: as far as it is directed to them by a certain providence or affection. Indeed, just as old men neglect or laugh at the games of boys, philosophers at the studies of common people, the waking at the dreams of the sleeping: unless necessity sometimes demands otherwise: so much more do segregated minds neglect these individual and contingent things of ours, unless a certain providence has been entrusted to them by the Father of all (whose nature is providence itself: whose action is to provide: whose office is to provide for all). Plotinus proves that such souls, both from the opinion of the ancients and from his own reason, care for their own: and often [Marginal note: A] publicly benefit the human race with prophecies and other good deeds. But since the providence of these (souls) agrees with the divine will, they are not touched by any disturbance from our affairs, but easily and tranquilly govern these things.
[Marginal note: B] But lest anyone should doubt that a separated soul can be raised to such light, because we see it in the body surrounded by such darkness, the Platonists bid us compare the intellect to sight, and the intelligible to the visible. Sight never comprehends the light itself in the sun in its fullest. For that (light) always exceeds the proportion of this (sight). Sometimes, even when impeded by a cataract, it does not see light in colors. Sometimes, obscured by a certain vapor, either red or yellow, it judges obscurely and differently from what it is. At other times, either because of contraction to internal imagination, it does not seem to look at external things, or because of simultaneous distraction to objects far distant from each other, it barely discerns either. And if it inclines a little more attentively to one, meanwhile it inclines more weakly or not at all to the other. Similarly, the human intellect never fully comprehends the immense fullness of divine light itself, overflowing in the absolute nature of God: since that (fullness) greatly exceeds the capacity of the mind. Moreover, the same divine light, either as if determined in the ideas of created things, or already contracted in angels, can indeed sometimes be clearly perceived: namely, when it has been almost as much removed from the contagion of the body as those (ideas/angels). **E** Here is also revealed that ancient secret celebrated by Plato above all others in the book *On Kingship*, that the present circuit of the world from east to west is Jovian and fatal: but that there will someday be another, opposite to this one, under Saturn, from west to east in turn, in which humans will be born spontaneously, and will proceed from old age into youth; and food will be supplied to them spontaneously in an eternal spring, according to their desire. Jupiter (as I believe) they call the soul of the world: by whose fatal law this manifest order of the manifest world is arranged. Moreover, he wishes the life of souls in elemental bodies to be Jovian, dedicated to the senses and action. But Saturn is the supreme intellect among the angels: by whose rays souls beyond the angels are illuminated and kindled, and are continuously raised towards an intellectual life according to their powers. And as often as they are converted to such a life, they are said to live under the reign of Saturn, insofar as they live by intelligence.

**F** Therefore, in that life, they are said to be spontaneously regenerated because by their own choice they are reformed for the better. Again, to rejuvenate daily, that is, daily (if indeed days are counted there), to flourish more and more. Hence that saying of the apostle Paul: "The inner man is renewed day by day." Finally, food is supplied to them spontaneously and abundantly in perpetual spring: because not through the senses and laborious discipline, but through an intimate light, and with the greatest tranquility and pleasure of life, they enjoy the wondrous spectacles of truth itself.

**G** The odor of such a life is indeed perceived by the mind separated according to its powers: but the taste is savored by the mind completely separated. He adds to these things in the *Symposium* that purified souls who have loved divine beauty above all others, finally immerse themselves completely into the very ocean of divine beauty: and there not only drink divine liquids, but also pour them out into others from themselves. Nine degrees in the homeland.

A Therefore, nine degrees of the blessed are arranged not only among Christians, but also among Platonists, both in angels and in souls, for this reason (as I believe), because divine contemplation there is perfected in nine principal ways. Indeed, just as we, from the power, order, and convenience of things, pursue God's power, wisdom, and goodness with whatever sagacity we can, so they in turn recognize these three similarly in things, from divine goodness, power, and wisdom, as from the final, efficient, and exemplary cause of the universe, namely, in such a way that some consider divine goodness primarily in itself, others refer it principally to things themselves, others principally refer things to it as to an end: yet each contemplates all things. Thus, therefore, a threefold intuition of divine goodness is fulfilled, by which the first three orders of the blessed are distinguished. In three ways also, similarly, power is conceived, and in as many ways, wisdom. Hence, six additional orders of the blessed are enu-B merated. To these nine degrees of the blessed among the Platonists, the eight celestial spheres and a ninth region conceived above the heavens seem to be appropriately accommodated. Among the Orphics, however, there are eight heavens: and beneath the moon, ethereal fire. Among Christians, nine circles beneath the Empyrean. For each is carried, by a certain similar habit, as if by natural lightness, to that particular region, to whose angelic inhabitants they themselves in life especially...

Indeed, the love of goodness alone transforms the soul into God. Therefore, love without inquiry and fear restores the soul to its homeland: but the opposite is by no means true. But now let us arrange in order the grades themselves by which one ascends to heaven. In the first are those who primarily love goodness, then fear power, lastly seek wisdom. [Marginal note: C] In the second, those who first love goodness, but in regard to the other two, they are equally disposed. In the fifth, those who first love good, then greatly fear power. In the sixth, those who similarly love good: but subsequently desire wisdom. In the seventh, those who absolutely and simply love good. In the eighth, those whom power moves first, goodness second, wisdom third. In the ninth, with whom wisdom prevails first, goodness second, power third. I believe a mystery of this kind is signified in the Gospel where the divine oracle calls its followers blessed nine times: because by nine grades of merits, with God as guide, the nine heavens are happily sought for the nine orders of contemplation. But behold, now the blessed commemoration of the holy Gospel seems to admonish us that, having dismissed philosophical digressions, we should seek blessedness by that shorter path by which Christian theologians lead, and Thomas Aquinas in particular, the splendor of Christian theology.

[G] But lest anyone consider it absurd to unite God with the intellect as a form, it is necessary to remember that the perfection of the mind consists in truth. But the True, Being, and the Intelligible are the same. Whatever, however, in this very genus is composed of essence and being, relates as being and true rather than as being-ness or truth; nor can it be the form of others in the same genus, since the form in itself is already contracted to its own quasi-matter. Therefore, no created mind can become the form of other minds; indeed, God alone relates to the genus of minds everywhere as form, who alone is Being itself and the most simple truth: as form, I say, not as part of a composite, but as a principle of operation, by which the mind operates more as God now, than as a mind; just as ignited gold acts more as fire than as gold, such as the Apocalypse of John commands to be bought.

In what manner the mind is united to God.

But to this end, that the mind may put on divine substance [A] as a form, it is not led by its own power, but is drawn by divine action. Indeed, an inferior nature cannot acquire the property and form of a superior without the action of the superior itself. Which is manifest in the elements, in which air becomes fire only through the agency of fire. Furthermore, nothing can ever be led to a more excellent action, unless its virtue is first strengthened in it. But if it is to be led to a customary kind of action, but nevertheless somewhat more vehement, it will certainly be enough if only the usual virtue is increased: for example, if air, which naturally heats by one degree, is sometimes to heat by two degrees, it will suffice to intensify the quality of its natural heat somewhat. However, if air is to claim for itself an action superior in kind and genus, namely, if it is to illuminate, which is proper to the ethereal body, it must now acquire a new form from the ether itself. What is the point of this? So that we may understand that the mind cannot be elevated to perceive divine substance by itself, through the mere increase of natural virtue and light, since such

--- Page 750 ---
PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...its operation differs more than in kind from the natural operation of the mind; but there is need of a certain new virtue, and a new (B) light descending from a higher principle. Which some call the light of grace and glory: by which the mind, illuminated and much more inflamed, now puts on the divine substance, with whose heat it now glows, like a flame—a flame, I say, not like the dry vapor lifted from the earth that rises near the sphere of fire in a comet, although that may seem very similar; but rather a supracelestial flame, shining healthily, not burning. Perhaps someone will deny that the mind can be led to perceive God by any light whatsoever: because if there is no proportion of sight itself to sound, then certainly there is no proportion of the mind, nor of the light received by the mind (and therefore finite), to the immense God. But we will respond that God, although He exceeds the faculty of the intellect, is not so alien from the intellect as sound is alien from sight; or something insensible from sense; since God is, as it pleases Christian theologians, the First Intelligible, and the beginning, middle, and end of all intellectual (C) virtue and action. Therefore, there is a certain proportion between the intellect and God: not because there is any commensuration, but rather a certain relationship, as it were, of intellectual matter to intelligible form, and of effect to cause. Furthermore, that infused light, even if it becomes limited in the mind, is nevertheless infused by God endowed with such a power, by which it may unite the mind to the divine substance, not indeed by a natural bond, but rather by an intellectual bond. But natural light cannot achieve this: because from the very beginning it entirely passed into the nature of the recipient, which was previously formless in itself; whence it itself became dim and weak. Nor can the mind, since it degenerates far from divine simplicity, obtain its entire perfection by the same (natural light); and therefore, in it, natural light is one thing, by which, insofar as it corresponds to its own species, it understands something; but divinely infused light is another, by whose uplifting the mind is wonderfully elevated to a degree above itself, more eminent than can be conceived. Finally, the very infinity of God does not signify a privation of form, such as the infinity that belongs to matter (and since it is inefficacious and formless, it is deservedly considered unfit for cognition); but it signifies absolute excellence, contracted by no subject whatsoever. But this, like the sun, has it in its nature, that it is wonderful

in such a way by shining and illuminating that it can move the intellectual sight most of all, and be seen; and by which power it surpasses the mind, it can elevate the mind itself above its own powers. Nor, however, is it to be thought that the mind, though formed by divine essence and understanding what it itself is, nevertheless fully comprehends it. For its power is limited, and the light within it is determined; and when it approaches the divine essence, it is not formed by every virtue of divinity from it. What then? Does it indeed perceive a part of the divine substance, but not perceive another part? It is certainly not to be said so, since God cannot be divided. D
Rather, it is to be thought that it beholds God, yet does not fully comprehend Him; that is, it does not perceive God with as many reasons, and with as much certainty, and as much perfection, as God is perceived by Himself, and in what magnitude. Added to this is that it (the mind) cannot see all things that God both sees and can do, by seeing God. But God sees and can do infinite things besides those which exist in nature, which we have proved elsewhere. For if it does not comprehend God's substance, certainly neither His intelligence nor His power. Therefore, it does not comprehend all things that God both understands and can do. Otherwise, since power is usually estimated by what it can do, if it fully comprehended whatever it sees and can do, it would likewise comprehend the power of seeing and doing, and the substance. What more? The higher the intellect, the more it ought to understand, either in number or by reason. From which it is consistent that the divine mind, contemplating itself from all sides, sees both more things and by more reasons than any intellect sees.

All species of minds can be joined to God.

E
**N**o one, however, ought to despair that human minds, because they are the lowest in the very genus of minds, can be led to the contemplation of the divine substance itself; since not even the angelic minds themselves arrive there by any natural power, but rather are drawn by divine, and (so to speak) supernatural power. But a work which is accomplished by supernatural power cannot be hindered by the diversity of natures, since nothing to the immense power of God

--- Page 752 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**
resists it anywhere. So easily does divine power move the whole machine, as easily as the smallest part of the world. So easily does it heal one gravely ill, as easily as one lightly ill. Wherefore, by the same divinely infused faculty by which the highest minds are rapt to sublime things, so too are the lowest. Moreover, the highest of created minds is distant from God by a certain immense space; but the lowest differs from this (the highest), since both are finite, by a finite interval. But no proportion is judged to exist between this interval and that (immense space). But if the finite added to the infinite brings no variation (as it appears), what then prevents the very power of God, which suddenly traverses the immense space up to an angel, from immediately embracing the tiny (space) between the angel and the soul, so that simultaneously both soul and angel may be rapt? Finally, if to the genus of minds, in so far as they are minds, F there is a natural instinct to perceive the highest intelligible, which they seek by seeking in every intelligible thing, and desire by desiring: it follows that such an instinct is as natural to the lowest minds as to the highest, and that these (the lowest) as well as those (the highest) can sometimes naturally attain the desired goal. But natural appetite itself shows this to us: which, since it draws towards the infinite, cannot be implanted or moved from anywhere else than from the infinite itself, and finally fulfilled. But if those lower things which are moved by nature are not moved in vain, much less are those which are led by the Supreme (Power). Indeed, the ray of this (Supreme Power), transferring itself through all orders of minds, both illuminates each one so that they may see, and ignites them so that they may love. But since fire and the sun are accustomed to propagate light more widely than heat, it is consistent that as far as the ray of the divine sun extends by heating, so much more can it extend by illuminating. Therefore, just as human minds, ignited by it, daily desire the divine good, so also, illuminated there, they sometimes behold the divine truth, and by beholding, they happily enjoy the true good.

Again, if the perpetual intelligence of the intelligent being itself is a kind of life, and there intelligence, because of its stability, becomes a participant in eternity: it follows that the blessed mind is rightly said to be translated into eternal life. Rightly so, indeed. For the human mind is placed in the middle, between eternal and temporal things. Therefore, just as its operation by which it is joined to temporal things is accustomed to become temporal: so also that by which it is joined to eternal things, is eternal. Finally, I do not see how the vision itself there could be mobile: where both the power of seeing, from the beginning and especially now, transcends time, and the object that is seen, and the form by which it is seen, is status itself, and eternity itself.

Hence it follows that souls, once adhering to God, will never depart from Him, if only they have already transcended motion and fulfilled their natural desire. And since this (desire/possession) is founded both in a stable substance, and is naturally directed towards a stable object: it certainly desires no other than a stable possession as its end. What wonder if the eternal mind desires that which it desires not for the sake of something else, but for its own sake, to be held forever? Moreover, where it ignores nothing natural beneath itself: it certainly does not ignore what kind of possession that is. Therefore, if it were to be lacking, it would foresee that lack and live unhappily, believing itself destined to be deprived of such a dear possession sometime, indeed soon. Add to this that whatever naturally adheres to a certain end: is not torn away from it except by some external force. Therefore, since the mind is naturally joined to God as to an end desired above all others, and the efficient cause of such a union is God Himself, and no greater opposing force can approach which might violently separate what God has willingly joined: without a doubt, the mind will never be compelled to depart from Him by anyone. Moreover, in what way it might turn itself away, either from certain truth through deceit, or from pure and complete good through will, cannot be conceived. All know: the blessed are known to all.
Here followers of pleasures, if only they have arrived, will enjoy complete
pleasure in the very cause of pleasures. Indeed, just as bodies are shadows of
divine things, so also the delights of the senses are shadows of divine joy.
For the mind is much more effective than the senses: and the true and whole
good is both more powerful than can be imagined and sweeter than some false
good. Moreover, the intellect is accustomed to penetrate its object from all
sides: since it separates both intrinsic from extrinsic, and proper from alien:
which the senses never accomplish. Likewise, the intelligible, due to the
wonderful purity and power of the intellect, completely glides into its innermost
parts: which indeed the sensible cannot do for the sense. Therefore, the pleasure
of the pure intellect concerning the highest intelligible is not only continuous
and pure, such as is not found in the senses: but also intimate and whole, and
at the same time completely comprehended: and it surpasses the pleasure of the
senses much more than the sweetness of tastes surpasses the empty allurements
of odors. We are accustomed, when we are restored to our proper state,
in whatever way that may happen, to be filled with pleasure. No greater
restoration can indeed be imagined, than when the soul, which had degenerated
from its Idea, indeed from itself, is restored on all sides to its Idea, indeed
to itself. There again, the very Idea of joy rejoices: and in one good, it enjoys
all goods. And since those things delight us which we desire, but we desire
all things, because they are good: there we are filled with the highest pleasure,
where, since every good exists, we perfectly obtain whatever can be desired.

--- Page 757 ---
...we attain. But diverse minds indeed especially enjoy every good according to the essence of good, and properly enjoy the degrees of good according to various ideas: inasmuch as, loving in the first place the various degrees of the whole good, they also proceed by various paths to the good itself. Finally, to speak summarily: there is one thing altogether which all the blessed enjoy; although some enjoy it in different ways and by different reasons than others, as each one's pleasure draws them differently, either from affection or from an object attracting them in different ways. Thus therefore, as Plato says, all envy is absent from the divine chorus. [Marginal note: A] For common charity in that chorus brings it about that individuals congratulate each other on their happiness as if it were their own. Moreover, where each person has attained what he loved, and by the reason he especially chose, and to the extent he desires, to his wish, there everyone lives entirely content and full, without envy and and far from any goad. For there both natural and acquired capacity is completely filled, nor is any greater capacity desired by anyone. For their own things are naturally dearest to each. It is added that nothing is more pleasing to the blessed, burning with divine love, than to will that very thing which they know God wills; and to possess the beloved God, both by the measure they comprehend, and by the reason they desire, and by the manner in which God himself shows himself to be possessed. But because they know that their good there cannot be entirely comprehended, they are wonderfully delighted by this very fact, choosing their treasure, namely, to be infinite rather than finite.

*Of the bodies of the blessed. Chapter 9.*

**A** twofold happiness is fitting for the pure soul: one from itself, of which we have treated; the other from the body, which among the Platonists is of this kind. For it is better to conceive of this by a certain example. [Marginal note: B] Indeed, your eye is round, clear, splendid, swiftest in motion, of wonderful keenness of sight. It sees my eye, and sees itself in mine. It shapes each of your soul's affections within itself, and transmits them into mine, and in turn receives my affections through mine. Such are those chariots of souls, both in themselves and mutually. For each of them is entirely an eye, and in almost all things they are as we see eyes themselves to be.

Therefore, they are, as it were, certain round eyes, clear, splendid,

of its own nature: whereby it follows that for the soul to remain
separate from the body is against the order of both universal
and its own nature. But they remain eternal [Marginal note: a]
after the destruction of the body. And since that which is against nature
cannot be eternal: it follows that souls will one day
receive their bodies.
Second reason. Individual souls are naturally inclined to
vivify and govern individual bodies. For thus both
nature and providence bear witness to life placed between eternity and time:
and having a natural inclination partly towards eternal things, partly
towards temporal things. But natural inclination remains
always as long as nature remains. Therefore, souls separated
from bodies will always be naturally inclined towards them.
But a natural inclination and propensity ought not always be in vain.
