For this is most alien from the order of the universe. Therefore, souls
will sometime receive their own bodies, to which they are always naturally drawn.

Third Reason. The soul is one part of the human species; the other
part, indeed, is the body. Therefore, separated from the body, insofar as it is a soul,
it is imperfect, just as a part itself usually is when outside the whole
for which it is constituted. For this reason, its natural appetite will never
be at rest. No soul will ever be blessed unless it is restored to its whole by the body being resumed, or hopes to be restored.

Fourth Reason. Due rewards are owed to virtues, and due punishments to
vices. Since these are not bestowed in this life, they are bestowed in
the next. The body, however, is a participant in both virtues and vices along with
the soul. Therefore, so that it may also be a participant in rewards or punishments
simultaneously, it is finally returned to the soul. Nor

But to the order of merits, as theologians teach, this also greatly corresponds, that bodies be thoroughly joined not only to all human souls in respect of life (which souls are a kind of life), but also to pure souls in respect of their qualities and actions, just as those souls are joined to God. Therefore, the intellect full of divine light, and the will, filled with incomparable joy and efficacy from it, completely transfuse splendor and a marvelous efficacy for movement into the body, so that just as those souls are raised to the celestial minds, so too are bodies raised to the clarity and power of celestial bodies. Nor should it seem strange that the human body, not a little similar to heaven by nature due to its temperance, when it is again endowed with a certain celestial form by some gift, is suddenly and completely elevated to the celestial region: drawn, namely, by the soul, supported by the infinite power of God, which even now on earth, though separated from God, connects, sustains, and raises the body against the nature of its elements, and then, joined to the supracelestial God, can also raise [the body] with itself to the sublime region of the aether. Nor by penetration then does that purest body, already made ethereal in virtue and quality, either offend the aether or is it offended.

The State of the Impure Soul. Chapter 10.

**E**T that we may understand what the state of the impure soul is after death, it must be observed what kind of lives...

--- Page 763 ---
...what kind of morals and habits living people have. For what kind of morals are those of youth, such for the most part are the habits of old age: and such also are the affections of the dead. In the present life, virtue and vice are born. With virtue, reward arises; but with vice, punishment. In the future life, virtue and vice are perfected. There, reward and punishment are fulfilled. Virtue is the emerging reward. Reward is mature virtue. Vice is nascent punishment: punishment is perfected vice. For it is the same which was seed, and which becomes the harvest. The same also which was the harvest, and which becomes fodder. Therefore, what kind of things we sow in this autumn, such things we shall reap in that summer. With such things, either in dark night we shall be fed in the Stygian swamp, or in serene day we shall be nourished in the Elysian fields. [Marginal note: F] Just as nature, the minister of divine providence, moves bodies intrinsically upwards by lightness and downwards by gravity, so also providence leads all things by an intrinsic law, and as if by a certain very similar natural inclination. By this law, supernal minds and souls, implanted universally in them...

For the greatest of evils is to descend to the underworld with a soul full of sins. He adds then there, and in the Theaetetus and Republic, that these things are not to be ridiculed as fables. Indeed, whoever denies such things, they themselves always bring ridiculous things into the discussion. Therefore, he enjoins that this above all must be striven for: that the best morals be acquired. For morals, he says, are paths either to the underworld or to
D the heavens.

I think it will be worthwhile to repeat more extensively what he writes about these things in the Republic and in the book on knowledge. Indeed, he says that those are to be utterly ridiculed who think that justice should be pursued, or injustice avoided, for the sake of human rewards or punishments. But that opinion is true which asserts that those are not true rewards or punishments which occur sometimes and by chance, but those which always and by necessary order follow virtues and vices. He adds in the book on knowledge that God is justice itself: and nothing is more similar to that which is just: and nothing, on the contrary, is more dissimilar to that which is unjust. Moreover, true wisdom and power are to be considered that which recognizes and attains that according to one's desire: but the contrary habit is to be judged as extreme ignorance and weakness. Therefore, he posits two extreme models in the universe, opposite to each other: at the highest, indeed, the most blessed divinity: but at the lowest, the opposite, devoid of divinity and most miserable. And he affirms that the unjust

--- Page 765 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVIII. 342
because of extreme ignorance, they never notice that because of injustice they are daily becoming more unlike the most blessed, but more like the most miserable. And such unlikeness or likeness is the proper punishment of injustice; but the reward of justice is properly judged to be the very likeness to the most blessed, or unlikeness to the most miserable. To these things he adds that the unjust are received neither in this life nor in the next by the very homeland of blessedness (inasmuch as they are unlike it); but rather, by a certain perverse habit, they are fittingly drawn back to the lowest state of misery (to which they have become similar), and always wander in a malignant region very similar to themselves, among evil ones similar to themselves. Finally, he adds that these things are usually ridiculed by some ambitious people; but if they are compelled to give and receive reasons diligently in these matters, then they (as we signified above) are truly convinced and depart to be ridiculed like children.

      But now let us return to morals: when these are distributed in order, we will understand by what reason rewards or punishments are distributed. But before we distinguish, it is necessary to remember that good morals only then lead to happiness if they are sought with a special love towards God, the author of happiness.
      But evil ones usually plunge those souls especially into misery in whom all love of God is extinguished. Hence that Platonic saying, "To the wise man, God is law; to the foolish, lust." Also that other saying, "Blessed will he be who humbly submits himself to divine law; but miserable he who proudly despises it." Now there are four types of morals among the living: the temperate man, the continent, the incontinent, the intemperate.
The temperate is he whose reason judges truly, and whose sensual affection willingly obeys reason.
The continent is he whose reason also judges truly, but whose affection obeys with difficulty. The incontinent is he in whom, although reason does not judge badly, yet bodily perturbation prevails. The intemperate is he in whom reason is either lulled to sleep or corrupted by an overly dominant affection, where all things are done at the command of fantasy, and reason does not oppose affection. When we speak here of temperance or continence, we understand, in the Platonic manner, to compose or dispose the soul against all kinds of perturbations, so that the duties of all moral virtues are comprehended in these. Moreover, when in the soul

--- Page 766 ---
THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY

when we set fancy apart, we understand either in the Platonic manner an inner sense, which they place in an ethereal and aerial vehicle, but properly with passion in the aerial [vehicle]; or in the manner of the Peripatetics, especially Avicenna, an affection and habit of even the rational part, which, by obeying the senses, it conceived in itself, inclining towards bodily passions and drawing towards matter: by which Avicenna says the soul, as if by a certain nature, even without choice or meditation, both here and in the other life, is twisted and tormented from the intelligible mode to the sensible. Therefore, to return now to our purpose: in the temperate soul, only the nutritive faculty cares for the body: Fancy does not love it; reason hates it. Wherefore, the ministry of caring for this body being fulfilled, that life-giving faculty is, as it were, content with its vehicle: whatever other faculties of the soul remain, just as they were accustomed in this very temperate man, dedicate themselves to contemplating the truth of all things: and so much more fervently than before, as they have been made freer. All therefore suddenly, with common effort and an ethereal chariot, return to the ether.

The soul of the continent man is indeed carried to heaven, like that one, but a little later, not suddenly. For in this man, the appetite of fancy was accustomed to barely obey reason, because of the body's allurements or terrors. Therefore, it reluctantly leaves bodily things in death: which difficulty for a short time occupies the keenness of reason with distress. But reason, which had been accustomed to conquer it, bids it be silent. Whence, the complaint of fancy being calmed, and the darkness dispelled, a heavenly spark glows faintly: and with all the faculties of the soul consenting, the heavenly homeland is revisited. The incontinent man, however, is freed late from these prisons; the intemperate, never. Indeed, the souls of these men, infected by bodily passions, have fallen into such madness in this life, that they rashly preferred shadows of good things to the good things themselves: they loved shadows, and feared shadows. And after this life, they are similarly compelled to be mad: the former (incontinent) for a long time, the latter (intemperate) always. For the madness of the incontinent finds some remedy: because although the disturbance of fancy was accustomed to dominate, reason nevertheless sometimes used to oppose it in life. If imagination, then you imagine most vehemently. This happens to such an extent in sleep, that what are images of things, we believe to be true things; and terrified by horrible visions, we tremble, sweat, cry out, and rise. Much more so for the impious, in death and after death, does the deception of terrible images occur. But through Alecto, from the indelible habit of love which he had contracted for corporeal things, certain such thoughts and affections again creep in: namely, just as old men who lived wantonly in their youth are tormented by a double punishment in old age, that is, because they burn with the desire for pleasures, and because they are deprived of all hope of obtaining them, unless perchance they rave; so the wretched in the underworld, because of their former habit, are troubled by the desires for human things, some by one, some by another, and for the most part they do not hope to be able to obtain them; although sometimes, like madmen, it seems to them that they are almost attaining their delights, but that they are immediately kept away from them for more bitter punishments. Sardanapalus is kept further away from embrace, Midas from gold, Tantalus from the feast, Sisyphus from the summit.

So great is the power of fantasy, so great its impulse, when either it alone commands, or some fantastic habit and affection alone, contracted in reason from long interaction with it.

Olympiodorus confirms the order laid down by us in previous sections in his commentaries on the Phaedo, setting forth three vices according to Plato's opinion.
The first indeed are those which are easily curable: which, namely, lack habit. But he says the second can be cured with difficulty, inasmuch as they are committed by habit, but have a certain resistance and repentance as a companion. Finally, the third cannot be cured: which, namely, are both perpetrated by habit and are entirely devoid of resistance and repentance.

Therefore, the first are assigned to Acheron, the second to Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus, the third to Tartarus among the Platonists, from which Plato says no one can ever escape. As many degrees are distributed to the good in the Phaedo, where it is asserted that innocent and pious souls, but lacking philosophy, together in the air...

Orpheus, however, distributes nine principal regions to souls. Indeed, to the good, either the eighth sphere or the planets, or the aether below the planets. Which spheres are indeed nine, if you divide them more diligently, appropriately with the nine degrees of contemplation which we mentioned elsewhere. But to the mediocre, the air, or water, and earth. Finally, to the reprobate, Acheron, Cocytus, Pyriphlegethon, where the Styx, flowing between, moreover restrains nine times. The number nine, however, is derived from this: that they sinned either by a certain affection, or by a changeable habit, or by an unchangeable habit; and in whichever of these ways they have transgressed, they have sinned either by thought, or even by speech, or moreover by action; whence nine degrees of faults and nine of punishments are rightly reckoned. Finally, that I may briefly comprehend the opinion of the ancient
theologians concerning the state of the soul after death: they believe
that only divine things (as we have said elsewhere) are true realities:
and that the rest are images and shadows of true realities. Therefore,
wise men, who apply themselves to divine things, watch more than others.
But unwise men who pursue other things are entirely deluded by dreams
as if sleeping: and if they die in this sleep before they have awakened,
they are tormented by similar and sharper visions after their departure.
And just as he who applied himself to true things in life, attains
the highest truth after death: so he who pursued false things is tormented
by extreme deceit: so that the former may be delighted by true things,
the latter vexed by false images. Therefore Christ, the master of life,
often commands thus. "Watch, I say, watch: lest the Lord find you
sleeping." Again, "Arise now: and let us go hence." What else is it
to awaken, than to recognize that one is dreaming in the senses? And what else is it to rise  C
and go away, than to turn oneself to God with one's very mind?
Nor do I think a certain cause of punishment should be passed over in silence,
indeed hidden from those who suffer, but most potent, which Plato
indicated in Timaeus, Gorgias, Republic, and Origen interpreted.
God tempered the soul from its beginning with a certain harmony of
spiritual parts, powers, and movements. This kind of tempering
is gradually dissolved in intemperate and unjust people, and is greatly
dissolved in the damned. It is necessary, however, from this loosening
and dissolution, that no small trouble and pain arise in the soul:
even if it does not know whence or for what reason it suffers:  D
just as when the natural tempering of bodily spirits, humors, and
members is dissolved, pain necessarily follows, even if the sick person
does not know the reason for their pain. Christian theologians will
not entirely deny these things, but will add (as I believe) some punishment
from a certain true judgment of the damned soul, because it will think
itself deprived of the divine vision forever. Which is therefore the greatest
punishment, because God is the end for whose sake we are born:
for whose sake we all desire and do all things. And therefore the natural
thirst which is for Him is much sharper than that which incites a thirsty
person for drink. But just as if someone by means of opium

cultivated orders of souls, than in manifest ranks of bodies,
and from this side many are most blessed: many from that
side most miserable: again from this side others less blessed, from that side others less miserable:
but equally the middle of all, who are neither properly miserable,
nor blessed? Since blessed is he who enjoys divine flavors in God:
but miserable is he who nowhere perceives any divine odor, and always hungers. [G in margin]
But less blessed from that side,
who enjoys fewer things in that. Conversely less miserable from this side,
who hungers and grieves less. Finally the middle, who in creation
perceives certain odors of the creator, and lives content with the odor.
Wherefore perhaps philosophers will say that the souls of infants ought not
to complain about divine justice: because if perhaps they are deprived of the faculty of the highest
good, they are also freed from the danger of extreme evil.
Again it is probable that they do not complain, if only into the clarity
of the soul, unobscured by any clouds of bodily affections,
the light of the divine sun, creating natural things, flows full of natural
forms: and to it, as Timaeus says, demonstrates the order
of the universe: and at the same time the ordainer in the order,
as much as the order itself comprehends of the ordainer: and by this good commands
and makes it to be content. Therefore just as in man between the gross
body and the soul there is spirit, and in emotion between pain [H in margin]
and pleasure there is freedom from pain, likewise in reason between knowl-
edge and ignorance there is right opinion: again in the universe a clear thing
between the lucid and the opaque: so in segregated spirits there seem
to be those who are blessed in the heavens, formed by both the light and the illumination of God:
and on the contrary, those around the earth to whom both are miserably
lacking. But among these, in purer air, are the middle ones, to whom, although not
light itself properly, yet illumination may reach.
But it is necessary to remember what we signify elsewhere,
just as one thing is the light remaining in the sun, another is the illumination flowing from it, and diffused through all things:
another is a certain ray naturally implanted in the eyes from it:
so it is another thing to be the infinite light in God, by which alone God
enjoys Himself, and blessed minds enjoy divine goodness:
another is the common illumination abundantly diffusing itself from there through all clear minds,
by which, as if a created and external thing, individual minds (provided they are not diverted from it) perceive all created things:
but the Creator Himself properly in Himself by no means: unless,
kindled by the illumination, they are transferred into the light. Another
is a certain ray now proper to each, and made from the beginning.

PLATONIC THEOLOGY
natural to minds, and in them somehow testifying even to those diverging and departing from it.

I
Indeed, in the first degree, they are blessed; but in the second, they are neither properly blessed nor miserable, provided they live content with this very thing. Finally, in the third, are human souls, whether bound to bodies or to bodily affections, and from this very fact almost already miserable, but happy, as it were, by hope alone. But the most miserable are under this very degree, for whom only a ray remains, and that indeed already both dim and burning, and deprived of the confidence of pure light.

K
But perhaps some Platonist will conjecture thus: If God created minds by the grace of the first light, and they themselves are prepared to attain it, both by the recognition of divine goodness and especially by love—since recognition forms by lumen from there, and love reforms from here to there by light—it would be probable that divine justice would not wish any mind whatsoever to always lack all faculty and opportunity for knowing and loving God. But since many die before the use of reason, and again, some are foolish from the beginning, and both are withdrawn by the malignant necessity of fate, therefore, it would be consistent that such a faculty be repaid by divine providence, either in this life sometimes in a wondrous way, or at least in the next life, so that no one, without their own fault, should lack the chief good. Wherefore, their souls, even if never here, yet separated from bodies, in that lumen we spoke of, while they recognize the Creator in creatures, are gradually so inflamed with the love of the Creator that they are disposed to attain light at a certain time. By time, I say, because only angelic minds, as if wholly in eternity, progress or fail in a moment; but souls, as if already naturally somehow inclining towards temporal things, perform their work over time, but indeed longer in the body, but outside the body, much shorter; but in a moment only then, when they have first been almost translated into an angelic nature. And if souls established in purgatorial torments, although they are in a worse state and place, nevertheless rise up to blessedness, nothing should seem strange, that their souls, placed in the middle region of freedom from pain, and nearer to blessedness, can progress even to blessedness. Philosophers would especially think these things about infants. But concerning those who are entirely foolish by nature...

--- Page 775 ---
DE IMMOR. ANI. LIB. XVIII. 347

...are, the question seems much more difficult than concerning infants. For if these (the foolish) live long, they contract a certain habit concerning matter (which is the lowest part of the universe), which tends to diverge from God, who is the highest part of the universe. This habit, accompanying the soul even when separated, perhaps still turns it towards matter, and meanwhile turns it away from God. But beatitude is considered to be fitting for none unless they are converted to God. But if these are miserable, since they could in no way be converted to the highest good, being prevented by fate, they are not miserable by their own fault: and God would have commanded those who could not convert in vain.

Here perhaps some Peripatetic will respond that in the foolish, due to the excessive intensity of their imagination, reason was so vacant that it created no habit through its inaction. But the habit proper to the imagination (which is not so much in the soul as in the animated body) ceases immediately when the composite is dissolved: so that the mind immediately, with no natural impediment preventing it, is converted to God: and receiving the divine light that is everywhere present, it is kindled: then, being kindled, it loves: and by loving more vehemently, it converts itself: and in a short time, by meriting something, it attains beatitude. But the Platonists, who think that habit remains somehow in the imagination, and also in the reason consenting to it, if indeed it consented to anything at all, and then indeed under duress, and is thence transfused: they will respond that the habit diverting to opposites must first be entirely destroyed before the higher (nature) can be elevated.

But in destroying this, both the power of the spirit (or genius) and of God work wonderfully. For under divine providence, no less provision and care is made for minds than for bodies. Therefore, just as with ailing bodies, where nature cannot expel the disease and return to health by its own power, it is accustomed to expel it with the aid of medical art: similarly, in minds lacking the natural faculty to purge corporeal habits and to revisit God: the omnipotent physician, either by his own virtue alone, or by the ministry of blessed ministers, happily accomplishes both. Nor will they think that this lacks order, that divine clemency, which is most proven in the ruler, shines forth most clearly here: while no one is condemned without their own fault: and he who is deprived of the faculty of merit for a time without fault, is sometimes divinely restored to that faculty: a safe faculty, I say: which cannot err: and

--- Page 776 ---
**PLATONIC THEOLOGY**
...nor may it quickly achieve much with God's help. So much for them. But lest we think childishly and foolishly about children and fools, it now seems that we must conclude thus. To this point, the conjectural path of philosophers almost leads us. But since human conjecture concerning divine matters is often and greatly mistaken, we judge it much better and safer to commit ourselves with obedient humility to the holier leaders among Christians.

**Conclusion.**

Since the end of life is not granted to us by God in the same way as to other living beings, as we have shown, firstly by common reasons, secondly by specific arguments, and thirdly by both signs and solutions to questions: I judge that we must guard with the utmost diligence lest we prefer this uncertain moment of fleeting life to infinite ages. Let us remember, however, if we are wise, that we cannot be well forever, or live perfectly, or understand happily, unless we are formed by His essence, by whose creation we received our being; let us live by His life, by whose breath we breathe and are moved. Let us understand Him by His intelligence, and through Him all things, by whose daily illumination we consider created things and seek the creator. But we shall reach this highest degree of nature, with God as our guide, if only we separate, as much as we can, the affection of the mind from matter itself, which is the lowest degree of nature: so that as much as we depart from it, so much we may approach God; and for whom we now live, setting aside, as far as we can, this fleeting moment of deceitful life, let us finally live by His life forever. Amen.

**The Author's Protestation concerning his writings**
In all things which are treated by me either here or elsewhere, I wish only that to be asserted which is approved by the Church.
